meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.
meta.notes: Exam 3 practice questions for Iggy chapters 16, 19, 31, 27, 29, 30, 32, 45, 58 and 59, Potter chapter 46, Enteral Nutrition, plus the Cardiac Assessment and Infusion Therapy skills. Built from the lecture PowerPoints and the skill course, with readings as support. Questions marked "new": true are the newest additions (addedBatch 16): per section 4 regular items in the instructor's short style and 2 hard items in long NCLEX format, each with a "cjmm" field. NGN style items are kept near 15% of each section. An independent NCLEX accuracy review fixed flagged items (reviewedBatch 18). All text says "patient", never "client". Batch 18 adds a "tag" field: "review" (4 NCLEX style items per section) and "case-study" (one unfolding 6 item case per section; show its items in caseStep order within the caseGroup). Case study items are counted apart from the standalone 15% NGN share.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: Six hours after a laceration is sutured, the wound edges are warm, red, swollen, and tender. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Report the findings as an early wound infection
options.rationale: Warmth, redness, swelling, and pain 6 hours after closure are expected inflammation. They do not establish infection, so labeling and reporting them as infection overreaches.

options.text: Recheck later and document only once a change appears
options.rationale: Rechecking is right, but the first set of findings is the baseline. Without it there is nothing to compare a change against.

options.text: Document measured findings; recheck on a schedule
options.rationale: These are the expected early findings of inflammation. Measured findings with a time give the baseline that later checks are compared with.

options.text: Tell the patient the redness means delayed healing
options.rationale: Redness this soon is expected. Vessels dilate and blood flow increases in the vascular response, so it does not mean healing is delayed.

questions.takeaway: Early warmth, redness, swelling, and pain at a wound are expected. Record measured findings with the time so that later findings can be compared with baseline.
questions.strategy: Infection is the tempting label. Decide first whether the findings are expected 6 hours after closure, then choose the option that sets a measured baseline without a wrong label or a wrong delay.

steps.detail: Four cardinal signs, 6 hours after closure.

steps.action: Check each option for one flaw
steps.detail: "As infection," "document once a change appears," and "delayed healing" are each one thing off.
Measured findings with a time, then a scheduled recheck.

elimination.verdict: Document measured findings and recheck on a schedule.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.nursesNote:
Yesterday 0800, day 1 after closure of a left forearm laceration: wound edges warm, redness 0.5 cm from wound edge, swelling limited to the wound edges, pain 4 of 10, makes a full fist with left hand, oral temperature 36.7 °C.

Today 0800: Wound edges are warm. Redness is 0.3 cm from wound edge. Swelling extends to the left wrist. Pain is 4 of 10. Unable to make a full fist with left hand. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing two days of notes for a patient with a sutured forearm laceration. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Wound edges are warm
segments.rationale: Warmth is a cardinal sign and matches yesterday's entry.

segments.text: Redness is 0.3 cm from wound edge
segments.rationale: Redness was 0.5 cm yesterday. It is smaller, which is not a worsening finding.

segments.text: Swelling extends to the left wrist
segments.rationale: Yesterday the swelling was limited to the wound edges. It has spread, and a worsening sign is followed up.

segments.text: Pain is 4 of 10
segments.rationale: Pain is a cardinal sign and the rating is unchanged from yesterday.

segments.text: Unable to make a full fist with left hand
segments.rationale: Yesterday the patient made a full fist. Decreased function is a cardinal sign, and a loss from baseline is followed up.

segments.text: Oral temperature is 36.8 °C
segments.rationale: This reading is close to yesterday's 36.7 °C and does not change the plan. The local findings are judged against their own baseline.

questions.takeaway: A cardinal sign that matches baseline is expected. A cardinal sign that is worse than baseline is followed up, and function counts as much as redness.
questions.strategy: Do not highlight a finding because it is a sign of inflammation. Line up each of today's findings with yesterday's entry and highlight only what is worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Six findings in each entry.

steps.action: Mark what changed for the worse
steps.detail: Swelling has spread and the fist is lost.

steps.action: Leave what matches or is better
steps.detail: Warmth, pain, and temperature match. Redness is smaller.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient whose forearm laceration was sutured 3 days ago. Yesterday at 0800 the nurse marked the edge of the redness 0.3 cm from the wound; swelling reached the wrist, pain was 4 of 10, and the patient could not make a full fist. Today at 0800 the redness extends 1 cm from the wound, past the marked line, and pain is 5 of 10. Swelling is back to the wound edges, and the patient makes a full fist. Oral temperature is 36.9 °C. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the wider redness and higher pain, with what has improved
options.rationale: Redness has crossed the marked line and pain has risen. Worsening findings are reported, and the report gives the whole picture, including what is better.

options.text: Document all four changes and recheck the wound at 2000
options.rationale: Two findings are better, but two are worse. Improvement in one sign does not cancel worsening in another, and waiting until 2000 delays the report.

options.text: Report the wider redness and higher pain as a new wound infection
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but the label goes beyond the findings. Redness and pain alone do not establish infection.

options.text: Redraw the line at 1 cm and use it as the new baseline
options.rationale: A new mark helps later checks, but resetting the baseline without reporting hides the change just found.

questions.takeaway: Compare every sign with baseline. Worsening in any sign is reported, even when other signs are better, and the report states findings without naming a cause.
questions.strategy: The trend is mixed and there is no fever, which makes waiting look reasonable. The deciding cue is that redness has passed the marked line and pain is up: two signs moved the wrong way. Then choose the report that states findings without adding a diagnosis.

steps.detail: Redness and pain are worse. Swelling and function are better.
Worsening symptoms are reported. Better signs do not cancel them.
One states findings. One adds "infection," which the findings do not establish.
Moving the baseline hides the change.

elimination.verdict: Report the wider redness and higher pain, with the improved swelling and function.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient whose deep forearm laceration into the muscle was sutured 3 weeks ago. Which finding should the nurse document as expected healing?

options.text: A pink scar with new thick yellow drainage
options.rationale: Pus is dead white cells, tissue, and fluid from an active fight against microorganisms. New drainage 3 weeks into repair is a change that needs follow up.

options.text: Warm redness spreading 2 cm past the scar
options.rationale: Redness that spreads after repair has begun is worsening, not healing. Worsening findings are reported.

options.text: Swelling and pain that returned after two weeks without them
options.rationale: Swelling and pain that come back after they had settled are a change from baseline. A return of signs needs follow up.

options.text: A firm scar with a stable, slightly weaker grip
options.rationale: Deep tissue often repairs with scar, and scar does not work like the muscle it replaced. A stable, slightly weaker grip fits that kind of repair.

questions.takeaway: Tissue repair can end in scar, and scar does not work like the tissue it replaced. A stable loss of some function can be expected; new or returning signs of inflammation are not.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options describe something new or spreading. The one finding that has stayed the same and fits scar repair is the expected one.

steps.detail: Three weeks after a deep cut, the area is in tissue repair.
New drainage, spreading redness, and returning swelling are each a change for the worse.
A firm scar with a stable, slightly weaker grip fits scar replacing muscle.

elimination.verdict: D. A firm scar with a stable, slightly weaker grip is expected after deep tissue repairs with scar.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A patient exposed to a disease this morning asks to skip immune globulin and take only the vaccine. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "The vaccine lasts longer, so I will ask to cancel the globulin."
options.rationale: The vaccine gives longer protection, but it takes time to build. After an exposure this morning, the vaccine alone leaves the patient unprotected now.

options.text: "Immune globulin protects you now; the vaccine takes time."
options.rationale: Immune globulin supplies antibodies from another source, so protection is immediate but temporary. The vaccine builds the patient's own lasting response, which takes time.

options.text: "Immune globulin builds memory too, so the vaccine can be skipped."
options.rationale: Passive protection does not create personal immune memory. The vaccine is the dose that builds lasting protection.

options.text: "Either one alone covers this morning's exposure."
options.rationale: Only immune globulin protects right away. A vaccine needs time for the body to build its own response.

questions.takeaway: After an exposure, immune globulin gives protection now because the antibodies come ready made. The vaccine builds the patient's own lasting protection, but not in time for today's exposure.
questions.strategy: The timing cue is "exposed this morning." Ask which product protects today, then which one builds memory.

steps.detail: The exposure was this morning, so protection is needed now.
Immune globulin: immediate, temporary. Vaccine: takes time, lasting.
A drops immediate protection, C gives passive immunity memory, D says the vaccine works today.

elimination.verdict: B. Immune globulin covers today's exposure; the vaccine builds lasting protection later.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A patient received immune globulin after an exposure and will get the vaccine next month. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "These antibodies were made by another source."
options.rationale: This is correct. Immune globulin is artificial passive immunity: antibodies from another source given as a product.

options.text: "My protection from this shot started right away."
options.rationale: This is correct. Passive immunity gives immediate protection because the antibodies are ready made.

options.text: "I still need the vaccine next month for longer lasting protection."
options.rationale: This is correct. Active immunity from the vaccine creates memory and often lasts longer than passive protection.

options.text: "My body will remember this, so I can skip the vaccine."
options.rationale: This needs follow up. Passive immunity creates no personal memory and fades, so canceling the vaccine would leave the patient without lasting protection.

questions.takeaway: Artificial passive immunity is immediate and temporary and builds no memory. A patient who plans to skip the vaccine because of immune globulin needs more teaching.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the statement that needs more teaching, so hunt the wrong idea. The one that leads the patient to drop the lasting protection is the one to act on.

steps.detail: You are looking for the incorrect statement.
Another source, immediate protection, and the vaccine for longer protection are all correct.
Memory from immune globulin is false, and it leads to canceling the vaccine.

elimination.verdict: D. Immune globulin builds no memory, so canceling the vaccine needs follow up.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient who is breastfeeding a 4 month old infant about the infant's protection against chickenpox. The patient had chickenpox as a child. The infant had chickenpox at 2 months of age and recovered. Which statement by the patient indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "Getting over chickenpox gave my baby its own lasting immunity. My milk adds temporary protection."
options.rationale: Recovering from a natural infection produces natural active immunity: the infant's own response, with memory and often long lasting protection. Antibodies in breast milk are natural passive immunity, which is immediate but temporary.

options.text: "My milk passes my chickenpox antibodies to my baby, and that is what keeps my baby protected."
options.rationale: Breast milk does carry maternal antibodies, but that protection is passive and temporary with no memory. The infant recovered from chickenpox and made its own response, which is what lasts.

options.text: "My baby got my chickenpox antibodies before birth, and those will protect my baby for years."
options.rationale: Antibodies across the placenta are natural passive immunity, which is temporary. They also did not prevent the infant's chickenpox at 2 months.

options.text: "Getting over chickenpox gave my baby passive immunity, so the protection will fade in a few months."
options.rationale: Recovering from a natural infection is active immunity, not passive. The infant made its own response.

questions.takeaway: Recovery from a natural infection is natural active immunity, with memory and longer protection. Maternal antibodies through the placenta or breast milk are natural passive immunity: immediate but temporary.
questions.strategy: A and B both describe real protection, and breastfeeding pulls toward B. The cue that decides is "the infant had chickenpox at 2 months of age and recovered": the infant made its own response, and that is the lasting one.

steps.detail: Chickenpox at 2 months, then recovery.
Natural active: own response, memory, longer lasting.
Natural passive: immediate, temporary, no memory.

steps.action: Reject the placenta and passive claims
steps.detail: Placental antibodies are temporary; recovery is active, not passive.

elimination.verdict: Recovery made the infant's own immunity with memory; milk antibodies add temporary protection.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with no prior immunity to a disease. The patient received immune globulin after an exposure 3 months ago and the first dose of the vaccine 2 days ago. Today the patient reports a new close exposure this morning and says, "I have had both, so I am covered." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The immune globulin from 3 months ago still protects you, so nothing more is needed."
options.rationale: Passive protection is temporary. The nurse cannot assume it is still present 3 months later.

options.text: "The vaccine from 2 days ago has given you memory, so nothing more is needed today."
options.rationale: Vaccines do create memory, but active immunity takes time to develop. Two days is too soon to count on it.

options.text: "Neither one can be counted on yet. I will report this new exposure to the provider."
options.rationale: Passive protection fades and active protection has not had time to form. The patient may be unprotected, so the nurse reports the exposure for a decision about protection now.

options.text: "Neither one can be counted on yet. I will give you another dose of immune globulin."
options.rationale: The reasoning is right and the product may be what is needed, but the nurse does not give it without an order. The exposure is reported first.

questions.takeaway: Passive immunity is temporary and active immunity takes time to develop. A patient can sit in the gap between the two.
questions.strategy: Each product sounds like it should cover the patient, and two options lean on one of them. The deciding cues are the two time points: 3 months since the temporary product and 2 days since the slow one.

steps.detail: Immune globulin: immediate but temporary. Vaccine: lasting but slow.
3 months is long for a temporary product, and 2 days is too early for the other.
One acts without an order. One reports so that a decision can be made.

elimination.verdict: Neither can be counted on today, so the exposure is reported.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A patient twisted an ankle for the first time an hour ago and asks why it already swelled. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Swelling this fast is unusual, so I will report it now."
options.rationale: The built in response needs no earlier exposure, so fast swelling after a first injury is expected. Reporting expected findings as unusual is not needed.

options.text: "This built in defense acts right away, even the first time."
options.rationale: Innate immunity is present at birth and acts immediately without prior exposure. The swelling is expected, and the nurse compares later checks with this baseline.

options.text: "Antibodies already waiting in your ankle caused the swelling."
options.rationale: Antibodies belong to the adaptive response, not to this fast swelling, which is the innate response.

options.text: "This built in defense acts fast and will be faster next time."
options.rationale: The innate response builds no memory, so it will not be faster next time. Memory belongs to adaptive immunity.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation is part of innate immunity: present at birth, fast, and needing no prior exposure. Fast swelling after a first injury is expected, so you set a baseline and compare.
questions.strategy: Decide whether the swelling is expected before you choose between reporting and explaining. The first injury cue tests whether you know the innate response needs no prior exposure.

steps.detail: Swelling within 1 hour is the innate inflammatory response.
Innate immunity needs no prior exposure, so a first injury still swells fast.
Expected findings are rechecked and compared, not reported as unusual.

elimination.verdict: B. The innate response is immediate without prior exposure.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.scenario: A patient twisted the right ankle 2 days ago. At 0800 today the nurse documented: right ankle warm, warmth limited to the ankle; redness 4 cm across over the outer ankle, edge marked with pen; right ankle circumference 26 cm, swelling limited to the ankle; pain 4 of 10 at rest; bears weight on the right leg with a limp. The nurse reassesses at 1600.
questions.stem: The nurse is reassessing a patient with a sprained ankle at 1600. For each 1600 finding, indicate whether it is expected with inflammation or requires follow up.

rows.text: Right ankle warm to the touch, warmth limited to the ankle
rows.rationale: Warmth is a cardinal sign of inflammation, and it is limited to the ankle, as at 0800.

rows.text: Redness over the outer right ankle 4 cm across, its edge on the line marked at 0800
rows.rationale: The redness reaches the marked line but does not pass it. It is the same 4 cm as at 0800, so it has not spread.

rows.text: Right ankle circumference 28 cm, swelling still limited to the ankle
rows.rationale: Swelling is still limited to the ankle, but the measurement is 2 cm larger than the 26 cm at 0800. Worsening swelling is documented and reported.

rows.text: Pain 6 of 10 at rest
rows.rationale: Pain at rest was 4 of 10 at 0800. A rise in a cardinal sign is a worsening finding to report.

rows.text: Bears weight on the right leg with a limp
rows.rationale: Decreased function is a cardinal sign, and this is the same function as at 0800.

questions.takeaway: Cardinal signs that match the 0800 baseline are expected with inflammation. A measured increase in a sign, even one that still looks limited to the ankle, is a change over time that is reported.
questions.strategy: Two rows are traps. Redness that reaches the line has not passed it, and swelling still limited to the ankle has grown by 2 cm. Compare each number with the 0800 entry instead of the description.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warmth, redness, swelling, pain, and function.

steps.action: Check the redness against the line
steps.detail: On the line, 4 cm, so unchanged.
28 cm now, 26 cm at 0800, so the swelling grew.
Pain rose from 4 to 6 of 10; weight bearing is unchanged.

elimination.verdict: Rows 3 and 4 require follow up. Rows 1, 2, and 5 are expected with inflammation.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A patient with deeply pigmented skin injured a wrist 4 hours ago. Which findings should the nurse document as cardinal signs of inflammation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Injured wrist warmer than the other wrist
options.rationale: Local warmth at the injured site, compared with the other wrist, is a cardinal sign of inflammation.

options.text: Skin over the injured wrist darker than the other
options.rationale: In deeply pigmented skin, the redness of inflammation can appear as a darker color. A color change at the site is the cardinal sign of redness.

options.text: Injured wrist 2 cm larger around than the other
options.rationale: A larger circumference on the injured side is measured swelling, a cardinal sign.

options.text: Unable to turn a doorknob with that hand
options.rationale: Decreased function is the fifth cardinal sign and the one most often left out. Losing a task the hand can normally do counts.

options.text: Oral temperature of 37.0 °C
options.rationale: Warmth as a cardinal sign is local, felt at the site. A core temperature within the reference range is not one of the five signs.

options.text: Capillary refill of 2 seconds in those fingers
options.rationale: This checks circulation beyond the injury and is within the reference range. It is not one of the five cardinal signs.

questions.takeaway: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain, and decreased function, all found at the site. In deeply pigmented skin, redness can show as a darker color, and lost function counts as fully as swelling.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Recite the five signs and match each option to one of them. Warmth means warmth at the site, not core temperature, and a color change is the redness sign even when it does not look red.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warmth, redness, swelling, pain, decreased function.
Warmer, darker, and larger injured wrist, and the lost doorknob task.

steps.action: Reject the systemic and circulation checks
steps.detail: Oral temperature and capillary refill are not among the five, and both are within reference ranges.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who touched a hot pan with the palm 1 hour ago. The palm is warm, red, and swollen, and the skin is intact. The patient asks what the body is doing to heal the burn. Place the events of the inflammatory response in the order in which they occur.

options.text: White blood cells move through the blood vessel walls into the burned area
options.rationale: This begins the cellular response, the second stage. Cells arrive after the vascular response has opened the way.

options.text: Blood vessels in the palm dilate and blood flow to the area increases
options.rationale: Vessel dilation starts the vascular response, the first stage. Histamine released at the site causes this dilation, which produces the warmth and redness.

options.text: The area heals by new cells, scar, or both and returns toward normal function
options.rationale: Tissue repair is the third stage. Damaged tissue heals by regeneration, scar formation, or both.

options.text: Fluid moves out of the vessels into the tissue and the palm swells
options.rationale: Still in the vascular response: fluid leaves the dilated vessels, causing swelling and helping deliver immune cells.

options.text: Neutrophils and macrophages engulf dead cells and harmful material
options.rationale: Once in the area, white blood cells remove harmful material and dead cells by phagocytosis, completing the cellular response.

options.text: Mast cells and basophils in the palm release histamine
options.rationale: Mast cells and basophils release histamine and other substances that promote inflammation. Histamine release comes first because it is what dilates the vessels in the vascular response.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation runs in three stages: vascular (histamine release, dilation, then fluid shift and swelling), cellular (white cells migrate in, then engulf), and tissue repair (regeneration, scar, or both).
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort the six events into the three stages first, then order the two events inside each stage. Within a stage, something has to arrive before it can act.

steps.detail: Histamine release, dilation, and fluid shift are vascular. Migration and engulfing are cellular. Healing is repair.
Histamine release comes first; it is what dilates the vessels.
Vessels dilate before fluid can leave them.
White cells must move into the area before they can engulf anything.
The area returns toward normal function at the end.

elimination.verdict: Histamine release, dilation, fluid shift and swelling, white cell migration, engulfing, tissue repair.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing measles protection with six patients. Which statements by the patients require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I had measles 10 years ago, so my own body makes protection against it."
options.rationale: This is correct. Recovering from a natural infection gives natural active immunity with memory.

options.text: "I got immune globulin with measles antibodies 2 months ago, so I am covered for years."
options.rationale: This needs follow up. Immune globulin is artificial passive immunity, which is temporary and builds no memory.

options.text: "My child got the measles vaccine at 12 months, so my child's own body is building protection."
options.rationale: This is correct. A vaccine gives artificial active immunity: the child's own response, with memory.

options.text: "My 3 month old got my measles antibodies before birth, so my baby is protected through childhood."
options.rationale: This needs follow up. Antibodies that cross the placenta are natural passive immunity, which gives temporary protection only.

options.text: "My measles vaccine 3 weeks ago used a weakened virus, so my body made its own antibodies."
options.rationale: This is correct. A vaccine with a weakened virus stimulates the patient's own response without causing disease.

options.text: "My blood test showed measles antibodies 1 day after immune globulin, so my body made its own protection."
options.rationale: This needs follow up. The antibodies came from the immune globulin, another source, so they are passive and will fade. A body response of its own takes time.

questions.takeaway: Passive immunity, from immune globulin or from a parent before birth, is immediate but temporary. Antibodies on a test do not prove active immunity; where they came from does.
questions.strategy: Treat each statement as true or false. For each one, ask where the antibodies came from, then whether the claim about lasting protection fits that source.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are selecting the statements that are wrong.
Illness and vaccines are active; immune globulin and antibodies before birth are passive.
In F, antibodies appeared 1 day after immune globulin, so they came from that product.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F. Each claims lasting protection from passive antibodies.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who got a splinter in an index finger yesterday. Within 1 hour the fingertip was warm, red, and swollen, the same timing and the same size as after a splinter in that finger 1 year ago. Today it looks as it did yesterday, with no drainage. The patient says, "My body should have remembered the first splinter, so the same swelling means something is wrong." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "This response builds no memory, so the same swelling is expected. Keep watching."
options.rationale: Inflammation is innate: fast, nonspecific, and without memory. The same timing and size as last time is what the innate response does, so the finding is expected and the plan is to watch for change.

options.text: "Your body formed memory after the first splinter, so this reaction shows a weak response."
options.rationale: Memory belongs to adaptive immunity. Inflammation does not form memory, so the same size reaction is not a weak response.

options.text: "A second reaction should be smaller than the first, so I will report this swelling now."
options.rationale: The innate response does not shrink with repeated exposure, so a same size reaction is expected. There is nothing here to report.

options.text: "Your body remembered the first splinter, which is why it swelled so fast. Keep watching."
options.rationale: This reaches the right plan for the wrong reason. A response from memory would be faster and stronger, but this one matched the first, which shows the innate response.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation is innate: it is equally fast every time and builds no memory. An identical reaction to a repeat injury is expected, not a sign of failure.
questions.strategy: A and D both call the finding expected. The cue that decides is "same size as the first time": a memory response would be faster and stronger, so only the innate explanation fits.

steps.detail: B and C report; A and D call the finding expected and keep watching.
Same timing and same size both times means no memory at work.
D credits memory; A names the innate response, which builds none.

elimination.verdict: A. The same reaction each time is the innate response, which has no memory.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the records of four patients who were exposed to measles at the clinic today. None of the patients has any other measles vaccine, illness, or antibody product on record. Which patient should the nurse report to the provider as lacking lasting protection?

options.text: A patient who received a measles vaccine 1 year ago
options.rationale: A vaccine gives artificial active immunity: the patient made the response, and memory remains. A year is not long for active immunity.

options.text: A patient who recovered from measles 40 years ago
options.rationale: Recovery from measles gives natural active immunity, the most effective and longest lasting type. Forty years sounds long, but this protection does not simply fade the way passive protection does.

options.text: A patient who received measles immune globulin 1 year ago
options.rationale: Immune globulin is artificial passive immunity: antibodies from another source, immediate but temporary, with no memory. A year later the patient has no lasting protection of the patient's own.

options.text: A patient, 78 years old, who recovered from measles as a child
options.rationale: Older age does affect immune function, so this pulls hard. But recovery from measles gave natural active immunity with memory. The source of protection, not age alone, decides here.

questions.takeaway: Lasting protection comes from active immunity, by illness or vaccine, even when that illness was long ago. Passive antibodies from immune globulin fade and leave no memory.
questions.strategy: Three options pull: A and C differ only in the product given 1 year ago, B has the oldest exposure, and D adds older age. The deciding cue is the source of protection: only one patient got antibodies from another source.

steps.detail: Vaccine and illness are active; immune globulin is passive.
A vaccine 1 year ago left memory; immune globulin 1 year ago did not.
Forty years after recovery, natural active immunity is still the longest lasting type.
Age affects immunity, but D still has active immunity from the illness.

elimination.verdict: C. Immune globulin gave temporary passive protection that is gone a year later.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who received the first dose of a vaccine in the upper arm 4 hours ago. The patient has never had this disease or this vaccine. Which findings should the nurse expect at this time? Select all that apply.

options.text: Redness and warmth at the injection site
options.rationale: Expected. Inflammation is innate, needs no prior exposure, and starts within hours of the injection.

options.text: High levels of antibodies that bind only the vaccine antigen
options.rationale: Not yet. Specific antibodies are adaptive and take time to develop after a first exposure.

options.text: Neutrophils and macrophages moving into the tissue at the injection site
options.rationale: Expected. Phagocytes act as part of the innate response, which begins right away.

options.text: A faster, stronger response than the patient has had to this antigen before
options.rationale: Not possible yet. A faster, stronger response comes from memory, which needs an earlier exposure, and this is the first.

options.text: Mild swelling and tenderness at the injection site
options.rationale: Expected. Swelling and pain are cardinal signs of the innate inflammatory response.

options.text: Full protection against the disease starting today
options.rationale: Not yet. Active immunity from a vaccine takes time to develop.

questions.takeaway: Hours after a first vaccine dose, only the innate response is at work: local inflammation and phagocytes. Specific antibodies, memory, and protection take time.
questions.strategy: The cues are "4 hours" and "never had". Sort each option into innate (immediate, no prior exposure) or adaptive (takes time, needs exposure).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At 4 hours after a first exposure, only fast responses can be present.
Redness, swelling, and phagocytes are innate; specific antibodies, memory, and protection are adaptive.
Choose the findings that need no prior exposure and no build up time.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E. Only the innate response is present 4 hours after a first dose.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who scraped a knee on gravel 4 days ago. On the day of the injury the knee was warm, red, and swollen, with redness 2 cm around the scrape. Today new pink skin covers the edges of the scrape, the redness is 0.5 cm around it, the swelling is gone, and the patient bends the knee fully. The patient asks, "Which stage is my knee in, and what comes next?" Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Your knee is in the cellular response. Next comes tissue repair, when new cells replace the damage."
options.rationale: The order of the stages is right, but the stage named is not. New pink skin and the return of full bending show damaged tissue being replaced and function returning, which is tissue repair.

options.text: "Your knee is in tissue repair, the last stage. It will keep returning toward normal function."
options.rationale: Tissue repair is the third and last stage, so no stage follows it: damaged tissue heals through regeneration and/or scar, and the area gradually returns toward normal function. New pink skin at the edges and full bending of the knee show this stage.

options.text: "Your knee is in the vascular response. Next comes the cellular response, when white cells clear debris."
options.rationale: The vascular response, with dilated vessels, warmth, redness, and swelling, fits the day of the injury. Today the swelling is gone and new skin is forming.

options.text: "Your knee is in tissue repair. Next comes the cellular response, when white cells clear debris."
options.rationale: The stage named is right, but the order is wrong. The stages run vascular, then cellular, then tissue repair, so the cellular response does not follow repair.

questions.takeaway: The stages run in order: vascular response, cellular response, then tissue repair. New tissue at the wound edges and returning function mark tissue repair, the last stage.
questions.strategy: A has the right order and D has the right stage, so both look defensible. The cue that decides is "new pink skin covers the edges" with full bending: that is regeneration and returning function, and repair is the last stage, so nothing follows it.

steps.detail: Vascular, then cellular, then tissue repair.
New pink skin at the edges, smaller redness, no swelling, full bending.
Regeneration with return toward normal function is tissue repair.
Repair is last, so A and D both fail on one point.

elimination.verdict: Tissue repair; the knee keeps returning toward normal function.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A new nurse is caring for a patient whose ankle swelled 2 hours after a sprain. Which statement by the new nurse requires correction?

options.text: "Fluid moved out of widened vessels into the tissue."
options.rationale: This is correct. In the vascular response, vessels dilate and fluid moves from the vessels into the tissue.

options.text: "I will measure both ankles now as a baseline."
options.rationale: This is correct. Measured findings form the baseline that later findings are compared with.

options.text: "The fluid also helps bring immune cells to the ankle."
options.rationale: This is correct. Fluid moving into the tissue helps deliver immune cells to the injury.

options.text: "It is getting worse, so I will report it now."
options.rationale: This needs correction. Swelling 2 hours after a sprain is part of the expected vascular response. What gets reported is worsening over time compared with baseline.

questions.takeaway: Early swelling is the vascular response: fluid leaves widened vessels and carries immune cells into the tissue. It is expected; you report worsening against baseline, not the swelling itself.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the statement to correct. Three explain or monitor the swelling; one turns an expected finding into a report.

steps.detail: You are looking for the wrong statement.
Dilated vessels, fluid into tissue, immune cells delivered.
Reporting expected early swelling as worsening is the error.

elimination.verdict: D. Early swelling is expected; worsening against baseline is what gets reported.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient who takes a daily immunosuppressant after a kidney transplant. The patient has a 2 cm abrasion on the shin from a fall 2 days ago, with redness 0.2 cm from the wound edge, no swelling, and pain 1 of 10. Oral temperature is 36.9 °C. The patient says, "It barely looks irritated, so I can stop the daily wound checks." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Keep checking daily, and report new redness, drainage, or pain even without a fever."
options.rationale: An immunosuppressant affects immune function, so the signs of inflammation and infection can be muted, and infection can be present without fever when immunity is decreased. Daily checks continue, and worsening local findings are reported.

options.text: "Keep checking daily, and call the clinic right away if you develop a fever or chills."
options.rationale: Daily checks are right, but this plan waits for fever. Infection can be present without fever, especially when immunity is decreased, as it is with this patient's medication.

options.text: "These findings are mild, so you can stop the checks once the redness fades."
options.rationale: For a patient with a typical immune response, mild signs with a temperature in range are reassuring. This patient's medication means mild signs cannot be taken at face value.

options.text: "Your medicine lowers your immune response, so the wound is already infected."
options.rationale: The first half is right. Mild findings do not establish infection, and the nurse does not label a cause from these findings.

questions.takeaway: Medications that suppress immunity can blunt the cardinal signs, and infection can be present without fever when immunity is decreased. Teach daily checks and reporting of new or spreading local findings, not waiting for fever.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options keep the daily checks. The deciding cue is the immunosuppressant: infection can be present without fever, so a plan that waits for fever can miss it.

steps.detail: Daily immunosuppressant after a transplant.
Mild findings are not reassuring when the immune response is muted.
Mild findings do not prove infection has started.

steps.action: Compare the two daily check plans
steps.detail: One waits for fever; the other reports local changes even without fever.

elimination.verdict: Check daily and report local changes even without fever.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A patient has an inherited condition in which neutrophils recognize and surround bacteria but cannot ingest them. Which teaching about new cuts should the nurse include?

options.text: "Your cuts will still heal at the usual pace."
options.rationale: Breakdown happens after ingestion. If the bacteria cannot be ingested, they are not broken down, so clearing is slower.

options.text: "New cuts will not turn red or swell at all."
options.rationale: Recognition works in this condition. The vascular response also does not depend on ingestion, so redness and swelling still occur.

options.text: "No defense will reach a new cut."
options.rationale: Crossing into the tissue is the step before recognition, and it works here. The cells reach the cut but stop before ingestion.

options.text: "Report spreading redness or drainage early."
options.rationale: Phagocytosis goes recognize, surround, ingest, then break down. Without ingestion there is no breakdown, so infection may set in and early reporting matters.

questions.takeaway: Phagocytosis runs in order: recognize, surround, ingest, break down. A break at one step stops every step after it, so teaching focuses on early signs of infection.
questions.strategy: Find the step that fails, then ask which later steps cannot happen. Steps before the failure still work.

steps.detail: Recognize and surround work; ingest fails.
Breakdown needs ingestion, so bacteria are not cleared.
Migration and recognition are intact, so B and C are wrong, and A ignores the failed step.

elimination.verdict: D. Without ingestion there is no breakdown, so teach early reporting of infection signs.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: A patient recovered from a viral illness 6 weeks ago. Which findings show that the adaptive immune response is working as expected? Select all that apply.

options.text: Antibodies that bind only that virus
options.rationale: Adaptive immunity targets a specific antigen. B lymphocytes become plasma cells that make antibodies against that one virus.

options.text: No illness after a new exposure to that virus
options.rationale: Memory cells from the first illness allow a faster, stronger response, so illness may not result.

options.text: Antibodies that bind viruses never met before
options.rationale: Antibodies are specific to the antigen that triggered them. Broad action without exposure describes innate immunity, not antibodies.

options.text: A faster antibody rise after the new exposure
options.rationale: A faster, stronger response on a second exposure than after the first illness is the mark of immune memory.

options.text: The same illness, just as severe, after reexposure
options.rationale: An identical second illness would suggest no memory was formed. This would need follow up, not reassure.

options.text: Redness and swelling around a new cut within an hour
options.rationale: This is innate inflammation. It is expected, but it does not show the adaptive response at work.

questions.takeaway: Adaptive immunity is specific and builds memory. Evidence that it worked is a specific antibody and a faster, stronger response, or no illness, on the next exposure to the same virus.
questions.strategy: Look for the two marks of adaptive immunity, specificity and memory. Findings that are broad or unchanged with a repeat exposure point to something else.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Adaptive immunity is specific and creates memory.
A is specific; B and D show memory.
C is broad, E shows no memory, F is innate.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D. Specific antibodies and a faster or protective response on reexposure.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who recovered from a cold 2 months ago; testing at that time identified the virus. This week a coworker has a cold, and testing shows the same virus. The patient asks, "Should I stay home from work so I do not catch it again?" Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Staying home is safest, since protection from a cold fades within a few weeks."
options.rationale: This sounds cautious, but natural active immunity creates memory and often lasts a long time. Two months is not long enough for it to be expected to fade.

options.text: "You made memory for this virus, so you may not get sick. Report any symptoms."
options.rationale: Recovering from the cold gave natural active immunity with memory. Against the same virus, the response is faster and stronger, so illness may not result, and new symptoms are still reported.

options.text: "Ask the provider about immune globulin to cover you after this week's exposure."
options.rationale: Immune globulin gives immediate passive protection after an exposure, so this sounds protective. But this patient already has active immunity with memory against the same virus, so borrowed antibodies add nothing needed.

options.text: "Your memory cells will keep you from getting sick, so you need no precautions at all."
options.rationale: The mechanism is right, but the promise is not. Memory makes illness less likely, not impossible, and symptoms are still watched for and reported.

questions.takeaway: Recovering from an illness gives natural active immunity with memory. Against the same virus the response is faster and stronger, so illness may not develop, but it is not guaranteed, and symptoms are still reported.
questions.strategy: Every option sounds like a nurse being careful or reassuring. The deciding cues are "recovered" and "the same virus": the patient has active immunity with memory, so passive cover is not needed, and the right answer says "may not" rather than promising no illness.

steps.detail: Recovery from the cold is natural active immunity, with memory.
The same virus means the memory cells match this exposure.
Immune globulin is for patients without their own protection.
B says "may not" and keeps reporting; D promises too much and drops it.

elimination.verdict: B. Memory from the same virus can protect the patient, and symptoms are still reported.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient, 78 years old, at a wellness visit. The patient has no wounds and says, "I had all my tetanus shots as a child more than 60 years ago, and vaccines create memory, so I am protected for life." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Those shots created memory cells that will respond fast enough if you ever get a deep wound."
options.rationale: Vaccines do create memory, but vaccine immunity needs booster doses to stay in place, and in older adults antibody duration is reduced further. Memory from 60 years ago cannot be counted on.

options.text: "Your protection has likely faded, so an injection of tetanus antibodies today will restore it."
options.rationale: Fading protection is the right concern, but antibodies from another source give passive immunity: immediate, temporary, and with no memory. The patient has no wound, so the goal is lasting protection.

options.text: "Your protection has likely faded, so a tetanus booster today will renew your own."
options.rationale: Vaccine immunity needs boosters, and at 78 antibody duration is reduced. A booster gives active immunity: the patient makes the response again and memory is renewed, which suits a patient seeking lasting protection.

options.text: "Childhood shots gave you antibodies from another source, so they have faded."
options.rationale: Childhood vaccines give artificial active immunity: the patient made the response. Antibodies from another source describe passive immunity.

questions.takeaway: Vaccination gives artificial active immunity with memory, and it needs boosters to stay in place; older adults have reduced antibody duration. When the goal is lasting protection rather than immediate cover, the patient's own response is renewed with a booster, not with passive antibodies.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: B and C both restore protection. The deciding cue is that the patient has no wound: the goal is lasting protection, and antibodies from another source give only immediate, short term protection with no memory.

steps.detail: Childhood tetanus shots: vaccination, artificial active immunity.
Vaccine immunity needs boosters, and at 78 antibody duration is shorter still.
Memory from 60 years ago cannot be counted on without a booster.
Antibodies from another source fade and leave no memory, and there is no wound calling for immediate cover.
Childhood shots made the patient's own response.

elimination.verdict: A tetanus booster so the patient makes antibodies again.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: A patient with a new kidney transplant says, "I will stop my antirejection medicine once I feel well." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "The donor kidney carries no tissue markers, so you may stop."
options.rationale: All body cells carry human leukocyte antigens (HLA). The donor kidney's HLA differ from the patient's, which is why it can be attacked.

options.text: "Self tolerance will protect the new kidney once it heals."
options.rationale: Self tolerance protects the patient's own tissue. The donor kidney is not self, so self tolerance does not cover it.

options.text: "It only prevents infection, so stop once the incision heals."
options.rationale: The medicine lowers the immune response to prevent rejection. It raises infection risk rather than preventing infection.

options.text: "Your body sees the new kidney as foreign; keep taking it."
options.rationale: Human leukocyte antigens (HLA) mark the body's own cells. The donor kidney carries different HLA, so it is recognized as non self. Stopping the medicine risks an attack on the kidney.

questions.takeaway: HLA mark cells as self. A donor organ carries different HLA, so the immune system sees it as non self, and the patient keeps taking the medicine that suppresses that response.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The patient's plan is unsafe. Choose the response that gives the correct reason and keeps the medicine going.

steps.detail: Stopping the medicine invites rejection.
Different HLA mean the kidney is seen as foreign.
No HLA, self tolerance for donor tissue, and infection prevention are all wrong.

elimination.verdict: D. The donor kidney is non self, so the medicine continues.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A patient takes an immunosuppressant that lowers T lymphocyte function after a kidney transplant. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: Report cold sores or other viral signs early
options.rationale: T lymphocytes target body cells infected with a virus. With lower T lymphocyte function, viral infections may be cleared more slowly, so early reporting matters.

options.text: Repeat all childhood vaccines to replace lost antibodies
options.rationale: B lymphocytes, through plasma cells, make antibodies. T lymphocytes do not make them, so lowering T lymphocyte function does not erase vaccine antibodies.

options.text: Expect new cuts to show no redness or swelling
options.rationale: Neutrophils, not T lymphocytes, are the first responders that engulf bacteria. The vascular response still occurs, so a cut will usually show some inflammation, though the signs may be milder.

options.text: Report new joint pain as an attack on your own tissue
options.rationale: Lowering T lymphocyte function reduces immune attacks; that is why it protects the transplant. It does not make the body attack its own tissue.

questions.takeaway: T lymphocytes target infected or abnormal body cells and help coordinate the immune response. When their function is lowered, teach the patient to report signs of viral infection early.
questions.strategy: Match the teaching to what T lymphocytes actually do. Each wrong option gives them another cell's job.

steps.detail: Target infected or abnormal cells and coordinate the response.
Antibodies belong to plasma cells; engulfing bacteria belongs to neutrophils.
Suppression lowers immune attack, so D runs the wrong way.

elimination.verdict: A. Lower T lymphocyte function slows clearing of virus infected cells, so report early.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the laboratory results of a patient who returned 4 weeks ago from travel to a tropical area where the patient often walked barefoot on soil. The patient reports loose stools for 3 weeks and a weight loss of 2 kg. The patient has seasonal allergies and today has no sneezing, itching, rash, or wheezing. White blood cell count is 7800 per mm3, neutrophils are 58%, and eosinophils are 14%. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The eosinophil rise most likely reflects the seasonal allergies
options.rationale: Eosinophils do rise with allergic responses, and the patient has an allergy history. But today there is no sneezing, itching, rash, or wheezing, so nothing shows an active allergic response.

options.text: The eosinophil rise most likely reflects bacteria picked up on the trip
options.rationale: Bacteria are a fair guess for loose stools after travel, but neutrophils are the first responders that engulf bacteria, and the neutrophils here are in range. Eosinophils defend against parasites and mediate allergic responses.

options.text: The results show no active immune response
options.rationale: The total count and neutrophils (55 to 70%) are in range, but eosinophils at 14% are well above 1 to 4%. One cell type can rise while the total stays in range.

options.text: The eosinophil rise most likely reflects a parasite from the soil
options.rationale: Eosinophils at 14% are well above the reference range of 1 to 4%. Eosinophils defend against parasites, and parasitic worms that enter through bare skin on soil are a classic cause of a high eosinophil count. Walking barefoot in a tropical area, weeks of loose stools, and weight loss fit a parasite better than an allergy with no active signs.

questions.takeaway: Eosinophils rise for two reasons: parasites and allergic responses. The history and current findings decide which one fits.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and D both link eosinophils to a correct function. The cue that decides is in the stem: today there is no sneezing, itching, rash, or wheezing, while walking barefoot on tropical soil and weeks of loose stools point to a parasite.

steps.detail: Eosinophils 14%; the total count and neutrophils are in range.
Parasites and allergic responses.

steps.action: Test the allergy option against the stem
steps.detail: No sneezing, itching, rash, or wheezing today.

steps.action: Test the parasite option against the stem
steps.detail: Barefoot on soil in a tropical area, loose stools for 3 weeks, 2 kg weight loss.
Neutrophils, not eosinophils, engulf bacteria.

elimination.verdict: A parasite from the soil; eosinophils defend against parasites.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is planning closer wound checks. Which patients are likely to clear bacteria from a new cut more slowly? Select all that apply.

options.text: A patient with a very low neutrophil count
options.rationale: Neutrophils are the first responders that engulf and destroy bacteria. Few neutrophils means slower clearing.

options.text: A patient with inherited low complement levels
options.rationale: Complement strengthens the defense and supports removal of invaders. Low complement slows clearing.

options.text: A patient with only a low eosinophil count
options.rationale: Eosinophils defend against parasites and mediate allergic responses. The cells that clear bacteria are not affected.

options.text: A patient taking a drug that blocks cytokine signaling
options.rationale: Cytokines carry signals that coordinate inflammation. Blocking them weakens the coordinated response to bacteria.

options.text: A patient never exposed to this bacterium before
options.rationale: Neutrophils, macrophages, and complement are innate and need no prior exposure. A first exposure does not slow this response.

options.text: A patient with seasonal allergies and high eosinophils
options.rationale: High eosinophils fit an allergic response. They do not slow the clearing of bacteria from a cut.

questions.takeaway: Neutrophils and macrophages engulf bacteria, complement helps remove them, and cytokines coordinate the response. A shortfall in any of these slows clearing; eosinophils target parasites and allergy.
questions.strategy: For each patient, ask whether the cell or protein that is low or blocked helps clear bacteria. Eosinophils and a lack of prior exposure are the traps.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Neutrophils, macrophages, complement, and coordinating cytokines.
Low neutrophils, low complement, and blocked cytokines each weaken clearing.
Eosinophils target parasites and allergy; innate defense needs no prior exposure.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D. Each lacks a part of the defense that clears bacteria.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with a skin reaction on both hands after starting a new hand cream. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient has red, warm, swollen, itchy patches on the backs of both hands 1 day after starting a new hand cream. The skin is intact. The patient rates the pain 3 of 10 and cannot fully close either hand. Oral temperature is 36.7 °C.

The findings on both hands are best explained by [[1]].

The cells that release histamine and promote this response are [[2]].

The patient's inability to fully close either hand is documented as [[3]].

options.text: an adaptive response that produces memory cells within 1 day
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity, a rapid, broad response. Adaptive responses take time to develop.

options.text: inflammation caused by microorganisms carried in the cream
options.rationale: Inflammation is the right idea, but nothing in the stem shows microorganisms entering the intact skin.

options.text: infection, because redness and swelling are present on both hands
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Inflammation can occur without infection.

options.text: inflammation without infection, triggered by an irritant
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur after exposure to an irritant, and it can occur without infection. Intact skin and a clear trigger fit this.

options.text: neutrophils and macrophages
options.rationale: Neutrophils and macrophages are phagocytes that engulf and remove material. They are not the histamine releasing cells.

options.text: basophils and mast cells
options.rationale: Basophils and mast cells release histamine and other substances that promote inflammation.

options.text: B lymphocytes and plasma cells
options.rationale: B lymphocytes and plasma cells produce antibodies in humoral immunity. They do not release histamine.

options.text: eosinophils and neutrophils
options.rationale: Neutrophils are phagocytes and do not release histamine. Basophils and mast cells are the cells that release histamine to promote inflammation.

options.text: a finding unrelated to the inflammation on the hands
options.rationale: Decreased function is one of the five cardinal signs, so it is part of the inflammatory picture.

options.text: evidence that an infection has developed in both hands
options.rationale: Decreased function is a sign of inflammation, and inflammation can occur without infection.

options.text: decreased function, a cardinal sign of inflammation
options.rationale: The five cardinal signs are warmth, redness, swelling, pain, and decreased function. Not being able to close the hands is decreased function.

options.text: swelling, a cardinal sign of inflammation
options.rationale: Swelling is a separate cardinal sign. Being unable to close the hand is a loss of function, which is documented as decreased function.

questions.takeaway: An irritant can trigger inflammation without infection. Basophils and mast cells release histamine that promotes it, and decreased function is one of the five cardinal signs.
questions.strategy: The trap in blank 1 is reading redness and swelling as infection. Name the trigger first: a new cream on intact skin is an irritant, not an invasion by microorganisms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new hand cream on intact skin: an irritant.

steps.action: Match the chemical to the cell
steps.detail: Histamine comes from basophils and mast cells.
Warmth, redness, swelling, pain, decreased function.
Cannot fully close the hands is decreased function.

elimination.verdict: Inflammation without infection, triggered by an irritant; basophils and mast cells; decreased function, a cardinal sign of inflammation.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: A patient with inherited low complement levels has had three bacterial skin infections this year. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: Expect new cuts to heal at the usual pace
options.rationale: Complement supports the removal of invaders, so with less of it bacteria are cleared more slowly. Cytokines carry signals and do not take over complement's role.

options.text: Get vaccine boosters to raise complement levels
options.rationale: Plasma cells make antibodies after vaccines, not complement. A booster does not raise complement levels.

options.text: Clean cuts and report spreading redness early
options.rationale: Complement strengthens the defense and supports the removal of invaders. With less of it, bacteria are cleared more slowly, so early care and reporting matter.

options.text: Watch for fever as the only sign of infection
options.rationale: The vascular response still produces redness and swelling, and infection can be present without fever, so watching only for fever misses it.

questions.takeaway: Complement strengthens immune defense and helps remove invaders. Low complement means slower clearing of bacteria, so teach early wound care and early reporting.
questions.strategy: Start from what complement does, then pick the teaching that protects against what is lost.

steps.detail: It strengthens the defense and supports removal of bacteria.
Bacteria are cleared more slowly, which fits three infections this year.
Usual healing and vaccine boosters ignore the loss; "fever as the only sign" misses local signs.

elimination.verdict: C. Low complement slows bacterial clearing, so teach early wound care and reporting.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: Which information should the nurse include when teaching a patient whose B lymphocytes cannot become plasma cells? Select all that apply.

options.text: "You may get infections more often."
options.rationale: B lymphocytes become antibody producing plasma cells when activated by antigens. Without plasma cells, few antibodies are made to neutralize or remove foreign material, so infections occur more often.

options.text: "A vaccine may not fully protect you."
options.rationale: Artificial active immunity depends on the body producing its own response. If B lymphocytes cannot become plasma cells, the patient may not make protective antibodies after a vaccine.

options.text: "Immune globulin can protect you for a short time."
options.rationale: Immune globulin is artificial passive immunity: antibodies come from another source, give immediate protection, and do not depend on the patient's plasma cells. The protection is temporary.

options.text: "You have no immune defenses at all."
options.rationale: Innate defenses such as skin and phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages do not depend on plasma cells, and T lymphocytes still work. Antibody protection is reduced, not all immune defense.

options.text: "Your T lymphocytes will make the antibodies instead."
options.rationale: T lymphocytes run cell mediated immunity: they target infected or abnormal cells and help coordinate the response. Antibodies come from plasma cells, which develop from B lymphocytes.

options.text: "Immune globulin will protect you for life."
options.rationale: Immune globulin is passive immunity: the antibodies come from another source and are used up over weeks, so the protection is temporary, not lifelong.

questions.takeaway: Humoral immunity runs from B lymphocytes to plasma cells to antibodies, and each antibody binds a specific antigen to neutralize or remove it. Without plasma cells the patient's own antibody response fails, but antibodies from another source can still give temporary protection.
questions.strategy: Trace the chain named in the stem: B lymphocytes, then plasma cells, then antibodies. Reject any option that hands the antibody job to another cell, claims every defense is gone, or makes passive protection permanent.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: B lymphocytes become plasma cells; plasma cells make antibodies that bind specific antigens.

steps.action: Apply the break in the chain
steps.detail: Few antibodies, more infections, and a vaccine may not produce protective antibodies.
Immune globulin brings antibodies from another source for a short time.
T lymphocytes do not make antibodies.
Innate and cell mediated defenses remain, and passive protection is not lifelong.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient whose knees are both swollen and painful. The patient reports no recent injury or illness. Cultures of fluid from both knees grew no microorganisms, and blood tests show antibodies that bind the patient's own joint tissue. The patient asks, "Why would my knees swell like this?" Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Your immune system is still reacting to an infection it cleared earlier."
options.rationale: Negative cultures with an active immune response make a leftover reaction sound right. But the patient reports no recent illness, and a leftover reaction would not explain antibodies that bind the patient's own joint tissue.

options.text: "Your knees are infected, and your immune cells are fighting it."
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection, and the cultures grew no microorganisms. Swelling alone does not establish infection.

options.text: "Your immune cells found foreign material in your knees."
options.rationale: Recognition of foreign material does start an immune response, so this sounds right. But the cultures grew nothing and there was no injury, and the antibodies bind the patient's own tissue, not a foreign target.

options.text: "Your immune cells are treating your own joint tissue as foreign."
options.rationale: The immune system normally distinguishes the body's cells from foreign substances, and self tolerance prevents attacks on healthy tissue. Antibodies that bind the patient's own joint tissue, with no injury, no recent illness, and no microorganism, mean the patient's own tissue is being treated as non self.

questions.takeaway: The immune system separates self from non self, and self tolerance keeps it from attacking healthy tissue. When antibodies bind the patient's own tissue and no injury, infection, or foreign material explains the response, self tolerance has failed and self is being treated as non self.
questions.strategy: A is the near miss: negative cultures plus an active immune response sound like a reaction left over from an infection. The deciding cues are no recent illness and antibodies that bind the patient's own joint tissue, which leave only the patient's own tissue as the target.

steps.detail: Antibodies bind the patient's own joint tissue.
Cultures grew no microorganisms, and there was no injury or recent illness.
Negative cultures rule out a current infection, and no recent illness removes a leftover reaction.
Nothing foreign was found; the target is self.

steps.action: Choose the failure of self tolerance
steps.detail: An attack on the patient's own tissue means self is treated as non self.

elimination.verdict: Self tolerance usually prevents attacks on healthy tissue; here the patient's tissue is being treated as non self.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who has an inherited condition that causes low complement levels. Antibody levels from childhood vaccines are in the expected range. Two hours ago the patient cut a palm on a metal edge, and bacteria of a type the patient has never been exposed to or vaccinated against entered the cut. Which statement by the nurse about the next few hours is accurate?

options.text: "Your vaccine antibodies will bind these bacteria, so removal will be at the usual pace."
options.rationale: Antibodies bind specific antigens. The patient was never exposed to or vaccinated against these bacteria, so the vaccine antibodies do not target them.

options.text: "Complement mainly supports memory, so only a later exposure to these bacteria is affected."
options.rationale: Memory cells belong to adaptive immunity. Complement is a group of proteins that strengthens defense and supports removal of invaders now, not memory for later.

options.text: "Complement helps the defense acting right now, so removal of these bacteria may be slower."
options.rationale: Innate immunity gives an immediate, broad defense without prior exposure, and complement is one of its proteins. With low complement, removal of the bacteria in the first hours is less efficient.

options.text: "Complement acts only after antibodies form, so removal will be at the usual pace for now."
options.rationale: This links complement to antibodies, which sounds plausible. But complement is part of the innate defense, and with no prior exposure the patient has no antibodies against these bacteria in the first hours; adaptive responses take time to develop.

questions.takeaway: Complement is a group of innate proteins that strengthens defense and supports removal of invaders. In the first hours after a new exposure, protection comes from innate immunity, so a low complement level slows removal of the bacteria right away.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: C and D both tie the effect to how complement works. The cue that decides is "never been exposed to or vaccinated against" within 2 hours: no specific antibodies exist yet, so the defense acting now is innate, and complement strengthens it.

steps.detail: Two hours after a first exposure, adaptive immunity has not developed yet.
Antibodies are specific, and none target these bacteria.
Complement works in the current response, not in immune memory.
Complement strengthens innate defense, which is the defense acting in the first hours.

elimination.verdict: Removal of the bacteria may be slower, because complement strengthens the innate defense acting now.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews immune events described in the records of five patients.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing immune events described in five patients' records. For each immune event, indicate whether it is part of antibody mediated (humoral) immunity or cell mediated immunity.

rows.text: Immune cells destroy liver cells in the patient's own body that a virus has infected
rows.rationale: Cell mediated immunity involves T lymphocytes and targets infected or abnormal cells. A virus is foreign, but the target here is the patient's own infected cells, which points to cell mediated immunity.

rows.text: Immunoglobulins bind a bacterial toxin circulating in the blood and neutralize it
rows.rationale: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) bind to specific antigens and neutralize or remove foreign material. Free toxin in the blood is a target for antibodies.

rows.text: Immune cells recognize abnormal cells in a growing tumor in the left lung and target them
rows.rationale: Cell mediated immunity targets abnormal cells. Tumor cells are the patient's own cells that have become abnormal.

rows.text: Activated B lymphocytes develop into plasma cells in a lymph node 5 days after a vaccine
rows.rationale: B lymphocytes differentiate into antibody producing plasma cells when activated by antigens. This is the humoral response.

rows.text: Antibodies received as immune globulin 1 day ago bind a virus in the blood before it enters body cells
rows.rationale: The antibodies came from another source, but they still act by binding a specific antigen and neutralizing it. The virus is free in the blood and has not entered cells, so antibodies, not T lymphocytes, act on it.

questions.takeaway: Humoral immunity uses B lymphocytes, plasma cells, and antibodies that bind antigens free in the body. Cell mediated immunity uses T lymphocytes that target the body's own cells once they are infected or abnormal. Ask where the target is: free in the blood or inside a body cell.
questions.strategy: Several rows involve a virus, which tempts one column for all of them. The cue in each row is where the target sits: a virus free in the blood is an antibody target, while a body cell the virus has infected is a cell mediated target.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
