steps.action: Find the target in each row
steps.detail: Free toxin or virus in the blood, or the patient's own infected or abnormal cells.
Antibodies bind specific antigens and neutralize them: rows 2 and 5.
T lymphocytes target infected or abnormal cells: rows 1 and 3.
B lymphocytes becoming plasma cells is the humoral response: row 4.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1 and 3 are cell mediated; rows 2, 4, and 5 are antibody mediated (humoral).

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A patient stopped an immunosuppressant that lowers T lymphocyte activity. Now the transplanted kidney is tender and urine output is falling. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: T lymphocytes are attacking the patient's own healthy tissue
options.rationale: Self tolerance protects the patient's own cells, which carry the patient's own HLA. The tenderness and falling urine output involve the donor kidney, whose cells are not self, so this is not an attack on the patient's own tissue.

options.text: T lymphocytes are targeting the donor kidney as non self
options.rationale: T lymphocytes support recognition of self and non self and target cells they identify as foreign. The donor kidney carries HLA that differ from the patient's, and the medication that held T lymphocyte activity down has been stopped. Tenderness over the graft and falling urine output fit an immune response against the donor kidney.

options.text: Neutrophils are engulfing the donor kidney's cells
options.rationale: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes, but phagocytosis still begins with recognizing harmful material. The medication the patient stopped acts on T lymphocytes, so its loss points to a T lymphocyte response, not a neutrophil one.

options.text: A new infection has reached the donor kidney
options.rationale: Stopping an immunosuppressant restores immune activity rather than lowering defenses. The timing after stopping the drug points to an immune response against the kidney, not a new infection.

questions.takeaway: T lymphocytes support recognition of self and non self. A transplanted organ carries the donor's HLA, so when a drug that holds T lymphocyte activity down is stopped, T lymphocytes recognize the organ as non self and target it.
questions.strategy: Link the stopped drug to the cell it controls, then ask what that cell recognizes. The drug acts on T lymphocytes, and the donor kidney is non self.

steps.action: Name the cell the drug controls
steps.detail: The medication lowers T lymphocyte activity, so stopping it frees T lymphocytes.
T lymphocytes support recognition of self and non self; donor kidney cells carry different HLA.

steps.action: Compare the self and non self options
steps.detail: Option A targets the patient's own tissue; the findings sit in the donor kidney, so option B fits.

elimination.verdict: B. T lymphocytes recognize the donor kidney as non self.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: A patient received a first dose of an inactivated virus vaccine today, and a household member has that illness. Which patient statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "The shot gave me antibodies, so I can help my family today."
options.rationale: Antibodies from another source describe passive immunity, such as immune globulin. A vaccine stimulates the patient's own response.

options.text: "The shot will give me a mild case of the illness."
options.rationale: An inactivated virus stimulates immunity without causing the disease.

options.text: "Protection takes time, so I will keep my distance for now."
options.rationale: Active immunity from a vaccine takes time to develop, so the patient is not yet protected. Keeping distance fits protection that is not yet in place, and an inactivated virus does not cause the illness.

options.text: "I will build protection without illness, so I can help today."
options.rationale: The body does build protection without the illness, but active immunity takes time, so the patient is not yet protected today.

questions.takeaway: A vaccine with an inactivated virus builds the patient's own immunity and memory without causing disease, but protection takes time to develop.
questions.strategy: C and D share the correct mechanism. The household exposure today is the cue that decides: active immunity is not ready yet.

steps.detail: A vaccine gives artificial active immunity: the patient's own response.
A describes passive immunity; B says the vaccine causes illness.
Active immunity takes time, so caring for the ill household member today is not yet safe.

elimination.verdict: C. The patient's own protection takes time, and the vaccine cannot cause the illness.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 2 week old infant brought to the clinic by the birth parent. An older sibling's school has a measles outbreak. The parent says, "I never had measles or the measles vaccine. My baby got my antibodies before birth, so my baby is covered for now, right?" Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Your baby can only receive antibodies you have, and you have none for measles."
options.rationale: Natural passive immunity is the transfer of maternal antibodies through the placenta or breast milk. A parent who never had measles and never got the vaccine has no measles antibodies to pass, so the infant has no borrowed protection and an immature immune system of its own.

options.text: "Your antibodies crossed before birth, so your baby is covered for a few months."
options.rationale: This is true for a disease the parent is immune to, since placental antibodies give immediate, temporary protection. The parent's own statement rules it out here: no illness and no vaccine means no measles antibodies to transfer.

options.text: "Your baby can get the measles vaccine today and will be protected within days."
options.rationale: The measles vaccine is not given to infants this young; it is first given at 12 months, or as early as 6 months during an outbreak or before international travel. An exposed infant this young is protected with immune globulin instead.

options.text: "Your breast milk will pass measles protection to your baby once feeding is set."
options.rationale: Breast milk does carry maternal antibodies, so this sounds right. But a parent with no measles antibodies has none to pass in the milk, and milk antibodies are temporary in any case.

questions.takeaway: Natural passive immunity comes from maternal antibodies through the placenta or breast milk, and it gives immediate but temporary protection. The infant can receive only the antibodies the parent has, so a parent with no immunity to a disease passes no protection against it.
questions.strategy: B and D are both true rules about natural passive immunity, one by the placenta and one by milk. The deciding cue is the parent's own history: no measles and no vaccine means there are no measles antibodies to pass by either route.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The parent never had measles and never got the vaccine, so the parent has no measles antibodies.
Placenta and milk can only pass antibodies the parent has.
The measles vaccine is not given to a 2 week old.

elimination.verdict: A. The parent has no measles antibodies to pass.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who received a kidney transplant 6 years ago and takes a daily medicine that lowers T lymphocyte activity. The patient says, "I have not had a single infection in 6 years, so I want to stop my yearly skin exam for new or changing growths." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Your medicine can hide the redness of a skin infection, so the exam still matters."
options.rationale: Lowered immune function can mute the signs of infection, so this is a reasonable concern. The exam the patient wants to stop looks for new or changing growths, which are abnormal cells, not infection.

options.text: "T lymphocytes remove abnormal cells, and your medicine lowers them. Keep the exam."
options.rationale: Cell mediated immunity targets infected or abnormal cells. With T lymphocyte activity lowered every day, abnormal cells in the skin may not be removed, so new or changing growths are watched for each year whether or not infections occur.

options.text: "Ask your provider whether you can stop, since you have had no infections in 6 years."
options.rationale: Deferring to the provider sounds respectful, but it accepts the patient's reasoning. Years without infection say nothing about abnormal skin cells, and the medicine still lowers T lymphocyte activity every day.

options.text: "Your medicine lowers antibody production by B lymphocytes, so the exam still matters."
options.rationale: This reaches the right plan for the wrong reason. The medicine acts on T lymphocytes, and targeting abnormal cells is cell mediated immunity, not antibodies from B lymphocytes.

questions.takeaway: Cell mediated immunity, carried out by T lymphocytes, targets infected or abnormal cells and supports recognition of self and non self. A medicine that lowers T lymphocyte activity raises the risk of infection and also of abnormal cells growing unchecked, so screening for new or changing skin growths continues.
questions.strategy: A, B, and D all keep the exam, and C sounds respectful. The deciding cue is what the exam looks for, new or changing growths, which are abnormal cells; then match that job to the cell the medicine lowers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The yearly exam looks for new or changing growths, which are abnormal cells.
T lymphocytes target infected or abnormal cells; the medicine lowers them.
A is a true concern, but it does not explain an exam for growths.
D blames B lymphocytes, which the medicine does not target.
C accepts that infection free years make the exam unneeded.

elimination.verdict: B. T lymphocytes target abnormal cells, and the medicine lowers them.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient who will receive a kidney from a sibling who is a close tissue match. Which statement by the patient indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "A close match means my body will see the kidney as self."
options.rationale: This is the near miss: a close match does lower the risk of rejection. But human leukocyte antigens (HLA) are identical only in an identical twin, so even a close sibling match leaves some markers that differ, and the kidney is not seen as self.

options.text: "Even a close match leaves markers my immune cells may attack."
options.rationale: HLA on the body's cells let the immune system tell self from non self. A close match is not an identical one, so some markers on the donor kidney differ from the patient's own and can be recognized as foreign, even with a close family match.

options.text: "Only my white blood cells carry these markers, so the kidney cannot be seen as foreign."
options.rationale: HLA are found on most body cells, not only on white blood cells. The kidney's own cells carry the sibling's markers, which is why the kidney can be recognized as foreign.

options.text: "I will need antirejection medicine only if the match is poor."
options.rationale: A close match lowers the risk, which makes this sound reasonable. But any donor other than an identical twin has markers that differ from the patient's, so antirejection medicine is needed even with a close match.

questions.takeaway: Human leukocyte antigens mark a person's own cells and are identical only in an identical twin. A close family match lowers the risk, but some markers still differ, the immune system can recognize those as non self, and antirejection medicine is still needed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and D both sound right because a close match does lower the risk. The deciding cue is the word close: close is not identical, so some markers differ and the kidney is never seen as self.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The donor is a close match, which is not the same as an identical match.
A treats a close match as self, and D treats it as safe without medicine; neither holds for a donor who is not an identical twin.
Option C is wrong because HLA sit on most body cells, including the kidney's.

elimination.verdict: B. A close match still leaves markers that can be recognized as non self.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who struck an elbow on a door frame 3 days ago. The skin is intact. The nurse compares findings today with findings yesterday. Which finding today requires follow up?

options.text: Cannot fully straighten the elbow, could yesterday
options.rationale: Decreased function is one of the five cardinal signs, and it is the only sign here that is worse than yesterday. A new loss of movement while the other signs settle is a change from baseline that is documented and reported.

options.text: Swelling extends down onto the forearm, as yesterday
options.rationale: Swelling that reaches the forearm sounds like the worst finding here, and it is the largest. But it is the same as yesterday; swelling after a blow often spreads downward with gravity and then holds, so it is not the sign that is worsening.

options.text: Redness 2 cm across, was 4 cm across yesterday
options.rationale: Redness is still present, which can make this look like a concern, but the area has shrunk by half. A shrinking area points toward healing.

options.text: Pain 2 of 10 at rest, was 4 of 10 yesterday
options.rationale: Pain is still present but has fallen since yesterday, so it is not the finding that is worsening.

questions.takeaway: Assess all five cardinal signs, warmth, redness, swelling, pain, and decreased function, and compare each with the patient's baseline. Decreased function is the sign most often skipped, and a new loss of function is worsening even when the other signs improve.
questions.strategy: B pulls hardest because swelling onto the forearm sounds alarming. Weigh each finding against yesterday, not against how bad it looks: the swelling matches yesterday, while the loss of the ability to straighten the elbow is new.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Swelling is large but unchanged, redness and pain are lower, and movement is newly limited.
The swelling looks worst but matches yesterday; shrinking and stable signs fit an injury that is settling.
Loss of the ability to straighten the elbow is new since yesterday.

elimination.verdict: A. Decreased function is new and worse than yesterday.

questions.objective: Identify the five cardinal signs of inflammation

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient with an inherited condition in which B lymphocytes cannot develop into plasma cells. The patient receives an infusion of immune globulin every 4 weeks. Which statements by the patient indicate understanding of the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Each infusion will train my B cells to start making their own antibodies."
options.rationale: Immune globulin supplies antibodies from another source. It does not change the patient's B lymphocytes, which still cannot become antibody producing plasma cells.

options.text: "The antibodies in each infusion start protecting me as soon as I get them."
options.rationale: Passive immunity provides immediate protection because the antibodies are given ready made.

options.text: "The protection from each infusion fades, so I keep every scheduled infusion."
options.rationale: Passive protection is temporary. Because the patient cannot make antibodies, the supply has to be replaced on schedule.

options.text: "After a year of infusions, my body will remember these germs and I can stop."
options.rationale: Passive immunity does not create personal immune memory, no matter how many infusions are given.

options.text: "I should still report a fever or a new cough, even between infusions."
options.rationale: The infusions lower the risk but do not restore the patient's own antibody response, so signs of infection are still reported early.

options.text: "Because these antibodies came from donors, a vaccine will now work better in me."
options.rationale: A vaccine works by having the patient's own B lymphocytes make antibodies. Donor antibodies do not fix the patient's inability to form plasma cells.

questions.takeaway: Immune globulin gives passive immunity: immediate, temporary protection with no personal memory. A patient who cannot make antibodies needs it replaced on schedule and still needs to report signs of infection.
questions.strategy: Test each statement against the three features of passive immunity: immediate, temporary, and no memory. Any statement that promises the patient's own cells will learn or remember is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Statements B and C match immediate and temporary protection.
Statements A, D, and F assume the patient's own B lymphocytes will respond.
Statement E reflects that protection is partial, so infection signs are still reported.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Distinguish active from passive immunity using examples

questions.scenario: A patient was bitten on the hand by a dog 2 weeks ago. The bite became infected and was treated, and the hand has now healed. The nurse reviews the immune events described in the patient's record.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the record of a patient treated for an infected dog bite on the hand. For each immune event, indicate whether it is part of innate immunity or adaptive immunity.

rows.text: Within minutes of the bite, mast cells released histamine and the hand swelled
rows.rationale: Mast cells and basophils release histamine, which promotes inflammation. Inflammation is part of innate immunity, which acts right away without prior exposure.

rows.text: Complement proteins were activated and helped remove the bacteria from the wound
rows.rationale: Complement is a group of proteins that strengthens immune defense and supports the removal of invaders. It acts in the early, broad defense, not as a response built for one antigen.

rows.text: B lymphocytes became plasma cells that made antibodies to the bacteria in the bite
rows.rationale: B lymphocytes differentiate into antibody producing plasma cells when an antigen activates them. The antibodies bind that specific antigen, which is the antibody mediated part of adaptive immunity.

rows.text: Macrophages cleared dead cells and debris from the wound
rows.rationale: Macrophages remove microbes, debris, and dead cells by phagocytosis. Phagocytosis is part of innate immunity, even though it happened days into the infection.

rows.text: Memory cells formed that will respond faster to these bacteria in the future
rows.rationale: Adaptive immunity creates memory cells that allow a faster, stronger response on a later exposure to the same antigen. Innate immunity builds no memory.

questions.takeaway: Innate immunity is present at birth, acts fast, is broad, and builds no memory: inflammation, histamine, complement, and phagocytosis. Adaptive immunity develops after exposure, targets one antigen, and creates memory: B lymphocytes, plasma cells, antibodies, and memory cells.
questions.strategy: Timing is the trap. The macrophage row happened days into the infection, which tempts an adaptive answer. Decide each row by what the response is, broad and without memory or specific with memory, not by when it happened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what kind of response it is
steps.detail: Broad with no memory is innate; specific to one antigen with memory is adaptive.
Histamine from mast cells, complement, and macrophage phagocytosis are innate: rows 1, 2, and 4.
Plasma cells making antibodies to these bacteria and memory cells are adaptive: rows 3 and 5.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 2, and 4 innate; rows 3 and 5 adaptive.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.scenario: A patient was stung by a bee on the forearm while gardening 30 minutes ago. The stinger has been removed. The area is red, warm, and swollen 5 cm across, and the patient reports itching and pain of 3 of 10. The patient has no hives elsewhere, no throat tightness, no hoarseness, and no wheezing. Respiratory rate 16/min, heart rate 84/min, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg, SpO2 98% on room air. The patient has been stung before with no reaction beyond the site.
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient 30 minutes after a bee sting on the forearm. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Apply a cold pack to the sting site
options.rationale: Cold narrows the dilated vessels at the site, which limits the fluid shift that causes swelling, and it eases pain and itching.

options.text: Mark the edge of the swelling and note the time
options.rationale: A measured, timed baseline lets the nurse compare the site later and tell whether the swelling is spreading.

options.text: Give epinephrine from the emergency kit
options.rationale: Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis. This patient has no hives elsewhere, no airway or breathing signs, and normal vital signs, so the reaction is local.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to draw out the venom
options.rationale: Heat dilates vessels further and increases the fluid moving into the tissue, so the swelling and itching worsen.

options.text: Report the site to the provider as infected
options.rationale: Redness, warmth, and swelling 30 minutes after a sting are inflammation from the sting itself. Inflammation can occur without infection, and there is no drainage or spreading redness.

options.text: Local inflammation from histamine released at the sting
options.rationale: Mast cells and basophils release histamine, which dilates vessels and lets fluid move into the tissue. The result is redness, warmth, swelling, itching, and pain limited to the site, with no systemic signs.

options.text: Anaphylaxis
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis involves the whole body: hives beyond the site, throat tightness, wheezing, or a falling blood pressure. None of these is present.

options.text: Infection at the sting site
options.rationale: Thirty minutes is too soon for an infection to develop, and there is no drainage or spreading redness.

options.text: Tissue repair after the sting
options.rationale: Tissue repair is the last stage of inflammation, after white blood cells have cleared the area. Thirty minutes after the sting, the vascular response is under way.

options.text: Breathing, voice, and swelling of the lips or throat
options.rationale: The patient has been stung before, and a reaction can spread beyond the site. New hoarseness, throat tightness, or wheezing would signal a systemic reaction that needs emergency care.

options.text: Size of the swelling compared with the marked edge
options.rationale: Comparing the swelling with the marked baseline shows whether the local reaction is growing or settling.

options.text: Oral temperature every hour to detect infection
options.rationale: Infection is not the concern 30 minutes after a sting, and hourly temperatures do not track the risk that matters here.

options.text: White blood cell count over the next week
options.rationale: A laboratory trend over a week does not help a patient whose risk is a reaction in the next minutes to hours.

questions.takeaway: A bee sting triggers mast cells and basophils to release histamine, starting the vascular response: dilated vessels, fluid moving into the tissue, and local redness, warmth, and swelling. Treat the site with cold, mark a baseline, and watch the airway for signs that the reaction is spreading.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Separate the site from the whole body. Every finding is limited to the forearm and the vital signs are normal, so the reaction is local; the past stings are why the airway still gets watched.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness, warmth, swelling, itching, and pain at the sting fit histamine driven inflammation.
No hives elsewhere, no airway signs, and normal vital signs rule out anaphylaxis for now.
Cold and a marked baseline now; watch breathing and voice and compare the swelling with the mark.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B; condition A; parameters A and B.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient at a clinic visit in the fall. Testing confirmed influenza in the patient last winter, and the patient recovered fully. The patient says, "I already made my own antibodies to the flu last year, so I can skip this year's flu vaccine." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Your antibodies fit last year's virus, and this year's virus may differ."
options.rationale: Adaptive immunity targets specific antigens, and antibodies bind the specific antigen that produced them. Influenza viruses change from season to season, so antibodies made against last winter's virus may not bind this year's virus. This answers the belief behind the request.

options.text: "Your protection from last year has faded, so this vaccine will renew it."
options.rationale: This sounds like booster logic, but immunity after a natural infection is long lasting against that same virus. The reason for a yearly vaccine here is that the virus itself may be different, not that the patient's protection has faded.

options.text: "Your memory cells will respond faster, so the vaccine is only a backup."
options.rationale: Memory cells do allow a faster response, but only to the same antigen. Calling the vaccine a backup supports skipping it, even though this year's virus may not match the patient's memory.

options.text: "The vaccine works faster than the antibodies you already made last year."
options.rationale: A vaccine produces active immunity, which takes time to develop. Existing memory responds faster than a new vaccine response, so this statement is false and does not address the real reason.

questions.takeaway: Adaptive immunity is specific: antibodies and memory cells respond to the antigen that produced them. A past influenza infection gives lasting protection against that virus, but a new season's virus may differ, which is why the vaccine is given every year.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Weigh the two stated cues together: the infection was last winter, and the request is about this year's vaccine. Ask which option explains the specificity of the patient's antibodies, not just whether immunity lasts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient made antibodies to last winter's virus, and the question is this year's vaccine.
Option B is wrong because natural active immunity lasts against the same virus.

steps.action: Reject the memory and speed claims
steps.detail: Memory helps only against the same antigen, and a new vaccine response takes time.

elimination.verdict: A. Antibodies are specific, and this year's virus may differ.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the laboratory results of a patient with seasonal allergies who has had sneezing, itchy watery eyes, and mild wheezing for 1 week, since the trees began to bloom. The patient has not traveled. White blood cell count 7,800/mm3, neutrophils 58%, eosinophils 11%. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: An allergic response to the tree pollen
options.rationale: Eosinophils mediate allergic responses. A high eosinophil percentage with a normal white blood cell count and normal neutrophils, in a patient whose symptoms began with the pollen season, fits an allergic response.

options.text: A bacterial infection of the airways
options.rationale: Neutrophils are the first responders to bacteria, so a bacterial infection would usually raise the white blood cell count and the neutrophil percentage. Both are in the expected range (neutrophils about 55% to 70%).

options.text: A parasitic infection needing stool tests
options.rationale: Eosinophils also defend against parasites, which makes this tempting. The patient has not traveled and the symptoms match the pollen season, so allergy explains the finding without a parasite.

options.text: A viral infection of the upper airways
options.rationale: Sneezing can come with a cold, but a viral infection does not explain a high eosinophil percentage, and the timing with the blooming trees points to allergy.

questions.takeaway: Read a white blood cell differential by matching the cell to its job: neutrophils rise with bacterial infection, eosinophils rise with allergic responses and parasites. Use the history to choose between two causes of the same cell change.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Two options explain a high eosinophil count: allergy and parasites. The history decides it: symptoms that began with the pollen season and no travel or exposure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Total count and neutrophils are in range; eosinophils are high (about 1% to 4% expected).
Eosinophils mediate allergy and fight parasites.
Pollen season onset and no travel point to allergy.
Neither explains the eosinophils, and neutrophils are not raised.

elimination.verdict: A. High eosinophils with a seasonal history mean an allergic response.

questions.objective: Compare innate and adaptive immunity

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who sprained an ankle 1 hour ago. The ankle is red, warm, and swollen, the patient rates the pain 7 of 10, and the patient reports new tingling in the toes of that foot. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply an ice pack wrapped in a towel
options.rationale: Cold limits the vascular response and eases pain, so it belongs in the plan. It does not come first when tingling suggests the swelling may be pressing on nerves or vessels.

options.text: Elevate the ankle above the level of the heart
options.rationale: Elevation helps fluid leave the tissue and is a correct intervention, but it treats the swelling before the nurse knows whether circulation to the toes is affected.

options.text: Check toe color, warmth, and capillary refill
options.rationale: Tingling in the toes is a new finding that can mean swelling is compressing nerves and vessels. Assessing circulation and sensation below the injury, and comparing with the other foot, comes before any intervention.

options.text: Wrap the ankle with an elastic bandage
options.rationale: Compression can limit swelling, but wrapping a swollen ankle when the toes already tingle could further reduce blood flow. It is unsafe until circulation has been assessed.

questions.takeaway: After an injury, the vascular response moves fluid into the tissue and causes swelling. When swelling comes with tingling, numbness, or color change below the injury, assess circulation and sensation first, then treat with cold and elevation.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options are correct treatments for a sprain, which makes them all look right. The deciding cue is the new tingling: assess before you intervene when a finding could signal compromised circulation.

steps.detail: New tingling in the toes after swelling.
Swelling may be compressing nerves or vessels.
Check color, warmth, and capillary refill before ice, elevation, or a wrap.
Compression could worsen blood flow.

elimination.verdict: C. Assess circulation below the injury first.

questions.objective: Describe the three stages of the inflammatory response

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for Patients With Infection

questions.stem: An older patient with a leg wound takes an immunosuppressant and has eaten poorly for 3 weeks. Which conclusion should guide the nurse's plan of care?

options.text: All three raise risk, so report the wound as infected
options.rationale: The history does raise concern, but risk factors alone do not establish infection.

options.text: Only age and the medicine raise risk
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function as well as healing. All three factors count.

options.text: All three raise risk, so watch closely once fever starts
options.rationale: The concern is right, but the trigger is wrong. The plan follows from the history now, without waiting for a fever.

options.text: All three raise risk, so watch closely starting now
options.rationale: Older age, an immunosuppressant, and poor nutrition each affect immunity. Reviewing the history identifies them so closer assessment can start now.

questions.takeaway: Age, nutritional status, disease, medications, and environmental exposures affect immunity. The history tells you whose protection is weak, and the plan starts from there.
questions.strategy: Three options accept that all three factors matter. They differ in what the nurse does next: label the wound, wait for a fever, or assess more closely now.

steps.detail: Older age, daily immunosuppressant, poor intake for 3 weeks.

steps.action: Drop the option that discounts one
steps.detail: Nutrition affects immune protection too.
Labeling infection overreaches, and waiting for fever delays.

elimination.verdict: All three raise concern, so closer assessment against baseline starts on admission.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the history of a patient with a wound. Which findings increase the patient's risk of infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Takes a daily immunosuppressant after a transplant
options.rationale: Immunosuppressants lower immune function, which raises infection risk and can mask its signs.

options.text: Has lost weight while eating half of each meal
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function and wound healing.

options.text: Has had diabetes mellitus for 12 years
options.rationale: Chronic disease such as diabetes mellitus lowers immune competence.

options.text: Received an influenza vaccine last month
options.rationale: A vaccine builds protection. It does not raise the risk of infection.

options.text: Has cared for a family member with influenza
options.rationale: Exposure to an ill contact raises the chance of infection.

options.text: Rates the wound pain 4 of 10
options.rationale: Pain is a finding at the wound, not a factor that raises infection risk.

questions.takeaway: Age, nutrition, chronic disease, medications, and exposure to ill contacts raise infection risk. Pick them out of the patient's own history to plan closer assessment.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into a factor that raises infection risk or a finding about the wound or a protective step.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age, nutrition, chronic disease, medications, and exposure to ill contacts.
Immunosuppressant, weight loss with poor intake, diabetes, and a sick contact each fit.
A vaccine builds protection; a pain rating is a wound finding.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E. Each is a history factor that raises infection risk.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario: An 82 year old patient was admitted 2 days ago after a fall and has a scrape on the left lower leg from the fall. The patient takes a daily immunosuppressant and has eaten about one quarter of each meal since admission. On admission and again today the redness extends 1 cm around the scrape, the area is warm with mild swelling, pain is 2 of 10, and the patient walks to the bathroom without help. Oral temperature today is 36.6 °C. The patient says, "I have no fever, so there is no infection in my leg."
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an older adult patient with a scrape from a fall. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Report the scrape to the provider today as infected because of the immunosuppressant
options.rationale: Immunosuppressants can affect immune function, but the scrape findings are unchanged from admission. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

options.text: Compare the scrape findings with the admission baseline at each assessment
options.rationale: Findings are compared with the patient's baseline and changes are documented over time.

options.text: Arrange a review of the patient's intake of protein, vitamins, and minerals
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function; adequate protein, vitamins, and minerals support immune responses and wound healing. The patient eats one quarter of each meal.

options.text: Use the oral temperature as the trigger for closer checks of the scrape
options.rationale: This patient's medication and age reduce immune protection, so the nurse watches the scrape findings and their trend, not the temperature alone.

options.text: Inflammation in a patient with reduced immune protection
options.rationale: The scrape shows cardinal signs that match admission. Older age, an immunosuppressant, and poor intake all reduce immune protection, so close assessment is needed.

options.text: Infection masked by the immunosuppressant
options.rationale: The medication raises concern, but every scrape finding is the same as on admission. Nothing is worsening that would point to infection.

options.text: Expected healing with no added risk
options.rationale: Age, the immunosuppressant, and poor intake are all factors that affect immunity, so the risk is not ordinary.

options.text: Failure of the tissue repair stage
options.rationale: The findings are unchanged after 2 days, which does not by itself show failed repair.

options.text: Size of the redness and swelling around the scrape, compared with admission
options.rationale: A change in size from baseline is a key sign of worsening.

options.text: Size of the redness alone, measured once a day
options.rationale: Redness alone leaves out swelling, pain, and function, and once a day may miss change.

options.text: Oral temperature as the main sign of infection
options.rationale: Temperature is one finding. With reduced immune protection, the scrape findings and function are trended alongside it.

options.text: Pain rating and ability to walk on the left leg
options.rationale: Pain and decreased function are cardinal signs to trend over time.

questions.takeaway: Age, immunosuppressants, and poor nutrition reduce immune protection. The nurse responds by comparing every cardinal sign with baseline over time and supporting nutrition, not by labeling unchanged findings as infection or waiting for a fever.
questions.strategy: The condition pool has a tempting choice: infection masked by the immunosuppressant. The cue that decides is that every scrape finding is the same as on admission; risk calls for closer comparison, not a diagnosis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 82, daily immunosuppressant, one quarter of meals.
Redness, warmth, swelling, pain, and walking are unchanged.
Inflammation in a patient with reduced immune protection.
Compare with baseline, review nutrition, trend size, pain, and function.

elimination.verdict: Actions: compare with the admission baseline and review nutrition. Condition: inflammation with reduced immune protection. Parameters: redness and swelling size against admission, and pain with walking.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient, 81 years old, who takes a daily immunosuppressant and was admitted 3 days ago with a wound on the lower leg. On admission the patient was alert and talkative and ate about one quarter of each meal. Today the redness is 1 cm around the wound and pain is 2 of 10, both unchanged, and oral temperature is 36.5 °C. The patient has slept through two meals, is slow to answer questions, and ate a few bites at breakfast. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the change in alertness and intake to the provider now
options.rationale: The patient has changed from baseline in behavior and function. In a patient with reduced immune protection, the nurse does not rely on the wound or on fever alone, and worsening is reported.

options.text: Wake the patient for lunch and report if alertness is no better by afternoon
options.rationale: Supporting intake is reasonable care, but it delays the report of a change from baseline in a patient with reduced immune protection.

options.text: Report to the provider that the wound has become infected
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but the wound findings have not changed. The report should state what changed, not name a cause.

options.text: Document the change and report it if the temperature rises
options.rationale: This patient takes an immunosuppressant and is 81 years old. The nurse does not wait for a fever before acting on a change in behavior.

questions.takeaway: Compare the whole patient with baseline, not only the wound. A change in behavior or function is reported, and fever is not required, especially when immune protection is reduced.
questions.strategy: The wound and the temperature both say nothing has changed, which makes waiting look reasonable. The deciding cue is the patient: alert and talkative on admission, now slow to answer and sleeping through meals.

steps.detail: Unchanged.
Alertness and intake are both worse than on admission.
Age 81 and an immunosuppressant: do not wait for fever.

steps.action: Choose the report that states findings
steps.detail: One report names infection, which the wound does not support.

elimination.verdict: Report the change in alertness and intake now.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who is alert and oriented. During the 0800 assessment the nurse finds a warm, red, swollen area 4 cm across on the patient's lower leg. The admission assessment at 2000 yesterday describes both legs with no redness or swelling, and the patient has not mentioned the area. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask about onset and recent injury, then assess pain and function
options.rationale: Assessment comes first: ask about symptom onset and recent injury, then assess warmth, color, swelling, pain, and functional ability. The patient is alert and oriented and can give this history now.

options.text: Report the new redness and swelling to the provider now
options.rationale: The area is new, which makes reporting tempting, but the report would have no onset, injury history, or full assessment. The nurse gathers these first.

options.text: Mark and measure the area and recheck it at the next assessment
options.rationale: Measuring helps, but this skips the history and the full assessment of pain and function, and treats a new finding as routine.

options.text: Report the area to the provider as an infection that began after admission
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and the history should come before any report.

questions.takeaway: A new finding is assessed before it is reported: ask about onset and recent injury, then assess the cardinal signs and function, then decide.
questions.strategy: A and B both respond to a new finding, and B feels urgent because the area was not there 12 hours ago. The cue that decides is "alert and oriented": the patient can give the onset and injury history right now, so assessment comes first.

steps.detail: Both legs had no redness or swelling at 2000.
The patient is alert and oriented.
Onset, recent injury, then warmth, pain, and use of the leg.
Reporting without data or calling it infection skips assessment.

elimination.verdict: Ask about onset and recent injury, then assess warmth, pain, and use of the leg.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who bumped the lower leg on a bed frame 2 days ago. The skin is intact. Yesterday and today the red area is 3 cm across, warm, and swollen, and pain is 5 of 10. A family member says, "It is still red and swollen after 2 days, so it must be infected." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Redness lasting 2 days can mean infection, so I will report it to the provider now."
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. The area has not changed since yesterday, so there is no worsening to report.

options.text: "The bump can cause these signs. I will keep comparing them and report any worsening."
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection after an injury. The findings match yesterday's baseline, so the nurse keeps comparing over time and reports worsening symptoms.

options.text: "The bump caused these signs, so the leg needs no more checks unless a fever develops."
options.rationale: Fever is not the trigger the nurse waits for. Findings are compared with baseline and changes are documented over time.

options.text: "The bump can cause these signs, but I will report them now since both are present."
options.rationale: This option names the injury as a cause but then treats redness and swelling as enough to report. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and nothing has changed.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation after an injury can last for days without infection. When the findings match the earlier baseline, the nurse keeps comparing and reports worsening, rather than acting on redness and swelling alone.
questions.strategy: A and D both feel cautious, and caution pulls students toward reporting; C sounds reassuring. The cue that decides is that every finding today matches yesterday: 3 cm, warm, swollen, 5 of 10, intact skin.

steps.detail: A bump on a bed frame with intact skin.
Size, warmth, swelling, and pain are unchanged.
Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.
The nurse compares over time, not only when a fever appears.

elimination.verdict: These signs can come from the bump; keep comparing and report any worsening.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.nursesNote:
Yesterday 0800, day 3 after a bump to the left lower leg: red area 2 cm across, warmth limited to the red area, pain 3 of 10 at rest and 3 of 10 when standing, walks to bathroom without help, skin intact, oral temperature 36.6 °C.

Today 0800: Red area on left lower leg is 2 cm across. Warmth extends from the red area to the left ankle. Pain is 3 of 10 at rest and 6 of 10 when standing. Walks to bathroom without help. Skin over the area is intact. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing two days of notes for a patient who bumped the lower leg. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Red area on left lower leg is 2 cm across
segments.rationale: The red area is the same size as yesterday.

segments.text: Warmth extends from the red area to the left ankle
segments.rationale: Yesterday the warmth was limited to the red area. Warmth spreading to the ankle is a worsening cardinal sign, even though the redness has not grown.

segments.text: Pain is 3 of 10 at rest and 6 of 10 when standing
segments.rationale: Pain at rest is unchanged, but pain when standing rose from 3 to 6 of 10. A rise in pain is a worsening symptom to report.

segments.text: Walks to bathroom without help
segments.rationale: Function is the same as yesterday.

segments.text: Skin over the area is intact
segments.rationale: The skin is intact, as yesterday.

segments.text: Oral temperature is 36.8 °C
segments.rationale: A difference of 0.2 °C from yesterday is not a meaningful change.

questions.takeaway: Compare each cardinal sign with yesterday, one by one. A sign can worsen while another stays the same, as when warmth spreads while the red area keeps its size.
questions.strategy: The traps hide inside unchanged findings. The red area is the same, so warmth looks the same too, but it now reaches the ankle. Pain at rest is the same, but pain when standing doubled.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 cm both days.
Limited to the red area yesterday; reaches the ankle today.
At rest 3 of 10 both days; standing 3 then 6 of 10.
Unchanged or a 0.2 °C difference.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who bumped the lower leg 5 days ago; the skin is intact. Yesterday at 0800 the red area was 2 cm across, pain was 5 of 10, and the patient walked to the bathroom with one person helping. Today at 0800 the red area is still 2 cm across, pain is 7 of 10, and the patient cannot stand on that leg. The patient slept in a chair with the leg bent and says, "I just slept on it wrong. Please do not bother anyone about it." Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document today's findings and recheck the leg in 4 hours, as the patient asks
options.rationale: Listening to the patient matters, but pain and function are clearly worse than baseline. A request not to bother anyone does not remove the duty to report worsening.

options.text: Give the ordered pain medication and report if the patient cannot stand in 1 hour
options.rationale: Treating the pain is reasonable care, but it delays the report of two findings that are already clearly worse than baseline.

options.text: Report the rise in pain and the loss of standing to the provider now
options.rationale: Pain has risen from 5 to 7 of 10 and the patient can no longer stand on that leg. Worsening is reported whatever the suspected cause, and the nurse explains to the patient why.

options.text: Help the patient try to stand again, and report if the patient still cannot
options.rationale: The assessment already shows the change. Repeating it delays the report and adds nothing.

questions.takeaway: Changes from baseline that show worsening are reported. A patient's explanation is heard and documented, and the report is still made.
questions.strategy: Three things pull toward waiting: the redness has not changed, the patient offers another cause, and the patient has asked the nurse not to report. The deciding cue is that pain and function are both worse than yesterday, and the nurse reports findings without having to settle the cause.

steps.detail: Redness same. Pain 5 to 7 of 10. Walking with help to unable to stand.
It is heard, but it does not change the findings.
Pain relief does not replace reporting a loss of function.

steps.action: Do not repeat what is known
steps.detail: Standing again only delays the report.

elimination.verdict: Report the rise in pain and the loss of standing now, and explain why.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A new nurse is caring for a patient with a red, swollen heel wound and poor intake. Which statement by the new nurse requires correction?

options.text: "I will compare today's findings with the earlier notes."
options.rationale: This is correct. Findings are compared with the patient's baseline.

options.text: "Infection can be present without a fever."
options.rationale: This is correct. The nurse does not rely on fever alone; findings at the site and changes from baseline are assessed as well.

options.text: "The redness is unchanged, so the wound is unchanged."
options.rationale: Redness is one finding. Swelling, pain, and functional ability are assessed and compared with baseline before the nurse can say nothing has changed.

options.text: "Poor protein intake can slow this wound's healing."
options.rationale: This is correct. Adequate protein, vitamins, and minerals support immune responses and wound healing.

questions.takeaway: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and one unchanged finding does not establish that nothing changed. The nurse assesses every sign, including pain and function, compares with baseline, and does not rely on temperature alone.
questions.strategy: The question asks for the wrong statement. The fever statement is true; the one that sounds careful judges the whole wound by a single finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the statement that is not accurate.
Infection can be present without a fever, so B is accurate.
C judges the whole wound by redness alone and skips swelling, pain, and function.
Comparing with earlier notes and linking nutrition to healing are accurate.

elimination.verdict: C. One unchanged finding does not show that the wound has not changed.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: Since yesterday, a patient's heel wound has developed spreading redness, more pain, and new thick yellow drainage. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document the findings as expected inflammation
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, but the drainage is new and the redness and pain are worse. This is more than inflammation.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider now
options.rationale: Spreading redness, rising pain, and new thick yellow drainage are worsening findings. Pus is a sign of local infection, and these findings are reported as suggesting infection.

options.text: Clean the wound and recheck it this evening
options.rationale: Wound care is appropriate, but waiting until evening delays the report of findings that are already worse.

options.text: Report the findings if a fever develops
options.rationale: The nurse does not wait for a fever. The local findings have already changed.

questions.takeaway: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Spreading redness, rising pain, and new pus are more than that: they are worsening findings that suggest infection and are reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Option A rests on a true rule, that redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and it is the trap. Ask what the stem adds beyond redness and swelling, and whether the wound matches yesterday.

steps.detail: Redness spreading, pain rising, drainage new.

steps.action: Test the rule against the stem
steps.detail: "Alone" no longer applies. Drainage is new.
Waiting until evening, or waiting for a fever.
It states the findings and what they suggest.

elimination.verdict: Report the worsening findings as findings that suggest infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with two injuries from a fall 1 day ago. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient fell on the sidewalk 1 day ago. The skin over the right wrist is intact. The right wrist is warm, red, and swollen; pain is 5 of 10, was 6 of 10 yesterday, and the swelling is the same size as yesterday. A scrape on the left palm from the same fall now has redness 3 cm around it, was 1 cm yesterday, and pain at the palm is 4 of 10, was 2 of 10 yesterday. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C.

The findings at the right wrist are best explained by [[1]].

The finding that most requires follow up is [[2]].

The nurse does not document the right wrist as infected because [[3]].

options.text: inflammation caused by microorganisms that entered through the skin
options.rationale: Inflammation is the right idea, but the skin over the right wrist is intact, so nothing shows microorganisms entering there.

options.text: inflammation without infection, a protective response to the injury
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur after injury without infection. The skin over the wrist is intact, and the pain is less than yesterday.

options.text: infection, because warmth, redness, and swelling are all present
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Inflammation can occur without infection.

options.text: an adaptive immune response directed at a specific antigen
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity, a rapid, broad response to the injury.

options.text: the oral temperature of 36.8 °C
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem shows a change in temperature. The palm findings are the ones that changed.

options.text: the pain of 5 of 10 at the right wrist
options.rationale: Pain at the wrist is lower than yesterday's 6 of 10, so it is not worsening.

options.text: the warmth and swelling at the right wrist
options.rationale: Warmth and swelling are cardinal signs of inflammation, and the swelling is the same size as yesterday.

options.text: the redness and pain at the left palm scrape
options.rationale: The palm redness spread from 1 cm to 3 cm and the pain rose from 2 to 4 of 10 since yesterday. Worsening findings over time are documented and reported, and this site has broken skin.

options.text: redness and swelling alone do not establish infection
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection, so redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. The wrist findings are also not worsening.

options.text: the pain at the right wrist is below 6 of 10
options.rationale: No single pain number rules out infection. What matters is the trend compared with baseline.

options.text: the injury happened only 1 day ago
options.rationale: Time since injury does not rule out infection. The palm scrape from the same fall is worsening within the same day.

options.text: the oral temperature is 36.8 °C
options.rationale: A temperature without fever does not rule out infection, and the nurse does not use it as the reason. Infection is judged on the findings and their change over time.

questions.takeaway: Injury can cause inflammation without infection, and redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. The finding that needs follow up is the one getting worse over time, here the scrape with spreading redness and rising pain.
questions.strategy: Blank 3 holds the trap: a temperature without fever feels like a reason, but it does not rule out infection. Blank 2 needs a comparison with yesterday at both sites, not a judgment from today's numbers alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wrist pain lower and swelling the same; palm redness and pain rising.
Inflammation without infection, skin intact.
The palm scrape.
Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

elimination.verdict: Inflammation without infection; the redness and pain at the left palm scrape; redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse educator is reviewing findings for six patients with a new nurse. None of the patients has a fever. Which findings suggest infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: A warm, swollen bruise on the thigh 2 days after a fall, the same size as yesterday, skin intact
options.rationale: Warmth and swelling after a fall with intact skin and no change fit inflammation without infection.

options.text: Redness around a stitched cut on the forearm that has spread past the line marked yesterday
options.rationale: Redness that extends beyond the marked edge is spreading. Extended redness around a wound points to infection.

options.text: Redness around a stitched cut on the shin that reaches the line marked yesterday, pain 2 of 10 as yesterday
options.rationale: Reaching the line is not passing it. The redness and pain are unchanged, so this fits inflammation.

options.text: A cut on an index finger that is red and swollen and now drains thick yellow fluid
options.rationale: Thick yellow drainage is pus, a sign of local infection, along with redness and swelling.

options.text: A blister on the heel from new shoes, filled with clear fluid, the covering skin unbroken
options.rationale: Clear fluid under intact skin after friction is inflammation from injury. Fluid alone is not pus.

options.text: Red, itchy skin on both hands after cleaning with a new chemical product without gloves, skin intact
options.rationale: An irritant can trigger inflammation without infection. The skin is intact and nothing shows pus or spread.

questions.takeaway: Infection is suggested by pus and by redness that spreads beyond a marked baseline. Unchanged redness, clear blister fluid, and irritant reactions fit inflammation without infection.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The item pairs near twins. Compare the two stitched cuts (past the line versus on the line) and the two fluids (thick yellow drainage versus clear fluid under intact skin).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Past the line is spread; on the line is unchanged.
Thick yellow drainage is pus; clear blister fluid under intact skin is not.

steps.action: Reject the injury and irritant findings
steps.detail: Bruise and chemical reaction with intact skin and no change.

elimination.verdict: B, D.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who was admitted 2 days ago and takes an immunosuppressant. The admission note describes a 4 cm bruise with mild swelling on the forearm at a blood draw site. Today the patient reports a sore, swollen area on the same forearm. The nurse has asked when it began and has assessed warmth, color, swelling, pain, and use of the arm. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Report the swollen area to the provider now
options.rationale: The immunosuppressant raises concern because it can mute the signs of infection, so this is tempting. But the nurse first needs to know whether this is the same bruise recorded on admission or a change.

options.text: Mark the edge of the swollen area and recheck it in 4 hours
options.rationale: Marking sets up later checks, but it skips the comparison that can be made right now with the admission note.

options.text: Document today's findings as the new baseline for the forearm
options.rationale: Replacing the baseline erases the comparison. A change from admission would be missed.

options.text: Compare today's findings with the admission note's bruise
options.rationale: Findings are compared with the patient's baseline. The admission note records a 4 cm bruise with swelling at this site, so the comparison shows whether the area is unchanged or worsening.

questions.takeaway: After assessing a finding, compare it with the recorded baseline. The comparison decides whether the finding is a change to report.
questions.strategy: A and D are both defensible, and the immunosuppressant pulls toward A; B sounds careful. The cue that decides is the admission note's 4 cm bruise with swelling at the same site: without comparing, the nurse cannot tell new from old.

steps.detail: History and assessment of the forearm.
Admission note: 4 cm bruise with mild swelling at a blood draw site.
Same as admission, or larger and more painful?
Rechecking in 4 hours or resetting the baseline skips the comparison.

elimination.verdict: Compare today's findings with the bruise in the admission note.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for six patients on a medical unit. Which findings require follow up today? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 3 week old infant who has fed less than yesterday; oral temperature 37.0 °C
options.rationale: Infants have immature immune systems, so infection may show first as subtle changes such as poor feeding. The change needs follow up even without fever.

options.text: A 34 year old with a sprained ankle that is warm, red, and swollen, the same as yesterday
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection. Unchanged findings after a sprain are expected and are compared over time.

options.text: A 79 year old admitted after a fall who is newly confused since this morning; oral temperature 37.1 °C
options.rationale: Older adults have reduced immune responses and may not develop a fever. New confusion is a change that needs follow up.

options.text: A 38 year old who takes a daily antirejection drug after a kidney transplant and has a new sore throat; oral temperature 36.9 °C
options.rationale: Antirejection drugs suppress immune function and can mask fever. A new sore throat needs follow up.

options.text: A 38 year old who donated a kidney 1 year ago, takes no daily medicines, and has a healed incision; oral temperature 36.8 °C
options.rationale: Donating a kidney does not suppress immune function, and this patient takes no immunosuppressant. Nothing here has changed.

options.text: A 52 year old with diabetes mellitus whose redness around a foot blister has spread 1 cm since yesterday; oral temperature 36.9 °C
options.rationale: Diabetes mellitus lowers immune competence, and spreading redness is worsening. It needs follow up even without fever.

questions.takeaway: In patients with reduced immune protection, infection can show as a small change with no fever. A change in a patient at risk needs follow up; stable findings in a patient not at risk do not.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for two things in each option: a factor that reduces immune protection and a change from before. E is the trap; the cue is "takes no daily medicines".

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Infant, older adult, antirejection drug, and diabetes each reduce immune protection.
Less feeding, new confusion, new sore throat, and spreading redness are changes.
B is an unchanged sprain; E has a past surgery but no immunosuppressant and no change.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F. Each pairs reduced immune protection with a new change.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A 34 year old with a sprained ankle; redness is 8 cm across and pain is 6 of 10, both the same as yesterday
options.rationale: The redness is large, but it and the pain match yesterday. Unchanged cardinal signs after an injury fit inflammation without infection.

options.text: A 58 year old with a shin wound; redness grew from 2 to 3 cm and pain from 3 to 5 of 10 since yesterday
options.rationale: Redness and pain have both worsened since yesterday. A temperature is not needed before acting on a change at the site.

options.text: A 78 year old with a hand wound and dementia; oral temperature 36.9 °C and confusion, both unchanged since admission yesterday
options.rationale: New confusion in an older adult can be the first sign of infection, which pulls hard. But this patient has dementia, and the confusion and temperature both match the baseline since admission, so nothing has changed.

options.text: A 45 year old with a rash on both forearms after using a cleaning product; the rash is smaller than yesterday
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow an irritant, and a rash that is smaller than at baseline is not a worsening finding.

questions.takeaway: Priority goes to the patient who has changed from baseline. A concerning finding that has not changed is less urgent than a worsening one, and the nurse does not wait for fever.
questions.strategy: Two options pull hard: an older patient with confusion, and a patient with a modest change at a wound. The deciding cue is "unchanged since admission yesterday" against "since yesterday": unchanged findings wait, worsening findings come first.

steps.detail: Ankle unchanged, temperature and confusion unchanged, rash smaller, shin wound worse.

steps.action: Do not let one finding decide
steps.detail: Confusion that matches baseline in a patient with dementia is not new.
Assess the patient whose findings have worsened.

elimination.verdict: Assess the patient whose shin wound redness and pain have worsened since yesterday.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A patient with an indwelling urinary catheter has bacteria in a urine culture and no symptoms. Which action should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Start an antimicrobial now
options.rationale: Bacteria without symptoms in a patient with a catheter is colonization, not infection. Antimicrobials are not expected, and treating colonization adds side effects and resistance.

options.text: Place the patient in a private isolation room
options.rationale: Colonization with common bacteria does not call for isolation; standard precautions apply. Transmission based precautions depend on the organism, such as a resistant one, not on a positive culture alone.

options.text: Monitor for signs of infection
options.rationale: Colonization means microorganisms are present without causing symptomatic disease. With no symptoms, no antimicrobial is expected; the nurse keeps monitoring for fever, pain, or changes in the urine and reviews whether the catheter is still needed.

options.text: Replace the catheter and culture the tip
options.rationale: Catheter tip cultures are not used for urinary catheters, and bacteria without symptoms do not call for a new catheter. The nurse does review daily whether the catheter is still needed.

questions.takeaway: Finding an organism is not the same as infection. Bacteria without symptoms in a patient with a catheter is colonization, which is monitored rather than treated with antimicrobials.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A positive culture pulls toward treatment. Decide by whether the patient shows signs of disease: no symptoms means colonization, which is watched, not treated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An organism is present with no symptoms: colonization.
Colonization does not call for an antimicrobial.
No isolation for common bacteria, and no tip culture or catheter change.
Watch for signs that colonization has become infection.

elimination.verdict: C. Colonization is monitored, not treated.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted yesterday with acute pancreatitis. Oral temperature is 38.4 °C, heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and white blood cell (WBC) count 13,500 per mm3. No source of infection has been found, and blood cultures show no growth so far. The patient is alert and oriented, as on admission; SpO2 is 97%, and urine output is 60 mL/hr. A new nurse says, "This meets the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria, so the patient has sepsis." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The SIRS criteria are met, so sepsis is present and the antimicrobial must start now."
options.rationale: SIRS describes a widespread inflammatory response and can occur with noninfectious causes such as pancreatitis. SIRS alone does not establish sepsis.

options.text: "This is widespread inflammation. Sepsis needs infection and organ dysfunction."
options.rationale: Sepsis requires infection plus organ dysfunction. Mentation matches admission, oxygen saturation and urine output are inside their ranges, and no infection source has been found.

options.text: "The blood cultures show no growth so far, so sepsis can be ruled out now."
options.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

options.text: "A respiratory rate of 22/min this early shows that sepsis is present."
options.rationale: A rising respiratory rate is concerning and is trended. Alone it does not show organ dysfunction when mentation, SpO2, and urine output are at baseline or inside their ranges.

questions.takeaway: SIRS is inflammation spread through the body, and pancreatitis can cause it without infection. Sepsis needs infection plus organ dysfunction, so look for new confusion, poor oxygenation, or falling urine output.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Option D is the pull: a fast respiratory rate is a common early sepsis cue, and A sounds like prompt action. The deciding cue is that every marker of organ function in the stem, mentation, SpO2, and urine output, is at baseline or inside its range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pancreatitis is a noninfectious cause of SIRS.
"Ruled out" ignores that sepsis is a clinical diagnosis.
Mentation at baseline, SpO2 97%, urine output 60 mL/hr: none shown.
It is concerning and is trended, but one number does not establish sepsis.

elimination.verdict: SIRS alone is not sepsis; sepsis needs infection with organ dysfunction, and none is shown.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A patient with a draining foot wound has a high white blood cell count with more band neutrophils and no fever. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Immature cells are rising; I will check the wound now."
options.rationale: A left shift means more immature band neutrophils are circulating because the marrow cannot keep up with a continuing infection, and immature neutrophils cannot phagocytose. Results are interpreted with the assessment and baseline.

options.text: "Immature cells are rising; I will act if fever develops."
options.rationale: The interpretation is right, but infection can be present without fever, and the nurse does not rely on fever alone.

options.text: "Memory cells are forming; I will check the wound now."
options.rationale: Memory cells come from lymphocytes, part of adaptive immunity. Band cells are immature neutrophils, part of innate defense.

options.text: "Memory cells are forming; I will act if fever develops."
options.rationale: This has two errors. Memory cells come from lymphocytes, part of adaptive immunity, while band cells are immature neutrophils. The nurse also does not wait for fever, because infection can be present without it.

questions.takeaway: A left shift means the marrow is sending out immature neutrophils that cannot phagocytose, a sign the body is losing ground to a continuing infection. Read the results now with the wound and the baseline, not alone and not by temperature.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option has an interpretation and an action. Judge each half on its own: two options name the right cell, two take the right action, and only one gets both.

steps.detail: Bands are immature neutrophils, which cannot phagocytose.
Memory belongs to lymphocytes, which removes C and D.
Waiting for fever removes B and D; reading the result with the wound and baseline now fits A.

elimination.verdict: A. Immature neutrophils signal a marrow that cannot keep up, and the result is read now with the wound and baseline.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A patient with an infected wound becomes newly confused and breathes faster, with low urine output and no fever. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Recheck the temperature and report if fever develops
options.rationale: Notifying the provider is the right idea, but tying it to fever is the error. New confusion, faster breathing, and low urine output are already present, and the nurse does not wait for fever.

options.text: Mark the redness and compare at the next dressing
options.rationale: Comparing the site with baseline is right in general, but the changes now are in breathing, mentation, and urine output, and they cannot wait.

options.text: Reassure the patient and reassess in 1 hour
options.rationale: Anxiety does not explain low urine output. New confusion is a change from baseline and is treated as a sepsis cue.

options.text: Notify the provider or rapid response team now
options.rationale: An infected wound plus new confusion, faster breathing, and low urine output are early cues of sepsis. When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is an immune response to infection that has become uncontrolled and disrupts organ function. New confusion, faster breathing, and falling urine output are the early cues, and a temperature inside the range does not delay escalation.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: No fever is the trap. Name the problem from the changes: mentation, breathing, and urine output.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Newly confused, breathing faster, low urine output, no fever.
An infected wound with organ dysfunction cues points to possible sepsis.
Waiting for fever, for the next dressing change, or for an hour of reassurance all postpone escalation.
Escalate now to the provider or the rapid response process.

elimination.verdict: D. Possible sepsis calls for immediate escalation, without waiting for fever.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A patient has had warm, swollen knees for 2 weeks and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), with no fever. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The ESR shows infection in both knees."
options.rationale: The ESR rises with inflammation and with infection. It does not name a cause or a location, and the knees have not yet been assessed.

options.text: "With no fever, this cannot be infection."
options.rationale: Infection can be present without fever, and the ESR cannot separate inflammation from infection.

options.text: "Something is inflamed or infected; I will assess each knee."
options.rationale: An ESR above 20 mm/hr indicates inflammation or infection somewhere in the body. Assessment begins with onset, recent injury, and illness history, then the findings at each site.

options.text: "Something is inflamed or infected; I will apply ice and recheck."
options.rationale: The interpretation is right, but comfort measures come after the history and the assessment of each knee. Assessment comes before intervention.

questions.takeaway: An ESR above 20 mm/hr says inflammation or infection is present somewhere in the body. It cannot say which, so the nurse reads it together with the history and the assessment of the site.
