questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and B each jump to a conclusion about cause. Ask what the ESR can tell you: that something is inflamed, not why. Then choose the option that gathers more data before acting.

steps.detail: The ESR is elevated.

steps.action: Reject the leap to a cause
steps.detail: The ESR rises with both inflammation and infection, so it cannot confirm infection (A), and no fever cannot rule it out (B).
C and D read the ESR correctly; D intervenes before the knees are assessed.
History, then a focused assessment of each knee.

elimination.verdict: C. The ESR shows inflammation or infection without naming which, so the nurse takes the history and assesses each knee.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient receiving chemotherapy who has a central venous catheter in the upper chest. Today the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 400 per mm3; the provider reviewed it at 0800, and neutropenic precautions are in place. At the catheter site the skin is pink 0.5 cm around the insertion point with no drainage, and site pain is 4 of 10, up from 1 of 10 yesterday. Oral temperature is 37.0 °C. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document the catheter site as showing no signs of infection
options.rationale: Little redness and no drainage would be reassuring with an ANC in range. With an ANC of 400 per mm3, few neutrophils reach the site, so these signs cannot be relied on.

options.text: Report the increase in site pain to the provider now
options.rationale: Pus forms from dead WBCs, and the ANC of 400 per mm3 is far below range. Local signs are blunted, so the rise in pain from 1 to 4 of 10 is reported as a change from baseline.

options.text: Report the ANC of 400 per mm3 to the provider now
options.rationale: The ANC is low, but the provider reviewed it at 0800 and neutropenic precautions are in place. The change that has not been reported is the rise in site pain.

options.text: Recheck the site and the temperature in 4 hours
options.rationale: Infection can be present without fever when immunity is low, so waiting for fever delays the report of pain that has already risen from 1 to 4 of 10.

questions.takeaway: Pus and much of the redness of infection come from neutrophils at the site. When the ANC is very low, those signs are muted, so a smaller change such as new pain is reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is partly covered in Reading (Iggy) and completed by standard NCLEX teaching.
questions.strategy: B and C both escalate. The deciding cue is that the provider reviewed the ANC at 0800 and precautions are in place, so the unreported change is the pain rising from 1 to 4 of 10.

steps.action: Read the ANC against its range
steps.detail: 400 per mm3 is far below the expected level.
Few neutrophils means little pus and muted redness.
Pain 1 to 4 of 10 since yesterday.
The ANC has already been reviewed and acted on.
Infection can be present without fever when immunity is low, so waiting for fever delays the report.

elimination.verdict: Report the new site pain now; a low ANC blunts redness and pus.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission note for a patient. Which findings increase the patient's risk for infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Capped peripheral IV catheter in the forearm, not in use
options.rationale: An IV catheter is an invasive device that raises the risk for infection whether or not fluids are running. Capped and unused sounds harmless, but the device still breaks the skin.

options.text: Arm cast for a closed fracture, skin intact at the edges
options.rationale: A cast is an outside device, not an invasive one, and the fracture is closed with intact skin. Intact skin is the best barrier, so this does not raise the current risk.

options.text: Daily nicotine patch since quitting smoking last month
options.rationale: Quitting sounds like the risk is gone, but nicotine use is a host factor that raises infection risk, and the patch delivers nicotine every day.

options.text: Stopped smoking 20 years ago
options.rationale: Smoking sounds like a risk, but this patient has used no nicotine for 20 years, so the host factor is not present today.

options.text: Burn on the forearm with open blisters
options.rationale: Burns break the skin, removing the best barrier against infection.

options.text: Received an influenza vaccine 1 month ago
options.rationale: A recent vaccine does not raise infection risk.

questions.takeaway: Host factors that raise infection risk include current alcohol or nicotine use, from any source, invasive devices even when not in use, and broken skin from surgery, trauma, or burns. Intact skin, outside devices, and past habits do not.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each risk has a near twin: a capped IV catheter versus a cast over intact skin, a nicotine patch now versus smoking that stopped 20 years ago. Ask whether the factor breaks the skin or is present today, not whether it sounds harmless.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The IV catheter is invasive even when capped; the cast sits on intact skin.
The burn has open blisters; the fracture is closed.
A daily patch counts; smoking that stopped 20 years ago does not.
A vaccine does not raise infection risk.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A patient with sepsis has received antimicrobials and IV fluids overnight. Which findings this morning require further escalation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Now alert and oriented; was confused last evening
options.rationale: Mental status moving back toward baseline is a sign of response to treatment.

options.text: Urine output up to 45 mL/hr from 15 mL/hr
options.rationale: Urine output is a key marker of perfusion, and it is now inside the range.

options.text: Capillary refill still 4 seconds, as last evening
options.rationale: Capillary refill is unchanged and still slow. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

options.text: Fever gone; oral temperature now 37.0 °C
options.rationale: The temperature has returned inside the range. It is one number and is judged with the rest of the trend.

options.text: Skin on both legs still cool and mottled
options.rationale: Skin findings are part of the perfusion assessment. Unchanged cool, mottled skin is a persistent sign of poor perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend, not one number. Mentation, urine output, and temperature moving toward baseline count as response, and persistent signs of poor perfusion still call for escalation.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The temperature drop is the eye catcher, and it pulls toward calling the whole picture a success. Judge each finding on its own trend: two perfusion signs have not moved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare each finding with last evening
steps.detail: Mentation, urine output, and temperature have moved toward baseline.
Capillary refill and skin findings are unchanged.
Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

elimination.verdict: C, E.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with an infected leg wound. Which new finding indicates that the infection has become systemic?

options.text: Thick yellow drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: New pus shows the wound infection is worsening and is reported, but pus is a local sign.

options.text: Pain at the wound rising to 6 of 10
options.rationale: Pain at the site is a local sign. Rising pain is a change from baseline, but it does not show spread to the whole body.

options.text: Warmth at the wound edges, unchanged since morning
options.rationale: Warmth at the site is a local sign, and it has not changed. Nothing here shows a systemic response.

options.text: New chills, malaise, and a fever
options.rationale: Fever, chills, and malaise are primary indicators of systemic infection. Spreading redness from the wound would also suggest systemic spread.

questions.takeaway: Pain, swelling, heat, redness, and pus at the site describe local infection. Fever with chills and malaise means the infection now involves the whole body.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A is the tempting answer because the wound now drains pus. The stem asks about systemic spread, so look for the option whose findings are outside the wound.

steps.detail: Systemic, not simply worse.
Pus, warmth, and pain at the site are local signs.
Warmth that has not changed is still local.
New fever, chills, and malaise.

elimination.verdict: New chills, malaise, and fever.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with an infected foot wound with thick yellow drainage. Oral temperature is 38.6 °C and heart rate is 108/min. At 1000 the provider prescribed a wound culture, two sets of blood cultures, and an IV antimicrobial to start as soon as possible. Laboratory staff drew both sets of blood cultures at 1015. At 1030 the antimicrobial arrives on the unit, and the wound culture has not been obtained. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Obtain the wound culture, then start the antimicrobial
options.rationale: Antimicrobial therapy should not begin until after the culture specimen is obtained. The wound culture is still outstanding, and collecting it takes minutes, so it comes first and the antimicrobial follows without delay.

options.text: Start the antimicrobial now that the blood cultures are drawn
options.rationale: Drawing the blood cultures first is correct, but the wound culture has not been obtained. Giving the antimicrobial now can keep the wound organism from growing and leave it unidentified.

options.text: Start the antimicrobial and obtain the wound culture at the next dressing change
options.rationale: This delays the wound culture until after the antimicrobial is running, so the specimen may not grow the organism.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial until culture results identify the organism
options.rationale: Culture results take time. The specimen must be collected first, but the antimicrobial is started once it is obtained, not after results return.

questions.takeaway: Culture is the best way to identify the organism, and every prescribed specimen is collected before the first antimicrobial dose. Collecting it promptly lets the dose start without delay.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and B both protect the cultures and both start treatment quickly. The cue that decides is "the wound culture has not been obtained": blood cultures drawn first do not cover the wound specimen.

steps.detail: Wound culture and two sets of blood cultures.
Blood cultures drawn at 1015; wound culture not obtained.

steps.action: Apply the rule to each specimen
steps.detail: Antimicrobial therapy begins after the culture specimen is obtained.
Waiting for a dressing change or for results postpones treatment or loses the specimen.

elimination.verdict: Obtain the wound culture now, then start the antimicrobial.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a wound on the shin who walks with a limp because of pain in that leg. At 0800 the nurse assesses the leg for signs of inflammation. Which documentation entry best supports comparing the patient's findings over time?

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm from wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Walks 10 m with a limp."
options.rationale: The entry names the side and time, measures and marks the redness, rates pain, and measures function. Each cardinal sign that is affected can be compared at the next assessment.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm from wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Dressing clean, dry, and intact."
options.rationale: This entry is well built, but the patient's walking is limited and the entry leaves out function, a cardinal sign the next nurse needs to compare. A dressing note is not a sign of inflammation to trend.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness past the wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Walks 10 m in the hallway with a limp."
options.rationale: Function is included, but the redness is described only as past the wound edge, not measured, so a change in its size cannot be measured at the next check.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm, wound appears infected. Provider made aware. Walks with a limp."
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. The entry labels a cause and leaves out pain and a measured distance.

questions.takeaway: A baseline entry names the side and time and measures each affected cardinal sign, including function, so later findings can be compared.
questions.strategy: A and B are both well built. The cue that decides is "walks with a limp because of pain in that leg": function is affected, so the entry must measure it.

steps.action: Read what the stem says is affected
steps.detail: Redness, pain, and walking.

steps.action: Check each entry for all three
steps.detail: Only A and C include walking.
C lacks a measured redness.
Redness alone does not establish infection.

elimination.verdict: The entry with time, measured and marked redness, pain rating, and walking distance.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario: An 87 year old patient with dementia who lives in a group home was admitted at 0900 today with an indwelling urinary catheter. Group home staff report that the patient is usually confused about the day and year. The nurse compares findings at 1400 with findings at 1000.
questions.stem: The nurse is reassessing an older adult patient with dementia and an indwelling urinary catheter. For each finding at 1400, indicate whether it requires follow up or no follow up is needed.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.3 °C, was 36.1 °C at 1000
rows.rationale: Older adults often have a lower baseline temperature and may have a fever at about 37.2 °C. A rise of 1.2 °C from this patient's baseline can be a fever.

rows.text: Hard of hearing in both ears, as at 1000
rows.rationale: This finding is unchanged from 1000 and does not point to infection or dehydration.

rows.text: Heart rate 104 beats per minute, was 76 beats per minute at 1000
rows.rationale: A new rise in heart rate can accompany systemic infection and is a sign of dehydration in an older adult.

rows.text: Confused about the day and year, as at 1000
rows.rationale: Group home staff report this confusion as the patient's usual baseline, and it is unchanged since 1000.

rows.text: Pulling at the catheter and trying to climb out of bed, was resting quietly at 1000
rows.rationale: Restlessness is a sign to assess for in an older adult with possible infection or dehydration, and it is new since 1000.

rows.text: Dark amber urine in the catheter bag, was pale yellow at 1000
rows.rationale: Darker urine is new and points to dehydration, which the nurse assesses for in an older adult with possible infection.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, compare each finding with the patient's own baseline. A small temperature rise from a low baseline, a faster heart rate, new restlessness, and darker urine need follow up; long standing confusion that matches the reported baseline does not.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two rows are traps. 37.3 °C looks close to normal, but the patient's baseline was 36.1 °C. Confusion looks alarming, but group home staff describe it as usual and it has not changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Anchor each row to its baseline
steps.detail: 1000 readings and the group home report.
Fever may appear near 37.2 °C; tachycardia, restlessness, and dark urine can signal infection or dehydration.
Hearing and the usual confusion.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 3, 5, and 6 require follow up. Rows 2 and 4 need no follow up.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is taking an exposure history from a patient with an oral temperature of 38.6 °C, chills, and 6 loose stools in the past 24 hours. The loose stools began yesterday. Which findings help the nurse identify a possible source of the infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Returned from travel abroad 3 days before the loose stools began
options.rationale: Recent travel is part of the infection history because it can expose the patient to organisms.

options.text: Returned from travel abroad 8 months ago, with no illness since then
options.rationale: Travel 8 months before an illness that began yesterday, with no illness in between, is too distant to point to this source.

options.text: A household member has had loose stools for 4 days
options.rationale: Exposure to ill contacts is a possible source, and the household member's illness began before the patient's.

options.text: Ate grilled chicken at a picnic 2 days ago, cooked through and eaten right after grilling
options.rationale: Food is part of the exposure history, but food that was cooked through and eaten right away is not described as contaminated.

options.text: Drank untreated water from a stream while camping 4 days ago
options.rationale: Contaminated water is a possible source of infection, and the timing fits.

options.text: Cleans a pet turtle's tank each week without gloves
options.rationale: Animal contact is part of the exposure history.

questions.takeaway: The exposure history looks for where an organism came from: travel, ill contacts, contaminated food or water, and animal contact. The timing and the details decide whether a given exposure fits this illness.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each category appears with a twin that fails on one detail: travel 8 months ago, and food that was cooked through and eaten right away. Ask of each whether it could have brought an organism to the patient in the days before the illness began.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loose stools began yesterday.
Travel 3 days before onset, ill household member, stream water, turtle tank.
8 months ago with no illness since.
Cooked through and eaten right away.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 3 week old infant who is breastfed. The parent had a contagious viral illness as a child and recovered, and an older sibling at home developed the same illness yesterday. The parent says, "My breast milk passes my antibodies to the baby, so the baby is protected the way I am." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Your milk gives the baby lasting immunity with memory, the same immunity you have."
options.rationale: Antibodies through breast milk are natural passive immunity. They are temporary and build no memory in the infant.

options.text: "Your antibodies protect the baby for now, so call only if the baby develops a fever."
options.rationale: The protection is real but temporary, and an infant's first sign of illness may be a subtle change such as poor feeding. Waiting for fever alone can miss it in an immature immune system.

options.text: "Your antibodies protect the baby for now, so the baby needs no extra watching at home."
options.rationale: The protection is real but temporary, and the infant's own immune system is immature. The infant's risk is higher than the parent's, so close watching is needed.

options.text: "This protection is temporary, and the baby's defenses are immature. Call with changes."
options.rationale: Natural passive immunity from breast milk is temporary, and infants have immature immune systems. With an ill sibling at home, the parent watches closely and calls early.

questions.takeaway: Antibodies in breast milk give an infant natural passive protection that is temporary. The infant's own immune system is immature, so an exposed infant still needs close watching.
questions.strategy: B, C, and D all agree that the milk antibodies protect the baby for now. The deciding cues are the age and the ill sibling: at 3 weeks the immune system is immature, so the infant needs close watching for any change, not only fever.

steps.detail: Antibodies in breast milk are natural passive: temporary, no memory.
A gives passive immunity memory.
A 3 week old has an immature immune system, so the risk is higher than the parent's.
No watching (C) and fever only (B) both miss early subtle changes.

elimination.verdict: D. Passive protection is temporary and the infant's immune system is immature, so watch closely and call early.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with a warm, red, swollen knee and pain of 6 of 10. The skin over the knee is intact, and oral temperature is 36.8 °C. The patient first noticed the swelling on waking this morning, and no one has examined the knee before today. Which question best helps the nurse identify the likely cause of these findings?

options.text: "Have you taken anything for the pain today, and did it help at all?"
options.rationale: A medication history is part of the assessment, but it does not point to what caused the knee findings.

options.text: "Is the knee more swollen now than it was when you first noticed it?"
options.rationale: Comparing findings over time matters, and this sounds like the baseline rule. But the swelling was first noticed only this morning and no one has examined the knee, so a trend says little about the cause, which is what the question asks.

options.text: "Did you injure, twist, or strain the knee recently?"
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur after an injury without infection, and an injury is a common cause of a single warm, red, swollen joint with intact skin. The answer helps separate inflammation from injury from inflammation with infection.

options.text: "Has anyone you live with had a cold or the flu this week?"
options.rationale: This sounds like infection screening, so it pulls. But a household cold or flu does not explain inflammation limited to one knee with intact skin, and warmth, redness, and swelling alone do not establish infection.

questions.takeaway: When a joint is warm, red, and swollen, the nurse asks about onset and recent injury, because inflammation can occur after an injury without infection. When no baseline exists yet, a question that explains the cause tells the nurse more than a trend.
questions.strategy: B and D both sound like sound assessment. The cue that decides is the question line, the likely cause, together with one inflamed knee and intact skin: a trend and a household cold do not explain it, while an injury can.

steps.detail: The swelling was first noticed this morning and no earlier exam exists.
With no earlier exam, B shows a trend but not a cause.

steps.action: Test each question against the cause
steps.detail: Pain medicine and a household cold do not explain one inflamed knee; an injury can.
Injury history helps tell inflammation without infection from infection.

elimination.verdict: Ask about recent injury.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient, 84 years old, who has had irritation on both forearms for 2 days after using a new cleaning product without gloves. Yesterday the patient scratched open a small area on one forearm. The nurse compares findings at 0800 today with findings at 0800 yesterday. Which findings today suggest that an infection has developed? Select all that apply.

options.text: Redness on both forearms, the same size as yesterday
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection, as with contact with an irritant. Redness on both forearms that has not changed fits the reaction to the cleaning product.

options.text: Oral temperature 37.3 °C, was 36.2 °C yesterday
options.rationale: Older adults often run a lower baseline temperature and may have a fever at about 37.2 °C. A rise of 1.1 °C from this patient's own baseline is a sign of infection even though the number looks close to the usual range.

options.text: Itching on both forearms, the same as yesterday
options.rationale: Itching on both forearms, unchanged, fits the irritant reaction. It does not point to microorganisms invading the tissue.

options.text: Thick yellow drainage from the scratched area, was dry yesterday
options.rationale: The scratch broke the skin, the best barrier against infection. New pus at that site suggests that microorganisms have invaded and are multiplying.

options.text: Redness around the scratched area spreading past the line marked yesterday
options.rationale: Redness that spreads past a marked edge around a break in the skin is a change from baseline that suggests infection at that site.

options.text: Swelling on both forearms, the same as yesterday
options.rationale: Swelling on both forearms that has not changed is part of the inflammation from the irritant. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation can occur without infection, as with an irritant reaction on intact skin. Infection is suggested by changes from the patient's baseline: new pus or spreading redness where the skin is broken, and in an older adult a temperature rise that may stay below the usual fever level.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate what is the same on both arms, which fits the irritant, from what changed at the one site where the skin is open. For an older adult, compare the temperature with the patient's own baseline, not with the usual fever level.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Unchanged redness, itching, and swelling on both arms fit the irritant reaction.
New pus and spreading redness at the scratch suggest invasion where the barrier broke.
A rise from 36.2 °C to 37.3 °C in an 84 year old can be a fever.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.scenario: A patient was admitted 3 days ago with dehydration and has a peripheral IV catheter in the forearm that was placed on admission. At 0800 the IV site had no redness, and oral temperature was 36.8 °C. At 1400 the skin is red and warm along the vein for 6 cm above the insertion site, and the site is tender, with pain of 4 of 10. The patient reports chills that began at 1300 and says, "I feel awful all over." Oral temperature is 38.5 °C, heart rate 112/min, and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. The patient is alert and oriented, as at 0800.
questions.stem: The nurse is reassessing a patient with a peripheral IV catheter who has new findings at 1400. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider now
options.rationale: Chills, malaise, and a new fever with a rising heart rate are primary signs that the infection has become systemic. These changes since 0800 are reported now.

options.text: Apply a warm compress and recheck the site in 4 hours
options.rationale: This treats the site as a local problem only. Fever, chills, and malaise show spread beyond the site, so waiting 4 hours delays care.

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: An infected IV site is not used. Stopping the infusion and removing the catheter takes away the source of the infection; any culture of the site or catheter is done as prescribed or by agency policy, and a new IV is placed at another site if still needed.

options.text: Flush the catheter to check that it is still patent
options.rationale: Patency is not the problem. An infected catheter is removed, not flushed, and flushing may push organisms into the bloodstream.

options.text: Document the site as inflamed and continue the infusion
options.rationale: Redness along the vein with fever and chills is more than inflammation, and an infected site is not used to continue the infusion.

options.text: Inflammation at the IV site without infection
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection, but it does not explain the fever, chills, and malaise that began today.

options.text: Infection at the IV site that has become systemic
options.rationale: Redness extending along the vein, with new fever, chills, malaise, and a fast heart rate, shows a local infection that has spread and become systemic.

options.text: Colonization of the IV catheter
options.rationale: Colonization means microorganisms are present without causing disease. This patient has local and systemic signs of disease.

options.text: Worsening of the dehydration from admission
options.rationale: Dehydration can raise the heart rate, but it does not explain redness along the vein or chills.

options.text: Oral temperature and heart rate
options.rationale: These track the systemic response and show whether treatment is working.

options.text: Extent of redness along the vein, compared with 1400
options.rationale: Comparing the red area with this baseline shows whether the local infection is spreading.

options.text: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate once a week
options.rationale: The sedimentation rate shows inflammation or infection somewhere in the body, but weekly checks are far too slow for a patient who is changing within hours.

options.text: Skin turgor on the forearm only
options.rationale: Turgor relates to fluid status, and a single site check does not track the infection.

questions.takeaway: Fever, chills, and malaise are the primary signs that an infection has become systemic, and redness extending from a site supports spread. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, and report the change now.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate the findings at the site from the findings in the whole body. The chills, malaise, and fever since 0800 move this past a local problem, so the site is not used again and the provider hears about it now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness extends 6 cm along the vein with tenderness.
New chills, malaise, a temperature of 38.5 °C, and heart rate 112/min point to systemic infection.
Report now and stop the infusion and remove the catheter; follow temperature, heart rate, and the red area.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and C; condition B; parameters A and B.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient, 83 years old, admitted with an infection that causes loose stools. The nurse compares findings at 1200 with findings at 0800. Which finding at 1200 requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Oral temperature 37.6 °C, was 37.4 °C at 0800
options.rationale: Older adults can have a fever at a lower reading than younger adults, so this is tempting. The patient is already known to have an infection, and the change since 0800 is small.

options.text: Abdominal cramping 4 of 10, was 3 of 10 at 0800
options.rationale: Cramping is expected with an infection that causes loose stools, and the rise is small.

options.text: Restless and pulling at the gown, was calm at 0800
options.rationale: In an older adult, new restlessness or acute confusion can be the first sign of dehydration or a worsening infection. A change in behavior from 0800 is the priority to assess now.

options.text: Two loose stools since 0800, was three overnight
options.rationale: Loose stools are expected with this infection, and the frequency has not risen.

questions.takeaway: Older adults often show infection and dehydration through behavior before vital signs change much. New restlessness or acute confusion requires immediate follow up, even when the temperature barely moves.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask which change is new in kind, not just a little higher. Expected symptoms of a known infection that change slightly lose to a new change in behavior.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loose stools, cramping, and a slightly raised temperature fit the known infection.
A rise of 0.2 °C in a patient already treated for infection is not the most urgent change.
New restlessness in an older adult can signal dehydration or a worsening infection.

elimination.verdict: C. New restlessness is the priority change.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching an older adult patient about signs of infection. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will tell my family to watch for new confusion."
options.rationale: In older adults, new confusion or restlessness can be the first sign of infection. This statement is correct.

options.text: "A high fever will be my first sign of infection."
options.rationale: With aging, the immune response weakens and fever is often lower or absent. Waiting for a high fever can delay care, so this statement needs more teaching.

options.text: "I will keep up with my recommended vaccines."
options.rationale: Vaccines build active immunity, which helps protect an older adult whose immune response is weaker. This statement is correct.

options.text: "I will eat protein at every meal to help healing."
options.rationale: Adequate protein supports immune cell function and wound healing. This statement is correct.

questions.takeaway: Older adults face a weakening immune response with age, so infection may appear as new confusion or a change in behavior with little or no fever. Teach patients and families not to wait for a high fever.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that relies on a sign older adults often do not show.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three statements are correct, and one is not.
A weaker immune response with aging often blunts fever.
Expecting a high fever first can delay care.

elimination.verdict: B. Fever is often low or absent in older adults.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A patient with a slow healing pressure injury has a low prealbumin level. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Dietitian referral for added protein
options.rationale: A low prealbumin level points to poor protein status. Protein supports immune cell function and wound healing, so a dietitian referral to raise protein intake fits.

options.text: Daily vitamin C supplement by itself
options.rationale: Vitamins support healing, but a vitamin alone does not replace the missing protein that the low prealbumin shows.

options.text: Extra fruit juice between meals
options.rationale: Juice adds fluid and sugar but little protein, so it does not address the deficit.

options.text: Strict bed rest until the wound closes
options.rationale: Bed rest does not correct the nutrition problem and adds pressure risk.

questions.takeaway: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function and slows wound healing. A low prealbumin level points to poor protein status, so expect a plan to raise protein intake.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Match the intervention to the deficit the lab result shows. Option B is the right idea with one thing off: it supports healing but leaves the protein deficit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low prealbumin means poor protein status.
Protein supports immune cells and wound repair.
A dietitian referral adds protein; the others do not.

elimination.verdict: A. The deficit is protein.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with diabetes mellitus and reduced feeling in both feet. A cut on the sole of one foot was found 2 days ago. Today the redness is 1 cm around the cut, the same as yesterday, but warmth and swelling now reach the ankle, and the patient cannot bear full weight on that foot. Oral temperature is 36.9 °C. The nurse has reported the findings to the provider. The patient says, "If it were getting worse, it would hurt." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The redness has not spread, so the cut is not getting worse."
options.rationale: Redness is the sign most people watch, and it has not changed, which makes this tempting. Warmth and swelling now reach the ankle and the patient cannot bear full weight, so the foot is worsening.

options.text: "Pain often returns as an infection worsens, so tell me if it starts."
options.rationale: This invites reporting, but reduced feeling in the feet can keep pain from ever appearing. Waiting for pain repeats the patient's mistaken belief.

options.text: "High blood sugar raises infection risk, so watch for a fever."
options.rationale: The risk is real, but the patient's temperature is 36.9 °C while the foot is already worse. This relies on another sign that may not appear and does not correct the belief about pain.

options.text: "Reduced feeling can hide pain, so swelling and warmth tell us more."
options.rationale: Reduced feeling in the feet can mask pain, one of the cardinal signs. The other signs, warmth, swelling, and decreased function, are worsening and are what the nurse and patient must compare over time.

questions.takeaway: Assess all five cardinal signs and compare them with the patient's baseline. When reduced feeling masks pain, warmth, swelling, and decreased function carry the decision, and no pain or fever does not mean the foot is healing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Several options rely on one sign: redness, pain, or fever. The deciding cue is the reduced feeling in the feet, which explains why pain is absent while warmth, swelling, and function are worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reduced feeling in both feet means pain may never appear.
Redness is unchanged, but warmth and swelling reach the ankle and weight bearing is lost.
Options A, B, and C each wait on redness, pain, or fever.

elimination.verdict: D. Reduced feeling hides pain, so the other signs decide.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing the abdominal incision of a patient on the fourth day after surgery. Which findings require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Redness 3 cm past the incision edges, was 0.5 cm yesterday
options.rationale: Redness close to the edges is expected inflammation. Redness that spreads beyond its earlier border over a day is a change from baseline that suggests infection.

options.text: Edges closed with all staples in place
options.rationale: Closed edges with intact staples are expected and show the wound is holding together.

options.text: Thick, cloudy yellow drainage on the dressing
options.rationale: Thick, cloudy, or purulent drainage is a sign of infection. Thin clear or pink drainage would be expected.

options.text: Incision pain 7 of 10, was 3 of 10 yesterday
options.rationale: Pain from surgery should lessen each day. Pain that rises sharply after it was decreasing suggests a new process such as infection.

options.text: Firm ridge forming under the incision
options.rationale: A healing ridge of new tissue under the incision is an expected sign of tissue repair as the wound heals.

options.text: Oral temperature 37.3 °C, was 37.2 °C yesterday
options.rationale: This temperature is essentially unchanged from yesterday and does not by itself show a change. The site findings are what require follow up.

questions.takeaway: Some redness, swelling, and tenderness at an incision are expected inflammation. Spreading redness, purulent drainage, and pain that worsens instead of easing signal infection. Compare each finding with the patient's baseline.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by whether it is expected for healing at day 4 or is a change for the worse since yesterday. Do not wait for a fever to act on changes at the site.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness spread from 0.5 to 3 cm and pain rose from 3 to 7: both worse.
Thick, cloudy yellow drainage suggests infection.
Closed edges, a healing ridge, and an unchanged temperature need no follow up.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with cellulitis of the hand after a cat scratch who has received IV antibiotics for 48 hours. On admission the nurse marked the border of the redness with a pen. Which finding best indicates that the treatment is effective?

options.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C, 1 hour after acetaminophen
options.rationale: A normal temperature is reassuring, but acetaminophen given an hour earlier lowers fever and can hide an infection that has not responded. This reading cannot judge the antibiotic.

options.text: Redness now 1 cm inside the line marked on admission
options.rationale: A measured border compared with the baseline mark is objective evidence that the inflammation from the infection is shrinking. This is the best measure of response to treatment.

options.text: Pain 2 of 10, 30 minutes after an analgesic
options.rationale: Lower pain is welcome, but a pain score taken right after an analgesic reflects the medicine, not the infection.

options.text: The patient says the hand feels better
options.rationale: The patient's report matters, but it is subjective and can reflect rest or pain medicine. A measured change at the site is stronger evidence.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an infection by comparing objective findings at the site with the documented baseline. A temperature or pain score taken soon after an antipyretic or analgesic can mask a lack of response.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options sound like the infection is better. Ask what each finding actually measures: two are affected by a medicine just given, one is subjective, and only the marked border measures the infection itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The temperature and pain were taken soon after an antipyretic and an analgesic.
Feeling better is subjective.
Redness inside the admission mark is measured and objective.

elimination.verdict: B. Redness inside the admission mark.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.nursesNote: Day 1, 1000. A 79 year old patient was admitted after a fall at home 2 days ago; imaging in the emergency department showed no fracture. History of type 2 diabetes for 20 years. A neighbor reports the patient has eaten about half of usual meals for 2 weeks. Knee: bruised, warm, and swollen, skin intact, pain 5 of 10 with movement. Shin of the other leg: 3 cm skin tear from the fall, edges pink, scant thin clear drainage; the nurse marked the edge of the redness, 0.5 cm from the wound. Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Oral temperature 37.2 °C, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 136/80 mm Hg. Blood glucose 248 mg/dL. Prealbumin 11 mg/dL.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission note of an older adult patient admitted after a fall. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: eaten about half of usual meals for 2 weeks
segments.rationale: Poor intake for 2 weeks points to malnutrition, which impairs immune cell function and wound healing. It needs a plan.

segments.text: bruised, warm, and swollen, skin intact
segments.rationale: Warmth and swelling 2 days after a fall with no fracture and intact skin are expected inflammation without infection.

segments.text: edges pink, scant thin clear drainage
segments.rationale: Pink edges and a small amount of thin clear drainage are expected early in healing.

segments.text: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time
segments.rationale: This is the patient's baseline mental status. It matters as a comparison point later.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.2 °C
segments.rationale: This temperature is not elevated. It is also a baseline, because older adults often show little fever with infection.

segments.text: Blood glucose 248 mg/dL
segments.rationale: High blood glucose impairs white blood cell function and wound healing. Chronic disease such as diabetes lowers immune competence.

segments.text: Prealbumin 11 mg/dL
segments.rationale: Prealbumin reflects recent protein status (about 15 to 36 mg/dL expected). A low value supports the history of poor intake and signals a higher risk of infection and slow healing.

questions.takeaway: On admission, look past the injuries to the factors that weaken immune protection: age, chronic disease, poor nutrition, and high blood glucose. Record the baseline findings at each site so later changes can be recognized.
questions.strategy: The injured sites look the most dramatic, but their findings are expected for day 2. The cues that need action are the ones that weaken the immune response.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Knee warmth and swelling with no fracture, and pink skin tear edges, are expected.
Two weeks of poor intake, a low prealbumin, and high blood glucose.
Orientation and temperature are normal and serve as baselines.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario:
Chart so far: 79 years old, type 2 diabetes, eating about half of meals, prealbumin 11 mg/dL. Day 1: knee bruised, warm, and swollen after the fall; shin skin tear with redness marked 0.5 cm from the edge and scant thin clear drainage; alert and oriented to person, place, and time; oral temperature 37.2 °C.

Day 2, 0800. The nurse reassesses the patient. Oral temperature 37.6 °C, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg.
questions.stem: The nurse is reassessing an older adult patient on the second day after admission for a fall. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with inflammation from the fall or suggests infection.
columns: Expected with inflammation from the fall

rows.text: Knee warmth and swelling the same as yesterday, bruise now purple and green
rows.answer: Expected with inflammation from the fall
rows.rationale: Unchanged warmth and swelling at an injury with intact skin, and a bruise changing color as blood is cleared, fit inflammation and tissue repair without infection.

rows.text: Shin redness 2.5 cm past the wound edge, beyond yesterday's mark
rows.rationale: Redness spreading past the border marked yesterday is a worsening change from baseline at a break in the skin.

rows.text: Thick, cloudy yellow drainage on the shin dressing
rows.rationale: Drainage changed from thin and clear to thick and cloudy, which suggests microorganisms have invaded the wound.

rows.text: Knee pain 4 of 10 with movement, was 5 of 10
rows.answer: Expected with inflammation from the fall
rows.rationale: Pain that is easing at the injury fits inflammation that is settling.

rows.text: Oriented to person and place, not to time
rows.rationale: The patient was fully oriented yesterday. New confusion in an older adult can be an early sign of infection, often before a high fever.

answer.r1: Expected with inflammation from the fall
answer.r4: Expected with inflammation from the fall

questions.takeaway: Inflammation can occur without infection, as at the knee. Infection shows as a worsening change from baseline: spreading redness past a marked border, purulent drainage, and in older adults new confusion with only a small rise in temperature.
questions.strategy: Both sites are red, warm, or swollen, so those signs alone cannot decide. Compare each finding with yesterday: unchanged or easing findings fit inflammation, while worsening or new findings suggest infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Unchanged swelling, easing pain, and a changing bruise fit inflammation.
Redness past the mark and new cloudy drainage suggest infection.
New disorientation to time in an older adult suggests infection.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1 and 4 expected with inflammation; rows 2, 3, and 5 suggest infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the second day findings of an older adult patient admitted after a fall. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
Chart so far: 79 years old, type 2 diabetes, poor intake, prealbumin 11 mg/dL. Day 2, 0800: knee swelling unchanged, pain easing; shin redness 2.5 cm past the wound edge, beyond yesterday's 0.5 cm mark; thick, cloudy yellow drainage; oriented to person and place, not to time; oral temperature 37.6 °C, was 37.2 °C yesterday.

The patient is most likely developing [[1]].

The finding that most strongly supports this is [[2]].

The temperature has risen only slightly most likely because of [[3]].

options.text: an infection of the shin skin tear
options.rationale: The changes are at the break in the skin: spreading redness past the mark and new purulent drainage, with new confusion. This fits an infection of the skin tear.

options.text: an infection inside the knee joint
options.rationale: The knee is warm and swollen, but those findings are unchanged and the pain is easing, with intact skin. Nothing at the knee has worsened.

options.text: worsening inflammation from the fall
options.rationale: Inflammation explains the knee, but it does not explain purulent drainage at a break in the skin or new confusion.

options.text: an allergic reaction to the dressing
options.rationale: A dressing reaction would cause redness under the dressing and itching, not thick cloudy drainage from the wound or new confusion.

options.text: the knee is still warm and swollen
options.rationale: Unchanged warmth and swelling after an injury fit inflammation, and redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

options.text: the redness now extends past the line marked yesterday
options.rationale: A measured spread past a documented baseline is the clearest objective change at the wound. Comparing with baseline is how worsening is recognized.

options.text: the temperature of 37.6 °C
options.rationale: The temperature has risen only slightly and could have many causes. It supports the picture but does not point to the wound.

options.text: the pain of 4 of 10 at the knee
options.rationale: Knee pain is easing, which argues against a problem at the knee.

options.text: a weaker immune response with aging
options.rationale: Immunosenescence blunts the immune response in older adults, so fever is often low or absent even when infection is spreading. New confusion may appear first.

options.text: an infection that is still minor
options.rationale: A small temperature rise does not mean a small infection. Redness is spreading and mental status has changed.

options.text: the knee injury using up white blood cells
options.rationale: Inflammation at another site does not use up the body's ability to make a fever. The blunted fever reflects age.

options.text: the high blood glucose lowering body heat
options.rationale: High blood glucose impairs white blood cell function and healing, but it does not lower body temperature.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, a worsening wound with new confusion is an infection until proven otherwise, even with only a small rise in temperature. The objective change from a marked baseline is the strongest evidence.
questions.strategy: Two sites compete for the explanation. Choose the one where findings have worsened since yesterday, and do not let a small temperature rise talk you out of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The shin worsened; the knee is unchanged or easing.
Redness past the marked line is measured against baseline.
Aging weakens the immune response and blunts fever.

elimination.verdict: 1: infection of the shin skin tear; 2: redness past yesterday's line; 3: weaker immune response with aging.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem:
Chart so far: 79 years old, type 2 diabetes, eating about half of meals, prealbumin 11 mg/dL, blood glucose 248 mg/dL on admission. Day 2, 0800: shin skin tear with redness 2.5 cm past the wound edge and thick, cloudy yellow drainage; new disorientation to time; oral temperature 37.6 °C. Knee swelling unchanged.

Day 2, 1000. The provider diagnoses an infected skin tear and prescribes an IV antibiotic, a wound culture, and blood glucose checks before meals and at bedtime. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mark the new edge of the redness with the time and compare each shift
options.rationale: A timed, marked border lets every nurse compare with the same baseline and recognize spread or improvement.

options.text: Assess orientation each shift and compare with the admission baseline
options.rationale: Mental status is an early cue of infection in this older adult. Tracking it against the baseline shows whether the patient is responding or worsening.

options.text: Request a dietitian consult to raise protein intake
options.rationale: Poor intake and a low prealbumin impair immune cell function and wound healing. Adequate protein supports both.

options.text: Report the blood glucose results that remain high
options.rationale: High blood glucose impairs white blood cell function and wound healing, so persistent hyperglycemia needs to be reported and treated.

options.text: Report worsening only if the temperature reaches 38.3 °C
options.rationale: Fever is often blunted in older adults. Waiting for a set temperature would delay care when the site or mental status worsens.

options.text: Treat the warm, swollen knee as a second site of infection
options.rationale: The knee findings are unchanged and the skin is intact. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

questions.takeaway: Plan care around the cues that showed the infection and the factors that weaken immunity: track the site and mental status against baseline, support nutrition, control blood glucose, and act on change rather than waiting for fever.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Each correct action ties back to a cue already in the chart. Reject options that wait for a sign this patient may never show or that treat inflammation as infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Marked border and orientation, each compared with baseline.
Protein through the dietitian and blood glucose control.
A fever threshold and an infected knee do not fit this patient.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem:
Chart so far: 79 years old, type 2 diabetes, poor intake. Infected shin skin tear; first IV antibiotic dose given at 1200. Day 2, 0800: redness 2.5 cm past the wound edge, oriented to person and place, oral temperature 37.6 °C, heart rate 96/min, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg.

Day 2, 2200. The patient is pulling at the IV line and is oriented to person only. Redness now reaches 5 cm past the wound edge. Oral temperature 38.0 °C, heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 102/60 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Treating the temperature is reasonable, but it lowers the one number that is rising and does nothing about the falling blood pressure and worsening confusion. Waiting an hour delays care.

options.text: Reorient the patient and dim the lights in the room
options.rationale: Reorientation helps with confusion, but this confusion is a new sign of a worsening infection, not a problem to manage on its own.

options.text: Mark the new edge of the redness and document it
options.rationale: Marking and documenting changes over time is correct practice, but documenting first delays reporting a patient whose condition is getting worse.

options.text: Report the worsening findings to the provider now
options.rationale: Spreading redness, deepening confusion, a faster heart rate and breathing, and a blood pressure that dropped from 132/78 to 102/60 mm Hg together suggest the infection is becoming systemic. Worsening findings must be reported right away.

questions.takeaway: Document changes over time and report worsening findings. When a local infection is joined by new or deeper confusion, a rising heart rate and respiratory rate, and a falling blood pressure, the infection may be spreading through the body, and the provider needs to know now.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Every option is something the nurse will do. The deciding cues are the trend across the whole body, not just the wound: confusion from oriented to person and place to person only, heart rate 96 to 112/min, and blood pressure 132/78 to 102/60 mm Hg. A systemic change outranks comfort, temperature, and documentation.

steps.detail: Confusion, heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure all worsened since 0800.
The infection may be becoming systemic.
Comfort, temperature, and documentation all wait behind reporting the change.

elimination.verdict: D. Report the worsening findings now.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario:
Chart so far: 79 years old, type 2 diabetes, eating about half of meals, prealbumin 11 mg/dL. Infected shin skin tear. Day 2, 2200: oriented to person only, redness 5 cm past the wound edge, oral temperature 38.0 °C, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 102/60 mm Hg. The provider adjusted the treatment and added IV fluids.

Day 4, 1000. The nurse reassesses the patient. Redness is 1 cm past the wound edge, inside the line marked on day 2. Drainage is scant and thin. The patient is oriented to person, place, and time. Oral temperature 37.1 °C (no antipyretic for 12 hours), heart rate 84/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 130/76 mm Hg. The patient ate about one third of breakfast. Blood glucose before breakfast was 286 mg/dL.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the response to treatment of an older adult patient with an infected skin tear. For each finding, indicate whether it shows progress or requires follow up.

rows.text: Redness 1 cm past the wound edge, inside the day 2 line
rows.rationale: The border has moved back inside the marked baseline, objective evidence that the infection is responding.

rows.text: Scant, thin drainage
rows.rationale: Drainage that changed from thick and cloudy to scant and thin fits a wound moving toward tissue repair.

rows.text: Oriented to person, place, and time
rows.rationale: Mental status is back to the admission baseline, which in this older adult was the early warning sign.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C with no antipyretic for 12 hours
rows.rationale: With no antipyretic masking it, this temperature reflects a real return toward baseline.

rows.text: Ate about one third of breakfast
rows.rationale: Intake is lower than on admission. Poor nutrition continues to impair immune cell function and wound healing.

rows.text: Blood glucose 286 mg/dL before breakfast
rows.rationale: High blood glucose impairs white blood cell function and healing, so it still needs to be reported and treated.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an infection against the baselines you documented: the marked border, the drainage, mental status, and a temperature not masked by medicine. A wound that is responding does not end the plan if the factors that weaken immunity, poor intake and high blood glucose, have not changed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Do not stop at the wound. The infection findings are all moving back toward baseline, which tempts a full pass, but two immune risk factors from admission are still unsolved or worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare the site with its mark
steps.detail: Redness inside the day 2 line and thin drainage: progress.
Orientation and an unmasked temperature are back to baseline: progress.
Intake fell and blood glucose is high: follow up.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1 to 4 show progress; rows 5 and 6 require follow up.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A patient admitted after 2 days of vomiting has a blood pressure of 78/42 mm Hg. Which interpretation of the mean arterial pressure (MAP) is accurate?

options.text: 54 mm Hg, too low to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: Mean arterial pressure is the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic pressure, divided by 3: (78 + 84) divided by 3 is 54 mm Hg, which is under 60 mm Hg, so perfusion of the major organs is at risk.

options.text: 60 mm Hg, at the lower limit for organ perfusion
options.rationale: This is the simple average of 78 and 42. The diastolic pressure is counted twice because the cycle spends more time in diastole, so the true value is lower.

options.text: 66 mm Hg, adequate to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: This doubles the systolic pressure instead of the diastolic pressure: (156 + 42) divided by 3. The diastolic pressure is the one counted twice.

options.text: 36 mm Hg, far too low to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: The interpretation that perfusion is at risk is right, but 36 mm Hg is the systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure, which is the pulse pressure, not the mean arterial pressure.

questions.takeaway: Mean arterial pressure equals the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic pressure, divided by 3. A value of 60 to 70 mm Hg is necessary to maintain perfusion of the major body organs, so anything under 60 mm Hg puts them at risk.
questions.strategy: Write the formula before you look at the choices. The wrong numbers come from the common slips: averaging the two pressures, doubling the wrong one, or subtracting them. Then check the interpretation against 60 to 70 mm Hg.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 42 times 2 is 84.

steps.action: Add the systolic and divide by 3
steps.detail: 78 plus 84 is 162; 162 divided by 3 is 54 mm Hg.
54 mm Hg is below 60 to 70 mm Hg, so perfusion is at risk.
60 is the simple average, 66 doubles the systolic, and 36 is the pulse pressure.

elimination.verdict: A. 54 mm Hg, below the level needed to perfuse the major organs.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.scenario: The nurse is completing admission assessments for several older adult patients. None of the patients has known heart disease.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the age related change in the cardiovascular system that best explains it.

rows.text: A soft murmur at the apex in a patient who reports no shortness of breath
rows.rationale: With age the mitral and aortic valves calcify. A murmur may be detected before any other symptom appears.

rows.text: Resting heart rate 56 beats per minute, with occasional premature ventricular contractions on the monitor
rows.rationale: Pacemaker cells decrease in number and conduction time increases. A rate below 60 beats per minute and premature ventricular contractions are common in older adults.

rows.text: Heart rate rises only to 96 beats per minute during a walk in the hallway, and the patient stops to rest after 20 meters
rows.rationale: A larger, stiffer left ventricle lowers stroke volume and cardiac output during exercise, and the maximum heart rate with exercise is lower. The result is activity intolerance.

rows.text: Dizziness each time the patient moves from lying to standing
rows.rationale: Less sensitive baroreceptors do not adjust the pressure quickly when position changes, which causes orthostatic dizziness.

rows.text: Lightheadedness 30 minutes after lunch, with a seated blood pressure of 98/60 mm Hg compared with 132/78 mm Hg before lunch
rows.rationale: A drop in pressure after eating is a postprandial change. It comes from the same less sensitive baroreceptors as the orthostatic change, not from the valves or the ventricle.

rows.text: During an exercise test, ejection fraction falls to 48%, although it was 62% at rest
rows.rationale: A larger, stiffer left ventricle lowers stroke volume, ejection fraction, and cardiac output during exercise, so the heart is less able to meet increased oxygen demands.

questions.takeaway: Five areas change with age: the valves calcify, pacemaker cells decrease, the left ventricle grows larger and stiffer, the large arteries stiffen, and the baroreceptors lose sensitivity. Each change has its own finding to assess.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Link each finding to the structure that produces it. Pressure drops with position or meals belong to the baroreceptors; a limited response to activity belongs to the left ventricle; rate and premature beats belong to the conduction system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A murmur with no symptoms points to calcified valves.
Below 60 with premature beats points to fewer pacemaker cells.
A limited rise in rate with early fatigue points to the left ventricle.
Both the positional and the after meal drops come from the baroreceptors.
A fall in ejection fraction with activity points to the stiff, enlarged left ventricle.

elimination.verdict: Cardiac valves; conduction system; left ventricle; baroreceptors; baroreceptors; left ventricle.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who has been on bed rest for 3 days and takes a diuretic. Before the patient first walks to the bathroom, the nurse checks orthostatic vital signs. Supine: blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg, heart rate 70/min. After 1 minute standing: blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, heart rate 80/min. The patient denies dizziness. Which conclusion by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: The 16 mm Hg systolic fall rules out orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: The systolic fall is under 20 mm Hg, which makes this tempting, but either pressure can meet the definition. The diastolic pressure fell 12 mm Hg, which is enough on its own.

options.text: The absence of dizziness rules out orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: Dizziness is observed and recorded, but the definition rests on the measured changes. The absence of symptoms does not cancel a diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg with a rising heart rate.

options.text: The 16 mm Hg systolic fall confirms orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: The label is right but the reason is wrong. A systolic fall must be more than 20 mm Hg to count, so 16 mm Hg does not meet the definition by itself; the diastolic fall is what meets it.

options.text: The 12 mm Hg diastolic fall confirms orthostatic hypotension.
options.rationale: The diastolic pressure fell from 82 to 70 mm Hg, more than 10 mm Hg, while the heart rate rose from 70 to 80/min, about 14%. This meets the definition even though the systolic fall is under 20 mm Hg and the patient feels well.

questions.takeaway: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall of more than 20 mm Hg systolic or more than 10 mm Hg diastolic, with a 10% to 20% rise in heart rate. Either pressure can meet it, and the patient does not have to feel dizzy.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options rest on a single number, and two of them are the same number read in opposite ways. Test each pressure against its own threshold: more than 20 mm Hg systolic or more than 10 mm Hg diastolic, with a 10% to 20% rise in heart rate. Either pressure is enough, and symptoms are not required.

steps.detail: Systolic 134 to 118 is 16 mm Hg; diastolic 82 to 70 is 12 mm Hg; heart rate 70 to 80 is about 14%.
16 mm Hg is not more than 20 mm Hg, so the systolic fall alone confirms nothing. C has the right label for the wrong reason.
12 mm Hg is more than 10 mm Hg with a 14% rise in heart rate, so the definition is met. A is wrong because the systolic is not the only test.
No dizziness does not cancel a measured change. Eliminate B.

elimination.verdict: D. The diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg, with a 14% rise in heart rate, meets the definition.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A patient with a family history of heart disease smokes, is obese, rarely exercises, and does not drink alcohol. Which topics should the nurse teach? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stopping smoking, with resources to quit
options.rationale: Cigarette smoking is a modifiable risk factor, and this patient smokes. It is one of the most useful changes the patient can make.

options.text: Losing weight through diet changes
options.rationale: Obesity is a modifiable risk factor, and this patient is obese. Diet change is a standard way to lower this risk.

options.text: Limiting alcohol to one drink a day
options.rationale: This patient drinks no alcohol, so the topic does not fit this patient. Teaching should target the risk factors the patient actually has.

options.text: Increasing physical activity
options.rationale: Physical inactivity is a modifiable risk factor, and this patient rarely exercises, so building up activity lowers risk.

options.text: Genetic testing to remove the family risk
options.rationale: Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor. No test removes it, so teaching targets the factors the patient can change.

options.text: Waiting to change until symptoms appear
options.rationale: Risk reduction works before disease shows itself. Waiting for symptoms throws away the benefit of changing the modifiable factors now.

questions.takeaway: Age, sex assigned at birth, ethnic origin and family history cannot be changed. Smoking, physical inactivity, obesity and psychological factors can. Teach the modifiable factors this patient actually has.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Test each option twice: can the factor be changed, and does this patient have it? Only options that pass both belong in the teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Family history cannot be changed, and waiting for symptoms is not risk reduction. Eliminate E and F.
The patient smokes, is obese and rarely exercises, so A, B and D fit. The patient drinks no alcohol, so C does not.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D. Smoking, weight and activity are the modifiable factors this patient has.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is performing a cardiovascular assessment on a patient who is 72 years old. Which findings require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Point of maximal impulse at fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
options.rationale: This is the expected location of the point of maximal impulse.

options.text: An extra sound just after S2
options.rationale: This is an S3, heard during rapid ventricular filling. It may be normal under 35 years of age, but at 72 it may indicate decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure.

options.text: S1 and S2 heard clearly
options.rationale: S1 and S2 are the normal heart sounds.

options.text: Warm, pink skin on both hands
options.rationale: Warm, pink skin is an expected finding of skin color and temperature.

options.text: A new whooshing sound between S1 and S2
options.rationale: A whooshing sound between S1 and S2 is a systolic murmur from turbulent flow, and it was not recorded at the last visit.

options.text: Equal radial pulses on both sides
options.rationale: Pulses that are equal on both sides are expected.

questions.takeaway: An S3 may be normal before 35 years of age but in an older adult may mean decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure. A murmur is a whooshing sound from turbulent flow, and a systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2.
questions.strategy: The S3 is the trap: it can be normal, so students leave it unselected. Read the patient's age. At 72 the same sound points to the ventricle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Point of maximal impulse location, S1 and S2, skin, and pulses are all expected.

steps.action: Read the age with the S3
steps.detail: At 72 years an S3 is not expected.
The systolic murmur was not present at the last visit.

elimination.verdict: B, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A patient with long standing hypertension has a short, low pitched extra sound just before S1 at the apex. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: An S3 gallop from decreased ventricular compliance
options.rationale: An S3 can also reflect decreased compliance, but it is heard during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. A sound just before S1 is timed to atrial contraction.

options.text: An S4 gallop from a stiff, noncompliant ventricle
options.rationale: An S4 is heard during atrial contraction, just before S1, and reflects a stiff, noncompliant ventricle. It may occur with hypertension.

options.text: A pericardial friction rub from an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: A friction rub comes from an inflamed pericardium. It is not tied to atrial contraction, and nothing in the stem suggests pericarditis.

options.text: A diastolic murmur from turbulent flow through a valve
options.rationale: A murmur is a whooshing or swishing sound from turbulent flow, not a short, low pitched extra sound.

questions.takeaway: S3 comes during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. S4 comes during atrial contraction, just before S1, and reflects a stiff, noncompliant ventricle, as seen with hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial infarction, or advancing age.
questions.strategy: A and B name nearly the same cause, so the cause cannot decide. Time the sound: just before S1 is atrial contraction, which is an S4.

steps.detail: Just before S1, which is atrial contraction.
A is an S3 after S2; B is an S4 before S1.
A rub comes from the pericardium, and a murmur is whooshing.

elimination.verdict: B. A sound just before S1 is an S4, which fits a stiff ventricle from long standing hypertension.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: Four patients each have a blood clot seen on imaging. Which patient should the nurse monitor most closely for a stroke if the clot breaks loose?

options.text: A clot in the left atrium
options.rationale: A clot here moves with the blood across the mitral valve into the left ventricle and out through the aortic valve, which can carry it to the arteries of the head.

options.text: A clot in a deep calf vein
options.rationale: Venous blood returns to the right atrium, right ventricle and pulmonary arteries. A clot from the calf lodges in the lungs, not the brain.

options.text: A clot in the right atrium
options.rationale: From the right atrium the clot crosses the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and is pumped through the pulmonic valve to the lungs.

options.text: A clot in a pulmonary artery
options.rationale: The pulmonary artery carries blood into the lungs, so a clot here moves farther into the lung vessels. It cannot reach the left heart without passing through the lungs.

questions.takeaway: Blood leaves the left atrium through the mitral valve to the left ventricle, then through the aortic valve to the arteries of the head and body. A clot on the left side can reach the brain; a clot on the right side or in a vein goes to the lungs.
questions.strategy: Trace each clot forward along the path of blood flow. Only a clot that starts after the lungs, in the pulmonary veins or the left heart, can reach the arteries of the head.

steps.detail: The calf vein, right atrium and pulmonary artery all send blood to the lungs. Eliminate B, C and D.
Left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, arteries of the head. A remains.

elimination.verdict: A. A clot in the left atrium can travel through the aorta to the brain.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A patient has a new whooshing sound at the apex between S1 and S2. Which entries belong in the nurse's documentation? Select all that apply.

options.text: New systolic murmur at the apex
options.rationale: A whooshing sound between S1 and S2 is a systolic murmur. That is the ejection phase, when the mitral and tricuspid valves are closed and the aortic and pulmonic valves are open.

options.text: Sound occurs with the carotid pulse
options.rationale: The carotid pulse is felt during ejection, between S1 and S2, so a systolic murmur occurs with it. Noting this confirms the timing.

options.text: Radiation and quality of the sound
options.rationale: Murmurs are described by location, timing, radiation and quality, so the record lets the next nurse tell whether it changes.

options.text: New diastolic murmur at the apex
options.rationale: Diastolic murmurs fall between S2 and S1, when the mitral and tricuspid valves are open and the ventricles fill. This sound falls between S1 and S2.

options.text: Pericardial friction rub at the apex
options.rationale: A rub is a scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium. A whooshing sound is a murmur from turbulent blood flow in or near the heart.

options.text: Atrial gallop heard before S1
options.rationale: An atrial gallop, the S4, is a single brief sound during atrial contraction just before S1. This sound falls after S1.
