options.rationale: The dietitian may review the sodium, sugar, fat, and fiber content of the foods chosen, but the nurse obtains the nutrition history as part of the cardiovascular assessment.

questions.takeaway: A cardiovascular nutrition history covers a 24 hour recall of food and fluid, self imposed or prescribed restrictions and supplements, and the amount and type of alcohol. Include the family member who shops and cooks, and consider culture, cost, and access to food.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Assess before you teach, and assess the person who controls the food. The cue is who does the shopping and cooking.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A printed list comes before anyone knows the intake.
The dietitian reviews the foods; the nurse takes the history.
The adult child shops and cooks, so the recall includes the adult child.

elimination.verdict: B. A 24 hour recall with the patient and the adult child.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient who reports fatigue. Which patient statements suggest a cardiac cause? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I get heartburn after spicy meals."
options.rationale: Burning pain after spicy food points to an esophageal or gastric source.

options.text: "I wake up gasping a few hours after falling asleep."
options.rationale: This is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Lying down shifts blood from the legs back to the heart, and a failing heart cannot pump the extra volume, so the lungs congest.

options.text: "My chest hurts where I bumped it last week."
options.rationale: Pain at the site of a recent injury points to the chest wall, not the heart.

options.text: "I need three pillows to sleep now instead of one."
options.rationale: This is orthopnea, dyspnea when lying flat. The number of pillows needed is a measure of its severity, and the increase shows it is worsening.

options.text: "I get short of breath climbing one flight of stairs."
options.rationale: Dyspnea on exertion is often an early symptom of heart failure. Breathlessness after a single flight of stairs is less exertion than should cause it.

options.text: "I feel tired after a long walk."
options.rationale: Tiredness after a long walk is an expected response to exertion.

questions.takeaway: Ask what brings dyspnea on, what relieves it, and the body position when it occurs. Dyspnea on exertion is often an early heart failure symptom, orthopnea is graded by the number of pillows, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea wakes the patient hours after lying down.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each statement, ask what brings the symptom on and what relieves it. Breathlessness tied to lying flat, sleep, or less exertion than before points to the heart.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Waking gasping, more pillows, and fewer stairs all point to the heart.
Heartburn after spicy meals is gastric; pain where the chest was bumped is the chest wall.
Tiredness after a long walk is expected.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: Before coronary CT angiography with IV contrast, a patient mentions having a coronary stent placed 3 years ago. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hold all oral fluids until after the scan
options.rationale: Contrast can damage the kidneys, so hydration is encouraged, not withheld. Oral fluids are encouraged after the test.

options.text: Report the stent to the provider now
options.rationale: Previous treatment for cardiovascular disease is part of the history. A coronary stent can make coronary CT angiography less reliable, so the provider needs to know before the scan.

options.text: Give a beta blocker to slow the heart rate
options.rationale: A beta blocker may be prescribed to slow the heart rate for the scan, but the nurse does not give a drug that has not been prescribed.

options.text: Record the stent in the past medical history
options.rationale: Past procedures are recorded, but this one bears directly on the test being done today. Recording it without telling the provider leaves the problem in place.

questions.takeaway: Ask about previous treatment for cardiovascular disease, including diagnostic procedures and invasive treatment. For coronary CT angiography, a stent makes the scan less reliable, the heart rate must be slow, and the contrast calls for checking kidney function and keeping the patient hydrated.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Connect the history to the test. The cue is a stent in the same arteries the scan is meant to show.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contrast calls for hydration, not restriction.
There is no prescription for it.
A stent can make the scan less reliable, so report it before the scan.

elimination.verdict: B. Report the stent before the scan.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.scenario: The nurse on a cardiac unit is preparing several patients for diagnostic tests ordered for today: a chest x ray, a resting 12 lead ECG, an echocardiogram, and a coronary CT angiography with intravenous contrast.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate the test it belongs to.

rows.text: Check kidney function before the test and encourage oral fluids afterward
rows.rationale: Intravenous iodinated contrast can damage the kidneys, so renal function is checked before and after and hydration is encouraged.

rows.text: Position the patient on the left side with the head raised 15 to 20 degrees
rows.rationale: For echocardiography the patient lies quietly on the left side with the head raised 15 to 20 degrees.

rows.text: Ask the patient to lie still and breathe normally while electrodes are placed on the chest, arms, and legs
rows.rationale: A resting ECG records electrical activity through electrodes on the chest and limbs. It shows dysrhythmias, ischemia, infarction, hypertrophy, and electrolyte effects.

rows.text: Explain that the test uses sound waves, takes 30 to 60 minutes, and needs no special preparation
rows.rationale: Echocardiography uses ultrasound, is painless and risk free, and needs no special preparation.

rows.text: Ask the patient to stand, take a deep breath, and hold it while a picture of the heart and lungs is taken
rows.rationale: A chest x ray is taken with a held deep breath and shows heart size and fluid in the lungs, with no needle or dye.

rows.text: Expect a prescribed drug to slow the heart rate before the images are taken
rows.rationale: Cardiac CT images are timed to the cycle and need a low resting heart rate, so a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker may be given.

questions.takeaway: Match the preparation to how the test works: contrast means kidney checks and fluids, ultrasound means left side positioning and no preparation, electrodes mean lying still for the ECG, and a chest x ray needs only a held breath.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what each test puts into or onto the body: dye, sound waves, electrodes, or radiation alone. The preparation follows from that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Kidney checks, fluids, and a slow heart rate go with coronary CT angiography.
Left side positioning and no special preparation go with echocardiography.
Electrodes on chest and limbs are the ECG; a held breath for a picture is the chest x ray.

elimination.verdict: Coronary CT angiography, echocardiography, resting 12 lead ECG, echocardiography, chest x ray, coronary CT angiography.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic heart failure has a blood pressure that has dropped to 78/46 mm Hg. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: New confusion about the date
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is now about 57 mm Hg. A mean arterial pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg is necessary to perfuse the major organs, so the brain is likely underperfused, which explains the new confusion.

options.text: Thin build, unchanged over 2 years
options.rationale: Chronic heart failure can leave a patient thin and cachectic, but the build has not changed in 2 years. It needs a plan, not urgent follow up.

options.text: Sits upright on 2 pillows, as usual
options.rationale: Breathing trouble when flat is common in heart failure, but this position is usual for the patient.

options.text: Warm, pink skin on both hands
options.rationale: Skin color and temperature are part of the assessment, and warm, pink skin on both hands is an expected finding. It is not the finding that changed today.

questions.takeaway: Physical assessment begins with general appearance: build, skin color, distress level, level of consciousness, shortness of breath, position, and verbal responses. Mean arterial pressure equals the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic, divided by 3, and 60 to 70 mm Hg is needed to perfuse the major organs. A new change in level of consciousness with a mean arterial pressure below that level signals poor perfusion of the brain.
questions.strategy: Separate chronic from new, then link the new finding to the numbers. Build, position, and skin match baseline; the mental status is new.

steps.detail: Build, position, and skin match prior visits.
Confusion about the date is new.
A mean arterial pressure of about 57 mm Hg is below the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to perfuse the brain.

elimination.verdict: A. The new confusion.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse sees distended neck veins and hears a swishing sound over one carotid artery. Which interpretations are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Distended neck veins suggest high right heart pressure
options.rationale: Neck vein pulsations reflect blood volume and central venous pressure. Distention means the filling volume and pressure on the right side of the heart are increased.

options.text: The swishing suggests turbulent flow through a narrowed artery
options.rationale: A bruit is a swishing sound from turbulent flow in a narrowed or atherosclerotic artery. An artery with uninterrupted flow makes no sound.

options.text: A loud swishing sound means near total blockage
options.rationale: A bruit may appear when the vessel is narrowed by half or more, but its loudness does not show how severe the disease is.

options.text: A swishing sound that disappears later means the narrowing resolved
options.rationale: Once a vessel is blocked 90% or more, the bruit often cannot be heard. A bruit that disappears can mean the narrowing has worsened.

options.text: Fluid volume overload may cause the distended neck veins
options.rationale: Jugular venous distention is usually caused by fluid volume overload or right ventricular failure.

options.text: Distended neck veins reflect increased carotid artery flow
options.rationale: The neck veins show venous pressure returning to the right heart, not arterial flow in the carotids.

questions.takeaway: Neck vein distention reflects increased volume and pressure on the right side of the heart, most often from fluid overload or right ventricular failure. A carotid bruit reflects turbulent flow in a narrowed artery, but its loudness does not show severity, and it can vanish when the artery is nearly closed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Keep the veins and the arteries apart. The neck veins tell about volume returning to the right heart; the carotid sound tells about flow through a narrowed artery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distention means more volume and pressure on the right side, often from fluid overload.
A bruit means turbulent flow through narrowing.
Loudness does not show severity, and a lost bruit can mean near blockage.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A systolic murmur recorded as faint at the last visit is now loud, and the nurse feels a vibration over the area. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document the murmur as unchanged, with the same timing and location
options.rationale: Timing and location match, but loudness has changed and a thrill is now present. Murmurs are categorized by loudness as well as timing.

options.text: Assign the murmur a grade III in the record
options.rationale: A loud murmur with a palpable thrill is grade IV or higher; grade III is loud without a thrill. Assigning a grade also does not communicate that the murmur has changed since the last visit.

options.text: Document a pericardial friction rub over the area
options.rationale: A friction rub is a scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium. A vibration felt over the area of a loud murmur is a thrill.

options.text: Document the louder murmur and thrill; report the change
options.rationale: The murmur has become louder and is now accompanied by a thrill, which reflects more turbulent flow. The nurse describes location, timing, radiation, and quality, notes the thrill, and reports the change.

questions.takeaway: Murmurs are categorized by timing, clinical nature, and loudness, and they are described by location, timing, radiation, and quality. Same timing and location does not mean unchanged: a murmur that has grown louder has changed, so the nurse describes it and reports the change.
questions.strategy: Compare today with the last visit on every category, not just timing and location. The cue is the change in loudness, and the trap is an option that labels the sound without reporting that it changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Faint before, loud with a thrill now.
A grade in the record does not tell anyone the murmur changed.
Describe the murmur and thrill and report it.

elimination.verdict: D. Describe the change and report it.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four patients on a medical unit. Which patient should the nurse assess first for poor perfusion of the major organs?

options.text: A patient with blood pressure 84/60 mm Hg
options.rationale: This is the lowest systolic pressure, but the mean arterial pressure is (84 + 120) / 3 = 68 mm Hg, within the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to perfuse the major organs.

options.text: A patient with blood pressure 102/36 mm Hg
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is (102 + 72) / 3 = 58 mm Hg, below the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to perfuse the major organs. The low diastolic pressure pulls the average down, because the heart spends about two thirds of each cycle in diastole.

options.text: A patient with blood pressure 90/56 mm Hg
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is (90 + 112) / 3 = 67 mm Hg, within the level needed to perfuse the major organs.

options.text: A patient with blood pressure 178/104 mm Hg
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is about 129 mm Hg. This pressure is high and needs follow up, but it is not a pressure too low to perfuse the organs.

questions.takeaway: Mean arterial pressure is the average pressure in the arteries during one cardiac cycle, calculated as [systolic + (2 x diastolic)] / 3. A mean arterial pressure between 60 and 70 mm Hg is necessary to perfuse the major organs, and because diastole is counted twice, a very low diastolic pressure can drop the mean below that level even when the systolic pressure looks acceptable.
questions.strategy: Do not rank by the systolic number alone. Calculate the mean arterial pressure for each patient; the diastolic value counts twice.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 68, 58, 67, and about 129 mm Hg.
The patient at 84/60 mm Hg has the lowest systolic pressure but a mean of 68 mm Hg.

steps.action: Choose the one below the level
steps.detail: Only 102/36 mm Hg gives a mean below 60 mm Hg.

elimination.verdict: B. Mean arterial pressure 58 mm Hg.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with bleeding from a stomach ulcer. At 0800 blood pressure was 116/72 mm Hg and heart rate was 86/min. At 1000 blood pressure is 108/92 mm Hg and heart rate is 118/min. A new nurse says, "The mean arterial pressure went up, so perfusion is holding." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The higher mean shows that each beat is ejecting more blood."
options.rationale: The mean rose because the diastolic pressure rose from vessel constriction. A pulse pressure that shrinks from 44 to 16 mm Hg points to less blood ejected with each beat, not more.

options.text: "The mean is adequate, so routine checks can continue."
options.rationale: The mean of about 97 mm Hg is adequate for now, which makes this tempting. It ignores the narrowing pulse pressure and the rising heart rate, which show that compensation is working hard during active bleeding.

options.text: "The faster heart rate has made up for the blood loss."
options.rationale: Cardiac output is heart rate x stroke volume. A faster rate can offset a falling stroke volume only for a time, and it does not replace lost blood.

options.text: "The narrow pulse pressure suggests a falling stroke volume."
options.rationale: Pulse pressure is the difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures and is an indirect measure of cardiac output. It narrowed from 44 to 16 mm Hg as the heart rate rose, which suggests falling stroke volume from blood loss, while vessel constriction keeps the mean up.

questions.takeaway: Pulse pressure, the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures, is an indirect measure of cardiac output. With blood loss, stretch receptors trigger a faster heart rate and constriction of the vessels, so the diastolic and mean pressures can hold or rise while the stroke volume falls; a narrowing pulse pressure is the early warning.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: When the mean looks reassuring, check the pulse pressure and the heart rate. A shrinking gap between systolic and diastolic pressure with a rising rate means compensation, not recovery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mean rose from about 87 to 97 mm Hg; pulse pressure fell from 44 to 16 mm Hg.
Vessel constriction raised the diastolic pressure, which lifts the mean.
A narrow pulse pressure with a rate of 118 beats per minute suggests less blood ejected per beat.

elimination.verdict: D. The pulse pressure has narrowed.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient on day 3 after a myocardial infarction. The patient jokes with staff and says, "It was just a bad case of indigestion, and I am over it now." The patient has taken every prescribed medication, walked the hallway three times today as planned, and asked when the cardiac rehabilitation class meets. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Restate the troponin results until the patient accepts the diagnosis
options.rationale: Pushing the patient to drop a defense mechanism removes a way of coping with a threatening event. Nothing in the patient's behavior shows that the denial is harming the care plan.

options.text: Accept the denial and continue teaching and monitoring adherence
options.rationale: Denial is a common and normal response that helps a patient cope with threatening circumstances, and it may show as excessive cheerfulness. It becomes maladaptive only when the patient does not follow the plan of care, and this patient takes every medicine, walks as planned, and asks about rehabilitation.

options.text: Request a mental health referral for maladaptive denial
options.rationale: Excessive cheerfulness can be a sign of denial, so concern is reasonable. Denial is maladaptive when the patient is not adherent, and this patient follows every part of the plan.

options.text: Delay discharge teaching until the patient accepts the diagnosis
options.rationale: Delaying teaching leaves the patient without the information needed at home. The patient is already taking part in the plan, so teaching continues.

questions.takeaway: Denial is a common and normal defense mechanism after a cardiac event, and the patient may deny the condition, say it is gone, or be excessively cheerful. It becomes maladaptive when the patient does not follow the interprofessional plan of care, so the nurse watches adherence rather than confronting the denial.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge denial by what the patient does, not only by what the patient says. Adherence to the plan is the cue that separates normal coping from a problem.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calling the infarction indigestion and joking fits denial.
The patient takes every medicine, walks as planned, and asks about rehabilitation.
Normal coping with full adherence calls for continued teaching and watching.

elimination.verdict: B. Accept the denial as normal coping and watch adherence.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.scenario: The nurse is completing the preoperative cardiovascular assessment of a patient who is 84 years old, has no known heart disease, walks 1 km each day, and is scheduled for hip surgery tomorrow.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected for this patient or requires follow up.

rows.text: A low pitched extra sound at the apex just after S2, during rapid ventricular filling
rows.rationale: This is an S3. It may be normal in patients under 35 years of age, but in an older adult it may indicate decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure.

rows.text: A low pitched extra sound at the apex just before S1, during atrial contraction, documented at clinic visits for the past 3 years
rows.rationale: This is an S4, heard during atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle. It may occur with advancing age as the left ventricle becomes stiffer and less distensible, and it has been documented unchanged for 3 years, so it is a known, stable finding. A new S4 would need follow up.

rows.text: Point of maximal impulse at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
rows.rationale: This is the expected location of the point of maximal impulse.

rows.text: Blood pressure 138/80 mm Hg lying and 112/72 mm Hg after 1 minute standing, with dizziness
rows.rationale: Baroreceptors become less sensitive with age, which explains the change, but a systolic drop of 26 mm Hg with dizziness is orthostatic hypotension and a fall risk that needs follow up before the patient gets up.

rows.text: Left dorsalis pedis pulse weak, right dorsalis pedis pulse strong
rows.rationale: Pulses are compared side to side. A pulse that is weaker on one side suggests reduced arterial flow to that limb, which aging alone does not explain.

rows.text: Heart rate 66 beats per minute at rest, 94 during a hallway walk, and 68 after 5 minutes of rest
rows.rationale: With aging the maximum heart rate during activity decreases. A rise with walking and a return to the resting rate within minutes is an expected response.

questions.takeaway: With aging, the left ventricle stiffens, so an S4 may occur, and the maximum heart rate with activity decreases. An S3 in an older adult may signal heart failure, and orthostatic drops from less sensitive baroreceptors or unequal pulses still require follow up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether aging explains it and whether it is safe. An S3 and an S4 sound alike; the timing, after S2 or before S1, decides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After S2 is an S3, which needs follow up at 84 years; before S1 is an S4, which may occur with advancing age and here is unchanged for 3 years.
Dizziness with a 26 mm Hg drop on standing is a fall risk.
A weak left pulse with a strong right pulse is not an aging change.

elimination.verdict: S3, orthostatic drop with dizziness, and the weak left pulse require follow up; the S4, the point of maximal impulse, and the heart rate response are expected.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who returned 1 hour ago from a left heart catheterization through the right femoral artery. A firm swelling at the right groin site is now 5 cm across and was 2 cm across 15 minutes ago, and there is fresh blood on the dressing. The patient denies chest pain, the monitor shows a regular rhythm at 92/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hold steady, firm pressure over the right groin site
options.rationale: For bleeding or hematoma formation after catheterization, the nurse holds steady, firm pressure on the access site until help arrives.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG before calling for help
options.rationale: A 12 lead ECG is obtained for chest pain or dysrhythmias. This patient has no chest pain and a regular rhythm, and the problem is bleeding at the site.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees so the patient can sit up
options.rationale: Sitting upright bends the right hip and puts strain on the femoral artery site, which can increase bleeding.

options.text: Call the rapid response team or provider while staying with the patient
options.rationale: A growing hematoma is a complication that needs prompt intervention. The nurse calls for help and remains with the patient, keeping pressure on the site.

options.text: Check the right dorsalis pedis pulse, skin color, and temperature
options.rationale: Peripheral pulses, skin temperature, and color in the affected limb are assessed with every check. A hematoma can compress the artery and reduce flow to the right foot.

options.text: Leave the bedside to get a pressure dressing, then reapply pressure
options.rationale: Leaving removes pressure from an actively bleeding arterial site. The nurse keeps pressure on and calls for help instead.

questions.takeaway: For bleeding or a growing hematoma after a femoral catheterization, hold steady, firm pressure on the site, call the rapid response team or provider, stay with the patient, and assess the pulses, color, and temperature of the affected limb. A 12 lead ECG is for chest pain or dysrhythmias.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each action to the problem in the stem. The problem is bleeding at the site, not ischemia, so pressure and help come first, and the ECG is not indicated without chest pain or a rhythm change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Firm pressure stays on; leaving or sitting the patient up works against it.
Call the rapid response team or provider from the bedside.

steps.action: Check the limb, not the rhythm
steps.detail: No chest pain and a regular rhythm, so assess the right foot instead of obtaining an ECG.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient, 81 years old, who has fainted twice this month. Both times the patient was seated in a car and turned the head quickly to look behind while backing out of the driveway. In the clinic, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg lying and 130/76 mm Hg standing, with no dizziness. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: Rise slowly from lying to sitting to standing
options.rationale: Less sensitive baroreceptors cause orthostatic changes in older adults, so this is a common and tempting instruction. This patient's lying and standing pressures barely differ, and both faints happened while seated.

options.text: Eat smaller meals and rest after eating
options.rationale: Postprandial hypotension also comes from less sensitive baroreceptors in older adults. Nothing in the stem links the faints to meals.

options.text: Turn your head slowly and avoid tight collars
options.rationale: In older adults, the carotid sinus in the neck can become oversensitive. Pressure on it from turning the head quickly or from a tight collar can trigger a vagal response that drops the heart rate and blood pressure, causing syncope. Both faints followed a quick head turn.

options.text: Drink a full glass of water before driving
options.rationale: Fluid intake helps when low volume causes dizziness, but nothing in the stem points to low volume, and it does not address what triggered the faints.

questions.takeaway: Syncope in an older adult can come from an oversensitive carotid sinus, from orthostatic changes, or from postprandial changes. Match the teaching to the circumstances of the episodes: faints after quick head turning point to the carotid sinus.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Explore the circumstances of each faint before choosing the teaching. Two causes from aging are tempting here, and the head turn while seated decides between them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both faints followed a quick head turn while seated.
Lying and standing pressures differ by only 2 mm Hg, with no dizziness.
Nothing in the stem links the faints to eating or low volume.

elimination.verdict: C. A quick head turn points to an oversensitive carotid sinus.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who has smoked for 30 years and stands all day at work. The patient reports an aching, heavy feeling in both lower legs by evening. Both feet are warm and pink, dorsalis pedis pulses are strong and equal, and there is 2+ pitting edema at both ankles. Which instruction should the nurse give to relieve the aching?

options.text: Let your legs hang over the side of the bed
options.rationale: Lowering the legs helps arterial flow and relieves claudication. This patient's warm pink feet and strong pulses show good arterial delivery, and lowering the legs would add to the pooling.

options.text: Walk until the ache starts, then stop to rest
options.rationale: This pattern fits claudication from poor arterial flow, which the long smoking history makes tempting. The ache here comes after standing, not walking, and the pulses are strong.

options.text: Apply a heating pad to your lower legs
options.rationale: Heat does not move pooled blood back toward the heart and can injure the skin.

options.text: Raise your legs above heart level to rest
options.rationale: Aching after long standing, with ankle edema, warm feet, and strong pulses, points to poor venous return. Raising the legs helps the veins return blood to the right side of the heart.

questions.takeaway: The venous system returns blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart. Leg pain after prolonged standing, with edema and intact pulses, fits venous insufficiency and is relieved by elevation; claudication from poor arterial flow is relieved by rest or by lowering the legs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Decide arterial or venous from the findings, not from the risk factors. Smoking points toward arterial disease, but warm feet, strong pulses, and edema after standing point to the veins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm pink feet with strong pulses show arterial delivery is intact.
The ache comes after standing all day, and both ankles have edema.
Elevation helps venous return; lowering the legs helps arterial flow.

elimination.verdict: D. Elevation relieves aching from poor venous return.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient whose heart rate rose suddenly from 84/min to 172/min, with a regular rhythm, 20 minutes ago. Blood pressure is 88/60 mm Hg, was 124/78 mm Hg before the change, and the patient reports lightheadedness. A new nurse says, "Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, so this faster rate should be raising the output." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The ventricles have too little time to fill, so stroke volume falls."
options.rationale: The ventricles fill during diastole, and a very fast rate shortens diastole. Less filling means less blood ejected with each beat, so stroke volume falls far enough that cardiac output drops. The falling blood pressure and lightheadedness fit low output.

options.text: "The output is rising, so the low pressure points to dilated arteries."
options.rationale: This accepts the formula without asking what the rate does to stroke volume. Nothing in the stem suggests dilated arteries.

options.text: "The fast rate raises afterload, so less blood leaves the ventricle."
options.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle pumps against, which depends on arterial pressure and vessel diameter. The pressure here is falling, so afterload is not the cause.

options.text: "The output is rising, so the lightheadedness points to anxiety."
options.rationale: Lightheadedness with a blood pressure that fell from 124/78 to 88/60 mm Hg points to poor perfusion of the brain, not anxiety.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume, but the two are linked. A very fast rate shortens diastolic filling time, so stroke volume and cardiac output can fall even as the rate climbs.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: When a formula seems to give an easy answer, check whether one term changes the other. The falling blood pressure and lightheadedness show what actually happened to output.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Options B and D both claim output is rising, which the falling pressure contradicts.
Afterload rises with arterial pressure, which is falling here.
A rate of 172/min shortens diastole, so less blood fills and leaves the ventricle.

elimination.verdict: A. Short filling time lowers stroke volume and output.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with heart failure whose furosemide dose was doubled 3 days ago. The patient has lost 3 kg and has a dry mouth. Today the patient reports palpitations with brief chest tightness that comes only with the skipped beats, and the monitor shows frequent premature ventricular contractions that were not present yesterday. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Which laboratory result should the nurse review first?

options.text: Troponin I
options.rationale: Chest tightness with new premature beats makes heart muscle injury tempting. Here the tightness comes only with the skipped beats, which points to the rhythm as the cause of the discomfort, and the recent diuretic change offers a more likely trigger for the rhythm. Troponin is still checked, but it is not first.

options.text: Serum magnesium
options.rationale: Loop diuretics also waste magnesium, and low magnesium can cause ventricular dysrhythmias, so this is a close second. Low potassium is the more common and more immediate result of a larger loop diuretic dose, so potassium is reviewed first, and magnesium next, especially if the potassium is low or hard to correct.

options.text: Hematocrit
options.rationale: The weight loss and dry mouth suggest fluid loss, and a raised hematocrit from hemoconcentration would confirm it. A high hematocrit does not explain new premature ventricular contractions.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: A doubled loop diuretic dose most often lowers potassium, and low potassium increases electrical instability and causes ventricular dysrhythmias. It explains the new beats, the most dangerous finding, and it is the first result to act on.

questions.takeaway: When premature ventricular contractions appear after a loop diuretic is increased, review potassium first, then magnesium. Both are wasted by the diuretic, but low potassium is the more common and more immediate cause of ventricular dysrhythmias. Chest tightness that comes only with the skipped beats points to the rhythm, not to new muscle injury.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Several results are reasonable. Tie the most dangerous new finding, the ventricular beats, to the most recent change in care, the doubled diuretic, and then ask which electrolyte that change lowers most often.

steps.detail: New premature ventricular contractions on the monitor.
The furosemide dose was doubled 3 days ago.
It comes only with the skipped beats, so the rhythm explains it; troponin is checked but is not first.
Weight loss and dry mouth fit a raised hematocrit, but that does not cause dysrhythmias.
The diuretic lowers potassium and magnesium; potassium is the more common and more immediate cause, so it comes first.

elimination.verdict: D. Review the serum potassium first, then the magnesium.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing an older adult patient whose aortic valve has stiffened with age. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient, 84 years old, has an aortic valve that has stiffened with age and no longer opens fully. A systolic murmur is heard at the right second intercostal space, unchanged from past visits. At rest, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, heart rate is 72/min, and the patient has no symptoms. This week the patient became lightheaded and had to sit down halfway up a flight of stairs.

The narrowed valve increases the [[1]] that the left ventricle must overcome.

Because of this, [[2]] is less able to rise when the patient is active.

The finding that requires follow up is [[3]].

options.text: preload
options.rationale: Preload is the stretch of the ventricle at the end of diastole, before it contracts. A narrowed aortic valve affects ejection, not filling.

options.text: afterload
options.rationale: Afterload is the pressure or resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood through the semilunar valves. The pressure needed to open a stiff aortic valve adds to it.

options.text: venous return
options.rationale: Venous return brings blood back to the right side of the heart. The aortic valve sits on the outflow of the left ventricle.

options.text: heart rate
options.rationale: The valve does not set the heart rate, which is 72/min at rest.

options.text: preload
options.rationale: Preload is the stretch of the ventricle at the end of filling. A narrowed aortic valve limits ejection, and filling can even rise as blood backs up, so preload is not what fails to rise.

options.text: systemic vascular resistance
options.rationale: Systemic vascular resistance is the resistance of the arteries beyond the valve, and it normally falls with exercise. The stiff valve adds resistance at the outflow, but what cannot rise is the amount of blood pumped.

options.text: cardiac output
options.rationale: Higher afterload lowers stroke volume, and with aging the heart already has less reserve. Output cannot rise to meet the demand of activity, so the brain is briefly underperfused.

options.text: the resting heart rate
options.rationale: The resting rate is 72/min and is not set by the valve. The rate can still rise with activity; it is the stroke volume behind each beat that the valve limits, so output falls short.

options.text: the murmur at the right second intercostal space
options.rationale: The murmur is tempting because it is abnormal, but it is unchanged from past visits.

options.text: the resting blood pressure of 128/76 mm Hg
options.rationale: This resting pressure does not show the problem, which appears only with exertion.

options.text: the absence of symptoms at rest
options.rationale: Changes from aging often stay hidden at rest and appear only under stress, so this is not reassuring by itself.

options.text: the lightheadedness on the stairs
options.rationale: Lightheadedness with exertion is new and shows that output cannot meet demand. Valve disorders such as a narrowed aortic valve can cause syncope, so this is reported.

questions.takeaway: A stiff aortic valve raises afterload, which lowers stroke volume and limits how much cardiac output can rise. Aging changes often appear only under physical stress, so new symptoms with exertion require follow up even when resting findings look unremarkable.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Follow the valve forward: outflow from the left ventricle means afterload, afterload limits output, and limited output shows up with exertion. Then pick the finding that is new, not the one that is merely abnormal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The aortic valve sits on the left ventricle's outflow, so it affects afterload, not preload.
Higher afterload lowers stroke volume, so cardiac output, not preload, resistance, or the resting rate, cannot rise with activity.
The murmur is unchanged; the lightheadedness on the stairs is new.

elimination.verdict: 1 afterload, 2 cardiac output, 3 the lightheadedness on the stairs.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: A patient whose mitral valve does not open fully now sleeps in a recliner to breathe. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Blood is backing up from the right atrium
options.rationale: Backup behind the right atrium goes into the neck veins and the body, not the lungs. The tricuspid valve, not the mitral valve, guards the right atrium.

options.text: Less blood is returning from the body
options.rationale: Venous return to the right side of the heart is not limited by the mitral valve, and it does not explain trouble breathing when lying down.

options.text: Blood is backing up from the left atrium
options.rationale: The mitral valve lets blood move from the left atrium into the left ventricle. When it does not open fully, blood backs up into the left atrium and the pulmonary veins, congesting the lungs. Lying flat worsens the congestion, so the patient sits up to breathe.

options.text: The left ventricle is overfilling each beat
options.rationale: A narrowed mitral valve lets less blood into the left ventricle, not more.

questions.takeaway: Blood flows from the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, through the mitral valve, and into the left ventricle. A narrowed mitral valve backs blood up into the lungs, causing shortness of breath that worsens when lying flat.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Trace the blood backward from the narrowed valve. Whatever sits upstream of the valve is where the congestion shows.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
Options A and C differ only by side; the mitral valve is on the left.
Behind the left atrium are the pulmonary veins and the lungs.

elimination.verdict: C. A narrowed mitral valve backs blood into the left atrium and lungs.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with heart failure who started a drug that relaxes the walls of the arteries. Before the first dose, blood pressure was 168/98 mm Hg, heart rate 78/min, and the patient stopped to rest after walking 10 meters. Today blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg, heart rate is 78/min, the patient walks 40 meters before resting, and urine output has doubled. The lungs are clear both days. A student nurse says, "The lower pressure means the heart is pumping less blood." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The drug lowered the preload, so the ventricle holds less blood."
options.rationale: Preload is the stretch of the ventricle at the end of diastole. The drug acts on the arteries, not the veins, and the clear lungs give no sign the ventricle was overstretched. Less filling would also lower output, which the findings do not show.

options.text: "The drug lowered the afterload, so more blood is ejected."
options.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Relaxed arteries lower that resistance, so each beat empties more blood. Better walking tolerance and more urine show more blood reaching the muscles and kidneys.

options.text: "The lower mean pressure means less blood is reaching the organs."
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure today is about 99 mm Hg, well able to perfuse the organs. More urine and longer walks show perfusion got better, not worse.

options.text: "The drug raised the heart rate, so the output rose each minute."
options.rationale: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, but the heart rate is 78/min on both days. Any rise in output came from stroke volume.

questions.takeaway: Afterload is the pressure or resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Relaxing the arteries lowers afterload, so stroke volume and cardiac output rise even though blood pressure falls. Judge output by perfusion findings such as activity tolerance and urine output, not by the pressure alone.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use the data to test each claim. The unchanged heart rate rules out a rate effect, the clear lungs and the drug's action on the arteries point away from preload, and the better walking and urine show output rose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart rate is 78/min on both days, so option D fails.
Longer walks and more urine show more output, so option C fails.

steps.action: Match the drug to the term
steps.detail: A drug that relaxes the arteries lowers resistance to ejection, which is afterload, not preload.

elimination.verdict: B. Lower afterload lets the ventricle eject more blood.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring a patient during a treadmill stress test. Which findings require the test to be stopped? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heart rate rising as the speed increases
options.rationale: The test is meant to raise the heart rate toward a planned target. A rising rate is the expected response to more work.

options.text: New chest pressure while walking
options.rationale: Chest pain during the test suggests the heart muscle is not getting enough oxygen for the workload. It is a reason to end the test.

options.text: Systolic pressure falling below the resting value
options.rationale: Systolic pressure should rise with exercise. A fall below the resting value means the heart cannot keep up with the demand and ends the test.

options.text: Sweating and faster breathing
options.rationale: Sweating and a faster respiratory rate are expected during exercise. Extreme shortness of breath, not ordinary faster breathing, would end the test.

options.text: Runs of premature ventricular contractions
options.rationale: Ventricular dysrhythmias during the test signal an unsafe response to the workload and end the test.

options.text: Systolic pressure rising as the speed increases
options.rationale: A rise in systolic pressure with more work is the expected response of a healthy heart.

questions.takeaway: A stress test continues until the target heart rate is reached or the protocol is done, unless chest pain, extreme shortness of breath, dizziness, hypotension, ventricular dysrhythmias, or significant ECG changes appear.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into expected response to exercise or sign that the heart cannot meet the demand. A rise in rate and pressure is the point of the test; a fall in pressure is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rising heart rate, rising systolic pressure, sweating, and faster breathing are normal with exercise.
New chest pressure suggests the heart muscle lacks oxygen.

steps.action: Stop for failure to keep up
steps.detail: Falling pressure and ventricular dysrhythmias mean the heart cannot handle the workload.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a cardiovascular history. Which patient statement reveals a risk factor that requires follow up?

options.text: "I walk my dog for 30 minutes every day."
options.rationale: Daily activity lowers risk. Physical inactivity, not this, is the modifiable risk factor.

options.text: "I quit smoking 10 years ago."
options.rationale: Smoking is a major risk factor, so this is tempting. The patient quit a decade ago, so the habit is no longer an active risk to change.

options.text: "I stay angry for hours over deadlines."
options.rationale: Hostility, anger, and stress over deadlines are psychological factors closely linked to heart disease. They are modifiable, so the nurse explores them and offers ways to manage stress.

options.text: "I eat fish for dinner twice a week."
options.rationale: Fish twice a week fits a heart healthy diet and is not a risk factor.

questions.takeaway: Psychological factors are part of the cardiovascular history. People who are highly competitive, worried about deadlines, and often hostile or angry are at higher risk for heart disease, and stress, anger, and depression can be changed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that describes a current, changeable habit or trait that raises risk. A past habit that has stopped and healthy habits do not need follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily walking and fish twice a week lower risk.
Smoking stopped 10 years ago, so it is not a current habit.
Lasting anger over deadlines is a psychological risk factor.

elimination.verdict: C. Anger and stress over deadlines are a modifiable risk factor.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse hears a new soft murmur in an older adult patient with no known heart disease. Which question should the nurse ask next?

options.text: "Do you get heartburn after large meals?"
options.rationale: Heartburn points to the stomach, not to a valve. It does not help judge whether the murmur is affecting the heart's function.

options.text: "Are you more short of breath lately?"
options.rationale: With aging, the mitral and aortic valves calcify and stiffen, and a murmur may be heard before other symptoms appear. Asking about shortness of breath checks whether the valve change is starting to limit the heart.

options.text: "Do your legs ache after standing all day?"
options.rationale: Aching legs after standing point to poor venous return. Leg veins are not where a heart murmur comes from.

options.text: "Do you feel lightheaded after you eat?"
options.rationale: Lightheadedness after meals comes from less sensitive baroreceptors, a different age related change. It does not follow up a valve finding.

questions.takeaway: Valves calcify with age, especially the mitral and aortic valves. When a murmur is found in an older adult, assess heart rhythm and sounds and ask about shortness of breath, because the murmur may appear before other symptoms.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match the follow up question to the structure that made the finding. A murmur comes from a valve, and valve problems show up as shortness of breath.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A murmur in an older adult points to a stiff, calcified valve.
Heartburn, leg aching, and lightheadedness after meals come from the stomach, the veins, and the baroreceptors.
Shortness of breath shows whether the valve is limiting the heart.

elimination.verdict: B. Ask about shortness of breath after a new murmur.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with hypertension who started amlodipine 2 weeks ago and returned from a 9 hour car trip yesterday. Blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg, was 158/94 mm Hg before the drug. The patient reports brief lightheadedness when standing quickly that passes within seconds. Both ankles have 1+ pitting edema that began after the drug was started. One calf is 3 cm larger around than the other and tender. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: The larger, tender calf
options.rationale: Edema in one extremity points to venous obstruction such as a clot. After a long period of sitting, a swollen, tender calf suggests a deep vein clot that could break loose and travel to the lungs.

options.text: The edema at both ankles
options.rationale: Edema is abnormal, so this is tempting. Dependent ankle edema on both sides is a common side effect of amlodipine and began when the drug was started; it is reported at the next contact, not ahead of a possible clot.

options.text: The brief lightheadedness when standing
options.rationale: Cardiovascular drugs can cause postural hypotension, so this is tempting. Symptoms that pass within seconds are usually transient; the nurse teaches slow position changes and checks orthostatic vital signs after the more urgent finding.

options.text: The blood pressure of 136/84 mm Hg
options.rationale: The fall from 158/94 mm Hg is the drug's intended effect. It is still slightly high and is followed over time, not urgently.

questions.takeaway: The location of edema helps find its cause: edema in both legs can come from heart failure, venous insufficiency, or drugs such as amlodipine, while edema in one extremity points to venous obstruction or lymph blockage. A new, tender, swollen calf after prolonged sitting needs immediate follow up for a clot.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Several findings are new here. Ask which one has an explanation already in the stem and which one could become dangerous quickly; the one sided swelling after a long trip is both unexplained and dangerous.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The pressure drop and ankle edema match the new drug.
Lightheadedness that passes in seconds is followed up, but it is not the most urgent.
A calf 3 cm larger and tender after a long car trip suggests a clot.

elimination.verdict: A. One sided calf swelling after prolonged sitting suggests a clot.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a history from a patient with coronary artery disease (CAD) at a routine clinic visit. Which statements by the patient require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: "My chest tightness now wakes me up at night."
options.rationale: Chest tightness that now comes at rest or during sleep is a change in pattern. Angina that changes from exertion only to rest suggests the disease is progressing and the heart muscle is at risk. It needs prompt follow up.

options.text: "I get tightness after two flights of stairs, the same as last year."
options.rationale: Tightness at the same level of effort, unchanged over a year, is a known, predictable pattern. It is documented, but it is not a new change.

options.text: "I need three pillows to breathe at night, and I used one last month."
options.rationale: Needing more pillows to breathe lying down is worsening orthopnea. A change over one month suggests fluid backing up into the lungs from a failing left ventricle.

options.text: "My heart races, and then I feel like I will pass out."
options.rationale: Palpitations with near fainting suggest an arrhythmia that is dropping cardiac output to the brain. This needs follow up before the patient leaves.

options.text: "I quit smoking 5 years ago and have not gone back."
options.rationale: Stopping smoking removes a modifiable risk factor. The nurse documents and praises it; it does not need follow up.

options.text: "I take my cholesterol pill every night with dinner."
options.rationale: Taking the lipid drug every night shows adherence. Nothing here needs follow up.

questions.takeaway: In a cardiovascular history, a CHANGE in a symptom is the finding that matters: chest pain that now comes at rest, more pillows to breathe, or palpitations with near fainting. A known pattern that has not changed, a risk factor already removed and good adherence are documented, not chased.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Sort every statement by one question: is this new or worse? The unchanged exertion pattern looks like the classic angina answer, but it is the one that has not changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rest pain and more pillows are both new or worse.
Racing heart with near fainting points to an arrhythmia.
An unchanged pattern, quitting smoking and taking the statin need no follow up.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted with pneumonia who reports sharp chest pain. A high pitched, scratchy sound is heard at the left lower sternal border. The nurse asks the patient to hold a breath, and the sound continues in time with each heartbeat. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: A pleural friction rub from inflamed lung lining
options.rationale: Pneumonia makes this tempting, and a pleural rub is also high pitched and scratchy. A pleural rub comes from the pleural layers rubbing with breathing, so it stops when the patient holds a breath. This sound kept going.

options.text: An S3 from rapid filling of the ventricle
options.rationale: An S3 is a low pitched, dull sound early in diastole. It is not high pitched or scratchy.

options.text: A pericardial rub from an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: A pericardial friction rub is a high pitched, scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium moving with each heartbeat. Because it follows the heart and not the lungs, it continues when the patient holds a breath. It may occur with pericarditis and is often transient, so the nurse documents it and reports it.

options.text: A systolic murmur from turbulent flow at a valve
options.rationale: A murmur is a whooshing or swishing sound from turbulent blood flow. A scratchy sound tied to movement of tissue is a rub, not a murmur.

questions.takeaway: A pericardial friction rub is a high pitched, scratchy sound from an inflamed pericardium and may occur with pericarditis. To tell it from a pleural rub, ask the patient to hold a breath: a pleural rub stops, a pericardial rub keeps going with each heartbeat.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Two options are rubs, and the pneumonia pulls you toward the lung. The deciding cue is what happened when breathing stopped: the sound kept the rhythm of the heart.

steps.detail: High pitched and scratchy: a rub, not an S3 or a murmur.
Pleural from the lung lining, pericardial from the sac around the heart.
The sound continued with each heartbeat: pericardial.

elimination.verdict: C. A pericardial rub from an inflamed pericardium.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing morning laboratory results for four patients on a cardiac unit. Which result requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Troponin I 0.62 ng/mL, was 0.03 ng/mL 6 hours earlier
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are released when heart muscle is injured. A rise from 0.03 to 0.62 ng/mL over 6 hours shows active myocardial injury, which is time critical. The small decimal numbers make it easy to skim past.

options.text: LDL cholesterol 188 mg/dL, statin started yesterday
options.rationale: The value is high, which makes it tempting, but a statin takes weeks to lower LDL. One day of therapy explains no change. This guides long term risk reduction, not urgent action.

options.text: Triglycerides 340 mg/dL after eating breakfast
options.rationale: Triglycerides rise after a meal, and a lipid panel is drawn fasting. This result is unreliable and is redrawn fasting; it is not an emergency.

options.text: INR 2.6 while taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation
options.rationale: The usual target INR for warfarin in atrial fibrillation is 2 to 3. An INR of 2.6 shows the anticoagulant is working as intended.

questions.takeaway: A rising troponin means heart muscle is being injured now and is the result to act on first. Lipid values guide long term risk and must be drawn fasting; a statin needs weeks to work. An INR in the target range on warfarin is the goal, not a problem.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three results look abnormal on paper. Ask which one is explained already (one day of a statin, a meal before the draw, a therapeutic anticoagulant) and which one shows harm happening right now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A statin started yesterday cannot have worked yet; triglycerides after breakfast are invalid.
An INR of 2.6 on warfarin for atrial fibrillation is on target.
Troponin rising twentyfold in 6 hours is active myocardial injury.

elimination.verdict: A. A rising troponin shows active injury to heart muscle.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: The nurse at a clinic is measuring the blood pressure of a patient with a large upper arm and no history of hypertension. The patient has rested quietly for 5 minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level. The standard adult cuff does not reach fully around the arm, and the result is 174/98 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Report the result as new hypertension
options.rationale: A cuff too small for the arm reads falsely high. Reporting this number could lead to treatment for a pressure the patient may not have.

options.text: Recheck with the same cuff on the other arm
options.rationale: Comparing arms is part of a full assessment, but the same small cuff gives the same falsely high value on either arm.

options.text: Have the patient rest 15 more minutes
options.rationale: Rest matters, but the patient has already rested 5 minutes in the correct position. More rest does not fix a cuff that is too small.

options.text: Repeat with a correctly sized cuff
options.rationale: The bladder of the cuff should circle about 80% of the arm and be about 40% of its width. A cuff that is too small squeezes the artery unevenly and reads falsely high, so the nurse repeats the measurement with the right size before reporting anything.

questions.takeaway: Cuff size is the most common equipment error in blood pressure measurement. Too small reads falsely high; too large reads falsely low. Fix the technique and repeat before you report or act on the number.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Every option is something a nurse does with blood pressure. The deciding cue is the cuff that does not reach around the arm: no other step corrects that error.

steps.detail: The cuff does not reach around the arm: too small, giving a falsely high value.

steps.action: Reject actions that keep the error
steps.detail: The other arm and more rest still use the wrong cuff.

steps.action: Reject acting on a bad number
steps.detail: Report only after an accurate measurement.

elimination.verdict: D. Repeat with a correctly sized cuff.

questions.nursesNote: 0900 Emergency department. Patient, 72 years old, has type 2 diabetes mellitus and takes metformin. Reports 2 days of unusual tiredness and nausea and says, "It is just indigestion." Describes an ache in the jaw that comes and goes. Denies chest pain. Skin cool and damp. Heart rate 106/min and regular, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air. Oral temperature 37.0 °C. Capillary blood glucose 142 mg/dL. Lungs clear. S1 and S2 heard, with an extra low pitched sound just before S1 at the apex. Radial and pedal pulses strong and equal.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the emergency department note of a patient with diabetes who reports tiredness and nausea. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Reports 2 days of unusual tiredness and nausea
segments.rationale: Unusual fatigue and nausea are common presentations of myocardial ischemia in older adults and in patients with diabetes, who often have less typical chest pain. They need follow up, not reassurance.

segments.text: an ache in the jaw that comes and goes
segments.rationale: Pain from the heart can be felt in the jaw, neck, arm or back. An ache that comes and goes, with fatigue and nausea, points to ischemia.

segments.text: Denies chest pain
segments.rationale: The absence of chest pain is not itself an abnormal finding. It also does not rule out a cardiac cause in an older adult with diabetes; the nurse weighs the other findings.

segments.text: Skin cool and damp
segments.rationale: Cool, damp skin shows the sympathetic nervous system constricting skin vessels and causing sweating, a response to reduced cardiac output.

segments.text: Heart rate 106/min and regular
segments.rationale: A fast rate with the other findings suggests the heart is compensating for a fall in stroke volume, and it raises the oxygen demand of the heart.

segments.text: respiratory rate 22/min
segments.rationale: A rate above normal for an adult at rest, with these findings, adds to the picture of a heart under strain.

segments.text: SpO2 97% on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygen saturation is within the expected range.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C
segments.rationale: There is no fever, which makes infection less likely as the cause of the fatigue.

segments.text: Capillary blood glucose 142 mg/dL
segments.rationale: For a patient with diabetes this is a reasonable random value. It does not explain the symptoms, and it rules out low glucose as the cause of the cool, damp skin.

segments.text: Lungs clear
segments.rationale: Clear lungs show no fluid backing up into the lungs at this time.

segments.text: an extra low pitched sound just before S1 at the apex
segments.rationale: A low pitched sound just before S1 is an S4, heard during atrial contraction into a stiff, noncompliant ventricle. It may occur with hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy or myocardial infarction and is new information here.

segments.text: Radial and pedal pulses strong and equal
segments.rationale: Strong, equal pulses show arterial flow to the extremities is intact.

questions.takeaway: Older adults and patients with diabetes often present with myocardial ischemia as fatigue, nausea, indigestion, or pain in the jaw or back, without classic chest pain. Look for the pattern: vague symptoms plus cool, damp skin, a fast heart rate and a new S4.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: The patient's own label, "just indigestion," and the denial of chest pain are the trap. Read each finding on its own and ask what the heart could be doing to cause it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fatigue, nausea and jaw ache in an older adult with diabetes can be ischemia.
Cool, damp skin, a fast heart rate and a fast respiratory rate.
An extra sound before S1 is an S4.
Normal SpO2, no fever, acceptable glucose, clear lungs, strong pulses.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing the findings of a patient with diabetes who reports tiredness, nausea and a jaw ache. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
0930. Chart so far: patient, 72 years old, with type 2 diabetes mellitus who takes metformin; 2 days of tiredness and nausea; an ache in the jaw that comes and goes; no chest pain; cool, damp skin; heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg at 0900; oral temperature 37.0 °C; glucose 142 mg/dL; an extra low pitched sound just before S1. A 12 lead ECG is being recorded.

The tiredness, nausea and jaw ache are most consistent with [[1]].

The cool, damp skin most likely reflects [[2]].

The extra sound just before S1 suggests [[3]].

options.text: myocardial ischemia
options.rationale: Fatigue, nausea and a jaw ache that comes and goes, with a sympathetic response, fit reduced oxygen to the heart muscle. Older adults and patients with diabetes often have these less typical symptoms.

options.text: indigestion from the stomach
options.rationale: This is the patient's own explanation and is the trap. Indigestion does not explain jaw pain, cool, damp skin and a new S4.

options.text: low blood glucose
options.rationale: Low glucose can cause sweating and fatigue in a patient with diabetes, but the glucose is 142 mg/dL.

options.text: anxiety about being in the emergency department
options.rationale: Anxiety can raise the heart rate, but it does not explain 2 days of symptoms or a new heart sound.

options.text: a sympathetic response to reduced cardiac output
options.rationale: When stroke volume falls, the sympathetic nervous system raises the heart rate and constricts skin vessels, and sweat glands fire. The skin turns cool and damp.

options.text: heat loss from a fever
options.rationale: The oral temperature is 37.0 °C, so there is no fever.

options.text: a drop in blood glucose
options.rationale: A drop in glucose can cause sweating, but the glucose is 142 mg/dL.

options.text: fluid loss from 2 days of nausea
options.rationale: The patient has nausea but no vomiting, and the blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Fluid loss does not fit.

options.text: a stiff, noncompliant ventricle
options.rationale: An S4 is heard during atrial contraction when the atria push blood into a stiff, noncompliant ventricle. It may occur with hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial infarction or advancing age.

options.text: rapid filling of an overloaded ventricle
options.rationale: This describes an S3, which comes after S2 during rapid ventricular filling, not just before S1.

options.text: an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: An inflamed pericardium produces a high pitched, scratchy friction rub, not a low pitched sound before S1.

options.text: turbulent flow across a valve
options.rationale: Turbulent flow produces a whooshing or swishing murmur, not a single low pitched sound.

questions.takeaway: Link each finding to its mechanism. Vague symptoms in an older adult with diabetes can be ischemia. Cool, damp skin is the sympathetic response to falling cardiac output. A sound just before S1 is an S4 from a stiff ventricle; a sound after S2 is an S3 from rapid filling.
questions.strategy: Use the chart to rule out the tempting explanations: the glucose rules out hypoglycemia, the temperature rules out fever, and the timing of the sound (before S1) separates an S4 from an S3.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Jaw ache, fatigue and nausea with a sympathetic response: ischemia.
No fever and normal glucose leave reduced cardiac output.
Before S1, low pitched: S4, a stiff ventricle.

elimination.verdict: 1: myocardial ischemia. 2: a sympathetic response to reduced cardiac output. 3: a stiff, noncompliant ventricle.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: At 1100 the nurse reassesses the patient in the emergency department. Chart so far: patient, 72 years old, with type 2 diabetes mellitus who takes metformin; 2 days of tiredness and nausea; an ache in the jaw that comes and goes; no chest pain; cool, damp skin; heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg at 0900; oral temperature 37.0 °C; glucose 142 mg/dL; an extra low pitched sound just before S1. New findings: troponin I 0.38 ng/mL, was 0.04 ng/mL at 0900. The 12 lead ECG shows ST depression and no ST elevation. Blood pressure 90/56 mm Hg, heart rate 118/min. The patient is restless and asks the same question twice. Crackles are now heard in both lung bases. The patient has voided 40 mL since 0900 and has not vomited. Which problem is the priority?

options.text: Unstable glucose related to diabetes and stress
options.rationale: Stress can raise glucose in diabetes, but the glucose is 142 mg/dL and the problem now is perfusion.

options.text: Decreased cardiac output with poor perfusion
options.rationale: The mean arterial pressure is (90 + 2 x 56) / 3, about 67 mm Hg, near the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to perfuse the major organs. A rising troponin shows heart muscle injury, new crackles show the left ventricle is failing to move blood forward, and restlessness and low urine output show the brain and kidneys are short of blood.

options.text: Anxiety related to the emergency department visit
options.rationale: Restlessness and repeated questions look like anxiety, but with a falling blood pressure they are signs of reduced blood flow to the brain.

options.text: Deficient fluid volume from 2 days of nausea
options.rationale: Low blood pressure, a fast heart rate and low urine output also fit fluid loss, which makes this tempting. But the patient has not vomited, and new crackles mean fluid is backing up into the lungs, so the pump is failing, not the volume.

questions.takeaway: Mean arterial pressure = (systolic + 2 x diastolic) / 3, and a MAP of 60 to 70 mm Hg is needed to perfuse the major organs. Falling blood pressure with restlessness, low urine output and new crackles after a rising troponin is a failing pump: decreased cardiac output.
questions.strategy: Low blood pressure, a fast heart rate and low urine output fit both a fluid deficit and a failing pump. The deciding cues are the new crackles and the rising troponin, which point to the pump, and the absence of vomiting.

steps.detail: (90 + 112) / 3 is about 67 mm Hg: organ perfusion is threatened.
Restless brain, low urine from the kidneys.
New crackles and a rising troponin point to the pump; there was no vomiting.
Glucose is acceptable; the restlessness is perfusion, not anxiety.

elimination.verdict: B. Decreased cardiac output with poor perfusion.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.scenario: At 1130 the provider admits the patient to the cardiac unit and plans a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery tomorrow. Blood pressure is now 98/60 mm Hg and heart rate 110/min with oxygen applied and the patient resting in bed. Chart so far: patient, 72 years old, with type 2 diabetes mellitus who takes metformin; 2 days of tiredness and nausea; an ache in the jaw that comes and goes; no chest pain; cool, damp skin; heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg at 0900; oral temperature 37.0 °C; glucose 142 mg/dL; an extra low pitched sound just before S1. Troponin I 0.38 ng/mL, was 0.04 ng/mL at 0900; the ECG shows ST depression; crackles in both lung bases.
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with a rising troponin before a cardiac catheterization. For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this patient now.

rows.text: Continuous cardiac monitoring
rows.rationale: Heart muscle injury raises the risk of arrhythmias, so the rhythm is watched continuously.

rows.text: Repeat troponin in 3 to 6 hours as prescribed
rows.rationale: Troponin is followed as a trend. Serial values show whether the injury is still evolving.

rows.text: An exercise ECG this afternoon to look for ischemia
rows.rationale: A stress test deliberately raises the heart's oxygen demand. With a rising troponin, ST depression and low blood pressure, ischemia is already proven and active, so exercise testing is unsafe.

rows.text: A new 12 lead ECG with any new or worse jaw ache
rows.rationale: An ECG recorded during symptoms shows whether the ischemia is changing.

rows.text: A basic metabolic panel before the catheterization
rows.rationale: The panel gives potassium, which affects heart rhythm, and creatinine, which shows whether the kidneys can clear the contrast dye.

rows.text: A walk in the hall to check activity tolerance
rows.rationale: Walking raises oxygen demand in a heart that is already short of oxygen, with a low blood pressure. The patient stays on rest.

questions.takeaway: With active myocardial injury, plan to watch (continuous monitoring, serial troponin, ECG with symptoms), to prepare (a basic metabolic panel before contrast), and to avoid raising oxygen demand (no stress test, no walking).
questions.strategy: Ask of each action: does it watch the injured heart, prepare it safely, or push it harder? Anything that raises oxygen demand while the troponin is rising is not indicated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Continuous ECG, serial troponin and an ECG with symptoms are indicated.
A basic metabolic panel checks potassium and kidney function before contrast.
A stress test and a walk raise oxygen demand: not indicated.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: rows 1, 2, 4, 5. Not indicated: rows 3 and 6.
