options.rationale: On time dosing matters, but this drug may not treat the organism. The provider needs the report before the dose so the order can change.

options.text: Hold the next dose until provider rounds
options.rationale: Questioning the dose is right, but holding it without reporting leaves the patient with no treatment and no new plan.

options.text: Report the result before the next dose
options.rationale: The culture and susceptibility test identifies the organism and guides the drug choice. The nurse supports appropriate antimicrobial use by following culture results, and the provider needs this result to change the treatment.

options.text: Check the blood count to judge the drug's effect
options.rationale: The blood count adds information about the immune response, read together with the assessment. It does not answer which drug the organism responds to.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides the antimicrobial choice. The complete blood count with differential adds information about the immune response. Read every result together with the assessment, and act on a susceptibility report that does not match the drug being given.
questions.strategy: Match each test to the question it answers: which organism and which drug, or how the body is responding. Then look for the choice that both protects the patient from an ineffective drug and gets a new plan.

steps.detail: Susceptibility answers which drug works. The blood count answers how the body is responding.
Giving the dose first and holding it silently both leave the patient without an effective plan.

steps.action: Choose the action that changes the plan
steps.detail: Report before the dose is due.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the result to the provider before the next dose.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a urinary tract infection who was alert at 0700 and is confused at 0900. Temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 112/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. At 0915 the provider documents probable sepsis without shock and orders blood cultures and an intravenous antimicrobial. Facility policy states that laboratory staff draw blood cultures, and they can reach the unit at 1115. The antimicrobial arrives at 0930, and the intravenous access works. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the antimicrobial at 1115, after the blood cultures are drawn
options.rationale: Specimens are obtained before the antimicrobial when that causes no delay, and 1115 is within 3 hours. The 3 hour window is for possible sepsis without shock. Probable sepsis calls for the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour, and waiting for cultures until 1115 delays it 2 hours.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial and give it if the blood pressure falls
options.rationale: Rechecking vital signs is right, but waiting for a falling blood pressure waits for shock. The provider has documented probable sepsis, which calls for the antimicrobial now.

options.text: Draw the cultures from the existing IV line, then give the antimicrobial
options.rationale: Getting the specimen first is the right idea, but facility policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff, and the existing line is not the way the specimen is obtained.

options.text: Give the antimicrobial now, and have the cultures drawn at 1115
options.rationale: For probable sepsis the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Cultures come first only when drawing them delays the antimicrobial by no more than 45 minutes; here the delay would be 2 hours.

questions.takeaway: Probable or definite sepsis, or septic shock: give the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: investigate rapidly and begin treatment within 3 hours if concern persists. Obtain cultures first only when that does not delay the antimicrobial.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: "Without shock" and the culture first habit both point toward waiting until 1115, which is still inside 3 hours. The deciding cue is the provider's word probable: the 3 hour window belongs only to possible sepsis without shock.

steps.detail: The provider documented probable sepsis, not possible sepsis.
Probable sepsis: antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour.
Cultures first is right only when it causes no delay. A 2 hour wait is a delay.
A falling blood pressure is not required to act.
Policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff.

elimination.verdict: D. Give the antimicrobial now, and have the cultures drawn at 1115.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A patient admitted for elective surgery has a nasal swab positive for methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and no signs of infection. Which statement to the team is accurate?

options.text: "The patient is colonized, so the nose is not a reservoir."
options.rationale: Colonization is correct, but the organism is still present and can still leave the patient and reach others. A colonized patient is a reservoir.

options.text: "The patient is colonized and spreads MRSA by droplets."
options.rationale: Colonization is correct, but MRSA spreads by contact, on hands and shared equipment, not mainly by droplets.

options.text: "The patient is infected but has no fever yet."
options.rationale: The nurse does not rely on fever alone, but this patient has no signs of infection at any site. Nothing shows the organism invading and growing.

options.text: "The patient is colonized, and hands can carry it."
options.rationale: Colonization differs from infection: the organism is present without symptomatic disease. A reservoir is where the agent lives, so hands and shared equipment can carry it to the next patient.

questions.takeaway: Colonization means the organism is present without disease. A colonized patient is still a reservoir, and an infection that develops during care can come from the patient's own organisms or an outside source.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate carrying an organism from being infected by it, then follow the organism: where it lives and how it leaves. Three options agree on colonization, so the decision rests on the reservoir and the route.

steps.detail: Positive screen, no signs of infection at any site: colonization. This removes the infection option.
Colonized still means a reservoir, which removes the option that says it is not one.
MRSA travels by contact on hands and equipment, which removes the droplet option.

elimination.verdict: D. The patient is colonized, and hands can carry it.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A patient who had a stroke coughs and has a wet voice after swallowing thin liquids. Which portal of entry is at risk?

options.text: Respiratory tract, through aspirated liquid
options.rationale: Coughing and a wet voice with thin liquids mean the liquid is going into the airway. Aspiration leads to respiratory infection such as pneumonia.

options.text: Gastrointestinal tract, through swallowed liquid
options.rationale: The liquid is swallowed, but the cough and wet voice show it is not staying in the gastrointestinal tract. Ask where the organism actually gets in.

options.text: Throat lining, through injury from coughing
options.rationale: Damaged mucous membranes in the throat do allow entry, but nothing shows a damaged membrane. The finding points to the airway.

options.text: Respiratory tract, through a weakened immune response
options.rationale: The portal is right, but the reason is not. The stem shows liquid entering the airway, not a change in immunity.

questions.takeaway: Infections enter through the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts, through broken skin or damaged mucous membranes, and through vascular access and other invasive devices that bypass natural barriers.
questions.strategy: Ask where the organism would actually get in, not which body part is named first. A swallow that ends in a cough enters the airway.

steps.detail: A wet cough with thin liquids is aspiration, so respiratory tract.
Swallowing names the gastrointestinal tract, but the liquid is not staying there.
Two options name the respiratory tract; only one gives the path the stem supports.

elimination.verdict: A. Respiratory tract, through aspirated liquid.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with no diagnosed infection. Which actions follow standard precautions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hand hygiene before and after patient contact
options.rationale: Hand hygiene before and after patient contact is part of standard precautions for every patient.

options.text: Gown and gloves to empty a drain that may splash
options.rationale: Equipment is chosen for the exposure expected. Gloves protect from body fluids, and a gown is worn when drainage may reach clothing or skin.

options.text: Gloves to count a radial pulse on intact skin
options.rationale: Gloves are right for body fluids and broken skin, but counting a pulse on intact skin carries no expected exposure.

options.text: Used needle into the sharps container uncapped
options.rationale: Sharps are handled safely: needles are not recapped and go into a puncture resistant container.

options.text: No eye protection while irrigating an incision
options.rationale: Standard precautions apply whether or not an infection has been diagnosed. Irrigation can splash, so eye protection is worn.

options.text: Sanitizer on drainage soiled hands after glove removal
options.rationale: Cleaning the hands after removing gloves is right, but visibly soiled hands are washed with soap and water.

questions.takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every patient: hand hygiene before and after contact, protective equipment matched to the expected exposure, safe sharps handling, and soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each task, ask what exposure is expected, not what the patient is diagnosed with. More equipment is not safer when no exposure is expected, and a missing diagnosis never lowers the precautions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drain: gown and gloves. Irrigation: eye protection. Pulse on intact skin: no gloves needed.
No recapping, into the container.
Soiled hands need soap and water, even after gloves.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse receives report at 0700 on four patients with infections. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Urinary tract infection, day 1: heart rate 98/min and respiratory rate 22/min, were 74/min and 14/min at 0300; temperature 37.0 °C; alert
options.rationale: Every number looks only mildly off, but the heart rate rose 24 beats and the respiratory rate rose 8 breaths per minute in 4 hours, now above 20. Two vital signs moving away from baseline together is an early sign of sepsis.

options.text: Pneumonia, day 3: temperature 38.3 °C, the same at each check since admission; heart rate 96/min; alert and oriented as on admission
options.rationale: This is the only fever, but it has not changed since admission, and mental status matches baseline. The nurse does not rank patients by fever alone.

options.text: Cellulitis of the leg, day 2: heart rate 106/min, between 104 and 108/min at every check since admission; respiratory rate 18/min; alert
options.rationale: The heart rate is above range, but it has not moved since admission. Compared with baseline, nothing has changed.

options.text: Infected abdominal wound, day 4: new purulent drainage on the dressing; heart rate 84/min and temperature 37.4 °C, unchanged since admission; alert
options.rationale: New drainage is a worsening local finding that the nurse will assess and report, which makes this tempting. Every finding outside the wound is unchanged, so it can follow the patient whose whole body findings are moving.

questions.takeaway: Compare every finding with the patient's baseline and look at the trend. Values that are moving away from baseline over hours outrank values that are out of range but unchanged.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three patients have something that looks worse: the only fever, the highest heart rate, and new purulent drainage. The deciding cue is the 0300 values: only one patient's vital signs have moved away from baseline in 4 hours, and two of them moved together.

steps.action: Mark what is out of range
steps.detail: Fever in the pneumonia patient, heart rate in the cellulitis patient.
New drainage in the wound patient is local. Only the urinary tract infection patient has whole body findings moving since 0300.
A worsening wound with unchanged vital signs is not yet a response beyond the site.
A worsening trend in vital signs comes before an abnormal value that has not changed.

elimination.verdict: A. The patient with the urinary tract infection whose heart rate and respiratory rate rose since 0300.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for two patients in adjacent rooms. One patient, 70 years old, has a draining leg wound whose culture grew methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). The other patient receives immunosuppressive treatment, has a fresh abdominal incision on day 1 after surgery with no drainage, and has a central venous catheter in the chest.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for two patients in adjacent rooms. For each nursing action, indicate the link in the chain of infection that the action interrupts.

rows.text: Covering the draining MRSA wound with an intact dressing
rows.rationale: This wound holds the organism, so the dressing contains drainage at the point where organisms leave the reservoir. The same action on a clean wound would protect entry instead.

rows.text: Covering the fresh surgical incision of the patient on immunosuppressive treatment with a sterile dressing
rows.rationale: This incision holds no known organism. A fresh surgical incision on day 1 after surgery has not yet sealed, so the dressing protects a place where organisms could get in. It acts on entry, not exit.

rows.text: Performing hand hygiene before touching the central venous catheter
rows.rationale: Hands carry organisms from one person or surface to the next. Clean hands remove the vehicle before it reaches the catheter, so the action works on transmission.

rows.text: Using sterile technique and placing a sterile dressing over the central venous catheter insertion site
rows.rationale: The catheter is a direct pathway into the bloodstream. A sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry point itself, not what carries organisms to it.

rows.text: Giving the prescribed antimicrobial to the patient with the MRSA wound
rows.rationale: Treatment acts on the organism where it lives, in the wound of the patient who is the reservoir.

rows.text: Offering the patient with the MRSA wound, 70 years old, a recommended vaccine before discharge
rows.rationale: This patient is the reservoir for MRSA, but the vaccine does nothing to that organism. It lowers this patient's risk for the infections the vaccine covers, so it acts on the patient as a host.

questions.takeaway: The same action can break different links. A dressing over a wound that holds the organism blocks the exit; over a fresh clean incision it protects the entry. Hand hygiene stops the carrier; a sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry. A vaccine always acts on the host, even in a patient who is also a reservoir.
questions.strategy: For each row, ask whether the action works on the organism's source, on what carries it, or on the place it would get in. The cue is in the row: does the wound hold the organism, and does the action clean the carrier or protect the entry point?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The MRSA wound holds the organism: portal of exit. The fresh incision on a patient on immunosuppressive treatment: portal of entry.
Hand hygiene cleans the carrier: method of transmission. A sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry: portal of entry.

steps.action: Place the antimicrobial and the vaccine
steps.detail: The antimicrobial acts on the agent in its reservoir. The vaccine changes the person's susceptibility: susceptible host.

elimination.verdict: Portal of exit; portal of entry; method of transmission; portal of entry; agent and reservoir; susceptible host.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: The nurse sustains a needlestick after giving a subcutaneous injection. The patient's record lists no known bloodborne infection. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Finish the medication pass, then report the injury
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but needlestick injuries are reported immediately. Delaying the report for routine medications delays evaluation and follow up care.

options.text: Report it and ask the provider if evaluation is needed
options.rationale: Reporting at once is right, but the record lists no known infection, which does not mean no infection. The facility exposure protocol, not a case by case decision, directs evaluation for every needlestick.

options.text: Report it now and follow the exposure protocol
options.rationale: Needlestick injuries and blood exposures are reported to supervisors immediately, documented at the scene, and followed through the facility exposure protocol for evaluation and follow up care. First aid is washing the site with soap and water; the report follows at once.

options.text: Get the patient's consent for testing, then report it
options.rationale: The nurse does not hold the report while collecting more information. The exposure protocol directs evaluation, and the report comes first.

questions.takeaway: Report a needlestick injury or blood exposure to the supervisor immediately, document it at the scene, and follow the facility exposure protocol whatever the patient's known history.
questions.strategy: Two options report at once. The difference is whether evaluation depends on the patient's record. A record with no known infection never makes the exposure protocol optional.

steps.detail: Finishing medications first puts routine work ahead of an exposure.
Getting the patient's consent first is another delay.

steps.action: Compare the two that report now
steps.detail: No known infection is not the same as no infection, so the protocol applies without asking.

elimination.verdict: C. Report it now and follow the exposure protocol.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an older adult with an infected pressure injury. Which findings should the nurse interpret as cues of sepsis in this patient? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cool, clammy skin and a low temperature
options.rationale: Temperature changes are common early signs of sepsis, and they include feeling cold and clammy as well as fever. A low temperature is a cue, not reassurance.

options.text: Wound pain unchanged at 2 of 10 since admission
options.rationale: Pain that has not changed from baseline is not a new cue, and it cannot explain the new changes in breathing or mentation.

options.text: Respiratory rate up from 16 to 26/min
options.rationale: Faster breathing is a concerning early cue. The body may be struggling to meet its metabolic demands.

options.text: New lethargy from an alert baseline
options.rationale: A sudden change in mental status from baseline is an early cue. New confusion or decreased alertness is evidence of organ dysfunction.

options.text: Eating half of each meal, as usual
options.rationale: Intake that matches the patient's usual pattern is not a change from baseline, so it is not a cue of sepsis.

options.text: Heart rate unchanged at 78/min
options.rationale: A heart rate that has not changed from baseline is not a cue. Sepsis is suspected from the other new changes even without a fast heart rate.

questions.takeaway: Early cues of sepsis are new changes from baseline: confusion or lethargy, faster breathing, and fever or feeling cold and clammy. A fever is not required, and findings unchanged from baseline are not cues.
questions.strategy: Test each finding against the patient's own baseline. A new change in mentation, breathing, or temperature is a cue, even without a fever; a finding that has not changed is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only new changes count as cues.
New lethargy and a rising respiratory rate: cues.
Cool, clammy skin with a low temperature: a cue, not reassurance.
Unchanged pain, usual intake, and an unchanged heart rate: not cues.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: The nurse calls a rapid response for a patient with an infected pressure injury who is newly lethargic, with heart rate up from 90 to 114/min. Which statement should open the report?

options.text: "Infected pressure injury. Heart rate 114, respiratory rate 26. Please assess."
options.rationale: The current values are accurate, but without the baseline of 90 the team cannot see the change, the new lethargy is left out, and no concern is stated.

options.text: "Lethargic with low urine output, but no fever, so likely local."
options.rationale: The findings are right, but the conclusion is wrong. The nurse does not rely on fever alone, and the change from baseline points toward sepsis.

options.text: "The patient looks septic and needs fluids now. Please come."
options.rationale: The concern is right, but the statement gives no findings. The team needs the changes that led the nurse to escalate.

options.text: "Infected wound, newly lethargic, heart rate 90 to 114. I suspect sepsis."
options.rationale: This names the likely source, gives the change from baseline in mentation and heart rate, and states the concern. Trends from baseline make the deterioration clear.

questions.takeaway: When escalating care, give the likely source, the change from the patient's baseline in breathing, mentation, circulation, and urine output, and the concern itself.
questions.strategy: Every option names something true. Pick the one that lets the team see the trend: current values alone hide how far the patient has moved from baseline.

steps.detail: No fever does not mean the infection is not spreading.
Urgency without findings gives the team nothing to act on.
Current values alone versus values with their baseline: the trend shows the deterioration.

elimination.verdict: The report that gives the source, the change from baseline, and the concern for sepsis.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: The nurse has intravenous antimicrobial doses ready at 0930 for four patients and can start only one at a time. Each order states to give the dose now. Which patient should the nurse give the antimicrobial to first?

options.text: Urinary tract infection: provider documented possible sepsis without shock at 0900; blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 108/min; alert
options.rationale: This patient was documented first and has the lower blood pressure, but possible sepsis without shock calls for rapid investigation and treatment within 3 hours if concern persists. That window allows this dose to follow the patient who needs it within 1 hour.

options.text: Pneumonia: provider documented infection without signs of sepsis at 0850; temperature 38.9 °C, respiratory rate 20/min; alert
options.rationale: This is the highest temperature, but the provider found no sepsis. The nurse does not rank patients by fever alone.

options.text: Cellulitis of the leg: provider documented probable sepsis at 0920; blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, heart rate 102/min; alert
options.rationale: For probable or definite sepsis, the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. The provider's category, not the blood pressure, sets the time limit, so this patient is first.

options.text: Infected foot wound: day 3 of treatment, dose due at 0930; temperature 37.4 °C, heart rate 88/min; alert
options.rationale: A dose on time matters, but this patient shows no sepsis and is on day 3 of treatment. It can follow the patients who have a sepsis time limit.

questions.takeaway: The Hour 1 bundle sets the time limit by category: septic shock or probable or definite sepsis gets the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour; possible sepsis without shock is investigated rapidly and treated within 3 hours if concern persists.
questions.strategy: The urinary tract infection patient looks sicker and was documented first. The deciding cue is the provider's category: possible sepsis without shock versus probable sepsis, which carries the shorter time limit.

steps.detail: Pneumonia without sepsis and the day 3 foot wound have no sepsis time limit.
One has possible sepsis without shock, the other probable sepsis.
Probable sepsis: within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: within 3 hours if concern persists. A lower blood pressure that is not shock does not change the category.

elimination.verdict: The patient with cellulitis and probable sepsis documented at 0920.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A patient with dehydration has cracked lips, a skin tear, and a urinary catheter and is due for vaccines. Which actions lower this patient's risk for infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give mouth care and moisten cracked lips
options.rationale: Intact skin and mucous membranes form barriers. Cracked lips and a dry mouth are breaks in that barrier, and mouth care helps restore it.

options.text: Cover a skin tear and prevent new tears
options.rationale: Broken skin gives organisms direct access. Covering the tear and preventing new ones protects the skin barrier.

options.text: Clean hands before and after touching the catheter
options.rationale: Hand hygiene and care of invasive devices help prevent exposure. The catheter bypasses natural barriers, so clean hands at every contact matter.

options.text: Offer recommended vaccines per protocol
options.rationale: Vaccination reduces risk for the infections covered by recommended vaccines. It strengthens the host's own defenses, and this patient is due for them.

options.text: Ask the provider for a preventive antibiotic
options.rationale: No infection has been identified. Antibiotics given without an indication do not strengthen defenses, and unnecessary use contributes to resistance.

options.text: Use alcohol based sanitizer on hands soiled with stool
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is right, but hands that are visibly soiled need soap and water. Alcohol based sanitizer is preferred only when hands are not visibly soiled.

questions.takeaway: The body defends itself with intact skin and mucous membranes and with inflammation and immune responses. Nurses support those defenses, offer recommended vaccines, and prevent exposure with hand hygiene and device care.
questions.strategy: For each action, ask whether it protects a barrier, strengthens the host, or blocks exposure. An action that only looks protective, or uses the wrong hand hygiene method, is false.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cracked lips and a skin tear are broken barriers: mouth care and covering the tear are true.
Hand hygiene around the catheter prevents exposure: true.
Recommended vaccines lower risk: true.
An antibiotic with no infection is not prevention; visibly soiled hands need soap and water: false, false.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient is at highest risk for developing sepsis?

options.text: Age 84, cellulitis shrinking on antimicrobials, no devices
options.rationale: Older age is a risk factor, but this infection is shrinking on treatment and there are no devices. A worsening infection, not an older age alone, is the stronger warning.

options.text: Age 61, chemotherapy, central port, worsening urinary infection
options.rationale: This patient combines reduced immune function, an invasive device, chronic illness, and an infection that is getting worse. Each is a listed risk factor for sepsis, and together they make this patient the highest risk.

options.text: Age 35, nasal swab positive for a resistant organism, no infection signs
options.rationale: A resistant organism sounds dangerous, but this is colonization, not infection. Sepsis is a response to an infection, and none is present.

options.text: Age 52, diabetes, heel blister with no signs of infection
options.rationale: Chronic illness is a risk factor, but the blister shows no sign of infection, and sepsis needs an infection to start.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for sepsis: older adults, reduced immune function, chronic illness or serious wounds, invasive devices or recent procedures, and anyone whose infection is worsening. Risk rises as factors add up on top of an active infection.
questions.strategy: Sepsis starts with an infection. Remove the patients who have none, then compare an improving infection with a worsening one in a patient with several risk factors.

steps.detail: Colonization with a resistant organism and an uninfected blister cannot lead to sepsis yet.
Cellulitis is shrinking on treatment; the urinary tract infection is worsening.
Chemotherapy, cancer, and a central port add reduced immunity, chronic illness, and a device.

elimination.verdict: The patient receiving chemotherapy with a central venous port and a worsening urinary tract infection.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.scenario: A patient is on day 2 after surgery on the hip. At 0700 the patient was alert and oriented, heart rate 84/min, respiratory rate 18/min, urine output 50 mL per hour. At 1100 the patient is confused, heart rate 116/min, respiratory rate 26/min, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C, and urine output 20 mL per hour. The hip incision is red with cloudy drainage. The patient has an indwelling urinary catheter and a peripheral intravenous catheter. The nurse has activated the rapid response process, and the provider has ordered blood cultures and a serum lactate.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient on day 2 after hip surgery whose condition has changed since 0700. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this patient now.

rows.text: Trend vital signs, oxygen saturation, mental status, and hourly urine output against the 0700 values
rows.rationale: Sepsis assessment trends vital signs, oxygenation, mental status, and urine output. The 0700 values are the baseline that shows how far the patient has moved.

rows.text: Inspect the hip incision, the urinary catheter, and the intravenous site for a likely source of infection
rows.rationale: The nurse assesses for a likely infection source. The cloudy drainage is a strong lead, but the catheter and the intravenous site are also possible sources.

rows.text: Prepare for the ordered blood cultures and serum lactate, and check that the intravenous access works
rows.rationale: The nurse anticipates ordered cultures and lactate testing, obtains ordered specimens, and assesses intravenous access so treatment is not delayed.

rows.text: Hold further assessments until the lactate result shows whether the patient has sepsis
rows.rationale: Clinical assessment remains essential alongside diagnostic information. No single test confirms sepsis, and the findings are already changing.

rows.text: Treat a single lactate result that is not elevated as ruling out sepsis
rows.rationale: No single test confirms or rules out sepsis, and a lactate result is interpreted with the assessment, not instead of it. New confusion, a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, and low urine output remain signs of organ dysfunction.

rows.text: Wait for organisms to grow in the blood cultures before treating the condition as sepsis
rows.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

questions.takeaway: In suspected sepsis, trend vital signs, oxygenation, mental status, and urine output; look for the source; anticipate cultures and lactate. Tests support the clinical assessment and never replace it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each action by whether it keeps the clinical assessment going or waits on a test result. Waiting on a lactate or a culture is the trap.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trending against 0700 and searching for the source are indicated.
Ordered cultures, lactate, and working intravenous access are indicated.
Holding assessment for a lactate, trusting one lactate value, or waiting for culture growth are not indicated.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: trend against 0700, find the source, prepare for cultures and lactate. Not indicated: holding assessment, trusting one lactate value, waiting for culture growth.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a cough for 6 weeks, night sweats, and weight loss. The provider documents suspected pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) and orders sputum specimens. The patient coughs often and is waiting in a private room with the door closed. Which precautions should the nurse implement?

options.text: Move to an airborne infection isolation room, and wear a fitted respirator
options.rationale: Tuberculosis spreads by particles that stay suspended in the air, so an airborne infection isolation room and respiratory protection are needed, along with standard precautions.

options.text: Keep the private room with the door closed, and wear a fitted respirator
options.rationale: The respirator is right, which makes this the near miss. A private room with the door closed lacks the monitored negative airflow of an airborne infection isolation room, so particles still leave the room.

options.text: Keep the private room with the door closed, and wear a surgical mask
options.rationale: A mask and a private room fit droplet precautions, where large droplets reach nearby mucous membranes. Tuberculosis particles remain suspended in the air, so a surgical mask is not enough.

options.text: Mask the patient, and use standard precautions until the sputum results return
options.rationale: Masking the patient is part of respiratory hygiene, but precautions start when the infection is suspected. Waiting for results leaves staff and other patients exposed.

questions.takeaway: Droplet precautions use a mask and patient placement; airborne precautions use an airborne infection isolation room and respiratory protection. Choose by how the organism travels, and start them when infection is suspected.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options sound protective: a respirator in the current room, a mask in the current room, and masking the patient. Decide by the route and then by both parts of the precaution: particles suspended in the air need the right room and the right respirator.

steps.detail: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis spreads by particles suspended in air.
Precautions begin on suspicion, so waiting for results is out.
A surgical mask is droplet protection; airborne needs a fitted respirator.
Two options have the respirator; only one moves the patient to an airborne infection isolation room.

elimination.verdict: A. Airborne infection isolation room and a fitted respirator.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is assigned a patient transferred from another hospital this morning. The transfer record shows a urine culture positive for carbapenem resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) 5 days ago. Which action should the nurse take before entering the room?

options.text: Wear gloves only when in contact with the urine
options.rationale: The culture came from urine, which makes limiting protection to urine contact tempting. CRE spreads by contact with the patient and the environment, not only through urine, so gloves for urine alone leave the nurse's clothing and other surfaces exposed. The guidance for CRE comes first.

options.text: Use standard precautions until a repeat urine culture is reported
options.rationale: The positive culture from 5 days ago is enough to act on. Waiting leaves other patients exposed.

options.text: Add a mask and eye protection for a resistant organism
options.rationale: CRE spreads by contact with the patient and the environment, not through the air.

options.text: Check the facility guidance for CRE before entering the room
options.rationale: Vancomycin resistant Enterococcus (VRE) and CRE require checking organism specific precautions before care. The nurse then adds what the guidance lists, typically contact precautions with a gown and gloves, to standard precautions.

questions.takeaway: Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), VRE, and CRE are resistant organisms, and VRE and CRE require checking the facility's organism specific precautions before care. Those precautions are typically contact precautions, added to the standard precautions that continue for every patient.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is a guess: gloves for the urine because that is where the culture came from, standard precautions because the culture is old, or a mask because the organism is resistant. The cue is the organism named: CRE means check the organism specific guidance before care, so the action before entry is the check, not a guess.

steps.detail: CRE, carbapenem resistant Enterobacterales.

steps.action: Reject waiting and the wrong route
steps.detail: The culture from 5 days ago is enough to act on, and CRE does not spread through the air.
Gloves for urine alone assume the organism stays in the urine; checking the guidance confirms the full precautions before care.

elimination.verdict: D. Check the facility guidance for CRE before entering the room.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to send a bedside commode used by a patient with confirmed Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) to the equipment room for another patient. On this unit the quaternary ammonium wipe is the routine for commodes after patients with methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Which action should the nurse take with the commode?

options.text: Clean the commode with the bleach based wipe
options.rationale: C. difficile spores persist in the environment, and standard disinfectants may not kill them. Shared equipment is cleaned with a sporicidal agent, and a bleach based (chlorine) product is sporicidal.

options.text: Clean the commode with the quaternary ammonium wipe
options.rationale: This is the unit routine and it works for many organisms, including MRSA, which makes it the near miss. Quaternary ammonium is not sporicidal, so C. difficile spores may survive it.

options.text: Scrub the commode with soap and water, then dry it
options.rationale: Soap and water is used for hand hygiene with C. difficile, which makes this tempting. It does not replace sporicidal cleaning of equipment.

options.text: Clean the commode twice with the quaternary ammonium wipe
options.rationale: Extra effort feels safer, but repeating a product that does not kill spores does not make it sporicidal.

questions.takeaway: C. difficile spores persist in the environment, and standard disinfectants such as quaternary ammonium may not be effective. Enhanced contact precautions include dedicated or appropriately cleaned equipment and sporicidal environmental cleaning, such as a bleach based product.
questions.strategy: Three options sound thorough: the unit's routine wipe, the hand hygiene method used for C. difficile, and a double wipe. The organism decides: spores persist and need a sporicidal agent such as bleach, whatever the routine is for MRSA.

steps.detail: C. difficile forms spores that persist on surfaces.
Quaternary ammonium is the routine disinfectant, not a sporicide. Bleach is sporicidal.
The quaternary ammonium wipe, once or twice, may not kill spores.
Soap and water is hand hygiene, not equipment cleaning.

elimination.verdict: A. Clean the commode with the bleach based wipe.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient in the clinic who has a sore throat, a cough, and thick green nasal drainage. The provider diagnoses a viral upper respiratory infection and prescribes rest and fluids. The patient says, "The green mucus means it is turning into an infection. Can I get an antibiotic just to be safe?" Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "I will ask the provider to reconsider, since the drainage is green."
options.rationale: This sounds like advocacy, but it reinforces the false belief about green mucus, and the diagnosis is already made. Teaching why an antibiotic will not help is the nurse's role here.

options.text: "The color of the mucus does not tell us what kind of infection you have."
options.rationale: This is a true correction, but it does not answer the request for an antibiotic.

options.text: "A decongestant from the pharmacy can ease the stuffiness and congestion while you rest."
options.rationale: This is caring, but it sidesteps the question and leaves the belief in place.

options.text: "Antibiotics do not work on viruses, and taking one you do not need can cause harm."
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections, and unnecessary use contributes to resistance. The response answers both the request and the belief behind "just to be safe" in plain language.

questions.takeaway: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections, and unnecessary use contributes to antimicrobial resistance. The nurse supports appropriate antimicrobial use through teaching.
questions.strategy: Three responses are things a nurse might say: relay the concern, correct the mucus myth, or offer comfort. The cue is "just to be safe": only one response answers the request itself and the belief behind it.

steps.detail: Viral upper respiratory infection, already made.
An antibiotic "just to be safe", driven by green mucus.

steps.action: Test each response against the request
steps.detail: Relaying it reinforces the myth; correcting the color does not answer it; a decongestant sidesteps it.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses and unneeded use causes harm.

elimination.verdict: D. "Antibiotics do not work on viruses, and taking one you do not need can cause harm."

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who had an indwelling urinary catheter placed on admission for a hip fracture. On day 5 the urine is cloudy, and the urine culture grows an organism from the patient's own bowel. A family member asks, "Since the germ came from the patient's own body, did this infection have anything to do with the hospital care?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "No, an infection from the patient's own germs is not counted as hospital related."
options.rationale: This is the common belief, but healthcare associated infections can come from the patient's own organisms or from an outside source.

options.text: "Yes, a caregiver's hands must have carried the germ in."
options.rationale: An outside source is possible, but the culture shows an organism from the patient's own bowel.

options.text: "Yes, it began during care, and the catheter let the patient's own germs in."
options.rationale: The infection developed on day 5 of care, after the catheter was placed. Organisms for a healthcare associated infection may come from the patient, and the catheter bypasses natural barriers.

options.text: "No, an infection like this comes from a weak immune system."
options.rationale: Age extremes and illness raise risk, which makes this sound reasonable, but the catheter placed in the hospital created a direct path for the organism.

questions.takeaway: A healthcare associated infection develops during healthcare delivery. The organism may come from the patient or an outside source, and invasive devices such as urinary catheters create a path past natural barriers.
questions.strategy: The source of the organism sounds like it decides. The cue that decides is when and how the infection developed: on day 5, after a catheter placed during care.

steps.detail: The infection appeared on day 5, after the catheter was placed.

steps.action: Compare the yes and no answers
steps.detail: Healthcare associated infections can come from the patient's own organisms.
The culture names the patient's bowel organism, not a caregiver's hands; the catheter gave it a path.

elimination.verdict: C. Yes, it began during care, and the catheter let the patient's own germs in.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.scenario: During a morning huddle on a medical unit, the nurse reviews findings and team comments about several patients and the unit as a whole.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings and team comments during a morning huddle on a medical unit. For each finding or comment, indicate the term that best describes it.

rows.text: A rectal swab taken on admission grows vancomycin resistant Enterococcus (VRE); the patient has formed stools and an oral temperature of 36.9 °C
rows.rationale: The organism is present, but there is no sign of disease. Colonization differs from infection, and the patient is still a source the team must contain.

rows.text: After 3 days of an antibiotic, the organisms that normally live in the patient's bowel are reduced, and liquid stools begin
rows.rationale: The microbiome is the set of microorganisms normally living in and on the body. Antibiotics can disturb it, which changes how the bowel works.

rows.text: One case of influenza on the unit was followed by 6 more cases in patients and staff within 4 days
rows.rationale: Communicability is the ability to spread. Fast spread from one case to many describes how readily the organism moves between people.

rows.text: A small number of organisms entered a cut on the hand and caused severe tissue damage within 24 hours
rows.rationale: Virulence is the ability to cause disease. Severe damage from few organisms in a short time describes a highly virulent organism, not how easily it spreads.

rows.text: The knee incision is red and swollen with purulent drainage, and the culture grows Staphylococcus aureus
rows.rationale: Infection is invasion and growth of a pathogen in the body. Here the organism has invaded and is producing signs of disease at the site.

rows.text: Skin swabs of a patient with no wounds or symptoms grow organisms that are always present on healthy skin
rows.rationale: These organisms normally live on the body and cause no harm. They are part of the microbiome, not colonization by a pathogen or an infection.

questions.takeaway: Infection is invasion and growth of a pathogen. Colonization is presence without disease. Virulence is how able an organism is to cause disease, communicability is how able it is to spread, and the microbiome is the organisms that normally live in and on the body.
questions.strategy: Ask what each statement is about: whether disease is present, how severe the disease is, how far it spread, or which organisms belong there normally.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Signs at the site mean infection; an organism with no signs means colonization.
Severe damage from few organisms is virulence; many cases from one is communicability.
Organisms that normally live on skin and in the bowel are the microbiome.

elimination.verdict: Colonization, microbiome, communicability, virulence, infection, microbiome.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient with dehydration. Which findings indicate a portal of entry that increases this patient's risk for infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Red, irritated eyes from frequent rubbing
options.rationale: Damaged mucous membranes, including the conjunctiva, allow organisms to enter.

options.text: A healed surgical scar with intact skin
options.rationale: A healed scar with intact skin is a barrier again. It does not provide a path for organisms.

options.text: A peripheral IV catheter placed today
options.rationale: An invasive device breaks the skin and gives organisms a direct path into the body.

options.text: Wears glasses for close work and hearing aids
options.rationale: Glasses and hearing aids do not break skin or mucous membranes and are not invasive devices.

options.text: Colonoscopy with biopsy 2 days ago
options.rationale: Medical procedures in the GI tract are a route for gastrointestinal infection.

options.text: Raw, cracked lining of the throat
options.rationale: Damaged mucous membranes in the throat allow organisms to enter.

questions.takeaway: Infections enter through mucous membrane lined tracts. Gastrointestinal infections can follow medical procedures, damaged membranes of the throat or conjunctiva let organisms in, and invasive devices such as IV catheters bypass natural barriers.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether a barrier is broken, a device bypasses it, or a tract has been entered by a procedure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red, irritated eyes and a raw, cracked throat lining.
A new IV catheter and a recent colonoscopy with biopsy.
A healed scar with intact skin; glasses and hearing aids.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: In a clinic waiting room, a patient with a new, undiagnosed cough is coughing near others without covering the mouth. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Wait for a diagnosis before choosing precautions
options.rationale: Standard precautions, including respiratory hygiene, apply to every patient whether or not an infection has been diagnosed. Waiting leaves the others exposed.

options.text: Put on a gown and gloves for this patient
options.rationale: Contact spread comes from touching a person or a contaminated item, such as wound drainage or shared equipment. A cough near other people is a respiratory concern, and gown and gloves do nothing to contain it.

options.text: Use a fitted respirator and an airborne isolation room
options.rationale: An airborne isolation room fits a suspected airborne infection. Nothing in the stem suggests one, and the first step is containing the cough at its source.

options.text: Give a mask and tissues and seat the patient apart
options.rationale: Standard precautions apply to every patient whether or not an infection has been diagnosed, and respiratory hygiene is one of them: covering the cough, a mask if tolerated, and separation from others. The uncovered cough near others is the reason to start it now.

questions.takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every patient whether or not an infection has been diagnosed, and they include respiratory hygiene. In practice that means covering the cough, a mask if tolerated, and hand hygiene after coughing.
questions.strategy: No diagnosis is needed for standard precautions. Match the precaution to the concern in the stem: a cough near other people.

steps.detail: They apply before any diagnosis, so waiting is wrong.
A cough near others calls for respiratory hygiene, not contact gear.
An airborne isolation room has no supporting cue.

elimination.verdict: D. Give a mask and tissues and seat the patient apart.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient who coughs often and has a respiratory infection spread by droplets. Which plan for placement and precautions is correct?

options.text: Gown and gloves, with dedicated equipment
options.rationale: These are contact precautions, for spread by touching a person or a contaminated item. Droplets reach nearby mucous membranes, so a mask is the key protection.

options.text: Airborne isolation room and a fitted respirator
options.rationale: These are airborne precautions, for particles that stay suspended in the air. Droplet spread needs a mask and placement, not an isolation room.

options.text: A mask, with placement away from other patients
options.rationale: Droplet precautions use a mask and appropriate placement. Droplets reach nearby mucous membranes, so the concern is coughing near another person. A private room is the usual way to meet this.

options.text: A mask, with a bed next to a postoperative patient
options.rationale: The mask is right, but placement is wrong. Coughing near another person is the concern with droplet spread, and a postoperative patient is a susceptible host.

questions.takeaway: Droplet spread happens when respiratory droplets reach nearby mucous membranes, so coughing near another person is the concern. Droplet precautions are a mask and appropriate placement that keeps the patient from coughing near others.
questions.strategy: Name the route first, then check both parts of the precaution: the protection and the placement.

steps.detail: The provider documents droplet spread.
Droplet means a mask and appropriate placement.
Only one places the patient away from a susceptible roommate.

elimination.verdict: C. A mask and placement away from other patients.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: Before collecting sputum from a patient with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID 19), the nurse puts on a gown, gloves, and a fitted respirator. What else should the nurse wear?

options.text: Goggles or a face shield
options.rationale: Precautions for COVID 19 call for appropriate respiratory protection and eye protection. The respirator covers the first; the eyes are still exposed to a cough at close range.

options.text: A second fitted respirator
options.rationale: A second respirator adds nothing once the first is fitted. The gap in protection is the eyes.

options.text: Sterile gloves
options.rationale: Clean gloves are already on for contact with sputum. Sterile gloves add nothing to COVID 19 precautions; eye protection is the missing piece.

options.text: No additional protection
options.rationale: The respirator alone leaves the eyes unprotected, and COVID 19 precautions include eye protection.

questions.takeaway: Precautions for COVID 19 combine appropriate respiratory protection with eye protection, with placement and other details per facility policy. Standard precautions continue alongside them.
questions.strategy: The nurse already has the respiratory protection. Ask which part of the COVID 19 precautions is still missing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Respiratory protection plus eye protection.
A gown and clean gloves cover contact with sputum; a fitted respirator covers the respiratory part.
The eyes are still exposed.

elimination.verdict: A. Goggles or a face shield.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is working on a medical unit. When should the nurse use alcohol based hand sanitizer? Select all that apply.

options.text: Before counting a pulse, hands not visibly soiled
options.rationale: Alcohol based sanitizer is preferred in most routine clinical situations when hands are not visibly soiled.

options.text: After using the restroom
options.rationale: Soap and water is used after using the restroom.

options.text: Before eating lunch
options.rationale: Soap and water is used before eating.

options.text: After removing intact gloves, hands not visibly soiled
options.rationale: Hands are cleaned after removing gloves. With no visible soil, sanitizer is the preferred method.

options.text: In place of gloves to empty a wound drain
options.rationale: Sanitizer does not replace appropriate protective equipment. Gloves are worn for expected contact with drainage.

options.text: After wound drainage soaks through the glove onto the hand
options.rationale: Hands that are visibly soiled are washed with soap and water.

questions.takeaway: Use alcohol based sanitizer for routine care when hands are not visibly soiled. Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled, before eating, and after using the restroom. Clean hands after removing gloves, and never use sanitizer in place of protective equipment.
questions.strategy: Sort each situation by two questions: are the hands visibly soiled, and is it eating or toileting? If neither, sanitizer is preferred.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drainage on the hand calls for soap and water.
Both call for soap and water.
Sanitizer never replaces gloves.
Before a pulse check and after glove removal with clean hands.

elimination.verdict: A, D.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The adult child of a patient on contact precautions asks, "I am family. Do I really need all this gear?" Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "It is the hospital rule, so please follow the sign on the door."
options.rationale: The visitor asked why. Citing a rule without explaining it does not help the visitor follow the precautions correctly.

options.text: "It spreads by touch, so let me show you the gear first."
options.rationale: Precautions are explained in plain language, and visitors are taught the required hand hygiene and protective equipment before entering the care area.

options.text: "Family is already exposed at home, so you can skip it."
options.rationale: Contact precautions address contact with the patient and the environment. Prior exposure does not remove the need for them.

options.text: "Go in now, and I will show you the gear next time."
options.rationale: Teaching after entry leaves the visitor unprotected during this visit. Visitors are taught before entering.

questions.takeaway: Explain precautions to patients, visitors, and staff in plain language, and teach visitors the required hand hygiene and protective equipment before they enter the care area.
questions.strategy: The visitor's question asks why. Choose the response that explains in plain words and teaches before entry.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The visitor wants to know why.
Teaching happens before entering, not after.
Prior exposure at home does not waive contact precautions.

elimination.verdict: B. Explain in plain language and teach before entry.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A patient who lives alone is going home on an oral antibiotic 4 times a day for cellulitis. Which finding is most likely to interfere with treatment?

options.text: No fever, and redness inside the skin marking
options.rationale: A receding border and no fever show the infection is responding. This finding supports discharge.

options.text: "I take my pills with orange juice."
options.rationale: The method of taking a pill is a minor teaching point. It does not stop the patient from taking the doses.

options.text: Blood glucose 168 mg/dL, near the usual home readings
options.rationale: Diabetes affects immune status and is part of the infection risk, but this value matches the patient's usual readings. It does not by itself stop the antibiotic from working.

options.text: "When unsure if I took a pill, I skip it."
options.rationale: The nurse considers the patient's ability to follow the care plan. Skipped doses of an antibiotic taken 4 times a day leave the infection undertreated.

questions.takeaway: The infection assessment considers the patient's immune status and the ability to follow the care plan. A patient who cannot follow the antibiotic schedule is at risk for an undertreated infection.
questions.strategy: Ask which finding directly stops the treatment from being carried out. A known, usual value is less urgent than a behavior that removes doses.

steps.detail: No fever and a receding border show response.
The glucose matches the patient's usual readings.

steps.action: Find the threat to the plan
steps.detail: Skipped doses undercut the antibiotic course.

elimination.verdict: D. The patient skips doses when unsure.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: A patient with a fever and fast breathing has a normal white blood cell count and a lung infiltrate on radiograph. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: The radiograph shows the site; breathing shows the effect.
options.rationale: Imaging helps locate the infection, and results are read together with the assessment. The fever and fast breathing show the infection's effect even though the cell count is not raised.

options.text: The normal cell count makes infection unlikely.
options.rationale: The blood count adds information about the immune response, but it is one piece. It does not outweigh the fever, the fast breathing, and the infiltrate.

options.text: Care must wait for the pending sputum culture.
options.rationale: The culture identifies the organism and guides the antimicrobial choice, but the other results and the assessment guide care now.

options.text: The radiograph identifies the organism, so cancel the culture.
options.rationale: Imaging locates the infection; it does not identify the organism. Culture and susceptibility does that.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides treatment, the complete blood count with differential adds information about the immune response, and imaging helps locate the infection or its effects. Each result is interpreted together with the assessment.
questions.strategy: Match each test to what it can tell you, then check which statement reads the results with the assessment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Culture names the organism; the blood count shows the immune response; imaging locates the source.
Imaging cannot replace the culture.
Fever and fast breathing outweigh a cell count that is not raised.

elimination.verdict: A. The radiograph locates the source, read with the assessment.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A patient with a urinary tract infection has fever, chills, and dry mucous membranes. The urine culture is collected. An IV antimicrobial is prescribed. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give the first antimicrobial dose now
options.rationale: The antimicrobial is prescribed and the culture is already collected, so nothing stands in the way of the first dose. The nurse treats the suspected cause as ordered.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial until the temperature comes down
options.rationale: The antimicrobial treats the cause of the fever. Holding it delays treatment.

options.text: Offer fluids often and record intake and output
options.rationale: Supporting hydration is part of infection treatment, and dry mucous membranes with fever point to fluid loss.

options.text: Change damp linen and offer a light blanket
options.rationale: Supporting comfort is part of treatment. Damp linen and chills add to the discomfort of fever.

options.text: Limit oral fluids during the infection
options.rationale: Limiting fluids worsens dehydration. Hydration is supported, not restricted.

options.text: Check the drug, dose, and route against the order
options.rationale: Prescribed antimicrobials are given safely, which includes checking the order before the dose. Checking allergies before a first dose is part of the same check.

questions.takeaway: Treat the suspected or identified cause as ordered, give prescribed antimicrobials safely, and support hydration and comfort.
questions.strategy: Sort each action into treating the cause, giving the drug safely, supporting hydration, supporting comfort, or getting in the way of treatment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Give the ordered dose now, after checking the order.
Offer fluids and track intake and output.
Dry linen and a light blanket for chills.
Holding the dose and limiting fluids.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.nursesNote: Day 3 of admission for an infected wound on the left foot, 1600. Dressing on the left foot dry and intact. Skin warm and flushed, heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 86 beats per minute at 1000. New pinpoint purple rash on both lower legs. Alert, oriented, and asking about dinner. Bowel sounds present in all 4 quadrants. Left foot pain 9 of 10, was 3 of 10 at 1000. Healed scar on the right knee. Oxygen saturation 91% on room air, was 96% at 1000.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 1600 note of a patient on day 3 of admission for an infected foot wound. Highlight the findings that suggest sepsis.

segments.text: Dressing on the left foot dry and intact.
segments.rationale: A dry, intact dressing shows no new drainage. It is not a sign of sepsis.

segments.text: Skin warm and flushed, heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 86 beats per minute at 1000.
segments.rationale: A fast heart rate with warm skin is a sign of sepsis. Warm skin does not mean the patient is doing well.

segments.text: New pinpoint purple rash on both lower legs.
segments.rationale: A new rash can be a sign of sepsis, especially away from the infected site.

segments.text: Alert, oriented, and asking about dinner.
segments.rationale: Mental status is at baseline. Sepsis can still be present, but this finding is not a cue of it.

segments.text: Bowel sounds present in all 4 quadrants.
segments.rationale: Bowel sounds in all quadrants are an expected finding.

segments.text: Left foot pain 9 of 10, was 3 of 10 at 1000.
segments.rationale: Extreme pain or discomfort is a sign of sepsis, and this is a sharp rise from 1000.

segments.text: Healed scar on the right knee.
segments.rationale: An old, healed scar is unrelated to the current infection.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 91% on room air, was 96% at 1000.
segments.rationale: Decreased oxygen saturation shows the body may be struggling to meet its demands.

questions.takeaway: Signs of sepsis include a fast heart rate, warm or clammy skin, a rash, extreme pain or discomfort, and decreased oxygen saturation. Normal mental status does not rule sepsis out.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with 1000 and ask whether it fits the whole body response to infection rather than the wound alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart rate, pain, and saturation all moved.
A new rash on both legs.
Intact dressing, bowel sounds, the healed scar, and baseline mental status.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: After a prescribed fluid bolus, a patient with sepsis has a lower blood pressure than before, cool mottled extremities, and falling urine output. Which condition should the nurse recognize?

options.text: Sepsis responding to treatment
options.rationale: Response is judged by the whole trend, not by finishing the fluids. Blood pressure and urine output are worse, and the skin shows poor perfusion.

options.text: Systemic inflammatory response alone
options.rationale: The patient already has sepsis, so a known infection is present; this is more than an inflammatory response alone.

options.text: Septic shock
options.rationale: Septic shock is the more severe form of sepsis, with significant circulatory and metabolic problems that can lead to organ failure and death. Blood pressure that falls despite fluids, cool mottled skin, and falling urine output show that circulation is failing.

options.text: Sepsis without shock
options.rationale: Some urine output does not rule out shock. Falling urine output with low blood pressure after fluids shows failing perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Septic shock is a more severe form of sepsis with significant circulatory and metabolic problems that can lead to organ failure and death. Low blood pressure that persists after fluids and signs of poor perfusion in the skin and urine output point to it, and persistent poor perfusion requires further escalation.
questions.strategy: Look at what the fluid bolus changed. When blood pressure, skin perfusion, and urine output all worsen after treatment, sepsis has progressed.

steps.detail: Blood pressure is lower than before the bolus.
Cool, mottled hands and feet and low urine output.
Output fell after the bolus instead of rising.

elimination.verdict: C. Septic shock.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.nursesNote: Day 5 after surgery on the left hip. Patient is 78 years old with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Peripheral intravenous catheter in the right forearm, capped, with no intravenous fluids or medications given since day 3. Incision edges together, dry, no redness. Indwelling urinary catheter drainage bag resting on the floor beside the bed. Oral temperature 36.9 °C. Received the influenza vaccine this season. Oral care not done since admission, lips dry and cracked.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the note of a patient on day 5 after hip surgery. Highlight the findings the nurse can act on to lower this patient's risk of a healthcare associated infection.

segments.text: Patient is 78 years old with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
segments.rationale: Older age and chronic illness do raise infection risk, but the nurse cannot change them. The question asks for findings the nurse can act on.

segments.text: Peripheral intravenous catheter in the right forearm, capped, with no intravenous fluids or medications given since day 3.
segments.rationale: A vascular access device bypasses the skin barrier. Nothing has been given through it for 2 days, so the nurse raises whether it is still needed. Unneeded devices add risk.

segments.text: Incision edges together, dry, no redness.
segments.rationale: A closed, dry incision with no redness is healing as expected. There is nothing to correct.

segments.text: Indwelling urinary catheter drainage bag resting on the floor beside the bed.
segments.rationale: Care of invasive devices helps prevent exposure. A bag on the floor contaminates the drainage system, and the catheter itself is a portal of entry whose need is reviewed.

segments.text: Oral temperature 36.9 °C.
segments.rationale: This value is not a risk the nurse can lower. Fever alone is also not relied on to judge infection.

segments.text: Received the influenza vaccine this season.
segments.rationale: Vaccination already lowers the risk for that infection. It needs no action now.

segments.text: Oral care not done since admission, lips dry and cracked.
segments.rationale: Intact skin and mucous membranes are barriers. Dry, cracked lips are broken barriers, and regular oral care helps restore them.

questions.takeaway: The nurse lowers infection risk by acting on what can change: unneeded devices, device care, and broken skin or mucous membranes. Age and chronic illness raise risk but cannot be changed.
questions.strategy: Read the stem twice: the findings must raise risk AND be something the nurse can act on. A true risk the nurse cannot change is the trap.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Incision, temperature, and the vaccine do not add risk now.
Age and diabetes are fixed risk factors.
Unused intravenous catheter, bag on the floor, broken mucous membranes.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with an infected foot wound and probable sepsis. The rapid response team is on the way, and the provider has ordered an intravenous antimicrobial now and an intravenous fluid bolus. The only intravenous catheter is in the hand. Its infusion runs slowly, the site is swollen, cool, and pale, and the patient rates pain at the site 4 of 10. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Start the antimicrobial through the current catheter without delay
options.rationale: Speed matters, but this catheter shows infiltration: swelling, coolness, pallor, and a slow infusion. A dose given here goes into the tissue, not the bloodstream, so the patient is not treated at all.

options.text: Remove the catheter and start the antimicrobial through new access
options.rationale: When sepsis is suspected the nurse assesses intravenous access as part of the immediate actions. A swollen, cool, pale site with a slow infusion is not working access. A new peripheral catheter at another site lets the antimicrobial and fluids reach the blood promptly.

options.text: Flush the catheter, and start the antimicrobial if it flushes
options.rationale: A catheter that flushes can still be infiltrated. The swelling, coolness, and pallor already show the fluid is going into the tissue.

options.text: Wait for the rapid response team to place new access
options.rationale: Escalation is already done. Waiting for the team delays treatment that the nurse can make possible now by placing a new peripheral catheter.

questions.takeaway: When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates, reassesses, obtains ordered specimens, and assesses the intravenous access, then gives the prescribed treatment promptly. Prompt treatment through access that does not work is not prompt treatment.
questions.strategy: Two options give the drug quickly. Ask whether the drug will actually reach the bloodstream through this site.

steps.detail: Swollen, cool, pale, slow infusion, and pain: infiltration.
Starting or flushing through this catheter sends the drug into tissue.
Waiting for the team postpones treatment the nurse can start.
New catheter at another site, then the antimicrobial.

elimination.verdict: B. Remove the catheter and start the antimicrobial through new access.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted 2 days ago with sepsis from pneumonia who is receiving the prescribed antimicrobial. White blood cell count 16,800/mm3 on admission, 3400/mm3 today. Blood pressure 92/54 mm Hg, was 116/70 mm Hg yesterday. Urine output 20 mL per hour, was 45 mL per hour yesterday. The patient is lethargic and was alert yesterday. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: With the other changes, the low count signals worsening sepsis
options.rationale: Results are interpreted together with the assessment. Falling blood pressure, falling urine output, and new lethargy show worse perfusion and organ dysfunction. In sepsis the white blood cell count may be normal or low as the condition worsens, so this low count fits deterioration.

options.text: The falling count shows the antimicrobial is clearing the infection
options.rationale: A falling count can follow successful treatment, which makes this option tempting. Here every other finding is worse than yesterday, so the count cannot be read as improvement.

options.text: The fall is too fast to be real and is likely a laboratory error
options.rationale: Nothing suggests an error. Assuming one delays the response to a patient whose perfusion is falling.

options.text: The low count shows the infection has stayed in the lungs
options.rationale: A white blood cell count does not show where an infection is. Low blood pressure, low urine output, and lethargy show a body wide response, not a confined infection.

questions.takeaway: A laboratory value is never read alone. In sepsis the white blood cell count can fall to normal or low while the patient worsens, so the nurse reads it against mentation, blood pressure, and urine output.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Both a falling count after treatment and a falling count in worsening sepsis are real patterns. The vital sign and urine output trends decide which one this is.

steps.detail: A and B read the same number as worse or better.
Blood pressure down, urine output down, new lethargy.

steps.action: Choose the interpretation that fits the patient
steps.detail: Worsening sepsis.

elimination.verdict: A. With the other changes, the low count signals worsening sepsis.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient who is going home after treatment for sepsis from a urinary tract infection, with 7 more days of an oral antibiotic. Which statements by the patient indicate understanding of the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I can stop the antibiotic once my temperature has been normal for 3 days."
options.rationale: A normal temperature for several days sounds like proof of cure, which makes this tempting. The entire course is completed even when the patient feels better; stopping early leaves organisms that can cause the infection to return and adds to resistance.

options.text: "I will take my temperature twice a day and write it down."
options.rationale: Checking the temperature twice a day is part of watching for early signs of a returning infection or sepsis at home.

options.text: "If I feel lightheaded when I stand, I will rest and mention it at my next visit."
options.rationale: Lightheadedness can be an early sign of sepsis from low blood pressure. After sepsis it is reported right away, not saved for the next visit. Resting first sounds sensible, which makes this the trap.

options.text: "A temperature lower than my usual is fine as long as I have no chills."
options.rationale: Linking concern to chills sounds sensible, but unusual coldness or a low temperature can signal sepsis on its own. It is reported, not explained away.

options.text: "If I pass much less urine than I am drinking, I will call the provider right away."
options.rationale: Urine output less than intake is an early sign of sepsis that the patient is taught to report immediately.

options.text: "If I feel that something is wrong, even without a fever, I will call."
