options.rationale: Sepsis does not always cause fever, and a sense that something is wrong is often an early cue. Calling is correct.

questions.takeaway: After sepsis, the patient takes the full antibiotic course, checks the temperature twice a day, and calls right away for early signs such as lightheadedness, urine output less than intake, unusual coldness, or feeling that something is wrong.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three wrong statements each sound careful: a temperature rule for stopping, rest before reporting, and a low temperature excused by the absence of chills. For each statement, ask whether the patient would get help at once for an early sign of sepsis and finish the full course.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The full course, not until the fever is gone.
Temperature twice a day.
Lightheadedness, less urine than intake, low temperature, and feeling wrong are all reported now.

elimination.verdict: B, E, F.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with confirmed Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) on enhanced contact precautions. The last liquid stool was 24 hours ago, and the patient has had 2 formed stools since. The patient asks, "Now that the diarrhea has stopped, can everyone stop wearing the gown and gloves today?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Yes, the precautions can end today now that your stools are formed."
options.rationale: The end of diarrhea is the right thing to watch, which makes this tempting. The precautions continue for at least 48 hours after the diarrhea stops, and only 24 hours have passed.

options.text: "The precautions stay in place until a repeat stool test shows no C. difficile."
options.rationale: The end of the precautions is timed from the last diarrhea, not from a repeat stool test.

options.text: "The precautions continue until at least 48 hours after your last liquid stool."
options.rationale: C. difficile spreads by direct and indirect contact, and its spores persist in the environment. Contact precautions continue for at least 48 hours after the diarrhea stops. With the last liquid stool 24 hours ago, they continue today.

options.text: "The precautions end on the day you finish the treatment for the infection."
options.rationale: Finishing treatment is not the measure used. The precautions are timed from when the diarrhea stops.

questions.takeaway: For C. difficile, enhanced contact precautions continue for at least 48 hours after the diarrhea stops, because spores persist and spread by contact.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and C both use the end of diarrhea. The time stated in the stem, 24 hours, decides between them.

steps.action: Find the timing in the stem
steps.detail: Last liquid stool 24 hours ago.
At least 48 hours after the diarrhea stops.
A repeat stool test and the end of treatment are not the measure.

elimination.verdict: C. "The precautions continue until at least 48 hours after your last liquid stool."

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient who receives immunosuppressive treatment after a kidney transplant. Over 2 days, clusters of fluid filled blisters have appeared on the chest, both arms, the back, and the face. The provider documents herpes zoster (shingles). Which precautions should the nurse implement?

options.text: Contact precautions in a private room
options.rationale: Contact precautions address the fluid in the blisters, which makes this tempting. They do not address the airborne spread that occurs once zoster has spread widely.

options.text: Airborne and contact precautions
options.rationale: Lesions on many areas of the body mean disseminated zoster, which spreads through the air and by contact. The patient also has reduced immune function. An airborne infection isolation room plus gown and gloves is required.

options.text: Droplet and contact precautions
options.rationale: A mask for droplets protects at close range only. The particles in disseminated zoster stay suspended in the air, so droplet precautions are not enough.

options.text: Standard precautions with the lesions covered
options.rationale: This fits zoster limited to one area in a patient with normal immune function. It does not fit lesions on the chest, arms, back and face in a patient on immunosuppressive treatment.

questions.takeaway: Zoster limited to one area in a patient with normal immunity needs standard precautions with covered lesions. Lesions spread over many areas, or zoster in an immunosuppressed patient, need airborne and contact precautions.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The diagnosis alone does not choose the precaution. Read where the lesions are and who the patient is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chest, both arms, back and face: spread well beyond one area.
Immunosuppressive treatment after a transplant.
Disseminated zoster needs airborne and contact precautions.

elimination.verdict: B. Disseminated zoster needs airborne and contact precautions.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient receiving chemotherapy whose white blood cell count is 900/mm3. Oral temperature is 38.3 °C, was 37.0 °C at 0800. Heart rate 98/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg. The patient feels tired and has no cough, the skin and mouth show no redness or drainage, and the central line site is clean and dry. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the temperature in 1 hour to confirm it
options.rationale: Confirming a single reading sounds careful. In a patient with very few white cells, a temperature of 38.3 °C is already an emergency, and waiting delays treatment.

options.text: Report the temperature to the provider now
options.rationale: Chemotherapy has left too few white cells to make redness, swelling or pus, so fever may be the only sign of a serious infection. It needs immediate escalation.

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen and reassess
options.rationale: Comfort matters, but lowering the temperature before it is reported hides the one sign of infection this patient can show.

options.text: Inspect the skin folds and perineum before reporting
options.rationale: A search for a source is reasonable later. With few white cells, an absent local sign does not rule out infection, so the search should not delay the report.

questions.takeaway: Immunosuppression is a major infection risk and also blunts the signs of infection. In a patient with very few white cells, fever may be the only cue, and it is escalated at once.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: No redness, no pus and a clean line site look reassuring. Ask whether this patient can make those signs at all.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chemotherapy with a white cell count of 900/mm3.
Too few white cells to cause redness or pus.

steps.action: Act on the cue that remains
steps.detail: A new temperature of 38.3 °C is reported now.

elimination.verdict: B. Fever in a patient with very few white cells is escalated at once.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with heart failure and probable sepsis from pneumonia. A prescribed intravenous fluid bolus of 2000 mL was started 30 minutes ago, and 750 mL has infused. Blood pressure 92/56 mm Hg, was 86/50 mm Hg before the bolus. Respiratory rate 32/min, was 24/min. Oxygen saturation (SpO2) 88% on 2 L nasal cannula, was 93%. New crackles are heard halfway up both lungs. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Continue the bolus, since the pressure is still low
options.rationale: Fluid for low pressure is part of early sepsis care, and the pressure is still low. The new crackles and falling SpO2 show the lungs are filling with the fluid.

options.text: Increase the oxygen and continue the bolus
options.rationale: More oxygen helps the SpO2, which makes this tempting. Continuing the fluid keeps adding to the cause of the problem.

options.text: Slow the bolus to half the rate and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: Slowing sounds cautious, but fluid keeps entering lungs that are already congested, and an hour is too long to wait.

options.text: Stop the bolus and raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: The response to treatment is fluid overload: new crackles, a faster respiratory rate and a falling SpO2. Stopping the fluid and sitting the patient up comes first, then the nurse escalates.

questions.takeaway: Give sepsis treatment promptly and reassess the response. When a fluid bolus causes new crackles and falling oxygenation, especially with heart failure, stop the fluid, sit the patient up and escalate.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: A better blood pressure is one number. Judge the whole response, including breathing and oxygenation.

steps.detail: Blood pressure slightly better, breathing clearly worse.
Heart failure limits how much fluid the patient can take.
Stop the fluid and raise the head of the bed.

elimination.verdict: D. Stop the fluid that is causing the overload.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.scenario: A patient, 84 years old, was admitted yesterday with a urinary tract infection and has had atrial fibrillation for 10 years. The family describes the patient's usual state: oriented to person and place but not to time, eats about half of each meal, and walks with a walker. At admission yesterday at 1600: oriented to person and place, respiratory rate 16/min, heart rate 82/min and irregular, urine output 50 mL per hour. The nurse assesses the patient at 1000 today.
questions.stem: The nurse is comparing the 1000 findings of an older patient with a urinary tract infection with the patient's baseline. For each finding, indicate whether it requires follow up or does not require follow up.

rows.text: Heart rate 86/min and irregular
rows.rationale: An irregular rhythm sounds alarming, but the patient has had atrial fibrillation for 10 years, and the rate is close to the 82/min at admission.

rows.text: Oriented to person only
rows.rationale: The patient was oriented to person and place at baseline and on admission. Losing place is new confusion, an early cue of sepsis in an older adult.

rows.text: Respiratory rate 24/min
rows.rationale: The rate was 16/min on admission. A respiratory rate above 20/min is concerning and may be an early cue of sepsis.

rows.text: Ate half of breakfast
rows.rationale: The family says the patient usually eats about half of each meal, so this matches the baseline.

rows.text: Urine output 90 mL over the past 4 hours
rows.rationale: That is about 22 mL per hour, down from 50 mL per hour. Falling urine output can signal poor perfusion.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C
rows.rationale: The temperature is in range. It does not lower concern for the other changes, because older adults often have infection or sepsis without a fever.

questions.takeaway: Compare each finding with the patient's own baseline, not only with normal values. In an older adult, new confusion, a faster respiratory rate and falling urine output can signal sepsis even without a fever.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by whether it is new for this patient. Long standing findings that look abnormal are the distractors here.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Atrial fibrillation for 10 years, oriented to person and place, eats half of meals.
Now oriented to person only, respiratory rate 24/min, urine output about 22 mL per hour.
A temperature in range does not cancel the other changes.

elimination.verdict: Requires follow up: oriented to person only, respiratory rate 24/min, urine output 90 mL in 4 hours. Does not require follow up: irregular rate of 86/min, half of breakfast, temperature 37.0 °C.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient on day 3 of an intravenous broad spectrum antimicrobial for cellulitis. Temperature is 37.0 °C, and the redness is now inside the border marked on admission. The culture and susceptibility report shows that the organism is sensitive to a narrower oral drug, and the provider switches to it. The patient says, "The IV one is working. Switching to a weaker pill seems risky." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "I will ask the provider to keep the IV drug, since it is working."
options.rationale: This sounds like advocacy, but it supports the belief that the broadest drug is best and ignores the culture result.

options.text: "Either drug would work, so the choice mostly comes down to cost."
options.rationale: The choice is guided by the culture and by resistance, not cost, and this response does not answer the patient's worry.

options.text: "The culture shows this drug kills your germ and limits resistance."
options.rationale: Culture and susceptibility results guide treatment. A narrower drug that the organism is sensitive to treats the infection and limits resistance, which answers the worry about a weaker drug.

options.text: "Pills are used once the fever is gone, so it is time for the switch."
options.rationale: The normal temperature supports the switch, but the reason this drug was chosen is the susceptibility report.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility results guide antimicrobial choice. Switching to a narrower drug the organism is sensitive to treats the infection and supports appropriate use, which limits resistance.
questions.strategy: Several responses sound helpful. Pick the one that answers the patient's actual worry with the reason the drug was chosen.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient thinks narrower means weaker.

steps.action: Find the reason for the switch
steps.detail: The susceptibility report shows the organism is sensitive to the new drug.
Narrower drugs limit resistance.

elimination.verdict: C. The culture guides the switch, and a narrower drug limits resistance.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient receiving immunosuppressive treatment whose incision has faint redness and no fever. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Infection may be present with only faint signs
options.rationale: Inflammation and immune responses produce the redness, swelling, and fever that point to infection. Immunosuppressive treatment weakens that response, so an infection can show only faint signs. The nurse watches the site and the overall condition closely.

options.text: Infection is unlikely without a fever
options.rationale: Fever is not relied on alone to judge infection, and a weakened immune response makes a fever less likely even when infection is present.

options.text: Faint redness is expected and needs no follow up
options.rationale: In this patient a faint sign may be the only early sign of infection, so it is followed, not dismissed.

options.text: The treatment lowers the risk of wound infection
options.rationale: The opposite is true. Immunosuppressive treatment is a patient factor that raises infection risk.

questions.takeaway: Immune status shapes both infection risk and how infection looks. A patient with weakened immune responses is more likely to get an infection and less likely to show strong signs of it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Ask what produces the classic signs of infection. If the immune response is weak, the signs will be weak too.

steps.action: Link the signs to the response
steps.detail: Redness and fever come from inflammation and immune responses.
Immunosuppression weakens those responses, so signs are muted.
No fever and faint redness do not rule out infection.

elimination.verdict: A. Infection may be present with only faint signs.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: A visitor arrives to see a patient on droplet precautions. Which instruction should the nurse give before the visitor enters the room?

options.text: "Put on a gown and gloves at the door."
options.rationale: Gown and gloves are the protective equipment for contact precautions. Droplets reach nearby mucous membranes, so the visitor needs a mask.

options.text: "Clean your hands and put on a mask."
options.rationale: Visitors are taught the required hand hygiene and protective equipment before they enter. Droplet precautions call for a mask, and hand hygiene applies with every precaution.

options.text: "Wear a fitted respirator during the visit."
options.rationale: A fitted respirator and an airborne infection isolation room are for infections spread by particles suspended in the air, not droplets.

options.text: "Put on a mask when you reach the bedside."
options.rationale: The mask is right, but the timing is wrong. Protective equipment goes on before entering the care area, and hand hygiene is missing.

questions.takeaway: The nurse explains precautions in plain language and teaches visitors the required hand hygiene and protective equipment before they enter. Droplet precautions mean a mask.
questions.strategy: Match the equipment to the route, then check the timing and the hand hygiene.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Droplet means a mask; gown and gloves and a respirator belong to other routes.
Only one puts the mask on before entering.
The key includes it.

elimination.verdict: B. Clean your hands and put on a mask.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The adult child of an older patient with pneumonia says, "Something is off today. This is not how my parent usually acts." Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Explain that confusion is common in older adults
options.rationale: This dismisses the family's report. A sudden change in behavior is a possible early cue of sepsis, not something to explain away.

options.text: Check the temperature for a new fever
options.rationale: Temperature is part of the picture, but the nurse does not rely on fever alone. Checking only for fever can miss the change the family is describing.

options.text: Note the concern and observe at the next check
options.rationale: Waiting delays the assessment of a possible early sign of deterioration.

options.text: Assess mental status against the usual baseline
options.rationale: New confusion, restlessness, or decreased alertness may signal sepsis. The family knows the patient's baseline, so the nurse compares mental status with it now, along with the vital signs.

questions.takeaway: A family member saying the patient is not acting right is a cue. The nurse compares current mental status with the patient's baseline and looks at the whole picture, not only the temperature.
questions.strategy: Two options dismiss or delay the concern. Of the two that assess, pick the one that looks at the change itself.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Explaining it away and waiting both ignore a possible early cue.
A fever check alone misses a change in behavior.

steps.action: Choose the assessment of the change
steps.detail: Mental status against the usual baseline.

elimination.verdict: D. Assess mental status against the usual baseline.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: The nurse in a long term care facility reviews four residents at the start of the shift. Which resident should the nurse assess first for a possible infection?

options.text: Shivering after a shower, temperature 36.2 °C, alert and walking as usual
options.rationale: Feeling cold can be a cue of infection, which makes this tempting. Here the shivering has a clear cause, and alertness and walking match the usual pattern.

options.text: Walked alone yesterday, needs two staff to stand, temperature 36.8 °C
options.rationale: A sudden loss of function is a change from baseline. Infection in an older adult often shows as a change in behavior or function rather than a fever, so the normal temperature does not rule it out.

options.text: Oriented to person only, as for the past year, temperature 36.9 °C
options.rationale: Confusion is an important cue only when it is new. This resident's orientation matches the long standing baseline.

options.text: Daily morning cough with white sputum for years, temperature 37.0 °C
options.rationale: A cough draws attention to the respiratory tract, but this cough and sputum are unchanged from a long history.

questions.takeaway: Do not rely on fever alone. Compare each finding with the resident's own baseline and look for new changes in behavior and function, which are often the first sign of infection in an older adult.
questions.strategy: Every option has something that sounds like infection: coldness, confusion, a cough. Ask which finding is new for that resident.

steps.detail: Shivering, confusion, and a cough each suggest infection at first glance.
The confusion and the cough are long standing; the shivering has a clear cause.
A sudden loss of the ability to stand and walk.
Fever is not required for infection.

elimination.verdict: B. Walked alone yesterday, needs two staff to stand.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a urinary tract infection who was alert at 0800 and is now confused, with a heart rate of 118/min, a respiratory rate of 26/min, and a blood pressure of 98/60 mm Hg. The nurse suspects sepsis. In which order should the nurse perform these actions?

options.text: Obtain the ordered blood cultures
options.rationale: Specimens are obtained once ordered, before the antimicrobial, so the organism can be identified to guide treatment.

options.text: Evaluate the response after the antimicrobial infuses
options.rationale: After treatment the nurse evaluates the response: mentation, blood pressure, and urine output. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation. This differs from the earlier reassessment, which tracks the change while help is on the way.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process
options.rationale: Sepsis is an emergency. When it is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately.

options.text: Give the prescribed IV antimicrobial
options.rationale: Prescribed treatment is given promptly once specimens are obtained. The antimicrobial is started as soon as possible.

options.text: Reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs
options.rationale: While help is on the way, the nurse reassesses breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs to track the change.

questions.takeaway: When sepsis is suspected: escalate, reassess, obtain ordered specimens and assess IV access, give the prescribed treatment promptly, then reassess the response.
questions.strategy: The nurse has already recognized the problem, so escalation comes first, then reassessment while help comes. After that, specimens come before the drug, and evaluating the response after the infusion closes the loop.

steps.detail: The cues are already recognized; sepsis is an emergency.
Reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs.
Cultures first, then the antimicrobial.
Evaluate the response once the antimicrobial has infused.

elimination.verdict: C, E, A, D, B.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with an infected abdominal wound. At 0800 the patient was alert, skin pale and dry, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, urine output 50 mL per hour. At 1200 the patient is restless, skin warm and pink, temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 116/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 104/62 mm Hg, urine output 25 mL per hour. A family member says, "Your color looks so much better now." Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Warm, pink skin with these changes suggests early sepsis
options.rationale: Warm skin is a listed sign of sepsis when vessels dilate early in the response, and a patient can look better while tissue perfusion falls. New restlessness, faster breathing and heart rate, a falling blood pressure, and half the urine output point to organ dysfunction.

options.text: Warm, pink skin shows that tissue perfusion is better
options.rationale: Skin color is one sign, but the whole trend decides. Blood pressure, urine output, and mentation are all worse than at 0800, so perfusion is not better.

options.text: The changes reflect a local wound infection only
options.rationale: An infection that stays local does not cause a fast heart rate, falling urine output, and new restlessness. These are signs of a body wide response.

options.text: The fever explains the skin, pulse, and breathing changes
options.rationale: Fever can raise the heart and respiratory rates and warm the skin, which makes this tempting. It does not explain new restlessness, a falling blood pressure, or urine output cut in half.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend, not one finding. In early sepsis the skin can be warm and pink while mentation, blood pressure, and urine output show falling perfusion.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options explain the changes away: one through skin color, one through fever. Check which findings each explanation leaves out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Restless, heart rate and breathing up, blood pressure down, urine output halved.
Fever does not explain restlessness, falling blood pressure, or low urine output.
One reassuring sign does not outweigh a worsening trend.

steps.action: Choose the explanation that fits all findings
steps.detail: Early sepsis.

elimination.verdict: A. Warm, pink skin with these changes suggests early sepsis.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted with an obstructing kidney stone and a urinary tract infection who had a ureteral stent placed yesterday. At 0800 the patient was alert, oral temperature 37.2 °C, respiratory rate 16/min, blood pressure 130/78 mm Hg. The nurse assesses the patient at 1200. Which findings require immediate follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Oral temperature 35.8 °C with shivering
options.rationale: Sepsis does not always bring a fever. Shivering and unusual coldness are early cues, and a temperature that drops below the patient's own 0800 value in a patient with an obstructed, infected urinary tract is a warning sign.

options.text: Pink tinged urine
options.rationale: Pink tinged urine is expected for a short time after a ureteral stent is placed. Bright red urine or clots would need follow up.

options.text: Respiratory rate 24/min
options.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20/min is concerning, and it was 16/min at 0800. Faster breathing is one of the earliest cues that the body is struggling to meet its demands.

options.text: Drowsy and slow to answer questions
options.rationale: The patient was alert at 0800. New lethargy or confusion compared with baseline is an early cue of sepsis and a sign of organ dysfunction.

options.text: Urine output 60 mL over 3 hours
options.rationale: That is 20 mL per hour. Falling urine output can signal poor perfusion of the kidneys, a marker of organ dysfunction.

options.text: Blood pressure 126/76 mm Hg
options.rationale: This is close to the 0800 value. A normal blood pressure does not rule out sepsis, because pressure often falls late, so the other cues still need action.

questions.takeaway: Do not wait for fever. Compare every finding with the patient's own baseline: new lethargy, a faster respiratory rate, unusual coldness or shivering, and falling urine output are early cues of sepsis. Expected procedure findings and a blood pressure that has not yet dropped do not lower the concern.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into one of two piles: expected after the procedure, or a change from this patient's 0800 baseline that fits a body wide response. A low temperature counts as a cue, not as reassurance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pink tinged urine and mild flank discomfort are expected with a new stent.
Alert to drowsy, respiratory rate 16/min to 24/min, temperature down with shivering.
60 mL over 3 hours is 20 mL per hour.

steps.action: Do not be reassured by one number
steps.detail: A blood pressure near baseline does not cancel the other cues.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, E.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: The nurse on a medical unit has one airborne infection isolation room open. Four patients are waiting for admission from the emergency department. Which patient should the nurse place in that room?

options.text: Influenza with a frequent cough and a fever
options.rationale: Influenza spreads by droplets. The patient needs a mask and placement away from other patients, not an airborne room.

options.text: Neutropenia from chemotherapy and a new fever
options.rationale: This patient is the most vulnerable, which makes the room tempting, but neutropenic precautions protect the patient from others. An airborne isolation room pulls hallway air into the room, which is the opposite of what this patient needs. A private room with protective precautions fits.

options.text: Cough for 3 months with blood streaked sputum
options.rationale: A cough for months with blood streaked sputum suggests pulmonary tuberculosis, which spreads by particles that stay suspended in the air. Only this patient needs an airborne infection isolation room and staff respiratory protection.

options.text: Draining wound with methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
options.rationale: MRSA in a draining wound spreads by contact. Gown, gloves and dedicated equipment are needed, not airborne isolation.

questions.takeaway: Match the room to the route. Airborne: an airborne infection isolation room and a fitted respirator. Droplet: a mask and placement away from others. Contact: gown, gloves and dedicated equipment. Neutropenic: protective precautions, meticulous hand hygiene and screening of visitors and staff.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: The question is not who is sickest or most vulnerable; it is whose organism stays suspended in the air. Name each patient's route first, then give the scarce room to the only airborne one.

steps.detail: Influenza: droplet. MRSA wound: contact. Months of cough with blood streaked sputum: airborne.
Neutropenia needs protection from others; an airborne room draws outside air in.
The only airborne route gets the airborne room.

elimination.verdict: C. Cough for 3 months with blood streaked sputum.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient on neutropenic precautions after chemotherapy. The patient's spouse arrives with a runny nose and a cough and says, "It is only a cold, and I will wear a mask. We have not seen each other in 2 days." Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the spouse to visit after the symptoms clear
options.rationale: Neutropenic precautions include screening visitors and staff for illness. A visitor with an active respiratory infection is kept out until well, even with a mask, because a cold can become a serious infection in a patient with few white blood cells. The nurse can offer a phone or video call in the meantime.

options.text: Allow the visit if the spouse keeps a mask on
options.rationale: A mask lowers but does not remove the risk, and the spouse would touch the patient and the room. The emotional pull of the 2 days apart does not change the screening rule.

options.text: Allow a short visit after hand hygiene
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is essential for every visitor, but it does not stop respiratory droplets from an ill visitor. A shorter visit still exposes the patient.

options.text: Allow the visit wearing a gown, gloves, and a mask
options.rationale: Adding more equipment feels safer, but the rule is to screen out ill visitors, not to dress them. The patient remains exposed to an active infection.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenic precautions protect the patient from others: meticulous hand hygiene, protective precautions as indicated, and screening of visitors and staff for illness. An ill visitor waits until well; a mask is not a substitute.
questions.strategy: Three options let the visit happen with some protection added. Ask what the precaution is actually for: keeping illness away from a patient with almost no defenses.

steps.detail: Neutropenic: protect the patient; screen visitors for illness.
Two days apart is compelling but does not change the risk.
A mask, hand hygiene or a gown still leaves an ill visitor at the bedside.

elimination.verdict: A. Ask the spouse to visit after the symptoms clear.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission based precautions

questions.stem: The nurse has taught the adult child of a patient with Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) how to help with care in the hospital room and at home. Which statement by the adult child indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will put on the gown and gloves every time I help in the room."
options.rationale: Correct. Enhanced contact precautions for C. difficile use a gown and gloves for all contact with the patient and the room.

options.text: "I will wash my hands with soap and water when I leave the room."
options.rationale: Correct. Soap and water with friction physically removes spores, which alcohol does not kill. Many facilities require it after C. difficile care.

options.text: "I will clean the bathroom at home with a bleach product."
options.rationale: Correct. C. difficile spores persist on surfaces and standard disinfectants may not kill them. A sporicidal cleaner, such as a bleach product, is used.

options.text: "Rubbing in alcohol gel for 20 seconds will clean my hands."
options.rationale: This needs correction. Alcohol based sanitizer does not kill C. difficile spores, however long it is rubbed in. After this patient's care, the adult child washes with soap and water.

questions.takeaway: C. difficile spores survive alcohol and many standard disinfectants. Teach gown and gloves for all contact, soap and water hand hygiene after care, and sporicidal cleaning such as a bleach product. Alcohol gel is preferred for most routine care, but not here.
questions.strategy: This is a negative stem: find the statement that is wrong. The 20 seconds makes it sound thorough, which is the trap; the problem is the product, not the time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the incorrect statement.
Gown and gloves, soap and water, and bleach all deal with spores.
Alcohol gel does not kill spores, however long it is rubbed in.

elimination.verdict: D. "Rubbing in alcohol gel for 20 seconds will clean my hands."

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.nursesNote: Day 3 of admission for influenza. Droplet precautions sign posted at the door. 0800: Alert and oriented, oral temperature 37.8 °C, heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air, dry cough. Ate most of breakfast. 1200: Restless and asks the same question twice. Oral temperature 39.1 °C with chills. Heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min. Blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg. SpO2 90% on room air. Cough now brings up thick yellow sputum. New crackles at one lung base. Urine output 80 mL since 0800. Family member at the bedside wearing a mask. Saline lock in the hand, site clean and dry.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 1200 note of a patient admitted with influenza. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow up.

segments.text: Restless and asks the same question twice
segments.rationale: The patient was alert and oriented at 0800. New restlessness and confusion are early cues of sepsis and a sign of organ dysfunction.

segments.text: Oral temperature 39.1 °C with chills
segments.rationale: A new high fever with chills on day 3, after the temperature was settling, signals a new or worsening infection.

segments.text: Heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min
segments.rationale: Both rose sharply from 0800. A respiratory rate above 20/min is concerning, and a fast heart rate fits a body wide response.

segments.text: Blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg
segments.rationale: The pressure fell from 128/76 mm Hg. Dilated, leaky vessels lower the pressure and the delivery of oxygen to tissues.

segments.text: SpO2 90% on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygenation fell from 95%. Impaired oxygenation is a sign of organ dysfunction and needs action now.

segments.text: Cough now brings up thick yellow sputum
segments.rationale: The cough was dry at 0800. New purulent sputum in a patient with influenza suggests a bacterial pneumonia on top of the viral infection.

segments.text: New crackles at one lung base
segments.rationale: New crackles in one area point to a lung infection in that area, the likely source.

segments.text: Urine output 80 mL since 0800
segments.rationale: That is 20 mL per hour over 4 hours. Falling urine output signals poor kidney perfusion.

segments.text: Ate most of breakfast
segments.rationale: Intake at breakfast was before the change and does not require follow up.

segments.text: Family member at the bedside wearing a mask
segments.rationale: A visitor following droplet precautions is expected.

segments.text: Saline lock in the hand, site clean and dry
segments.rationale: The site shows no problem. The size and location of the access will matter for treatment, but the finding itself is not abnormal.

questions.takeaway: Compare the 1200 findings with 0800. New confusion, fever with chills, a rising heart and respiratory rate, a falling blood pressure, lower SpO2 and low urine output, together with a new purulent cough and focal crackles, signal sepsis from a likely lung source.
questions.strategy: Read the note twice: once for what changed between 0800 and 1200, and once for what changed in the cough and lungs. Everything that changed for the worse needs follow up; routine items do not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mental status, temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure and SpO2 all worsened.
A dry cough became thick yellow sputum with new crackles.
80 mL over 4 hours is 20 mL per hour.
Breakfast, a masked visitor and a clean site are not abnormal.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing the 1200 findings of a patient admitted with influenza. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
Chart so far: day 3 of admission for influenza on droplet precautions. At 0800 alert, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. At 1200 restless and repeating questions, oral temperature 39.1 °C with chills, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, SpO2 90% on room air, new thick yellow sputum and crackles at one lung base, urine output 80 mL since 0800.

The new thick yellow sputum and crackles at one lung base suggest [[1]].

The findings that show organ dysfunction are [[2]].

Together, these findings point to [[3]].

options.text: worsening of the viral influenza alone
options.rationale: Influenza can worsen, but a dry cough that turns into thick yellow sputum with new crackles in one area points to a bacterial infection added on top.

options.text: a secondary bacterial pneumonia
options.rationale: Bacterial pneumonia is a common complication of influenza. New purulent sputum and focal crackles on day 3 fit it, and the lung is the likely source of the infection.

options.text: aspiration of food at breakfast
options.rationale: Aspiration is a cause of pneumonia, but nothing in the chart describes coughing or choking with meals.

options.text: the new confusion and the low urine output
options.rationale: New confusion shows the brain is affected, and 20 mL per hour shows the kidneys are affected. These are signs of organ dysfunction.

options.text: the fever and the chills
options.rationale: Fever and chills show an infection and an inflammatory response, but they are not organ dysfunction.

options.text: the fast heart rate and the productive cough
options.rationale: A fast heart rate is a response to fever and stress, and the cough shows the source. Neither one by itself shows organ dysfunction.

options.text: sepsis
options.rationale: Sepsis is infection plus life threatening organ dysfunction. This patient has a likely lung infection with new confusion, low urine output, falling oxygenation and a falling blood pressure.

options.text: a systemic inflammatory response without sepsis
options.rationale: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) alone describes inflammation. Here there is both an infection and organ dysfunction, which is sepsis.

options.text: a local lung infection only
options.rationale: A local infection does not cause new confusion and falling urine output. Those findings show a body wide response.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is infection plus organ dysfunction. Fever, chills and a fast heart rate show an infection and inflammation; new confusion, low urine output and impaired oxygenation show organs failing. In a patient with influenza, a new purulent cough and focal crackles point to a bacterial pneumonia as the source.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into three groups: the source, the inflammation and the organ dysfunction. Only organ dysfunction turns an infection into sepsis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New purulent sputum and focal crackles: bacterial pneumonia.
Fever and heart rate are inflammation; confusion and low urine output are organ dysfunction.
Infection plus organ dysfunction is sepsis.

elimination.verdict: 1: a secondary bacterial pneumonia. 2: the new confusion and the low urine output. 3: sepsis.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: At 1215 the nurse has applied oxygen as prescribed, and SpO2 is 94% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Blood pressure is now 94/56 mm Hg, heart rate 120/min, and the patient is still restless. The patient's oral temperature remains 39.1 °C, and droplet precautions are in place. Chart so far: day 3 of admission for influenza on droplet precautions. At 0800 alert, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. At 1200 restless and repeating questions, oral temperature 39.1 °C with chills, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, SpO2 90% on room air, new thick yellow sputum and crackles at one lung base, urine output 80 mL since 0800. Which problem is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Risk for spread of the infection to others
options.rationale: Droplet precautions are already in place and are working. Spread to others is a real concern but not the most urgent threat to this patient.

options.text: Impaired tissue perfusion from sepsis
options.rationale: With oxygenation now corrected on 2 L/min, the most dangerous change is falling perfusion: the blood pressure keeps dropping, the heart rate keeps rising, and the brain and kidneys are already affected. Without prompt treatment this moves toward septic shock.

options.text: Hyperthermia from the infection
options.rationale: A temperature of 39.1 °C is uncomfortable and is treated, but fever itself is not what threatens organs here. Treating the fever does not fix perfusion.

options.text: Impaired gas exchange from pneumonia
options.rationale: This was the first concern at 1200, and the ABCs make it tempting. The oxygen has brought SpO2 to 94%, so breathing is now supported, while circulation is getting worse.

questions.takeaway: Use the ABCs with the current data, not the earlier data. Once oxygenation is supported, a falling blood pressure with new confusion and low urine output makes impaired perfusion from sepsis the priority, because it is the problem that leads to septic shock and organ failure.
questions.strategy: Two options are physiological and both feel urgent. Ask which one has already been addressed and which one is still getting worse at 1215.

steps.detail: SpO2 is 94% on oxygen: breathing is supported for now.

steps.action: Look at the trend in circulation
steps.detail: Blood pressure 98/58 to 94/56 mm Hg, heart rate 118 to 120/min, still restless.

steps.action: Set aside the real but lesser problems
steps.detail: Fever and spread to others are managed and are not the main threat.
Falling perfusion from sepsis is the priority.

elimination.verdict: B. Impaired tissue perfusion from sepsis.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.scenario: At 1220 the nurse has activated the rapid response process for probable sepsis, and the provider is giving prescriptions. SpO2 is 94% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg. Chart so far: day 3 of admission for influenza on droplet precautions. At 0800 alert, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. At 1200 restless and repeating questions, oral temperature 39.1 °C with chills, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, SpO2 90% on room air, new thick yellow sputum and crackles at one lung base, urine output 80 mL since 0800.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing potential prescriptions for a patient with influenza and probable sepsis. For each potential prescription, indicate whether it is anticipated or not anticipated for this patient.

rows.text: Two sets of blood cultures
rows.rationale: Cultures identify the organism and guide treatment. They are drawn before the antimicrobial when this does not delay it.

rows.text: Serum lactate level
rows.rationale: Lactate testing is anticipated when sepsis is suspected. A high lactate signals poor tissue perfusion and is trended to judge the response.

rows.text: Portable chest x ray
rows.rationale: Imaging helps locate the source. New purulent sputum and focal crackles make the lung the likely source, and a portable film avoids moving the patient.

rows.text: Broad spectrum IV antimicrobial within 1 hour
rows.rationale: For probable sepsis the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour.

rows.text: IV bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Dilated, leaky vessels drop the blood pressure. An isotonic fluid bolus expands the circulating volume to restore perfusion.

rows.text: IV bolus of 0.45% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: A hypotonic solution shifts water into cells and does little to expand the circulating volume. It is avoided in hypotension.

rows.text: Hold the antimicrobial until the culture results return
rows.rationale: Culture results take days. Waiting delays the treatment that most improves survival in sepsis.

rows.text: End droplet precautions now that the infection is bacterial
rows.rationale: The patient still has influenza. A bacterial pneumonia on top does not end the precautions for the virus.

questions.takeaway: The sepsis bundle the nurse anticipates: blood cultures, a lactate level, imaging such as a chest x ray to find the source, an IV antimicrobial within 1 hour, and an isotonic fluid bolus for low blood pressure. Precautions for the original infection continue.
questions.strategy: Picture the four jobs: find the organism, find the source, treat the infection, restore perfusion. Each anticipated order does one of these jobs; each wrong one delays treatment, uses the wrong fluid or drops a precaution still needed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the organism and the source
steps.detail: Cultures, lactate and a chest x ray.
Antimicrobial within 1 hour and an isotonic bolus.
Hypotonic fluid, waiting for cultures and stopping droplet precautions.

elimination.verdict: Anticipated: rows 1 to 5. Not anticipated: rows 6, 7 and 8.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: At 1240 the nurse has drawn two sets of blood cultures and the lactate level. The radiology technician is on the way with a portable machine for the chest x ray. The IV antimicrobial and a 0.9% sodium chloride bolus are ready, and the only access is a 22 gauge saline lock in the hand. Blood pressure 92/54 mm Hg, SpO2 94% on 2 L/min. Chart so far: day 3 of admission for influenza on droplet precautions. At 0800 alert, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. At 1200 restless and repeating questions, oral temperature 39.1 °C with chills, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, SpO2 90% on room air, new thick yellow sputum and crackles at one lung base, urine output 80 mL since 0800. Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insert a second IV catheter of a larger size
options.rationale: A 22 gauge in the hand is too small to run a rapid bolus and an antimicrobial together. Assessing IV access is part of the immediate actions for sepsis, and an 18 or 20 gauge catheter allows faster flow.

options.text: Delay the antimicrobial until the chest x ray is taken
options.rationale: The x ray locates the source but does not change the need for the drug. Every hour of delay in probable sepsis raises the risk of death.

options.text: Start the fluid bolus at the prescribed rate
options.rationale: The blood pressure is still falling. The bolus restores circulating volume and perfusion.

options.text: Hold the fluid bolus until the lactate result returns
options.rationale: The lactate helps judge perfusion, but the falling blood pressure already shows the need for fluid. Waiting delays treatment.

options.text: Keep droplet precautions in place during the x ray
options.rationale: The patient still has influenza. The technician wears a mask at the bedside, and the portable film keeps the patient in the room.

options.text: Reassess mentation, blood pressure, and breathing during the bolus
options.rationale: The nurse gives treatment and then reassesses the response. Breathing is watched closely because the patient has pneumonia and is receiving a large volume of fluid.

questions.takeaway: Once cultures are drawn, the antimicrobial and the fluid bolus start without waiting for imaging or the lactate result. Make sure the access can deliver them, keep the original precautions, and reassess the response, including the lungs, during fluid.
questions.strategy: Look for any option that makes treatment wait for a test. In probable sepsis, tests run alongside treatment, not ahead of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A 22 gauge in the hand cannot carry both quickly: add a larger catheter.
Antimicrobial and bolus now, not after the x ray or lactate.
Droplet precautions continue, and the nurse reassesses during the bolus.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.scenario: At 1630, about 4 hours after treatment began, the nurse reassesses the patient. The antimicrobial was given at 1250 and the prescribed bolus has finished. Chart so far: day 3 of admission for influenza. At 1200 restless and repeating questions, oral temperature 39.1 °C, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, urine output 20 mL per hour, new crackles at one lung base. At 1240 lactate 4.1 mmol/L, respiratory rate 26/min and SpO2 94% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the response of a patient with influenza and sepsis to treatment. For each finding, indicate whether it indicates improvement or indicates no improvement.

rows.text: Alert, oriented, and answering questions clearly
rows.rationale: Mental status has moved back toward the 0800 baseline, a sign that brain perfusion is better.

rows.text: Blood pressure 110/66 mm Hg
rows.rationale: The pressure has risen from 98/58 mm Hg, showing a response to the fluid.

rows.text: Urine output 40 mL in the past hour
rows.rationale: Output doubled from 20 mL per hour. Urine output is a key marker of adequate perfusion.

rows.text: Lactate 2.2 mmol/L
rows.rationale: The lactate fell from 4.1 mmol/L, showing tissue perfusion is better.

rows.text: Oral temperature 38.2 °C
rows.rationale: The fever has come down from 39.1 °C.

rows.text: Respiratory rate 32/min
rows.rationale: The rate was 26/min at 1240 and is rising. The patient is working harder to breathe.

rows.text: SpO2 89% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula
rows.rationale: Oxygenation fell from 94% on the same oxygen. This needs escalation now, even though perfusion is better.

rows.text: Crackles now at both lung bases
rows.rationale: Crackles spread from one base to both, after a large fluid volume in a patient with pneumonia. Fluid or spreading infection in the lungs needs prompt reporting.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend, not one system. Here perfusion responded (mentation, blood pressure, urine output, lactate) while breathing got worse after fluid. Persistent or new signs of failing oxygenation require further escalation even when other numbers look better.
questions.strategy: Group the rows by system. Circulation and kidneys moved one way; the lungs moved the other. A mixed picture is not success.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mentation, blood pressure, urine output and lactate all moved toward normal.
Respiratory rate up, SpO2 down on the same oxygen, crackles spreading.
Improvement in one system does not cancel worsening in another.

elimination.verdict: Indicates improvement: rows 1 to 5. Indicates no improvement: rows 6, 7 and 8.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

chapters.title: Acute Coronary Syndromes: Coronary Artery Disease

questions.stem: A patient who smokes and has a high low density lipoprotein (LDL) level has no plaque on imaging. Which teaching by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: "Quitting and lowering LDL protect your artery lining now."
options.rationale: Smoking and dyslipidemia injure the endothelium. Injury lets LDL enter the wall, where it is oxidized and draws in macrophages to form a fatty streak and then plaque. Reducing these risks now targets the first steps.

options.text: "These changes matter once plaque narrows an artery."
options.rationale: The order is reversed. Injury to the lining comes first and plaque follows, so the changes matter most before plaque forms.

options.text: "These changes can wait until a later scan shows plaque."
options.rationale: Injury to the lining begins before plaque shows on a scan. Waiting lets the process continue.

options.text: "A stent now would keep plaque from forming."
options.rationale: A stent opens an artery that is already narrowed. It does nothing to prevent plaque in an artery with no narrowing.

questions.takeaway: Atherosclerosis starts with endothelial injury from hypertension, smoking, diabetes or dyslipidemia. LDL then enters the wall, is oxidized, attracts macrophages, and forms a fatty streak and then a fibrous plaque that narrows the artery. Risk reduction works best before plaque forms.
questions.strategy: Put the steps in order, then ask where this patient is. Teaching aimed at the first step fits a patient who has risks but no plaque yet.

steps.detail: Risks are present but there is no plaque, so the patient is at the stage of lining injury.
B says plaque causes the injury, which reverses the sequence.
C waits for a scan and D relies on a stent that does not prevent plaque, so A remains.

elimination.verdict: A. Removing the causes of lining injury keeps LDL out of the wall and prevents plaque.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.nursesNote: Patient, 59 years old, seen for a wellness visit. Parent died of a myocardial infarction at 62 years old. Has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years. Blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg. LDL cholesterol 172 mg/dL. Works at a desk and does not exercise. Body mass index 23 kg/m2. Fasting blood glucose 118 mg/dL. Eats fried food or fast food 5 days each week.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the wellness visit note of a patient. Highlight the findings that are modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease.

segments.text: Patient, 59 years old
segments.rationale: Increasing age is a risk factor, but it is nonmodifiable. The patient cannot change it.

segments.text: Parent died of a myocardial infarction at 62 years old
segments.rationale: Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor. It raises risk but cannot be changed.

segments.text: Has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years
segments.rationale: Cigarette smoking is a modifiable risk factor. It injures the endothelium, and the patient can stop.

segments.text: Blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg
segments.rationale: 148/94 mm Hg is above the normal range of below 120/80 mm Hg. Hypertension is modifiable with lifestyle change and medication.

segments.text: LDL cholesterol 172 mg/dL
segments.rationale: 172 mg/dL is above the reference of below 100 mg/dL. Dyslipidemia is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Works at a desk and does not exercise
segments.rationale: A sedentary lifestyle is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Fasting blood glucose 118 mg/dL
segments.rationale: 118 mg/dL is above the reference of 70 to 99 mg/dL, which points to insulin resistance. Diabetes and insulin resistance are modifiable risk factors.

segments.text: Eats fried food or fast food 5 days each week
segments.rationale: An atherogenic diet, high in fat, is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Body mass index 23 kg/m2
segments.rationale: A body mass index of 23 kg/m2 is inside the reference range of 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2, so obesity is not present.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease are dyslipidemia, hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes and insulin resistance, obesity and a sedentary lifestyle, and an atherogenic diet. Age and family history raise risk but cannot be changed.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions of each finding: does it raise risk, and can the patient change it? Age and family history pass the first test and fail the second. A value inside its range fails the first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 59 and a parent's myocardial infarction cannot be changed.

steps.action: Check each value against its range
steps.detail: Blood pressure, LDL, and glucose are above range. Body mass index 23 kg/m2 is inside 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2.
Smoking, no exercise, and frequent fried or fast food are all changeable.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient whose blood pressure was 164/98 mm Hg and 160/96 mm Hg at two clinic visits. Low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is 92 mg/dL, and the patient has never smoked. The provider prescribes an antihypertensive. The patient says, "Plaque comes from cholesterol, and mine is in range, so I don't need a pressure pill to protect my heart arteries." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Your LDL is in range, so the pill mainly protects your kidneys and brain."
options.rationale: The pill does protect the kidneys and brain, but this agrees that plaque risk is low. Hypertension is a cause of plaque even with LDL in range.

options.text: "Take the pill for your kidneys, and ask about a statin for your arteries."
options.rationale: This repeats the patient's mistake. High pressure injures the lining of the heart arteries, so the pill protects them too.

options.text: "High pressure makes your heart work harder, and the pill eases that strain."
options.rationale: This is true and gives a reason to take the pill. But the patient asked about protecting the heart arteries, and this answer does not address plaque.

options.text: "High pressure injures the lining and lets cholesterol in to form plaque."
options.rationale: Hypertension causes endothelial injury, the first step of atherosclerosis. Once the lining is injured, LDL in range can still enter the wall and start plaque. This answers the belief the patient stated.

questions.takeaway: Hypertension is a cause of endothelial injury, the first step of atherosclerosis. Once the lining is injured, LDL enters the wall even at levels in range, so blood pressure control protects the coronary arteries.
questions.strategy: Two options give true reasons to take the pill. Pick the one that answers the belief the patient actually stated: plaque in the heart arteries.

steps.detail: A and B both accept that plaque depends only on cholesterol, so both are out.
C explains workload and oxygen demand. D explains how pressure starts plaque.
The patient said the pill is not needed to protect the heart arteries. Only D answers that.

elimination.verdict: D. High pressure injures the arterial lining, so plaque can form even with LDL in range.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A patient has had chest pressure after 5 minutes of uphill walking that ends with rest, unchanged for 1 year. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The narrowed artery cannot raise flow during hard work."
options.rationale: In predictable angina, a plaque narrows the artery so flow meets the heart's needs at rest but not during exertion. Resting lowers the need, and the pressure ends.

options.text: "A clot blocks the artery while you walk and clears when you sit."
options.rationale: A clot blocking the artery is an acute coronary syndrome, and it would not clear each time the patient sits.

options.text: "Steady walking widens the narrowed artery until the pressure passes."
options.rationale: Exercise does not widen a narrowed artery during the walk. Continuing raises demand further.

options.text: "Each episode is a small heart attack that ends when you sit."
options.rationale: Pressure that comes with exertion and ends with rest in an unchanged pattern is not a heart attack. Activity is paced, not stopped.

questions.takeaway: In predictable angina, plaque narrows the artery so flow meets the heart's needs at rest but falls short during exertion. Rest lowers demand and ends the pressure. New, worsening or rest pressure points instead to an acute coronary syndrome.
questions.strategy: Each option offers a mechanism. Match it to the pattern: pressure with exertion that ends with rest and has not changed for a year.

steps.detail: Pressure with exertion, relief with rest, and no change for 1 year is predictable angina.
A clot or a heart attack would not start and stop with each walk, so B and D are out.
Exercise does not widen a narrowed artery during the walk, so C is out.

elimination.verdict: A. The narrowed artery cannot raise its flow to meet the demand of exertion.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who has had chronic angina for 2 years. The chest pressure has always started after climbing two flights of stairs and ended within 3 minutes of rest. Over the past 2 weeks, the same pressure starts after walking from the bedroom to the kitchen, and it still ends within 3 minutes of rest. The patient has no pressure now. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Reinforce resting at the first sign of pressure
options.rationale: Relief with rest fits chronic angina, and teaching rest is reasonable. But the pressure now starts with far less exertion. That is a worsening pattern, and reinforcing the old plan leaves it unevaluated.

options.text: Teach taking nitroglycerin before walking to the kitchen
options.rationale: Taking nitroglycerin before a known trigger is reasonable teaching for a predictable pattern. This pattern is no longer predictable: the threshold has dropped from two flights of stairs to a short walk, and that change needs evaluation, not prevention.

options.text: Report the change in pattern to the provider today
options.rationale: Angina that is new, worsening, or at rest is unstable and needs urgent evaluation. Pressure that once needed two flights of stairs and now comes with walking to the kitchen is worsening.

options.text: Document the episodes for review at the 3 month visit
options.rationale: Documenting is part of care, but waiting 3 months delays evaluation of angina that is getting worse.

questions.takeaway: Chronic angina is predictable: the same trigger, the same relief. A change in the pattern, such as pressure that now starts with less exertion, means unstable angina and urgent evaluation, even when rest still relieves it.
questions.strategy: Relief with rest makes the old plan look right. The deciding cue is the trigger: two flights of stairs before, a walk to the kitchen now. A lower threshold is a worsening pattern.

steps.action: Compare the trigger then and now
steps.detail: Two flights of stairs, now bedroom to kitchen.
Worsening angina is unstable, even with relief by rest.
Reinforcing rest and waiting 3 months both leave the change unevaluated.

steps.action: Reject prevention of the old pattern
steps.detail: Nitroglycerin before exertion treats a predictable pattern. The pattern has changed.

elimination.verdict: Report the worsening pattern for urgent evaluation.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: An older patient with coronary artery disease and diabetes calls the clinic about symptoms this week. Which reports may be manifestations of myocardial ischemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Jaw ache while raking leaves that stops with rest
options.rationale: Angina may radiate to the jaw. Onset with exertion and relief with rest fit ischemia.

options.text: Unusual fatigue while making the bed
options.rationale: Fatigue and weakness can accompany ischemia, and some patients, especially older patients and patients with diabetes, have atypical symptoms rather than chest pain.

options.text: Shortness of breath and sweating carrying groceries upstairs
options.rationale: Dyspnea and diaphoresis can occur with ischemia, and they came on with exertion.

options.text: Calf cramping after walking one block, relieved by standing
options.rationale: The exertion and rest pattern looks like angina, but the discomfort is in the calf. Angina radiates to the jaw, neck, shoulder, arm, or back, not the leg.

options.text: Upper back pressure that comes on with exertion
options.rationale: Angina may radiate to the back, and pressure is a common description.

options.text: Shoulder pain since lifting a box, worse with arm movement
options.rationale: The shoulder is a site angina can reach, but this pain began with a lift and changes with arm movement, which points to the muscle or joint rather than the heart.

questions.takeaway: Angina is pressure, heaviness, squeezing, or pain that may radiate to the jaw, neck, shoulder, arm, or back, and it may come with dyspnea, diaphoresis, pallor, fatigue, or weakness. Some patients have atypical or silent ischemia, so ask about associated symptoms, not only chest pain.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options borrow one feature of angina: the exertion and rest pattern, or the shoulder location. Check every report for both a site angina reaches and a pattern ischemia follows.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Jaw, back, and shoulder are sites angina reaches. The calf is not.
Fatigue, weakness, dyspnea, and diaphoresis can all accompany ischemia.
Shoulder pain that started with a lift and changes with arm movement points to a muscle or joint.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A patient with 3 years of angina only on exertion now has chest pressure that began while sitting at a desk. Which process best explains the change?

options.text: Slow plaque growth limiting flow on exertion
options.rationale: Slow growth of a fixed plaque explains angina with exertion. This pressure began at rest, so exertion is not the trigger.

options.text: Plaque rupture with a clot cutting flow
options.rationale: Plaque rupture with thrombosis turns chronic narrowing into an acute coronary syndrome. Pressure that starts at rest in a patient whose pressure came only with exertion fits that change.

options.text: A new fatty streak blocking the artery
options.rationale: A fatty streak is an early lesion that develops over time. It does not form in a day or block an artery.

options.text: Higher demand from a rise in blood pressure
options.rationale: Higher pressure does raise demand, but the patient is sitting at a desk. A sudden change to pressure at rest points to rupture and a clot, not to a blood pressure rise.

questions.takeaway: Plaque rupture and thrombosis are what turn chronic coronary artery disease into an acute coronary syndrome or acute myocardial infarction. Angina that changes to occurring at rest is the cue.
questions.strategy: Ask what changed. Angina with exertion is a narrowing problem. Pressure at rest in a patient whose angina came only with exertion means something new happened in the artery: rupture and a clot.

steps.detail: Pressure has always come with exertion. Now it began at rest.
Gradual growth and a new fatty streak do not cause sudden pressure at rest.
A blood pressure rise at a desk does not explain the abrupt change.
Rupture and a clot cut flow at rest.

elimination.verdict: Plaque rupture with a clot.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.scenario: A patient with coronary artery disease diagnosed 6 months ago arrives at the emergency department. Chest pressure began 40 minutes ago while lying on the sofa. Pain 7 of 10, radiating to the left arm, with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. Blood pressure 156/92 mm Hg, heart rate 106 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Lungs are clear in both bases, and there is no edema in either ankle.
questions.stem: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a patient with coronary artery disease who has chest pressure that began at rest. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Draw blood for a troponin level as prescribed
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are the preferred biomarkers for acute myocardial infarction.

options.text: Obtain a chest X ray
options.rationale: A chest X ray can show congestion, but the lungs are clear in both bases, so it does not answer the question this presentation raises.

options.text: Teach a low sodium diet before discharge
options.rationale: Diet teaching is part of risk reduction, but it does not address pressure at rest happening now.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: The 12 lead ECG is a core diagnostic test for coronary artery disease and acute coronary syndrome.

options.text: Draw a B type natriuretic peptide level
options.rationale: B type natriuretic peptide points to ventricular stretch and fluid overload. Clear lungs and no edema do not suggest heart failure; ischemia is the problem.

options.text: Left sided heart failure
options.rationale: Left sided failure causes pulmonary congestion with crackles. The lungs are clear in both bases.

options.text: Acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Pressure at rest, 7 of 10, with diaphoresis and dyspnea in a patient with known coronary artery disease fits an acute coronary syndrome.

options.text: Chronic angina with a predictable pattern
options.rationale: Predictable angina comes with exertion and ends with rest. This pressure began while lying on the sofa.

options.text: Hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: Hypertensive crisis is a blood pressure of 180/120 mm Hg or higher. This measurement is 156/92 mm Hg.

options.text: Orthostatic blood pressure
options.rationale: Orthostatic checks are a hypertension and medication assessment. Standing a patient with active ischemia raises demand and is not the priority.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario points to a glucose problem; pain and rhythm show whether ischemia continues.

options.text: Heart rhythm on the cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Ischemic muscle is irritable, and a heart rate of 106 beats per minute is already above range.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid in heart failure. Lungs are clear and there is no edema.

options.text: Chest pain intensity
options.rationale: Pain intensity shows whether ischemia is continuing or easing with treatment.

questions.takeaway: Chest pressure at rest with diaphoresis and dyspnea in a patient with coronary artery disease is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. Obtain a 12 lead ECG and a troponin, and watch pain intensity and heart rhythm.
questions.strategy: Rule out each condition with one stem fact: the pressure began at rest, the pressure is below 180/120 mm Hg, and the lungs are clear. Then choose the actions that diagnose the problem now and the parameters that show whether ischemia is continuing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressure at rest with diaphoresis and dyspnea: acute coronary syndrome.
Not predictable angina, not 180/120 mm Hg or higher, lungs clear.
12 lead ECG and troponin.
Lungs clear, no edema.
Pain intensity and heart rhythm.

elimination.verdict: Actions: 12 lead ECG and troponin. Condition: acute coronary syndrome. Parameters: pain intensity and heart rhythm.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for several patients with coronary artery disease. Which findings suggest an acute coronary syndrome rather than predictable chronic angina? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heaviness on stairs, relieved by rest, unchanged for months
options.rationale: A predictable trigger and relief with rest, unchanged for months, is chronic angina.

options.text: Chest pressure that began while resting in bed
options.rationale: Angina at rest is unstable and needs urgent evaluation.

options.text: Jaw ache with yard work, relieved by sitting, for 1 year
options.rationale: Radiation to the jaw can occur with any angina. The trigger, relief, and 1 year pattern make this predictable.

options.text: A first episode of chest squeezing yesterday
options.rationale: New angina is unstable. There is no established pattern to call predictable.

options.text: Chest pressure with an elevated troponin level
options.rationale: Troponin is the preferred biomarker for acute myocardial infarction. An elevated level with chest pressure points to infarction.

options.text: Pressure with brisk walking, relieved by a nitrate as usual
options.rationale: Predictable angina is relieved by rest or nitrates.

questions.takeaway: Chronic angina is predictable with exertion or stress and relieved by rest or nitrates. Angina that is new, worsening, or at rest is unstable, and an elevated troponin points to myocardial infarction; both are acute coronary syndromes.
questions.strategy: Ignore how dramatic a symptom sounds. Jaw ache can be part of a predictable pattern. Sort each finding by trigger, relief, and whether the pattern is new or changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Look for rest or new onset
steps.detail: Pressure in bed and a first episode are unstable.
An elevated troponin points to infarction.

steps.action: Look for the same trigger and relief over time
steps.detail: Stairs, yard work, and brisk walking with relief by rest or a nitrate are predictable.
Jaw ache does not by itself make angina unstable.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: The nurse in the emergency department is caring for a patient with chest pressure, 5 of 10, that began 45 minutes ago while watching television. The 12 lead ECG shows no ST elevation, and the first troponin I is 0.01 ng/mL. The provider prescribes continuous cardiac monitoring and repeat troponin levels. The patient says, "My heart tracing and blood test are normal, so can I go home now?" Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "These results point to unstable angina, and the repeat tests are routine."
options.rationale: Unstable angina does not raise troponin, so this sounds reasonable. But the pressure began only 45 minutes ago, too early for troponin to separate unstable angina from an infarction without ST elevation. The repeat levels are not a formality.

options.text: "Troponin can take hours to rise, and one normal result is not enough."
options.rationale: In infarction without ST elevation, troponin may be normal at first and rise over 3 to 12 hours. The pressure began 45 minutes ago, so the first value is too early to rule out infarction.

options.text: "You can go home later if a treadmill stress test today shows no changes."
options.rationale: A stress test is part of the workup, but it is done after the acute stage. Exercise now would raise demand while pressure from 45 minutes ago may still be an acute event.

options.text: "No ST elevation means no heart attack; the repeat tests look for other causes."
options.rationale: Infarction can occur without ST elevation, and in that case troponin rises over 3 to 12 hours.

questions.takeaway: Troponin T and I are the preferred markers for acute myocardial infarction, but they are drawn as a series. In infarction without ST elevation the first value may be normal and rise over 3 to 12 hours, so an early normal result does not rule out infarction.
