options.text: Chronic incomplete emptying, residual unchanged from yesterday
options.rationale: This is ongoing incomplete emptying that has not changed. It needs follow up but is not a sudden change.

options.text: Leaks small amounts with coughing for 3 years
options.rationale: Leakage with coughing is a long standing pattern of stress incontinence. It affects quality of life but is not urgent.

options.text: Mild burning on day 2 of antibiotics for cystitis
options.rationale: Mild burning on the second day of treatment is expected to ease as the antibiotic works. The patient is being treated.

options.text: No void for 8 hours, palpable bladder, severe pain
options.rationale: Sudden inability to void with severe pain and a palpable bladder is acute retention. A sudden inability to void needs urgent attention.

questions.takeaway: Acute retention is a sudden inability to urinate and needs urgent attention. Chronic retention and long standing incontinence patterns are ongoing problems that can wait for the acute one.
questions.strategy: Sort acute from chronic. A new, sudden problem with severe pain outranks problems that are unchanged or already treated.

steps.detail: No void for 8 hours with severe pain and a palpable bladder.
Residual the same as yesterday; leakage for 3 years.
Cystitis on day 2 of an antibiotic.
The patient with acute retention.

elimination.verdict: D. No void for 8 hours, palpable bladder, severe pain.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: After knee surgery, a patient allowed up with help cannot void on a bedpan with the curtain open. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Insert a straight catheter to empty the bladder
options.rationale: Catheterization is considered only after measures that promote normal voiding are tried. The patient has not yet tried a usual position with privacy.

options.text: Close the curtain and assist to a commode
options.rationale: The patient cannot void lying on a bedpan with no privacy. A usual sitting position, privacy, and adequate time help the bladder empty, and the nurse then reassesses with the void amount or a bladder scan.

options.text: Leave the patient on the bedpan and check back later
options.rationale: Staying in the same position without privacy does not change what is keeping the patient from voiding, and the bladder keeps filling.

options.text: Give extra oral fluid to strengthen the urge
options.rationale: The problem is emptying, not the urge. More fluid adds volume without helping the bladder empty.

questions.takeaway: For suspected retention, provide safe positioning, privacy, and time before an invasive step, and reassess after each intervention.
questions.strategy: The stem names the barriers: lying on a bedpan and an open curtain. Pick the option that removes them safely.

steps.detail: Lying on a bedpan with no privacy.
The patient is allowed up with help.
A catheter comes after normal voiding measures.
Neither removes a barrier.

elimination.verdict: B. Close the curtain and assist to a commode.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the histories of six patients who each have urinary retention.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the histories of patients who have urinary retention. For each history, indicate whether it points to obstructive or non obstructive retention.

rows.text: Spinal anesthesia for surgery 5 hours ago
rows.rationale: Anesthesia interferes with the nerve signals and muscle function that empty the bladder. Nothing blocks the outflow.

rows.text: A stone lodged at the outlet of the bladder
rows.rationale: A bladder stone at the outlet physically blocks urine from leaving the bladder.

rows.text: Nerve damage from diabetes for 20 years
rows.rationale: Nerve damage weakens the signals that tell the bladder it is full and trigger contraction.

rows.text: A new medication that slows bladder muscle contraction
rows.rationale: Medications can cause retention by reducing bladder contraction. The outflow path is open.

rows.text: A tumor that narrows the urethra
rows.rationale: A tumor narrowing the urethra blocks the path urine takes out of the body.

rows.text: A spinal cord injury at the level of the waist
rows.rationale: Spinal cord injury interrupts the nerve pathways that coordinate bladder contraction and sphincter relaxation.

questions.takeaway: Obstructive retention comes from something blocking the outflow, such as stones, tumors, an enlarged prostate, or pelvic organ prolapse. Non obstructive retention comes from nerve damage, spinal cord injury, medications, or anesthesia that interfere with the signals and muscles of emptying.
questions.strategy: Ask one question for each row: is something in the way, or are the nerves and muscle not working?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stone at the bladder outlet and the tumor narrowing the urethra.

steps.action: Find the signal and muscle problems
steps.detail: Anesthesia, diabetic nerve damage, the medication, and spinal cord injury.

elimination.verdict: Obstructive: rows 2 and 5. Non obstructive: rows 1, 3, 4, and 6.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A patient leaks small amounts of urine when sneezing, laughing, or lifting, with no urgency. Which intervention should the nurse plan?

options.text: Teach pelvic floor muscle exercises
options.rationale: Leakage with sneezing, laughing, and lifting is stress incontinence. Pelvic floor muscle training strengthens the muscles around the urethra so that they hold urine when abdominal pressure rises.

options.text: Schedule toileting every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting addresses functional or urgency patterns. This patient leaks with pressure, not with a full bladder or difficulty reaching the toilet.

options.text: Repeat a bladder scan after each void
options.rationale: Nothing suggests incomplete emptying. Repeated scans do not address leakage with pressure.

options.text: Advise the patient to limit fluid intake
options.rationale: Restricting fluid concentrates the urine and irritates the bladder. It does not strengthen the muscles that fail under pressure.

questions.takeaway: Stress incontinence is leakage with coughing, sneezing, or activity. Match care to the cause: pelvic floor muscle training for stress leakage.
questions.strategy: Name the incontinence type from the trigger first, then pick the intervention that treats that cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sneezing, laughing, lifting: rises in abdominal pressure.
No urgency and no sign of incomplete emptying.
Pelvic floor muscle training.

elimination.verdict: A. Teach pelvic floor muscle exercises.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A patient with long standing diabetes reports constant dribbling and small voids. The bladder is still palpable after voiding. Which problem is most likely?

options.text: Urgency incontinence from sudden bladder contractions
options.rationale: Urgency incontinence follows a sudden strong urge, and the bladder empties. This bladder stays full after voiding.

options.text: Stress incontinence from weak pelvic floor muscles
options.rationale: Stress leakage follows coughing, sneezing, or activity, and the bladder empties normally between episodes.

options.text: Overflow incontinence from incomplete bladder emptying
options.rationale: Constant dribbling, small voids, and a bladder still palpable after voiding show leakage from a bladder that does not empty. Long standing diabetes can damage the nerves that signal fullness.

options.text: Functional incontinence from difficulty reaching the toilet
options.rationale: Functional incontinence happens when the patient cannot get to or use the toilet in time. Nothing in the stem describes a barrier to the toilet.

questions.takeaway: Overflow incontinence is leakage with incomplete emptying. Small voids or leakage can occur with retention, so a palpable bladder and a high residual after voiding point to overflow.
questions.strategy: Look for the finding that only one type explains: urine left in the bladder after voiding.

steps.detail: Bladder still palpable after a void.
No urge or pressure trigger is described.
No barrier to the toilet is described.

elimination.verdict: C. Overflow incontinence from incomplete bladder emptying.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A patient who walks independently leaks urine after a sudden strong urge, before reaching the nearby bathroom. Which intervention best addresses the cause?

options.text: Place a bedside commode next to the bed
options.rationale: A commode helps when reaching the toilet is the problem. This patient walks independently and the bathroom is close; the leakage starts with the urge itself.

options.text: Limit fluid intake to reduce leakage
options.rationale: Restricting fluid concentrates urine, which irritates the bladder and can worsen urgency.

options.text: Apply an absorbent product and change it often
options.rationale: An absorbent product contains leakage but does not treat its cause, and leaves the skin wet between changes.

options.text: Start bladder training to lengthen intervals
options.rationale: A sudden strong urge with leakage is urgency incontinence. Bladder training teaches the patient to delay voiding and gradually lengthen the interval, which reduces urgency and leakage.

questions.takeaway: Urgency incontinence is a sudden strong urge followed by leakage. Bladder training lengthens the time between voids and treats the cause.
questions.strategy: The cue is that the patient is independent and close to the bathroom, so access is not the problem. The urge is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden strong urge, then leakage: urgency incontinence.
Walks independently, bathroom nearby.
Absorbent products and fluid limits do not treat the urge.
Bladder training.

elimination.verdict: D. Start bladder training to lengthen intervals.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A patient with frequent urinary incontinence has red perineal skin with no open areas. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash with soap and a washcloth using firm strokes
options.rationale: Firm scrubbing and soap residue damage skin that is already red. Cleansing after incontinence is gentle.

options.text: Cleanse gently after each episode and pat dry
options.rationale: Gentle cleansing removes urine without friction, and patting dry avoids rubbing the reddened skin.

options.text: Leave each pad in place until it is fully soaked
options.rationale: A soaked pad keeps urine against the skin and worsens the moisture damage.

options.text: Apply a barrier cream after cleansing
options.rationale: A barrier cream protects the skin from urine between episodes.

options.text: Request an indwelling catheter to keep the skin dry
options.rationale: A catheter is used only when indicated and carries a risk of infection. Incontinence alone is not an indication.

options.text: Inspect the perineal skin with each episode of care
options.rationale: Inspecting the perineal skin is indicated with ongoing incontinence, so early damage is found and the plan can change.

questions.takeaway: Incontinence care includes gentle cleansing, skin protection with a barrier cream, and regular inspection of the perineal skin. A catheter is not a skin care measure.
questions.strategy: Judge each option by whether it shortens contact between urine and skin without adding friction or risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gentle cleansing, patting dry, barrier cream.
Inspect the skin with each episode of care.
Scrubbing, soaked pads, and a catheter without an indication.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.nursesNote: Clinic visit. Patient is 81 years old, 2 weeks after starting a plan for functional incontinence with a bedside commode and toileting every 2 hours. Leakage 1 time this week, was 6 times in the week before the plan. Uses the commode at night without help. Perineal skin red with a 2 cm open area on the buttock. Pain with voiding 0 of 10. Says, "If my urine turns cloudy or I get a fever, I will wait for my next visit." Drinks 1,800 mL of fluid per day as planned. A family member reports that toileting at 1400 is skipped when the patient naps.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the clinic note of a patient 2 weeks after a plan of care for functional incontinence began. Highlight the findings that show the plan of care needs revision.

segments.text: Leakage 1 time this week, was 6 times in the week before the plan
segments.rationale: Leakage has dropped from 6 episodes to 1, which shows the plan is working on this outcome.

segments.text: Uses the commode at night without help
segments.rationale: Independent use of the commode meets the goal of greater independence.

segments.text: Perineal skin red with a 2 cm open area on the buttock
segments.rationale: The outcome is intact skin. An open area means skin protection in the plan needs revision.

segments.text: Pain with voiding 0 of 10
segments.rationale: No pain with voiding meets the comfort outcome.

segments.text: Says, "If my urine turns cloudy or I get a fever, I will wait for my next visit."
segments.rationale: Cloudy urine and fever are reportable changes. The patient does not know to report them, so teaching needs revision.

segments.text: Drinks 1,800 mL of fluid per day as planned
segments.rationale: Fluid intake matches the plan.

segments.text: A family member reports that toileting at 1400 is skipped when the patient naps
segments.rationale: A missed scheduled toileting time means the patient cannot fully manage the plan as written. The schedule needs to be revised with the patient and family.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the pattern is better, the patient has comfort, the skin is intact, the patient can manage the plan, and the patient knows reportable changes. A no to any of these means the plan needs revision.
questions.strategy: Hold each finding against one evaluation question. Findings that meet their outcome are not the cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leakage down from 6 to 1, uses the commode alone: met.
Open area on the buttock: not met.
Would wait with fever and cloudy urine; 1400 toileting skipped: not met.
Pain 0 of 10 and 1,800 mL per day: met.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse needs a urine culture from a patient with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Drain urine from the bag spout into a sterile cup
options.rationale: Urine in the bag has been standing and can grow bacteria, so a specimen from the bag gives an inaccurate culture. A specimen is never collected from the drainage bag.

options.text: Aspirate from the cleansed sampling port after clamping
options.rationale: Clamping below the port lets fresh urine collect. Cleansing the port and using a sterile syringe and container avoids contaminating the specimen and keeps the drainage system closed.

options.text: Disconnect the catheter and let urine drip into a sterile cup
options.rationale: Disconnecting opens the closed drainage system, which lets bacteria enter and raises the risk of infection.

options.text: Withdraw urine from the balloon inflation port
options.rationale: The balloon port leads to the balloon, not the bladder. It holds sterile water, not urine.

questions.takeaway: Avoid contaminating a specimen. With an indwelling catheter, collect urine from the sampling port with sterile technique, never from the bag, and never by opening the closed system.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Two options open the system or use old urine. One uses the wrong port. Choose the one that gets fresh urine with the system closed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Urine in the bag has been standing.
Disconnecting invites infection.
The balloon port holds water.
Sampling port after clamping below it.

elimination.verdict: B. Aspirate from the cleansed sampling port after clamping.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is collecting urinalysis specimens from three patients. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Label all three specimens together in the utility room
options.rationale: Labeling away from the patient after collecting several specimens risks switching them. Each specimen is labeled at the bedside.

options.text: Verify each order and use two patient identifiers
options.rationale: The nurse verifies the order and the patient's identity before collection so that the right test is done on the right patient.

options.text: Label each container at the bedside
options.rationale: Specimens are labeled according to requirements so the laboratory can match the result to the right patient. Labels usually include the name, date, time, and type of collection.

options.text: Leave the specimens at the bedside until pickup
options.rationale: Specimens are transported according to requirements. Urine left standing at the bedside grows bacteria and changes the results.

options.text: Use urine that has stood in the bedpan
options.rationale: Urinalysis needs fresh urine. Urine left standing grows bacteria and changes the results.

options.text: Explain the collection method to each patient first
options.rationale: The nurse explains the collection method so the patient can help collect the specimen correctly and without contamination.

questions.takeaway: Specimen collection: verify the order and identity, explain the collection method, use the correct container and technique, avoid contamination, and label and transport according to requirements.
questions.strategy: Look at each step from order to laboratory and ask whether it keeps the right specimen with the right patient and the result accurate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Verify the order and two identifiers; explain the method.
Fresh urine, not urine that has stood in a bedpan.
Label at the bedside; transport, do not leave it waiting.

elimination.verdict: B, C, F.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.scenario: A nurse observes the urine of six patients during the morning assessment and reviews each patient's history.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the urine findings and histories of six patients during the morning assessment. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or requires follow up.

rows.text: Dark amber urine in a patient who drank 600 mL in the past 24 hours and has a dry mouth
rows.rationale: Dark urine sits at the concentrated end of the urine color chart. With low intake and a dry mouth, the finding points to a fluid deficit that needs follow up.

rows.text: Cloudy, foul smelling urine with burning and urgency on voiding
rows.rationale: A change in urine appearance with burning and urgency fits a urinary tract infection.

rows.text: Pale yellow, clear urine in a patient who drinks 2,000 mL per day
rows.rationale: Pale, clear urine fits the dilute end of the color chart and the patient's intake.

rows.text: Dark yellow first morning void that lightens to pale yellow after the patient drinks 720 mL
rows.rationale: Urine held overnight is more concentrated. It lightens as intake increases, and the trend matches the history.

rows.text: Urine output of 120 mL in 8 hours with an intake of 1,600 mL
rows.rationale: Output far below intake is a significant decrease that is compared with intake and reported promptly.

rows.text: Light yellow urine with a mild odor, 250 to 300 mL every 3 to 4 hours
rows.rationale: Light color, mild odor, and regular voids of this size are an expected pattern.

questions.takeaway: Observe color, clarity, and odor, measure output, and combine the findings with symptoms and history. Dark urine with low intake, cloudy foul urine with burning, and output well below intake need follow up.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether the history explains it. If the history makes it worse rather than explains it, follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Use the color chart with the history
steps.detail: Dark with low intake: follow up. Dark in the morning that lightens with fluid: expected.
Cloudy and foul with burning and urgency: follow up.
120 mL out against 1,600 mL in: follow up.

elimination.verdict: Requires follow up: rows 1, 2, and 5. Expected: rows 3, 4, and 6.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A patient with cystitis starts an oral antibiotic today, and the urine culture is pending. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "The culture takes a few days to grow."
options.rationale: This is correct. Bacteria need time to grow, so a culture usually takes 48 to 72 hours.

options.text: "I will start the antibiotic today."
options.rationale: This is correct. Treatment starts once the culture has been collected, and the result is used to adjust it later.

options.text: "If the clinic changes my antibiotic, I will switch."
options.rationale: This is correct. The culture and sensitivity result shows which antibiotics the organism responds to, so a change is possible.

options.text: "Today's urine test showed which antibiotic works."
options.rationale: This needs teaching. The urinalysis screens for signs of infection, such as nitrites and white blood cells. Only the culture identifies the organism and the antibiotics it responds to, so the antibiotic may still change.

questions.takeaway: A urinalysis screens urine for signs of infection; a culture identifies the organism and the antibiotics it responds to, in about 48 to 72 hours. Teach the patient that the antibiotic started today may change once the culture returns.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. Match each test to the question it answers, then find the statement that gives the urinalysis the culture's job.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Urinalysis screens; the culture identifies the organism and its sensitivity.
A, B and C fit a pending culture that may change the antibiotic; D credits the urinalysis with the culture's result.

elimination.verdict: D. "Today's urine test showed which antibiotic works."

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: Before an imaging study of the urinary tract tomorrow, which patient finding requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: Signed consent form is on the chart
options.rationale: A signed consent on the chart is expected preparation. It does not need action.

options.text: Vital signs are at the patient's baseline
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs give no reason to delay or change the preparation for the study.

options.text: Says, "Nobody told me why I need this test."
options.rationale: The nurse explains the purpose of each test. The patient does not know why the study is ordered or what will happen, so the nurse explains the purpose and the procedure before the test.

options.text: Plans to collect urine in the bathroom with a device
options.rationale: Using the collection device in the bathroom supports privacy and independence. It does not need correction.

questions.takeaway: For laboratory and diagnostic tests, the nurse explains the purpose so the patient understands what is being done and why.
questions.strategy: Three options describe preparation that is already in place. Find the cue that shows a need the nurse can meet now.

steps.detail: Consent signed, vital signs at baseline.
Using the device in the bathroom is correct.
The patient does not know the purpose of the test.

elimination.verdict: C. Says, "Nobody told me why I need this test."

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is matching three patients to the urinary catheter each one needs. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse matches three patients to the catheter each needs.

A patient who needs continuous irrigation after bladder surgery to keep blood clots from forming needs a [[1]] catheter.

A patient whose urethra is blocked by scar tissue and who needs long term drainage is expected to have a [[2]] catheter.

A patient with a postvoid residual of 450 mL and an order to drain the bladder one time needs a [[3]] catheter.

options.text: three way
options.rationale: A three way catheter includes a separate channel for irrigation, which allows continuous irrigation through a closed system.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter is inserted briefly for drainage and removed. It cannot deliver continuous irrigation.

options.text: suprapubic
options.rationale: A suprapubic catheter drains the bladder through the abdominal wall. It is not chosen for continuous irrigation.

options.text: indwelling urethral
options.rationale: An indwelling urethral catheter passes through the urethra, which is blocked in this patient.

options.text: suprapubic
options.rationale: A suprapubic catheter enters the bladder through the abdomen, so it drains urine when the urethra is blocked.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter also passes through the urethra and is removed after one drainage.

options.text: straight
options.rationale: A straight catheter is inserted briefly to drain the bladder and then removed, which fits a one time order.

options.text: three way
options.rationale: A three way catheter stays in place for irrigation. Nothing here calls for irrigation.

options.text: indwelling
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter remains in the bladder and adds infection risk when only one drainage is ordered.

questions.takeaway: Straight catheters drain once and are removed, indwelling catheters remain in the bladder, three way catheters add an irrigation channel, suprapubic catheters enter through the abdomen, and external devices collect urine outside the urethra.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each patient: does the catheter stay or come out, and which path can it take?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Continuous irrigation needs an irrigation channel: three way.
A blocked urethra needs a path through the abdomen: suprapubic.
One drainage needs a catheter that is removed: straight.

elimination.verdict: Three way; suprapubic; straight.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: Before inserting an indwelling urinary catheter for hourly output after major surgery, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear clean gloves for the insertion
options.rationale: Catheter insertion uses aseptic technique with sterile gloves and sterile equipment to keep bacteria out of the bladder.

options.text: Ask about a latex allergy
options.rationale: Catheters and gloves can contain latex. The nurse checks for relevant allergies before insertion.

options.text: Choose a larger catheter size than usual
options.rationale: The smallest appropriate catheter is used. A larger catheter increases trauma to the urethra and the risk of infection.

options.text: Confirm the order documents the indication
options.rationale: The nurse confirms the indication before insertion. Hourly output after major surgery is the indication here.

options.text: Secure the catheter to the patient's upper thigh
options.rationale: Securing the catheter prevents movement and pulling that injure the urethra and raise infection risk.

options.text: Leave the catheter unsecured after insertion
options.rationale: An unsecured catheter moves and pulls with each position change, which causes trauma.

questions.takeaway: Catheter safety: confirm the indication, consider an alternative, check allergies, use aseptic technique and sterile equipment, use the smallest appropriate catheter, and secure it after insertion.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is the opposite of a safety step. Find the pairs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sterile, not clean.
Smallest appropriate, not larger.
Secured to the thigh, not left free.
Indication and latex allergy.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: On day 3 after abdominal surgery, a patient walks with help. The catheter was placed for hourly output, which has ended. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Keep the catheter in place until discharge
options.rationale: Each day a catheter remains raises the risk of a catheter associated infection. The risk of retention is managed by monitoring voiding after removal.

options.text: Replace the catheter with a new one today
options.rationale: Routine catheter changes do not prevent infection. The question is whether the catheter is still needed.

options.text: Remove the catheter per order or protocol
options.rationale: The reason for the catheter, hourly output, no longer exists. Catheters are removed promptly when no longer indicated, per order or protocol, and voiding is monitored after removal.

options.text: Send a urine culture before removing the catheter
options.rationale: The patient has no signs of infection. A culture without symptoms does not decide whether the catheter stays.

questions.takeaway: Prevent catheter associated urinary tract infection: use a catheter only when needed, review the indication regularly, and remove it promptly when no longer indicated.
questions.strategy: Ask why the catheter was placed and whether that reason still exists.

steps.detail: Hourly output, which has ended.
Walks with help, no output order.
Review the indication and remove per protocol.

elimination.verdict: C. Remove the catheter per order or protocol.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: A long term urinary catheter with gritty sediment has stopped draining, and the bladder is full. There is no irrigation order. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Notify the provider of the blocked drainage
options.rationale: The catheter is likely blocked by sediment, and the bladder is filling. Irrigation is done only when indicated and ordered, and changing a blocked catheter is often safer than flushing debris into the bladder. The provider needs the findings to decide.

options.text: Irrigate the catheter through a closed system
options.rationale: Closed irrigation is the right technique, but irrigation is done only when it is prescribed, and there is no prescription.

options.text: Reposition the patient and recheck in 2 hours
options.rationale: The bladder is already full. Waiting 2 more hours lets it keep filling.

options.text: Disconnect the tubing and flush the catheter
options.rationale: Disconnecting opens the closed drainage system, and flushing without a prescription risks pushing debris into the bladder.

questions.takeaway: Irrigate only when indicated and ordered, and follow the approved procedure. When a catheter is blocked and there is no order, report the findings so the provider can order irrigation or a change.
questions.strategy: One option uses the right technique without the order. The cue that decides is the missing irrigation order.

steps.detail: Sediment present, no drainage, full bladder.
No order for irrigation.

steps.action: Reject delay and opening the system
steps.detail: Waiting 2 hours; disconnecting to flush.
Report and obtain an order.

elimination.verdict: A. Notify the provider of the blocked drainage.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse evaluates discharge teaching for a patient with a new continent urinary reservoir. Which patient statement shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "My spouse will do all of my stoma care."
options.rationale: Self management support aims for the patient to take part in device care. Avoiding the stoma also means the patient cannot check drainage and skin.

options.text: "I will call if the skin gets sore or urine changes."
options.rationale: The patient names reportable changes in skin and drainage, which shows the patient knows what to watch for and can manage the plan.

options.text: "I will wait for my next visit if the skin breaks down."
options.rationale: Skin breakdown is a reportable change. Waiting for the next visit leaves it untreated.

options.text: "An internal reservoir needs no drainage checks."
options.rationale: Drainage and skin are assessed with every urinary diversion, including a continent reservoir.

questions.takeaway: With a urinary diversion, care includes assessing drainage and skin, supporting device care and self management, and individualized teaching. Evaluation checks whether the patient can manage the plan and knows reportable changes.
questions.strategy: Use the evaluation questions: can the patient manage the care, and does the patient know what to report?

steps.detail: Handing all care to a spouse.
Waiting for the next visit with skin breakdown.
Drainage is checked with every diversion.
Reports skin and urine changes.

elimination.verdict: B. "I will call if the skin gets sore or urine changes."

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: On day 3 after creation of an ileal conduit, which patient finding requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: Clear, pale yellow urine, 900 mL in 8 hours
options.rationale: Clear, pale urine with this output is an expected drainage finding.

options.text: Pouch emptied and output recorded every 4 hours
options.rationale: Emptying the pouch and recording output supports device care and accurate intake and output.

options.text: Watched the pouch change and asks to do the next one
options.rationale: Asking to take part in device care shows readiness for self management.

options.text: Red, weeping skin where urine has leaked
options.rationale: Assessing drainage and skin is part of continuing care, and the outcome is intact skin. Red, weeping skin where urine leaked needs follow up.

questions.takeaway: With an ileal conduit, assess drainage and skin, support device care, and support self management. Skin damage from leaking urine needs follow up.
questions.strategy: Three options describe care and drainage that are on track. Find the one that describes harm.

steps.detail: Clear, pale urine and output recorded: on track.
Asks to try the next change: on track.
Red and weeping where urine leaked: requires follow up.

elimination.verdict: D. Red, weeping skin where urine has leaked.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse admits a patient with new nighttime urine leakage. Which findings can affect the patient's urinary elimination? Select all that apply.

options.text: Takes a new diuretic each evening
options.rationale: Medications affect urinary elimination. A diuretic increases urine output, and an evening dose produces more urine overnight.

options.text: Allergy to penicillin
options.rationale: A drug allergy does not change how the patient stores or empties urine.

options.text: Hand arthritis and pants with small buttons
options.rationale: Clothing management is a factor. Stiff hands and small buttons slow undressing once the patient reaches the toilet.

options.text: Does crossword puzzles each afternoon
options.rationale: Puzzle habits do not affect urinary elimination.

options.text: Finds it hard to void with a roommate behind the curtain
options.rationale: Privacy affects the ability to void. A shared room can make the patient hold urine or not empty fully.

options.text: Drinks 4 cups of coffee each evening
options.rationale: Fluid intake and habits are factors. A large volume of a caffeinated drink in the evening adds to urine overnight.

questions.takeaway: Factors that influence urinary elimination include fluid intake and habits, growth and development, illness and medications, mobility and clothing management, privacy and culture, and toilet access.
questions.strategy: For each finding, ask whether it changes how much urine is made, how fast the patient can get to and use the toilet, or how easily the patient can void.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Evening diuretic and evening coffee add overnight urine.
Small buttons with arthritis; a roommate behind the curtain.
Penicillin allergy and afternoon puzzles.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: A patient reports hesitancy and a feeling of incomplete emptying that began 4 days ago, with no burning. Which question should the nurse ask next?

options.text: "Do you leak urine when you cough, sneeze, or lift?"
options.rationale: This question screens for stress incontinence. The patient reports trouble starting and emptying, not leakage.

options.text: "How much coffee or tea do you drink?"
options.rationale: Fluid habits matter, but caffeine does not explain a new delay in starting the stream.

options.text: "Have you started any new medicines this week?"
options.rationale: Hesitancy and incomplete emptying that began suddenly 4 days ago suggest retention. Medications are a common non obstructive cause, so a recent medication history is the most useful next question.

options.text: "Do you need help getting to the bathroom?"
options.rationale: Toilet access does not explain hesitancy or incomplete emptying.

questions.takeaway: The nursing history covers pain, urgency, hesitancy, leakage, the feeling of incomplete emptying, fluid intake, and medication history. A new onset of hesitancy and incomplete emptying calls for the medication history.
questions.strategy: Ask what could have changed 4 days ago to cause a new problem with starting and emptying.

steps.detail: Leakage with coughing and toilet access do not cause hesitancy.
Caffeine does not explain a new delay in the stream.

steps.action: Find the cause of a new change
steps.detail: A recently started medication.

elimination.verdict: C. "Have you started any new medicines this week?"

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: During the night, the nurse finds an alert patient incontinent of urine in bed while the roommate is awake. Which statement best supports dignity?

options.text: "Let's get your diaper changed so you won't wet the bed again."
options.rationale: "Diaper" and "wet the bed" are childlike terms that shame an adult. Respectful language uses neutral words.

options.text: "I'll close the curtain and explain each step as we change."
options.rationale: Closing the curtain gives privacy from the awake roommate, neutral words respect the patient, and explaining each step before touching supports dignity.

options.text: "Next time, please call before you have an accident."
options.rationale: This places blame on the patient. The patient may have been unable to call in time, and blame increases embarrassment.

options.text: "Don't worry, this happens to everyone your age."
options.rationale: This minimizes the patient's feelings and is not true of every older adult. It does not provide privacy or explain care.

questions.takeaway: Support dignity with privacy, respectful language, and an explanation of care before exposing or touching the patient.
questions.strategy: Eliminate the options that shame, blame, or dismiss. Then confirm the remaining option includes privacy.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Diaper and wet the bed.
Calling before an accident.
Happens to everyone your age.
Curtain closed, each step explained.

elimination.verdict: B. "I'll close the curtain and explain each step as we change."

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.stem: A patient who needs help to reach the commode wants to stop leaking to eat in the dining room. Which outcome is most appropriate?

options.text: Patient will have 1 or fewer leaks daily by 1 week
options.rationale: This outcome is set with the patient's goal in mind, is measurable by the number of episodes, includes a time frame, and is realistic for a patient who still needs help to transfer.

options.text: Patient will understand the importance of the toileting schedule
options.rationale: Understanding cannot be measured as written. It names no observable behavior.

options.text: Nurse will offer toileting assistance every 2 hours while awake
options.rationale: This is a nursing intervention, not a patient outcome. Outcomes describe what the patient will do or experience.

options.text: Patient will never leak urine again once the toileting plan begins
options.rationale: Never is absolute and unrealistic for a patient who still needs help to reach the commode.

questions.takeaway: Set priorities with the patient and choose measurable outcomes: a patient behavior, a number, and a time frame, realistic for the patient's situation.
questions.strategy: Check each option for three parts: the patient as the subject, something you can count or observe, and a time frame.

steps.detail: Offering toileting is an intervention.
Understand names no behavior.
Never is unrealistic.
1 or fewer leaks daily by 1 week.

elimination.verdict: A. Patient will have 1 or fewer leaks daily by 1 week.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who had knee surgery under spinal anesthesia 7 hours ago and has received 1,800 mL of IV fluid since surgery. The patient has not voided since before surgery and says, "I do not feel any need to go." Which interpretation should guide the nurse's next action?

options.text: The bladder is not yet full enough to cause an urge
options.rationale: An urge depends on nerve signals that report bladder fullness, and anesthesia can block them. After 7 hours and 1,800 mL with no void, the missing urge does not show an empty bladder, and waiting risks overdistention.

options.text: The patient is holding urine to avoid using a bedpan
options.rationale: Privacy and position can make voiding hard, which makes this tempting. This patient reports no need to go at all; a patient holding urine back still feels the urge.

options.text: Anesthesia may be blocking the sense of fullness
options.rationale: Nerve signals communicate bladder fullness, and anesthesia is a non obstructive cause of retention that can interrupt them. The nurse assesses the bladder now, by palpation and a bladder scan, instead of relying on the patient's urge.

options.text: The bladder will empty by leaking once it is full
options.rationale: Urination needs coordinated bladder contraction and sphincter relaxation. Anesthesia causes retention, not free leakage, so waiting for leakage leaves a full bladder unrecognized.

questions.takeaway: Voiding depends on nerve signals of fullness, bladder contraction, and sphincter relaxation. Anesthesia can block the fullness signal, so after surgery the nurse compares intake and time since the last void with the bladder findings, not with the patient's urge.
questions.strategy: Three options explain the missing urge in ways that let the nurse wait. The 7 hours and 1,800 mL of intake decide that the bladder is likely full and the sensation is what is missing.

steps.detail: 7 hours, 1,800 mL in, no void.

steps.action: Ask what the urge depends on
steps.detail: Nerve signals that spinal anesthesia can block.
A patient holding urine back still feels the urge.
Waiting for an urge or for leakage leaves a full bladder unassessed.

elimination.verdict: C. Anesthesia may be blocking the sense of fullness.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with chronic urinary retention managed with double voiding, whose daily postvoid residual is about 200 mL. At 0900 the patient says, "I have not been able to pass any urine since 0400, and my lower belly hurts." Pain is 7 of 10, and the bladder is palpable above the symphysis pubis. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Have the patient double void as usual, then scan the bladder
options.rationale: Double voiding is the patient's usual plan, which makes it tempting. The patient has passed no urine for 5 hours, which is a new, sudden problem that the chronic plan does not address.

options.text: Scan the bladder and report the new inability to void
options.rationale: Chronic retention is ongoing incomplete emptying. A sudden inability to void with pain and a palpable bladder is acute retention, which needs urgent attention. The nurse obtains the bladder scan and reports the findings so they can be acted on.

options.text: Give the prescribed analgesic and reassess in 1 hour
options.rationale: Pain of 7 of 10 needs relief, but treating the pain alone delays care for its cause. A sudden inability to void needs urgent attention, not a 1 hour wait.

options.text: Help the patient to the toilet with water running in the sink
options.rationale: Running water and privacy help a patient who is able to void. This patient has been unable to pass urine for 5 hours and has a painful, palpable bladder, so simple measures delay the urgent report.

questions.takeaway: Chronic retention means ongoing incomplete emptying. A patient with chronic retention who suddenly cannot void at all has a new acute problem, and sudden inability to void needs urgent attention.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is something a nurse would do for chronic retention or for pain. Compare with baseline: a patient who usually voids now cannot void at all, which is acute retention.

steps.detail: Usual: voids with a residual of about 200 mL. Now: no urine for 5 hours.
Sudden inability to void with pain 7 of 10 and a palpable bladder.

steps.action: Reject the usual plan and comfort measures
steps.detail: Double voiding, running water, and an analgesic all delay the report.
Bladder scan now and report.

elimination.verdict: B. Scan the bladder and report the new inability to void.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient who fell at home last week and now needs standby help to walk, but toilets without help once seated. The patient says, "At home I always rinse with water after I use the toilet. Paper alone does not feel clean to me." Which action by the nurse best supports the patient's dignity?

options.text: Place warm water in the bathroom for rinsing
options.rationale: Supporting the patient's preferred toileting method when it is safe respects the patient's culture and comfort. Standby help is needed for walking, not for toileting once seated, so staff help the patient to and from the toilet, and water within reach lets the patient rinse alone with privacy.

options.text: Offer moist wipes to use in place of rinsing
options.rationale: Wipes may seem safer because water could spill on the floor of a patient at risk for falls. Water placed within reach of the seated patient keeps the floor dry, so substituting wipes gives up the patient's routine for no safety gain.

options.text: Help the patient rinse with water after each void
options.rationale: The recent fall makes hands on help look like the safe choice, which is the trap. The patient needs standby help to walk but toilets without help once seated, so doing the rinse takes away self care and privacy. Staff stay nearby and help the patient back from the toilet.

options.text: Ask the family to bring a rinse bottle from home
options.rationale: A familiar bottle from home is reasonable, but the patient goes without the preferred method until it arrives, when the nurse can provide water now.

questions.takeaway: Dignity supporting care asks about the usual routine, supports the preferred toileting method when safe, provides privacy, and encourages participation in self care. Match the help to the task the patient actually needs help with: standby help to walk does not mean help with toileting once seated.
questions.strategy: The fall makes hands on help and wipes look safer. The deciding cue is which task needs help: walking needs standby help, toileting once seated does not, so the patient rinses alone with water within reach.

steps.detail: Rinsing with water after toileting.

steps.action: Find the safety and ability cue
steps.detail: Standby help to walk after a fall, but toilets without help once seated.

steps.action: Reject options that substitute or delay
steps.detail: Wipes instead, or waiting for a bottle from home.
Help with walking only, so the seated patient rinses alone with water within reach.

elimination.verdict: A. Place warm water in the bathroom for rinsing.

questions.objective: Select dignity supporting interventions

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the plan of care for a patient with urgency incontinence who started bladder training 3 weeks ago. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient, 70 years old, with urgency incontinence started bladder training 3 weeks ago. The patient now voids every 2.5 hours, was every 1 hour before training. Leakage occurred 2 times this week, was daily before training. Perineal skin is intact. The patient drinks 4 cups of coffee each afternoon, and both leakage episodes this week happened between 1500 and 1700. The patient says, "I can hold it now when the urge starts."

The nurse evaluates the plan as [[1]].

The finding that most supports revising the plan is [[2]].

The change the nurse discusses with the patient is [[3]].

options.text: effective, needing no change
options.rationale: The interval is longer and leakage is less often, which makes this tempting. Leakage still occurs, and it follows a pattern that can be addressed, so the plan is not finished.

options.text: partly effective, needing revision
options.rationale: The voiding interval lengthened and leakage fell from daily to 2 times a week, so the training is working. Leakage that remains with a clear pattern means the plan needs revision.

options.text: ineffective, needing to stop
options.rationale: The interval lengthened and leakage fell from daily to 2 times a week. Stopping the training would discard a plan that is working.

options.text: the voiding interval of 2.5 hours
options.rationale: A longer interval is the goal of bladder training. It shows progress, not a need for change.

options.text: the patient's report of holding the urge
options.rationale: The patient's report shows better urge control, which is progress. It does not point to what still causes the leakage.

options.text: the timing of leakage after the afternoon coffee
options.rationale: Both episodes occurred in the hours after the coffee. Caffeine is a bladder irritant that can cause contractions, urgency, and leakage, so this pattern points to the revision.

options.text: shortening the voiding interval back to every 1 hour
options.rationale: Going back to a 1 hour interval undoes the progress of training and does not address the cause of the remaining leakage.

options.text: replacing the afternoon coffee with a drink without caffeine
options.rationale: Replacing the caffeine targets the identified contributing factor while keeping fluid intake within the plan.

options.text: limiting total fluids to 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restricting all fluids is not the answer. Adequate fluids are supported within the care plan, and the problem is the irritant, not the volume.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the urinary pattern has changed toward the goal, whether the skin is intact, and whether the plan needs revision. A plan can be working and still need revision when a contributing factor, such as a bladder irritant, is found.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Judge each finding against the outcome. Improvement shows the plan works; a leakage pattern tied to one cause shows what to revise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Better interval and less leakage, but leakage remains: partly effective.
Leakage only after the afternoon coffee.
Remove the irritant, keep the fluids and the training.

elimination.verdict: Partly effective, needing revision; the timing of leakage after the afternoon coffee; replacing the afternoon coffee with a drink without caffeine.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a 24 hour urine collection that begins at 0800, and the laboratory instructions require the urine to be kept cold. At 0800 the patient voids 350 mL. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Discard the 0800 void and record 0800 as the start time
options.rationale: The timed period begins after the patient urinates. The first void is discarded because that urine was made before the collection period began.

options.text: Save the 0800 void as the first specimen
options.rationale: Saving every void sounds thorough, which makes this the trap. The 0800 urine was made before the period began, so adding it makes the result inaccurate.

options.text: Keep the collection container on ice
options.rationale: The laboratory instructions call for cold storage, so the container stays on ice and the urine does not change before testing.

options.text: Note any flushed void and continue the collection
options.rationale: A missed specimen makes the whole collection inaccurate. The nurse follows agency and laboratory policy, which usually means starting again.

options.text: Add the 0800 void tomorrow to the container
options.rationale: The period ends with a final void at the end of the 24 hours, and that urine is included.

options.text: Post a sign and tell the team that all urine is saved
options.rationale: Signs and verbal communication help every caregiver save all urine during the timed collection.

questions.takeaway: A 24 hour collection starts after a discarded first void and ends with a saved final void. Every void in between is saved, kept cool if required, and a missed void makes the collection inaccurate.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Picture the 24 hours as a box. Urine made before 0800 is outside the box; the final void at 0800 tomorrow is inside it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Discard the 0800 void today.
Save the 0800 void tomorrow.
Ice if required, signs posted, every void saved.
The collection is no longer accurate.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with continuous bladder irrigation through a three way catheter after bladder surgery. From 1200 to 1400, 800 mL of irrigant infused and the drainage bag collected 650 mL. The drainage is light red with small clots, and the patient reports bladder spasms and lower abdominal pressure. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Increase the irrigation rate to flush the clots
options.rationale: Clots make a faster rate tempting. The drainage is 150 mL less than the irrigant, so fluid is already staying in the bladder. More inflow adds to the pressure until the outflow is open.

options.text: Give the prescribed antispasmodic medication
options.rationale: The spasms are real and need relief, but they are a sign of the problem. Fluid going in without coming out is the cause, and medicating first leaves the bladder filling.

options.text: Record 650 mL as the urine output
options.rationale: Drainage during irrigation includes the irrigant. The 650 mL is less than the 800 mL infused, so true urine output cannot be 650 mL, and recording it hides a blocked catheter.

options.text: Stop the irrigation and check for a blockage
options.rationale: Drainage 150 mL less than the irrigant, clots, spasms, and lower abdominal pressure show the outflow is blocked and the bladder is filling. Stopping the inflow and checking patency comes first, then the nurse reports and follows the irrigation order.

questions.takeaway: During irrigation, drainage must equal the irrigant plus urine. Drainage less than the irrigant, with spasms and pressure, means the outflow is blocked: stop the inflow, then check the catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Compare what went in with what came out before reading the clots or the spasms.

steps.detail: 800 mL in, 650 mL out: 150 mL is held in the bladder.
Spasms and pressure fit a filling bladder.
A faster rate worsens the distention.
The antispasmodic and the 650 mL entry leave the blockage in place.

elimination.verdict: D. Stop the irrigation and check for a blockage.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: At 1000 the nurse finds a capped urine specimen for culture, labeled with the patient's identifiers, on the bedside table. The patient says, "I collected it at 0630, midstream, the way you showed me." The specimen has no preservative and has stayed at room temperature. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: It is usable because the patient used the right technique
options.rationale: Correct midstream technique limits contamination at collection. It does not protect urine that then stands for 3.5 hours at room temperature.

options.text: It is usable if it is placed on ice before sending
options.rationale: Cooling slows bacterial growth only from the time it starts. The urine has already stood for 3.5 hours without cooling or a preservative.

options.text: It is no longer accurate, and a new specimen is needed
options.rationale: Most urine specimens must reach the laboratory within 2 hours of collection or be preserved. Urine standing at room temperature grows bacteria, so after 3.5 hours the culture would not reflect the bladder. The nurse collects a new specimen and sends it promptly.

options.text: It is usable for urinalysis but not for culture
options.rationale: Urine that stands at room temperature changes in ways that affect the accuracy of testing, so the urinalysis is also unreliable.

questions.takeaway: A correct collection can still give a wrong result. Urine that stands at room temperature without a preservative past the time limit grows bacteria, so the nurse recollects it and sends it promptly.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Several options rescue the specimen. Ask what happened to the urine after it was collected, not only how it was collected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Collected 0630, found 1000: 3.5 hours.
No preservative, room temperature.
Ice now and a urinalysis only both use urine that has already changed.
Good technique does not undo the delay.

elimination.verdict: C. It is no longer accurate, and a new specimen is needed.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted with pneumonia who is alert, walks to the bathroom with standby assistance, and voids 300 to 400 mL every 3 to 4 hours. The provider prescribes strict intake and output and an indwelling urinary catheter "for accurate output." Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Insert the smallest catheter that will drain the urine
options.rationale: Using the smallest appropriate catheter is part of catheter safety, which makes this tempting. The earlier steps are to confirm the indication and consider an alternative, and this patient needs neither a catheter nor a smaller one.

options.text: Discuss measuring output with a urine hat instead
options.rationale: Catheter safety starts with confirming the indication and considering an appropriate alternative. The patient is alert, walks to the bathroom, and voids normal amounts, so output can be measured accurately with a collection device in the toilet, with no infection risk from a catheter.

options.text: Insert the catheter and review the need for it daily
options.rationale: Daily review prevents catheter associated infection once a catheter is in, but it does not justify inserting one that is not needed.

options.text: Apply an absorbent pad and weigh each pad
options.rationale: The patient is continent and walks to the bathroom. Pads take away independence and are less accurate than measuring each void.

questions.takeaway: Before any catheter, the nurse confirms the indication and considers an alternative. A patient who is alert and voids on their own can have accurate output measured with a collection device, without the infection risk of a catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options are good catheter practice. Ask first whether this patient needs a catheter at all.

steps.detail: Alert, walks, voids 300 to 400 mL: no need to drain the bladder.
Accurate output, which a urine hat provides.
Smallest size and daily review are care for a catheter that should not be placed.
Less accurate and takes away continence.

elimination.verdict: B. Discuss measuring output with a urine hat instead.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.scenario: A patient is preparing for discharge 6 days after creation of an ileal conduit. The nurse asks the patient to describe care at home.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating discharge teaching for a patient with a new ileal conduit. For each patient statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs further teaching.

rows.text: "Urine will drain all the time, so I will wear the pouch day and night."
rows.rationale: An ileal conduit gives no sensation or control over the continuous flow of urine, so a pouch collects it at all times.

rows.text: "I will wash the skin around the stoma with soap so it stays clean."
rows.rationale: Soap leaves a residue that keeps the pouch from sealing. The skin is cleansed with warm water and patted dry.

rows.text: "I will put a catheter into the stoma 4 to 6 times a day to drain it."
rows.rationale: Catheterizing the stoma 4 to 6 times a day is care for a continent reservoir. An ileal conduit drains on its own into a pouch.

rows.text: "I will measure the stoma and cut the pouch opening to fit."
rows.rationale: A pouch that fits snugly around the stoma prevents urine from leaking onto the skin.

rows.text: "A red, moist stoma is what I expect to see each day."
rows.rationale: A healthy stoma is red and moist.

rows.text: "If urine leaks under the pouch, I will wait to change it until the weekend."
rows.rationale: Urine leaking under the pouch damages the skin. A leaking pouch is changed promptly, and ongoing leaks are reported so the fit can be checked.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the patient can manage the care plan. For an ileal conduit, that means a pouch at all times, a snug fit, water without soap on the skin, a red and moist stoma, and prompt changes for leaks.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask which diversion each statement describes. Catheterizing the stoma belongs to the continent reservoir, not the conduit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Continuous drainage into a pouch.
Warm water without soap; change a leaking pouch now.
Cut the opening to fit; red and moist is expected.
Catheterizing 4 to 6 times a day is the continent reservoir.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 4 and 5 show understanding; rows 2, 3 and 6 need further teaching.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who wakes 4 times each night to void and fell last week on the way to the bathroom at 0300. The patient drinks 3 cups of tea between 1900 and 2200, takes a diuretic at 0800, and voids 250 to 300 mL each time with no burning or leakage. Which intervention best addresses the cause of the nocturia?

options.text: Move the evening tea to earlier in the day
options.rationale: Three cups of tea in the 3 hours before bed add both volume and caffeine, a bladder irritant, at the time the patient sleeps. Avoiding fluids in the 2 hours before bedtime reduces nocturia while keeping the total intake.

options.text: Take the diuretic at bedtime instead of 0800
options.rationale: A diuretic taken in the evening causes nocturia. The 0800 dose is timed correctly, and moving it to bedtime would add more voids at night.

options.text: Place a bedside commode for use at night
options.rationale: After a fall, the commode is a sound safety measure and is tempting for that reason. It shortens the walk but does not reduce how often the patient wakes to void.

options.text: Limit total fluid intake to 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restricting all fluids risks dehydration and concentrated urine, which irritates the bladder. The problem is the timing of the tea, not the total amount.

questions.takeaway: Fluid intake and habits shape the voiding pattern. Nocturia from evening fluids and caffeine is managed by moving fluids earlier and avoiding them 2 hours before bed, not by cutting total fluids.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The fall makes the commode tempting. The question asks about the cause of the nocturia, so match the option to the timing of the intake.

steps.detail: 3 cups of tea from 1900 to 2200; the diuretic is in the morning.
Voids 250 to 300 mL without burning or leakage.
The commode helps the fall risk but not the waking.
A bedtime diuretic and a total fluid limit both make things worse.

elimination.verdict: A. Move the evening tea to earlier in the day.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient, 84 years old, in long term care who has always been continent and oriented. Since yesterday the patient has had 3 episodes of urine leakage, is confused about the day, and is eating less. Oral temperature is 37.3 °C. The assistive personnel suggests absorbent briefs and toileting every 2 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Start a toileting schedule every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting is sound incontinence care, which makes it tempting. It treats the leakage as a lasting pattern before the nurse knows why the leakage started yesterday.

options.text: Assess the urine and voiding for infection
options.rationale: Incontinence that begins suddenly with new confusion and poor appetite in an older adult points to a reversible cause, and infection is a common one. Older adults often show infection as confusion, appetite loss, or new leakage instead of burning or a high fever, so 37.3 °C does not rule it out. The nurse assesses before choosing an incontinence plan.

options.text: Apply absorbent briefs and protect the skin
options.rationale: Skin protection matters once leakage occurs, but briefs only contain the urine. They take away continence the patient had until yesterday and leave the cause unexamined.

options.text: Place a bedside commode near the bed
options.rationale: Better toilet access fits functional incontinence. Nothing states a new mobility problem, and a commode does not explain a sudden change in a patient who was continent.

questions.takeaway: New incontinence is a change to investigate, not a pattern to manage. In an older adult, sudden leakage with new confusion and poor appetite suggests a reversible cause such as infection, even without a high fever, so the nurse assesses first.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Every option is reasonable incontinence care. Ask what is new: a continent, oriented patient changed in one day, and a sudden change calls for assessment before a plan.

steps.detail: Continent and oriented until yesterday; now leakage, confusion, and poor appetite.
37.3 °C does not rule out infection in an older adult.
A schedule, briefs, and a commode all manage leakage without finding its cause.
Assess the urine and voiding pattern before choosing a plan.

elimination.verdict: B. Assess the urine and voiding for infection.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.scenario: The nurse is caring for a patient, 82 years old, on day 5 after hip surgery. An indwelling urinary catheter was placed for surgery, and the need for it has not been reviewed since day 1. Nurse's note, 0800: Oral temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 104/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. Urine in the tubing is cloudy and foul smelling. Reports tenderness above the pubic bone. Oriented to person only, was oriented to person, place, and time on day 4. Incision dry with edges closed.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the note of a patient with an indwelling urinary catheter after hip surgery. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Obtain a urine specimen from the sampling port
options.rationale: A culture identifies the organism. Urine from the cleansed sampling port is fresh and keeps the drainage system closed.

options.text: Report the findings and the need for the catheter
options.rationale: Fever, cloudy foul urine, suprapubic tenderness, and new confusion need prompt reporting. The catheter has not been reviewed since day 1, and removing a catheter that is no longer needed is a key step in managing this infection.

options.text: Irrigate the catheter to clear the cloudy urine
options.rationale: Irrigation is done only when indicated and ordered. Cloudy urine is a sign of infection, not a blockage, and opening the system adds risk.

options.text: Collect urine from the drainage bag spout
options.rationale: Urine in the bag has stood at room temperature and is not fresh, so a culture from it is not accurate.

options.text: Restrict fluids to reduce the urine output
options.rationale: Adequate fluids support bladder health. Restricting them concentrates the urine and does nothing for the infection.

options.text: Catheter associated urinary tract infection
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter for 5 days, fever, cloudy foul smelling urine, suprapubic tenderness, and new confusion in an older adult fit an infection linked to the catheter.

options.text: Acute urinary retention
options.rationale: The catheter drains the bladder, and nothing suggests it is blocked. Retention does not explain the fever or cloudy urine.

options.text: Infection of the surgical incision
options.rationale: The incision is dry with closed edges. The urine findings place the infection in the urinary tract.

options.text: Functional incontinence
options.rationale: The patient has a catheter in place, and functional incontinence does not cause fever or cloudy urine.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Temperature shows whether the infection is responding to treatment or progressing.

options.text: Urine color, clarity, and odor
options.rationale: Cloudy, foul smelling urine is a cue of infection, and its change shows the response to treatment.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Bowel sounds do not track a urinary tract infection.

options.text: Hip range of motion
options.rationale: Range of motion is part of recovery after hip surgery, but it does not track this problem.

options.text: Pedal pulses
options.rationale: Pedal pulses check circulation and do not reflect the urinary infection.

questions.takeaway: A catheter left in without review raises the risk of infection. In an older adult with a catheter, fever, cloudy foul urine, suprapubic tenderness, and new confusion point to a catheter associated infection: obtain a proper specimen, report, and question the need for the catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Name the problem from the cues that cluster, then choose actions that fit it and keep the system closed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Catheter for 5 days without review, fever, cloudy foul urine, suprapubic tenderness, new confusion.
Incision is intact; the catheter drains; no retention or functional problem.
Fresh specimen from the sampling port; report and review the catheter's need.
Temperature and urine appearance track the infection.

elimination.verdict: Actions: obtain a specimen from the sampling port and report the findings and the catheter's need. Condition: catheter associated urinary tract infection. Monitor: temperature and urine color, clarity, and odor.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient, 79 years old, with urgency incontinence who started an antimuscarinic medication for overactive bladder 5 days ago. The patient now has constant dribbling, voids of about 50 mL every hour, and lower abdominal fullness. The bladder is palpable after voiding. The urine is clear, with no burning. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's next action?

options.text: The medication may be causing urinary retention
options.rationale: The medication relaxes the bladder muscle, and in an older adult it can keep the bladder from emptying. A bladder still palpable after voiding, small frequent voids, and constant dribbling point to retention with overflow leakage, which started after the new medication.

options.text: Urgency incontinence is worsening despite treatment
options.rationale: Small, frequent voids look like urgency, which makes this tempting. Urgency incontinence empties the bladder, so it does not leave a palpable bladder after voiding or cause constant dribbling.

options.text: A urinary tract infection is causing the frequency
options.rationale: Infection causes frequency and urgency, but the urine is clear and there is no burning. Infection also does not explain a bladder that stays full after voiding.

options.text: Stress incontinence is causing the dribbling
options.rationale: Stress incontinence leaks small amounts with coughing, sneezing, or activity, and the bladder empties. Constant dribbling with a full bladder after voiding is not this pattern.

questions.takeaway: Small voids or leakage can mean the bladder is not emptying. When a patient on a medication that relaxes the bladder has a palpable bladder after voiding and constant dribbling, the nurse suspects retention, not a worsening of the condition being treated.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: The frequent small voids pull toward urgency. Ask what the bladder looks like after the patient voids, and what changed 5 days ago.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new antimuscarinic medication 5 days ago.
Palpable after voiding, small voids, constant dribbling: incomplete emptying.
Clear urine and no burning.
Both empty the bladder; neither leaves it full after voiding.

elimination.verdict: A. The medication may be causing urinary retention.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: A parent asks the nurse whether a 2 year old is ready to begin toilet training. Which finding best indicates readiness?

options.text: Wakes dry from sleep each morning
options.rationale: Control develops during the day first. Night dryness often comes later, so waiting for it would delay training a child who may be ready.

options.text: Has just reached 2 years of age
options.rationale: Age alone does not show that the nervous system can signal fullness. Readiness depends on what the child can sense, hold, and communicate.

options.text: Watches an older sibling use the toilet
options.rationale: Interest helps, but watching an older sibling does not show the child can feel the urge or hold urine.

options.text: Stays dry 2 hours and names the urge
options.rationale: A child is ready when the child recognizes bladder fullness, can hold urine for 1 to 2 hours, and can communicate the urge. This finding shows all three.

questions.takeaway: Urinary control depends on nerve signals that report bladder fullness. A child is ready for toilet training when the child senses fullness, holds urine for 1 to 2 hours, and communicates the urge.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Match readiness to what the child's body can do, not to age or interest.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sense fullness, hold urine 1 to 2 hours, and communicate the urge.
Neither shows bladder control.
Day control comes first, so it is not the sign to wait for.
Dry for 2 hours and names the urge.

elimination.verdict: D. Stays dry 2 hours and names the urge.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions

questions.stem: A patient with frequent incontinence empties the bladder fully with each void and needs accurate output. Which device should the nurse plan to use?

options.text: Indwelling catheter to a drainage bag
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter measures output exactly, which makes it tempting, but it adds infection risk when the bladder empties on its own.

options.text: Absorbent pads weighed after each leak
options.rationale: Weighing pads estimates output but is less accurate, and wet pads in place add skin risk.

options.text: External collection device to a bag
options.rationale: An external device collects urine without entering the bladder. It suits a patient who is incontinent and empties the bladder fully, and it measures output with less infection risk than a catheter.

options.text: Straight catheter every 4 hours
options.rationale: Straight catheterization drains a bladder that does not empty. This patient empties fully, so repeated insertions add risk without benefit.

questions.takeaway: Catheter safety starts with considering an alternative. A patient who is incontinent but empties the bladder fully can have output collected and measured with an external device instead of a catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Ask whether the bladder empties. If it does, nothing needs to go inside it.

steps.detail: Empties the bladder fully with each void.
Accurate output with the least risk.
Both indwelling and straight catheters enter a bladder that empties.
Less accurate and harder on the skin.
