elimination.verdict: C. External collection device to a bag.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient going home with a suprapubic catheter. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will clean around the tube site each day."
options.rationale: Daily inspection and cleansing of the insertion site is part of suprapubic catheter care.

options.text: "I will keep the bag below my bladder."
options.rationale: Keeping the bag below the bladder lets urine drain and prevents backflow.

options.text: "I will call if urine stops draining."
options.rationale: No drainage can mean a blocked catheter, which is a reportable change.

options.text: "I will drink less so the bag fills slowly."
options.rationale: Adequate fluids support bladder health and help prevent infection and sediment. Drinking less concentrates the urine and raises those risks.

questions.takeaway: Home teaching is effective when the patient can manage the care plan: site care, a bag below the bladder, adequate fluids, and knowing what to report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that trades bladder health for convenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs further teaching: find the wrong statement.
Daily site care and a bag below the bladder are correct.
No drainage is reportable, so that statement is correct.
Limiting fluids for convenience needs correction.

elimination.verdict: D. "I will drink less so the bag fills slowly."

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient on day 2 after creation of an ileal conduit. Which findings require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stoma is dark purple
options.rationale: A healthy stoma is red or pink and moist. A dark purple or dusky stoma means its blood supply is failing, and tissue without blood flow dies. This is reported to the surgeon at once.

options.text: Mucus threads in the urine
options.rationale: The conduit is made from a segment of ileum, and bowel tissue keeps making mucus. Mucus in the urine is expected and is the classic trap for this patient.

options.text: Stoma is red and swollen
options.rationale: Swelling of a new stoma is expected for several weeks after surgery, and red, moist tissue means good blood flow. The pouch opening is resized as the swelling goes down.

options.text: No urine in the pouch for 2 hours
options.rationale: An ileal conduit has no valve and drains urine all the time. No output for 2 hours means a blockage or a fall in urine production, and either one needs prompt follow up.

options.text: Urine is light pink tinged
options.rationale: Urine is often blood tinged for the first few days after the surgery. Bright red urine or clots would need follow up; light pink on day 2 does not.

options.text: Flank pain with a temperature of 38.6 °C
options.rationale: Fever with flank pain suggests that infection has climbed toward the kidneys, a risk with urinary diversion. It needs prompt follow up.

questions.takeaway: A new ileal conduit is red, moist and swollen, drains urine constantly, and the urine carries mucus and may be pink for a few days. A dark or dusky stoma, no urine output, and fever with flank pain need follow up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into expected for a new conduit or a threat. Ask what the stoma needs (blood flow), what the conduit does (drains all the time), and what infection looks like.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red or pink and moist is healthy; dark purple is not.
Mucus and swelling are expected after surgery.
The conduit drains constantly, so no urine for 2 hours is a problem.
Fever with flank pain needs follow up.

elimination.verdict: A, D, F.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with an indwelling urinary catheter. Drainage was 60 mL/hr earlier in the shift and has been 15 mL in the last 2 hours. The patient reports lower abdominal pressure, and the bladder is palpable above the pubic bone. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The kidneys are making less urine
options.rationale: Low drainage tempts this answer. A palpable, full bladder shows the kidneys are still making urine; it is collecting instead of leaving.

options.text: The patient needs more IV fluid
options.rationale: Low intake lowers production, and the bladder would then be small, not palpable. More fluid would only add to a bladder that is not draining.

options.text: Urine is not draining from the bladder
options.rationale: Low drainage with a full, palpable bladder and pressure means the urine is trapped. The nurse checks the system for a kink, a loop of tubing below the bag or a blocked catheter and follows protocol.

options.text: The bladder is spasming around the balloon
options.rationale: Spasms cause cramping and leaking around the catheter. They do not explain a bladder full enough to palpate.

questions.takeaway: Low catheter drainage has two very different meanings. With an empty bladder, the kidneys are making little urine. With a full, palpable bladder, the urine is made but not draining, so the nurse checks the drainage system.
questions.strategy: Put the output beside the bladder exam. Low output with a full bladder points to the drainage, not to the kidneys.

steps.detail: The bladder is palpable and the patient feels pressure.
Less urine from the kidneys or too little fluid would leave the bladder small.
Spasm does not fill the bladder.
Urine is made but not draining.

elimination.verdict: C. Urine is not draining from the bladder.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is inserting an indwelling urinary catheter using sterile technique. While the nurse lubricates the catheter, the tip touches the patient's thigh. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Discard it and open a new sterile catheter
options.rationale: The catheter tip is now contaminated, and a contaminated catheter carries skin bacteria into the bladder. The nurse discards it and uses a new sterile catheter, changing gloves too if they touched anything nonsterile.

options.text: Wipe the tip with an antiseptic swab and insert
options.rationale: Wiping sounds like a fix, but it does not make the catheter sterile again. Anything sterile that touches a nonsterile surface is contaminated.

options.text: Insert it, since the perineum was cleansed
options.rationale: Perineal cleansing lowers the bacteria at the urethral opening; it does not make the thigh or the catheter sterile.

options.text: Rinse the tip with sterile water and insert
options.rationale: Rinsing a contaminated item with a sterile solution does not restore sterility.

questions.takeaway: Catheter insertion is a sterile procedure because catheters are a major route for bacteria into the bladder. Once the catheter touches anything nonsterile, it is contaminated and replaced.
questions.strategy: Sterile is all or nothing. Any option that tries to clean a contaminated catheter and use it is wrong.

steps.detail: The sterile catheter touched skin and is contaminated.
Wiping, rinsing and relying on the perineal prep all assume a contaminated catheter can still be used.
Discard it and use a new sterile catheter.

elimination.verdict: A. Discard it and open a new sterile catheter.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an older adult with functional incontinence who walks with a walker. Last night the patient fell without injury while hurrying alone to the bathroom. The perineal skin is red with no open areas. The patient says, "I am embarrassed to keep asking for help." Which problem should the nurse address first?

options.text: Embarrassment about needing to ask for help
options.rationale: The statement is emotionally compelling, and it matters because it drives the patient to go alone. It is psychosocial, and physical safety comes first.

options.text: Skin breakdown from urine contact
options.rationale: The skin is red but intact. Gentle cleansing and a barrier protect it, but this is a lower risk than another fall.

options.text: Sleep loss from nighttime voiding
options.rationale: Waking to void disturbs sleep, but nothing in the stem makes sleep the most dangerous problem.

options.text: Injury from falls on the way to the toilet
options.rationale: The patient has already fallen once and is still hurrying alone with a walker. Injury is the most serious risk, so safety comes first. Scheduled toileting and a commode within reach address the fall risk and the leakage together.

questions.takeaway: Functional incontinence means the bladder works but the patient cannot reach the toilet in time. When it leads to hurrying alone, the fall risk is the priority over skin and feelings, and scheduled toileting addresses both the fall risk and the leakage.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real problem. Rank them by harm: an injury from a fall is worse than red skin, lost sleep or embarrassment.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: A fall last night while hurrying to the bathroom alone.
Physical safety before skin, comfort and feelings.
The embarrassment matters because it drives the risky behavior, so fixing the fall risk respects it too.
Injury from falls.

elimination.verdict: D. Injury from falls on the way to the toilet.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.nursesNote: 0600. Patient is 79 years old, day 2 of treatment for pneumonia. Received diphenhydramine 50 mg orally at 2200 for sleep. Last void was 250 mL at 2130. Since 0300 has voided 3 times, 30 to 50 mL each time. Reports lower abdominal pressure, 5 of 10. Bladder palpable above the pubic bone. IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusing at 75 mL/hr as prescribed. Oral temperature 37.4 °C, heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg. SpO2 94% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, unchanged since admission. Crackles in the right lower lobe, as on admission. Alert and oriented. Restless and asks to get up to the bathroom again.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 0600 note of a patient being treated for pneumonia. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Received diphenhydramine 50 mg orally at 2200 for sleep
segments.rationale: Diphenhydramine has strong anticholinergic effects that weaken bladder contraction, and older adults are most sensitive to them. A medication that causes retention, followed by small voids, needs follow up.

segments.text: Last void was 250 mL at 2130
segments.rationale: A 250 mL void before bed is a usual amount and shows the bladder was emptying before the medication.

segments.text: Since 0300 has voided 3 times, 30 to 50 mL each time
segments.rationale: Small, frequent voids can mean the bladder is full and only spilling over. With 75 mL/hr of IV fluid running, these small amounts do not match what the kidneys are making.

segments.text: Reports lower abdominal pressure, 5 of 10
segments.rationale: Pressure over the bladder is a symptom of a distended bladder.

segments.text: Bladder palpable above the pubic bone
segments.rationale: An empty bladder sits behind the pubic bone. A bladder felt above it is distended.

segments.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride infusing at 75 mL/hr as prescribed
segments.rationale: The infusion is prescribed for the pneumonia and is running as ordered. It explains why urine keeps forming, but it is not the problem.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.4 °C
segments.rationale: A temperature of 37.4 °C in a patient being treated for pneumonia does not need follow up.

segments.text: SpO2 94% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, unchanged since admission
segments.rationale: Oxygenation is unchanged from admission on the prescribed oxygen. It is monitored, but it is not a new finding.

segments.text: Crackles in the right lower lobe, as on admission
segments.rationale: Crackles over the area of pneumonia are expected and unchanged.

segments.text: Restless and asks to get up to the bathroom again
segments.rationale: Restlessness and repeated urges can come from a distended bladder, and getting up again and again raises the fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Retention can look like frequent voiding. Small voids after an anticholinergic drug, with pressure and a bladder palpable above the pubic bone, mean the bladder is full and not emptying.
questions.strategy: Ask which findings are new or do not fit. The breathing findings match admission; the voiding pattern, the bladder and the new drug do not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oxygen and crackles are unchanged since admission.
30 to 50 mL voids do not match 75 mL/hr of IV fluid.
Pressure and a palpable bladder.
Diphenhydramine at 2200 in an older adult.

questions.objective: Assess patterns & concerning changes

questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing the 0600 findings of a patient being treated for pneumonia who has voided small amounts since 0300. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
Chart so far: 79 years old, day 2 of treatment for pneumonia; diphenhydramine 50 mg at 2200; 3 voids of 30 to 50 mL since 0300; lower abdominal pressure 5 of 10; bladder palpable above the pubic bone; IV fluid at 75 mL/hr.

The findings are most consistent with [[1]]. The most likely cause is [[2]]. The small, frequent voids mean the bladder is [[3]].

options.text: acute urinary retention
options.rationale: Sudden small voids with bladder pressure and a palpable bladder are acute retention, an inability to empty the bladder.

options.text: a urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Frequent small voids fit infection, but there is no burning and the bladder would not be distended.

options.text: urgency incontinence
options.rationale: Urgency incontinence is leakage after a sudden strong urge. It does not leave the bladder full.

options.text: low urine output from the pneumonia
options.rationale: Low production leaves the bladder small. This bladder is palpable.

options.text: the anticholinergic effect of diphenhydramine
options.rationale: Anticholinergic drugs weaken the bladder muscle contraction that empties the bladder. Medications are a non obstructive cause of retention.

options.text: the IV fluid rate
options.rationale: IV fluid fills the bladder but does not stop it from emptying.

options.text: an obstruction from a bladder stone
options.rationale: Stones can obstruct, but nothing suggests one, and the problem began right after a new drug.

options.text: the antibiotic for pneumonia
options.rationale: The antibiotic was given before last night without any change in voiding.

options.text: overfilled and only partly emptying
options.rationale: Urine spills out in small amounts while most of it stays behind. Small voids or leakage can occur with retention.

options.text: nearly empty after each void
options.rationale: A palpable bladder after voiding is not empty.

options.text: irritated by an infection
options.rationale: There is no burning or change in the urine to suggest infection.

options.text: contracting too often
options.rationale: An overactive bladder empties with each strong urge; this one is staying full.

questions.takeaway: Small, frequent voids are not proof of good bladder function. After an anticholinergic drug, with a palpable bladder, they mean retention with spillover.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Potter).
questions.strategy: Link each cue to its meaning: palpable bladder means full, small voids mean spillover, and the new drug is the reason it will not empty.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Full bladder plus small voids: acute retention.
A new anticholinergic drug in an older adult.
Overflow from a bladder that is not emptying.

elimination.verdict: 1: acute urinary retention. 2: the anticholinergic effect of diphenhydramine. 3: overfilled and only partly emptying.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.stem: At 0615 the nurse considers this patient's problems. Chart so far: day 2 of treatment for pneumonia; SpO2 94% on 2 L/min and right lower lobe crackles, both unchanged since admission; 3 voids of 30 to 50 mL since 0300 after diphenhydramine at 2200; bladder palpable; lower abdominal pressure 5 of 10; restless; walks with a walker. Which problem is the priority?

options.text: Impaired gas exchange from pneumonia
options.rationale: Breathing problems usually come first, which makes this tempting. The oxygen need and crackles are unchanged since admission and already treated, so they are not the new problem.

options.text: Acute urinary retention with bladder distention
options.rationale: This is the new, unexpected change. A bladder that keeps filling while it cannot empty causes pain and can be injured by overdistention, and the urge is what keeps a restless older adult getting up. Sudden inability to void needs urgent attention.

options.text: Risk for falls from restlessness and walker use
options.rationale: Falls are a real risk, but the risk comes from the retention. Relieving the bladder removes the reason the patient keeps getting up.

options.text: Risk for infection from urine stasis
options.rationale: Stagnant urine can lead to infection, but that is a later, potential problem. The distended bladder is actual and happening now.

questions.takeaway: The ABCs win when the airway or breathing finding is new or worsening. When it is unchanged and treated, the new, unexpected, actual problem comes first, and here that is acute retention.
questions.strategy: Mark each problem as new or unchanged and as actual or potential. Only one is both new and actual.

steps.detail: Unchanged since admission and already treated.
Retention began overnight after a new drug.
Falls and infection are risks; the distended bladder is happening now.
Acute urinary retention.

elimination.verdict: B. Acute urinary retention with bladder distention.

questions.objective: Differentiate retention, infection, incontinence

questions.scenario: At 0620 the nurse plans care. Chart so far: diphenhydramine 50 mg at 2200; 3 voids of 30 to 50 mL since 0300; bladder palpable; lower abdominal pressure 5 of 10; restless; walks with a walker and standby assistance; IV fluid at 75 mL/hr as prescribed for pneumonia. The protocol allows a straight catheterization if a bladder scan shows more than 500 mL and the patient cannot void.
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with suspected acute urinary retention. For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated at this time.

rows.text: Obtain a bladder scan
rows.rationale: A scan measures how much urine is in the bladder and decides whether the protocol applies. Assess before acting.

rows.text: Help the patient to the toilet with the walker and provide privacy
rows.rationale: Sitting upright, privacy and time are the first measures that help a patient void, and standby help keeps the walk safe.

rows.text: Insert an indwelling catheter for continuous drainage
rows.rationale: The cause is a drug that will wear off. An indwelling catheter adds infection risk, and the protocol calls for a straight catheter only if needed.

rows.text: Slow the IV fluid to reduce bladder filling
rows.rationale: The rate is prescribed for the pneumonia, and making urine is not the problem. A prescribed rate is not changed without a prescription.

rows.text: Report the diphenhydramine as a likely cause
rows.rationale: The provider needs to know that a drug is causing retention so the as needed order can be reviewed. Reporting findings is part of care for suspected retention.

rows.text: Apply an absorbent brief for the small voids
rows.rationale: A brief contains the spillover but leaves the bladder full and takes away the patient's dignity. It treats the symptom, not the cause.

questions.takeaway: For suspected retention: assess with a bladder scan, help the patient void with privacy and an upright position, report findings and a likely drug cause, and follow the catheter protocol. Do not jump to an indwelling catheter, change prescribed fluids, or hide the problem with a brief.
questions.strategy: Follow the order of care for suspected retention: assess, position and privacy, report and follow protocol. Reject anything that skips assessment, adds risk or hides the cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bladder scan.
Upright on the toilet with privacy and safe help.
A drug the provider can stop.
Indwelling catheter, a slower IV, a brief.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: bladder scan, toilet with privacy, report the drug. Not indicated: indwelling catheter, slower IV, brief.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.stem: At 0700 the nurse returns. Chart so far: diphenhydramine 50 mg at 2200; small voids since 0300; bladder palpable. The patient sat on the toilet with privacy and running water for 10 minutes and voided 40 mL. A bladder scan now shows 780 mL, and lower abdominal pressure is 6 of 10. The protocol allows a straight catheterization if the scan shows more than 500 mL and the patient cannot void. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter to drain the bladder
options.rationale: This drains the bladder, which makes it tempting. The cause is a drug that will wear off, and an indwelling catheter adds infection risk the patient does not need. The protocol calls for a straight catheter.

options.text: Have the patient try again in 1 hour
options.rationale: Measures to help voiding have already failed, the bladder holds 780 mL and the pain is rising. Waiting lets the bladder stretch further.

options.text: Perform a straight catheterization per protocol
options.rationale: The scan is above 500 mL and the patient could not void after privacy, position and running water, so the protocol applies. A straight catheter empties the bladder and comes out, with the least infection risk. The nurse then reassesses voiding.

options.text: Report to the provider and wait for orders
options.rationale: Reporting sounds safe, but the protocol already authorizes the action. Waiting for a call delays relief of a distended bladder.

questions.takeaway: When first measures fail and the scan meets the protocol, a straight catheter is the least risky way to empty a bladder with retention that should resolve. Use an indwelling catheter only when there is an ongoing indication.
questions.strategy: Two options drain the bladder. Pick the one that matches the protocol and adds the least risk, then reject the two that delay.

steps.detail: Scan above 500 mL and unable to void after first measures.
Trying again later or waiting for orders lets the bladder stretch.
Temporary cause, so the catheter should not stay in.
Straight catheterization per protocol.

elimination.verdict: C. Perform a straight catheterization per protocol.

questions.objective: Describe specimen collection & catheter care

questions.scenario: At 1400 the nurse reassesses the patient. Chart so far: acute urinary retention after diphenhydramine; straight catheterization at 0710 drained 760 mL; the provider discontinued the diphenhydramine. The nurse reviews findings recorded since 0710.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the response of a patient treated for acute urinary retention. For each finding, indicate whether it shows the plan is effective or requires follow up.

rows.text: Voided 300 mL at 1030 and 350 mL at 1330
rows.rationale: Voids of usual size at usual intervals show the bladder is emptying again.

rows.text: Bladder scan after voiding shows 60 mL
rows.rationale: A small residual after voiding means the bladder is emptying nearly completely. Most adults keep less than about 50 to 100 mL.

rows.text: Lower abdominal pressure 0 of 10
rows.rationale: The pressure from the distended bladder is gone.

rows.text: Urine is clear and pale yellow
rows.rationale: Clear, pale urine shows good hydration and no sign of infection after the catheterization.

rows.text: Says, "I will take my sleeping pill again tonight at home."
rows.rationale: The sleeping pill is likely the same over the counter diphenhydramine that caused the retention. The patient does not yet know the drug to avoid, so the teaching needs revision.

rows.text: Walked to the bathroom alone twice without the walker
rows.rationale: The patient still needs a walker and standby help. Walking alone without it raises the fall risk, so the toileting plan and call light use need review with the patient.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether voiding is back, the bladder empties, the patient is free of pain, the patient is safe, and the patient can manage the plan at home. Normal voids do not finish the job if the patient plans to take the drug that caused the problem.
questions.strategy: Check each finding against an outcome: emptying, comfort, safety and the home plan. Two findings fail an outcome even though the bladder has recovered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Normal voids and a small residual.
No pressure; clear urine.
The planned sleeping pill is the cause.
Walking alone without the walker.

elimination.verdict: Effective: rows 1 to 4. Requires follow up: rows 5 and 6.

questions.objective: Evaluate nursing care outcomes

questions.stem: A patient who uses a cane limits fluids to avoid leaking, is constipated, and has a cluttered path to the bathroom. Which recommendations should the nurse make? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear absorbent briefs in place of walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Briefs used in place of toileting leave urine against the skin and do nothing to remove the contributors named. The patient can still walk to the bathroom with a cane once the path is safe.

options.text: Spread fluids through the day for pale urine
options.rationale: The kidneys need enough fluid to produce dilute urine. Restricting fluid concentrates the urine, which irritates the bladder and raises the risk of infection, and it does not prevent leakage.

options.text: Wait until the urge is strong before walking to the bathroom
options.rationale: Waiting for a strong urge leaves less time to reach the toilet. With a long walk and a cane, the patient needs more time, not less.

options.text: Clear the clutter from the path
options.rationale: A cluttered path is an environmental barrier to reaching the toilet in time, and it adds fall risk for a patient who walks with a cane.

options.text: Stop drinking fluids after the noon meal
options.rationale: Fluid is limited only in the 2 to 4 hours before bed, not for the whole afternoon. The patient is already taking in too little fluid for dilute urine.

options.text: Add fiber and fluid to relieve constipation
options.rationale: Constipation places pressure on the bladder and urethra and contributes to incontinence. It is a reversible contributor.

questions.takeaway: Normal elimination depends on enough fluid for dilute urine, regular bowel movements, and a safe, short path to the toilet. Fluid restriction, constipation, limited mobility and environmental barriers all work against continence.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each option by whether it removes a contributor named in the stem: low fluid, constipation, or a cluttered path.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Limited fluid, constipation, a cluttered path and a cane are each a contributor.
Fluid spread through the day, bowel regularity, and a clear path.
Waiting for a strong urge, briefs in place of toileting, and stopping fluid at noon add risk.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions and factors that support normal elimination

questions.stem: A resident with dementia voids about every 2 hours, does not recognize the urge, and needs help to walk. Which toileting program should the nurse plan?

options.text: Bladder training with voids every 45 minutes
options.rationale: Bladder training depends on a patient who is aware of bladder fullness and able to resist the urge. This resident does not recognize the urge.

options.text: Scheduled toileting with staff assistance every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting relies on a time schedule set from the voiding pattern and does not require the resident to sense fullness or delay voiding. The 2 hour interval matches the resident's pattern, and the goal is to reach the toilet before leakage.

options.text: Absorbent briefs changed every 2 hours in place of toileting
options.rationale: Briefs used in place of timed toileting undermine the program and leave urine on the skin. They also lead residents to get up alone, a common cause of falls.

options.text: Prompted voiding alone, with the resident asking for help
options.rationale: Prompted voiding supplements scheduled toileting by prompting the resident to ask for help. Used alone, it fails for a resident who does not recognize the need to void.

questions.takeaway: Match the toileting program to cognition. Bladder training needs an alert patient who can suppress the urge. Scheduled toileting works on a timed interval set from the voiding diary and suits cognitive impairment, with prompted voiding added as a supplement.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Prompted voiding is the right idea with one thing off: it depends on the resident asking. The cue that decides is that the resident does not recognize the need to void.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The resident does not sense the urge to void.
It requires suppressing the urge between intervals.
It depends on the resident asking for help.
Briefs replace toileting and harm skin and safety.

elimination.verdict: B. Scheduled toileting with staff assistance every 2 hours.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.scenario: A patient, 74 years old, has urge incontinence. The provider is choosing between an antimuscarinic drug, oxybutynin, and mirabegron. The nurse prepares teaching and monitoring points for each drug.
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing teaching for a patient with urge incontinence whose provider is choosing between an antimuscarinic and mirabegron. For each item, indicate the drug it applies to.

rows.text: Blocks the nerve signals that trigger bladder contraction
rows.rationale: Antimuscarinics block the acetylcholine signals that trigger involuntary bladder contractions. Mirabegron works on beta 3 receptors instead.

rows.text: Relaxes the detrusor muscle by stimulating beta 3 receptors
rows.rationale: Mirabegron relaxes the bladder muscle while urine is stored, which increases bladder capacity.

rows.text: Report new forgetfulness or confusion
rows.rationale: Cognitive effects are an antimuscarinic side effect and are a particular concern in older adults, so they are monitored closely.

rows.text: Ask about glaucoma before the first dose
rows.rationale: Antimuscarinics can raise eye pressure in narrow angle glaucoma, so the nurse asks about glaucoma before the first dose.

rows.text: Check the blood pressure at follow up visits
rows.rationale: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure, so blood pressure is monitored while the patient takes it.

rows.text: Use sugarless hard candy for dry mouth and add fiber for constipation
rows.rationale: Dry mouth and constipation are expected antimuscarinic side effects managed with these measures.

questions.takeaway: Antimuscarinics block the nerve signals that trigger bladder contraction and cause dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and cognitive effects; ask about glaucoma first. Mirabegron relaxes the bladder during storage through beta 3 receptors and requires blood pressure monitoring.
questions.strategy: Learn one unique point for mirabegron, blood pressure, and its beta 3 action. Antimuscarinic points follow the drying, slowing pattern: dry mouth, constipation, confusion and the glaucoma check.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Beta 3 relaxation of the detrusor and blood pressure.
Blocked nerve signals for contraction, with dry mouth, constipation, cognitive effects and a glaucoma check.
Every drying or slowing side effect belongs to the antimuscarinic.

elimination.verdict: Mirabegron: beta 3 relaxation of the detrusor and blood pressure. Antimuscarinic: blocked contraction signals, confusion, glaucoma check, dry mouth and constipation.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse evaluates a patient's pelvic floor muscle training. Which patient statement shows the exercises are done correctly?

options.text: "I hold each squeeze as long as I can without relaxing between."
options.rationale: Training is a controlled contraction followed by complete relaxation. Holding without relaxing fatigues the muscle and is not the method.

options.text: "I do the squeezes only on days when the leaking is worse."
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training needs consistent, regular practice over time. Practicing only on bad days does not build strength.

options.text: "I squeeze, then fully relax, and I practice when not voiding."
options.rationale: Correct muscle identification is essential, and stopping the stream once can help find the muscles. Each controlled contraction is followed by complete relaxation, and practice happens outside of urination.

options.text: "I practice by stopping and starting my stream every time I void."
options.rationale: Stopping the stream is a way to identify the muscles, not the exercise itself. Practice is done outside of urination.

questions.takeaway: Pelvic floor training: identify the correct muscles, contract with control, relax completely, practice outside of urination, and keep practicing regularly over time on an individualized plan.
questions.strategy: Option D is the right idea with one thing off: stopping the stream identifies the muscles, but practice happens outside of urination.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Option A skips complete relaxation.
Option B practices only on bad days.
Option D practices during urination.
Option C identifies, contracts, relaxes and practices outside of urination.

elimination.verdict: C. "I squeeze, then fully relax, and I practice when not voiding."

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with diabetic neuropathy who reports leaking small amounts of urine many times a day and night for 3 weeks, with a weak stream and a feeling of urgency. An antimuscarinic was started for urgency 4 weeks ago. The patient denies burning. Intake over 24 hours was 2,000 mL, and voided output was 700 mL. The area above the pubic bone is firm, and a bladder scan right after voiding shows 450 mL. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Urge incontinence that needs a higher antimuscarinic dose
options.rationale: Urgency and frequent leakage fit urge incontinence, and that is the reason the drug was started. The postvoid volume of 450 mL shows the bladder is not emptying, and an antimuscarinic adds to retention.

options.text: Cystitis causing urgency and frequent leakage
options.rationale: Urgency with frequent small leaks fits cystitis, which makes this tempting. The patient denies burning, and infection does not explain 450 mL left in the bladder after voiding.

options.text: Reduced urine production by the kidneys
options.rationale: Output far below intake suggests low production, but the urine is being made and held: the area above the pubic bone is firm and the bladder holds 450 mL right after voiding. More fluid adds to a bladder that is not emptying.

options.text: Overflow leakage from retention the drug may worsen
options.rationale: Leakage can occur with incomplete emptying. A postvoid volume of 450 mL, output far below intake, and a firm suprapubic area point to retention. Diabetic neuropathy and the antimuscarinic are both contributors.

questions.takeaway: Leakage does not always mean an overactive bladder. When output is well below intake and the bladder holds a large volume right after voiding, the leakage comes from incomplete emptying, and antimuscarinics, which cause retention, can make it worse.
questions.strategy: Urge incontinence, cystitis, and low kidney output each explain part of the picture. The 450 mL scan right after voiding, with a firm suprapubic area, decides it: the bladder is not emptying, and an antimuscarinic adds to retention.

steps.detail: 450 mL remains in the bladder right after voiding, and the suprapubic area is firm.
Involuntary contractions empty the bladder; a full bladder after voiding means it is not emptying.
Diabetic neuropathy and an antimuscarinic both promote retention.
No burning argues against cystitis, and a full bladder rules out low production.

elimination.verdict: D. Overflow leakage from retention the drug may worsen.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.nursesNote: 1015. Patient is 34 years old. Oral temperature 37.0 °C. Has type 1 diabetes. Denies flank pain and denies chills. Reports burning during voiding since yesterday. Drank 1800 mL of fluid yesterday. Voids small amounts every 30 to 45 minutes and feels a sudden need to void. Reports no change in vision. Urine is pink tinged. Reports aching above the pubic bone, 4 of 10.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the clinic note of a patient who reports burning with voiding. Highlight the findings that are cues for a lower urinary tract infection, including risk factors.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C
segments.rationale: The temperature is within the expected range. Fever would suggest spread beyond the bladder.

segments.text: Has type 1 diabetes
segments.rationale: Diabetes and reduced immunity are risk factors for urinary infection.

segments.text: Denies flank pain and denies chills
segments.rationale: Flank pain and chills point to the kidney. Their absence fits a lower urinary infection.

segments.text: Reports burning during voiding since yesterday
segments.rationale: Dysuria, a stinging or burning pain during voiding, is a hallmark of cystitis.

segments.text: Drank 1800 mL of fluid yesterday
segments.rationale: This intake is adequate and is not a cue for infection.

segments.text: Voids small amounts every 30 to 45 minutes and feels a sudden need to void
segments.rationale: Frequency and urgency, often with small amounts, are signs of cystitis.

segments.text: Reports no change in vision
segments.rationale: Vision is unrelated to the urinary findings.

segments.text: Urine is pink tinged
segments.rationale: Hematuria, with pink, red or tea colored urine, warrants evaluation and occurs with cystitis.

segments.text: Reports aching above the pubic bone, 4 of 10
segments.rationale: Suprapubic discomfort is a sign of bladder inflammation.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis presents with dysuria, urgency and frequency in small amounts, suprapubic discomfort and hematuria. Diabetes raises infection risk. Fever, chills and flank pain suggest the infection has spread to the kidney.
questions.strategy: Read each phrase against the cystitis signs and the infection risk factors. Leave expected and absent findings unhighlighted.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Type 1 diabetes.
Burning, small frequent voids with urgency, pink urine, suprapubic aching.
Normal temperature, no flank pain or chills, adequate intake and normal vision.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A patient started on an antibiotic for cystitis yesterday reports slightly less burning. The culture shows an organism resistant to that antibiotic. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Report the susceptibility result to the provider
options.rationale: Culture identifies the organism, and susceptibility testing guides the antibiotic choice. An organism resistant to the current drug will not be treated by it, so the result is reported.

options.text: Reassure the patient that the antibiotic is working
options.rationale: A slight drop in pain in less than a day is not evidence that the drug works. The culture shows the organism is resistant to it.

options.text: Repeat the urinalysis before changing the antibiotic
options.rationale: The infection is already supported by symptoms, urinalysis and culture. Repeating the urinalysis delays effective treatment.

options.text: Request phenazopyridine and continue the antibiotic
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort but does not treat infection. Continuing a drug the organism resists leaves the infection untreated.

questions.takeaway: Urinalysis suggests infection; culture identifies the organism; susceptibility testing guides antibiotic choice. Results are interpreted together with the symptoms, and a resistant organism means the antibiotic needs to change.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A small drop in pain is tempting evidence. The culture result outweighs it because it shows the drug cannot kill this organism.

steps.detail: The organism is resistant to the current antibiotic.
A slight drop in pain does not override resistance.
Repeating the urinalysis adds no new information.
Phenazopyridine treats discomfort, not infection.

elimination.verdict: A. Report the susceptibility result to the provider.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: A patient with cystitis is prescribed an oral antibiotic and phenazopyridine. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm drug allergies before the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Allergies are checked before any antibiotic, because antibiotic allergies are common and change the drug choice.

options.text: Teach the patient to expect orange or red urine
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine turns the urine orange or red. Knowing this ahead prevents alarm.

options.text: Teach the patient to stop the antibiotic when burning ends
options.rationale: The full course is taken exactly as prescribed even when symptoms end early, to prevent recurrence and resistance. Adverse effects are reported rather than handled by stopping the drug.

options.text: Teach the patient to report fever, flank pain, or vomiting
options.rationale: Fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms suggest the infection is spreading upward and need immediate reporting.

options.text: Explain that phenazopyridine treats the infection
options.rationale: The roles are reversed. Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort but does not treat infection; the antibiotic treats the infection.

options.text: Encourage regular fluid intake and bladder emptying
options.rationale: Unless fluids are restricted, appropriate hydration and regular bladder emptying flush bacteria from the bladder.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis care: check allergies before antibiotics, monitor for improvement and adverse effects, encourage fluids within limits, and give ordered pain relief. Teach the full course, report adverse effects rather than stop, and report fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening at once. Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red and does not treat infection.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option has the patient stopping a drug or misreading what phenazopyridine does. Keep the options that complete treatment and report danger signs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Allergy check before the antibiotic.
Orange or red urine with phenazopyridine; complete the antibiotic course.
Fever, flank pain or vomiting are reported right away.
Stopping when the burning ends, and calling phenazopyridine a treatment, are errors.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A patient with an indwelling catheter now walks with help, has red perineal skin, and needs a urine culture. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review with the provider whether the catheter is needed
options.rationale: Necessity is reviewed daily and the catheter is removed promptly. A patient who now walks with help may no longer need it.

options.text: Collect the culture from the sampling port using aseptic technique
options.rationale: A proper specimen comes from the sampling port without opening the closed system, so the result reflects the bladder and not the bag.

options.text: Pour the culture specimen from the bag into a sterile cup
options.rationale: Urine in the bag has been standing and is not a proper specimen. Specimens are collected properly so they can be interpreted.

options.text: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing to obtain the specimen
options.rationale: The closed drainage system is maintained. Disconnecting opens a route for bacteria.

options.text: Keep the drainage bag below the bladder and off the floor
options.rationale: The bag stays below the bladder and off the floor so urine drains away from the bladder and the bag is not contaminated.

options.text: Cleanse the red skin gently, with privacy
options.rationale: Skin protection and dignity are part of catheter care: gentle cleansing keeps the irritated skin intact, and privacy preserves dignity.

questions.takeaway: CAUTI prevention: use an indwelling catheter only for an appropriate indication, keep the drainage system closed and the tubing unobstructed, keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and review necessity daily and remove promptly. Collect specimens properly and protect skin and dignity.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The specimen options test the closed system. Keep the port with aseptic technique; reject the bag and the disconnection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient now walks with help, so review the need today.
Port with aseptic technique, not the bag or a disconnection.
Bag below the bladder and off the floor.
Gentle cleansing, dry skin and privacy.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E, F.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a resident in long term care, 88 years old, who became confused this morning and was alert and oriented at 2000 yesterday. A new sleeping medication was given at 2100. Temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate 78/min, and blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. The resident has no dysuria, urgency, frequency, or suprapubic or flank pain. A urine culture sent 2 days ago grew bacteria. A family member asks the nurse to request an antibiotic for a urinary infection. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Bacteria alone are not an infection. I will check other causes, like the new sleeping pill."
options.rationale: Bacteria in urine without attributable infection symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria, and confusion alone does not establish a urinary infection. The nurse assesses other causes; a sleeping medication started the night before is a likely one.

options.text: "Confusion is often the only sign of infection at this age. I will ask the provider for an antibiotic."
options.rationale: Confusion can be the main sign of infection in older adults, which makes this tempting. With normal vital signs, no urinary findings, and a sleeping medication started the night before, a positive culture plus confusion does not establish infection, and most asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults is not treated.

options.text: "The culture grew bacteria, which confirms an infection. I will call the provider now."
options.rationale: A positive culture alone does not establish symptomatic infection. Results are matched with clinical findings.

options.text: "I will send a new urine sample, and if it grows bacteria again, we can treat it then."
options.rationale: A second positive culture still shows only bacteria in the urine. Treatment depends on infection symptoms, not on culture results.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, bacteria in the urine without urinary or systemic findings is asymptomatic bacteriuria and usually is not treated. Confusion or falls alone do not establish a urinary infection; assess other causes and look for urinary or systemic findings.
questions.strategy: Both the antibiotic request and the search for other causes are defensible, because confusion can signal infection in older adults. The cue that decides is the absence of any urinary or systemic findings, with a sleeping medication started the night before.

steps.detail: New confusion, normal vital signs, no urinary symptoms, positive culture.
A positive culture plus confusion alone is not a urinary infection.
A new sleeping medication started at 2100 yesterday.
Treating or repeating the culture ignores the missing symptoms.

elimination.verdict: A. Bacteria alone are not an infection; check other causes, like the new sleeping pill.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.scenario: A nurse on a medical unit reviews urinary findings recorded today for several patients.
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical unit is reviewing urinary findings recorded today for several patients. For each finding, indicate the term that describes it.

rows.text: Voids 15 times while awake, 50 to 80 mL each time, with a 24 hour output of 1400 mL
rows.rationale: Urinating more often than usual is frequency. The voids are small, but the 24 hour output of 1400 mL shows the total output is not decreased, so this is not oliguria.

rows.text: Sleeps from 2200 to 0600 and is woken 3 times by the need to void
rows.rationale: Waking from sleep to urinate is nocturia. The problem is the timing during sleep, not the number of voids while awake.

rows.text: Total urine output 300 mL over 24 hours, with 3 voids
rows.rationale: Oliguria is decreased urine output. Few voids with a low 24 hour total point to less urine, not to a voiding pattern problem.

rows.text: Reports a sudden, compelling need to void while in the shower and rushes out to reach the toilet
rows.rationale: A sudden, compelling need to urinate is urgency. One episode with a rush to the toilet describes the sensation, not how often voiding occurs.

rows.text: Indwelling catheter has drained 18 mL per hour for 4 hours, was 60 mL per hour yesterday
rows.rationale: A falling hourly output through a draining catheter is decreased urine output, oliguria. Urgency, frequency and nocturia do not apply to a patient whose urine drains through a catheter.

rows.text: Wakes at 0200 and 0430 each night to void 250 mL, with 6 voids while awake
rows.rationale: Six voids while awake is not more often than usual. The finding that stands out is waking from sleep to void: nocturia.

questions.takeaway: Each term names one thing: nocturia is waking from sleep to urinate, frequency is urinating more often than usual, urgency is a sudden compelling need, and oliguria is decreased urine output. Small voids are not oliguria when the 24 hour total is not decreased.
questions.strategy: Ask which part of the pattern is off for each finding: the time of night, the number of voids, the sensation, or the total amount.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 300 mL in 24 hours and 18 mL per hour are decreased output: oliguria. 1400 mL is not.
15 voids while awake: frequency.
Woken from sleep to void: nocturia. Sudden compelling need: urgency.

elimination.verdict: Frequency, nocturia, oliguria, urgency, oliguria, nocturia.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with new urine leakage. Which findings are risk factors or contributors for incontinence? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pelvic surgery 2 years ago
options.rationale: Pelvic surgery is a cause of pelvic floor weakness, a patient factor for incontinence. Aging adds to the weakness.

options.text: Levothyroxine taken each morning
options.rationale: The medications that contribute are those affecting awareness, urine production or emptying, such as diuretics, sedatives and anticholinergics. Levothyroxine is not one of them.

options.text: Stroke with arm and leg weakness
options.rationale: Neurologic conditions such as stroke impair bladder control, and the weakness limits mobility to reach the toilet.

options.text: Drinks 8 glasses of fluid spread through the day
options.rationale: Adequate fluid spread through the day supports dilute urine and normal elimination. It does not contribute to leakage.

options.text: Urethral stricture with incomplete emptying
options.rationale: Obstruction causes incomplete emptying, and leakage can occur when the bladder does not empty.

options.text: Burning, urgency, and positive nitrites
options.rationale: Urinary infection is a clinical contributor to incontinence and is reversible with treatment.

questions.takeaway: Incontinence risk factors: pelvic floor weakness from childbirth, pelvic surgery or aging; neurologic disease such as stroke, spinal cord injury or diabetic neuropathy; obstruction with incomplete emptying; urinary infection; constipation; medications affecting awareness, production or emptying; and limited mobility or environmental barriers.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into a known category of contributor. A drug counts only when it changes awareness, urine production or emptying.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pelvic surgery and stroke.
Stricture with incomplete emptying, and urinary infection.
Levothyroxine and adequate fluid spread through the day are not contributors.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A resident has woken wet for 5 nights without sensing the urge. A bedtime sedative began 6 days ago; a morning diuretic began years ago. Which contributor is most likely?

options.text: The long standing morning diuretic
options.rationale: Diuretics raise urine production, but this one is taken in the morning and has been taken for years without nighttime leakage. Its effect is greatest during the day.

options.text: A urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Infection is a reversible contributor, but nothing in the findings points to it, and the onset matches the new sedative.

options.text: The bedtime sedative
options.rationale: Sedatives affect awareness. The leakage began the night after the sedative started, occurs during sleep, and the resident does not sense the urge.

options.text: Pelvic floor weakness from aging
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness causes leakage with coughing or lifting while awake, not wetting during sleep without sensing the urge.

questions.takeaway: Medications contribute to incontinence by changing awareness (sedatives), urine production (diuretics) or emptying (anticholinergics). Timing points to the cause: the new drug whose start matches the onset is the first to consider.
questions.strategy: The diuretic is the right idea with one thing off: it raises production, but it is old and taken in the morning. The cue that decides is the sedative starting the day before the leakage began.

steps.detail: Leakage started 5 nights ago; the sedative started 6 days ago.
No sensation of the urge during sleep fits reduced awareness.
The diuretic is long standing and taken in the morning, nothing points to infection, and pelvic floor weakness causes leakage with exertion.

elimination.verdict: C. The bedtime sedative.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: An external urine collection device keeps coming loose, the linens are wet, and the skin under its edge is red. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The device is not effective, and its fit needs reassessment
options.rationale: External devices are evaluated for fit, skin contact and effectiveness. Repeated loosening, wet linens and red skin show the device fails on all three.

options.text: The device is effective, and the plan can continue
options.rationale: Collecting some urine is not the measure. Most of the output is leaking onto the linens, and the skin is red.

options.text: The device has failed, and an indwelling catheter is needed
options.rationale: Indwelling catheters are used only for an appropriate indication. Incontinence is not one, and the skin has no open areas.

options.text: The device is loose and needs to be applied more tightly
options.rationale: A tighter fit adds pressure to skin that is already red. The fit itself needs to be reassessed, with another size or device considered.

questions.takeaway: External collection devices are evaluated on 3 points: fit, skin contact and effectiveness. Wet linens and red skin mean the device is failing, and the answer is to reassess the device, not to switch to an indwelling catheter.
questions.strategy: Options C and D both accept that the device failed but choose a fix that adds risk. The global option names all 3 evaluation points.

steps.detail: Wet linens and repeated loosening.
Red skin under the edge.
An indwelling catheter lacks an indication; a tighter fit adds pressure.

elimination.verdict: A. The device is not effective, and its fit needs reassessment.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: After an onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) bladder injection for urge incontinence, a patient no longer leaks but strains to void and retains urine after voiding. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Add an antimuscarinic to the injection therapy
options.rationale: Combining approaches is reasonable in some patients, but antimuscarinics cause retention. Adding one now worsens the problem.

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter until the leaking returns
options.rationale: Indwelling catheters are used only for an appropriate indication and removed promptly, and device therapy includes intermittent catheterization for incomplete emptying.

options.text: Arrange an artificial urinary sphincter
options.rationale: An artificial sphincter controls leakage at the urethra; it does not empty the bladder. Surgical options are individualized and do not treat retention.

options.text: Teach intermittent self catheterization
options.rationale: Botox relaxes the bladder muscle, which stops the leakage, and straining with urine left after voiding shows incomplete emptying. Self catheterization is a device therapy that empties the bladder for a patient able to perform it. The retention after Botox is usually temporary.

questions.takeaway: Botox relaxes the bladder muscle and relieves urge incontinence. When the bladder then does not empty, device therapy with intermittent self catheterization empties it. Treatment is individualized, and approaches are combined only when they do not add to the problem, as an antimuscarinic adds retention.
questions.strategy: The cue that decides is the urine left in the bladder after voiding. Treat the retention with the device therapy that empties the bladder.

steps.detail: Leakage stopped, but urine remains after voiding: retention.
Botox relaxes the bladder muscle.

steps.action: Choose the fix that empties the bladder
steps.detail: Intermittent self catheterization, taught to a patient able to perform it.
The antimuscarinic adds retention, an indwelling catheter needs an appropriate indication and prompt removal, and a sphincter does not empty the bladder.

elimination.verdict: D. Teach intermittent self catheterization.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: At a clinic visit, a patient looks away and says, "Leaking is normal for my age. I just deal with it." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Leaking is often treatable. When does it happen?"
options.rationale: Urinary concerns are assessed directly and with dignity. Normalizing the topic and asking when leakage happens starts identifying the type and cause.

options.text: "Leaking is part of aging, and pads manage it well."
options.rationale: Incontinence is not a normal part of aging, and accepting pads without assessment skips identifying a cause that may be reversible.

options.text: "I will note that you have no urinary concerns."
options.rationale: Recording no concerns when there are cues of leakage denies the problem and leaves it unassessed.

options.text: "Your family may know, so I can ask them for you."
options.rationale: Asking a family member without consent breaks privacy and dignity. The patient is the source of this history.

questions.takeaway: Assess urinary concerns directly, in private, and with dignity. Patients often hide leakage from embarrassment or the belief that it is normal with age. Specific questions about how often and when it happens identify the type and cause.
questions.strategy: Options B and C both close the topic. The patient centered option keeps the patient talking and gathers data.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Looking away and calling leakage normal for age.
Calling it normal for age, or noting no concerns, ends the assessment.
Asking the adult child without consent.
Normalize, then ask how often and when.

elimination.verdict: A. "Leaking is often treatable. When does it happen?"

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A patient receiving pelvic radiation has burning, urgency, and frequency, but the urinalysis and urine culture are negative. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: A lower urinary tract infection that needs an antibiotic
options.rationale: Symptoms alone do not establish infection. Urine tests are matched with the clinical findings, and here they show no organism.

options.text: Bladder inflammation without an infection
options.rationale: Bladder inflammation can occur without infection, from irritation by other sources. Cystitis symptoms with no nitrites and no organism on culture fit inflammation without infection. Pelvic radiation is one such irritant.

options.text: Asymptomatic bacteriuria that needs no antibiotic
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is bacteria in the urine without symptoms. This patient has symptoms and no bacteria, the opposite pattern.

options.text: A contaminated specimen that needs to be repeated
options.rationale: A contaminated specimen grows mixed organisms. No growth with a negative urinalysis does not suggest contamination.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis is inflammation of the bladder, and bladder inflammation can occur without infection. Urine tests are interpreted with the symptoms: the culture identifies organisms, and symptoms with no organism point away from infection. Radiation, drugs and chemicals are examples of irritants.
questions.strategy: Options B and C are an opposite pair. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is bacteria without symptoms; this patient has symptoms without bacteria.

steps.detail: Classic symptoms, but no nitrites and no growth.
No organism identified, so there is no infection to treat.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria needs bacteria and no symptoms.

elimination.verdict: B. Bladder inflammation without an infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent cystitis often holds urine for a whole work shift. Which patient statement shows understanding of how the infection developed?

options.text: "Bacteria reached my bladder through my blood."
options.rationale: Spread through the blood is uncommon. Bacteria most often ascend through the urethra to the bladder.

options.text: "I will drink less during my shift so I void less."
options.rationale: Less fluid concentrates the urine and means fewer voids to flush bacteria, adding to the risk.

options.text: "Bacteria move up the urethra, so I will void often."
options.rationale: Upward migration through the urethra is the most frequent route. Regular voiding flushes bacteria out before they multiply in the bladder.

options.text: "I will scrub with antiseptic soap several times a day."
options.rationale: Perineal hygiene is gentle. Harsh, repeated scrubbing goes against that teaching.

questions.takeaway: Bacteria most commonly ascend through the urethra to the bladder. Prevention follows from the route: adequate hydration, emptying the bladder regularly, and gentle perineal hygiene.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option is a prevention idea with one thing off: the wrong route, too little fluid, or harsh hygiene. Match the teaching to the ascending route.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Upward through the urethra.

steps.action: Check the habit in the stem
steps.detail: Holding urine for a whole shift.

steps.action: Keep the statement that fixes it
steps.detail: Voiding often flushes bacteria.

elimination.verdict: C. "Bacteria move up the urethra, so I will void often."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A patient with a urethral stricture has had 4 bladder infections this year, each cleared by antibiotics. Fluid intake and glucose are normal. Which factor most likely explains the recurrence?

options.text: Urine stasis from the stricture
options.rationale: Obstruction and incomplete emptying cause stasis, and bacteria multiply in urine that stays in the bladder. The stricture keeps the bladder from emptying.

options.text: Low fluid intake concentrating the urine
options.rationale: Fluid intake is adequate and does not explain the repeated infections.

options.text: Antibiotic resistance from repeated courses
options.rationale: Each episode resolved with treatment, so the drugs are working. The problem is that the infections keep returning.

options.text: Reduced immunity from diabetes
options.rationale: Diabetes is a risk factor, but the glucose is normal.

questions.takeaway: Incomplete emptying and obstruction, such as strictures, tumors, stones or reflux, cause stasis that lets bacteria multiply. Recurrent infection plus a high volume after voiding points to the obstruction.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real risk factor; the stem rules out all but one. Use the data given to test each.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Intake is adequate.
Glucose is normal.
Each episode resolved.
The stricture causes incomplete emptying.

elimination.verdict: A. Urine stasis from the stricture.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy is on day 2 of an antibiotic for cystitis and calls about vomiting and worse burning. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Without a fever or side pain, waiting for your visit is fine."
options.rationale: Fever and flank pain are only two of the findings to report. Vomiting and worsening symptoms are reported immediately on their own.

options.text: "Extra water will flush your bladder. Call back if a fever starts."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged, but they do not replace evaluation, and waiting for fever ignores vomiting and worsening burning.

options.text: "Stop the antibiotic, since it may be causing the vomiting."
options.rationale: Adverse effects are reported rather than managed by stopping. Stopping also leaves the infection untreated.

options.text: "Vomiting and worse burning need to be checked today."
options.rationale: Vomiting and worsening symptoms are reported immediately. Reduced immunity from chemotherapy raises the risk of infection, so these signs need evaluation now.

questions.takeaway: Teach patients with cystitis to report fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms immediately. Any one of them is enough. Reduced immunity is a risk factor for urinary infection, which makes prompt reporting matter more.
questions.strategy: Options A and B wait for fever, which is the trap: the findings to report are fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening, and this patient has two of the four.

steps.detail: Chemotherapy: reduced immunity.
Vomiting and burning worse than yesterday.
Waiting for a visit, waiting for fever, or stopping the antibiotic.
Arrange a visit today.

elimination.verdict: D. "Vomiting and worse burning need to be checked today."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse cares for several patients with indwelling urinary catheters. Which actions help prevent catheter associated urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Declines a catheter to keep an incontinent patient dry
options.rationale: An indwelling catheter is used only for an appropriate indication. Keeping linens dry is staff convenience, not an indication.

options.text: Clamps the drainage tubing while the patient walks
options.rationale: Tubing is kept unobstructed. Backflow is prevented by keeping the bag below the bladder, not by clamping.

options.text: Disconnects the tubing to flush slow drainage
options.rationale: Opening the connection breaks the closed drainage system and lets bacteria enter.

options.text: Inserts a catheter for acute retention using aseptic technique
options.rationale: Acute retention is an appropriate indication, and hand hygiene with aseptic insertion keeps bacteria out of the bladder.

options.text: Straightens tubing kinked under a patient's thigh
options.rationale: A kink obstructs flow and causes urine to pool. Keeping tubing unobstructed is a prevention step.

options.text: Leaves a catheter in overnight in case of retention
options.rationale: Necessity is reviewed daily and the catheter is removed promptly. In case is not an indication.

questions.takeaway: Prevent catheter associated urinary tract infection: use an indwelling catheter only for an appropriate indication, perform hand hygiene and insert aseptically, keep the drainage system closed and the tubing unobstructed, keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and review necessity daily and remove promptly.
questions.strategy: Test each action against the 6 prevention steps. Any action that breaks the system, blocks flow, or keeps a catheter without an indication is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Incontinence and in case are not indications; acute retention is.
Disconnecting the tubing breaks closed drainage.
Clamping blocks flow; straightening a kink restores it.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure on a 1,500 mL daily fluid limit starts an antibiotic for cystitis. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will spread my 1,500 mL over the day."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged within prescribed limits. Spreading the allowed amount through the day supports regular voiding without exceeding the limit.

options.text: "I will drink as much water as I can."
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged only within prescribed limits. Drinking without limit can overload a patient with heart failure.

options.text: "If I get diarrhea, I will call instead of stopping."
options.rationale: Patients report adverse effects rather than stopping the antibiotic, so the provider can adjust treatment.

options.text: "I will call for fever, side pain, or vomiting."
options.rationale: Fever, flank pain, vomiting or worsening symptoms are reported immediately because they suggest the infection is spreading.

questions.takeaway: Encourage fluids within prescribed limits. For a patient with a fluid restriction, the limit wins over the usual advice to drink more. Teach the patient to report adverse effects instead of stopping the antibiotic.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. The fluid limit in the stem is the cue that turns usual advice into an error.

steps.detail: Find the statement that is incorrect.
Heart failure with 1500 mL a day.
A, C and D follow the plan; B ignores the limit.

elimination.verdict: B. "I will drink as much water as I can."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a patient on day 3 of treatment for cystitis. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient, 45 years old, is on day 3 of a 5 day oral antibiotic and a 2 day course of phenazopyridine for cystitis. Today: dysuria 1 of 10, was 6 of 10 on day 1; voids every 3 hours, was every 30 minutes on day 1; urine is orange; oral temperature 36.8 °C; 4 watery stools since 0600, with none before today.

The orange urine is [[1]].

The change in dysuria and voiding shows [[2]].

The nurse [[3]].

options.text: a sign of new hematuria that needs a culture
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine explains the color, and the other findings are moving the right way.

options.text: an expected effect of phenazopyridine
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red. It is expected and not a sign of bleeding.

options.text: a sign of dehydration from the stools
options.rationale: Concentrated urine is dark yellow or amber. Orange urine on phenazopyridine is a drug effect.

options.text: an allergic reaction to the antibiotic
options.rationale: Urine color is not a sign of allergy.

options.text: a response to treatment, with the full course still to be finished
options.rationale: Symptoms are decreasing, which is the expected improvement. The full course is completed even when symptoms ease.

options.text: a cure, so the remaining antibiotic doses can be stopped
options.rationale: Stopping early leaves bacteria behind. The full course is completed.

options.text: masking by phenazopyridine, so the antibiotic is failing
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine eases pain, but the voiding interval has also returned toward normal, which is an antibiotic effect.

options.text: spread of infection toward the kidney
options.rationale: Spread brings fever, flank pain or vomiting. The temperature is 36.8 °C and symptoms are easing.

options.text: tells the patient to stop the antibiotic until the stools end
options.rationale: Patients report adverse effects rather than stopping. The provider decides on a change.

options.text: tells the patient that watery stools are expected and need no follow up
options.rationale: Four new watery stools in a few hours are an adverse effect to report.

options.text: asks the provider to extend the phenazopyridine course
options.rationale: Pain is 1 of 10, and phenazopyridine does not treat infection.

options.text: reports the watery stools to the provider as a possible adverse effect
options.rationale: Monitoring includes adverse effects. New watery stools after starting an antibiotic are reported rather than ignored or managed by stopping the drug.

questions.takeaway: During cystitis treatment, monitor both improvement and adverse effects. Decreasing dysuria and frequency show response, but the full course is completed. Orange urine on phenazopyridine is expected. New adverse effects are reported, not managed by stopping the drug.
questions.strategy: Evaluate each finding separately: expected drug effect, treatment response, or adverse effect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Orange urine from phenazopyridine.
Pain 6 to 1 and voids every 30 minutes to every 3 hours, with the course unfinished.
4 new watery stools today: report.

elimination.verdict: 1: expected effect of phenazopyridine. 2: response to treatment, finish the course. 3: report the watery stools.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient in an urgent care clinic who has had burning and urgency with voiding for 2 days and has taken no antibiotic. Prescriptions are a clean catch midstream urine for urinalysis and culture with susceptibility, and the first dose of an oral antibiotic now. The patient says, "Please give me the antibiotic first, then I will give you the urine." Place the actions in the order the nurse should perform them.

options.text: Have the patient pass the first part of the stream into the toilet
options.rationale: Third. The first urine flushes organisms from the urethral opening, so it is not collected.

options.text: Confirm drug allergies and give the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Sixth. The allergy check comes right before the dose, and the dose comes after the culture specimen is collected and labeled. An antibiotic given first can reduce the organisms in the specimen and make the culture and susceptibility result unreliable, so the patient's request does not change the order.

options.text: Explain the method and give a sterile cup and towelettes
options.rationale: First. The patient needs to understand the method before starting, or the specimen is likely to be contaminated.

options.text: Cap the cup and label it in front of the patient
options.rationale: Fifth. The specimen is capped and labeled at the bedside, in the patient's presence, right after it is collected, then sent to the laboratory promptly.

options.text: Have the patient cleanse the urethral opening with the towelettes
options.rationale: Second. Cleansing removes organisms from the skin around the opening before any urine is passed.

options.text: Have the patient catch the middle of the stream in the cup without touching the inside
options.rationale: Fourth. Midstream urine is the sample that reflects the bladder, and touching the inside of the cup contaminates it.
