questions.takeaway: Collect the urine culture specimen before the first antibiotic dose, using a clean catch midstream method: teach, cleanse, pass the first stream into the toilet, catch the midstream without touching the inside of the cup, then cap and label the cup in front of the patient and send it. The culture and susceptibility result guides the antibiotic choice.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: The patient's request makes giving the antibiotic first look kind. The prescription for culture and susceptibility is the cue that decides: the specimen has to be collected before the antibiotic, because the result is what guides the antibiotic choice.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A culture with susceptibility is prescribed, and no antibiotic has been taken yet.
It goes last, after the specimen is collected and labeled, with the allergy check right before it.
Teach, cleanse, first stream into the toilet, midstream into the cup, then cap and label at the bedside.

elimination.verdict: Explain and give supplies; cleanse; first stream into the toilet; midstream into the cup; cap and label in front of the patient; confirm allergies and give the antibiotic.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a resident in long term care, 86 years old, who became confused at 0600 and was oriented at 2100 yesterday. Since last evening the resident has voided small amounts every 30 to 60 minutes, reports burning with voiding, and has tenderness above the pubic bone. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 30 mL. Temperature is 38.3 °C, heart rate 102/min, and blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg. No new medications were started. A urine culture 3 months ago grew bacteria without symptoms and was not treated. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Confusion alone does not indicate a urinary infection
options.rationale: This rule is correct when confusion is the only finding. Here the confusion comes with new frequency, burning, suprapubic tenderness and a temperature of 38.3 °C, so it is not alone.

options.text: The earlier culture shows harmless bladder colonization
options.rationale: The culture 3 months ago was asymptomatic bacteriuria and was rightly not treated. The resident now has symptoms, which changes the decision; an old result does not explain new findings.

options.text: Small frequent voids show retention with overflow
options.rationale: Small, frequent voids can come from a bladder that does not empty, which makes this tempting. The scan shows only 30 mL after voiding, so the bladder is emptying, and retention does not explain burning or fever.

options.text: Urinary symptoms with fever point to infection
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated, but these are infection symptoms. Urinary findings plus fever and a heart rate of 102 make a urinary infection likely, so the resident needs evaluation with urine testing.

questions.takeaway: Confusion or falls alone do not establish a urinary infection, and bacteria without symptoms are not treated. When confusion comes with urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency or suprapubic pain, or with systemic findings such as fever, infection is likely and needs evaluation.
questions.strategy: Two options rest on true rules about older adults, and one reads the small voids as retention. Combine the cues: new burning, suprapubic tenderness, and fever, with only 30 mL left after voiding, point to infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New frequency, burning, suprapubic tenderness and a temperature of 38.3 °C.
Confusion alone does not show infection, but this confusion is not alone.
30 mL after voiding shows the bladder empties.
Bacteria 3 months ago with no symptoms do not cancel today's symptoms.

elimination.verdict: D. Urinary symptoms with fever point to infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who had abdominal surgery yesterday and whose indwelling catheter was removed at 0800. At 1500 the patient feels an urge but cannot void on a bedpan in bed, and a bladder scan shows 380 mL. The prescribed activity is out of bed with assistance, and the patient stood at the bedside with 1 staff member at 1300. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Insert a straight catheter to drain the bladder now
options.rationale: Catheterization adds infection risk, and simple measures to help the patient void have not been tried yet.

options.text: Help the patient onto a bedside commode in private
options.rationale: Sitting upright on a commode is a normal voiding position, and privacy promotes the urge. The activity prescription and the patient's standing at 1300 show this is safe.

options.text: Close the curtain and offer the bedpan again
options.rationale: Privacy and a raised head of bed help, so this is a defensible choice. The patient already could not void on the bedpan, and the activity prescription allows a more normal position on the commode.

options.text: Wait 1 hour and repeat the bladder scan
options.rationale: Rescanning gathers more data, but the bladder already holds 380 mL and the patient has an urge. Waiting lets the bladder keep filling without helping it empty.

questions.takeaway: Normal voiding is supported by a normal position (sitting or standing), privacy and cues such as running water. Try these before invasive measures such as catheterization.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options use privacy to help the patient void, and one waits for more data. The activity prescription and the patient standing at 1300 decide: the patient can use the commode, which gives a normal voiding position.

steps.detail: Out of bed with assistance, and the patient stood at 1300.
The commode gives a normal sitting position; the bedpan already failed.
Catheterization comes after simple measures.
A repeat scan in 1 hour adds data but lets the bladder keep filling.

elimination.verdict: B. Help the patient onto a bedside commode in private.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions and factors that support normal elimination

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 24 hour intake and output record of a patient. Intake is 2,200 mL, and output is 650 mL from 3 voids measured in a collection hat. During the night the assistive personnel changed the patient's soaked bed pad 4 times and discarded the pads. The urine in the hat is light yellow, the bladder is not palpable after voiding, and serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, unchanged since admission. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The patient has oliguria to report to the provider
options.rationale: The recorded output is low, so this looks right. The 4 soaked pads were never measured, so the record does not show the true output.

options.text: The patient is retaining urine in the bladder
options.rationale: Low recorded output with leakage can mean overflow from a full bladder, which makes this tempting. The bladder is not palpable after voiding, so urine is not being held.

options.text: The recorded output is incomplete
options.rationale: The night leakage was not counted. Weighing wet pads and subtracting the dry weight measures that urine, and the light yellow urine and unchanged creatinine fit an output that is not truly low.

options.text: The patient is retaining fluid in the tissues
options.rationale: Daily weights track fluid balance, but the gap between intake and output here is explained by urine that was not measured.

questions.takeaway: Intake and output is only as accurate as what is measured. Urine lost to pads or linens is part of output; weigh wet pads (1 g equals about 1 mL) before concluding that output is low.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three conclusions accept 650 mL as the real output. The 4 soaked pads discarded without measurement decide it, supported by light yellow urine, an unchanged creatinine, and a bladder that is not palpable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four soaked pads during the night were not measured.
Light yellow urine, a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL unchanged, and no palpable bladder.

steps.action: Reject the conclusions built on a false total
steps.detail: Oliguria, urine held in the bladder, and fluid in the tissues all assume the 650 mL is the real output.
Complete the record by weighing wet pads.

elimination.verdict: C. The recorded output is incomplete.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a resident in long term care who walks slowly with a walker and wets the brief about 4 times a day when the bathroom cannot be reached in time. The resident does not leak when coughing, and a bladder scan right after voiding shows 40 mL. The perineal skin is red with no open areas. Staff have been layering 2 pads inside the brief, and an assistive personnel asks for an indwelling catheter to keep the skin dry. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Request an indwelling catheter for the resident
options.rationale: Keeping skin dry sounds protective, but incontinence is not an appropriate indication for an indwelling catheter, and the skin has no open areas. A catheter adds infection risk.

options.text: Assist the resident to the toilet every 2 hours while awake
options.rationale: The leakage happens when the bathroom is not reached in time, and the bladder empties (40 mL after voiding). Scheduled toileting gets the resident there before the urge becomes urgent.

options.text: Cleanse the skin with a no rinse cleanser after each episode
options.rationale: Gentle cleansing removes urine without adding friction to reddened skin.

options.text: Continue layering 2 pads inside the brief
options.rationale: Layered pads trap heat and sweat, which can cause dermatitis even when urine is kept off the skin.

options.text: Apply a moisture barrier to the reddened skin
options.rationale: A barrier protects the skin from urine between changes.

options.text: Scrub the skin with soap and a washcloth
options.rationale: Scrubbing adds friction and damages reddened skin. Perineal hygiene is gentle.

questions.takeaway: For incontinence with reddened skin, protect the skin with gentle cleansing and a moisture barrier, avoid layered pads, and treat the cause of leakage. Leakage from not reaching the toilet in time responds to scheduled toileting. Incontinence alone is not an indication for an indwelling catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options sound like skin protection: the catheter and the extra pad. Decide each by its risk. The intact skin and the cause of leakage (not reaching the bathroom) point to toileting and gentle skin care instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leakage only when the bathroom is not reached in time, with 40 mL left after voiding.
Toilet every 2 hours while awake.
Gentle no rinse cleanser and a moisture barrier.
No catheter for incontinence alone; no layered pads that trap heat and sweat.
Do not scrub reddened skin.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: The nurse receives a call from a patient with type 1 diabetes who has had burning with voiding and frequency since yesterday. Oral temperature at home is 37.0 °C, there is no flank pain, and blood glucose this morning was 214 mg/dL, was 120 mg/dL last week. The patient says, "This happened years ago and went away with water. I will drink extra and mention it at my visit next month." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Extra water is a good plan. Call back if a fever starts."
options.rationale: Fluids and reporting fever are sound teaching for cystitis, which makes this tempting. Diabetes lowers the body's defenses and raises the risk of complications, and the glucose has risen, so waiting for a fever delays care.

options.text: "With diabetes, these symptoms need a check today."
options.rationale: Burning and frequency are symptoms of cystitis, and diabetes is a risk factor for urinary infection and its complications. A patient with diabetes is taught to have urinary symptoms checked right away, and the rise in glucose from 120 to 214 mg/dL suggests the body is already under stress, so the nurse arranges an evaluation today.

options.text: "Burning often eases on its own, so watch it for now."
options.rationale: This accepts the patient's past experience and ignores the diabetes and the rising glucose.

options.text: "Bring a urine sample to next month's visit for testing."
options.rationale: Testing is the right idea, but a month is far too long for urinary symptoms in a patient with diabetes.

questions.takeaway: Diabetes changes the threshold for action: it reduces defenses against urinary infection and raises the risk of complications, so urinary symptoms need prompt evaluation even without fever or flank pain.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The normal temperature and the patient's past recovery both pull toward waiting. The diabetes and the rising glucose decide the timing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning and frequency since yesterday.
Type 1 diabetes; glucose 214 mg/dL, was 120 mg/dL.
Waiting for fever, watching the burning, and testing next month all delay evaluation.
Evaluation today.

elimination.verdict: B. "With diabetes, these symptoms need a check today."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient on day 2 of an oral antibiotic and phenazopyridine for cystitis. The patient says the burning with voiding is much less than yesterday. Oral temperature is 37.4 °C. Which finding requires follow up by the nurse?

options.text: Reddish orange urine in the collection hat
options.rationale: Red tinged urine looks like bleeding, which is the trap. Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red, so this is an expected drug effect.

options.text: Small voids still about every hour
options.rationale: Frequency that lingers can look like treatment failure. Lower tract symptoms ease over a few days, and with the burning much less on day 2, the cystitis is responding.

options.text: A dull ache in the flank since this morning
options.rationale: Flank pain is a hallmark of pyelonephritis, an infection that has moved up from the bladder to the kidney, and it needs prompt follow up. Phenazopyridine eases bladder burning without treating infection, so less burning does not reassure, and a temperature of 37.4 °C does not rule it out because fever may not have appeared yet.

options.text: Mild nausea after doses taken on an empty stomach
options.rationale: Nausea can be a sign of kidney infection, which makes this tempting. Nausea that follows doses taken on an empty stomach is a common antibiotic adverse effect, handled by taking the dose with food.

questions.takeaway: During treatment for cystitis, a new flank ache is a sign the infection may be ascending to the kidney, even when bladder burning is easing on phenazopyridine. Red orange urine, lingering frequency and nausea tied to doses taken on an empty stomach are expected.
questions.strategy: Each distractor looks like trouble: red urine, ongoing frequency, nausea. Ask what explains each one: the drug, a slow but improving course, or dose timing. The deciding cue is location: a new ache in the flank points above the bladder, and easing burning on phenazopyridine does not cancel it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red.
It follows doses taken on an empty stomach, a common antibiotic effect.
Burning is much less and frequency eases over a few days.
A flank ache, which points above the bladder, even at 37.4 °C.

elimination.verdict: C. A dull ache in the flank since this morning.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a resident in long term care who has moderate memory loss, cannot follow a plan to delay voiding, and walks to the bathroom with 1 staff member. When staff ask, the resident correctly says whether the brief is wet or dry and asks to use the toilet. The resident's goal is to ask for help without waiting to be taken. Which toileting approach should the nurse plan?

options.text: Bladder training to lengthen the voiding interval
options.rationale: Bladder training depends on the patient following a plan to delay voiding, which this resident cannot do.

options.text: Scheduled toileting by staff every 2 hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting works for patients with cognitive impairment and prevents leaks, which makes it tempting. It relies completely on a time schedule, so it does not build the resident's awareness or the goal of asking for help.

options.text: Absorbent briefs checked every 2 hours
options.rationale: Briefs used in place of toileting undermine continence, and they do nothing toward the resident's goal.

options.text: Prompted voiding with regular staff check ins
options.rationale: The resident recognizes wet or dry and asks to void when prompted. Prompted voiding builds awareness of the need to void and prompts the resident to ask for toileting help, which matches the stated goal.

questions.takeaway: Match the toileting program to the patient's ability and goal: bladder training needs the ability to delay voiding, scheduled toileting relies on staff timing, and prompted voiding builds awareness and asking for help in a patient who responds when prompted.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Scheduled toileting is a correct answer for many residents with memory loss. The resident's response to prompts and the goal of asking decide here.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cannot follow a plan to delay voiding.
They replace toileting instead of supporting it.

steps.action: Compare the two staff led programs
steps.detail: Schedule only versus prompting the resident to ask.
Responds to prompts and wants to ask for help.

elimination.verdict: D. Prompted voiding with regular staff check ins.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the history of a patient with urge incontinence before giving the first dose of a newly prescribed antimuscarinic. Which findings increase this patient's risk of harm from the drug? Select all that apply.

options.text: Postvoid residual of 260 mL with a weak stream
options.rationale: Antimuscarinics reduce bladder contractions and can cause urinary retention. A patient who already empties incompletely is at risk for worse retention.

options.text: Drinks 1,800 mL of fluid spread through the day
options.rationale: Fluid intake spread through the day supports normal elimination and helps offset the constipation these drugs can cause.

options.text: Voids 10 times a day with sudden strong urges
options.rationale: Urgency and frequency are the reason the drug is prescribed, not a risk from it.

options.text: Glaucoma treated with eye drops
options.rationale: Antimuscarinics can raise the pressure in the eye and worsen glaucoma, so the nurse asks about it before the drug is started.

options.text: Family reports new forgetfulness this month
options.rationale: Antimuscarinics can cause cognitive effects, and new forgetfulness could worsen or be blamed on the drug later. The change needs to be reported before the first dose.

options.text: Leaks a large amount on the way to the toilet
options.rationale: Leaking on the way to the toilet is the typical pattern of urge incontinence that the drug treats.

questions.takeaway: Before an antimuscarinic, the nurse looks for conditions the drug can worsen: incomplete emptying, glaucoma, and changes in thinking. Symptoms of urge incontinence are the indication, not a risk.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Treat each finding as either the reason for the drug or something the drug could make worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 260 mL left after voiding: the drug can worsen it.
Glaucoma: the drug can raise eye pressure.
New forgetfulness: the drug can cause cognitive effects.
Urges, leaks on the way, and spread fluids are not risks.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the findings of a resident in long term care with new urine leakage. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A resident in long term care, 84 years old, has had new urine leakage with urgency for 1 week and voids small amounts every 1 to 2 hours. The last bowel movement was 6 days ago, and the lower abdomen is firm. The resident denies burning with voiding. Urinalysis is negative for nitrites and white blood cells. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 90 mL.

The most likely contributor to the new leakage is [[1]].

The finding that most argues against cystitis is [[2]].

The nurse plans to [[3]].

options.text: cystitis
options.rationale: Urgency and small frequent voids fit cystitis, which makes this tempting. There is no burning, and the urinalysis is negative for nitrites and white blood cells.

options.text: constipation
options.rationale: Six days without a bowel movement and a firm lower abdomen point to stool pressing on the bladder and urethra, which causes urgency and leakage.

options.text: pelvic floor weakness
options.rationale: Aging can weaken the pelvic floor, but that develops slowly and causes leakage with coughing or activity, not new urgency over 1 week.

options.text: retention with overflow
options.rationale: Overflow comes from incomplete emptying. A residual of 90 mL right after voiding does not show a bladder that stays full.

options.text: the urgency with small voids
options.rationale: This pattern supports cystitis rather than arguing against it.

options.text: the negative urinalysis with no burning
options.rationale: Burning is a key symptom of cystitis, and a urinalysis without nitrites or white blood cells does not suggest infection. Together they argue against cystitis.

options.text: the firm lower abdomen
options.rationale: The firm abdomen supports constipation, but it does not by itself rule out an infection.

options.text: request an antibiotic for the urgency
options.rationale: Nothing suggests infection, and an antibiotic does not treat stool pressing on the bladder.

options.text: begin pelvic floor muscle training
options.rationale: Training does not address the new cause and takes weeks to work.

options.text: restore bowel elimination with fluid and fiber
options.rationale: Treating the constipation removes the pressure on the bladder, which is a reversible cause of the new leakage. Fluid and fiber are given within the care plan.

options.text: limit fluids to reduce the leakage
options.rationale: Limiting fluids worsens constipation and concentrates the urine.

questions.takeaway: New leakage has reversible causes. Constipation presses on the bladder and urethra and can cause urgency and leakage; treating the bowel removes the cause.
questions.strategy: Weigh each tempting diagnosis against the data that rules it out: the urinalysis and no burning for cystitis, the residual for overflow, the 1 week onset for pelvic floor weakness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 6 days without a bowel movement and a firm abdomen: constipation.
No burning and a negative urinalysis argue against cystitis.
Treat the reversible cause with bowel care, fluid, and fiber.

elimination.verdict: Constipation; the negative urinalysis with no burning; restore bowel elimination with fluid and fiber.

questions.objective: Explain urinary system functions and factors that support normal elimination

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a urinary history from a patient at a clinic visit. Which patient statement requires further assessment?

options.text: "I void about every 3 to 4 hours while awake."
options.rationale: Voiding every 3 to 4 hours while awake is a usual adult pattern and needs no follow up.

options.text: "I void right before bed each night."
options.rationale: Emptying the bladder at bedtime is a healthy habit that supports normal elimination.

options.text: "My urine has looked pink for 2 days."
options.rationale: Pink, red, or tea colored urine can mean hematuria, blood in the urine, and it always warrants evaluation. The nurse asks about onset, pain, burning, foods, and medications and reports the finding.

options.text: "My first morning urine is darker yellow."
options.rationale: Urine collected after a night without fluid is more concentrated, so a darker morning color is expected.

questions.takeaway: Pink, red, or tea colored urine suggests hematuria and needs evaluation. Concentrated first morning urine and a regular voiding schedule are expected.
questions.strategy: Sort each statement into a usual pattern or a change in the urine itself. A color change toward pink or red is the one that needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every 3 to 4 hours and voiding at bedtime are usual.
Morning urine is concentrated after the night.
Pink urine for 2 days suggests blood in the urine.

elimination.verdict: C. "My urine has looked pink for 2 days."

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient with recurrent cystitis about perineal hygiene. Which patient statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will scrub the area with a washcloth daily."
options.rationale: Scrubbing irritates the perineal and urethral tissue, and irritated tissue lets bacteria take hold more easily. Hygiene is gentle, not vigorous.

options.text: "I will wash gently with mild soap and water."
options.rationale: Gentle perineal hygiene with mild soap and water keeps the area clean without irritating the tissue, which is the self care teaching for preventing cystitis.

options.text: "I will use a scented spray to stay fresh."
options.rationale: Scented products irritate the perineal and urethral tissue and do not lower the risk of infection.

options.text: "I will use an antibacterial wipe after each void."
options.rationale: Cleaning after voiding sounds protective, which makes this tempting. Harsh antibacterial products used many times a day irritate the tissue, and the teaching is gentle hygiene.

questions.takeaway: Perineal hygiene for cystitis prevention is gentle: mild soap and water. Scrubbing, scented products, and harsh antibacterial cleansers irritate the tissue.
questions.strategy: Every option is about cleanliness. Choose the one that cleans without irritating, and reject the options that are more aggressive than the teaching.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vigorous cleaning irritates the tissue.
Fragrance irritates and does not prevent infection.
Harsh products many times a day irritate the tissue.
Mild soap and water, washed gently.

elimination.verdict: B. "I will wash gently with mild soap and water."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A patient is started on mirabegron for urge incontinence. Which assessment should the nurse plan at follow up visits to detect an adverse effect?

options.text: Mouth and eye dryness
options.rationale: Dryness is a classic adverse effect of antimuscarinic drugs, which block bladder contractions. Mirabegron works by a different action.

options.text: Stool frequency
options.rationale: Constipation is an antimuscarinic adverse effect. It is not the effect that is monitored for mirabegron.

options.text: Memory and attention span
options.rationale: Cognitive effects are a concern with antimuscarinic drugs, especially in older adults, not the key adverse effect of mirabegron.

options.text: Blood pressure readings
options.rationale: Mirabegron relaxes the bladder during the storage phase and can raise blood pressure, so blood pressure is checked periodically and an increase is reported.

questions.takeaway: Know which monitoring goes with which drug: antimuscarinics cause dry mouth, constipation, retention, and cognitive effects; mirabegron can raise blood pressure.
questions.strategy: Three options belong to the same drug class. The odd one out matches the drug named in the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mirabegron, not an antimuscarinic.
Dryness, constipation, and memory are antimuscarinic effects.
Mirabegron can raise blood pressure.

elimination.verdict: D. Blood pressure readings.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching bladder training to an alert patient with urge incontinence who can resist the urge briefly. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Void as soon as any urge is felt
options.rationale: Voiding with every urge keeps the bladder small and the urgency in control. Bladder training teaches the patient to control the bladder instead.

options.text: Void at set times, even without an urge
options.rationale: Bladder training uses a fixed voiding schedule based on the patient's current pattern, so the patient voids at the set time whether or not an urge is present.

options.text: Start with a 4 hour interval right away
options.rationale: The first interval is based on the patient's current pattern, often 30 to 45 minutes. A 4 hour start would lead to leaks and discouragement.

options.text: Use slow breathing to hold off urges
options.rationale: Relaxation and distraction help the patient suppress the urge between scheduled voids, which is the core skill of bladder training.

options.text: Limit fluids to keep the bladder empty
options.rationale: Limiting fluids concentrates the urine, which irritates the bladder and raises infection risk. Fluids are spread through the day.

options.text: Lengthen the interval in small steps once dry
options.rationale: When the patient stays dry between voids, the interval is lengthened by about 15 to 30 minutes at a time until 3 to 4 hours is reached.

questions.takeaway: Bladder training is for an alert patient who can resist the urge: void on a schedule, suppress urges between voids, and lengthen the interval gradually once continent.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stem says the patient is alert and can resist the urge, which is what bladder training requires. Keep the options that build control on a schedule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Void at set times, even without an urge.
Slow breathing to hold off urges between voids.
Lengthen the interval in small steps once dry.
Voiding with every urge, a 4 hour start, and limiting fluids.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with heart failure who has wet the bed on 4 of the last 5 nights and wakes 3 times a night to void large amounts. Last week the patient began taking the daily furosemide at 2000 instead of 0800 to avoid leaking during morning errands. The patient has had 1 cup of tea with dinner for many years and reports a weak stream. There is no burning, and the urinalysis is negative for nitrites and white blood cells. A bladder scan right after voiding shows 35 mL. Which contributor is most likely?

options.text: The evening diuretic dose
options.rationale: Diuretics increase urine production, often in large amounts. Moving the dose to 2000 places that output during sleep, which explains the new timing, the large night voids, and the wet bed that began last week.

options.text: The cup of tea at dinner
options.rationale: Caffeine can irritate the bladder, which makes this tempting. The tea is a habit of many years and cannot explain a change that started last week.

options.text: A urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Urgency at night can come from cystitis, but there is no burning and the urinalysis has no nitrites or white blood cells.

options.text: Overflow from retention
options.rationale: The weak stream suggests incomplete emptying, which makes this tempting. A residual of 35 mL right after voiding shows the bladder empties well, so overflow is unlikely.

questions.takeaway: When new leakage appears, look for what changed. Diuretics affect urine production, and taking one in the evening moves the large output into the night.
questions.strategy: Each distractor has a cue that makes it tempting: the tea, a weak stream, nighttime urgency. Weigh each against the data that rules it out and against the timing of the change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The furosemide moved from 0800 to 2000 last week.
Large night voids fit increased urine production.
A habit of many years cannot cause a new problem.
Negative urinalysis, no burning, residual 35 mL.

elimination.verdict: A. The evening diuretic dose.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the home bladder diary of a patient with a spinal cord injury who does not sense bladder fullness and performs intermittent self catheterization every 8 hours. Each catheterization drains 650 to 750 mL, and urine leaks between catheterizations. Fluid intake is 2,000 mL spread through the day, the urine is clear yellow, and oral temperature is 36.9 °C. The patient asks to switch to an indwelling catheter to stop the leaking. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Limit fluid intake to 1,000 mL a day
options.rationale: Less fluid would lower the volumes, which makes this tempting. The intake of 2,000 mL is appropriate, and limiting it concentrates the urine and raises infection risk.

options.text: Change to an indwelling catheter
options.rationale: This answers the patient's request, but an indwelling catheter is a major infection risk, and intermittent catheterization is the preferred method for a neurogenic bladder. The leaking has a correctable cause.

options.text: Catheterize at shorter intervals
options.rationale: Volumes of 650 to 750 mL show the bladder is overdistended between catheterizations, and the leaking is overflow. A regular schedule that empties the bladder more often prevents distention and mucosal trauma and stops the leaking.

options.text: Catheterize only when an urge is felt
options.rationale: Catheterizing by urge works only when the patient can sense fullness. This patient does not, so the bladder would overfill even more.

questions.takeaway: Intermittent self catheterization works only if the schedule keeps the bladder from overfilling. Large volumes with leaking between catheterizations call for a shorter interval, not a fluid limit or an indwelling catheter.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Every option would change the volume or the leaking. Weigh the cues: intake is appropriate, sensation is absent, and the infection risk of an indwelling catheter is avoidable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 650 to 750 mL means overdistention; the leak is overflow.
2,000 mL a day is appropriate intake.
The patient does not sense fullness.
An indwelling catheter adds infection risk when the schedule can be fixed.

elimination.verdict: C. Catheterize at shorter intervals.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient to the medical unit. Which findings increase this patient's risk for a urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Postvoid residual of 250 mL
options.rationale: Urine left in the bladder after voiding gives bacteria time to multiply. Incomplete emptying is a major risk factor for infection.

options.text: Indwelling catheter placed 2 days ago
options.rationale: Catheters and instrumentation are a major risk because they carry bacteria into the bladder and give them a path along the tubing.

options.text: Takes a diuretic each morning
options.rationale: A diuretic contributes to urgency and incontinence by increasing urine production. It does not raise the risk of infection; frequent voiding actually flushes the bladder.

options.text: Blood glucose of 280 mg/dL
options.rationale: High glucose with diabetes impairs the immune response, and glucose in the urine feeds bacteria. Diabetes is a risk factor for infection.

options.text: Walks with a cane
options.rationale: Limited mobility is a risk factor for functional incontinence, not for infection. This is the trap of mixing the two risk lists.

options.text: Receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma
options.rationale: Chemotherapy reduces immunity, so bacteria that reach the bladder are less likely to be cleared.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for urinary infection: incomplete emptying or obstruction, catheters and instrumentation, diabetes and reduced immunity. Diuretics and limited mobility raise the risk of incontinence, not infection.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each finding helps bacteria reach the bladder, stay there, or escape the immune system. If it only changes how often or how fast the patient gets to the toilet, it is an incontinence factor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A residual of 250 mL lets bacteria multiply.
A catheter brings bacteria in.
High glucose and chemotherapy weaken it.
A diuretic and a cane affect leakage, not infection.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a resident in long term care who was continent until 4 days ago and now leaks small amounts of urine many times a day. The bladder is palpable after voiding. The resident has not had a bowel movement in 6 days, and hard stool is felt on rectal exam. Oral temperature is 36.9 °C, and a urinalysis is negative for nitrites and white blood cells. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: A new urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Frequent small leaks suggest infection, which makes this tempting. The urinalysis is negative for nitrites and white blood cells and there is no fever, so infection is unlikely.

options.text: Constipation pressing on the bladder
options.rationale: Six days without a bowel movement and hard stool in the rectum press on the bladder outlet, so the bladder cannot empty and spills over in small leaks. The palpable bladder after voiding confirms incomplete emptying. Constipation is a reversible cause; relieving it often ends the leakage.

options.text: Urgency incontinence from normal aging
options.rationale: Aging can bring urgency, but this began suddenly 4 days ago in a continent resident, and urgency incontinence does not leave a full bladder. Leakage is not a normal part of aging.

options.text: Pelvic floor muscle weakness
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness causes leakage with coughing or lifting that develops over time. It does not explain a sudden change or a bladder that stays full.

questions.takeaway: New incontinence is a signal to look for a reversible cause. Constipation presses on the bladder and urethra and can cause incomplete emptying with overflow leakage. A full bladder after voiding plus no stool for days points there, especially when the urine tests are negative.
questions.strategy: Combine three cues: sudden onset, a bladder still full after voiding, and 6 days without stool. Then let the negative urinalysis rule out infection.

steps.detail: Sudden change 4 days ago means a reversible cause.
Palpable after voiding: incomplete emptying.
No stool for 6 days with hard stool in the rectum.
Negative urinalysis and no fever.

elimination.verdict: B. Constipation pressing on the bladder.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients on a medical unit. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Cystitis on phenazopyridine, urine bright orange
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine turns urine orange or red. This is an expected drug effect.

options.text: Positive urine culture, no symptoms, oriented
options.rationale: Bacteria in the urine without symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria. It usually needs no antibiotic and is not urgent.

options.text: Started oxybutynin yesterday, dry mouth
options.rationale: Dry mouth is a common, expected side effect of an antimuscarinic. It is taught and monitored but is not urgent.

options.text: Indwelling catheter, new chills and confusion
options.rationale: New chills and new confusion in a patient with a catheter suggest a catheter associated infection spreading into the blood. New confusion is an early sepsis warning sign, so this patient is seen first.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis warning signs from a urinary infection progress from new confusion to low blood pressure and poor perfusion to rapid breathing and low urine output. A patient with a catheter and new systemic signs is assessed first.
questions.strategy: Three patients have expected or harmless findings. Find the one whose change is new, systemic and possibly life threatening.

steps.detail: Expected with phenazopyridine.
Bacteria without symptoms is not an urgent infection.
Expected antimuscarinic effect.
Chills and confusion with a catheter.

elimination.verdict: D. Indwelling catheter, new chills and confusion.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating teaching for a patient with cystitis who is going home with an oral antibiotic and phenazopyridine. Which statements by the patient indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will finish every antibiotic dose even when the burning stops."
options.rationale: Symptoms ease before the bacteria are gone. Completing the full course prevents relapse and resistance.

options.text: "I will stop the antibiotic if it upsets my stomach."
options.rationale: Patients report adverse effects instead of stopping. The provider decides whether to change the drug.

options.text: "I will call right away if I get a fever or pain in my side."
options.rationale: Fever and flank pain suggest the infection is moving toward the kidney, and they are reported immediately.

options.text: "The orange urine means the infection is clearing."
options.rationale: Orange urine is a color effect of phenazopyridine. It says nothing about whether the infection is clearing.

options.text: "I will empty my bladder regularly instead of holding it."
options.rationale: Regular emptying flushes bacteria out before they multiply.

options.text: "The pain pill treats the infection if I miss an antibiotic dose."
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort but does not treat infection. It can hide worsening symptoms.

questions.takeaway: Self care after cystitis: take the antibiotic exactly as prescribed and finish it, report side effects rather than stopping, empty the bladder regularly, and report fever, flank pain, vomiting or worse symptoms right away. Phenazopyridine only relieves pain and turns urine orange.
questions.strategy: Test each statement against what each drug actually does. The antibiotic treats; phenazopyridine only soothes and colors the urine.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Finish the course; do not stop for side effects.
It does not treat, and the color is not a sign of healing.
Regular voiding; report fever and flank pain.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.nursesNote: 0800. Day 3 after knee replacement surgery. Indwelling urinary catheter removed on day 1. Today reports burning with voiding, 5 of 10, and voids 50 to 100 mL every hour. Urine cloudy with a strong odor. Lower abdominal discomfort, 3 of 10. Incision dry, edges approximated. Oral temperature 37.8 °C, heart rate 90/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 130/78 mm Hg. Alert and oriented. Knee pain 3 of 10 after an oral analgesic. Walks to the bathroom with a walker.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 0800 note of a patient on day 3 after knee replacement surgery. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: reports burning with voiding, 5 of 10
segments.rationale: Dysuria, burning with voiding, is a key cue for cystitis.

segments.text: voids 50 to 100 mL every hour
segments.rationale: Urgency and frequency with small amounts is a cystitis pattern, and it is new for this patient.

segments.text: Urine cloudy with a strong odor
segments.rationale: Cloudy, strong smelling urine suggests bacteria and white blood cells in the urine.

segments.text: Lower abdominal discomfort, 3 of 10
segments.rationale: Suprapubic discomfort is a cue for bladder inflammation.

segments.text: Incision dry, edges approximated
segments.rationale: The incision is healing as expected.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.8 °C
segments.rationale: A new low grade temperature with urinary symptoms needs follow up and trending, because a rising fever would suggest spread beyond the bladder.

segments.text: Alert and oriented
segments.rationale: Orientation is intact. New confusion would be a warning sign.

segments.text: Knee pain 3 of 10 after an oral analgesic
segments.rationale: Knee pain is controlled after surgery.

segments.text: Walks to the bathroom with a walker
segments.rationale: Walking with a walker is expected after knee replacement.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis cues are dysuria, urgency and frequency with small voids, suprapubic discomfort, and changes in the urine. A recent indwelling catheter is a major risk factor.
questions.strategy: Separate the surgical recovery findings from the new urinary ones. Every urinary change here is new since the catheter came out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning and hourly small voids.
Cloudy with a strong odor.

steps.action: Find the comfort and fever cues
steps.detail: Lower abdominal discomfort and 37.8 °C.
Incision, knee pain, walker.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings

questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing the 0815 findings of a patient with new urinary symptoms after knee replacement surgery. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
Chart so far: day 3 after knee replacement; indwelling catheter removed on day 1; burning with voiding 5 of 10; voids 50 to 100 mL every hour; urine cloudy with a strong odor; oral temperature 37.8 °C. At 0815 a bladder scan right after voiding shows 40 mL.

The cloudy, strong smelling urine most likely reflects [[1]]. The small hourly voids with a postvoid scan of 40 mL point to [[2]]. The history finding that most raised this patient's risk is [[3]].

options.text: bacteria and white blood cells in the urine
options.rationale: Cloudiness and a strong odor come from bacteria and white blood cells, which is what the urinalysis will look for.

options.text: concentrated urine from low intake
options.rationale: Concentrated urine is dark, not cloudy, and does not explain the burning.

options.text: blood from the surgery
options.rationale: Knee surgery does not put blood in the urine, and blood makes urine pink or red, not cloudy.

options.text: an effect of the oral analgesic
options.rationale: The analgesic does not make urine cloudy or foul smelling.

options.text: bladder irritation from infection
options.rationale: An inflamed bladder sends urgent signals at small volumes. A residual of 40 mL shows the bladder is emptying, so the small voids are irritation, not retention.

options.text: retention with overflow
options.rationale: Retention is a tempting thought after catheter removal, but a 40 mL residual shows the bladder empties.

options.text: low urine production
options.rationale: Hourly voids of 50 to 100 mL add up to a normal output.

options.text: urgency incontinence from aging
options.rationale: The patient is not leaking, and the change is new and has an infectious cause.

options.text: the indwelling catheter
options.rationale: Catheters and instrumentation are a major risk factor because they carry bacteria into the bladder.

options.text: the knee surgery itself
options.rationale: The surgery raised the risk only through the catheter placed for it.

options.text: use of a walker
options.rationale: A walker affects how quickly the patient reaches the toilet, not infection.

options.text: the oral analgesic
options.rationale: The analgesic does not raise infection risk.

questions.takeaway: Small, frequent voids can mean retention or irritation. A postvoid scan separates them: a small residual means the bladder empties and the urge comes from irritation, here from a catheter associated cystitis.
questions.strategy: Use the scan to decide between the two bladder explanations, then trace the infection back to the catheter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bacteria and white cells.
40 mL residual: emptying, so irritation.
The recent indwelling catheter.

elimination.verdict: 1: bacteria and white blood cells in the urine. 2: bladder irritation from infection. 3: the indwelling catheter.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.scenario: At 0830 the nurse completes the assessment. Chart so far: day 3 after knee replacement; catheter removed on day 1; burning with voiding; hourly small voids; cloudy, strong smelling urine; oral temperature 37.8 °C; postvoid bladder scan 40 mL. New findings: no flank pain, no costovertebral angle tenderness, no chills, no nausea. No known drug allergies are recorded yet. Prescriptions: clean catch midstream urine for urinalysis and culture, an oral antibiotic, and phenazopyridine.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 0830 findings of a patient with new urinary symptoms after knee replacement surgery. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Collect the urine specimen before the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: A specimen taken after the antibiotic may not grow the organism, and the culture with susceptibility testing guides the antibiotic choice.

options.text: Confirm drug allergies before giving the antibiotic
options.rationale: Allergies are checked before any antibiotic, and none are recorded yet.

options.text: Reinsert a catheter to obtain a sterile specimen
options.rationale: The patient can give a clean catch specimen. Reinserting a catheter adds the very risk that caused the infection.

options.text: Limit fluids to reduce how often the patient voids
options.rationale: Fluids within the care plan help flush bacteria. Limiting them concentrates the urine.

options.text: Teach that phenazopyridine treats the infection
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort only.

options.text: Cystitis
options.rationale: Dysuria, urgency and frequency, suprapubic discomfort and cloudy urine, with no flank pain, chills or costovertebral angle tenderness, point to a lower urinary tract infection.

options.text: Pyelonephritis
options.rationale: Kidney infection brings flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, chills and systemic signs, none of which are present.

options.text: Acute urinary retention
options.rationale: A residual of 40 mL shows the bladder empties.

options.text: Asymptomatic bacteriuria
options.rationale: This patient has symptoms of infection, so the term does not apply.

options.text: Temperature and chills
options.rationale: A rising temperature with shaking chills would signal spread beyond the bladder.

options.text: Flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness
options.rationale: Flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness are the hallmark of kidney infection and need immediate attention.

options.text: Urine color after phenazopyridine
options.rationale: The urine will turn orange or red from the drug, so its color stops being a useful sign.

options.text: Knee incision appearance
options.rationale: The incision is part of surgical care, not a measure of this infection.

options.text: Postvoid bladder scan each shift
options.rationale: The bladder already empties; repeated scans add nothing to monitoring the infection.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis is a lower urinary tract infection with local bladder symptoms. Collect the specimen before the antibiotic, check allergies first, and watch for fever, chills and flank pain that mean the infection is climbing.
questions.strategy: Name the condition from what is present and what is absent. Then pick the actions that protect the culture and the patient, and the parameters that would show spread to the kidney.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bladder symptoms without flank pain or chills: cystitis.
Specimen before the antibiotic, allergy check before the dose.
Fever and chills; flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness.

elimination.verdict: Actions: specimen before the antibiotic, confirm allergies. Condition: cystitis. Parameters: temperature and chills, flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis

questions.scenario: At 1000 the urinalysis shows nitrites and white blood cells, and the culture is pending. The first antibiotic dose and phenazopyridine have been given. Chart so far: cystitis after catheter removal; no fluid restriction; walks with a walker after knee replacement; urgent voids about every hour; no leakage.
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with cystitis after knee replacement surgery. For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.

rows.text: Encourage fluids spread through the day
rows.rationale: The patient has no fluid restriction. Regular fluids within the care plan help flush bacteria from the bladder.

rows.text: Place a bedside commode and answer the call light promptly
rows.rationale: Hourly urgent voids with a walker after knee surgery raise the fall risk. Quick access to a toilet keeps the patient safe and continent.

rows.text: Teach that the urine will turn orange or red
rows.rationale: Phenazopyridine colors the urine, and knowing this ahead of time prevents alarm.

rows.text: Teach that phenazopyridine treats the infection
rows.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort but does not treat infection.

rows.text: Apply an absorbent brief in case of urgency
rows.rationale: The patient is not leaking. A brief is not needed and does not support dignity or independence.

rows.text: Teach the patient to hold urine longer between voids
rows.rationale: Holding urine keeps bacteria in the bladder longer. Delaying voids is bladder training for urgency incontinence, not care for cystitis.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis care: fluids within the plan, regular bladder emptying, teaching about phenazopyridine, and safe, quick toilet access. Do not delay voiding or use products the patient does not need.
questions.strategy: Match each action to cystitis. Ask whether it helps clear bacteria, keeps the patient safe, or prepares the patient for a drug effect.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluids spread through the day.
A commode and a prompt call light response.
Orange or red urine is expected.
Holding urine, a brief, and the idea that phenazopyridine cures.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: fluids, commode and call light, orange urine teaching. Not indicated: phenazopyridine treats infection, brief, holding urine.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.stem: At 0600 the next day the nurse assesses the patient. Chart so far: cystitis after catheter removal; oral antibiotic since 1000 yesterday; temperature was 37.8 °C, blood pressure 130/78 mm Hg, and alert and oriented yesterday. Now: oral temperature 38.9 °C with shaking chills, flank pain 7 of 10 with costovertebral angle tenderness, vomited once, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg, does not know the day or place, and urine output 120 mL since 2200. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the findings to the provider now
options.rationale: Fever with chills and flank pain mean the infection has reached the kidney, and new confusion, falling blood pressure, rapid breathing and low output are sepsis warning signs. The provider or rapid response team is called at once for blood cultures, IV antibiotics and fluids.

options.text: Give the prescribed acetaminophen for fever
options.rationale: Acetaminophen eases the fever, which makes it tempting, but it treats a symptom and does nothing for the spreading infection or low blood pressure.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids to raise urine output
options.rationale: Fluids help perfusion, but the patient is vomiting and confused, and oral fluid cannot correct sepsis. This delays the call.

options.text: Recheck the vital signs in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Assessment usually comes first, but this assessment is done and the trend is clear. Waiting lets sepsis progress.

questions.takeaway: Cystitis can climb to the kidney. Fever, chills and flank pain signal pyelonephritis, and new confusion, hypotension, rapid breathing and falling urine output signal sepsis. That cluster is reported right away.
questions.strategy: Every option helps a little. Ask which one gets the patient the treatment that stops sepsis: only the provider can order IV antibiotics and fluids.

steps.detail: Kidney infection signs plus sepsis warning signs.
The assessment is already complete; rechecking only delays.
Acetaminophen and oral fluids do not treat sepsis.
Report now.

elimination.verdict: A. Report the findings to the provider now.

questions.objective: Prioritize nursing interventions, including catheter safety, specimen collection, dignity, and skin protection

questions.scenario: Forty eight hours after IV antibiotics and IV fluids began, the nurse reassesses the patient. Chart so far: cystitis progressed to a kidney infection with sepsis warning signs; at its worst, oral temperature 38.9 °C, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg, flank pain 7 of 10, and urine output 15 mL/hr. The patient will switch to an oral antibiotic for home.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the response of a patient receiving IV antibiotics for a kidney infection. For each finding, indicate whether it shows the plan is effective or requires follow up.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
rows.rationale: The fever has resolved, which shows the infection is responding.

rows.text: Blood pressure 126/76 mm Hg, heart rate 84/min
rows.rationale: Blood pressure and heart rate have returned toward the patient's baseline, so perfusion is restored.

rows.text: Urine output 45 mL/hr over 8 hours
rows.rationale: Output has recovered from 15 mL/hr, which shows the kidneys are perfused and working.

rows.text: Flank pain 2 of 10
rows.rationale: Flank pain has dropped from 7 of 10, which fits response to treatment.

rows.text: Six watery stools since yesterday
rows.rationale: New frequent watery stools after antibiotics can mean Clostridioides difficile infection. The nurse reports it, and contact precautions and a stool test may be needed.

rows.text: Says, "I will stop the pills at home once I feel better."
rows.rationale: Stopping early leaves bacteria behind and risks a relapse or kidney scarring. The patient needs teaching to finish the full course.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate a kidney infection by fever, vital signs, urine output and flank pain, then check for antibiotic adverse effects and whether the patient can follow the home plan. Watery stools on antibiotics and a plan to stop early both need follow up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Four findings track the infection and all have moved the right way. Then look past the infection to the drug's effects and the patient's plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Temperature, blood pressure, output and flank pain all better.
Six watery stools on antibiotics.
Plans to stop the antibiotic early.

elimination.verdict: Effective: rows 1 to 4. Requires follow up: rows 5 and 6.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan

questions.stem: A patient who has had burning on urination for 4 days now has a high fever, chills, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Cystitis confined to the bladder
options.rationale: Burning is a lower tract symptom and can be present in pyelonephritis too. Cystitis does not explain a high fever, chills, and costovertebral angle tenderness.

options.text: Pyelonephritis involving the kidney
options.rationale: Fever and chills signal that infection has spread beyond the lower tract, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of kidney involvement. Dysuria may still be present.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis from kidney injury
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis presents with cola colored urine, facial and peripheral edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output. None of those findings are described, and fever with flank tenderness points to infection.

options.text: Urinary retention from a bladder not emptying
options.rationale: Retention causes a distended bladder and incomplete emptying. It does not explain fever, chills, and costovertebral angle tenderness.

questions.takeaway: Lower tract symptoms (dysuria, urgency) can occur in both cystitis and pyelonephritis. Fever with chills and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness are what move the infection up to the kidney.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into local bladder symptoms and systemic or kidney findings. The option that accounts for every finding wins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning is lower tract; high fever, chills, and flank tenderness are systemic and kidney findings.
Costovertebral angle tenderness points to the kidney.
Cystitis explains only the burning.
Glomerulonephritis needs edema, high blood pressure, and cola colored urine, which are absent.

elimination.verdict: B. Pyelonephritis involving the kidney.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A patient with a recent ureteral stone is admitted with fever, tachycardia, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Which diagnostic tests should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: 24 hour urine collection for total protein
options.rationale: Measuring urine protein levels belongs to the workup for glomerulonephritis, where damaged glomeruli leak protein. It does not identify the organism or the spread of a kidney infection.

options.text: Urinalysis and urine culture with susceptibility
options.rationale: Urinalysis shows findings such as white blood cells and nitrites, and the culture identifies the organism. Susceptibility testing guides the antibiotic choice.

options.text: Blood cultures
options.rationale: Blood cultures are drawn when sepsis is a risk. Fever with tachycardia raises that risk.

options.text: Imaging of the kidneys and ureters
options.rationale: Imaging is used when obstruction or complications are suspected. A recent ureteral stone makes obstruction a real concern.

options.text: Serum creatinine and electrolytes
options.rationale: Kidney function tests and electrolytes show whether the infection is affecting kidney function and give a baseline to trend.

questions.takeaway: The pyelonephritis workup has four parts: urinalysis and urine culture, blood cultures when sepsis is a risk, kidney function tests and electrolytes, and imaging when obstruction or a complication is suspected.
questions.strategy: Match each test to a question the nurse needs answered: which organism, has it reached the blood, how are the kidneys working, and is something blocking flow. A test that answers none of these is out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Urinalysis and culture with susceptibility testing.
Fever with tachycardia justifies blood cultures.
Creatinine and electrolytes.
The recent ureteral stone justifies imaging.
Urine protein measurement is a glomerulonephritis test.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, E.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: A patient with pyelonephritis is going home on a 10 day oral antibiotic. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will drink the fluid amount you told me each day."
options.rationale: Taking the prescribed fluid intake is part of the plan. This statement is correct.

options.text: "I will keep my appointment for a repeat urine test."
options.rationale: Follow up testing confirms the infection has cleared. This statement is correct.

options.text: "If the pills upset my stomach, I will stop and call."
options.rationale: Adverse effects are reported to the provider rather than handled by stopping the drug, and the full course is completed even when the patient feels better. Stopping early risks a return of the kidney infection.

options.text: "I will call right away if the chills or flank pain return."
options.rationale: Fever, chills, or worsening symptoms are reported promptly. This statement is correct.

questions.takeaway: Pyelonephritis teaching: complete the full antibiotic course, report adverse effects instead of stopping, report fever, chills, or worsening, take the prescribed fluids, and keep follow up testing.
questions.strategy: In a need for further teaching item, look for the statement with one wrong step hidden inside a correct one. Calling is right; stopping the drug on its own is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Fluids, follow up testing, and calling about chills or pain are all correct.
Stopping the antibiotic for stomach upset abandons the full course.
Adverse effects are reported, not treated by stopping.

elimination.verdict: C. "If the pills upset my stomach, I will stop and call."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.scenario: A patient, 67 years old, weighing 70 kg, was admitted at 0800 with pyelonephritis and started on IV antibiotics. The nurse reassesses the patient at 1600.
questions.stem: The nurse is reassessing a patient with pyelonephritis 8 hours after IV antibiotics began. For each finding at 1600, indicate whether it is expected with pyelonephritis or signals progression toward sepsis.

rows.text: Confused about the date and place, was oriented at 0800
rows.rationale: New confusion is an early warning sign in the progression from urinary infection to sepsis.

rows.text: Flank pain 6 of 10 with costovertebral angle tenderness, was 7 of 10 at 0800
rows.rationale: Flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of pyelonephritis, and the pain has not grown worse since 0800.

rows.text: Blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg, was 126/78 mm Hg at 0800
rows.rationale: Hypotension with poor perfusion signals that the infection is progressing to sepsis.

rows.text: Respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, was 20 at 0800, and urine output 60 mL over the past 4 hours
rows.rationale: Rapid breathing and output below 0.5 mL/kg per hour are signs of sepsis and organ hypoperfusion. An output of 60 mL in 4 hours in a patient weighing 70 kg is about 0.2 mL/kg per hour.

rows.text: Burning and urgency with each void
rows.rationale: Dysuria and urgency may be present with pyelonephritis because the infection usually ascends from the bladder.

rows.text: Nausea with one episode of vomiting
rows.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are associated findings in pyelonephritis.

questions.takeaway: New confusion, hypotension with poor perfusion, rapid breathing and decreased urine output each signal progression from urinary infection toward sepsis, and new confusion is an early warning sign. Flank pain, dysuria, and nausea belong to the kidney infection itself.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each finding is the kidney infection itself or a sign that the infection is now affecting the brain, circulation, lungs, or kidney output. Changes from the 0800 baseline are the cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, dysuria, urgency, and nausea are pyelonephritis findings.
New confusion, a fall in blood pressure from 126/78 to 88/52 mm Hg, a respiratory rate rising to 30, and 60 mL of urine in 4 hours.
New confusion is an early sign, and hypotension, rapid breathing and low urine output also signal sepsis.

elimination.verdict: Expected: flank pain with tenderness, burning and urgency, nausea. Sepsis progression: new confusion, hypotension, rapid breathing with low urine output.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: On day 2 of IV antibiotics for pyelonephritis, a patient's creatinine and blood urea nitrogen have doubled and urine output has fallen. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Kidney function is declining
options.rationale: Creatinine is excreted only by the kidneys, so a creatinine that doubles reflects about a 50% loss of filtration. When blood urea nitrogen and creatinine rise together and output falls, the kidneys themselves are failing to clear waste.

options.text: A fluid volume deficit is raising the BUN
options.rationale: Dehydration does raise the blood urea nitrogen (BUN), but it raises the BUN faster than the creatinine. Here both values doubled at the same rate, which points to kidney dysfunction rather than low blood volume.

options.text: The infection is resolving
options.rationale: Falling urine output on day 2 is a warning sign, not a sign of recovery. Response to treatment is judged by fever, pain, and kidney function trends.

options.text: Fluid overload is causing the changes
options.rationale: Low output can lead to fluid retention, but overload is a possible result of failing kidneys, not the cause of a doubling creatinine.

questions.takeaway: Rising creatinine with falling urine output means kidney dysfunction. When BUN and creatinine rise together, the cause is the kidney itself, not dehydration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use creatinine as the kidney specific value. Then check whether the BUN rose alone or alongside the creatinine.

steps.detail: The creatinine has doubled.
BUN also doubled, so the ratio is unchanged and dehydration does not fit.
Falling urine output with a rising creatinine means the kidneys are clearing less.
Overload does not raise creatinine, and falling output is not recovery.

elimination.verdict: A. Kidney function is declining.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the laboratory results of a patient with pyelonephritis who has vomited 6 times in 2 days and has dry oral mucosa. BUN is 36 mg/dL, was 15 mg/dL on admission 2 days ago. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, unchanged since admission. Urine is dark amber, 180 mL over 8 hours, and the bladder is not palpable. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: A fluid volume deficit is raising the BUN
options.rationale: Dehydration concentrates the blood and raises the BUN faster than the creatinine. Creatinine is excreted only by the kidneys, and an unchanged value of 0.9 mg/dL shows filtration has not fallen. Vomiting, dry mucosa, and dark amber urine fit fluid loss.

options.text: Infection is damaging the kidney tissue itself
options.rationale: Pyelonephritis can damage the kidney, and the output is low, which makes this tempting. Kidney damage raises creatinine along with BUN, and the creatinine is unchanged at 0.9 mg/dL.

options.text: The antibiotic is injuring the kidneys
options.rationale: Some antibiotics can injure the kidneys, which makes this tempting. Kidney injury from any cause raises creatinine along with BUN, and the creatinine has not changed.

options.text: The bladder is not emptying completely
options.rationale: Low output can come from urine held in the bladder, but the bladder is not palpable, and retention does not explain a rising BUN with a steady creatinine.

questions.takeaway: BUN rises with dehydration as well as with kidney dysfunction. Creatinine is the kidney specific value: a high BUN with an unchanged creatinine points to low blood volume, while both rising together points to the kidney.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options blame the kidneys or the bladder for the high BUN and low output. The unchanged creatinine decides it, because any kidney injury would raise creatinine too, and the vomiting points to fluid loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: BUN 15 to 36 mg/dL; creatinine 0.9 to 0.9 mg/dL.

steps.action: Use creatinine as the kidney marker
steps.detail: No change means filtration has not fallen, which rules out infection or drug injury to the kidney.
Vomiting 6 times, dry mucosa, and dark amber urine fit fluid loss.
The bladder is not palpable.

elimination.verdict: A. A fluid volume deficit is raising the BUN.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: Two weeks after a sore throat, a patient has puffy eyelids, cola colored urine, and new high blood pressure, with no fever. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Pyelonephritis from an ascending infection
options.rationale: Pyelonephritis is a kidney infection with fever, chills, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness. This patient has no fever.

options.text: Cystitis with bladder inflammation
options.rationale: Cystitis causes dysuria, urgency, frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. It does not cause facial edema or new high blood pressure.

options.text: Urinary retention with a full bladder
options.rationale: Retention holds urine in the bladder but does not cause cola colored urine, eyelid edema, or hypertension.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis after infection
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis may follow a bacterial infection. Damaged glomeruli leak blood into the urine, giving cola or tea colored urine, and reduced filtration causes fluid retention with facial edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis cues: cola or tea colored urine, facial and peripheral edema, elevated blood pressure, and decreased urine output, often after a recent infection. Fever and flank pain point instead to pyelonephritis.
questions.strategy: Two options name the kidney. Decide between them by asking whether the picture is infection (fever, flank pain) or fluid retention with blood in the urine (edema, hypertension, low output).

steps.detail: A sore throat 2 weeks ago can precede glomerulonephritis.
Cola colored urine, eyelid edema, and new hypertension.

steps.action: Rule out infection of the kidney
steps.detail: No fever.
Cystitis and retention do not cause edema or hypertension.

elimination.verdict: D. Acute glomerulonephritis after infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the results of a patient with acute glomerulonephritis. Which results indicate glomerular injury or reduced kidney filtration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Urine protein 3+
options.rationale: Damaged glomeruli leak protein into the urine, so protein on the urinalysis is a direct sign of glomerular injury.

options.text: Negative urine nitrites
options.rationale: Nitrites point to bacteria in the urine. A negative result says nothing about the glomeruli.

options.text: Serum creatinine more than doubled recently
options.rationale: Creatinine is cleared by the kidneys, so a creatinine that more than doubles shows reduced filtration.

options.text: Hemoglobin level unchanged since the last clinic visit
options.rationale: A stable hemoglobin does not reflect glomerular leakage or filtration.

options.text: Many red blood cells in the urine
options.rationale: Damaged glomeruli also leak blood, which is why the urine can look cola or tea colored.

options.text: Elevated serum potassium
options.rationale: When filtration and urine output fall, the kidneys excrete less potassium, so the serum level rises. Electrolytes are checked for this reason.

questions.takeaway: The glomerulonephritis workup is urinalysis for protein and blood, urine protein levels, creatinine, and electrolytes. Protein and blood show leaky glomeruli; creatinine and potassium show reduced filtration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
