questions.strategy: For each result ask two questions: is it abnormal, and does it come from the glomerulus leaking or from the kidney filtering less? Only results that answer yes to both are selected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Protein 3+ and many red blood cells.
Creatinine more than doubled and potassium elevated.
Negative nitrites relate to bacteria, not the glomerulus.
Hemoglobin does not measure kidney filtration.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with acute glomerulonephritis on a prescribed fluid and sodium restriction. Findings at 1200: blood pressure 166/100 mm Hg, was 168/102 mm Hg at 0800; urine output 25 mL/hr, unchanged since 0800, when it was reported to the provider; weight 74.2 kg, was 73.9 kg yesterday; crackles in both lower lobes with a respiratory rate of 28/min, lungs were clear with a respiratory rate of 18/min at 0800. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Blood pressure 166/100 mm Hg, was 168/102 mm Hg
options.rationale: Elevated blood pressure is an expected cue in glomerulonephritis, and it has not risen since 0800.

options.text: Crackles in both lower lobes, respiratory rate 28/min
options.rationale: Reduced filtration causes fluid retention, and fluid in the lungs is the dangerous form of it. Crackles and a respiratory rate rising from 18 to 28 since 0800 are new and show respiratory distress, which is reported immediately.

options.text: Urine output 25 mL/hr, unchanged since reported at 0800
options.rationale: Decreased urine output signals kidney dysfunction and is a serious finding, but it is unchanged since 0800 and the provider already knows it.

options.text: Weight 74.2 kg, was 73.9 kg yesterday
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid retention, and the trend is documented. A gain of 0.3 kg in a day is not the most urgent change here.

questions.takeaway: Report respiratory distress or worsening kidney function immediately. A finding that is new since the last assessment outranks a serious finding that is unchanged and already reported.
questions.strategy: Both the low urine output and the crackles are reportable. The cue that decides is the 0800 comparison: output is unchanged and the provider already knows; the crackles are new and affect breathing.

steps.detail: Blood pressure and urine output are unchanged; the lungs have changed.
Urine output was reported at 0800.
New crackles with a rising respiratory rate threaten oxygenation.
A 0.3 kg gain is documented for the trend.

elimination.verdict: B. Crackles in both lower lobes, respiratory rate 28/min.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient with acute glomerulonephritis who is going home on sodium and fluid restrictions. Which statement indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will weigh myself once a week and call if it rises."
options.rationale: Weight is the right measure, but it is checked daily, not weekly. A weekly weight misses fluid gained over a few days.

options.text: "I will drink extra water every day to flush my kidneys."
options.rationale: Reduced filtration causes fluid retention, so the prescribed fluid limit is followed. Extra water adds to the fluid overload.

options.text: "I will call if I become short of breath."
options.rationale: Respiratory distress signals fluid in the lungs and is reported immediately.

options.text: "I can use regular salt once the puffiness is gone."
options.rationale: The sodium restriction is part of the prescribed plan and is not stopped on the patient's own judgment when the edema goes down.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis home care: follow the prescribed fluid, sodium, and dietary limits, weigh daily, take medications as ordered, and report respiratory distress or worsening kidney function immediately.
questions.strategy: Check each statement against the plan. The weekly weight option is the right idea with the wrong frequency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluid and sodium limits, daily weight, report breathing changes.
Weighing is correct, but weekly is not daily.
Extra water and resuming salt break the restrictions.
Shortness of breath is reported right away.

elimination.verdict: C. "I will call if I become short of breath."

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the history of a patient admitted with pyelonephritis. Which findings increase this patient's risk for pyelonephritis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Drinks plenty of fluid each day
options.rationale: A steady fluid intake keeps urine moving through the tract. It does not cause obstruction, reflux, or stasis.

options.text: A ureteral stone seen on recent imaging
options.rationale: A ureteral stone obstructs urine flow. Obstruction lets bacteria multiply above the blockage.

options.text: A small postvoid residual on a recent bladder scan
options.rationale: This is the right idea with one thing off: incomplete emptying is a risk, but a small residual means the bladder is emptying, so urine is not pooling.

options.text: Vesicoureteral reflux since childhood
options.rationale: Reflux carries bladder urine back up the ureter toward the kidney, giving bacteria a route from the bladder to the renal pelvis.

options.text: Spinal cord injury with urinary retention
options.rationale: Urine held in the bladder is urinary stasis. Stagnant urine lets bacteria multiply and ascend to the kidney.

options.text: Hypertension controlled with one daily drug
options.rationale: Treated hypertension does not block urine flow, reverse it, or cause it to pool, so it does not raise the risk of an ascending kidney infection.

questions.takeaway: The three pyelonephritis risk factors are urinary obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, and urinary stasis. Each one lets bacteria multiply or travel upward toward the kidney.
questions.strategy: Ask of every history item: does it block urine, push it backward, or let it sit? Only those three raise the risk of an ascending kidney infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pyelonephritis usually starts as an ascending urinary infection.
The ureteral stone blocks flow.
Vesicoureteral reflux carries urine back toward the kidney.
The spinal cord injury leaves urine sitting in the bladder.
A small residual shows the bladder empties, so there is no stasis.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A patient with vesicoureteral reflux has had three episodes of pyelonephritis this year, and creatinine is rising. Which long term complication is the patient at greatest risk for?

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis from the repeated infections
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis can follow a bacterial infection, so this option sounds connected. It presents with cola colored urine, edema, and high blood pressure, none of which are described, and repeated pyelonephritis damages the kidney through scarring instead.

options.text: Urinary incontinence from pelvic floor weakness
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness is an incontinence risk factor. Nothing in the stem describes leakage, and reflux with repeated kidney infections threatens the kidney rather than bladder control.

options.text: Kidney scarring and lost function
options.rationale: Recurrent kidney infections can scar the kidney and cause permanent impairment. A creatinine that rises over a year of repeated infections suggests that loss has already begun.

options.text: Bacteriuria needing lifelong antibiotics
options.rationale: Most asymptomatic bacteriuria does not need antibiotics, and each episode here was a symptomatic kidney infection. This is not the long term threat.

questions.takeaway: Recurrent pyelonephritis can scar the kidney and cause permanent kidney impairment. A creatinine that climbs across repeated episodes is the cue that damage is accumulating.
questions.strategy: The cues are a repeated kidney infection plus a rising creatinine. Pick the complication that explains a slow rise in creatinine; the others describe different organs or different diseases.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Creatinine is rising across 3 kidney infections.
Repeated infection of the kidney leads to scarring.
Glomerulonephritis needs edema, high blood pressure, and cola colored urine.
Incontinence and bacteriuria do not explain a rising creatinine.

elimination.verdict: C. Kidney scarring with permanent loss of function.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A patient with pyelonephritis is prescribed an IV antibiotic, an analgesic, and IV fluids. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check drug allergies before the first dose
options.rationale: Antibiotics are given after an allergy check. Asking before the first dose is the step that prevents an allergic reaction to a drug the patient has never received in this admission.

options.text: Hold all oral fluids during treatment
options.rationale: Fluids are encouraged within prescribed limits during pyelonephritis treatment. Withholding oral fluids is not part of the prescriptions and does not rest an infected kidney.

options.text: Give the analgesic for flank pain
options.rationale: Ordered analgesics are part of pyelonephritis treatment, and flank pain is expected with a kidney infection.

options.text: Measure intake and output every shift
options.rationale: Intake and output are monitored to track hydration and to catch a fall in urine output, which can signal worsening infection or kidney dysfunction.

options.text: Teach that phenazopyridine will clear the kidney infection
options.rationale: Phenazopyridine relieves urinary discomfort and turns urine orange or red, but it does not treat infection. The antibiotic treats the kidney infection.

options.text: Recheck vital signs and report new confusion
options.rationale: Vital signs and response to treatment are monitored to watch for worsening. New confusion is an early warning sign of progression toward sepsis.

questions.takeaway: Pyelonephritis care: antibiotics after an allergy check, ordered analgesics, fluids within prescribed limits, vital signs and intake and output, and a watch for worsening or adverse effects.
questions.strategy: Sort each option by whether it treats the infection, relieves pain, supports fluid balance, or monitors for worsening. An option that misstates what a drug does or invents a restriction is out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The allergy check comes before the first antibiotic dose.
The analgesic is ordered for the flank pain of a kidney infection.
Intake and output, vital signs, and mental status catch worsening.
Fluids are encouraged within limits, not withheld.
Phenazopyridine relieves discomfort only.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.scenario: A patient, 74 years old, was admitted 48 hours ago with pyelonephritis and has received IV antibiotics since admission. The nurse compares the findings now with the findings on admission.
questions.stem: The nurse is comparing current findings with admission findings for a patient with pyelonephritis. For each finding, indicate whether it shows an effective response to treatment or a response that is not effective.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.2 °C, was 39.2 °C on admission
rows.rationale: The fever that signaled spread of infection to the kidney has resolved, which shows the antibiotic is working.

rows.text: Flank pain 2 of 10, was 8 of 10 on admission
rows.rationale: Flank pain is the hallmark of kidney infection. A drop from 8 of 10 to 2 of 10 shows the inflammation is settling.

rows.text: Urine output 140 mL over the past 8 hours, was 520 mL over 8 hours on admission
rows.rationale: Falling urine output is a warning sign of progression toward sepsis or of kidney dysfunction. It needs follow up even though other findings are better.

rows.text: Heart rate 84 beats per minute, was 118 beats per minute on admission
rows.rationale: Tachycardia is an associated finding of pyelonephritis. A return to 84 beats per minute shows the systemic response is easing.

rows.text: Asking repeatedly where the patient is, was oriented on admission
rows.rationale: New confusion is an early warning sign in the progression from urinary infection to sepsis. It cannot be dismissed as age related because it is new since admission.

rows.text: Eating breakfast with no nausea, was vomiting on admission
rows.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are associated findings of pyelonephritis. Eating without nausea shows the systemic illness is resolving.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate each finding against its own baseline. Resolving fever, flank pain, tachycardia, and nausea show response to treatment, but new confusion or falling urine output means worsening even when the other numbers look better.
questions.strategy: Read each row as now versus admission. A finding that moved toward normal is effective; a finding that is new or moving the wrong way is not, regardless of how the rest of the picture looks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Temperature, pain, heart rate, and nausea all moved toward normal.
Confusion is new since admission.
Urine output fell from 520 mL to 140 mL over 8 hours.
Several good findings do not cancel two warning signs.

elimination.verdict: Effective: temperature, flank pain, heart rate, nausea. Not effective: urine output and new confusion.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: A patient with an immune mediated disease and new glomerulonephritis asks, "My cousin's kidney inflammation cleared after a throat infection. Will mine?" Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Yes, this kind almost always clears in a few weeks."
options.rationale: This is false reassurance. Recovery from glomerulonephritis varies by cause, and the patient's cause is different from the cousin's.

options.text: "This cannot happen without an infection first."
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis can occur with immune mediated disease as well as after a bacterial infection, so a missing infection does not rule it out.

options.text: "No, with an immune disease it always leads to failure."
options.rationale: The absolute word always makes this inaccurate. Severity and recovery vary, so the nurse does not promise either a full recovery or a permanent loss.

options.text: "Recovery depends on the cause, and yours differs."
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis may follow an infection or occur with immune mediated disease, as it does for this patient, and severity and recovery vary by cause. This response is honest and does not promise an outcome either way.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis can follow a bacterial infection or occur with an immune mediated disease, and severity and recovery vary by cause. A missing infection history does not rule it out.
questions.strategy: Two options promise an outcome in opposite directions, and one denies the diagnosis. The accurate answer names the cause and avoids predicting the outcome.

steps.detail: The patient has an immune mediated disease, not a recent infection like the cousin.
Almost always clears and always leads to failure are absolutes in opposite directions.
Glomerulonephritis does not require a preceding infection.

elimination.verdict: D. Recovery depends on the cause, which differs from the cousin's.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a patient with acute glomerulonephritis after 3 days of fluid and sodium restriction. Which finding best indicates the plan is achieving its goal?

options.text: Weight down 2.4 kg and urine output rising
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis causes fluid retention. Weight loss with rising urine output shows retained fluid is leaving, which is the goal of the fluid and sodium restriction and medications.

options.text: Took every dose and kept to the fluid limit
options.rationale: This shows the patient is following the plan, which matters, but adherence is not an outcome. The nurse evaluates the patient's response, not the patient's actions.

options.text: Blood pressure slightly lower, with new crackles
options.rationale: The small drop in blood pressure is outweighed by new crackles, a sign of fluid overload and possible respiratory distress that is reported immediately.

options.text: Puffiness looks smaller; output still falling
options.rationale: A subjective report of less swelling is not a measured trend, and urine output is still falling, which suggests worsening kidney function.

questions.takeaway: Glomerulonephritis outcomes are judged by documented trends: daily weight, blood pressure, intake and output, and lung sounds. Falling weight with rising output means retained fluid is leaving.
questions.strategy: Evaluate outcomes with measured trends in the patient, not with adherence or impressions. Any option that contains a new warning sign is out even if one value moved the right way.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Remove retained fluid and protect kidney function.
Taking doses and limiting fluid are actions, not outcomes.
New crackles signal fluid overload despite a small blood pressure drop.
Puffiness looking smaller is an impression, and output is falling.
Weight down and output up: both moved toward the goal.

elimination.verdict: A. Weight down 2.4 kg and urine output rising.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient with pyelonephritis. Temperature is 38.9 °C and flank pain is 7 of 10. Serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL, was 0.9 mg/dL 2 months ago. The patient has no fluid restriction. Urine and blood cultures were collected at 1000, with results expected in 48 hours. Prescriptions include a broad spectrum IV antibiotic, acetaminophen as needed for pain or fever, and ibuprofen as needed for pain. The patient asks for ibuprofen because it works best at home. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until culture results are available
options.rationale: Culture results guide a later change to a more specific antibiotic. The cultures are already collected, so the broad spectrum antibiotic starts now instead of waiting 48 hours.

options.text: Confirm drug allergies and give the first antibiotic dose
options.rationale: With the cultures collected, the antibiotic starts after the allergy check.

options.text: Give acetaminophen for the flank pain and fever
options.rationale: Acetaminophen treats both the pain and the fever and does not interfere with the kidney's control of its own blood flow.

options.text: Limit oral fluids to 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: The patient has no fluid restriction. Restricting fluid concentrates the urine and does not rest the kidneys.

options.text: Clarify the ibuprofen prescription with the provider
options.rationale: The patient prefers it, but the creatinine rose from 0.9 to 1.5 mg/dL. An NSAID can reduce kidney blood flow, so the nurse clarifies it instead of giving it.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids spread through the day
options.rationale: Without a restriction, steady fluid intake that keeps urine pale yellow and dilute supports treatment.

questions.takeaway: In pyelonephritis, start the antibiotic once cultures are collected, check allergies first, give fluids within any prescribed limit, and treat pain and fever. Acetaminophen is preferred over NSAIDs, and a rising creatinine makes an NSAID a prescription to clarify.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options look reasonable on their face: honoring the patient's preference for ibuprofen and waiting for the culture. The creatinine trend decides the first, and the cultures already collected decide the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, was 0.9 mg/dL 2 months ago.
Give acetaminophen; clarify the ibuprofen.
Cultures are collected, so the first dose goes now after the allergy check.
No restriction, so encourage fluids for pale yellow urine.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient on day 3 of an IV antibiotic for pyelonephritis, with every dose given on time. Temperature is 39.0 °C, was 39.2 °C on admission; flank pain is 7 of 10, was 8 of 10. Heart rate is 104/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, and urine output 50 mL/hr, and the patient is alert and oriented. The urine culture grew an organism susceptible to the antibiotic being given. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The organism has become resistant to the antibiotic
options.rationale: Resistance is a common reason an infection does not respond, which makes this tempting. The susceptibility result shows the organism is not resistant to the drug being given.

options.text: An obstruction or abscess may be present
options.rationale: The fever and pain have barely changed after 3 days of an antibiotic the organism is susceptible to. When the drug matches the organism and doses are on time, a complication such as obstruction or an abscess is suspected, and imaging looks for it.

options.text: The infection is responding to treatment
options.rationale: A drop from 39.2 to 39.0 °C and from 8 to 7 of 10 after 3 days is not a meaningful response, and the heart rate is 104 beats per minute.

options.text: The infection has progressed to sepsis
options.rationale: A fever with a heart rate of 104/min raises concern for sepsis. The blood pressure, urine output, and mental status are normal, so there is no sign of organ dysfunction; the problem is an infection that is not clearing.

questions.takeaway: Use the culture and susceptibility result when a patient is not responding. If the organism is susceptible and doses are on time, suspect a complication such as obstruction or abscess and anticipate imaging.
questions.strategy: Resistance, sepsis, and a resolving infection each explain part of the picture. Combine the cues: a susceptible organism with on time doses rules out resistance, normal perfusion rules out sepsis, and barely changed fever and pain mean the infection is not clearing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The organism is susceptible to the antibiotic, and every dose was on time.
Temperature and pain have barely changed in 3 days.
Blood pressure, urine output, and mental status are normal.
Obstruction or abscess, found with imaging.

elimination.verdict: B. An obstruction or abscess may be present.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with pyelonephritis who has an indwelling urinary catheter. Urine output was 60 mL/hr from 0800 to 1200 and has been 5 mL in total from 1200 to 1400. Blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg, was 134/78 mm Hg at 0800; heart rate is 88/min; and the patient is alert and oriented. The patient reports new lower abdominal pressure, and the area above the pubic bone is firm. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the drop in urine output to the provider
options.rationale: A sudden fall in output can signal kidney dysfunction or sepsis, so this is defensible. The firm area above the pubic bone and the new pressure show urine is being made but not draining, so the nurse checks the catheter first.

options.text: Irrigate the catheter with sterile saline
options.rationale: A blocked catheter may need irrigation, which makes this tempting. Irrigation needs a prescription, and the nurse first checks the tubing for a simple kink and confirms the bladder volume.

options.text: Recheck the urine output in 1 hour
options.rationale: A falling output is trended, but a firm bladder with new pressure means urine is being made and held now. Waiting 1 hour lets the bladder keep filling.

options.text: Check the tubing and scan the bladder
options.rationale: A full, firm bladder with output that stopped suddenly, while the vital signs and mental status are unchanged, points to a kinked or blocked catheter. Keeping the tubing unobstructed is part of catheter care, and a bladder scan confirms the volume.

questions.takeaway: When catheter output drops suddenly, assess drainage first: a firm bladder and new suprapubic pressure mean urine is being made but not draining. Decreased output with hypotension, new confusion or rapid breathing points to sepsis or kidney dysfunction instead.
questions.strategy: Reporting, irrigating, and rechecking all respond to low output. The firm bladder with unchanged vital signs and mental status decides that the problem is drainage, which the nurse assesses first.

steps.detail: Firm area above the pubic bone and new lower abdominal pressure.
Blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, heart rate 88/min, alert and oriented: none present.
Check the tubing and scan the bladder; irrigation needs a prescription.
Rechecking in 1 hour lets the bladder keep filling.

elimination.verdict: D. Check the tubing and scan the bladder.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.scenario: A patient, 24 years old, has acute glomerulonephritis. Prescriptions: a daily fluid allowance equal to the previous 24 hour urine output plus 500 mL, a sodium restriction, and daily weight. Findings at 0800: urine output 350 mL over the past 24 hours; weight 68.9 kg, was 67.4 kg yesterday; blood pressure 168/104 mm Hg; crackles in both lower lobes with a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, lungs were clear yesterday. The patient reports a dry mouth and thirst.
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with acute glomerulonephritis. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this patient now.

rows.text: Offer extra water for the dry mouth and thirst
rows.rationale: Thirst is real, but the patient has a fluid allowance, a weight gain of 1.5 kg and new crackles. Extra water adds to the fluid overload; mouth care and counted sips are used instead.

rows.text: Set today's fluid allowance at 850 mL, spread across the day
rows.rationale: The prescription is the previous 24 hour output plus 500 mL: 350 mL plus 500 mL is 850 mL. Spreading it out helps with thirst.

rows.text: Request an IV fluid bolus to raise the low urine output
rows.rationale: The low output comes from reduced filtration, not from a low fluid volume. The weight gain and crackles show the patient already holds too much fluid.

rows.text: Raise the head of the bed and report the new crackles to the provider
rows.rationale: New crackles with a respiratory rate of 26 show fluid overload reaching the lungs, which is reported right away. Raising the head of the bed eases breathing.

rows.text: Weigh before breakfast on the same scale and compare with yesterday
rows.rationale: Daily weight at the same time on the same scale is the most direct trend of fluid retention; the 1.5 kg gain since yesterday is about 1.5 L of fluid.

rows.text: Offer broth at lunch to replace the sodium lost in the urine
rows.rationale: Glomerulonephritis causes sodium and fluid retention, not loss, and the patient is on a sodium restriction.

questions.takeaway: In acute glomerulonephritis with low output, weight gain and crackles, the problem is fluid and sodium retention. Follow the fluid allowance (previous 24 hour output plus the prescribed amount), restrict sodium, weigh daily, and report respiratory changes right away.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each row is decided by one cue: the fluid allowance math, the weight gain and crackles that rule out more fluid, and the sodium restriction.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 350 mL plus 500 mL equals 850 mL.
Weight up 1.5 kg and new crackles with a respiratory rate of 26.
Extra water, a bolus and broth all worsen retention.
Daily weight, raise the head of the bed, report the crackles.

elimination.verdict: Not indicated, indicated, not indicated, indicated, indicated, not indicated.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient with acute glomerulonephritis who is going home on sodium, fluid, and potassium restrictions. Serum potassium today is 5.7 mEq/L. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will count soup and ice as part of my fluid allowance."
options.rationale: Soup, ice, and other foods that are liquid at room temperature count toward a fluid allowance. The statement may sound overly strict, but it is correct.

options.text: "I will use a salt substitute so my food still has flavor."
options.rationale: This sounds like it follows the sodium restriction. Most salt substitutes contain potassium chloride, and with a potassium of 5.7 mEq/L and a potassium restriction, using one can raise the potassium further.

options.text: "I will limit bananas and oranges, even though they are healthy."
options.rationale: Bananas and oranges are high in potassium, so limiting them fits the potassium restriction even though they are healthy foods. The statement is correct.

options.text: "I will season my food with herbs and lemon instead of salt."
options.rationale: Herbs and lemon add flavor without sodium or potassium, which fits both restrictions.

questions.takeaway: Sodium restriction does not mean switching to a salt substitute when potassium is also high or restricted, because most salt substitutes are potassium chloride. Herbs, spices and lemon flavor food without either.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Two statements describe ways to flavor food without salt, and two sound overly strict. The potassium of 5.7 mEq/L and the potassium restriction decide which one is unsafe.

steps.detail: Needs further teaching: find the unsafe statement.
Potassium 5.7 mEq/L with a potassium restriction.
Herbs and lemon have no potassium; most salt substitutes are potassium chloride.
Counting soup and ice and limiting bananas and oranges are correct.

elimination.verdict: B. The salt substitute statement.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients on a medical unit. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis, cola colored urine, puffy eyelids
options.rationale: Cola colored urine and puffy eyelids are the expected key cues of acute glomerulonephritis. They need monitoring, not the first visit.

options.text: Pyelonephritis, newly unsure of the date, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg
options.rationale: New confusion is an early warning sign of sepsis and can appear while the blood pressure is still normal. The normal blood pressure is the trap: waiting for it to fall means missing the early cue.

options.text: Pyelonephritis, flank pain 8 of 10, asking for the prescribed analgesic
options.rationale: Flank pain is the hallmark of pyelonephritis and the pain needs treatment soon, but it is expected and a prescription is in place. A possible change in perfusion to the brain comes first.

options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis, blood pressure 150/94 mm Hg, was 156/96 mm Hg
options.rationale: The blood pressure is high, but it is expected in acute glomerulonephritis and is slowly coming down, so it is not a new change.

questions.takeaway: In a patient with a urinary infection, new confusion is an early warning sign of sepsis and can appear while the blood pressure is still normal. A normal blood pressure does not make new confusion safe to delay.
questions.strategy: Every patient has an abnormal finding. Sort expected from unexpected: pain, cola colored urine and a high blood pressure that is falling are expected; new confusion is a change that signals possible sepsis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Mark each finding expected or unexpected
steps.detail: Flank pain, cola colored urine, puffy eyelids and a falling high blood pressure are expected for the diagnosis.
New confusion about the date in a patient with pyelonephritis.

steps.action: Reject the normal blood pressure as reassurance
steps.detail: New confusion can appear while the blood pressure is still normal.
The patient with new confusion is assessed first.

elimination.verdict: B. Pyelonephritis, newly unsure of the date, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a spinal cord injury who has had an indwelling urinary catheter for 3 weeks and is admitted with pyelonephritis. Prescriptions: replace the catheter and drainage system, obtain a urine culture, and start an IV antibiotic. Blood cultures were drawn at 0900, and the patient has no known drug allergies. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the first dose of the IV antibiotic
options.rationale: The blood cultures are drawn and allergies are checked, so this is tempting. A catheter in place for 3 weeks carries a film of organisms, so it is replaced before the antibiotic starts and the urine culture is collected before the first dose.

options.text: Collect urine for culture from the drainage bag
options.rationale: Urine in the drainage bag has been sitting at room temperature and does not reflect the urine in the bladder, so it is never used for a culture.

options.text: Collect urine for culture from the current catheter port
options.rationale: The sampling port is the right site on a new catheter. On a catheter in place for 3 weeks, the specimen picks up organisms living on the old device instead of the organism in the bladder.

options.text: Replace the catheter and the drainage system
options.rationale: A catheter in place for 3 weeks holds a film of concentrated organisms. Replacing it and the closed drainage system first removes that source, lets the culture come from the new catheter, and then the antibiotic is started.

questions.takeaway: For a patient with a long term indwelling catheter who develops pyelonephritis, replace the catheter and the closed drainage system before starting the antibiotic, and collect the urine culture from the new catheter, never from the bag.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options look correct: starting the antibiotic, since the blood cultures are drawn, and collecting the culture from the sampling port. The 3 weeks of catheter use decides, because the old catheter is the source of organisms that would cloud the culture and blunt treatment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The catheter has been in place for 3 weeks.
Urine in the bag is never cultured.
A specimen through the old catheter reflects the device, not the bladder.
Replace the catheter and drainage system, collect the culture from the new catheter, then give the antibiotic.

elimination.verdict: D. Replace the catheter and the drainage system.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.nursesNote: 0900. Day 2 of admission for acute glomerulonephritis that began 10 days after a sore throat. Urine is cola colored. Vomited twice since 0600 and reports nausea and no appetite. Eyelids and hands puffy, unchanged since admission. Blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg, was 164/98 mm Hg on admission. Neck veins distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees. An S3 heart sound is heard. Urinalysis shows protein and red blood cells. Serum potassium 6.1 mEq/L, was 5.0 mEq/L on admission.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the day 2 note of a patient with acute glomerulonephritis. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Urine is cola colored.
segments.rationale: Cola colored urine comes from blood leaking through the damaged glomeruli. It is an expected cue of acute glomerulonephritis.

segments.text: Vomited twice since 0600 and reports nausea and no appetite.
segments.rationale: Nausea, vomiting and loss of appetite in a patient with reduced kidney filtration point to uremia, a sign that kidney function is getting worse.

segments.text: Eyelids and hands puffy, unchanged since admission.
segments.rationale: Facial and hand edema is present in most patients with acute glomerulonephritis, and it has not changed.

segments.text: Blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg, was 164/98 mm Hg on admission.
segments.rationale: The blood pressure is falling from the admission value, which shows a response to treatment.

segments.text: Neck veins distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees.
segments.rationale: Distended neck veins with the head raised show fluid volume excess from sodium and water retention.

segments.text: An S3 heart sound is heard.
segments.rationale: An S3 heart sound is a sign of fluid overload that can lead to pulmonary edema.

segments.text: Urinalysis shows protein and red blood cells.
segments.rationale: Protein and blood in the urine are expected because the inflamed glomeruli leak them.

segments.text: Serum potassium 6.1 mEq/L, was 5.0 mEq/L on admission.
segments.rationale: Potassium is high and rising. Reduced filtration lets potassium build up, which threatens the heart rhythm.

questions.takeaway: In acute glomerulonephritis, cola colored urine, protein and blood in the urine, and facial edema are expected. Follow up on cues that the condition is worsening: uremic symptoms such as nausea and vomiting, signs of fluid overload such as neck vein distention and an S3, and a rising potassium.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate the findings the disease always brings from the ones that show it getting worse. Ask of each: is this new, rising or a sign of overload or uremia?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cola colored urine, protein and red blood cells, unchanged puffiness.
Blood pressure is falling from 164/98 mm Hg, so it is responding.
Distended neck veins at 45 degrees and an S3.
New vomiting and nausea, and potassium 6.1 mEq/L, was 5.0 mEq/L.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an older adult with heart failure who is admitted with a weight gain of 2 kg in 4 days and crackles in both lung bases. The patient had a skin infection on the leg 2 weeks ago. The provider is considering acute glomerulonephritis as well as worsening heart failure. Which finding most strongly supports acute glomerulonephritis?

options.text: Urine output 300 mL over 24 hours
options.rationale: Decreased urine output is a key cue of acute glomerulonephritis, but worsening heart failure also lowers urine output by reducing blood flow to the kidneys, so it does not tell the two apart.

options.text: Cola colored urine with 3+ protein
options.rationale: Blood and protein in the urine come from damaged glomeruli leaking them. Heart failure does not cause this, so it points to the kidney, and the recent skin infection fits.

options.text: Pitting edema of both ankles
options.rationale: Edema occurs in both conditions. Dependent ankle edema is typical of heart failure, so it does not point to the kidney.

options.text: Blood pressure 170/100 mm Hg
options.rationale: High blood pressure is a key cue of acute glomerulonephritis, but it is common in heart failure too and does not separate them.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, acute glomerulonephritis is easily mistaken for worsening heart failure because both cause fluid overload. Blood and protein in the urine come from the glomeruli and point to the kidney.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: All four options are key cues of acute glomerulonephritis, which makes them all look right. Ask which one heart failure cannot produce: only the cola colored urine with protein.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Heart failure history versus a skin infection 2 weeks ago.

steps.action: Test each cue against heart failure
steps.detail: Low output, edema and high blood pressure all occur in heart failure.

steps.action: Find the cue only the kidney explains
steps.detail: Cola colored urine with 3+ protein.
Blood and protein in the urine support glomerulonephritis.

elimination.verdict: B. Cola colored urine with 3+ protein.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient with acute glomerulonephritis from an immune mediated disease who is going home on prednisone, a sodium restriction and a daily fluid allowance. Urine output is still below the patient's usual amount. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will take the prednisone with breakfast, even when I feel well."
options.rationale: Taking a corticosteroid every day as prescribed, even after the swelling eases, is correct. Morning dosing with food matches the body's natural rhythm and protects the stomach.

options.text: "I will keep to my fluid allowance even when my mouth is dry."
options.rationale: Staying within the fluid allowance despite thirst sounds harsh but is correct; mouth care and spreading fluids through the day ease the dryness.

options.text: "I will weigh myself each morning and call if it jumps suddenly."
options.rationale: Daily weight at the same time and reporting a sudden rise is how fluid retention is tracked at home.

options.text: "I will season my food with a salt substitute instead."
options.rationale: This sounds like following the sodium restriction, and prednisone can lower potassium, which makes it tempting. Most salt substitutes are potassium chloride, and with urine output still low the kidneys cannot excrete potassium well, so hyperkalemia can develop. The patient uses herbs and spices and checks any substitute with the provider.

questions.takeaway: With glomerulonephritis and low urine output, potassium is retained, so salt substitutes made of potassium chloride are avoided even though they fit a sodium restriction. Corticosteroids are taken daily as prescribed, infection exposure is limited, the fluid allowance is kept, and weight is checked daily.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three statements sound strict or routine but are correct. The statement that sounds most compliant, using a salt substitute for the sodium restriction, is the unsafe one. The deciding cue is the low urine output: the kidneys cannot clear the potassium in most substitutes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needs further teaching: find the unsafe statement.
Daily prednisone with food, the fluid allowance despite thirst, and daily weights are correct.
Low urine output means potassium is retained.
A potassium chloride salt substitute can cause hyperkalemia, so it needs teaching.

elimination.verdict: D. The statement about using a salt substitute.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: The nurse is following up by phone with a patient on day 2 of an oral antibiotic and phenazopyridine for cystitis. The patient says the burning with urination is much less and the urine is orange. Since this morning the patient has had nausea, chills, and an ache in the back just below the ribs. The patient's temperature is 37.6 °C. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The antibiotic is causing an expected stomach upset
options.rationale: Nausea can be an antibiotic adverse effect, so this is tempting. It does not explain new chills and a new ache below the ribs.

options.text: The bladder infection is clearing, since burning is less
options.rationale: The burning is less, but phenazopyridine relieves discomfort without treating the infection. Less burning while the patient takes it does not show the infection is clearing.

options.text: The infection may be spreading to the kidney
options.rationale: New chills, an ache below the ribs and nausea are the local and systemic signs of an infection that has moved up from the bladder to the kidney. A temperature of 37.6 °C does not rule this out, because fever can lag behind chills. The patient needs prompt evaluation.

options.text: The phenazopyridine is causing the nausea and ache
options.rationale: The orange urine is the expected effect of phenazopyridine. It does not explain chills or a new ache below the ribs.

questions.takeaway: Phenazopyridine eases bladder discomfort but does not treat infection, so less burning can hide a worsening infection. New chills, an ache below the ribs and nausea during treatment for cystitis suggest the infection is ascending to the kidney and need prompt evaluation, even before a fever appears.
questions.strategy: Three options each explain one finding: the nausea, the lesser burning or the orange urine, and the near normal temperature makes them feel safe. Only one option explains the chills and the ache below the ribs together.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New chills, an ache just below the ribs and nausea since this morning.
Less burning is from the phenazopyridine, and 37.6 °C does not rule out a kidney infection.
Orange urine is the expected effect of phenazopyridine.

steps.action: Choose the option that explains every new finding
steps.detail: An infection spreading from the bladder to the kidney.

elimination.verdict: C. The infection may be spreading to the kidney.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient with fever, chills, and suspected pyelonephritis. Which assessment best checks for the hallmark finding?

options.text: Fist percussion at the costovertebral angle
options.rationale: Flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of pyelonephritis. Striking a fist placed over the angle where the lowest rib meets the spine checks for kidney tenderness.

options.text: Deep palpation above the pubic bone
options.rationale: Discomfort above the pubic bone points to the bladder, as in cystitis, not to the kidney.

options.text: Bladder scan right after the patient voids
options.rationale: A bladder scan measures urine left after voiding. It checks for retention, not kidney inflammation.

options.text: Auscultation of bowel sounds in all four quadrants
options.rationale: Bowel sounds assess the gut. They do not check the kidney.

questions.takeaway: In suspected pyelonephritis, check for costovertebral angle tenderness with fist percussion over the angle where the lowest rib meets the spine. Tenderness there points to the kidney; tenderness above the pubic bone points to the bladder.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real assessment. Match the location of the organ involved: pyelonephritis is in the kidney, so the check is at the flank.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pyelonephritis is infection of the kidney and renal pelvis.
Suprapubic palpation and a bladder scan assess the bladder.
Bowel sounds assess the gut.
Fist percussion at the costovertebral angle.

elimination.verdict: A. Fist percussion at the costovertebral angle.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 24 hour intake and output of a patient with pyelonephritis who has had a temperature of 38.6 to 39.0 °C with heavy sweating all day. Intake is 2,400 mL and urine output is 1,300 mL. Weight is 72.0 kg, unchanged from yesterday. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, unchanged since admission. Lungs are clear, there is no edema, the oral mucosa is moist, and the bladder is not palpable after voiding. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Losses from fever and sweating explain the gap
options.rationale: Fever and heavy sweating cause fluid losses that intake and output records do not measure. The unchanged weight shows the patient's total fluid is the same as yesterday, so the 1,100 mL difference left the body unmeasured.

options.text: The kidneys are retaining the unexcreted fluid
options.rationale: Intake higher than output looks like retention, but retained fluid would raise the weight and could cause edema or crackles. The weight is unchanged, the lungs are clear, and the creatinine has not risen.

options.text: A fluid volume deficit is beginning to develop
options.rationale: Fever and sweating do raise the risk of a deficit, so this is tempting. The weight is unchanged and the mucosa is moist, so the losses are being replaced.

options.text: Urine is collecting in a bladder that is not emptying
options.rationale: Retention would leave a full bladder after voiding. The bladder is not palpable after voiding.

questions.takeaway: Intake and output does not capture losses through the skin and lungs, which rise with fever and sweating. Daily weight is the best check on total fluid balance: an unchanged weight with moist mucosa and a steady creatinine means the gap is unmeasured loss, not retention or a deficit.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Two options are tempting from the numbers alone: retention because intake exceeds output, and a deficit because of the fever. The unchanged weight rules out both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight 72.0 kg, unchanged from yesterday.
No weight gain, clear lungs, no edema and an unchanged creatinine.
No weight loss and moist mucosa.
The bladder is not palpable after voiding.
Unmeasured losses from fever and sweating explain the gap.

elimination.verdict: A. Losses from fever and sweating explain the gap.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the clinic findings of a patient with repeated kidney infections. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient with vesicoureteral reflux has had four kidney infections in 2 years. At today's clinic visit the patient has no fever, no flank pain and no burning with urination, and the urine is clear yellow. There is no edema. The patient now gets up three times each night to void, which began in the past few months. Blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg, was 124/78 mm Hg a year ago. Serum creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL, was 1.0 mg/dL a year ago.

These findings are best explained by [[1]].

The new need to void at night most likely reflects [[2]].

To protect the remaining kidney function, the nurse reinforces [[3]].

options.text: kidney scarring from the repeated infections
options.rationale: Repeated kidney infections, especially with reflux, cause scarring and permanent loss of kidney function. The rising creatinine and blood pressure with no signs of active infection fit scarring.

options.text: urinary retention from the reflux
options.rationale: Nothing in the findings shows a bladder that is not emptying, and retention does not explain the rising creatinine and blood pressure.

options.text: acute glomerulonephritis
options.rationale: There is no edema and the urine is clear yellow, not cola colored.

options.text: an active kidney infection
options.rationale: There is no fever, no flank pain, no burning and the urine is clear, so there are no signs of an active infection.

options.text: a new bladder infection
options.rationale: There is no burning, no fever and the urine is clear.

options.text: weakness of the pelvic floor muscles
options.rationale: Pelvic floor weakness causes leakage, not a new need to wake and void.

options.text: loss of the kidney's ability to concentrate urine
options.rationale: A scarred kidney cannot concentrate urine well, so more dilute urine is made and the patient wakes to void.

options.text: a full bladder that does not empty
options.rationale: No finding suggests retention.

options.text: drinking fluids spread through the waking hours
options.rationale: Dehydration can further reduce kidney function, so steady intake during waking hours protects the remaining function.

options.text: starting leftover antibiotics at the first symptom
options.rationale: Antibiotics are taken only as prescribed, as a full course; new symptoms are reported for evaluation.

options.text: limiting fluids after supper to stop waking at night
options.rationale: This sounds practical for the night voiding, but less fluid risks dehydration, which further reduces kidney function.

options.text: ibuprofen for any flank discomfort
options.rationale: NSAIDs can reduce blood flow to the kidney and are avoided in a patient with declining kidney function.

questions.takeaway: Repeated pyelonephritis scars the kidney. A rising creatinine, new hypertension and new night voiding without signs of active infection point to lost kidney function. Protect what remains with steady fluids, no NSAIDs and prescribed antibiotics only.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: First decide whether the infection is active: no fever, flank pain or burning means it is not. Then link each finding to a scarred kidney that filters and concentrates less.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No fever, flank pain or burning, and clear urine.
No edema and no cola colored urine.
Creatinine 1.0 to 1.8 mg/dL and blood pressure 124/78 to 156/94 mm Hg over a year mean lost kidney function.
A scarred kidney cannot concentrate urine.
Fluids through the waking hours; reject the fluid limit, the NSAID and leftover antibiotics.

elimination.verdict: 1: kidney scarring from the repeated infections. 2: loss of the kidney's ability to concentrate urine. 3: drinking fluids spread through the waking hours.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a patient with cola colored urine, puffy eyelids, and new high blood pressure. Which history question is most important to ask?

options.text: "How much coffee do you drink each day?"
options.rationale: Caffeine can irritate the bladder, but it does not cause cola colored urine, puffy eyelids or high blood pressure.

options.text: "Have you had burning when you urinate?"
options.rationale: Burning points to cystitis. These findings point to the kidney's filters, not the bladder.

options.text: "Have you had a recent throat infection?"
options.rationale: Cola colored urine, facial edema and new high blood pressure are the key cues of acute glomerulonephritis, which may follow a bacterial infection such as a sore throat. A recent infection supports the diagnosis and its cause.

options.text: "Do you leak urine when you cough or sneeze?"
options.rationale: Leaking with coughing is a sign of incontinence and does not explain these findings.

questions.takeaway: Cola colored urine, facial edema and new high blood pressure suggest acute glomerulonephritis. Ask about a recent bacterial infection, such as a sore throat, because it may trigger the glomerular injury.
questions.strategy: Each question fits some urinary problem. Pick the one that matches all three findings and asks about their likely cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cola colored urine, puffy eyelids and new high blood pressure.
Acute glomerulonephritis.
It may follow a bacterial infection.
Ask about a recent throat infection.

elimination.verdict: C. "Have you had a recent throat infection?"

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning ongoing assessment for a patient with acute glomerulonephritis and falling urine output. Which assessments should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Postvoid residual by bladder scan
options.rationale: The output is falling because the kidney filters less, not because the bladder holds urine. A bladder scan checks retention.

options.text: Lung sounds for new crackles
options.rationale: Reduced filtration causes fluid retention, which can reach the lungs. Lung sounds are part of ongoing monitoring.

options.text: Urine culture every day
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the filters, not an active urinary infection, and a daily culture is not part of monitoring.

options.text: Weight at the same time each morning
options.rationale: Daily weight shows the trend of fluid retention.

options.text: Costovertebral angle tenderness each shift
options.rationale: Costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of pyelonephritis, not a monitoring point for glomerulonephritis.

options.text: Blood pressure trends
options.rationale: Blood pressure rises with fluid and sodium retention, so its trend is monitored.

questions.takeaway: Ongoing monitoring in acute glomerulonephritis tracks fluid retention: daily weight, blood pressure, intake and output, and lung sounds, documented as trends.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real urinary assessment. Keep the ones that track fluid retention from reduced filtration and drop the ones meant for the bladder or for infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reduced filtration with fluid retention.
Lung sounds, daily weight and blood pressure.
A bladder scan checks retention.
A daily culture and costovertebral angle checks belong to infection.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who weighs 80 kg and was admitted 12 hours ago with pyelonephritis. The patient is receiving an IV antibiotic and IV fluids. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Temperature 38.4 °C, was 38.9 °C on admission
options.rationale: The patient still has a fever, which makes this tempting, but the temperature is falling. Fever often takes 48 to 72 hours of antibiotics to clear, so a falling fever at 12 hours is the expected course.

options.text: Flank pain 5 of 10 after an analgesic, was 8 of 10
options.rationale: Flank pain is expected with a kidney infection, and this pain is responding to the analgesic. It needs continued pain management, not immediate follow up.

options.text: Urine output 96 mL over the past 4 hours
options.rationale: 96 mL over 4 hours is 24 mL per hour, or 0.3 mL/kg/hr for an 80 kg patient. Output below 0.5 mL/kg/hr is decreased urine output. In a kidney infection it can signal poor perfusion from early sepsis or worsening kidney function, and it needs follow up now.

options.text: Burning and urgency with each void
options.rationale: Dysuria and urgency are expected with a urinary infection that has reached the kidney, and they ease as the antibiotic works. They are not a sign of worsening.

questions.takeaway: In pyelonephritis, watch for the shift from local infection to systemic trouble. Decreased urine output (below 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is an early sign of poor perfusion or kidney dysfunction. Fever and flank pain that are trending down on treatment are the expected course.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Convert every urine output to mL per hour and compare it with the weight. A number that looks harmless over 4 hours can hide oliguria. Then ask which finding is getting worse rather than which one is still abnormal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 96 mL over 4 hours is 24 mL/hr, or 0.3 mL/kg/hr at 80 kg: decreased urine output.
Still febrile, but falling on treatment: the expected course.
Flank pain is easing and dysuria is expected with this infection.
The only finding that signals worsening is the low urine output.

elimination.verdict: C. Urine output 96 mL over the past 4 hours.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an older adult admitted after a fall at home. The patient is alert and oriented, has no fever, and denies burning, urgency or flank pain. A urine culture grew bacteria, and a family member asks why no antibiotic was started. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The provider may be waiting for the culture susceptibility results."
options.rationale: Susceptibility testing guides the choice of antibiotic once treatment is needed. This answer suggests an antibiotic is coming and does not explain why none is needed.

options.text: "Bacteria in the urine without symptoms usually is not treated."
options.rationale: This is asymptomatic bacteriuria: bacteria in the urine with no symptoms of infection. A positive culture alone does not establish a urinary infection, and most asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults does not need antibiotics. The team still looks for other causes of the fall.

options.text: "A fall is often the first sign of a bladder infection."
options.rationale: A fall or confusion alone does not establish a urinary infection. This statement reinforces the belief that leads to unneeded antibiotics.

options.text: "I will ask the provider to order an antibiotic to be safe."
options.rationale: This sounds like advocacy, but treating bacteria without symptoms adds adverse effects and antibiotic resistance with no benefit.

questions.takeaway: Asymptomatic bacteriuria: bacteria in the urine without infection symptoms. A positive culture, a fall or confusion alone does not establish a urinary infection. Look for urinary or systemic findings and other causes; treat only when infection symptoms are present.
questions.strategy: The fall and the positive culture both pull toward infection. Check the symptoms: no fever, no dysuria, no urgency, no flank pain and normal mental status. Without symptoms, the culture alone is not an infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Positive culture, but no fever, no urinary symptoms and alert and oriented.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria.
A fall alone does not establish infection, and an antibiotic to be safe causes harm.
The answer that explains why no treatment is needed.

elimination.verdict: B. "Bacteria in the urine without symptoms usually is not treated."

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: The nurse at a clinic receives a call from a patient on day 1 of an oral antibiotic for pyelonephritis. The patient has vomited after both doses, cannot keep fluids down, and has a temperature of 38.9 °C. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Arrange for the patient to be seen today
options.rationale: Vomiting every dose means the antibiotic is not being absorbed, and no fluid intake leads to dehydration. With a fever, this patient is at risk for worsening infection and sepsis and likely needs IV therapy. Vomiting and fever are findings to report immediately.

options.text: Advise taking the next dose with a light meal
options.rationale: Food can ease mild stomach upset from an antibiotic. It does not solve a patient who cannot keep fluids or any dose down.

options.text: Advise waiting 24 hours for the antibiotic to work
options.rationale: Antibiotics can take a day or two to bring a fever down, which makes this tempting. A drug that is vomited back up is not working at all, and waiting lets the infection progress.

options.text: Advise sipping clear fluids until the vomiting stops
options.rationale: Small sips are reasonable for nausea, but this delays treatment of a kidney infection that is not being treated and a patient who is already unable to keep fluids down.

questions.takeaway: Teach patients with pyelonephritis to report fever, chills, vomiting or worsening symptoms immediately. Vomiting every dose means no treatment and no hydration, so the patient needs to be seen the same day.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the treatment is actually reaching the patient. Every home option assumes the antibiotic is working; the vomiting says it is not.

steps.detail: Vomited both doses, no fluids kept down, fever 38.9 °C.
No antibiotic absorbed and no hydration: the infection is untreated.
A meal, waiting or sips all delay treatment.
Same day evaluation.

elimination.verdict: A. Arrange for the patient to be seen today.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating discharge teaching for a patient with acute glomerulonephritis who is going home on a sodium restriction, a daily fluid allowance and an antihypertensive. Which statements by the patient indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will use a salt substitute to flavor my food."
options.rationale: Most salt substitutes are potassium chloride. With reduced kidney filtration, potassium can build up, so salt substitutes are avoided unless the provider approves them. This needs further teaching.

options.text: "I will weigh myself each morning after I void, on the same scale."
options.rationale: Daily weight at the same time, after voiding and on the same scale is the most sensitive measure of fluid retention in glomerulonephritis.

options.text: "I will call if I get short of breath or my eyelids get puffier."
options.rationale: Shortness of breath and more edema signal fluid overload. Respiratory distress is reported immediately.

options.text: "I will drink extra water on hot days to protect my kidneys."
options.rationale: The fluid allowance is set to match what the kidneys can excrete. Extra water adds to the fluid the damaged glomeruli cannot remove.

options.text: "I will stop the blood pressure pill once the swelling is gone."
options.rationale: Less swelling does not mean the blood pressure or kidney is back to normal. Medications are taken as prescribed until the provider changes them.

options.text: "I will call if I am passing much less urine than usual."
options.rationale: Decreased urine output signals worsening kidney function and is reported.

questions.takeaway: For glomerulonephritis at home: daily weight with the same scale and timing, the prescribed sodium and fluid limits, medications as prescribed, no salt substitutes without approval, and report shortness of breath, more edema or less urine.
questions.strategy: Picture kidneys that cannot filter well. Every correct statement watches for or limits fluid buildup. Every wrong one adds fluid, adds potassium or stops treatment early.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily weight, more edema, shortness of breath, less urine.
Extra water and a potassium salt substitute.
Swelling gone does not end the antihypertensive.

elimination.verdict: B, C, F.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.nursesNote: 0900. Admitted with 3 days of burning and frequency with voiding. History of type 2 diabetes and a kidney stone seen on imaging last month. Since last night has had shaking chills and has vomited 3 times. Temperature 39.2 °C. Heart rate 112 beats per minute. Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg. SpO2 97% on room air. Alert and oriented to person, place and time. Costovertebral angle tenderness on the side of the known stone. Oral mucosa dry. Urine cloudy and dark amber. Blood glucose 264 mg/dL. Weight 80 kg.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission note of a patient with suspected pyelonephritis. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: shaking chills
segments.rationale: Shaking chills mean the infection has spread beyond the lower urinary tract. With dysuria they point to a kidney infection.

segments.text: vomited 3 times
segments.rationale: Vomiting is an associated symptom of pyelonephritis and causes fluid loss. It also means oral fluids and oral drugs may not stay down.

segments.text: Temperature 39.2 °C
segments.rationale: A high fever signals a systemic infection, not a bladder infection alone.

segments.text: Heart rate 112 beats per minute
segments.rationale: Tachycardia comes with fever and fluid loss, and it is an early sign of sepsis. It needs trending.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute
segments.rationale: Within the expected range for an adult. It sets the baseline for later checks.

segments.text: Blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg
segments.rationale: Within the expected range now. It is the baseline for watching for a fall.

segments.text: SpO2 97% on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygenation is adequate.

segments.text: Alert and oriented to person, place and time
segments.rationale: Normal mental status. It is the baseline: new confusion would be an early warning sign of sepsis.

segments.text: Costovertebral angle tenderness on the side of the known stone
segments.rationale: Flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness is the hallmark of pyelonephritis. A stone on the same side raises concern for obstruction and urinary stasis.

segments.text: Oral mucosa dry
segments.rationale: Dry mucosa after vomiting points to fluid volume deficit.

segments.text: Urine cloudy and dark amber
segments.rationale: Cloudy urine suggests infection, and dark amber urine is concentrated, which fits fluid loss.

segments.text: Blood glucose 264 mg/dL
segments.rationale: Diabetes is a risk factor for urinary infection, and infection raises glucose. Hyperglycemia also adds fluid loss through the urine.

questions.takeaway: Recognize a kidney infection by its local and systemic signs: fever, shaking chills, flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness, nausea and vomiting, and tachycardia. Note the risk factors (diabetes, a stone that can block flow) and record a baseline blood pressure and mental status for the hours ahead.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into abnormal now or baseline. Normal blood pressure, oxygen and mental status do not need follow up yet, but they are what the nurse compares with later.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shaking chills, fever, tachycardia, costovertebral angle tenderness, cloudy urine.
Vomiting, dry mucosa, dark amber urine.
Blood glucose 264 mg/dL with diabetes.
Respiratory rate, blood pressure, SpO2 and mental status are normal for now.

questions.objective: Assess urinary patterns, symptoms, intake and output, and key diagnostic findings.

questions.scenario: Chart so far: admitted at 0900 with suspected pyelonephritis; type 2 diabetes; a known kidney stone; shaking chills, vomited 3 times, temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg, alert and oriented, costovertebral angle tenderness, dry oral mucosa, cloudy dark amber urine, blood glucose 264 mg/dL, weight 80 kg. At 1000 the nurse reviews the first results and history: urinalysis positive for nitrites with many white blood cells; abdominal CT shows the stone lodged in the ureter with swelling of the kidney above it; weight 80 kg, was 82 kg at a clinic visit last week.
questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing the findings of a patient admitted with suspected pyelonephritis. For each finding, indicate the problem it best supports.

rows.text: Costovertebral angle tenderness with shaking chills
rows.rationale: Flank tenderness with chills and fever is the hallmark of infection in the kidney and renal pelvis.

rows.text: Nitrites and many white blood cells in the urine
rows.rationale: Nitrites and white blood cells suggest a urinary infection. Matched with the fever and flank findings, they support pyelonephritis.

rows.text: Dry oral mucosa after repeated vomiting
rows.rationale: Vomiting removes fluid and dry mucosa shows the result.

rows.text: Weight 80 kg, was 82 kg last week
rows.rationale: A 2 kg loss in a week with vomiting and poor intake is mostly fluid.

rows.text: Stone lodged in the ureter with swelling of the kidney above it
rows.rationale: A stone blocking the ureter backs urine up into the kidney. Obstruction causes stasis, which lets bacteria multiply, and it needs to be relieved for the infection to clear.

questions.takeaway: Pyelonephritis seldom travels alone. Link each cue to its problem: flank tenderness, chills and positive urine findings to the kidney infection; vomiting, dry mucosa and weight loss to fluid volume deficit; a lodged stone with a swollen kidney to obstruction, the risk factor that keeps the infection going.
questions.strategy: For each row ask what is causing this finding. Infection explains inflammation and urine findings, fluid loss explains dryness and weight change, and blocked flow explains a swollen kidney above a stone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flank tenderness, chills, nitrites and white blood cells.
Dry mucosa after vomiting and a 2 kg drop in a week.
Lodged stone with a swollen kidney above it.

elimination.verdict: Kidney infection: rows 1 and 2. Fluid volume deficit: rows 3 and 4. Urinary obstruction: row 5.

questions.objective: Differentiate incontinence, retention, cystitis/UTI, pyelonephritis, and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
Chart so far: admitted at 0900 with suspected pyelonephritis; type 2 diabetes; a known kidney stone; shaking chills, vomited 3 times, temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg, alert and oriented, costovertebral angle tenderness, dry oral mucosa, cloudy dark amber urine, blood glucose 264 mg/dL, weight 80 kg. Urine and blood cultures were collected at 1000, and the first dose of IV ceftriaxone was given at 1015. A 1,000 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride finished at 1130, and the IV now runs at 125 mL/hr. A procedure to relieve the blockage is planned for 1600.

At 1300 the nurse reassesses the patient. The patient is restless, slow to answer and says it is Sunday; it is Tuesday. Temperature 39.5 °C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. Hands are cool. Urine output is 40 mL since 1000. Flank pain is 7 of 10. Lactate 3.6 mmol/L. Blood glucose 288 mg/dL.

The patient is most likely developing [[1]], as shown by the new [[2]] and the [[3]]. The priority problem now is [[4]].

options.text: fluid overload from the bolus
options.rationale: Fluid overload raises blood pressure and brings crackles. This patient is hypotensive after only 1,000 mL.

options.text: sepsis from the kidney infection
options.rationale: New confusion, a falling blood pressure, rapid breathing, decreased urine output and a raised lactate in a patient with a kidney infection are the progression of urinary infection to sepsis.

options.text: diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: The glucose is high, which makes this tempting, but 288 mg/dL does not explain hypotension and confusion, and the infection is the driver.

options.text: acute glomerulonephritis
options.rationale: Glomerulonephritis brings cola colored urine, edema and high blood pressure. This patient's blood pressure is falling.

options.text: blood glucose
options.rationale: The glucose is high but is not a new sign of poor perfusion.

options.text: burning with voiding
options.rationale: Dysuria is a local symptom of the urinary infection and does not show spread.

options.text: confusion
options.rationale: New confusion is the earliest warning sign in the progression of urinary infection to sepsis. The patient was alert and oriented at 0900.

options.text: flank pain
options.rationale: Flank pain was present on admission and is unchanged. It is expected with the kidney infection.

options.text: falling blood pressure with low urine output
options.rationale: A blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg, was 124/76 mm Hg, and 40 mL of urine in 3 hours show poor perfusion. These come after confusion in the sepsis warning progression.

options.text: cloudy urine
options.rationale: Cloudy urine shows the urinary infection, not its spread.

options.text: costovertebral angle tenderness
options.rationale: This is the hallmark of pyelonephritis and was present on admission.

options.text: SpO2 of 95%
options.rationale: Oxygenation is adequate and is not the cue that shows sepsis.

options.text: fever
options.rationale: The fever is real and will be treated, but it is not what threatens organs now.

options.text: flank pain
options.rationale: Pain needs management, but it does not outrank failing circulation.

options.text: high blood glucose
options.rationale: Hyperglycemia needs management, but it is not the immediate threat.

options.text: poor tissue perfusion
options.rationale: Hypotension, cool hands, low urine output and a raised lactate show organs are not getting enough blood flow. Circulation comes first.

questions.takeaway: Urinary infection becomes sepsis in a recognizable order: new confusion, then hypotension and poor perfusion, then rapid breathing and decreased urine output. Once perfusion fails, circulation is the priority over fever, pain and glucose.
questions.strategy: Separate what was already there at 0900 (flank pain, dysuria, cloudy urine, high glucose) from what is new at 1300 (confusion, hypotension, rapid breathing, low urine output, lactate). The new findings name the problem, and the one that threatens organs is the priority.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
