steps.detail: Confusion, blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28/min and low urine output are all new.
Sepsis from the kidney infection.
Flank pain, dysuria and cloudy urine were present on admission.
Poor tissue perfusion: circulation comes first.

elimination.verdict: 1: sepsis from the kidney infection. 2: confusion. 3: falling blood pressure with low urine output. 4: poor tissue perfusion.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.scenario: Chart so far: admitted at 0900 with suspected pyelonephritis; type 2 diabetes; a known kidney stone; shaking chills, vomited 3 times, temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg, alert and oriented, costovertebral angle tenderness, dry oral mucosa, cloudy dark amber urine, blood glucose 264 mg/dL, weight 80 kg. At 1300: restless and says the wrong day, temperature 39.5 °C, heart rate 126 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg, urine output 40 mL since 1000, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, blood glucose 288 mg/dL. The first ceftriaxone dose was given at 1015, a 1,000 mL fluid bolus finished at 1130, and a procedure to relieve the blockage is planned for 1600. The nurse has notified the provider and is planning care while prescriptions are written.
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with pyelonephritis whose condition is worsening. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this patient now.

rows.text: Measure urine output every hour
rows.rationale: Hourly output is the bedside measure of kidney perfusion in sepsis. It shows whether fluid resuscitation is working.

rows.text: Restrict IV fluids to protect the kidneys
rows.rationale: The low output comes from poor perfusion, not fluid overload. Restricting fluid would worsen the kidney injury; this patient needs more fluid, not less.

rows.text: Recheck blood pressure and mental status every 15 minutes
rows.rationale: Frequent checks show whether the patient responds to treatment or keeps declining.

rows.text: Hold the next antibiotic dose until culture results return
rows.rationale: Cultures were collected before the first dose. Antibiotics are never delayed for results in sepsis; the next dose is given on time.

rows.text: Encourage oral fluids to replace the vomiting losses
rows.rationale: The patient is vomiting and confused, so oral fluids risk aspiration and cannot restore circulating volume quickly. Fluid goes in by IV.

rows.text: Delay the procedure to relieve the blockage until the fever resolves
rows.rationale: The blocked, infected kidney is the source of the sepsis. The fever will not resolve while urine stays trapped, so relieving the obstruction is not delayed.

rows.text: Monitor blood glucose closely
rows.rationale: Infection and stress raise glucose in a patient with diabetes. Hyperglycemia adds fluid loss and impairs healing, so it is monitored and treated as prescribed.

questions.takeaway: In urinary sepsis, plan for perfusion: IV fluids, hourly urine output, frequent vital signs and mental status, antibiotics on time, source control of an obstruction, and glucose monitoring in diabetes. Fluid restriction, oral replacement and delays all lose ground.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Ask of each action: does it restore or track perfusion and treat the source, or does it delay or limit them? Hourly output and frequent checks track perfusion; fluid limits, waiting for cultures and waiting on the procedure delay treatment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hourly urine output, blood pressure and mental status every 15 minutes.

steps.action: Keep what treats the person with diabetes
steps.detail: Close glucose monitoring.
Fluid restriction, holding the antibiotic, delaying source control.
Oral fluids in a vomiting, confused patient.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: rows 1, 3 and 7. Not indicated: rows 2, 4, 5 and 6.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.stem: At 1310 the nurse is caring for a patient with pyelonephritis and a blocked ureter who is now confused, with a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg, heart rate 126 beats per minute, temperature 39.5 °C, and 40 mL of urine since 1000. Prescriptions: 0.9% sodium chloride 1,400 mL IV bolus now, insert an indwelling urinary catheter for hourly output, acetaminophen 650 mg now, repeat lactate at 1500, and transfer to intermediate care when a bed opens. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the acetaminophen for the fever
options.rationale: The fever is high and will be treated, but it is not the threat to organs. Acetaminophen does not raise the blood pressure.

options.text: Insert the indwelling urinary catheter
options.rationale: Hourly output is an appropriate reason for a catheter in a critically ill patient and will track the response. Measuring output does not restore it, so this follows the fluid.

options.text: Call the intermediate care unit about a bed
options.rationale: The patient needs a higher level of care, but arranging a bed does not treat the hypotension happening now.

options.text: Start the 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Hypotension, confusion and low urine output show poor perfusion. The bolus completes 30 mL/kg for an 80 kg patient (2,400 mL total) and treats circulation, which comes first.

questions.takeaway: In sepsis with hypotension, restore circulation first: the IV fluid bolus. Then set up monitoring (hourly output), treat comfort (fever) and arrange the level of care.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: All four are prescribed and all four will be done. Apply the ABCs: the airway and breathing are holding, and circulation is failing, so the action that treats circulation goes first.

steps.detail: Blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg, confusion and low output: circulation is failing.
Only the fluid bolus raises circulating volume.
Catheter to measure, acetaminophen for comfort, the bed for the level of care.
Start the bolus.

elimination.verdict: D. Start the 0.9% sodium chloride bolus.

questions.objective: Recognize worsening infection, sepsis, decreased urine output, and kidney dysfunction.

questions.scenario: Chart so far: pyelonephritis with a stone blocking the ureter and type 2 diabetes; at 1300 confused, blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg, heart rate 126 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, urine output 40 mL in 3 hours, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, blood glucose 288 mg/dL, lungs clear. The 1,400 mL bolus finished at 1415, and a stent was placed at 1600 to relieve the blockage. Antibiotics continue on schedule. At 1900 the nurse reassesses the patient.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the response to treatment of a patient with sepsis from pyelonephritis. For each finding at 1900, indicate whether it shows an effective response or needs follow up.

rows.text: Oriented to person, place and time and answers promptly
rows.rationale: Mental status has returned to the 0900 baseline, which shows the brain is perfused again.

rows.text: Blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg
rows.rationale: The pressure has risen from 88/50 mm Hg with a mean arterial pressure near 80 mm Hg, enough to perfuse organs.

rows.text: Urine output 50 mL/hr for the past 2 hours
rows.rationale: Above 0.5 mL/kg/hr for an 80 kg patient. The kidneys are perfused and the relieved blockage is draining.

rows.text: Lactate 1.8 mmol/L, was 3.6 mmol/L
rows.rationale: Lactate falls as tissue perfusion returns.

rows.text: Crackles in both lung bases, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 91% on room air
rows.rationale: The lungs were clear before 2.4 L of fluid. New crackles with low oxygen saturation suggest fluid overload and need follow up now, even though the perfusion goals were met.

rows.text: Blood glucose 312 mg/dL, was 288 mg/dL
rows.rationale: Glucose is still rising. Hyperglycemia worsens fluid loss and infection control and needs treatment as prescribed.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate sepsis care against perfusion goals: mental status, blood pressure, urine output and lactate. Then look for what the treatment itself can cause: crackles and falling oxygen saturation after large fluid volumes, and glucose that keeps rising in diabetes.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with its 1300 value. Four perfusion measures moved the right way. The two that need follow up are a new problem (crackles after fluid) and a trend still going the wrong way (glucose).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oriented, blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, urine 50 mL/hr, lactate falling: effective.
Crackles with SpO2 91% after 2.4 L of fluid: needs follow up.
Glucose 312 mg/dL, was 288 mg/dL: needs follow up.

elimination.verdict: Effective response: rows 1, 2, 3 and 4. Needs follow up: rows 5 and 6.

questions.objective: Evaluate outcomes and teach patients when to report changes and how to follow the care plan.

questions.stem: An older adult who eats red meat several times a week has low iron and vitamin B12 levels. Which age related change best explains these findings?

options.text: Slowed peristalsis in the colon
options.rationale: Slower peristalsis and dulled nerve impulses decrease the sensation to defecate and lead to constipation and impaction. They do not explain low iron and vitamin B12.

options.text: Atrophy of the gastric mucosa
options.rationale: Gastric mucosal atrophy decreases absorption of iron and vitamin B12. Low levels in a patient whose intake includes red meat point to poor absorption rather than poor intake.

options.text: Dilation of the pancreatic ducts
options.rationale: Lower lipase reduces fat digestion and absorption and causes steatorrhea. It does not account for low iron and vitamin B12.

options.text: Fewer and smaller liver cells
options.rationale: Fewer and smaller hepatic cells depress drug metabolism and raise the risk of drug toxicity. This change does not explain poor absorption of iron and vitamin B12.

questions.takeaway: Atrophy of the gastric mucosa in older adults decreases absorption of iron and vitamin B12 and allows bacteria to proliferate, which can cause atrophic gastritis. Low levels with adequate intake point to an absorption problem.
questions.strategy: Match the nutrient to the change that affects its absorption. The diet history rules out poor intake, so look for the change that blocks absorption of iron and vitamin B12.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Red meat several times a week supplies iron and vitamin B12.

steps.action: Name the effect of each change
steps.detail: Peristalsis causes constipation, lipase causes steatorrhea, liver cells cause drug toxicity.
Gastric mucosal atrophy decreases iron and vitamin B12 absorption.

elimination.verdict: B. Atrophy of the gastric mucosa.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: An older adult reports pale, greasy stools that float and weight loss without trying. Which explanation should the nurse consider most likely?

options.text: Slower drug metabolism from fewer liver cells
options.rationale: This change leads to accumulation of drugs, possibly to toxic levels. Drug accumulation does not produce fatty stools.

options.text: Less urge to defecate from dulled nerve impulses
options.rationale: Dulled nerve impulses lead to postponed bowel movements, constipation and impaction, not fatty stools.

options.text: Bacterial overgrowth from gastric mucosal atrophy
options.rationale: Gastric mucosal atrophy causes bacterial overgrowth, atrophic gastritis and poor absorption of iron and vitamin B12. It is not the source of fatty stools.

options.text: Poor fat digestion from pancreatic duct changes
options.rationale: Distention and dilation of the pancreatic ducts lower lipase, so fat is poorly digested and absorbed. The result is steatorrhea, fatty stools that are pale, greasy and float, with weight loss from lost calories.

questions.takeaway: Distention and dilation of the pancreatic ducts with aging decrease lipase. Fat is poorly digested and absorbed, which produces steatorrhea and can cause unintended weight loss.
questions.strategy: Name the stool first. Pale, greasy, floating stool is fatty stool, and fat digestion depends on lipase from the pancreas.

steps.detail: Pale, greasy, floating stool is steatorrhea.
Fat digestion depends on lipase.
Age related pancreatic duct changes lower lipase.

elimination.verdict: D. Poor fat digestion from pancreatic duct changes.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: An older adult with constipation says, "I never feel the urge anymore, so I just wait." Which patient statement indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I will sit on the toilet after breakfast, urge or not."
options.rationale: With age, peristalsis slows and nerve impulses are dulled, so the urge to defecate is weaker. Waiting for the urge postpones bowel movements and leads to constipation and impaction. A set daily time does not depend on a sensation the patient no longer feels.

options.text: "I will wait until I feel a strong urge before I go."
options.rationale: Waiting for the urge is the behavior causing the problem. The patient reports the urge rarely comes, and postponement leads to constipation and impaction.

options.text: "I will cut back on fluids during the day and evening."
options.rationale: Less fluid makes stool harder and worsens constipation.

options.text: "I will take a stimulant laxative at bedtime every night."
options.rationale: Nightly laxative use does not address the cause and builds dependence on the drug. A regular toileting time works with the slowed bowel instead.

questions.takeaway: Decreased peristalsis and dulled nerve impulses in older adults weaken the sensation to defecate. Postponing bowel movements leads to constipation and impaction, so teaching focuses on a regular toileting time that does not rely on the urge.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The patient's own words name the problem: waiting for an urge that no longer comes. The right statement removes the waiting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: The patient waits for an urge that has weakened with age.

steps.action: Reject options that keep the cause
steps.detail: Waiting for a strong urge repeats the problem.
Less fluid hardens stool; nightly laxatives build dependence.

elimination.verdict: A. Sit on the toilet at a set time each day.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: The nurse is obtaining a focused history from a patient with watery diarrhea. Which questions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: "What have you taken for the diarrhea, and did it help?"
options.rationale: The history includes actions taken to relieve diarrhea or constipation and whether they were successful.

options.text: "Is your tetanus immunization up to date?"
options.rationale: Tetanus status does not describe the diarrhea, its cause, or its effect on nutrition and elimination.

options.text: "What color are the stools, and have you seen any blood?"
options.rationale: Color and consistency of the feces and the presence of frank blood or tarry stools are part of the bowel history.

options.text: "Would you rather use a stool softener or a fiber supplement?"
options.rationale: Choosing a treatment comes after assessment, and a stool softener does not fit watery diarrhea.

options.text: "Have you had nausea or vomiting along with the diarrhea?"
options.rationale: Nausea and vomiting are common GI symptoms included in the nutrition and current health history.

options.text: "Have you lost weight since this started, without trying?"
options.rationale: Unintentional weight gain or loss is part of the assessment of changes in bowel habits.

questions.takeaway: A focused GI history covers the pattern, color and consistency of stool, blood or tarry stools, what the patient did for the symptom and whether it worked, associated symptoms such as nausea and vomiting, and unintentional weight change.
questions.strategy: Keep each question that describes the symptom, its associated symptoms, or its effect on nutrition. Reject questions about unrelated systems or treatment choices.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stool color and blood.
Actions taken and whether they worked.
Nausea, vomiting and unintentional weight loss.
Tetanus status is unrelated; a treatment choice skips assessment.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: A patient with a history of peptic ulcer disease calls to report black, sticky stools and a racing heart. Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: Hematochezia from lower gastrointestinal bleeding
options.rationale: Hematochezia is bright red blood in the stool and usually comes from the lower bowel. Black, sticky stool is digested blood.

options.text: Steatorrhea from poor fat digestion
options.rationale: Steatorrhea is pale, greasy, floating stool. It is not black or tarry.

options.text: Melena from upper gastrointestinal bleeding
options.rationale: Black, sticky, tarry stool is melena, blood that has been digested on its way through the bowel. With a history of peptic ulcer disease and a fast heart rate, it points to upper GI bleeding.

options.text: Acholic stool from blocked bile flow
options.rationale: Acholic stool is pale or clay colored because bile pigment is missing. It is the opposite of black stool.

questions.takeaway: Melena is black, tarry stool from digested blood and points to bleeding high in the GI tract. Hematochezia is bright red blood from lower in the tract. Both are reported findings in the bowel history.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Color and texture decide. Black and sticky means the blood has been digested, so the source is high in the tract; the ulcer history and fast heart rate fit.

steps.detail: Black, sticky and shiny is tarry stool.
Melena is black and from high in the tract; hematochezia is red and from low in the tract.
Steatorrhea and acholic stool are pale.

elimination.verdict: C. Melena from upper GI bleeding.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.scenario: A patient is admitted with abdominal pain. The nurse uses the PQRST approach (precipitating or palliative factors, quality or quantity, region or radiation, severity, timing) to organize the pain assessment and records the patient's statements.
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient admitted with abdominal pain. For each patient statement, indicate the part of the pain assessment it describes.

rows.text: "It feels like a deep burning, like acid."
rows.rationale: Quality describes how the pain feels, such as burning, sharp, dull or crushing.

rows.text: "It began 3 days ago, and each episode lasts about 2 hours."
rows.rationale: Timing covers onset, duration and frequency: when the pain started and how long each episode lasts.

rows.text: "Lying still with my knees pulled up makes it ease off a little."
rows.rationale: Palliative factors are what make the pain better or worse.

rows.text: "It starts under my ribs on the right and spreads to my right shoulder blade."
rows.rationale: Region is where the pain is, and radiation is where it spreads.

rows.text: "At its worst it is 8 of 10, and it makes me stop and sit down."
rows.rationale: Severity covers the rating, how bad it is at its worst, and whether it forces the patient to sit, lie down or slow down.

rows.text: "It came on after a big fried dinner."
rows.rationale: Precipitating factors are what brings the pain on.

questions.takeaway: PQRST organizes a pain assessment: P is what brings it on or relieves it, Q is how it feels, R is where it is and where it spreads, S is how severe it is and how it limits activity, and T is onset, duration and frequency.
questions.strategy: Ask what question each statement answers: what causes or eases it, what it feels like, where it is, how bad it is, or when it happens.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The fried dinner brings it on; lying still with knees up eases it.
Burning is quality; right ribs to shoulder blade is region and radiation.
8 of 10 and having to sit is severity; began 3 days ago with 2 hour episodes is timing.

elimination.verdict: Quality, timing, palliative, region, severity, precipitating.

questions.objective: Assess abdominal pain using the PQRSTU framework and recognize associated GI symptoms

questions.stem: A patient reports yellow eyes and a dull ache in the right upper quadrant. Which questions about skin changes should the nurse ask? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Have you had itching anywhere?"
options.rationale: Itching is a skin change that can result from liver and biliary obstruction.

options.text: "Do your fingers turn white in the cold?"
options.rationale: Color change of the fingers with cold is a vascular finding, not a skin change from a GI disorder.

options.text: "Do you bruise or bleed more easily?"
options.rationale: Increased bruising or a tendency to bleed is a skin change linked to GI disorders. The liver makes clotting proteins.

options.text: "Have you noticed rashes or skin color changes?"
options.rationale: Skin discolorations, including jaundice, and rashes are skin changes the nurse asks about.

options.text: "Have you had a recent sunburn?"
options.rationale: Sunburn does not explain yellow eyes or a right upper quadrant ache.

options.text: "Do new shoes give you blisters?"
options.rationale: Friction blisters from footwear are not linked to GI or liver disorders.

questions.takeaway: Skin changes linked to GI disorders such as liver and biliary obstruction are discoloration or rashes, itching, jaundice, and increased bruising or a tendency to bleed.
questions.strategy: Yellow eyes and right upper quadrant pain point to the liver and biliary tract. Keep the questions that match the 4 skin changes linked to that system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Yellow eyes with a right upper quadrant ache points to the liver and biliary tract.
Discoloration or rash, itching, jaundice, bruising or bleeding.
Cold induced finger color change, sunburn and friction blisters from shoes do not fit.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Assess abdominal pain using the PQRSTU framework and recognize associated GI symptoms

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the laboratory results of a patient with epigastric pain that goes through to the back, rated 7 of 10, with nausea. The pain began 6 days ago and is unchanged. The serum amylase today is within the expected range, and the urine amylase is elevated. Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: The normal serum amylase rules out pancreatitis
options.rationale: This conclusion would fit the first days of symptoms, when serum amylase is elevated. Serum amylase falls within days of onset, so after 6 days a normal level does not rule out pancreatitis.

options.text: The urine amylase likely reflects a collection error
options.rationale: Normal serum and elevated urine amylase together are the expected pattern later in pancreatitis, not a sign of error.

options.text: The pattern fits pancreatitis that began days ago
options.rationale: Renal clearance of amylase increases in acute pancreatitis. Urine amylase stays elevated 5 to 7 days after onset, even after the serum level returns to normal. With symptoms for 6 days, this pattern supports pancreatitis.

options.text: The pattern shows that pancreatitis is resolving
options.rationale: This is the near miss: it reads the timing correctly but draws the wrong conclusion. A normal serum amylase on day 6 is the expected time course, not proof of recovery, and pain that is still 7 of 10 and unchanged argues against resolution.

questions.takeaway: In acute pancreatitis, serum amylase rises early and falls within days, while urine amylase stays elevated for 5 to 7 days after onset. Urine amylase matters for a patient who has had symptoms for several days.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options accept the time course: one calls it active pancreatitis, the other calls it resolving. Combine the timing (6 days, when serum amylase has already fallen) with the unchanged pain of 7 of 10 to decide.

steps.detail: Symptoms began 6 days ago.
Serum amylase falls within days; urine amylase stays high 5 to 7 days.
A normal serum level late in the illness does not rule out pancreatitis or show an error.
Pain still 7 of 10 and unchanged, so the illness is not resolving.

elimination.verdict: C. The pattern fits pancreatitis that began days ago.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A patient reports tenderness in the left lower quadrant. After inspecting the abdomen, which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Lightly palpate the left lower quadrant
options.rationale: Touch before listening stimulates the bowel and changes the sounds. A tender area is also palpated last, not first.

options.text: Percuss over the left lower quadrant
options.rationale: Percussion also comes after auscultation, and percussion of the abdomen may be left to the provider. It does not come next.

options.text: Auscultate with the bell, starting in the left lower quadrant
options.rationale: Listening is the right step, but bowel sounds are high pitched and are heard with the diaphragm, and listening starts in the right lower quadrant.

options.text: Auscultate with the diaphragm in the right lower quadrant
options.rationale: Auscultation follows inspection so touch does not change the bowel sounds. The diaphragm picks up high pitched sounds, and listening begins in the right lower quadrant. The tender quadrant is palpated last.

questions.takeaway: Assess the abdomen in this order: inspection, auscultation, then palpation. Listen with the diaphragm starting in the right lower quadrant, and palpate the tender area last, even when the patient's pain pulls you toward it.
questions.strategy: The patient's pain tempts you to go straight to the sore spot. Decide the step first, then the tool, then where to start.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: After inspection comes auscultation, which removes A and B.
The diaphragm hears high pitched bowel sounds, which removes C.
Begin in the right lower quadrant and leave the tender quadrant for last.

elimination.verdict: D. Diaphragm, right lower quadrant, before any palpation.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: The nurse is supervising a student performing an abdominal assessment. Which actions by the student require the nurse to intervene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspects all 4 quadrants before auscultating
options.rationale: Inspection comes first in the abdominal assessment.

options.text: Presses about 5 cm into each quadrant
options.rationale: Pressing more than 1 inch is deep palpation, which determines organ size and shape. Deep palpation is performed by the health care provider, not the nurse generalist.

options.text: Listens with the diaphragm from the right lower quadrant
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are heard with the diaphragm, starting in the right lower quadrant.

options.text: Percusses the right upper quadrant to size the liver
options.rationale: Percussion to determine the size of solid organs may be performed by the health care provider. The nurse generalist performs inspection, auscultation and light palpation.

options.text: Presses about 2 cm into each quadrant for tenderness
options.rationale: Light palpation, 0.5 to 1 inch deep, detects large masses and tenderness and is within the nurse generalist's role.

questions.takeaway: The nurse generalist performs inspection, auscultation and light palpation of 0.5 to 1 inch to detect large masses and tenderness. Deep palpation of more than 1 inch and percussion to size the liver and spleen are performed by the health care provider.
questions.strategy: Sort each action by depth and technique. Anything deeper than 1 inch or any percussion falls outside the nurse generalist's role.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inspection, then auscultation with the diaphragm from the right lower quadrant, is correct.
About 2 cm is light palpation; 5 cm is deep palpation.
Percussion to size the liver belongs to the provider.

elimination.verdict: B, D.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.nursesNote: 0900. Patient is 70 years old and reports nausea since last night. Abdomen rises and falls with each breath. No flatus or stool for 2 days. Umbilicus midline. Abdomen distended, with taut, glistening skin. Skin warm and dry, with no scars. Lungs clear in all lobes. Visible waves moving across the left upper quadrant toward the right. Oral temperature 37.1 °C. Loud, high pitched gurgling sounds heard in the upper quadrants. Oriented to person, place and time. Vomited 300 mL of green fluid at 0700.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission note of a patient with nausea and vomiting. Highlight the findings that require further evaluation.

segments.text: Abdomen rises and falls with each breath
segments.rationale: Rising and falling with breathing is a normal abdominal movement.

segments.text: No flatus or stool for 2 days
segments.rationale: No passage of flatus or stool suggests that bowel contents are not moving forward.

segments.text: Umbilicus midline
segments.rationale: A midline umbilicus is an expected finding.

segments.text: Abdomen distended, with taut, glistening skin
segments.rationale: Distention with taut, glistening skin is an abnormal inspection finding that suggests trapped gas or fluid.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry, with no scars
segments.rationale: Warm, dry, intact skin is an expected finding.

segments.text: Lungs clear in all lobes
segments.rationale: Clear lungs are an expected finding.

segments.text: Visible waves moving across the left upper quadrant toward the right
segments.rationale: Peristaltic movements are rarely seen. Visible waves are reported with the quadrant of origin and direction because they may indicate an intestinal obstruction.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
segments.rationale: The temperature is within the expected range.

segments.text: Loud, high pitched gurgling sounds heard in the upper quadrants
segments.rationale: Loud, high pitched gurgling sounds (borborygmus) can be heard above a complete intestinal obstruction.

segments.text: Oriented to person, place and time
segments.rationale: Orientation is an expected finding.

segments.text: Vomited 300 mL of green fluid at 0700
segments.rationale: Vomiting with nausea and no stool or flatus fits a bowel that is not moving contents forward.

questions.takeaway: Visible peristaltic waves, distention with taut glistening skin, loud high pitched bowel sounds above a blockage, vomiting and no flatus or stool together point to a possible intestinal obstruction and need further evaluation.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read each phrase as normal or abnormal for the abdomen. Then check whether the abnormal ones form one picture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distention with taut skin and visible peristaltic waves.
Loud, high pitched gurgling in the upper quadrants.
No flatus or stool for 2 days and green vomit.
Breathing movement, midline umbilicus, warm dry skin, normal temperature and orientation.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: The nurse is inspecting the abdomen of a patient with hypertension who reports a vague ache in the lower back, rated 3 of 10. The nurse observes a bulging mass just above the umbilicus that pulsates with each heartbeat. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Auscultate over the mass for a bruit
options.rationale: Listening for a bruit seems to gather useful data, and bruits over the aorta are part of the assessment. But the nurse does not auscultate or palpate a bulging, pulsating mass, which may be an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

options.text: Continue with auscultation and light palpation
options.rationale: This is the usual sequence after inspection. A bulging mass that pulses changes the plan, because routine auscultation and palpation would place a stethoscope and hands over it.

options.text: Avoid touching the mass and notify the provider
options.rationale: A bulging, pulsating mass may be an abdominal aortic aneurysm, a life threatening problem. The nurse does not touch the area with hands or a stethoscope and notifies the health care provider immediately.

options.text: Document the finding as a normal aortic pulsation
options.rationale: This is the near miss. A faint aortic pulsation can be a normal finding in some patients, but a bulging mass that pulses is not that finding. Documenting it as normal delays care for a possible aneurysm.

questions.takeaway: A bulging, pulsating abdominal mass may be an abdominal aortic aneurysm. The nurse does not auscultate, palpate or percuss it and notifies the health care provider immediately.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options treat the pulsation as normal and one gathers more data. The deciding cue is the word bulging: a visible pulsation can be normal, but a bulging, pulsating mass is a possible aneurysm that is not touched or auscultated.

steps.detail: The mass bulges and pulses with each heartbeat.
A faint pulsation can be normal; a bulging mass is not.
A possible abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Auscultating, palpating or continuing the routine places a stethoscope or hands on the mass.

elimination.verdict: C. Avoid touching the mass and notify the provider.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: Two days after colon surgery, a patient has absent bowel sounds, a rigid abdomen, worsening pain and a new fever. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Peritonitis
options.rationale: Absent bowel sounds occur with peritonitis. A new fever, worsening pain and a rigid abdomen point to inflammation of the peritoneum, not just a slowed bowel.

options.text: Paralytic ileus
options.rationale: Absent bowel sounds fit paralytic ileus, but ileus does not explain a new fever, a rigid abdomen and worsening pain.

options.text: Gastroenteritis
options.rationale: Gastroenteritis increases motility and produces loud, gurgling bowel sounds. This patient has no bowel sounds.

options.text: Bowel obstruction
options.rationale: Loud, high pitched sounds are heard above a complete obstruction. This patient has no bowel sounds in any quadrant.

questions.takeaway: Bowel sounds are diminished or absent after abdominal surgery and with paralytic ileus or peritonitis. A new fever, worsening pain and a rigid abdomen separate peritonitis from an ileus.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Absent bowel sounds fit two conditions here. The new fever and rigid abdomen are what separate inflammation from a slowed bowel.

steps.detail: Absent sounds rule out gastroenteritis and the loud sounds of obstruction.
Ileus and peritonitis both have absent sounds.
A new fever, worsening pain and a rigid abdomen point to peritonitis.

elimination.verdict: A. Peritonitis.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient admitted with right lower quadrant pain, rated 8 of 10, that began around the umbilicus 12 hours ago. The provider's admission note states that appendicitis is suspected and a CT scan is pending. The nurse has inspected and auscultated the abdomen. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Lightly palpate the right lower quadrant to find the tender point
options.rationale: Light palpation is within the nurse's role, but a painful area is assessed last, never first. When appendicitis is suspected, palpation is not done at all.

options.text: Omit palpation and document the findings so far
options.rationale: Palpation is not done when appendicitis is suspected. The nurse has completed the parts of the assessment that are safe for this patient and records them.

options.text: Lightly palpate all quadrants, leaving the right lower quadrant last
options.rationale: This is the near miss: it follows the general rule of palpating a painful area last, and light palpation is within the nurse's role. The suspected appendicitis overrides the rule, because palpation is not done at all.

options.text: Apply a warm pack to the right lower quadrant for comfort
options.rationale: Comfort matters with pain rated 8 of 10, but heat is avoided when appendicitis is suspected because it can speed inflammation toward rupture. A comfort measure also does not replace a safe assessment.

questions.takeaway: The nurse generalist inspects, auscultates and lightly palpates the abdomen, assessing painful areas last. If appendicitis or an abdominal aneurysm is suspected, palpation is not done, and heat is not applied to a possibly inflamed appendix.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options are light palpation done the way that would be correct for most patients, and one is a comfort measure for severe pain. The deciding cue is the documented suspicion of appendicitis: it removes palpation from the assessment and rules out heat to the area.

steps.detail: Appendicitis is suspected.
Palpation is not done when appendicitis is suspected.
Palpating the painful quadrant last is still palpation, and heat is avoided with suspected appendicitis.

elimination.verdict: B. Omit palpation and document the findings so far.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: Before an abdominal CT scan with IV contrast, which patient finding should the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: Ate a light breakfast 6 hours ago
options.rationale: The patient must be NPO for at least 4 hours before a contrast CT. A light breakfast 6 hours ago meets that requirement.

options.text: Has a peripheral IV in place
options.rationale: IV access is required for the contrast injection, so this is expected preparation.

options.text: Had hives and wheezing with contrast before
options.rationale: The nurse asks about past contrast reactions and severe allergies before a contrast CT. Hives and wheezing are an allergic reaction, and the team needs this before contrast is given again.

options.text: Had a metallic taste with contrast in the past
options.rationale: A warm, flushed feeling or a metallic taste during the injection is expected. The nurse explains it, but it is not a reaction.

questions.takeaway: Before an abdominal CT with contrast, the nurse asks about past contrast reactions and severe allergies, keeps the patient NPO for at least 4 hours, establishes IV access, and explains that a warm, flushed feeling or metallic taste is expected.
questions.strategy: Two options describe past contrast experiences. Separate an expected sensation from a reaction that involves the skin and airway.

steps.detail: 6 hours is more than the 4 required.
An IV is required, so it is expected.
A metallic taste is expected; hives and wheezing are a reaction.

elimination.verdict: C. Hives and wheezing after contrast.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A patient at average risk for colorectal cancer has a negative stool DNA home test. Which patient statement indicates understanding of the screening plan?

options.text: "I will repeat the kit in 1 year."
options.rationale: Yearly screening is the interval for the fecal immunochemical test and the guaiac based fecal occult blood test, not the stool DNA test.

options.text: "I will repeat the kit in 3 years."
options.rationale: The multitargeted stool DNA test is performed every 3 years.

options.text: "I will not need more screening."
options.rationale: Screening for colorectal cancer continues at regular intervals. A single negative result does not end screening.

options.text: "I will test my stool for parasites next year."
options.rationale: A stool test for ova and parasites looks for parasitic infection. It does not screen for colorectal cancer.

questions.takeaway: Stool screening for colorectal cancer is an annual fecal immunochemical test, an annual guaiac based fecal occult blood test, or a multitargeted stool DNA home test every 3 years.
questions.strategy: Two options differ only in the interval. Match the interval to the test the patient used.

steps.detail: Multitargeted stool DNA.
Every 3 years.
Yearly is for the other stool tests; parasite testing is not cancer screening.

elimination.verdict: B. Repeat in 3 years.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.scenario: A patient had an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with removal of a gallstone at 0900. The gag reflex returned at 1000. At 1500 the patient reports severe pain in the upper abdomen that goes through to the back, 8 of 10, and has vomited twice. Blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg, was 124/78 mm Hg at 1000. Heart rate 112 beats per minute. Oral temperature 37.9 °C. Serum lipase 1250 units/L.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with new severe abdominal pain 6 hours after an endoscopic procedure. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Withhold oral food and fluids
options.rationale: Severe pain with vomiting after ERCP suggests a complication, so oral intake is withheld.

options.text: Offer clear liquids by mouth
options.rationale: Oral intake is withheld while a post procedure complication with vomiting is being evaluated.

options.text: Encourage the patient to walk in the hall
options.rationale: Gas pain is colicky, not severe pain through to the back with vomiting, a rising heart rate and a high lipase.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider
options.rationale: Pancreatitis is a severe post ERCP complication that needs prompt treatment.

options.text: Prepare the patient for discharge as planned
options.rationale: Severe pain, vomiting and falling blood pressure are not findings that allow discharge.

options.text: Expected gas pain from air instilled during the test
options.rationale: Gas pain is colicky and mild. It does not raise the lipase or the heart rate.

options.text: Aspiration from an absent gag reflex
options.rationale: The gag reflex returned at 1000, and the findings are abdominal, not respiratory.

options.text: Acute pancreatitis
options.rationale: Severe upper abdominal pain through to the back, vomiting and an elevated lipase after ERCP point to pancreatitis, the complication the nurse observes for.

options.text: Respiratory depression from sedation
options.rationale: The findings are severe pain and vomiting 6 hours after the test, not slowed breathing.

options.text: Return of the gag reflex
options.rationale: The gag reflex returned at 1000.

options.text: Serum amylase and lipase levels
options.rationale: Amylase and lipase elevate in acute pancreatitis and are trended.

options.text: Passage of a capsule in the stool
options.rationale: Capsule passage applies to small bowel capsule endoscopy, not ERCP.

options.text: Abdominal pain severity and location
options.rationale: Severe abdominal pain is the key sign of pancreatitis after ERCP and is reassessed.

questions.takeaway: After ERCP, the nurse observes for pancreatitis, shown by severe abdominal pain, and monitors for bleeding, sedation effects and respiratory depression. Elevated amylase and lipase support pancreatitis.
questions.strategy: Start with the condition: severe pain through to the back, vomiting and a high lipase after ERCP. Then choose actions and parameters that fit that condition.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Severe pain to the back, vomiting and lipase 1250 units/L point to pancreatitis.
Withhold oral intake and report the findings.
Amylase and lipase levels and abdominal pain.

elimination.verdict: Actions: withhold oral intake, report the findings. Condition: acute pancreatitis. Parameters: amylase and lipase, abdominal pain.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: After an EGD with moderate sedation, a patient rouses only to a loud voice and has slow, shallow breathing. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the gag reflex and offer sips of water
options.rationale: Fluids are withheld until the gag reflex returns and the patient is alert. A drowsy patient with slow, shallow breathing is at risk for aspiration and needs breathing support first.

options.text: Lower the side rails and turn the patient
options.rationale: Side rails stay raised while sedation wears off. Lowering them adds fall risk without improving breathing.

options.text: Document vital signs and recheck in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Slow, shallow breathing after sedation needs action now, not a recheck in 30 minutes.

options.text: Rouse the patient and coach deep breaths
options.rationale: Sedation drugs depress the rate and depth of breathing. When the respiratory rate falls below 10 breaths per minute, the nurse stimulates the patient to encourage deeper, faster breathing. This patient opens the eyes to a loud voice, so a verbal and light touch stimulus is enough to rouse the patient and coach deep breaths.

questions.takeaway: After endoscopy with moderate sedation, the nurse monitors respiratory rate and depth, oxygen saturation and capnography. A respiratory rate below 10 breaths per minute calls for a stimulus that rouses the patient, matched to how the patient responds, to promote deeper, faster breaths.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Apply the ABCs. Breathing is failing, so the first action supports breathing.

steps.detail: Slow, shallow breathing in a patient who rouses only to a loud voice.
The patient rouses to voice, so call the name, touch the shoulder and coach deep breaths.
Fluids, lowered rails and a delayed recheck do not support breathing.

elimination.verdict: D. Rouse the patient and coach deep breaths.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient with type 2 diabetes who is scheduled for an outpatient colonoscopy tomorrow. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: "You may drive yourself home after the test once you feel awake."
options.rationale: Moderate sedation impairs judgment and reaction time. Another person drives the patient home, and the patient does not drive for the rest of the day.

options.text: "Drink clear liquids today, nothing red, orange or purple."
options.rationale: A clear liquid diet the day before helps empty the colon. Red, orange and purple drinks and gelatin can look like blood or residue in the colon.

options.text: "Ask your provider about your diabetes medicine for tomorrow."
options.rationale: The patient is NPO before the test, so the primary provider decides how to adjust diabetes medication that day.

options.text: "Eat a full meal tonight before the prep."
options.rationale: A full meal leaves residue in the colon. Poor bowel preparation decreases visualization and can lead to an unsuccessful colonoscopy.

options.text: "Drink extra fluids after the test."
options.rationale: The bowel prep causes watery diarrhea and fluid loss, so the nurse encourages fluid intake to rehydrate after the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Colonoscopy teaching covers the bowel prep and a clear liquid diet the day before without red, orange or purple drinks, a plan for diabetes medication while NPO, a driver home because of sedation, and fluids afterward to rehydrate.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check each instruction against two goals: a clean colon for viewing and safety around sedation and fluid loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear liquids without red, orange or purple; no full meal.
A driver home; a plan for diabetes medicine while NPO.
Fluids after the test.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who had a colonoscopy with removal of 2 polyps at 1000. At 1230 the patient is awake and alert, reports cramping rated 3 of 10, and has passed flatus. The first stool after the procedure has a small streak of red blood. Blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, was 130/80 mm Hg at 1030. Heart rate 84/min, was 80/min at 1030. Which interpretation and action are appropriate?

options.text: Expected findings; continue monitoring and offer fluids
options.rationale: A small amount of blood in the first stool is expected after polyp removal. Cramping and flatus are expected for several hours, and fluids are permitted once flatus shows that peristalsis has returned. Blood pressure and heart rate are near their 1030 values.

options.text: Possible hemorrhage; report the bleeding to the provider now
options.rationale: Any blood after a colonoscopy seems worth reporting, and excessive bleeding is reported immediately. A small streak after polyp removal, with blood pressure and heart rate near baseline, is not excessive.

options.text: Possible perforation; keep the patient nothing by mouth
options.rationale: Perforation causes severe pain and guarding. Cramping of 3 of 10 with flatus is expected.

options.text: Expected findings; withhold fluids until the cramping stops
options.rationale: This is the near miss: the findings are expected, but fluids are permitted once the patient passes flatus. Cramping is expected for several hours and is not a reason to withhold fluids.

questions.takeaway: After colonoscopy, fullness, cramping and flatus are expected for several hours, and a small amount of blood in the first stool is expected if a polyp was removed or a biopsy taken. Excessive bleeding, severe pain or a rapid drop in blood pressure is reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options call the findings expected, and one calls the blood a hemorrhage. Decide twice: the removal of 2 polyps with stable vital signs makes the streak expected, and the passage of flatus is what allows fluids.

steps.detail: 2 polyps were removed.
A small streak, with blood pressure and heart rate near the 1030 values.
Cramping 3 of 10 with flatus is expected, not perforation.
Flatus shows peristalsis has returned, so fluids are permitted even while cramping continues.

elimination.verdict: A. Expected findings; continue monitoring and offer fluids.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: An older adult is prescribed a new gastrointestinal medication at the usual adult dose. Which action should the nurse include in the plan of care?

options.text: Ask the provider to increase the dose
options.rationale: A higher than usual dose is never the starting point in an older adult. Age related changes in the liver make toxic levels more likely, not less.

options.text: Monitor closely for adverse effects
options.rationale: Fewer and smaller hepatic cells lower protein synthesis and enzyme activity, which depresses drug metabolism. Drugs can accumulate to toxic levels even at a usual dose, so the nurse monitors closely.

options.text: Ask the provider to reduce the dose by half
options.rationale: Older adults do not automatically need a lower dose. The safe plan is close monitoring at the prescribed dose.

options.text: Hold the dose if the patient reports nausea
options.rationale: Nausea is not an expected effect of a correctly dosed medication in an older adult. New nausea after a medication starts is a possible sign of toxicity to report, not a routine reason to hold.

questions.takeaway: A decrease in the number and size of hepatic cells lowers liver mass, protein synthesis and enzyme activity. Drug metabolism slows, so an older adult can reach toxic drug levels at a usual dose and needs close monitoring.
questions.strategy: Link age to fewer and smaller liver cells, then ask what slower drug metabolism means for a usual dose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Aging brings fewer and smaller liver cells with less protein synthesis and enzyme activity.
Slower metabolism lets drugs build up toward toxic levels.
Raising the dose adds risk, and halving it without cause is an extreme.
Close monitoring for adverse effects at the prescribed dose.

elimination.verdict: B. Watch closely for adverse effects.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: An older adult who has lost weight says, "I just do not feel hungry." Stools and blood counts are normal. Which age related change should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Atrophy of the gastric mucosa
options.rationale: Gastric mucosal atrophy lowers iron and vitamin B12 absorption and can lead to anemia. Normal blood counts do not suggest that picture, and it does not explain the loss of appetite.

options.text: Slowed peristalsis in the colon
options.rationale: Slower peristalsis lowers the sensation to defecate and leads to constipation. The patient's stools are normal.

options.text: Dilation of the pancreatic ducts
options.rationale: Lower lipase causes steatorrhea and weight loss from poorly absorbed fat. The patient's stools are normal.

options.text: Disrupted gut microbial balance
options.rationale: Disrupted intestinal microbial balance in older adults contributes to anorexia and the undernutrition that follows. Poor appetite with weight loss and no other GI finding fits this change.

questions.takeaway: Disruption of microbial balance in the aging gut contributes to anorexia and then undernutrition. Rule out the other changes by their own signs: anemia, constipation and steatorrhea.
questions.strategy: Each age related change has its own signature. Match the one finding left, poor appetite, to the change that explains it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Normal blood counts do not suggest poor iron or vitamin B12 absorption.
Normal stools argue against slowed peristalsis.
Normal stools argue against low lipase.
Disrupted microbial balance explains anorexia and the weight loss.

elimination.verdict: D. Disruption of the microbial balance in the gut.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: A patient reports bloating and loose stools after meals. Which nutrition and family history questions should the nurse ask? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Do symptoms follow milk, cheese or ice cream?"
options.rationale: Lactose intolerance is part of the nutrition history. Bloating, gas and loose stools after dairy point toward it.

options.text: "Has anyone in your family had colon cancer or polyps?"
options.rationale: Family history of GI disorders matters because some GI problems carry a genetic predisposition.

options.text: "Would you like a dietitian referral today?"
options.rationale: A referral may come later, but it is an intervention, not a history question. The nurse finishes collecting data first.

options.text: "How much alcohol or caffeine do you drink weekly?"
options.rationale: Alcohol and caffeine intake belong in the nutrition history and can contribute to GI symptoms.

options.text: "Have you had an influenza vaccine this season?"
options.rationale: Immunization status is general health data, not part of a focused GI nutrition and family history.

options.text: "Has food tasted different, or is swallowing hard?"
options.rationale: Changes in taste and dysphagia are listed nutrition history items and may reveal another GI problem.

questions.takeaway: A focused GI history covers the nutrition history (special diets, food allergies, lactose intolerance, anorexia, taste change, dysphagia, pain with eating, nausea, dyspepsia, weight loss, alcohol and caffeine) and family history with genetic risk.
questions.strategy: Sort each option into history data or something else. Keep questions that gather nutrition or family data; drop interventions and unrelated health data.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dairy, alcohol and caffeine, taste and swallowing.
Colon cancer, polyps and bowel disorders in relatives.
A referral is a next step, not data collection.
Vaccination status is not part of this focused history.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: A patient with fatigue has a falling hemoglobin. Which patient statement requires further assessment by the nurse?

options.text: "I take ibuprofen several times a day for arthritis."
options.rationale: Regular use of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen predisposes the patient to peptic ulcer disease and GI bleeding. With a falling hemoglobin, this is the statement to explore: dose, duration, and any black or bloody stools.

options.text: "My dentures still fit well after 10 years of wearing them."
options.rationale: Well fitting dentures support chewing and nutrition. Nothing here needs follow up.

options.text: "I eat bran cereal to stay regular."
options.rationale: Fiber supports regular bowel movements. This is a healthy habit, not a concern.

options.text: "I avoid hot peppers because I dislike them."
options.rationale: Avoiding spicy food is a preference. It does not suggest a GI problem.

questions.takeaway: Regular NSAID use, such as ibuprofen, predisposes patients to peptic ulcer disease and GI bleeding. A medication history is part of a focused GI history, and a falling hemoglobin makes it urgent.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that could explain the abnormal data in the stem. The others describe healthy habits or preferences.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A falling hemoglobin with fatigue.
Frequent ibuprofen can cause ulcers and GI bleeding.
Fitting dentures, fiber and a taste preference are not concerns.

elimination.verdict: A. The ibuprofen statement.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.scenario: The nurse in a gastrointestinal clinic reviews the bowel histories that patients gave during intake today.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing bowel histories in a gastrointestinal clinic. For each stool description, indicate the stool finding it describes.

rows.text: "My stools have been pale, almost like clay, for a week, and my urine is dark."
rows.rationale: Acholic stool is pale or clay colored because bile is not reaching the bowel. Dark urine often comes with it.

rows.text: "I pass small, hard, separate lumps every 4 days, and I have to strain."
rows.rationale: Small, hard, separate lumps passed with straining are pebble stools, a sign of constipation.

rows.text: "There is bright red blood on the outside of my stool."
rows.rationale: Bright red blood in or on the stool is hematochezia and points to bleeding low in the GI tract.

rows.text: "My stools are bulky and greasy, they float, and they are hard to flush."
rows.rationale: Bulky, greasy, floating stools are steatorrhea, caused by poor fat digestion or absorption.

rows.text: "My stools look gray, my skin itches, and my eyes have turned yellow."
rows.rationale: Gray stool with itching and jaundice suggests that bile is blocked from the bowel, producing acholic stool.

rows.text: "My stools are black and sticky, like tar, with a very strong odor."
rows.rationale: Black, tarry stool is melena, from digested blood high in the GI tract.

questions.takeaway: Name the stool: acholic (pale, clay colored, no bile), pebble (small hard lumps, constipation), hematochezia (bright red blood, lower GI), melena (black and tarry, upper GI), steatorrhea (greasy, floating, fat). Each name points to a different problem to explore.
questions.strategy: Use color first, then consistency. Pale or gray means bile, red means low bleeding, black means high bleeding, greasy means fat, and hard lumps mean constipation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clay and gray are acholic; bright red is hematochezia; black and tarry is melena.
Greasy and floating is steatorrhea; small hard lumps are pebble stool.
Dark urine, itching and yellow eyes support blocked bile.

elimination.verdict: Acholic, pebble, hematochezia, steatorrhea, acholic, melena.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: A patient with diarrhea since a recent move looks away and asks quietly, "Do we have to talk about this?" Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Skip to the physical examination and return to it later
options.rationale: Skipping the history delays data the nurse needs now. Avoiding the topic also tells the patient the subject is too awkward to discuss.

options.text: Close the door, acknowledge it, and ask about stress
options.rationale: Elimination topics are often embarrassing, so the nurse provides privacy and acknowledges the feeling. Recent stress is linked to the onset or flare of some GI disorders, so asking about the recent move is relevant data.

options.text: Ask a family member about the bowel pattern
options.rationale: Asking a family member breaks confidentiality and bypasses the patient, who is able to answer and is the primary source.

options.text: Reassure the patient that stress diarrhea will pass
options.rationale: This reassurance assumes a cause before assessment is complete and dismisses ongoing diarrhea, which needs evaluation.

questions.takeaway: GI and elimination topics can feel embarrassing. Provide privacy, acknowledge the feeling, ask about recent stressful events, and refer for ongoing support when needed.
questions.strategy: Choose the option that keeps the patient as the source, protects privacy and still gathers the data. Eliminate options that avoid, bypass or dismiss.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Looking away and a quiet question show embarrassment.
A recent move is a stressful event worth exploring.
Postponing, asking family and premature reassurance all fail the patient.
Privacy, acknowledgment and a stress question.

elimination.verdict: B. Close the door, acknowledge, ask about stress.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: Before an abdominal assessment, a patient lying with the legs straight says the bladder feels full. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Have the patient void, then lie supine with knees bent
options.rationale: Emptying the bladder and lying supine with knees bent and arms at the sides relaxes the abdominal muscles. A full bladder and tensed muscles distort the findings.

options.text: Begin inspection, then have the patient void before listening
options.rationale: Stopping halfway interrupts the sequence. Preparation, including voiding, comes before inspection begins.

options.text: Turn the patient to the side with knees drawn up
options.rationale: The side lying position is used for some procedures, such as colonoscopy. The abdomen is assessed with the patient supine.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees
options.rationale: Sitting upright folds and tenses the abdomen. The supine position with knees bent relaxes it.

questions.takeaway: Prepare for abdominal assessment by having the patient empty the bladder and lie supine with knees bent and arms at the sides to keep the abdominal muscles relaxed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Preparation comes before the first step of the assessment. Pick the option that fixes both problems in the stem: the full bladder and the tensed position.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A full bladder and straight legs that tense the abdomen.
Supine, knees bent, arms at the sides.
Voiding happens before inspection, not midway.

elimination.verdict: A. Empty the bladder, then supine with knees bent.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing bowel sound findings for four patients. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: After abdominal surgery yesterday: hypoactive sounds, soft abdomen
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are often diminished after surgery while peristalsis returns. With a soft abdomen, this is expected.

options.text: Watery diarrhea: loud, frequent, high pitched gurgling
options.rationale: Loud, frequent gurgling is hyperactive, called borborygmus. It matches a bowel moving fast enough to cause watery stools, so it is expected.

options.text: Knee replacement: gurgling in all 4 quadrants, soft abdomen
options.rationale: Gurgling in each quadrant with a soft, flat abdomen is a normal finding that needs no follow up.

options.text: Diarrhea: no bowel sounds, rigid abdomen, severe pain
options.rationale: Diarrhea should give active or hyperactive sounds. Absent sounds with a rigid abdomen and severe pain point to peritonitis or a paralytic ileus, so this patient needs follow up now.

questions.takeaway: Grade bowel sounds as hypoactive, normal or hyperactive, then ask whether the grade fits the patient. Hyperactive sounds fit diarrhea and quiet sounds fit the first day after surgery; absent sounds with a rigid, painful abdomen fit peritonitis or ileus and need follow up.
questions.strategy: Grade each patient's sounds, then match the grade to that patient's situation. The finding that needs follow up is the one where the grade does not fit the story.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A hypoactive, B hyperactive, C normal, D absent.
Quiet after surgery and loud with diarrhea are both expected; C is normal.
Diarrhea with absent sounds, a rigid abdomen and severe pain does not fit.

elimination.verdict: D. Absent sounds with a rigid, painful abdomen need follow up.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: Percussion of a bloated abdomen finds high pitched, musical notes throughout and liver dullness within the rib margin. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?

options.text: Fluid is filling the abdominal cavity
options.rationale: Fluid gives a dull note. Loud, high pitched musical notes are tympany from air.

options.text: The liver extends below the rib margin
options.rationale: A dull note over the liver is expected. The note stays within the rib margin, so it does not suggest an enlarged liver.

options.text: Air fills the bowel; liver size is normal
options.rationale: Tympany is the high pitched, musical sound of an air filled intestine and fits the bloating. Dullness over a normal sized liver is expected.

options.text: A solid mass is present in the lower abdomen
options.rationale: Solid tissue such as an organ or mass gives a dull, thudlike note, not tympany.

questions.takeaway: Percussion, often done by the health care provider, sizes solid organs. Tympany is a high pitched, air filled sound; dullness is a thudlike sound over a solid organ such as the liver.
questions.strategy: Match each note to what lies beneath: air sounds musical and high pitched, solid tissue and fluid sound dull. Then ask whether the dull area is the expected size.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Musical and high pitched is tympany; thudlike is dullness.
Air in a distended bowel, which fits the bloating.
Dullness confined within the rib margin is an expected liver size.

elimination.verdict: C. Air in the bowel, expected liver dullness.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: One day after abdominal surgery, a patient has hypoactive bowel sounds. Which finding best indicates that peristalsis is returning?

options.text: Reports feeling hungry and asks for breakfast
options.rationale: Hunger is welcome, but it does not show that the bowel is moving contents forward.

options.text: One bowel sound heard after 2 minutes
options.rationale: A single faint sound still fits hypoactive bowel sounds and does not confirm that contents are moving.

options.text: Reports passing flatus twice this morning
options.rationale: Passing flatus is a favorable indicator that peristalsis is returning after surgery. Gas is moving through the whole bowel.

options.text: Soft abdomen with no nausea this morning
options.rationale: A soft abdomen without nausea is reassuring, but neither shows forward movement of bowel contents.

questions.takeaway: After abdominal surgery, bowel sounds are diminished or absent. The patient's report of passing flatus is a favorable indicator that peristalsis is returning, so ask about it first.
questions.strategy: Choose the finding that proves contents are moving all the way through, not one that is only reassuring.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypoactive bowel sounds are expected after surgery.
Hunger, one faint sound and a soft abdomen do not show movement through the bowel.
Flatus has traveled the length of the bowel.

elimination.verdict: C. Passing flatus.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis who bruises easily is scheduled for an EGD with possible biopsy. Which finding should the nurse report before the procedure?

options.text: Prothrombin time 19 seconds
options.rationale: A prolonged prothrombin time means blood takes longer to clot, which fits the easy bruising. Bleeding is a known challenge of EGD, especially with a biopsy, so this is reported before the procedure.

options.text: Potassium 4.1 mEq/L
options.rationale: This potassium value is within the expected range and does not change the plan.

options.text: Nothing by mouth since midnight
options.rationale: Being NPO for more than 6 to 8 hours is the expected preparation for EGD.

options.text: Blood glucose 104 mg/dL
options.rationale: A glucose of 104 mg/dL after fasting since midnight does not threaten the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Prothrombin time is a serum test of clotting. Before EGD, bleeding risk matters: bleeding is a challenge of the procedure, and anticoagulants are avoided. Increased bruising or a tendency to bleed is a skin change linked to GI disorders such as liver disease, where the liver makes fewer clotting proteins.
questions.strategy: Ask which value changes safety for the planned procedure. A biopsy cuts tissue, so the clotting value matters most.

steps.detail: Easy bruising shows a tendency to bleed.
A prothrombin time of 19 seconds is prolonged.
Potassium, glucose and NPO status are expected for this procedure.

elimination.verdict: A. Prothrombin time 19 seconds.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with cirrhosis who has new confusion and yellow sclera. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient with cirrhosis is newly confused and slow to answer questions, and the sclera are yellow. The nurse expects the confusion to be linked to an elevated serum [[1]].

The nurse expects the yellow sclera to be linked to an elevated serum [[2]].

Today the AST and ALT are both several times higher than at the last visit. The nurse interprets this as [[3]].

options.text: ammonia
options.rationale: The liver converts ammonia to urea. Hepatocellular injury, such as cirrhosis, raises serum ammonia, which is linked to hepatic encephalopathy and confusion.

options.text: amylase
options.rationale: Amylase rises with acute pancreatitis. It does not explain confusion in liver disease.

options.text: carcinoembryonic antigen
options.rationale: This oncofetal antigen monitors GI cancer therapy and recurrence. It does not cause confusion.

options.text: lipase
options.rationale: Lipase rises with pancreatitis, not with jaundice from liver disease.

options.text: bilirubin
options.rationale: Bilirubin is the main pigment in bile. Impaired excretion by the liver raises serum bilirubin and produces jaundice.

options.text: potassium
options.rationale: Potassium shifts with vomiting and diarrhea. It does not cause yellow sclera.

options.text: ongoing injury to liver cells
options.rationale: AST and ALT are liver enzymes. Injured liver cells release them into the blood, so a sharp rise points to ongoing liver cell injury, highest with necrosis such as hepatitis and cirrhosis.

options.text: recovery of liver function
options.rationale: Rising AST and ALT reflect enzymes leaking from damaged cells, not a healing liver. Recovery would bring the levels down.

options.text: a problem with the pancreas
options.rationale: AST and ALT are liver enzymes. Amylase and lipase reflect the pancreas.

questions.takeaway: Liver tests: ammonia rises with hepatocellular injury and is linked to confusion, bilirubin rises with impaired excretion and causes jaundice, and AST and ALT rise when injured liver cells release them.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each finding to the substance the failing liver can no longer process: ammonia for the brain, bilirubin for the color, enzymes for the damaged cells.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Confusion in cirrhosis points to ammonia that the liver cannot convert to urea.
Yellow sclera point to bilirubin that the liver cannot excrete.
A sharp rise in AST and ALT means liver cells are still being injured and releasing enzymes.

elimination.verdict: Ammonia; bilirubin; ongoing injury to liver cells.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A patient with 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea has a low potassium level and an irregular pulse. Which plan of care should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Restrict oral and IV fluids until vomiting stops
options.rationale: Vomiting and diarrhea cause fluid loss, not overload. Restricting fluid worsens the deficit.

options.text: Replace potassium and fluids as prescribed
options.rationale: Excessive vomiting or diarrhea depletes sodium and potassium and requires replacement. Rechecking the results evaluates the response.

options.text: Give a potassium bolus by IV push
options.rationale: Potassium is never given by IV push; a rapid rise can cause a fatal dysrhythmia. Replacement is diluted and given slowly as prescribed.

options.text: Offer high fiber foods with each meal
options.rationale: Fiber does not correct a low potassium level, and food is not the first step with active vomiting.

questions.takeaway: Electrolytes are altered in GI dysfunction; excessive vomiting or diarrhea causes sodium and potassium depletion that requires replacement. A high hemoglobin and hematocrit with fluid loss reflect hemoconcentration.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Read the losses and the low potassium as one picture of fluid and electrolyte loss, then pick the safe replacement plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low potassium follows vomiting and diarrhea, and the irregular pulse shows its effect on the heart.
Vomiting and diarrhea cause fluid loss, so restricting fluid worsens it.
Potassium is never given by IV push.
Prescribed replacement with a recheck.

elimination.verdict: B. Replace potassium and fluids, recheck.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A patient treated for colon cancer has a rising carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level. Which patient statement indicates understanding of the purpose of the test?

options.text: "Since this test is followed, I can stop colonoscopies."
options.rationale: CEA does not replace other monitoring. A blood value alone is not enough, so colonoscopy continues.
