options.text: "This test is how my cancer was first found."
options.rationale: CEA and CA 19 9 are used to monitor therapy and recurrence, not to make the first diagnosis.

options.text: "A rising level proves my cancer is back."
options.rationale: These antigens can also rise in benign GI conditions, so a rising level calls for further testing rather than proving recurrence.

options.text: "This test tracks my treatment and any recurrence."
options.rationale: Oncofetal antigens such as CEA and CA 19 9 monitor the efficacy of cancer therapy and assess for recurrence of GI cancer.

questions.takeaway: Oncofetal antigens (CA 19 9 and CEA) monitor how well GI cancer therapy is working and screen for recurrence. They can rise in benign GI conditions, so a rise leads to more testing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Find the statement that matches the purpose of the test without overstating it. Words like proves and stop are the warning signs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Monitor therapy and recurrence.
A rise does not prove recurrence; benign conditions can raise it.
It is not the initial diagnostic test and does not replace colonoscopy.

elimination.verdict: D. Tracks treatment and possible recurrence.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: After drinking stream water while camping and finishing an antibiotic, a patient has greasy, floating diarrhea. Which stool tests should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ova and parasites
options.rationale: Drinking untreated water followed by diarrhea suggests a parasitic infection. A stool sample for ova and parasites aids the diagnosis.

options.text: Fecal fats
options.rationale: Greasy, floating stools are steatorrhea. Fecal fat testing is done when steatorrhea or malabsorption is suspected.

options.text: Multitargeted stool DNA kit
options.rationale: This home kit screens average risk adults for colorectal cancer every 3 years. It is not used to diagnose acute diarrhea.

options.text: Annual fecal immunochemical test
options.rationale: The FIT screens for hidden blood as a colorectal cancer screening option. It does not identify the cause of acute diarrhea.

options.text: Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile)
options.rationale: Recent antibiotic therapy is a risk factor for Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile), a common infectious cause of diarrhea. The stool is tested for it.

questions.takeaway: Stool studies for diarrhea include ova and parasites for parasitic infection, fecal fats for steatorrhea or malabsorption, and C. difficile after antibiotic therapy. FIT, gFOBT and stool DNA kits are screening tests for colorectal cancer.
questions.strategy: Tie each test to a cue in the stem. Screening tests are for people without symptoms, not for working up acute diarrhea.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Untreated stream water points to ova and parasites.
Greasy, floating stools point to fecal fats.
A recent antibiotic points to C. difficile.
FIT and stool DNA screen for colorectal cancer.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: A patient with an insulin pump is scheduled for an abdominal radiograph and then an abdominal MRI. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Have the patient remove jewelry and belts for the radiograph
options.rationale: No preparation is needed for an abdominal radiograph except a hospital gown and removal of jewelry and belts that can interfere with the film.

options.text: Keep the patient NPO from midnight for the radiograph
options.rationale: An abdominal radiograph needs no preparation, so fasting is not required for it.

options.text: Report the insulin pump to the MRI team
options.rationale: MRI uses powerful magnets. The nurse screens for metal implants and devices such as insulin pumps, pacemakers and aneurysm clips.

options.text: Explain that the MRI is long and requires lying still
options.rationale: The MRI takes longer than a CT, and the patient must lie still for clear images.

options.text: Explain that the MRI uses a small dose of radiation
options.rationale: MRI uses magnets and gives no radiation exposure.

options.text: Explain that the radiograph is taken sitting upright
options.rationale: The abdominal radiograph is taken with the patient lying supine.

questions.takeaway: Abdominal radiograph: no preparation, hospital gown, remove jewelry and belts, taken supine. MRI: screen for metal implants and devices such as insulin pumps, remove all metal, longer than CT, lie still, no radiation.
questions.strategy: Sort each statement by test, then check it against that test's preparation. The radiograph needs almost nothing; the MRI needs metal screening.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gown and removal of metal; no fasting; supine.
Screen the insulin pump; lie still; longer than CT.
MRI uses magnets, not radiation.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: After an EGD with anesthetic throat spray, an alert patient says, "My throat still feels numb. Can I have some water?" Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the patient 30 mL of water by mouth
options.rationale: Being awake does not mean the gag reflex has returned. A numb throat after anesthetic spray means swallowing is not yet safe.

options.text: Discontinue the IV infusion
options.rationale: The IV fluid is discontinued only when the patient tolerates oral fluids without nausea or vomiting, which has not happened yet.

options.text: Check the gag reflex
options.rationale: The priority after EGD is preventing aspiration. The patient stays NPO until the gag reflex returns, usually in 30 to 60 minutes.

options.text: Lower the side rails
options.rationale: The side rails stay raised while sedation wears off. Being alert does not show that sedation has fully cleared.

questions.takeaway: After EGD, keep the patient NPO until the gag reflex returns (usually 30 to 60 minutes), check vital signs every 30 minutes until sedation wears off, keep the side rails raised, and stop IV fluids once oral fluids are tolerated without nausea or vomiting.
questions.strategy: The patient's own words give the cue: a numb throat means the gag reflex may not be back. Assess it before anything goes by mouth.

steps.detail: "My throat still feels numb."
Aspiration if fluids are given before the gag reflex returns.
The IV and side rails stay until fluids are tolerated and sedation clears.
Check the gag reflex first.

elimination.verdict: C. Check the gag reflex.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A patient who takes a daily anticoagulant is scheduled for an EGD tomorrow. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will not eat or drink for 6 to 8 hours before."
options.rationale: NPO for 6 to 8 hours before EGD is correct and lowers the risk of aspiration.

options.text: "I will take my anticoagulant tomorrow morning as usual."
options.rationale: Anticoagulants are usually avoided before EGD because of the bleeding risk, unless the provider says otherwise. The patient needs to clarify this drug with the provider before the test.

options.text: "My throat will be sprayed, so swallowing will feel hard."
options.rationale: An anesthetic spray inactivates the gag reflex, and swallowing will be difficult until it wears off. This is correct.

options.text: "A block between my teeth will protect them."
options.rationale: A bite block keeps the patient from biting the scope and protects the teeth. This is correct.

questions.takeaway: Before EGD: avoid anticoagulants unless told otherwise, NPO 6 to 8 hours, moderate sedation, anesthetic throat spray that inactivates the gag reflex, atropine to dry secretions, and a bite block.
questions.strategy: Negative polarity: look for the wrong statement. Bleeding risk is the safety issue the patient has missed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is unsafe.
NPO, throat spray and bite block are correct.
Taking the anticoagulant as usual raises bleeding risk.

elimination.verdict: B. Taking the anticoagulant as usual.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.nursesNote: 1500. Patient, 61 years old, had an EGD with dilation of an esophageal stricture at 1100. Gag reflex returned at 1200. Took sips of water at 1230 without nausea. Reports new pain behind the sternum, 7 of 10, was 0 of 10 at 1200. Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Oral temperature 37.0 °C, was 36.9 °C at 1100. Alert and oriented to person, place and time. Heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 82 beats per minute at 1100. SpO2 97% on room air. Spit up saliva streaked with bright red blood at 1445. IV fluid infusing at 75 mL per hour as prescribed.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the note of a patient who had an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with dilation of an esophageal stricture. Highlight the findings that require further evaluation.

segments.text: Gag reflex returned at 1200
segments.rationale: Return of the gag reflex within 30 to 60 minutes is expected after EGD.

segments.text: Took sips of water at 1230 without nausea
segments.rationale: Tolerating fluids after the gag reflex returns is an expected finding.

segments.text: Reports new pain behind the sternum, 7 of 10, was 0 of 10 at 1200
segments.rationale: After endoscopy the nurse monitors for perforation and assesses pain. New, severe pain after dilation of a stricture suggests perforation.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute
segments.rationale: This respiratory rate is within the expected range.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C, was 36.9 °C at 1100
segments.rationale: The temperature is essentially unchanged and within the expected range.

segments.text: Alert and oriented to person, place and time
segments.rationale: Orientation shows the sedation has worn off, an expected finding.

segments.text: Heart rate 118 beats per minute, was 82 beats per minute at 1100
segments.rationale: A rising heart rate supports a developing complication such as perforation or bleeding.

segments.text: SpO2 97% on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygen saturation is within the expected range.

segments.text: Spit up saliva streaked with bright red blood at 1445
segments.rationale: After endoscopy the nurse monitors for bleeding, a known challenge of EGD. Fresh blood with new pain needs evaluation.

segments.text: IV fluid infusing at 75 mL per hour as prescribed
segments.rationale: An infusion running as prescribed is expected.

questions.takeaway: After endoscopy, monitor for perforation, bleeding and aspiration, and assess pain. Esophageal stricture and bleeding are challenges of EGD. Expected findings are a returned gag reflex and tolerated fluids.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with its earlier value and with what is expected after EGD. Changes that point to one complication need follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain 0 to 7 of 10 and heart rate 82 to 118; temperature barely changed.
Blood streaked saliva.
New pain, a rising heart rate and bleeding after stricture dilation point to perforation or bleeding.
Gag reflex, fluids tolerated, temperature, orientation, respiratory rate, SpO2, IV.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: A patient with bleeding of unknown source is scheduled for small bowel capsule endoscopy. Which patient statement indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I will watch my stools for the capsule to pass."
options.rationale: The capsule passes naturally in the stool. The patient observes stools for its passage and reports if it does not pass.

options.text: "I will return so the capsule can be removed with a scope."
options.rationale: The capsule is a single use device that is excreted naturally. No scope is needed to remove it.

options.text: "I can eat my usual dinner tonight before the test."
options.rationale: A clear liquid diet is required the day before, with NPO status as ordered.

options.text: "I will stay in the hospital until an x ray shows it is gone."
options.rationale: The patient goes home during the test. Passage is confirmed by stool observation, not a hospital stay.

questions.takeaway: Small bowel capsule endoscopy: clear liquid diet the day before and NPO as ordered, swallow the capsule, then watch the stool for capsule passage and report if it does not pass.
questions.strategy: Picture the capsule's path. It is swallowed and leaves in the stool, so the teaching centers on preparation and on watching for it to pass.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A clear liquid diet the day before rules out the usual dinner.
The capsule is excreted, not retrieved.
Watching the stool for passage.

elimination.verdict: A. Look for the capsule in the stool.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: After a sigmoidoscopy with biopsy, a patient passes several bloody stools with clots and feels lightheaded when sitting up. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Assist the patient to walk in the hall
options.rationale: Mild cramping is expected after sigmoidoscopy, but this patient is lightheaded and at risk for falling.

options.text: Reassure the patient and recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: A small amount of blood is expected after biopsy, but repeated clots with lightheadedness are excessive.

options.text: Report the findings to the provider now
options.rationale: After sigmoidoscopy the nurse monitors for bleeding, especially after a biopsy, and excessive bleeding is reported. Lightheadedness suggests significant blood loss and makes it urgent.

options.text: Give a cleansing enema before reassessing
options.rationale: An enema is part of the preparation before sigmoidoscopy, not a treatment for bleeding afterward. It delays reporting the bleeding.

questions.takeaway: After sigmoidoscopy, mild cramping and gas pain are expected, and a small amount of bleeding may follow a biopsy. Monitor for bleeding and report excessive bleeding immediately.
questions.strategy: Separate expected from excessive. A small streak is expected after biopsy; repeated clots with lightheadedness are not.

steps.detail: Several bloody stools with clots and lightheadedness when sitting up.
Repeated stools of blood with clots is excessive.
Report now; do not wait or walk the patient.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the bleeding now.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.scenario: A patient is scheduled for an abdominal ultrasound in the morning and a liver spleen scan in the afternoon. The nurse plans the teaching.
questions.stem: The nurse is planning teaching for a patient scheduled for two abdominal imaging tests. For each statement, indicate whether the teaching is appropriate or not appropriate.

rows.text: "A gel will be placed on your skin, and the ultrasound uses no needles or radiation."
rows.rationale: Ultrasonography uses gel on the skin and is noninvasive, with no radiation.

rows.text: "You may need to fast before the ultrasound, depending on the organs being viewed."
rows.rationale: Ultrasonography may require fasting, depending on the organ, such as NPO for an abdominal ultrasound.

rows.text: "After the liver spleen scan, limit fluids so the tracer stays in your body longer."
rows.rationale: Hydration is encouraged after a liver spleen scan to help eliminate the radionuclide.

rows.text: "The scan uses a small amount of radioactive material, and the exposure is minimal."
rows.rationale: A small amount of radioactive material is used, and the exposure is minimal and safe.

rows.text: "You will need to stay on bed rest for 6 hours after the ultrasound."
rows.rationale: After ultrasonography there are no specific requirements; patients resume normal activities right away.

rows.text: "For the liver spleen scan, you will swallow the tracer with a cup of water."
rows.rationale: The radionuclide for a liver spleen scan is injected through IV access, not swallowed.

questions.takeaway: Ultrasonography: possible fasting, gel, noninvasive, no follow up care. Liver spleen scan: IV radionuclide, minimal and safe exposure, then fluids to help eliminate it.
questions.strategy: Check each statement against the test it names. Ultrasound needs almost no aftercare; the scan needs IV access and fluids afterward.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gel, fasting as ordered, normal activity afterward.
IV radionuclide, minimal exposure, encourage fluids.
Limiting fluids, bed rest and a swallowed tracer.

elimination.verdict: Appropriate, appropriate, not appropriate, appropriate, not appropriate, not appropriate.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a patient for endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) with possible biopsy. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teach that eating can resume once awake
options.rationale: After EUS the nurse confirms that the gag reflex has returned before any oral intake.

options.text: Teach that driving home is safe once awake
options.rationale: EUS uses sedation, so the patient needs a driver. Feeling awake does not mean sedation has cleared.

options.text: Explain that a brief sore throat may follow
options.rationale: The scope passes through the throat, so a sore throat is a possible side effect.

options.text: Teach NPO for 6 to 8 hours before the procedure
options.rationale: EUS requires NPO status for 6 to 8 hours before the procedure.

options.text: Confirm signed consent before sedation
options.rationale: EUS is an invasive procedure that requires informed consent, obtained before sedation.

options.text: Explain that a biopsy cannot be taken
options.rationale: EUS can include biopsy collection, and the nurse prepares for it.

questions.takeaway: EUS: NPO 6 to 8 hours, informed consent, sedation with possible biopsy, possible sore throat, and gag reflex return before oral intake, with monitoring for bleeding or perforation.
questions.strategy: EUS is an endoscopy, so apply the endoscopy rules: NPO, consent, sedation precautions and gag reflex before eating.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPO 6 to 8 hours and informed consent.
Sore throat is possible; gag reflex before food or fluid.
Driving after sedation, early eating, and denying biopsy.

elimination.verdict: C, D, E.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with upper abdominal pain and has documented: "Burning pain in the epigastric area that spreads to the back. Began 3 days ago, comes in episodes that last about 2 hours, and woke the patient twice last night. Rated 6 of 10 at its worst; the patient had to lie down at work." Which question should the nurse ask next to complete the pain assessment?

options.text: "At what time of day does the pain usually begin, and how long does it last?"
options.rationale: This is a timing question. Onset, duration, frequency and waking at night are already documented, so asking it again adds nothing new.

options.text: "Can you point to the spot where the pain feels the worst?"
options.rationale: This is a region question. The epigastric location and the spread to the back are already documented.

options.text: "On a scale of 0 to 10, how bad does the pain get at its worst?"
options.rationale: This is a severity question. The rating of 6 of 10 at its worst and the effect on work are already documented.

options.text: "Does anything you do or take make the pain better or worse?"
options.rationale: Precipitating and palliative factors are the only part of PQRST missing from the note. What eases or worsens the pain, including any medicine taken, is the next piece of data the nurse needs.

questions.takeaway: PQRST: precipitating or palliative factors, quality or quantity, region or radiation, severity, timing. A complete abdominal pain assessment covers every letter, so the nurse looks for the part that has not been collected yet.
questions.strategy: Label each documented phrase with its letter. The question that fills the empty letter is the next question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Burning is quality, epigastric and spreading to the back is region, 6 of 10 is severity, 3 days and 2 hour episodes are timing.
Nothing in the note says what brings the pain on or what makes it better or worse.
The timing, region and severity questions ask for data already recorded.
Ask about precipitating and palliative factors.

elimination.verdict: D. Ask what makes the pain better or worse.

questions.objective: Assess abdominal pain using the PQRSTU framework and recognize associated GI symptoms

questions.nursesNote: 1000. Patient, 58 years old, reports fatigue and a smaller appetite for 3 weeks. Weight 81.6 kg, was 76.2 kg 3 weeks ago. Oral temperature 37.0 °C. Sclera yellow. Abdomen rounded and symmetric. Umbilicus midline. Skin over the abdomen taut and glistening. Gurgling sounds heard in all 4 quadrants. Bruises on both forearms, and the patient recalls no injury. Light palpation: no tenderness or masses. Scratch marks on both lower legs from itching.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the assessment note of a patient with fatigue and a smaller appetite. Highlight the findings that require further evaluation.

segments.text: Weight 81.6 kg, was 76.2 kg 3 weeks ago
segments.rationale: A gain of 5.4 kg while eating less cannot come from food. Combined with taut, glistening abdominal skin, it suggests fluid collecting in the abdomen.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C
segments.rationale: The temperature is within the expected range.

segments.text: Sclera yellow
segments.rationale: Jaundice is a skin change linked to liver and biliary disorders and needs further evaluation.

segments.text: Abdomen rounded and symmetric
segments.rationale: A rounded, symmetric contour can be a normal finding. On its own it does not require follow up.

segments.text: Umbilicus midline
segments.rationale: A midline umbilicus is an expected finding.

segments.text: Skin over the abdomen taut and glistening
segments.rationale: Taut, glistening skin is an abnormal inspection finding that suggests the abdomen is stretched by fluid or gas.

segments.text: Gurgling sounds heard in all 4 quadrants
segments.rationale: Irregular gurgles in every quadrant are normal bowel sounds.

segments.text: Bruises on both forearms, and the patient recalls no injury
segments.rationale: Increased bruising or a tendency to bleed is a skin change linked to GI disorders, such as a liver that makes fewer clotting proteins.

segments.text: Light palpation: no tenderness or masses
segments.rationale: No tenderness and no masses on light palpation is an expected finding.

segments.text: Scratch marks on both lower legs from itching
segments.rationale: Itching is one of the skin changes the nurse asks about in a GI history because it can come from liver or biliary obstruction.

questions.takeaway: Skin changes tied to GI disorders are discoloration or rashes, itching, jaundice and increased bruising or bleeding. Weight gain while eating less points to fluid, especially with taut, glistening abdominal skin.
questions.strategy: Mark each finding normal or abnormal. For the weight, compare it with the appetite: a gain while eating less is not a nutrition gain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Yellow sclera, unexplained bruising and scratch marks from itching.

steps.action: Read the weight with the appetite
steps.detail: Gaining 5.4 kg while eating less points to fluid, not food.
Taut, glistening skin over the abdomen.
A rounded, symmetric contour, a midline umbilicus, gurgles in all quadrants, a soft nontender abdomen and a temperature of 37.0 °C.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with cirrhosis who passed a large black stool this morning. At 0800 the patient was alert and oriented. At 1400 the patient is drowsy, states the wrong year, and does not know where they are. Blood pressure and heart rate are unchanged from yesterday. Several laboratory results drawn at 1300 are now available. Which result should the nurse review first to explain the change in mental status?

options.text: Serum ammonia
options.rationale: The liver normally converts ammonia to urea for excretion, and a cirrhotic liver cannot. Blood in the gut is digested into protein, which adds more ammonia. A black stool followed by new confusion points to hepatic encephalopathy, so ammonia is the result that explains the change.

options.text: Hemoglobin and hematocrit
options.rationale: The black stool suggests bleeding, so hemoglobin and hematocrit matter and will be reviewed. But blood pressure and heart rate are unchanged, and blood loss alone does not explain the confusion the way rising ammonia from digested blood does.

options.text: Prothrombin time
options.rationale: A prolonged prothrombin time reflects poor synthesis of clotting proteins and helps explain why a patient with cirrhosis bleeds, which fits the black stool. It describes bleeding risk, not the toxin that clouds thinking.

options.text: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
options.rationale: AST is a liver enzyme that rises when liver cells are injured, so it fits the known cirrhosis. It measures injury, not the toxin that causes confusion, so it does not explain the new change in mental status.

questions.takeaway: Serum ammonia evaluates hepatic function: an injured liver cannot convert ammonia to urea, and levels rise in cirrhosis, hepatitis and hepatic encephalopathy. Gastrointestinal bleeding is a common trigger, because digested blood adds protein that becomes ammonia. Match the lab to the new finding, not only to the known disease.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The black stool pulls toward the bleeding results, and each one matters. The question asks what explains the new confusion: in cirrhosis, digested blood raises ammonia, so ammonia links both cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Black stool this morning; alert at 0800, drowsy and disoriented at 1400.
Hemoglobin and prothrombin time fit the black stool, but vital signs are unchanged and neither explains confusion.
Digested blood adds protein, and a damaged liver cannot clear the ammonia, causing hepatic encephalopathy.
AST measures liver cell injury, not the cause of the mental status change.

elimination.verdict: A. Serum ammonia.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient during an abdominal CT scan with IV contrast. The patient has no history of contrast reaction and no known allergies. As the contrast is injected, the patient says, "My whole body suddenly feels warm, and I taste metal." The patient speaks in full sentences and has no itching, hives or wheezing. SpO2 98% and blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, both unchanged from before the injection. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Stop the injection and report a possible contrast reaction
options.rationale: Stopping is right for a reaction, such as hives, itching or wheezing. None of those signs is present, and the vital signs and SpO2 have not changed, so stopping would interrupt the scan without cause.

options.text: Explain that these sensations are expected and keep observing
options.rationale: A warm, flushed feeling and a metallic taste are expected during the contrast injection; patients are told about them before the test. With no hives, no wheezing and unchanged vital signs, the nurse reassures and keeps watching for a true reaction.

options.text: Give the prescribed antihistamine and recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: An antihistamine treats an allergic reaction. The patient has no signs of one, so the drug is not needed.

options.text: Ask the technologist to slow the injection and recheck vital signs
options.rationale: This is the near miss: it seems a cautious middle path. Warmth and a metallic taste are expected effects of contrast, not a sign that the rate is unsafe, so there is nothing to slow down for.

questions.takeaway: Before a CT with contrast, ask about past contrast reactions and severe allergies, keep the patient NPO for at least 4 hours, start IV access, and explain that a warm, flushed feeling or a metallic taste may occur during the injection. Itching, hives or wheezing signal a reaction.
questions.strategy: Three options respond to the symptoms as a possible problem, and one of them sounds like a cautious compromise. Decide whether this is an expected sensation or a reaction by looking for hives, itching, wheezing and vital sign changes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warmth and a metallic taste during injection are expected.
No itching, hives or wheezing, and the SpO2 and blood pressure are unchanged.
An antihistamine treats a problem the patient does not have, and slowing the injection treats an expected sensation.
Reassure and keep observing rather than stopping the scan.

elimination.verdict: B. Explain that the sensations are expected and keep observing.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient at average risk for colorectal cancer how to use a guaiac based fecal occult blood test (gFOBT) kit. The patient takes ibuprofen for back pain and a 1,000 mg vitamin C tablet each day. Which statements by the patient indicate a need for further teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will bring the kit to my next office visit so it can be done during a rectal exam."
options.rationale: The gFOBT is a take home test with several samples collected at home. A single sample taken during a rectal exam is not how this screening is done.

options.text: "Food does not change the result of this test, so I can eat as I usually do."
options.rationale: This is true of the fecal immunochemical test, not the guaiac test. With gFOBT, red meat is avoided for 3 days before and during collection.

options.text: "I will ask my provider about stopping the ibuprofen for 7 days before and during collection."
options.rationale: NSAIDs are avoided for 7 days before and during a gFOBT collection. Checking with the provider about the back pain plan is appropriate.

options.text: "I can keep taking my vitamin C tablet while I collect the samples."
options.rationale: Vitamin C above 250 mg a day is avoided for 3 days before and during a gFOBT collection. The patient's 1,000 mg tablet must be stopped.

options.text: "I will avoid red meat for 3 days before and while I collect the samples."
options.rationale: This is correct preparation for the guaiac test.

options.text: "If the result is negative, I will repeat this test in 3 years."
options.rationale: The gFOBT is repeated every year. The 3 year interval belongs to the multitargeted stool DNA test.

questions.takeaway: The gFOBT is an annual take home test. The patient avoids NSAIDs for 7 days and red meat and vitamin C over 250 mg a day for 3 days before and during collection. The FIT has no food or drug restrictions, and the stool DNA test is repeated every 3 years.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The test named in the stem is the guaiac test. Check each statement against that test, not against the FIT or the stool DNA kit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Guaiac based, so diet and drug limits apply.

steps.action: Flag the diet and drug errors
steps.detail: Eating as usual and continuing 1,000 mg of vitamin C both interfere.

steps.action: Flag the method and interval errors
steps.detail: It is collected at home and repeated every year.
Asking about stopping ibuprofen and avoiding red meat.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who returned 15 minutes ago from an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with moderate sedation and an anesthetic throat spray. The patient is drowsy but answers questions and asks for something to drink. An IV infusion is running. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should be performed.

options.text: Offer a sip of water
options.rationale: Fluids are offered only after the gag reflex has returned, because the throat spray and sedation raise the risk of aspiration.

options.text: Discontinue the IV infusion
options.rationale: The IV is stopped only once the patient tolerates oral fluids without nausea or vomiting, so it is last.

options.text: Check respiratory rate, depth and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: The patient is still drowsy from sedation that can depress breathing, so breathing is checked first.

options.text: Watch for coughing, nausea or vomiting after the sip
options.rationale: The first sip shows whether the patient swallows safely and keeps fluids down, which decides whether the IV can stop.

options.text: Check for return of the gag reflex
options.rationale: The patient is asking to drink, but the throat spray blocks the gag reflex. It must return before anything is taken by mouth.

questions.takeaway: After an EGD, confirm breathing first while sedation wears off, keep the patient nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns, then offer fluids, and stop the IV only after oral fluids are tolerated without nausea or vomiting.
questions.strategy: The patient's request for a drink pulls toward the water early. Order by risk: breathing under sedation, then airway protection, then fluids, then removing the IV.

steps.detail: The patient is drowsy after moderate sedation.
Throat spray blocks the gag reflex, so check it before any water.
Offer a sip and watch for coughing, nausea or vomiting.
Only after fluids are tolerated.

elimination.verdict: C, E, A, D, B.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring a patient 20 minutes after an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with moderate sedation. The patient receives oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula, and the SpO2 is 97%, unchanged from before the procedure. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Reports a sore, scratchy throat when swallowing
options.rationale: A sore throat is an expected effect of the scope and is taught before the procedure.

options.text: Gag reflex has not returned at 20 minutes
options.rationale: This is tempting because it affects safety, but the gag reflex usually returns in 30 to 60 minutes; at 20 minutes the patient simply stays nothing by mouth.

options.text: Blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, was 116/72 mm Hg before
options.rationale: A small drop is common as sedation takes effect and does not show bleeding on its own.

options.text: Respiratory rate 9/min, rising end tidal carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Slow breathing with a rising end tidal carbon dioxide shows the sedation is causing hypoventilation. Supplemental oxygen keeps the SpO2 normal for a while, so the SpO2 of 97% hides the problem.

questions.takeaway: After moderate sedation, monitor respiratory rate and depth and capnography, not only pulse oximetry. A patient on oxygen can keep a normal SpO2 while retaining carbon dioxide from slow breathing.
questions.strategy: The unchanged SpO2 of 97% makes every option look minor. The oxygen therapy decides: it masks hypoventilation, so the rising end tidal carbon dioxide with a slow rate is the true warning.

steps.detail: SpO2 97% on 2 L/min of oxygen.
Sore throat and a gag reflex not yet back at 20 minutes.
A small drop with no other sign of bleeding.
Respiratory rate 9/min with rising end tidal carbon dioxide.

elimination.verdict: D. Respiratory rate 9/min, rising end tidal carbon dioxide.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is obtaining a gastrointestinal health history from a patient who was told yesterday that a colon biopsy showed cancer. When asked about bowel habits, the patient says loudly, "Why does it matter now? Nobody caught this in time anyway." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "You sound angry about how this was found. Tell me more."
options.rationale: Naming the feeling and inviting the patient to talk accepts the anger as part of grieving a new cancer diagnosis and keeps the conversation open. The history can continue once the patient feels heard.

options.text: "Anger is a normal part of grief, and it often passes."
options.rationale: The statement is true, but it labels the patient and tells them the feeling will pass instead of letting them express it.

options.text: "I can arrange for a counselor to see you after we finish."
options.rationale: A referral may be needed later, but offering it now and finishing the history first puts off the feeling the patient just expressed.

options.text: "These questions help your team plan your cancer treatment."
options.rationale: Explaining the purpose is accurate, but it answers the question literally and steers back to the task without acknowledging the anger.

questions.takeaway: A patient newly diagnosed with cancer may be angry, depressed or in denial as part of grieving. Acknowledge and explore the feeling first; referral and the rest of the history follow.
questions.strategy: Three options are things a nurse might reasonably say: a true fact about grief, a referral, and an explanation of the questions. The new diagnosis and the angry outburst decide that the feeling needs to be acknowledged before anything else.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Cancer diagnosis yesterday and an angry statement.
Telling the patient anger passes dismisses it.

steps.action: Reject the deferral and the redirect
steps.detail: The referral and the explanation both move away from the feeling.
Acknowledge the anger and invite the patient to say more.

elimination.verdict: A. "You sound angry about how this was found. Tell me more."

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an older adult in a long term care facility who has had small amounts of liquid stool leaking several times a day for 2 days. The patient has not passed a formed stool in 6 days and reports a feeling of fullness in the rectum. Oral temperature 37.0 °C, and the patient has taken no antibiotics in the past 3 months. Which explanation should the nurse consider most likely?

options.text: An infection that needs a stool test for Clostridioides difficile
options.rationale: Liquid stool in a long term care facility makes this test tempting, but the patient has no fever and no recent antibiotics, and has passed no formed stool in 6 days.

options.text: Poor fat digestion from changes in the pancreatic ducts
options.rationale: Age related pancreatic duct changes cause greasy, pale stools that float, not a small liquid leak with rectal fullness.

options.text: Fecal impaction from slowed peristalsis and dulled sensation
options.rationale: Slowed peristalsis and a dulled urge to defecate with aging lead to constipation and impaction. Liquid stool leaks around the hard mass, which explains the leaking with no formed stool in 6 days and rectal fullness.

options.text: Intolerance of milk products in the usual diet
options.rationale: Lactose intolerance causes bloating and loose stools after milk products, but it does not stop formed stool for 6 days or cause rectal fullness.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, liquid stool leaking with no formed stool for days and a feeling of rectal fullness points to fecal impaction from slowed peristalsis and dulled sensation, not to diarrhea.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: The liquid stool pulls toward an infection. Combine the cues: no formed stool in 6 days plus rectal fullness, with no fever and no recent antibiotics, means the liquid is leaking around an impaction.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Liquid leak, no formed stool in 6 days, rectal fullness.
Temperature 37.0 °C and no antibiotics in 3 months.
Greasy floating stools and loose stools after milk do not fit.
Fecal impaction from slowed peristalsis.

elimination.verdict: C. Fecal impaction from slowed peristalsis and dulled sensation.

questions.objective: Describe age related changes in the GI system and their impact on digestion, absorption, and elimination

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted 1 hour ago after vomiting about 500 mL of bright red blood at home. Heart rate 118/min and blood pressure 94/58 mm Hg, was 128/80 mm Hg at a clinic visit last week. Hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL and hematocrit 42%, unchanged from that visit. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The bleeding was minor, since the hemoglobin is unchanged
options.rationale: This is the trap. Whole blood is lost all at once, so the hemoglobin and hematocrit stay the same until fluid shifts in and dilutes the remaining blood, hours later.

options.text: The hemoglobin does not yet show the blood lost an hour ago
options.rationale: After a sudden bleed, the hemoglobin and hematocrit lag behind the loss. The heart rate of 118/min and the blood pressure fall from 128/80 to 94/58 mm Hg show the volume loss now.

options.text: The heart rate reflects anxiety, since the hemoglobin is unchanged
options.rationale: Anxiety can raise the heart rate, but it does not explain the blood pressure falling from 128/80 to 94/58 mm Hg after a 500 mL bleed.

options.text: The low blood pressure reflects dehydration from the vomiting
options.rationale: One episode of vomiting does not explain this drop. The vomit was blood, so the fluid lost was blood volume.

questions.takeaway: Right after an acute bleed, the hemoglobin and hematocrit can still be at baseline. Judge the loss by the vital signs, and expect the values to fall over the next hours.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options lean on the unchanged hemoglobin to explain away the vital signs. The timing, 1 hour after the bleed, decides: the lab has not caught up, and the heart rate and blood pressure show the loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The bleed was 1 hour ago.
Heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 94/58 mm Hg, was 128/80 mm Hg.
Hemoglobin and hematocrit lag behind a sudden loss.
Minor bleed, anxiety and dehydration do not fit a 500 mL bleed.

elimination.verdict: B. The hemoglobin does not yet show the blood lost an hour ago.

questions.objective: Identify common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate GI function and disorders

questions.stem: The nurse is obtaining a nutrition history from a patient with unintentional weight loss. Which patient statement requires further assessment by the nurse?

options.text: "I drink one cup of coffee each morning."
options.rationale: One cup of coffee is a small caffeine intake. It is worth recording but does not explain weight loss or point to a GI disorder.

options.text: "It hurts when I swallow food."
options.rationale: Pain or difficulty with swallowing can come from an esophageal disorder and can lead the patient to eat less. With unintentional weight loss, which some GI cancers present with, this needs further assessment.

options.text: "I eat my largest meal at lunchtime."
options.rationale: Meal timing is part of the history, but eating the main meal at midday is a usual pattern, not a symptom.

options.text: "I like to snack on fruit in the afternoon."
options.rationale: Snacking on fruit is a healthy habit and does not suggest a problem with eating or digestion.

questions.takeaway: In a nutrition history, pain or difficulty with swallowing is a symptom, not a habit. With unintentional weight loss it needs follow up, because esophageal disorders and some GI cancers present this way.
questions.strategy: Three statements describe ordinary eating habits. Look for the one that is a symptom and could explain why the patient is losing weight.

steps.detail: Weight loss the patient did not intend.
Coffee, meal timing and fruit snacks are habits.
Painful swallowing makes a patient eat less.
"It hurts when I swallow food."

elimination.verdict: B. "It hurts when I swallow food."

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: The nurse is inspecting the abdomen of a patient admitted with nausea. Which finding requires further evaluation?

options.text: Bulge in one lower quadrant only
options.rationale: A bulge on one side that is not present on the other breaks the expected symmetry and may be a mass, hernia or distended bowel, so it needs further evaluation.

options.text: Healed scar from a past appendectomy
options.rationale: A healed scar the patient can explain is documented with the surgical history. It is not a new problem.

options.text: Abdomen rises and falls with breathing
options.rationale: Gentle movement of the abdomen with each breath is an expected inspection finding.

options.text: Flat contour with a midline umbilicus
options.rationale: A flat contour and a midline umbilicus are expected findings.

questions.takeaway: During inspection, compare the quadrants for contour and symmetry. A bulge on one side only is abnormal and is evaluated further, while a healed, explained scar is recorded with the history.
questions.strategy: Every option is something the nurse documents during inspection. Ask which one breaks the expected pattern of a symmetric abdomen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contour, symmetry, skin and movement.
Breathing movement, flat contour, midline umbilicus.
Healed and explained by past surgery.
A bulge on one side only.

elimination.verdict: A. Bulge in one lower quadrant only.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: The nurse is performing an abdominal assessment on a patient admitted yesterday with pneumonia. The patient reports passing flatus this morning, and the abdomen is soft and nontender. After inspection, the nurse places the diaphragm of the stethoscope in the right lower quadrant and hears no bowel sounds after 1 minute. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Report absent bowel sounds to the provider
options.rationale: This is tempting because absent bowel sounds are abnormal. But sounds cannot be called absent after only 1 minute, and the patient passed flatus this morning, which shows peristalsis is present.

options.text: Proceed to light palpation of each quadrant
options.rationale: Palpation follows auscultation, but the auscultation is not finished. Moving on now leaves the bowel sound finding incomplete, and palpating first could change the sounds.

options.text: Document absent bowel sounds and move on
options.rationale: Recording sounds as absent after 1 minute documents a finding that has not been confirmed and conflicts with the flatus the patient reports.

options.text: Keep listening for up to 5 minutes
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are irregular, so a quiet minute is common. The nurse keeps listening before concluding they are absent. Flatus this morning and a soft, nontender abdomen make true absence unlikely.

questions.takeaway: Bowel sounds are irregular. Listen with the diaphragm, starting in the right lower quadrant, for up to 5 minutes before calling them absent, and weigh the patient's report of flatus, the best sign that peristalsis is working.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Absent bowel sounds look like a reason to report or document. Two cues decide: only 1 minute of listening, and flatus this morning. The finding is not yet confirmed, so the assessment continues.

steps.detail: Only 1 minute in the right lower quadrant.
Flatus this morning, soft and nontender abdomen.
Reporting or documenting absent sounds is premature.
Finish auscultation before palpation.

elimination.verdict: D. Keep listening for up to 5 minutes.

questions.objective: Demonstrate the correct sequence and techniques for abdominal assessment, including inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient scheduled for an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Which patient statement indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I can have black coffee the morning of the test."
options.rationale: The patient stays NPO for 6 to 8 hours before an ERCP. Black coffee is still oral intake.

options.text: "No dye is used, so allergies do not matter."
options.rationale: ERCP combines endoscopy with x rays and uses contrast, so allergies are reviewed before the test.

options.text: "I can eat as soon as I am awake afterward."
options.rationale: Being awake is not enough. The gag reflex must return before anything is taken by mouth.

options.text: "I will report belly pain after the test."
options.rationale: Abdominal pain after ERCP may signal pancreatitis, so the patient is taught to report it.

questions.takeaway: Before ERCP: NPO 6 to 8 hours, consent, and an allergy review because contrast is used. After ERCP: no oral intake until the gag reflex returns, and report abdominal pain, which may signal pancreatitis.
questions.strategy: Each wrong statement is one step off the plan: intake before the test, the contrast, and eating after. Choose the statement that matches the complication the patient must watch for.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPO 6 to 8 hours, so no coffee.
ERCP uses contrast, so allergies matter.
Gag reflex before eating, not just being awake.
Report abdominal pain afterward.

elimination.verdict: D. "I will report belly pain after the test."

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing discharge teaching for a patient after a sigmoidoscopy with biopsy. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Your throat will be numb, so wait to drink."
options.rationale: A sigmoidoscopy enters through the anus. There is no throat spray, so this applies to upper endoscopy, not this test.

options.text: "Mild cramping after the test is expected."
options.rationale: Mild cramping is an expected effect after sigmoidoscopy and is part of the teaching.

options.text: "Stay on clear liquids for 3 days."
options.rationale: No extended diet restriction is needed. The patient resumes a usual diet as tolerated.

options.text: "Report heavy bleeding or passing clots."
options.rationale: A biopsy was taken, so bleeding is the complication to watch for and report.

options.text: "Return to your usual diet as tolerated."
options.rationale: After sigmoidoscopy the patient is encouraged to resume a normal diet as tolerated.

questions.takeaway: After sigmoidoscopy, teach that mild cramping is expected, the usual diet resumes as tolerated, and bleeding must be reported, especially when a biopsy was taken.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options belong to other tests or invent restrictions. Match each instruction to a lower endoscopy with a biopsy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sigmoidoscopy enters through the anus, so no throat spray.
A biopsy raises the risk of bleeding.
Usual diet as tolerated, no 3 day restriction.
Mild cramping.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is calling a patient who had small bowel capsule endoscopy 3 days ago for bleeding of unknown source. The patient has not seen the capsule in the stool. Since last night the patient has had cramping abdominal pain, a swollen abdomen and two episodes of vomiting, and asks whether to take a laxative to help the capsule pass. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Capsules can take up to 2 weeks to pass, so keep checking."
options.rationale: This is true for a patient with no symptoms, which makes it tempting. But cramping pain, a swollen abdomen and vomiting are signs of obstruction, so waiting is unsafe.

options.text: "A mild laxative may help, so take one and call tomorrow."
options.rationale: This answers the patient's request, but a laxative pushes against a possible blockage and delays evaluation of obstruction signs.

options.text: "This may be a blockage, so you need to be seen today."
options.rationale: Pain, swelling and vomiting with no capsule seen suggest the capsule may be blocking the bowel. Signs of GI obstruction are reported and evaluated promptly, not managed at home.

options.text: "Drinking extra clear liquids can help the capsule move along."
options.rationale: This sounds supportive, but a vomiting patient may not keep fluids down, and it treats a possible obstruction as a slow capsule.

questions.takeaway: After capsule endoscopy, the patient watches for the capsule in the stool and reports it if not passed within 2 weeks. Signs of GI obstruction, such as cramping pain, distention and vomiting, are reported right away whatever the timing.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The 2 week window and the patient's question about a laxative both pull toward waiting at home. The symptoms decide: pain, a swollen abdomen and vomiting with no capsule seen point to a blockage.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No capsule seen, cramping pain, swollen abdomen, vomiting.
Up to 2 weeks applies only without symptoms.
A laxative or extra fluids treats a blockage as a slow capsule.
Possible blockage, seen today.

elimination.verdict: C. "This may be a blockage, so you need to be seen today."

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four patients in a procedure recovery area. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: After a colonoscopy: cramping and bloating, passing flatus
options.rationale: Air is inflated during a colonoscopy, so mild cramping and bloating are expected, and passing flatus is how the air leaves.

options.text: After an EGD: mild sore throat, gag reflex returned
options.rationale: A sore throat after an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is an expected effect of the scope. The returned gag reflex means oral intake can start.

options.text: After a sigmoidoscopy with biopsy: a streak of blood on the tissue
options.rationale: A small streak of blood after a biopsy is expected. Bleeding with clots, many bloody stools or lightheadedness would need follow up.

options.text: After an ERCP: epigastric pain going to the back, 8 of 10
options.rationale: Severe abdominal pain after endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a sign of pancreatitis, the complication the nurse watches for after this procedure. It needs follow up now.

questions.takeaway: Know the expected and the dangerous finding after each procedure. Colonoscopy: cramping from air is expected. EGD: sore throat is expected. Biopsy: a small streak of blood is expected. ERCP: severe abdominal pain, often going to the back, suggests pancreatitis.
questions.strategy: Three findings are expected effects of the procedure. Look for the one finding that matches the named complication of its procedure.

steps.detail: Cramping from air, sore throat from the scope, a streak of blood after biopsy.
Severe epigastric pain going to the back after ERCP: pancreatitis.
The ERCP patient.

elimination.verdict: D. After an ERCP: epigastric pain going to the back, 8 of 10.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient with cramping abdominal pain that comes in waves, abdominal distention and vomiting. The patient has passed no flatus since yesterday. Bowel sounds are loud and high pitched, with rushes. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?

options.text: An early bowel obstruction is likely
options.rationale: Loud, high pitched rushes with cramping in waves, distention, vomiting and no flatus fit a bowel obstruction. Above the blockage, peristalsis works hard against it. An abdominal radiograph can confirm it.

options.text: Peristalsis is returning to normal
options.rationale: Active bowel sounds can be reassuring, which makes this tempting. Normal peristalsis moves gas, and this patient has passed no flatus and is distended and vomiting.

options.text: A paralytic ileus is developing
options.rationale: An ileus is the other cause of distention with no flatus, but in an ileus bowel sounds are diminished or absent, not loud and high pitched.

options.text: Gastroenteritis is the likely cause
options.rationale: Gastroenteritis brings hyperactive bowel sounds with diarrhea. It does not cause distention with no passage of flatus.

questions.takeaway: Bowel sounds help sort the cause of distention with no flatus: loud, high pitched rushes point to a mechanical obstruction; diminished or absent sounds point to a paralytic ileus or peritonitis. A radiograph can show an obstruction and abnormal gas patterns.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Two options explain distention with no flatus: obstruction and ileus. The bowel sound quality decides between them. Hyperactive sounds alone tempt you toward normal or gastroenteritis, but neither explains no flatus.

steps.detail: Cramping in waves, distention, vomiting, no flatus, loud high pitched rushes.
Obstruction or ileus both explain no flatus.
Ileus is quiet; obstruction is loud and high pitched.
Early bowel obstruction.

elimination.verdict: A. An early bowel obstruction is likely.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an older adult who is drinking a prescribed bowel prep for a colonoscopy tomorrow. The patient has had 10 watery stools and stands up to walk to the bathroom, then says, "I feel dizzy and my legs are shaky." Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check orthostatic vital signs
options.rationale: Assessment before intervention makes this tempting, and the nurse will check vital signs. A dizzy patient who is standing can fall during the check, so safety comes first.

options.text: Offer a cup of clear broth
options.rationale: Clear fluids replace losses from the prep and are part of the plan, but they do not prevent the fall that can happen in the next few seconds.

options.text: Help the patient sit down
options.rationale: A dizzy, shaky older adult who is standing is at immediate risk of falling. Fluid loss from the prep and the reduced reserve of aging cause orthostatic changes. Sitting the patient down prevents injury, then the nurse assesses.

options.text: Report the symptoms to the provider
options.rationale: The provider may need to know about dizziness and possible fluid or electrolyte loss, but the nurse first makes the patient safe and gathers data to report.

questions.takeaway: During a bowel prep, especially in older adults, watch for fluid and electrolyte loss: dizziness, weakness and orthostatic changes. A dizzy patient who is standing is protected first by sitting or lying down, then assessed, then given fluids and reported as needed.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Assessment usually comes before intervention, but not when a patient is about to fall. The deciding cue is that the patient is standing while dizzy.

steps.detail: Standing, dizzy and shaky after 10 watery stools.
Orthostatic vital signs are needed, but a standing dizzy patient can fall during them.
Fluids and reporting follow once the patient is safe.
Sit the patient down.

elimination.verdict: C. Help the patient sit down.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating discharge teaching for a patient going home after an outpatient esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with moderate sedation and a biopsy. Which statements by the patient indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "A mild sore throat for a day or two is expected."
options.rationale: The scope and the throat spray can leave a sore throat that eases in a day or two.

options.text: "If I vomit blood once, I will wait to see if it happens again."
options.rationale: Vomiting blood after a biopsy is a sign of bleeding and is reported right away. Waiting delays care.

options.text: "A friend will drive me home today."
options.rationale: Moderate sedation impairs judgment and reaction time, so the patient does not drive after the procedure.

options.text: "I will wait until tomorrow to sign any legal papers."
options.rationale: Sedation can affect judgment for the rest of the day, so important decisions and legal documents wait.

options.text: "I will restart my anticoagulant tonight on my own."
options.rationale: Anticoagulants are avoided around an EGD, and after a biopsy the provider decides when to restart. Restarting on its own raises the risk of bleeding.

options.text: "I will call if I have chest pain, a fever or black stools."
options.rationale: Chest pain and fever can signal perforation, and black stools can signal bleeding, which are the complications watched for after an EGD with biopsy.

questions.takeaway: After an EGD with sedation and biopsy: expect a mild sore throat, have someone drive, delay legal decisions, restart anticoagulants only as directed, and report chest pain, fever, black stools or vomiting blood at once.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Sort statements into expected effects, sedation safety and warning signs. Every wrong statement delays reporting bleeding or adds to the bleeding risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mild sore throat.
No driving and no legal papers today.
Chest pain, fever, black stools: report. Vomiting blood: report at once, not wait.
Anticoagulant restarts only on the provider's direction.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.nursesNote: 1400. Admitted with fatigue for 2 weeks and black, sticky stools for 3 days. Takes naproxen twice daily for knee arthritis. Reports burning epigastric pain before meals, 4 of 10. Lying: heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg. Standing: heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg, reports dizziness. Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Oral temperature 36.9 °C. SpO2 97% on room air. Skin and conjunctivae pale. Abdomen soft and nondistended. Bowel sounds active in all 4 quadrants. Hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, was 13.4 g/dL 6 months ago.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission note of a patient with fatigue and a change in stool color. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: black, sticky stools for 3 days
segments.rationale: Black, sticky, tarry stool is melena, a sign of bleeding high in the GI tract.

segments.text: Takes naproxen twice daily
segments.rationale: Regular use of a nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID) such as naproxen predisposes the patient to peptic ulcer disease and GI bleeding.

segments.text: burning epigastric pain before meals
segments.rationale: Burning epigastric pain when the stomach is empty fits a peptic ulcer, a common source of upper GI bleeding.

segments.text: Lying: heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg
segments.rationale: Within the expected range lying down. Alone it would not suggest blood loss, which is why the standing values matter.

segments.text: Standing: heart rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg, reports dizziness
segments.rationale: A heart rate rise and a blood pressure fall on standing with dizziness are orthostatic changes. They show a loss of circulating volume and a fall risk.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute
segments.rationale: Within the expected range.

segments.text: Oral temperature 36.9 °C
segments.rationale: No fever.

segments.text: SpO2 97% on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygenation is adequate.

segments.text: Skin and conjunctivae pale
segments.rationale: Pallor fits anemia from blood loss.

segments.text: Abdomen soft and nondistended
segments.rationale: No rigidity or distention, which makes perforation less likely.

segments.text: Bowel sounds active in all 4 quadrants
segments.rationale: Active bowel sounds are expected; blood in the gut can increase them.

segments.text: Hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, was 13.4 g/dL 6 months ago
segments.rationale: A large drop in hemoglobin confirms significant blood loss.

questions.takeaway: Recognize an upper GI bleed from the history and the body: melena, NSAID use, epigastric burning, pallor, a falling hemoglobin and orthostatic changes. A normal lying blood pressure can hide volume loss that standing reveals.
questions.strategy: Read the history as carefully as the vital signs. The drug, the stool and the pain each require follow up, and the lying values look normal only until you compare them with the standing values.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Black, sticky stools, naproxen twice daily, epigastric burning before meals.
Orthostatic changes with dizziness, pallor.
Hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, was 13.4 g/dL.
Lying vital signs, respiratory rate, temperature, SpO2, soft abdomen, bowel sounds.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
Chart so far: admitted at 1400 with fatigue, black, sticky stools for 3 days and naproxen twice daily; burning epigastric pain before meals; heart rate 98 rising to 126 beats per minute and blood pressure 118/72 falling to 92/58 mm Hg on standing, with dizziness; pale skin; hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, was 13.4 g/dL 6 months ago.

The black, sticky stools are called [[1]] and point to bleeding in the [[2]]. The naproxen most likely [[3]]. The change in heart rate and blood pressure on standing shows [[4]].

options.text: steatorrhea
options.rationale: Steatorrhea is pale, greasy, floating stool from poor fat absorption.

options.text: acholic stool
options.rationale: Acholic stool is clay colored from a lack of bile.

options.text: melena
options.rationale: Melena is black, tarry, sticky stool from blood that has been digested on its way through the gut.

options.text: hematochezia
options.rationale: Hematochezia is bright red or maroon blood in the stool, usually from bleeding lower in the GI tract.

options.text: stomach or duodenum
options.rationale: Blood from the upper GI tract is digested before it leaves the body, which turns stool black and tarry.

options.text: rectum or anus
options.rationale: Bleeding this low appears as bright red blood, not black stool.

options.text: liver or gallbladder
options.rationale: Liver and gallbladder problems change stool color through bile, giving clay colored stool, not tarry stool.

options.text: pancreatic ducts
options.rationale: Pancreatic duct problems reduce lipase and cause steatorrhea.

options.text: reduced iron absorption
options.rationale: Reduced iron absorption comes with gastric mucosa atrophy in aging. It causes anemia slowly but not black stool.

options.text: injured the lining of the stomach
options.rationale: NSAIDs such as naproxen damage the protective mucosa and predispose the patient to peptic ulcers and GI bleeding.

options.text: turned the stool black directly
options.rationale: Iron and bismuth can darken stool. Naproxen does not; it causes bleeding that makes stool black.

options.text: slowed peristalsis
options.rationale: Slowed peristalsis causes constipation, not black stool and a falling hemoglobin.

options.text: an expected change with aging
options.rationale: Aging can blunt blood pressure responses, but a 28 beat rise with dizziness and a falling hemoglobin is not an expected change.

options.text: a side effect of naproxen
options.rationale: Naproxen does not cause orthostatic changes directly; the bleeding it caused does.

options.text: anxiety about the admission
options.rationale: Anxiety can raise the heart rate but does not drop the blood pressure on standing.

options.text: loss of circulating blood volume
options.rationale: A rising heart rate and falling blood pressure on standing, with dizziness, show the body cannot maintain pressure after blood loss.

questions.takeaway: Melena means digested blood from the upper GI tract (stomach or duodenum). NSAIDs injure the gastric lining and cause ulcers and bleeding. Orthostatic changes show loss of circulating volume.
questions.strategy: Link each finding to its mechanism. Black and tarry means digested, which means high in the tract. A rise in pulse with a fall in pressure on standing means volume is missing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Black, sticky: melena.
Digested blood: stomach or duodenum.
NSAID injury to the gastric lining.
Orthostatic change: blood volume loss.

elimination.verdict: 1: melena. 2: stomach or duodenum. 3: injured the lining of the stomach. 4: loss of circulating blood volume.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.scenario:
Chart so far: admitted at 1400 with fatigue, black, sticky stools for 3 days and naproxen twice daily; burning epigastric pain before meals; heart rate 98 rising to 126 beats per minute and blood pressure 118/72 falling to 92/58 mm Hg on standing, with dizziness; pale skin; hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, was 13.4 g/dL 6 months ago. Naproxen is held, IV pantoprazole has been started, and 0.9% sodium chloride runs at 100 mL/hr. Prescriptions include a 500 mL bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride for a systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg, and an EGD tomorrow at 0900.

At 2200 the patient calls from the bathroom, feeling faint after passing a large maroon stool. The nurse helps the patient back to bed. Heart rate 134 beats per minute, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C. Skin is cool and clammy, and the patient is restless. The abdomen is soft, with no rigidity.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with an upper GI bleed who feels faint after passing a large maroon stool. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Give the prescribed 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: The systolic pressure is below 90 mm Hg, so the prescribed bolus is given now to restore circulating volume.

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: A heart rate of 134 beats per minute, hypotension and restlessness show a patient deteriorating from ongoing bleeding who needs a rapid team response.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler position
options.rationale: Sitting a hypotensive patient upright lowers blood flow to the brain further. The patient is kept flat.

options.text: Offer juice for energy
options.rationale: The patient is bleeding and has an EGD planned. Oral intake is not the treatment and may need to stop.

options.text: Give the next pantoprazole dose early
options.rationale: Acid suppression supports ulcer healing over days. It does not treat hypovolemia now.

options.text: Hypovolemia from ongoing GI bleeding
options.rationale: A large maroon stool with tachycardia, hypotension, cool clammy skin and restlessness shows continued blood loss with falling circulating volume.

options.text: Vasovagal fainting from straining
options.rationale: Straining can cause fainting, but vasovagal episodes slow the heart. This heart rate is 134 beats per minute.

options.text: Perforation of a peptic ulcer
options.rationale: Perforation brings severe pain and a rigid abdomen. The abdomen is soft.

options.text: Orthostatic change from aging
options.rationale: Aging does not explain a maroon stool and a blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg lying in bed.

options.text: Heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: They show whether the fluid replaces volume or the bleeding continues.

options.text: Hemoglobin and hematocrit
options.rationale: Serial values show the amount of blood lost and guide transfusion.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Blood in the gut can make bowel sounds active, but they do not measure blood loss.

options.text: Blood glucose
options.rationale: Nothing here suggests a glucose problem.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: There is no fever, and temperature does not track bleeding.

questions.takeaway: A large maroon stool with tachycardia, hypotension and cool, clammy skin in a patient with an upper GI bleed signals brisk ongoing bleeding and hypovolemia. Give the prescribed fluid, call for rapid help, keep the patient flat, and trend vital signs and hemoglobin and hematocrit.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Rule out the look alikes with one cue each: a fast heart rate rules out a vasovagal episode, and a soft abdomen rules out perforation. Then choose actions that restore volume and bring help, and parameters that measure blood loss.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Maroon stool, heart rate 134, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg: hypovolemia from bleeding.
Fast heart rate: not vasovagal. Soft abdomen: not perforation.
The prescribed bolus and the rapid response team.
Heart rate and blood pressure; hemoglobin and hematocrit.

elimination.verdict: Actions: give the bolus, call the rapid response team. Condition: hypovolemia from ongoing GI bleeding. Parameters: heart rate and blood pressure, hemoglobin and hematocrit.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a patient with an upper GI bleed for an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with moderate sedation at 0900. Overnight the patient received a fluid bolus and 2 units of packed red blood cells. At 0700, heart rate is 94 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mm Hg with no dizziness on sitting, and hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL. Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm the patient has been NPO since midnight
options.rationale: Patients are NPO for 6 to 8 hours before an endoscopy to lower the risk of aspiration under sedation.

options.text: Give the prescribed bowel prep
options.rationale: A bowel prep cleans the colon before a colonoscopy. An EGD views the esophagus, stomach and duodenum and does not need one.

options.text: Verify the informed consent is signed
options.rationale: Informed consent is obtained before an invasive procedure with sedation. The provider explains it, and the nurse verifies it is signed.

options.text: Explain that a sore throat may follow
options.rationale: A sore throat after the scope is a common, expected effect, and knowing this lowers worry afterward.

options.text: Screen for metal implants
options.rationale: Metal screening is part of the MRI checklist. An EGD uses no magnet.

options.text: Review drug allergies and medical history
options.rationale: Sedatives and other drugs are given during the EGD, so allergies and history are reviewed first.

questions.takeaway: Before an EGD: NPO 6 to 8 hours, signed informed consent, allergies and history reviewed, sedation planned, and teaching about the procedure and a possible sore throat afterward.
questions.strategy: Match each action to the procedure. The two wrong options are correct for other tests: the bowel prep for colonoscopy, metal screening for MRI.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPO, consent, allergies and history.
Expected sore throat.
Bowel prep belongs to colonoscopy; metal screening belongs to MRI.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.
