questions.objective: Explain nursing responsibilities and patient education for GI diagnostic procedures, including preparation, monitoring, and post procedure care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who had an EGD at 0900 that found a duodenal ulcer, treated with clips. The gag reflex returned at 1000, clear liquids were tolerated, and IV fluids were stopped at 1300. At 1600 the patient passes a soft black stool. The patient is alert, denies dizziness, and rates epigastric pain 2 of 10. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Reassure the patient that this is old blood
options.rationale: Blood already in the gut can keep coming out as black stool for a few days after bleeding stops, so this may be true. The nurse cannot conclude it without first assessing for rebleeding.

options.text: Compare vital signs with earlier values
options.rationale: A black stool after treatment is either old blood passing or new bleeding. Heart rate, blood pressure and orthostatic changes compared with earlier values tell the two apart, so the nurse assesses first.

options.text: Make the patient NPO and restart the IV
options.rationale: These would fit active rebleeding, but nothing yet shows rebleeding. Acting before assessing treats a conclusion the nurse has not reached.

options.text: Report rebleeding to the provider
options.rationale: The provider will need data, but calling this rebleeding is a conclusion the findings do not yet support. The nurse gathers the data first.

questions.takeaway: After an upper GI bleed is treated, black stool may continue for a few days as old blood passes. Signs of new bleeding are a rising heart rate, a falling blood pressure, orthostatic dizziness, vomiting blood or coffee ground material, maroon stools and a falling hemoglobin. Assess before deciding.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Two options are conclusions in opposite directions (old blood or rebleeding), and one is an action based on a conclusion. When the stem gives a finding that has two explanations, assess to tell them apart.

steps.detail: Old blood passing or new bleeding.
Reassurance and reporting rebleeding each assume an answer.
NPO and IV fluids treat bleeding not yet shown.
Compare vital signs with earlier values.

elimination.verdict: B. Compare vital signs with earlier values.

questions.objective: Differentiate normal and abnormal GI assessment findings and identify findings that require further evaluation

questions.scenario: Chart so far: admitted with melena from a duodenal ulcer linked to twice daily naproxen; hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL on admission; hypovolemia at 2200 treated with a fluid bolus and 2 units of packed red blood cells; ulcer treated with clips during an EGD. A soft black stool at 1600 yesterday came with unchanged vital signs. On the morning of discharge the nurse reviews findings and the patient's teaching.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a patient with an upper GI bleed before discharge. For each finding, indicate whether it shows an effective outcome or needs follow up.

rows.text: Heart rate 82 beats per minute lying and 88 standing, no dizziness
rows.rationale: No orthostatic change, which shows circulating volume has been restored.

rows.text: Hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, was 9.0 g/dL yesterday
rows.rationale: The hemoglobin is holding steady after transfusion, which shows no ongoing blood loss.

rows.text: Says, "I will take my naproxen with food from now on."
rows.rationale: Food may ease stomach upset but does not prevent NSAID injury to the gastric lining. The patient needs teaching to avoid NSAIDs unless the provider directs otherwise.

rows.text: Says, "I will call if I vomit something that looks like coffee grounds."
rows.rationale: Coffee ground vomit is digested blood and a sign of rebleeding. The patient knows to report it.

rows.text: Reports new dizziness walking to the bathroom this morning
rows.rationale: New dizziness on walking can signal renewed blood loss or volume deficit, even with a steady hemoglobin. It needs assessment before discharge.

rows.text: Stool this morning brown and formed
rows.rationale: Return to brown stool shows the old blood has passed and no new bleeding is reaching the stool.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an upper GI bleed on two fronts: the body (no orthostatic change, steady hemoglobin, brown stool) and the teaching (avoid NSAIDs, report coffee ground vomit, black stools or dizziness). A plausible but wrong plan, like taking an NSAID with food, needs follow up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Check each finding against the cause and the danger. The cause was the NSAID, so any plan that keeps it needs follow up. The danger is rebleeding, so a new symptom of volume loss needs follow up even when the numbers look good.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No orthostatic change, steady hemoglobin, brown stool: effective.
Reports coffee ground vomit: effective. NSAID with food: needs follow up.
Dizziness on walking: needs follow up.

elimination.verdict: Effective outcome: rows 1, 2, 4 and 6. Needs follow up: rows 3 and 5.

questions.objective: Obtain a focused GI health history, including nutritional habits, bowel patterns, and common GI symptoms

questions.stem: After a stroke, a patient coughs and has a wet voice with sips of water. Bowel sounds are active. Which nutrition plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition
options.rationale: Unsafe swallowing makes oral intake unsafe, but parenteral nutrition is used when the GI tract cannot be adequately used. This patient's GI tract works.

options.text: Continuation of the current oral diet
options.rationale: A working bowel does not make swallowing safe. Coughing and a wet voice after sips signal a high risk of aspiration with oral intake.

options.text: Enteral nutrition by feeding tube
options.rationale: Enteral nutrition is indicated when the GI tract functions but oral intake is unsafe or inadequate. Active bowel sounds show function; coughing with sips shows unsafe swallowing.

options.text: Peripheral parenteral nutrition
options.rationale: Peripheral parenteral nutrition is still an intravenous route, used when the GI tract cannot be adequately used. Active bowel sounds show a working GI tract, so the route stays enteral.

questions.takeaway: Choose the route by asking two questions: does the GI tract work, and is oral intake safe and adequate? A working gut with unsafe swallowing means enteral nutrition; a gut that cannot be adequately used means parenteral nutrition.
questions.strategy: Two options choose parenteral nutrition by different routes. Check the bowel findings first: if the gut works, the intravenous route is not needed.

steps.detail: Coughing and a wet voice with sips: oral intake is unsafe. Active bowel sounds: the GI tract works.
A working bowel does not protect the airway.
A working gut does not need the intravenous route.
Enteral nutrition fits a working gut with unsafe swallowing.

elimination.verdict: C. Enteral nutrition by feeding tube.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: A patient with dysphagia no longer needs a large bore nasogastric tube for suction. Feedings are prescribed for 2 to 3 weeks. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Begin feedings through the existing tube
options.rationale: A large bore double lumen tube is meant for decompression, lavage and medications. Using it for weeks of feeding ignores what the tube is built for.

options.text: Replace it with a small bore tube confirmed by x ray
options.rationale: Small bore single lumen tubes of 8 to 12 Fr are used for feeding and medications. Decompression is no longer needed, and a blindly inserted tube needs x ray confirmation before anything goes through it.

options.text: Keep the tube to suction and give medications through it
options.rationale: Suction is no longer needed. Keeping the tube to suction removes gastric contents and does not provide nutrition.

options.text: Request a gastrostomy tube for the feedings
options.rationale: Gastrostomy and jejunostomy tubes are for long term feeding. A nasal tube suits a short course of 2 to 3 weeks.

questions.takeaway: Large bore nasogastric tubes (14 to 18 Fr, double lumen) are for decompression, lavage and medications. Small bore tubes (8 to 12 Fr, single lumen) are for feeding and medications. When the goal changes from draining the stomach to feeding it, the tube changes too.
questions.strategy: Ask what the patient needs now, not what tube is already in. Then match the need and the expected duration to the tube built for it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Suction is no longer needed, so the goal is feeding and medications, not decompression.
Feeding is the job of a small bore single lumen tube, which removes A and C.
2 to 3 weeks is short term, so a nasal tube, which removes D.

elimination.verdict: B. Replace it with a small bore tube confirmed by x ray.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: The nurse aspirates fluid with a pH of 4 from a newly inserted nasogastric feeding tube. The placement x ray has not been read yet. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Wait for the x ray result
options.rationale: A newly inserted tube needs x ray confirmation before first use, and the nurse reviews the result before giving anything through the tube.

options.text: Start the feeding as prescribed
options.rationale: An acidic aspirate supports gastric placement, but pH alone cannot guarantee it. A new tube still needs x ray confirmation before first use.

options.text: Inject air and auscultate, then feed
options.rationale: Air bolus auscultation does not reliably verify placement. A sound over the stomach can be heard even when the tube sits in the airway or esophagus.

options.text: Flush with water, then start the feeding
options.rationale: Water is held until placement is confirmed, the same as formula and medications. Water given through a tube in the airway enters the lungs.

questions.takeaway: A blindly inserted feeding tube is confirmed by x ray before first use. Formula, water, and medications all wait for the documented result; pH and air bolus checks do not replace it.
questions.strategy: Three options put something into the tube before confirmation. Ask what the tube must have before anything goes in.

steps.detail: A new tube, and the x ray has not been read.
pH alone cannot guarantee placement; air bolus auscultation is not reliable.
Water is a substance given through the tube, so it also waits.
Hold all tube use until the documented x ray result confirms placement.

elimination.verdict: A. Wait for the x ray result.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give a bolus feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube. After x ray confirmation 2 days ago, the tube was marked and documented at 55 cm at the naris. The nurse now finds the mark at 49 cm and the tape loose. The patient has no cough, and SpO2 is 96% on room air. The aspirate has a pH of 4. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the feeding and document the acidic aspirate
options.rationale: An acidic aspirate and quiet breathing make this tempting, but aspirate pH alone cannot guarantee placement. The cue is the mark: 6 cm of tube has come out since the confirmed baseline.

options.text: Advance the tube to the 55 cm mark and give the feeding
options.rationale: This is the near miss: it restores the documented length. Advancing the tube does not prove where the tip now lies, and a tube that has moved needs verification, not a blind adjustment followed by a feeding.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees and give the feeding
options.rationale: Raising the head of the bed reduces aspiration risk, but it does not address a tube that may be displaced. Placement comes before feeding.

options.text: Hold the feeding and verify placement per policy
options.rationale: The external length differs from the documented baseline, a sign of displacement. When placement is uncertain, the nurse holds tube use, secures the tube and obtains further verification.

questions.takeaway: Before each feeding and medication, compare the external tube length with the documented baseline. If the length has changed, hold tube use and obtain further verification, even when the aspirate is acidic.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option is something a nurse does during tube feeding: check pH, restore the mark, raise the head of the bed. Weigh the acidic pH against the 6 cm change in the mark; pH alone cannot guarantee placement, and the moved mark makes placement uncertain.

steps.detail: Mark at 49 cm now, documented at 55 cm, with loose tape.
An acidic aspirate supports gastric placement but cannot guarantee it.
Pushing the tube back or raising the bed does not confirm the tip.
Hold tube use and obtain further verification.

elimination.verdict: D. Hold the feeding and verify placement per policy.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: During continuous nasogastric tube feeding, which findings require the nurse to act to reduce the risk of aspiration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Head of the bed at 10 degrees with the pump running
options.rationale: Lying nearly flat while formula runs lets it reflux toward the airway. The head of the bed is raised 30 to 45 degrees during feeding, so you raise it now.

options.text: Tube mark at the documented length
options.rationale: The mark matches the documented length, which supports that the tube has not moved. No action is needed for this finding.

options.text: Tape at the naris loose and peeling
options.rationale: A tube that is not secured can slip out of the stomach and deliver formula into the esophagus or airway. You resecure it and check placement.

options.text: Reports fullness and formula in the mouth
options.rationale: Reflux and regurgitation are warning signs that come before aspiration. You act on them now rather than waiting for coughing or a drop in oxygen.

options.text: Soft abdomen, bowel sounds present, no nausea
options.rationale: These show the patient is tolerating the feeding and need no action.

options.text: Breathing unlabored, oxygen saturation 97%
options.rationale: Breathing shows no sign of aspiration. These are baseline values to keep comparing, not a reason to act.

questions.takeaway: Aspiration prevention during enteral feeding is head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees, a verified and secured tube, and watching for reflux, vomiting and intolerance. On rounds, act on a lowered bed, a loose tube and any sign of reflux.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings by the three defenses: position, tube security and signs of reflux. Any finding that weakens one of them needs action; findings that confirm a defense is holding do not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 10 degrees with the pump running is too low: act on A.
The mark matches (B, no action), but the tape is loose (C, act).
Fullness and formula in the mouth are reflux (D, act); a soft abdomen and normal breathing need no action.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.nursesNote: 1400: Patient, 66 years old, receiving continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube at 55 mL per hour. Head of bed at 40 degrees. Coughing during the last hour, was not coughing at 1000. External tube mark at 60 cm at the right naris, matches the documented baseline. One soft formed stool at 1200. SpO2 90% on room air, was 96% at 1000. Oral temperature 37.0 °C. Abdomen firm and distended, was soft at 1000. Abdominal pain 0 of 10. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 breaths per minute at 1000.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the note of a patient receiving continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Head of bed at 40 degrees
segments.rationale: A head of bed angle of 40 degrees is within the 30 to 45 degrees used during feeding.

segments.text: Coughing during the last hour, was not coughing at 1000
segments.rationale: New coughing during feeding can signal aspiration of formula.

segments.text: External tube mark at 60 cm at the right naris, matches the documented baseline
segments.rationale: A mark that matches the baseline does not suggest displacement.

segments.text: One soft formed stool at 1200
segments.rationale: A soft formed stool does not suggest diarrhea or intolerance.

segments.text: SpO2 90% on room air, was 96% at 1000
segments.rationale: Oxygen desaturation during feeding can signal aspiration.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C
segments.rationale: No fever is present at this time.

segments.text: Abdomen firm and distended, was soft at 1000
segments.rationale: New distention is a sign of feeding intolerance and raises the risk of vomiting and aspiration.

segments.text: Abdominal pain 0 of 10
segments.rationale: No abdominal pain is reported.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 breaths per minute at 1000
segments.rationale: A rising respiratory rate with coughing and desaturation points to a breathing problem during feeding.

questions.takeaway: Monitor tolerance with the abdomen (fullness, nausea, distention), the stool, and the lungs (coughing, dyspnea, oxygen desaturation). Compare each finding with its earlier value.
questions.strategy: Look for what changed since 1000. Findings that match a baseline or a target are not the cues.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Coughing, SpO2, abdomen, and respiratory rate all changed since 1000.
Head of bed 40 degrees and the matching tube mark meet the plan.
A formed stool, no pain, and 37.0 °C need no follow up.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.scenario: A patient receives continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube at 60 mL per hour. At 0300 the patient vomits formula and begins coughing. Respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute, was 18 breaths per minute at 2400. SpO2 is 87% on room air, was 95% at 2400. Crackles are heard in the right lower lobe. Oral temperature is 37.2 °C.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who vomits and begins coughing during a continuous tube feeding. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Stop the feeding pump
options.rationale: With suspected aspiration, the first priority is to stop the feeding so no more formula reaches the airway.

options.text: Check the gastric residual volume
options.rationale: Residual volume does not reliably predict aspiration, and checking it delays stopping the formula.

options.text: Lower the rate to 30 mL per hour and recheck the SpO2 in 1 hour
options.rationale: A lower rate still delivers formula, and an hour is too long with SpO2 87%.

options.text: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water
options.rationale: More fluid through the tube adds to the risk while aspiration is suspected.

options.text: Assess the airway and breathing and call for help
options.rationale: After stopping the feeding, the nurse assesses the airway and breathing and obtains help.

options.text: Feeding intolerance from too high a rate
options.rationale: Vomiting can reflect intolerance, but coughing, desaturation, and new right lower lobe crackles point to formula in the lungs.

options.text: Refeeding syndrome
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is an electrolyte shift after nutrition restarts, not a sudden breathing change after vomiting.

options.text: Aspiration of formula
options.rationale: Vomiting followed by coughing, SpO2 87%, a respiratory rate of 30, and new crackles in the right lower lobe fit aspiration.

options.text: Clogged feeding tube
options.rationale: A clogged tube stops delivery; it does not cause vomiting with desaturation and crackles.

options.text: SpO2
options.rationale: Shows whether oxygenation recovers after the feeding is stopped.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Weight tracks fluid and nutrition over days, not the airway now.

options.text: Respiratory rate and lung sounds
options.rationale: Show whether the breathing problem and the right lower lobe crackles are worsening or clearing.

options.text: Stool frequency
options.rationale: Stool pattern tracks tolerance of the gut, not the lungs.

options.text: Serum phosphate
options.rationale: Phosphate is monitored for refeeding syndrome, which is not the problem here.

questions.takeaway: Suspected aspiration during feeding: stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, and obtain help. Watch the SpO2, respiratory rate, and lung sounds.
questions.strategy: Name the problem from the sequence: vomiting, then coughing, desaturation, and new crackles. Then pick actions that stop more formula and protect the airway now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vomiting followed by respiratory changes and right lower lobe crackles: aspiration.
Stop the pump; assess airway and breathing and call for help.
Residual checks, rate changes, and flushes delay or add fluid.
SpO2, respiratory rate, and lung sounds change within minutes.

elimination.verdict: Stop the feeding pump and assess the airway and breathing and call for help; aspiration of formula; SpO2 and respiratory rate with lung sounds.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient receiving continuous feeding at 50 mL/hour through a small bore nasogastric tube. Facility policy is to check gastric residual volume every 4 hours and to hold the feeding for a residual greater than 500 mL. The residual is 240 mL at 1200, was 160 mL at 0800. The abdomen is soft and not distended, the patient denies nausea, and the patient has not vomited. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the feeding for 1 hour and recheck the residual
options.rationale: A rise from 160 mL to 240 mL looks like a warning. The residual alone does not predict aspiration, it is below the policy limit, and there is no vomiting, distention or nausea, so holding the feeding only reduces intake.

options.text: Hold the feeding and report the rising residual
options.rationale: This is the near miss: reporting a trend sounds like safe practice. But the residual alone does not reliably predict aspiration, it is under the policy limit, and no other sign of intolerance is present, so there is no reason to stop the feeding.

options.text: Continue the feeding and monitor for intolerance
options.rationale: Residual volume is interpreted with vomiting, distention and other intolerance findings. None are present and the value is below the policy limit, so the feeding continues with monitoring.

options.text: Request a change to feeding into the small intestine
options.rationale: There are no other signs of intolerance, so a change of route is not indicated by this number.

questions.takeaway: Gastric residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration. Follow facility policy and interpret the residual with vomiting, distention, nausea, and other intolerance findings.
questions.strategy: Three options react to the rising number in ways that sound careful. Decide by the rest of the picture and the policy: no vomiting, no distention, no nausea, and a value under the 500 mL limit.

steps.detail: No vomiting, distention or nausea, and 240 mL is under the 500 mL policy limit.
A rising residual alone does not predict aspiration.
Holding, with or without a report, cuts intake without a sign of intolerance.
Continue the feeding and keep monitoring for intolerance.

elimination.verdict: C. Continue the feeding and monitor for intolerance.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the findings of a newly admitted patient. Which findings indicate undernutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Unintended 5 kg weight loss in 2 months
options.rationale: Unintentional weight loss is a key assessment finding of undernutrition.

options.text: Blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg
options.rationale: This blood pressure does not reflect nutrient intake or absorption.

options.text: Sacral pressure injury unhealed after 4 weeks
options.rationale: Poor wound healing is an assessment finding of undernutrition, because healing needs protein and calories.

options.text: Weak grip and daytime fatigue
options.rationale: Muscle weakness and fatigue are assessment findings of undernutrition.

options.text: Urine output 1,500 mL in 24 hours
options.rationale: This output does not suggest a nutrient deficit.

options.text: Eats 30% of meals, refuses the supplement
options.rationale: Undernutrition is inadequate intake to meet the body's needs, and poor appetite is a risk factor. This intake does not meet needs.

questions.takeaway: Undernutrition shows as unintentional weight loss, muscle weakness, fatigue, and poor wound healing, often with poor intake. Identify deficits early so nutrition support can start.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each finding reflects intake, muscle, energy, or healing. Normal vital signs and output do not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A 5 kg loss without trying is unintentional.
A sacral injury not healing in 4 weeks, weak grip, and fatigue.
30% of meals with the supplement untouched.
Blood pressure and urine output do not reflect nutrition here.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with advanced cancer of the tongue who can no longer swallow safely. The gastrointestinal tract is functional. The patient is alert and oriented, accurately explains the risks and benefits of a gastrostomy tube, and has a written advance directive declining artificial nutrition. The patient declines the tube again today. The patient's adult child, who is the durable power of attorney for health care, insists that the tube be placed. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Obtain consent for the tube from the durable power of attorney
options.rationale: A durable power of attorney makes health decisions only when the patient cannot make them. This patient is alert and able to decide.

options.text: Support the patient's refusal and inform the provider
options.rationale: The patient has decision making capacity and an advance directive that matches the spoken choice. The nurse honors the patient's preference, documents it, and communicates it to the provider.

options.text: Request an ethics consultation before any decision is made
options.rationale: This is the near miss: an ethics committee helps with real conflict, and the family disagrees. But it fits when a patient cannot express wishes and no directive exists. This patient is alert, explains the choice, and has a directive, so the decision belongs to the patient.

options.text: Encourage the patient to reconsider the tube with the family
options.rationale: Family involvement sounds supportive, and the functional gut makes feeding possible. But pressing a capable patient to revisit a clear, informed refusal does not respect the patient's decision.

questions.takeaway: A working gut makes enteral feeding possible, not required. A patient with decision making capacity decides, and an advance directive guides care; the durable power of attorney and ethics committee step in when the patient cannot express wishes.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three options each sound like respect for someone: the proxy, the process, the family. Ask whether the patient can decide now: alert, oriented and explaining the risks means yes, and the directive confirms the choice.

steps.detail: Alert, oriented, accurately explains risks and benefits, with a directive declining artificial nutrition.
The durable power of attorney acts only when the patient cannot decide.
Ethics review fits when wishes cannot be known.
A capable patient's informed refusal is not reopened to satisfy the family.
Honor and document the patient's decision and inform the provider.

elimination.verdict: B. Support the patient's refusal and inform the provider.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: Two days after enteral feeding starts, a severely undernourished patient has weakness, an irregular pulse, and low potassium, magnesium and phosphorus. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Refeeding syndrome
options.rationale: Severe undernutrition, a recent restart of feeding, and low phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium with weakness and a new irregular rhythm fit refeeding syndrome.

options.text: Fluid overload
options.rationale: Fluid overload would bring edema, crackles, or a rising weight, and it does not explain three low electrolytes.

options.text: Dehydration
options.rationale: No diarrhea, dry mucous membranes, or low output is reported, and dehydration does not explain three low electrolytes.

options.text: Aspiration of formula
options.rationale: Aspiration presents with coughing, dyspnea, or desaturation, not low electrolytes.

questions.takeaway: Refeeding syndrome is a dangerous electrolyte shift after nutrition restarts in a severely undernourished patient. Watch potassium, magnesium, and phosphate, with I&O and daily weights.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real complication of enteral feeding. Choose the one that explains the history and all three low electrolytes.

steps.detail: Severe undernutrition, with feeding restarted 2 days ago.
Low phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium; weakness; a new irregular rhythm.
Overload, dehydration and aspiration do not explain three low electrolytes.
Refeeding syndrome.

elimination.verdict: A. Refeeding syndrome.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A patient at risk for refeeding syndrome receives continuous enteral feeding. Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weigh the patient daily on the same scale
options.rationale: Daily weights track fluid balance and the response to feeding.

options.text: Advance the rate faster than prescribed
options.rationale: Continuous feeding rates are advanced only as ordered. Faster advancement raises the risk of dangerous electrolyte shifts.

options.text: Review ordered potassium, magnesium and phosphate
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome shifts potassium, magnesium, and phosphate, so the nurse monitors the ordered values.

options.text: Count water flushes in total fluid intake
options.rationale: Flushes are included in total fluid intake, so I&O is accurate.

options.text: Omit the prescribed water flushes
options.rationale: Flushes keep the tube open and are given as ordered. Holding them risks a clogged tube and does not prevent refeeding syndrome.

questions.takeaway: For a patient at risk for refeeding syndrome, monitor I&O (including flushes), daily weights, and ordered potassium, magnesium, and phosphate values, and advance feeding only as ordered.
questions.strategy: Keep the monitoring actions; reject anything that changes the plan without an order.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Daily weight and the ordered electrolytes.
Flushes count in total fluid intake.
Rate increases need an order; holding flushes risks clogging.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A patient's nasogastric feeding tube has caused a small area of nonblanching redness on the naris, and the lips are dry. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Remove the tape and leave the tube unsecured
options.rationale: An unsecured tube can be pulled and displaced. The tube stays secured, but away from the injured skin.

options.text: Apply additional tape over the red area
options.rationale: More tape over the area keeps the pressure on injured skin and hides it from inspection.

options.text: Document the redness and recheck the area in 24 hours
options.rationale: Nonblanching redness is a pressure injury, not an expected finding, and waiting lets it worsen.

options.text: Move the tape off the red area and give lip care
options.rationale: The nurse inspects the nares for pressure injury, secures the tube to reduce pressure, provides oral and lip care, and documents the site condition.

questions.takeaway: For a nasal feeding tube, inspect the nares and securement for pressure injury, secure the tube to reduce pulling and pressure, give frequent oral and lip care, and document the site.
questions.strategy: Two options act on the naris. Keep the tube secured and move the pressure, rather than removing securement or adding more tape.

steps.detail: Nonblanching redness where the tube presses; dry lips.
An unsecured tube risks displacement.
A pressure injury is not expected.
Resecure off the area, give oral and lip care, and document.

elimination.verdict: D. Move the tape off the red area and give lip care.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing four patients who need tube feeding. For which patient should the nurse anticipate a gastrostomy tube rather than a nasal tube?

options.text: Stroke, failed swallow screen, recovery expected in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Feeding is expected to last only a short time, so the less invasive nasal route fits.

options.text: Jaw surgery, eating again in 10 days
options.rationale: This is short term feeding, and a nasal tube is less invasive and preferred when the duration is brief.

options.text: Stroke with aspiration, feeding needed 6 more months
options.rationale: Expected duration guides the route. Months of feeding call for a gastrostomy, which is meant for long term support, rather than a nasal tube meant for short periods.

options.text: Paralytic ileus with a distended abdomen
options.rationale: The GI tract cannot be used, so neither tube fits. This patient needs parenteral nutrition, not a gastrostomy.

questions.takeaway: Nasal tubes are for short term feeding; gastrostomy and jejunostomy tubes are for long term feeding. Duration, GI function and gastric emptying guide the route, and a gut that cannot be used rules out both.
questions.strategy: First ask whether the gut can be used. Then ask how long the feeding is expected to last; only a long expected course moves the patient to a tube through the abdomen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Paralytic ileus rules out enteral feeding entirely, which removes D.
10 days and 2 weeks are short term, which removes A and B.
At least 6 more months of feeding fits a gastrostomy.

elimination.verdict: C. The patient expected to need feeding for at least 6 more months.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a patient's percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube site. Which findings require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dry, intact skin of normal color
options.rationale: Dry, intact skin with no color change is the expected site condition.

options.text: Formula leaking and soaking the gauze
options.rationale: Leakage at the site irritates the skin and can signal a problem with the tube or stoma, so it is assessed and reported.

options.text: External mark matches the documented mark
options.rationale: A matching mark shows the tube has not moved.

options.text: Site pain rising from mild to severe
options.rationale: New or rising pain at the site needs follow up for infection or tube problems.

options.text: Tubing secured with no tension
options.rationale: Securing the tubing to reduce pulling and pressure is the goal of site care.

questions.takeaway: Assess gastrostomy and jejunostomy sites for redness, pain, drainage, leakage, and swelling. Keep the site clean and dry and secure the tubing to reduce pulling.
questions.strategy: Separate findings that meet the goals of site care from findings on the list of warning signs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leakage soaking the gauze; pain rising from mild to severe.
Intact skin, a matching mark, and secured tubing.

elimination.verdict: B, D.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a spouse to give bolus gastrostomy feedings at home. Which statement by the spouse indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will keep the head raised 30 to 45 degrees."
options.rationale: This is correct. Elevation during feeding reduces aspiration risk.

options.text: "If coughing starts, I will slow the feeding and finish."
options.rationale: Coughing or trouble breathing during a feeding can mean aspiration. The caregiver stops the feeding and seeks help, so this statement needs more teaching.

options.text: "I will flush the tube with water before and after each feeding."
options.rationale: This is correct. Flushes before and after intermittent feedings keep the tube open.

options.text: "I will call if the site becomes red or leaks."
options.rationale: This is correct. Redness, swelling, and leakage at the site need follow up.

questions.takeaway: Teach when to stop a feeding and seek help, and confirm understanding with teach back and return demonstration. Coughing or trouble breathing means stop, not slow down.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that keeps the feeding going when it should stop.

steps.detail: A need for more teaching means find the unsafe statement.
Elevation, flushes, and reporting site changes are correct.
Slowing and finishing a feeding during coughing or trouble breathing is unsafe.

elimination.verdict: B. Slowing and finishing the feeding when coughing starts.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse is hanging a new container of formula for a continuous gastrostomy feeding. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check formula, rate and expiration against the order
options.rationale: The nurse verifies formula, route, volume, rate, and expiration date before hanging formula.

options.text: Connect the set with an ENFit connector
options.rationale: ENFit connections fit only enteral devices, which prevents wrong route administration such as formula entering an intravenous line.

options.text: Use a Luer adapter if the ENFit set does not fit
options.rationale: Luer connectors also fit intravenous devices, which defeats the protection against wrong route administration.

options.text: Label the formula and the set
options.rationale: Labeling the formula and equipment supports safe hang times and correct identification.

options.text: Add new formula to the formula still hanging
options.rationale: Adding fresh formula to old formula breaks hang time limits and increases handling and contamination.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene and minimize handling
options.rationale: Hand hygiene and minimal handling reduce contamination of the formula.

questions.takeaway: Before hanging formula, verify it against the order, perform hand hygiene, minimize handling, label the formula and set, follow hang time limits, and use ENFit connections to prevent wrong route administration.
questions.strategy: Treat each option as true or false against two goals: the right formula by the right route, and no contamination.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Verify against the order; ENFit, never a Luer adapter.
Hand hygiene, minimal handling, labeling; never top off old formula.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give two liquid medications at 0900 through the gastrostomy tube of a patient receiving continuous feeding. The pharmacist has confirmed that both are appropriate for the tube and the delivery site and that neither requires a longer feeding interruption. In which order should the nurse perform the actions?

options.text: Give the second medication
options.rationale: The second medication follows the flush that cleared the first, so the two never mix in the tube.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water to clear the first medication from the tube
options.rationale: A 30 mL flush between medications keeps them separate and prevents clogging.

options.text: Pause the pump and check the tube placement
options.rationale: Placement is checked before medications, and the feeding is paused so medications are given separately from formula.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water and restart the feeding at the ordered rate
options.rationale: A final 30 mL flush clears the last medication; the feeding then resumes as ordered.

options.text: Give the first medication
options.rationale: The first medication goes in after the tube has been flushed.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water before any medication enters the tube
options.rationale: A 30 mL flush before medications clears formula from the tube.

questions.takeaway: Give each medication separately with a 30 mL water flush before, between, and after, after checking placement. Include the flushes in total fluid intake.
questions.strategy: Start with the check that makes the tube safe to use, then alternate flush and medication, and end with a flush before the feeding restarts.

steps.detail: Pause the pump and check placement.
Flush, first medication, flush, second medication.
Flush and restart the feeding.

elimination.verdict: Pause and check placement; flush; first medication; flush; second medication; flush and restart.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing medications for a patient who receives feedings through a gastrostomy tube and takes nothing by mouth. The prescription reads "diltiazem SR 120 mg by gastrostomy tube daily," and the tablet form is the only one on the unit. Tube placement has been checked, and the tube flushes with no resistance. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the tablet and contact the pharmacist
options.rationale: Each medication must be appropriate for the tube. SR means sustained release; crushing it releases the full dose at once, so the nurse holds it and asks the pharmacist about a form that is safe for the tube.

options.text: Crush the tablet, dissolve it in water, and give it with flushes
options.rationale: This is the near miss: it is the correct method for a tablet that can be crushed. The cue is the letters SR after the drug name: a sustained release tablet must not be crushed.

options.text: Crush the tablet and mix it into the formula bag
options.rationale: Mixing into formula seems to keep the dose slow, but medications are not mixed with formula, and crushing the tablet still destroys the sustained release design.

options.text: Give the tablet whole, followed by a 60 mL water flush
options.rationale: Giving it whole seems to protect the sustained release design, but a whole tablet cannot pass through a feeding tube and will clog it.

questions.takeaway: Verify that each medication is appropriate for the tube before giving it. Sustained or extended release (SR, ER, XL) tablets are not crushed; ask the pharmacist about a liquid or other safe form.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option protects something real: the routine crushing method, the slow delivery, or the intact tablet. The subtle cue is SR after the drug name, which means sustained release: it cannot be crushed, and a whole tablet cannot go down the tube.

steps.detail: SR after the drug name means sustained release.
Correct for most tablets, unsafe for a sustained release one, whether flushed or mixed into formula.
A whole tablet clogs the tube.
Hold the tablet and ask the pharmacist about another form.

elimination.verdict: A. Hold the tablet and contact the pharmacist.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: The feeding pump alarms for occlusion, and a water flush through the gastrostomy tube meets resistance. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Instill 30 mL of cola and clamp the tube
options.rationale: Carbonated beverages and juice are avoided when unclogging tubes, because their acid can make formula proteins clump and worsen the clog.

options.text: Use a 10 mL syringe to flush with more force
options.rationale: A clogged tube is never forced. A small syringe creates high pressure that can rupture the tube.

options.text: Keep the pump running at the prescribed rate
options.rationale: The pump cannot clear the clog, and the patient receives no formula while the tube is blocked.

options.text: Flush gently with water, then follow policy
options.rationale: For a clogged tube, the nurse attempts gentle water flushing, never forces it, and follows policy if the clog remains.

questions.takeaway: For a clogged feeding tube, attempt gentle water flushing and never force it. Do not use carbonated beverages or juice. Prevent clogs with 30 mL flushes before, between, and after medications.
questions.strategy: Three options apply force or the wrong fluid. Find the option that uses water gently.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Occlusion alarm and resistance to a water flush.
A 10 mL syringe or pump pressure forces the tube.
Carbonated drinks and juice worsen clogs.
Gentle water flushing, then policy.

elimination.verdict: D. Flush gently with water, then follow policy.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: Six days after bowel surgery, a patient with a paralytic ileus has absent bowel sounds and a distended abdomen. Which nutrition plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Feeding through the existing nasogastric tube
options.rationale: A tube already in place is convenient, but enteral nutrition needs a functional GI tract. Formula put into a bowel that is not moving adds to the distention.

options.text: An oral diet advanced slowly
options.rationale: Oral intake does not help when the bowel cannot move or absorb food, and it would worsen the ileus.

options.text: Parenteral nutrition
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition delivers nutrients intravenously when the GI tract cannot be adequately used. Peripheral (PPN) and total parenteral nutrition (TPN) are its two types.

options.text: Feeding through a new small bore tube
options.rationale: Tube size does not solve the problem. Any enteral route still relies on a working bowel.

questions.takeaway: Enteral nutrition delivers nutrients into a functional GI tract. Parenteral nutrition, peripheral or total, delivers nutrients intravenously when the GI tract cannot be adequately used.
questions.strategy: Ask first whether the gut works. Absent bowel sounds and distention mean it does not, whatever tube is in place.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ileus, absent bowel sounds and distention: the GI tract cannot be used.
Three options feed into the GI tract; only one bypasses it.
Parenteral nutrition.

elimination.verdict: C. Parenteral nutrition.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing an older adult who lives alone. Which findings place the patient at risk for undernutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Walks 20 minutes daily with a neighbor
options.rationale: Regular activity with social contact is a healthy habit, not a risk factor.

options.text: Has heart failure and kidney disease
options.rationale: Chronic illness is a risk factor for undernutrition.

options.text: Poor appetite since a spouse died
options.rationale: Poor appetite is a risk factor for undernutrition, whatever its cause.

options.text: Coughs when drinking thin liquids
options.rationale: Coughing with liquids suggests difficulty swallowing, a risk factor for undernutrition and for aspiration.

options.text: No longer drives and has no bus to a store
options.rationale: Limited access to food is a risk factor for undernutrition.

options.text: Takes a daily multivitamin
options.rationale: A multivitamin does not create risk, and it does not replace adequate intake.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for undernutrition are poor appetite, difficulty swallowing, chronic illness and limited food access. The nursing priority is to identify deficits early.
questions.strategy: Test each finding against the four risk factors: appetite, swallowing, chronic illness and access to food.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Grief has reduced the appetite.
Coughing with thin liquids.
Heart failure and kidney disease.
No car and no bus to a store.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, E.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.stem: A patient with delayed gastric emptying has had aspiration pneumonia with nasogastric feedings. Long term feeding and gastric drainage are needed. Which tube should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A dual access gastrojejunostomy tube
options.rationale: Long term feeding calls for an enterostomal tube. Delayed gastric emptying and aspiration point to feeding into the small intestine, and the gastric port allows the stomach to be drained.

options.text: A large bore double lumen nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Large bore tubes are for decompression and lavage, and nasal tubes are for short term use. Feeding into a slow stomach keeps the aspiration risk.

options.text: A gastrostomy tube
options.rationale: A gastrostomy is long term, but it still feeds a stomach that empties slowly. No route removes aspiration risk completely.

options.text: A nasojejunal tube
options.rationale: Feeding into the jejunum fits the delayed emptying, but nasal tubes are for short term feeding, not long term feeding.

questions.takeaway: Route selection depends on expected duration (nasal tubes for short term; G and J tubes for long term) and on GI anatomy and gastric emptying. Small intestine feeding may lower aspiration risk but does not eliminate it.
questions.strategy: Apply two filters in order: duration first (months means an enterostomal tube), then gastric emptying (a slow stomach means feeding beyond it).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Long term feeding rules out the nasal tubes.
Delayed emptying and aspiration point past the stomach.
Removes the aspiration risk is never true.
A gastrojejunostomy tube that feeds the jejunum and drains the stomach.

elimination.verdict: A. A dual access gastrojejunostomy tube.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: Before the first feeding through a new gastrostomy tube in a patient with dysphagia, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review weight, intake and output, and ordered laboratory results
options.rationale: Weight, hydration, intake and output, and laboratory results give the baseline for monitoring the response to feeding.

options.text: Offer 30 mL of water by mouth to test swallowing
options.rationale: The patient has dysphagia. Testing with water by mouth risks aspiration; the swallow is evaluated, not challenged.

options.text: Verify the order and identify the patient
options.rationale: Verifying the order and identifying the patient come first before any feeding.

options.text: Assess consciousness and airway protection
options.rationale: Swallowing, consciousness and airway protection affect aspiration risk during feeding.

options.text: Send a stool culture before the first feeding
options.rationale: A stool culture is not part of the routine assessment before feeding. The nurse assesses bowel patterns.

options.text: Record baseline respiratory status
options.rationale: A baseline respiratory status lets the nurse recognize aspiration if it occurs.

questions.takeaway: Before feeding: verify the order and identify the patient; assess weight, hydration, I&O and labs; assess the abdomen, nausea, vomiting and bowel pattern; evaluate swallowing, consciousness and airway protection; and establish baseline respiratory status.
questions.strategy: Each correct option gives a baseline or confirms safety. Reject any option that puts the patient at risk or is not part of the routine assessment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Order and identity.
Weight, I&O, labs and respiratory status.
Consciousness and airway protection.
Water by mouth with dysphagia; a stool culture.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: A patient taking an acid suppressor has a nasogastric feeding tube at its confirmed length, unlabored breathing and no new cough. Aspirate pH is 6. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: The tube has moved into the airway
options.rationale: Airway placement is the dangerous possibility, but the length matches the confirmed mark and breathing is unlabored with no new cough.

options.text: The tube has moved up into the lower esophagus
options.rationale: Esophageal placement can give a higher pH, but the external length still matches the confirmed mark and respiratory status is unchanged. The acid suppressing medication already explains the pH.

options.text: The pH test strip is defective
options.rationale: A defective strip is possible but unlikely. The medication already explains the result.

options.text: Acid suppression has raised the gastric pH
options.rationale: Acid suppressing medications can raise gastric pH. The matching length and unchanged breathing support this, and pH is read with the overall assessment.

questions.takeaway: Gastric aspirate is usually acidic (pH 5 or less), but acid suppressing medications and formula change the result. pH alone cannot confirm or rule out placement; interpret it with length, securement and the patient's condition, and hold use if placement is uncertain.
questions.strategy: Weigh the single abnormal value against all the other placement data before deciding what it means.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The length matches the confirmed mark, and breathing is unlabored with no new cough.
A daily acid suppressing medication.
A pH above 5 does not always mean the tube has moved.
The medication raised the gastric pH.

elimination.verdict: D. The medication raised the gastric pH.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: Ten minutes after a bolus gastrostomy feeding, a patient asks to lie flat for a nap. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Lower the head of the bed flat for the nap
options.rationale: Aspiration risk continues after the formula is in. The head stays raised at least 30 degrees for 1 hour after a bolus.

options.text: Keep the head raised for 1 hour after the feeding
options.rationale: Upright positioning after intermittent feeding is maintained as directed. The head stays raised at least 30 degrees for 1 hour after a bolus feeding.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed and turn the patient to the side
options.rationale: Side lying does not replace head elevation. Lying flat soon after a bolus still allows reflux and aspiration.

options.text: Keep the head raised for 15 minutes, then lower it
options.rationale: The angle is right, but 15 minutes falls short of the 1 hour that bolus feeding requires.

questions.takeaway: Prevent aspiration by keeping the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding and raised for 1 hour after a bolus feeding, as directed.
questions.strategy: The head of the bed stays raised for 1 hour after a bolus. Pick the option that meets both the angle and the time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At least 30 degrees for 1 hour after each bolus.
Only 10 minutes have passed.
15 minutes meets the angle but not the time.

elimination.verdict: B. Keep the head raised for 1 hour after the feeding.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.scenario: A nurse on a rehabilitation unit reviews the feeding plans of several patients who receive enteral nutrition.
questions.stem: The nurse on a rehabilitation unit is reviewing the feeding plans of patients who receive enteral nutrition. For each feeding plan, indicate the feeding method.

rows.text: A patient wants the daytime free for therapy; formula runs by pump at 80 mL per hour from 2000 to 0600.
rows.rationale: Cyclic feeding runs by pump over a designated period, such as overnight, leaving the rest of the day free.

rows.text: A patient receives 240 mL by syringe over 10 minutes every 4 hours while awake.
rows.rationale: A larger volume given over a short period is a bolus feeding.

rows.text: A patient receives formula at 55 mL per hour by pump around the clock.
rows.rationale: A prescribed hourly rate by pump, without a planned stop, is continuous feeding.

rows.text: A patient at home gives 200 mL by syringe over 15 minutes at 5 scheduled times a day.
rows.rationale: A larger volume over a short period, even at scheduled times, is a bolus feeding.

rows.text: A patient receives formula by pump only during sleep, from 2200 to 0600.
rows.rationale: Pump feeding limited to a designated period each day is cyclic feeding.

questions.takeaway: Bolus: a larger volume over a short period. Continuous: a prescribed hourly rate by pump, advanced only as ordered. Cyclic: pump feeding over a designated period, such as overnight.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions: is a pump used, and does it stop? Short syringe feedings are bolus; pump all day is continuous; pump for part of the day is cyclic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 240 mL over 10 minutes is a bolus.

steps.action: Find the round the clock pump
steps.detail: 55 mL per hour with no planned stop is continuous.
2000 to 0600 and 2200 to 0600 are cyclic.

elimination.verdict: Cyclic, bolus, continuous, bolus, cyclic.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: A tube medication requires holding the feeding 1 hour before the dose, but the continuous feeding was never paused. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the medication now while the feeding keeps running
options.rationale: Giving the drug with formula running ignores the required hold and can lower absorption.

options.text: Add the medication to the formula bag
options.rationale: Medications are never added to formula. They are given separately, and this drug interacts with the formula.

options.text: Pause the feeding and ask the pharmacist about timing
options.rationale: Medication and feeding interactions and required interruptions are assessed before giving the drug. The required hold was missed, so the nurse pauses and clarifies the timing.

options.text: Give the medication now and hold the feeding 2 hours
options.rationale: Extending the hold after the dose does not remove formula already in the stomach. The nurse does not change the schedule without clarification.

questions.takeaway: Verify that each medication suits the tube and site, give medications separately with ordered flushes, and assess medication and feeding interactions and any required feeding interruptions.
questions.strategy: The order's hold was missed, so the drug cannot be given as ordered. Choose the option that stops the interaction and gets direction rather than inventing a new schedule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The 1 hour hold before the dose did not happen.
Formula is in the stomach and lowers absorption.
Mixing in formula or extending the hold changes the order.
Pause and clarify the timing.

elimination.verdict: C. Pause the feeding and clarify the timing.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: A continuous gastrostomy feeding in an open bag has hung for 10 hours. Facility policy limits hang time to 8 hours. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Discard it and hang fresh, labeled formula
options.rationale: The formula has hung for 10 hours, past the 8 hour limit. Old formula grows bacteria, so it is discarded and fresh formula is hung and labeled.

options.text: Add a new can of formula to the bag
options.rationale: Adding fresh formula to formula past its hang time contaminates the new formula as well.

options.text: Let the remaining formula infuse, then replace it
options.rationale: Running the remaining formula delivers formula that is already past the hang time limit.

options.text: Relabel the bag with the current time
options.rationale: Relabeling hides the true hang time and leaves expired formula running.

questions.takeaway: Follow manufacturer and facility hang time limits. Label the formula and equipment, minimize handling, and never add new formula to formula already hanging.
questions.strategy: Ten hours is past the 8 hour limit. Every option that keeps the old formula running is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 10 hours exceeds the 8 hour limit.
New formula on old formula is contaminated.
Finishing or relabeling still gives expired formula.
Discard and hang fresh, labeled formula.

elimination.verdict: A. Discard and hang fresh formula.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: Because of frequent pauses, a patient received two thirds of the prescribed tube feeding, without nausea or distention. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?

options.text: The formula is tolerated, and the intake goal is met
options.rationale: The patient is tolerating the formula, but two thirds is not the prescribed amount.

options.text: The rate should be raised to catch up
options.rationale: Continuous feeding rates are advanced only as ordered. The nurse does not change the rate to catch up.

options.text: The feeding should be held for intolerance
options.rationale: There are no signs of intolerance. Holding the feeding would widen the shortfall.

options.text: The formula is tolerated, but intake falls short
options.rationale: Tracking formula delivered against the prescribed amount shows a shortfall, which is reported so the plan can be adjusted.

questions.takeaway: Monitoring tolerance includes tracking formula delivered against the prescribed amount, along with intake and output, weight and ordered laboratory values. Interruptions add up.
questions.strategy: Separate two questions: is the formula tolerated, and is enough being delivered? The stem answers yes to the first and no to the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No nausea or distention.
Two thirds of the prescribed volume.
Rates are advanced only as ordered.
Report the delivery gap.

elimination.verdict: D. Tolerated, but delivery is short.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A patient on tube feeding who started an IV antibiotic 4 days ago has frequent liquid stools. Which causes should the nurse assess? Select all that apply.

options.text: The need for a larger bore tube
options.rationale: Tube size is not a cause of diarrhea, and faster delivery would not help.

options.text: Signs of infection and stool testing as ordered
options.rationale: Infection can cause diarrhea, and recent antibiotic therapy raises the risk.

options.text: All medications, including the antibiotic
options.rationale: Medications are a common cause of diarrhea during tube feeding and are assessed first.

options.text: Formula handling, labeling and hang time
options.rationale: Contamination from handling or formula past its hang time can cause diarrhea.

options.text: Whether water flushes can be stopped
options.rationale: Stopping flushes does not address the cause and raises the risk of dehydration with ongoing diarrhea.

questions.takeaway: When diarrhea occurs during tube feeding, assess medications, infection, contamination and formula tolerance before blaming the formula.
questions.strategy: Diarrhea during tube feeding has four causes to assess. Match each correct option to one of them and reject options that are actions or that create new risks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The antibiotic and other medications.
Signs of infection and stool testing.
Handling, labeling and hang time.
Tube size and stopping flushes.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with heart failure who receives continuous tube feeding. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient with heart failure receives continuous feeding at 65 mL per hour with 30 mL water flushes every 4 hours. Today the weight is 61.5 kg, was 59.0 kg 2 days ago. Crackles are heard in both lung bases, and both ankles have 2+ edema. Intake was 2,600 mL and output 1,100 mL in the past 24 hours. The findings fit [[1]].

To monitor this problem, the nurse tracks [[2]].

When totaling the intake, the nurse counts [[3]].

options.text: aspiration of formula
options.rationale: Aspiration would bring coughing, desaturation or crackles in one area, but not weight gain, ankle edema or intake far above output.

options.text: fluid overload
options.rationale: Weight gain of 2.5 kg in 2 days, bilateral crackles, edema and intake far above output point to fluid overload.

options.text: refeeding syndrome
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is an electrolyte shift in a severely undernourished patient. Nothing here suggests it.

options.text: gastric residual volume every 4 hours
options.rationale: Gastric residual volume reflects gastric emptying, not total body fluid.

options.text: stool frequency and consistency
options.rationale: Stool pattern monitors tolerance, not fluid balance.

options.text: daily weights and intake and output
options.rationale: Daily weights and intake and output are the nursing measures for fluid imbalance.

options.text: the formula, the water flushes and any IV fluid
options.rationale: Water flushes are included in total fluid intake, along with formula and other fluids.

options.text: only the IV fluid
options.rationale: Formula is mostly water and is counted in the intake.

options.text: only the formula
options.rationale: Flushes are water the patient absorbs and are counted in intake.

questions.takeaway: Metabolic complications of enteral feeding include dehydration and fluid overload. Monitor intake and output, including water flushes, daily weights and ordered laboratory values.
questions.strategy: Group the findings: weight, lungs, ankles and intake all point the same way. Then pick the measures that track fluid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid weight gain, bilateral crackles, edema and positive balance mean fluid overload.
Weight and intake and output measure fluid.
Every fluid the patient receives counts, including flushes.

elimination.verdict: Fluid overload; daily weights and intake and output; formula, flushes and IV fluid.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A patient on new gastrostomy feedings says, "Dinner was family time. Now I sit apart with my formula." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "The tube keeps you strong, and that matters most."
options.rationale: This shifts the focus to the medical goal and dismisses the patient's sense of loss.

options.text: "Tell me about family dinners and what you would like now."
options.rationale: An open question invites the patient to share the loss and their preferences. It opens planning for ways to join family meals, such as feeding at the table.

options.text: "Many patients feel this way, and it passes in weeks."
options.rationale: False reassurance minimizes the feeling and closes the conversation.

options.text: "You could feed in another room so the family eats as usual."
options.rationale: This advice increases the isolation the patient describes and ignores what the patient wants.

questions.takeaway: Support emotional concerns, cultural needs and treatment preferences. Meals carry social and cultural meaning, and tube feeding can feel like losing that connection.
questions.strategy: Choose the response that explores the feeling and the patient's preferences. Reject responses that dismiss, falsely reassure or isolate.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Loss of family connection at meals.
The medical goal and "it passes" both minimize the loss.
Another room increases the separation.
An open question about family meals and preferences.

elimination.verdict: B. Explore family meals and preferences.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: A nursing student documents and hands off care after an intermittent nasogastric feeding. Which entries are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Placement confirmed by air heard over the stomach."
options.rationale: Air bolus auscultation does not reliably verify placement and is not documented as a placement check.

options.text: "300 mL formula and 60 mL flushes recorded as intake."
options.rationale: The feeding and flushes are documented, and flushes count in total fluid intake.

options.text: "Family member is difficult and asks too many questions."
options.rationale: A personal judgment about the family is not objective documentation.

options.text: "Nares intact; no nausea or distention during feeding."
options.rationale: Site condition and tolerance are documented after each feeding.

options.text: "Handoff: 300 mL every 6 hours, head raised 30 to 45 degrees."
options.rationale: Communicating the feeding plan during handoff supports safe continuity of care.

options.text: "Tube length not checked; tape appeared secure."
options.rationale: The external length is compared with the baseline before each feeding. Tape that looks secure does not replace the check.

questions.takeaway: Document placement checks, feeding, flushes, site condition and tolerance, report complications, and communicate the feeding plan during handoff.
questions.strategy: Ask whether each entry is objective and reflects a current standard. Reject outdated checks, skipped checks and personal judgments.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Volumes, flushes, site and tolerance.
Feeding plan, schedule and positioning.
Air bolus and no length check.
Opinions about the family.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient receiving continuous nasogastric tube feeding by pump. The prescription reads: increase by 10 mL/hour every 8 hours to a goal of 60 mL/hour as tolerated. At 0800 the rate was increased to 40 mL/hour; the abdomen was soft and the patient had no nausea. At 1600, when the next increase is due, the patient reports fullness and nausea, and the abdomen is firm and distended. The patient has not vomited. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Increase the rate to 50 mL/hour as scheduled
options.rationale: The schedule allows an increase only as tolerated. Fullness, nausea and new distention are signs of intolerance, so raising the rate now does not follow the order.

options.text: Stop the feeding and flush the tube with 30 mL of water
options.rationale: A temporary hold may be part of the provider's plan, but the extra 30 mL flush adds volume to a distended stomach. The nurse does not stop and flush on the nurse's own when aspiration or displacement is not suggested.

options.text: Keep the rate at 40 mL/hour and notify the provider
options.rationale: Continuous rates are advanced only as ordered, and this order requires tolerance. New fullness, nausea and a firm, distended abdomen mean the increase is not met, so the nurse holds the current rate and reports the intolerance so the provider can adjust the plan.

options.text: Check the residual and increase the rate if under 500 mL
options.rationale: Gastric residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration or tolerance. A low residual does not cancel the nausea and distention.

questions.takeaway: Advance continuous feeding rates only as ordered. When the order says as tolerated, intolerance findings (fullness, nausea, vomiting, pain, distention) mean the rate is not increased, and the provider is notified.
questions.strategy: Two options follow the order on paper. The phrase as tolerated plus the new findings decides whether the increase is allowed, and intolerance is reported so the plan can change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Increase every 8 hours only as tolerated.
Fullness, nausea and a distended, firm abdomen are new since 0800.
The scheduled increase ignores the condition; the residual check relies on a measure that is not reliable alone; stopping and adding a flush puts more volume into a distended stomach.
Hold at 40 mL per hour and notify the provider.

elimination.verdict: C. Keep the rate at 40 mL/hour and notify the provider.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: The nurse is checking a patient receiving continuous feeding at 55 mL/hour through a small bore nasogastric tube. Placement was confirmed by x ray 3 days ago, and the tube was documented at 58 cm at the naris. Facility policy is to obtain an x ray if the external length, securement or respiratory status changes. At 1200 the mark is at 58 cm, the tape is intact, and the aspirate looks like formula with a pH of 6.5. The patient takes no acid suppressing medication. Respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, no cough. Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: The tube has likely moved out of the stomach
options.rationale: A pH above 5 can raise concern, but the length, securement and breathing all match the baseline. Under this policy none of the findings that call for an x ray is present.

options.text: Formula is raising the pH, and placement is supported
options.rationale: Formula makes pH results less reliable, and aspirate pH alone cannot confirm or rule out placement. The mark matches the documented 58 cm, the tape is intact and the respiratory status has not changed, so the findings taken together support placement.

options.text: Acid suppressing medication is raising the gastric pH
options.rationale: Acid suppressing drugs can raise gastric pH, but the patient takes none. The cause named here does not fit this patient.

options.text: The tube tip has likely moved into the small intestine
options.rationale: This is the near miss: intestinal fluid is less acidic, so a pH of 6.5 seems to point there. But the mark is unchanged at 58 cm, and aspirate pH cannot confirm where the tip lies.

questions.takeaway: Gastric aspirate is usually acidic (pH 5 or less), but formula and acid suppressing drugs can raise it. pH alone cannot confirm placement; interpret it with the external length, securement and respiratory status, and hold tube use only when placement is uncertain.
questions.strategy: Three options read the pH alone and each names a real cause of a higher pH. Read the pH with everything else: the matching mark, intact tape, unchanged breathing and the formula in the aspirate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mark at 58 cm as documented, tape intact, no respiratory change.
Formula in the stomach during continuous feeding can raise the pH.
The patient takes no acid suppressor, and the unchanged mark argues against a tip that has moved.
No trigger for an x ray is present, so placement is supported.

elimination.verdict: B. Formula is raising the pH, and placement is supported.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.scenario: A patient, 79 years old, with heart failure receives continuous feeding through a gastrostomy tube at 65 mL per hour, with 60 mL water flushes every 4 hours and water flushes before, between and after medications. The intake record lists only the formula volume; the flushes have not been recorded. Weight 66.4 kg today, was 64.2 kg 2 days ago. Both ankles have 2+ edema, were without edema 2 days ago. Crackles are heard in the bases of both lungs. Respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, was 18 breaths per minute 2 days ago. SpO2 92% on room air. Head of the bed at 40 degrees. No vomiting, coughing or choking during the feedings.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with heart failure who receives continuous gastrostomy tube feeding. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Add all water flushes to the intake record, and compare total intake with output
options.rationale: Flushes count as fluid intake. Without them the record hides part of what the patient is receiving, so the nurse totals all intake and compares it with output.

options.text: Stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, and call for help
options.rationale: This is the priority action for suspected aspiration. The patient has not vomited, coughed or choked, and the crackles are in both bases with edema and weight gain, which point to fluid, not formula in the airway.

options.text: Report the weight gain, edema and lung findings to the provider
options.rationale: A gain of 2.2 kg in 2 days with new edema and crackles in a patient with heart failure needs the provider's review of the fluid volume in the feeding plan.

options.text: Increase the water flushes to keep the tube from clogging
options.rationale: More water adds to the fluid the patient already cannot handle.

options.text: Check the gastric residual volume before the next flush
options.rationale: Residual volume addresses gastric intolerance. It does not measure the fluid problem shown by the weight, edema and lungs.

options.text: Fluid overload
