options.rationale: Weight gain over 2 days, new edema in both ankles and crackles in both lung bases in a patient with heart failure fit fluid overload. Unrecorded flushes add to the intake.

options.text: Aspiration of formula
options.rationale: Aspiration usually follows vomiting, coughing or choking during feeding. None is present, and aspiration does not explain the weight gain and ankle edema.

options.text: Refeeding syndrome
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is an electrolyte shift in a severely undernourished patient after nutrition restarts. Nothing here describes severe undernutrition or electrolyte results.

options.text: Dehydration
options.rationale: Dehydration causes weight loss, not a gain with edema and crackles.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight on the same scale shows whether fluid is building up or being removed.

options.text: Lung sounds and SpO2
options.rationale: Crackles and oxygen saturation show whether fluid in the lungs is worsening or clearing.

options.text: Stool frequency and consistency
options.rationale: Stool pattern tracks feeding tolerance in the gut, not fluid volume.

options.text: Gastric residual volume
options.rationale: Residual volume does not measure fluid overload and does not reliably predict aspiration.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Glucose is unrelated to the fluid findings in this scenario.

questions.takeaway: Fluid imbalance is a metabolic complication of enteral nutrition. Water flushes are part of total fluid intake; monitor intake and output, daily weights and ordered labs, and report signs of overload.
questions.strategy: Two conditions share the lung findings. Weight gain, new edema in both ankles and no vomiting or coughing during feedings separate fluid overload from aspiration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Crackles in both bases and a lower SpO2 fit both aspiration and fluid.
A 2.2 kg gain, new ankle edema and no vomiting or coughing point to fluid overload.
Count every flush in the intake, compare with output, and report the findings.
Daily weight, lung sounds and SpO2.

elimination.verdict: Add the flushes to intake and compare with output, and report the findings; fluid overload; daily weight and lung sounds with SpO2.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who takes nothing by mouth and receives 4 intermittent feedings a day through a gastrostomy tube between 0800 and 2000. The feedings are tolerated. The patient says, "Next month I will fast from sunrise to sunset for Ramadan, as I do every year. I would like to keep the fast if I can." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "Tell me about the fast. I can ask about an overnight pump schedule."
options.rationale: The nurse supports the patient's cultural and treatment preferences and explores them. A cyclic feeding by pump over a set period, such as overnight, may fit the fast, but any change in the method or timing needs a new order.

options.text: "You can skip the daytime feedings and take larger ones after sunset."
options.rationale: Moving feedings to the evening is the right idea, but the nurse cannot change the schedule without an order. Larger volumes over a short time also add to the risk of intolerance and aspiration.

options.text: "Tube feedings do not count as eating, so you can keep your schedule."
options.rationale: This answers a religious question for the patient. Whether a tube feeding breaks the fast is the patient's decision, and the response closes the conversation.

options.text: "People who are ill do not have to fast, so you can skip it this year."
options.rationale: This dismisses a preference the patient has stated clearly. The nurse explores the wish instead of deciding for the patient.

questions.takeaway: Support emotional concerns, cultural needs and treatment preferences. Feeding methods include bolus, intermittent, continuous and cyclic (pump feeding over a set period, such as overnight); a change in method or rate is made only by order.
questions.strategy: Two options move the feeding to the night. The one that keeps the change inside an order and keeps the patient talking is the better response.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient wants to keep the fast and asks if it can be done.
Telling the patient what the fast allows or that fasting is not needed overrides the patient's choice.
Skipping daytime feedings changes the order without approval.
Explore the fast and ask the team about an overnight cyclic schedule.

elimination.verdict: A. Explore the fast and ask about an overnight pump schedule.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating discharge teaching for a patient going home with a new gastrostomy tube and bolus feedings. Weakness in both hands prevents the patient from handling the syringe, so the patient's adult child will give every feeding. Which findings indicate that the teaching is effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: The adult child gives a bolus feeding with flushes while the nurse watches
options.rationale: Return demonstration by the person who will do the feedings shows that the skill can be performed correctly.

options.text: The patient explains every step of the feeding correctly, in order
options.rationale: Teach back is useful, but the patient will not be the one giving the feedings. The adult child must show the skill.

options.text: The adult child watches a feeding and says, "I understand, that looks easy."
options.rationale: Saying "I understand" is not evidence of learning. It shows neither teach back nor return demonstration.

options.text: The adult child explains when to stop the feeding and get help
options.rationale: Teach back by the caregiver shows understanding of when to stop feeding and seek help, which is part of the required teaching.

options.text: The adult child plans to clear a blocked tube with a little cola
options.rationale: Carbonated drinks and juice are avoided for clogged tubes. This plan shows a need for more teaching.

options.text: The adult child cleans the site and names findings to report
options.rationale: Performing site care and naming the findings to report shows the caregiver can carry out tube care at home.

questions.takeaway: Use teach back and return demonstration with the person who will perform the care. Teach when to stop the feeding and seek help, site care and what to report, and that cola or juice is not used to clear a blocked tube.
questions.strategy: Ask who will do the feedings at home. Effective teaching is shown by that person, through teach back or return demonstration, not by agreement alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The adult child gives every feeding because of the patient's hand weakness.
Return demonstration of the feeding and site care, and teach back about when to stop.
The patient's explanation and the caregiver's "I understand" do not show the caregiver's skill.
Cola is not used to unclog a tube.

elimination.verdict: A, D, F.

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a confused patient receiving continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube that was documented at 56 cm at the naris after x ray confirmation. The patient is found pulling at the tape, and the mark is now at 44 cm. The patient is coughing, and SpO2 is 89% on room air, was 96% at 0800. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the feeding and assess breathing
options.rationale: Coughing and a fall in SpO2 from 96% to 89% during feeding point to suspected aspiration. The priority action is to stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, and obtain help.

options.text: Hold tube use and obtain an x ray
options.rationale: The tube has moved 12 cm, so displacement is likely and placement must be verified before the tube is used again. That is correct, but the coughing and desaturation make the airway the first concern.

options.text: Advance the tube back to the 56 cm mark
options.rationale: Pushing the tube back in does not confirm where the tip lies and delays the response to the breathing changes.

options.text: Check the aspirate pH for placement
options.rationale: Aspirate pH alone cannot confirm placement, and testing it delays the response to the coughing and desaturation.

questions.takeaway: Suspected displacement calls for stopping tube use and verifying placement, but when respiratory signs appear during feeding, treat it as suspected aspiration first: stop the feeding, assess the airway and breathing, and obtain help.
questions.strategy: Two options stop the tube. The coughing and the fall in SpO2 decide which complication the nurse acts on first.

steps.detail: The mark moved from 56 cm to 44 cm (displacement), and the patient is coughing with SpO2 89%, was 96% (aspiration).
Breathing changes outrank verifying the tube position.
Advancing the tube and checking pH do not confirm placement and delay airway care; the x ray is right but comes after breathing is assessed.
Stop the feeding and assess breathing.

elimination.verdict: A. Stop the feeding and assess breathing.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give 3 medications through the gastrostomy tube of a patient with heart failure who is on a fluid restriction. The pharmacist has confirmed that each medication is appropriate for the tube. The prescription reads: use 15 mL of water for each flush with medication administration. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Flush 15 mL before and after only
options.rationale: Skipping the flushes between doses saves fluid for a patient on a restriction, which makes it tempting. But without a flush between medications, the drugs mix in the tube, which risks clogging and interactions.

options.text: Flush 15 mL each time and record the flushes as intake
options.rationale: Each medication is given separately with a 15 mL flush before, between and after, as the individualized order allows, and every flush is counted in total intake, which matters most under a fluid restriction.

options.text: Give all three after one 15 mL flush
options.rationale: One flush with all three drugs together uses the least fluid, but medications are given separately with a flush between each, to prevent clogging and interactions.

options.text: Flush 15 mL each time and leave flushes off the intake record
options.rationale: The flush sequence is right, but flush water is fluid intake. For a patient on a fluid restriction, leaving it off the record hides fluid the patient received.

questions.takeaway: Flush before, between and after each medication. The usual volume is 30 mL of water, but follow individualized orders, and include every flush in total fluid intake.
questions.strategy: Every option uses the ordered 15 mL, and the fluid restriction makes the options that save water look careful. Two rules decide: a flush between every medication, and every flush counted as intake.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 15 mL per flush for a patient on a fluid restriction; the sequence is still before, between and after.
Dropping the between flushes or giving all three together lets the drugs mix and clog the tube.
Flush water is intake; leaving it off hides fluid from a restricted patient's total.
Flush 15 mL each time and record the flushes as intake.

elimination.verdict: B. Flush with 15 mL each time and record the flushes as intake.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients receiving enteral feeding. Which patient should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Gastric residual 280 mL, was 200 mL; abdomen soft; no nausea
options.rationale: The residual rose, but gastric residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration. A soft abdomen and no nausea show no intolerance.

options.text: Three loose stools in 24 hours since an antibiotic started
options.rationale: Diarrhea needs assessment of medications, infection, contamination and formula tolerance, but it is not an immediate threat to the airway.

options.text: Pump alarming for occlusion; formula not infusing
options.rationale: A clogged tube needs gentle flushing, but a paused feeding does not threaten breathing.

options.text: Nasojejunal feeding running; head of bed flat since a bath
options.rationale: Feeding into the small intestine lowers but does not eliminate aspiration risk. Feeding with the head of the bed flat is an immediate airway risk that the nurse corrects now by raising it to 30 to 45 degrees.

questions.takeaway: Keep the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees during feeding for every tube, including small intestine tubes. A risk to the airway comes before problems that are real but not dangerous right now.
questions.strategy: Every patient needs something. The one whose problem threatens the airway is seen first, and a jejunal tube does not remove that risk.

steps.detail: Head of bed flat during feeding is an airway risk; the others are tolerance, diarrhea and patency problems.
A nasojejunal tube lowers aspiration risk but does not eliminate it.
A residual under the policy limit with no intolerance, loose stools, and a clogged tube can wait a few minutes.
The patient with the nasojejunal feeding and the head of the bed flat.

elimination.verdict: D. The nasojejunal feeding with the head of the bed flat.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the plans of care for patients on a medical unit. For which patients should the nurse anticipate enteral nutrition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cancer of the tongue; cannot chew or swallow; bowel sounds active
options.rationale: The gastrointestinal tract works, but the patient cannot ingest food safely. This is the classic indication for enteral nutrition.

options.text: Extensive small bowel removal; cannot absorb nutrients from the gut
options.rationale: Enteral nutrition depends on a gut that digests and absorbs. When the tract cannot be adequately used, parenteral nutrition is anticipated.

options.text: Dysphagia after a stroke; passed a repeat swallow test; eats 90% of meals
options.rationale: Dysphagia is a risk factor, but this patient now swallows safely and meets needs by mouth, so a feeding tube is not indicated.

options.text: Eats 30% of meals despite supplements; weight down 6 kg in 2 months
options.rationale: The gastrointestinal tract works, but oral intake cannot meet nutritional needs. Enteral nutrition is indicated.

options.text: Unresponsive after a head injury; bowel sounds present in all quadrants
options.rationale: The patient cannot swallow or protect the airway, and the gastrointestinal tract works, so enteral nutrition is indicated.

options.text: Functional gut; declined a tube after discussing risks and benefits
options.rationale: Selection considers treatment goals and patient preferences. An informed refusal means a tube is not planned.

questions.takeaway: Anticipate enteral nutrition when the gastrointestinal tract works but oral intake is unsafe or not enough to meet needs, consistent with the patient's goals and preferences. When the tract cannot digest or absorb, anticipate parenteral nutrition.
questions.strategy: Check two things for each patient: can the gut digest and absorb, and is eating unsafe or inadequate? Then check the patient's preference.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient with extensive small bowel removal cannot absorb nutrients, so parenteral nutrition fits.
The patient after a stroke now swallows safely and eats 90% of meals.
An informed refusal rules out the tube.
Cancer of the tongue, intake of 30% with weight loss, and unresponsiveness with bowel sounds present.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Compare enteral and parenteral nutrition and identify who needs enteral feeding

questions.scenario: A patient admitted 3 weeks ago with undernutrition receives continuous gastrostomy tube feeding at 60 mL per hour for 24 hours. Weight 49.0 kg on admission, 49.8 kg 2 days ago, 51.6 kg today. Both ankles have new 1+ edema today. Sacral pressure injury 2 cm, was 3 cm on admission. Phosphorus 2.0 mg/dL, was 3.4 mg/dL on admission. Pump shows 1,420 mL delivered in the past 24 hours. Grip strength is stronger, and the patient naps once a day, was 3 times a day on admission.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the response to enteral feeding of a patient with undernutrition. For each finding, indicate whether it shows progress or requires follow up.

rows.text: Sacral pressure injury 2 cm, was 3 cm
rows.rationale: Poor wound healing is a sign of undernutrition. A wound that is shrinking shows that nutrition is supporting healing.

rows.text: Weight 49.8 kg 2 days ago, was 49.0 kg on admission
rows.rationale: A gain of 0.8 kg over about 19 days is gradual and fits the rebuilding of body tissue.

rows.text: Weight 51.6 kg today, was 49.8 kg 2 days ago, with new ankle edema
rows.rationale: A gain of 1.8 kg in 2 days with new edema is too fast to be tissue. It points to fluid imbalance, which needs intake and output review and reporting.

rows.text: 1,420 mL of formula delivered in the past 24 hours
rows.rationale: The prescribed amount is 1,440 mL. Delivery that nearly matches the prescription shows the patient is receiving the planned nutrition.

rows.text: Phosphorus 2.0 mg/dL, was 3.4 mg/dL on admission
rows.rationale: A falling phosphorus during nutrition support is an electrolyte imbalance and can signal a dangerous shift. The nurse reports it.

rows.text: Stronger grip and one nap a day, was 3 naps a day
rows.rationale: Muscle weakness and fatigue are signs of undernutrition. Their improvement shows response to the feeding.

questions.takeaway: Monitor the response to feeding with weight, wound healing, strength and energy, formula delivered versus prescribed, intake and output, and ordered laboratory results. A rapid gain with edema is fluid, not nutrition, and a falling phosphorus is an electrolyte problem.
questions.strategy: Two weight rows look alike. The rate of gain and the new edema separate tissue from fluid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.8 kg over about 19 days is gradual; 1.8 kg in 2 days with new edema is fluid.
Phosphorus fell from 3.4 mg/dL to 2.0 mg/dL during feeding.
1,420 mL delivered of 1,440 mL prescribed.
A smaller wound, stronger grip and fewer naps show progress.

elimination.verdict: Requires follow up: the 2 day weight gain with edema and the falling phosphorus. The other four show progress.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: A patient receiving feedings through a small bore nasogastric tube develops a bowel obstruction, and gastric decompression is prescribed. Which tube should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A small bore nasojejunal feeding tube
options.rationale: A nasojejunal tube places formula in the small intestine. It is a feeding tube and does not drain the stomach.

options.text: The current small bore tube set to suction
options.rationale: Small bore tubes are single lumen and used only for feeding and medications. They are too narrow for decompression and collapse under suction.

options.text: A large bore double lumen nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Large bore, double lumen nasogastric tubes are used for gastric decompression and lavage, which is what this patient now needs.

options.text: A small bore tube advanced into the duodenum
options.rationale: Moving a small bore tube deeper still leaves a single lumen feeding tube that cannot decompress the stomach.

questions.takeaway: Small bore tubes are for feeding and medications only. Gastric decompression needs a large bore, double lumen nasogastric tube.
questions.strategy: Three options are small bore tubes. Ask what each tube is built to do: feed or drain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gastric decompression, not feeding.
Small bore, single lumen tubes feed; large bore, double lumen tubes decompress.
The nasojejunal tube, the current tube on suction and the duodenal tube are all small bore feeding tubes.
A large bore double lumen nasogastric tube.

elimination.verdict: C. A large bore double lumen nasogastric tube.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: The nurse reads the x ray result confirming placement of a newly inserted small bore nasogastric tube. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Inject air and listen over the stomach
options.rationale: Air bolus auscultation does not reliably verify placement, and the x ray has already confirmed it.

options.text: Measure nose to earlobe to xiphoid again
options.rationale: That measurement estimates insertion length before the tube is placed. It does not help once the tube is in.

options.text: Wait for a second x ray before feeding
options.rationale: One documented x ray confirmation is enough to begin use. A repeat film delays nutrition without a reason.

options.text: Mark and record the length at the naris
options.rationale: Marking and documenting the external length at the exit site sets the baseline for every later placement check.

questions.takeaway: After x ray confirmation, mark and document the tube length at the exit site. Every ongoing check compares the external length with that baseline.
questions.strategy: Placement is already confirmed. Look for the step that makes later checks possible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The x ray result is in and confirms placement.
Later checks need a documented baseline length.
Air auscultation is unreliable, remeasuring is a step done before insertion, and a second x ray is not needed.
Mark and record the length at the naris.

elimination.verdict: D. Mark and record the length at the naris.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with decreased consciousness who receives continuous nasogastric feeding. Which actions should the nurse take to reduce aspiration risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lay the patient flat to turn with the pump running
options.rationale: Lowering the head of the bed while formula is running raises the risk of reflux and aspiration.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees during feeding is the core aspiration prevention measure.

options.text: Rely on residual volume alone to judge risk
options.rationale: Gastric residual volume alone does not reliably predict aspiration. It is interpreted with vomiting, distention and other findings.

options.text: Check the external length and securement
options.rationale: A tube that has moved can deliver formula into the esophagus. Checking the length against the baseline and keeping the tube secured reduces that risk.

options.text: Switch to bolus feeding to shorten feeding time
options.rationale: A bolus delivers a larger volume over a short period, which increases reflux. It does not lower aspiration risk.

options.text: Monitor for reflux and vomiting
options.rationale: Reflux and vomiting are warning signs that formula may reach the airway, so the nurse watches for them throughout the feeding.

questions.takeaway: Prevent aspiration by keeping the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees, verifying placement and securement, and monitoring reflux, vomiting and intolerance. Residual volume alone is not a safety check.
questions.strategy: Test each action: does it keep formula moving down and out of the airway?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees, length and securement checks, and monitoring for reflux and vomiting.
Lying flat with the pump running invites reflux.
Residual volume alone does not predict aspiration.
A larger volume in a short time increases reflux.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Prevent aspiration during enteral feeding

questions.stem: Before an intermittent nasogastric feeding, which finding should cause the nurse to hold the feeding?

options.text: External mark at the documented length
options.rationale: A mark that matches the baseline supports correct placement.

options.text: New cough and hoarse voice
options.rationale: New respiratory findings raise concern that the tube has moved or formula has been aspirated. Tube use is held until placement and breathing are assessed.

options.text: Aspirate pH of 4 with a gastric appearance
options.rationale: An acidic aspirate fits gastric placement and is used with the overall assessment.

options.text: Bowel sounds active in all quadrants
options.rationale: Active bowel sounds fit a working gastrointestinal tract and support feeding.

questions.takeaway: Compare respiratory status with the baseline before each feeding. A new cough or voice change makes placement uncertain, so tube use is held for further assessment.
questions.strategy: Three findings support feeding. The one that is new and involves breathing is the one that stops it.

steps.detail: Matching mark, acidic aspirate and active bowel sounds all support feeding.
A new cough and hoarse voice involve the airway.
Breathing concerns come before giving formula.
New cough and hoarse voice.

elimination.verdict: B. New cough and hoarse voice.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with delayed gastric emptying who receives continuous feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube. The patient has vomited formula twice today with the head of the bed at 45 degrees. Bowel sounds are active. The provider expects the patient to resume eating in about 10 days. Which plan should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Hold feedings and request parenteral nutrition
options.rationale: Vomiting is tempting as a reason to stop using the gut, but bowel sounds are active and the intestine works. Parenteral nutrition is for a gastrointestinal tract that cannot be adequately used.

options.text: Request a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy
options.rationale: A gastrostomy gives long term access, but it still delivers formula into a stomach that empties slowly, so the vomiting and aspiration risk remain.

options.text: Request a direct percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy
options.rationale: Feeding into the jejunum fits the delayed gastric emptying, but this is a long term enterostomal route placed through the abdominal wall. About 10 days of feeding calls for a less invasive nasal tube.

options.text: Request a nasojejunal feeding tube
options.rationale: Feeding past the stomach bypasses the delayed gastric emptying and may reduce aspiration risk, and a nasal route is preferred when feeding is needed for a short time.

questions.takeaway: Route selection weighs two things: where the tube should end (gastric emptying and anatomy) and how long it is needed (nasal for short term, gastrostomy or jejunostomy for long term).
questions.strategy: Each distractor answers one cue. Only one option fits both the slow stomach and the 10 day timeline.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Delayed gastric emptying with vomiting means formula should go past the stomach.
About 10 days means a short term, nasal route.
Parenteral nutrition ignores a working gut; the gastrostomy still feeds the stomach; the jejunostomy is right on site but too invasive for 10 days.
A nasojejunal feeding tube.

elimination.verdict: D. Request a nasojejunal feeding tube.

questions.objective: Describe feeding tube types and the factors that guide route selection

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to resume intermittent feeding through a small bore nasogastric tube that was confirmed by x ray 2 days ago. Overnight the patient retched and vomited forcefully three times. The external mark is at the documented length, and the tape is intact. The patient has no cough, and breathing is unlabored. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?

options.text: Placement is supported because the mark is unchanged
options.rationale: An unchanged mark is reassuring, but forceful vomiting can move the tip up into the esophagus without changing the length at the naris.

options.text: Placement is supported if the aspirate is acidic
options.rationale: Aspirate pH is used according to policy, but pH alone cannot guarantee correct placement, especially after an event that may have moved the tip.

options.text: Placement is uncertain and must be verified
options.rationale: Forceful vomiting is a known cause of tube displacement. When placement is uncertain, the nurse holds tube use and obtains further verification before giving formula.

options.text: The vomiting reflects intolerance, not displacement
options.rationale: Vomiting is a sign of intolerance and needs assessment, but it does not rule out displacement. Both must be considered before the feeding resumes.

questions.takeaway: Ongoing checks compare the length, securement and respiratory status with the baseline, but an event that can move the tip makes placement uncertain even when the mark has not changed. Hold tube use and verify.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Three options sound reassuring or explain the vomiting. The forceful vomiting overnight is the cue that outweighs the unchanged mark and the normal breathing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mark at the documented length, tape intact, no cough.

steps.action: Find the cue that outweighs them
steps.detail: Forceful vomiting three times can move the tip without changing the external length.
The mark and pH alone do not confirm placement after this event, and calling it intolerance ignores possible displacement.
Placement is uncertain and must be verified.

elimination.verdict: C. Placement is uncertain and must be verified.

questions.objective: Assess the patient before feeding and verify tube placement

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who ate almost nothing for 2 weeks before admission and has lost 9 kg. Continuous tube feeding started 48 hours ago and is now at 40 mL/hour. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: Gastric residual volume of 150 mL
options.rationale: A residual of this size, with no vomiting or distention described, does not by itself predict aspiration. It is interpreted with other intolerance findings and is not the most urgent finding here.

options.text: Two loose stools since midnight
options.rationale: Loose stools need assessment of medications, contamination and formula tolerance, but two stools are not an immediate threat.

options.text: Phosphorus of 1.3 mg/dL
options.rationale: A severely undernourished patient who has just restarted nutrition is at risk for refeeding syndrome. A very low phosphorus (normal about 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dL) is a dangerous electrolyte shift that can affect the heart and breathing muscles, so it needs immediate reporting.

options.text: Weight up 0.4 kg since yesterday
options.rationale: A small gain is expected as nutrition resumes. Daily weights are tracked, but this change alone does not signal danger.

questions.takeaway: In a severely undernourished patient who just restarted nutrition, a falling phosphorus, potassium or magnesium is the warning sign of refeeding syndrome and outranks residual volume, stool changes or a small weight gain.
questions.strategy: Every option is something the nurse monitors. Ask which finding fits the most dangerous complication for this patient's history.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two weeks of almost no intake and a 9 kg loss: high risk for refeeding syndrome.
Refeeding syndrome shows as dangerous electrolyte shifts, especially phosphorus.
The residual, the stools and the small weight gain need monitoring, not immediate action.
Phosphorus of 1.3 mg/dL.

elimination.verdict: C. Phosphorus of 1.3 mg/dL.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: The nurse is totaling the intake from 0700 to 1500 for a patient receiving continuous gastrostomy feeding prescribed at 60 mL/hour. The feeding was paused for 40 minutes for a procedure, and the pump shows 440 mL delivered. The tube was flushed with 30 mL of water when the pump restarted, and with 30 mL at 1100 and 1500. Which amount should the nurse record as the enteral intake for the shift?

options.text: 480 mL
options.rationale: This is the prescribed rate times 8 hours. It counts formula that was never delivered and leaves out every flush.

options.text: 530 mL
options.rationale: Formula actually delivered (440 mL) plus all three water flushes (90 mL) equals 530 mL. Intake reflects what the patient received, and flushes count toward total fluid intake.

options.text: 570 mL
options.rationale: This adds the flushes to the prescribed 480 mL. It still counts the 40 mL of formula that was not delivered during the pause.

options.text: 440 mL
options.rationale: This is the formula delivered, but water flushes are part of total fluid intake and must be included.

questions.takeaway: Record what the patient actually received: formula delivered by the pump, not the prescribed amount, plus every water flush. Tracking delivered versus prescribed formula also shows whether nutrition goals are met.
questions.strategy: Two separate errors hide in the distractors: using the prescribed amount and leaving out the flushes. Only one answer avoids both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The pump shows 440 mL delivered because of the 40 minute pause.
Three flushes of 30 mL each add 90 mL.
440 mL plus 90 mL equals 530 mL.
480 mL and 570 mL use the prescribed amount; 440 mL leaves out the flushes.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to start a continuous feeding through a patient's gastrostomy tube, which has an ENFit port. The only feeding set on the unit has a Luer tip that does not fit the port. The patient also has a peripheral IV. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Get a feeding set with an ENFit connector
options.rationale: ENFit connectors fit only enteral devices, which prevents formula from being connected to an IV line. The correct set keeps the system closed and the route safe.

options.text: Tape the Luer tip securely into the port
options.rationale: A taped connection can leak or separate, and a Luer tip on a feeding set is exactly what allows a wrong route connection to an IV line.

options.text: Give the formula by Luer syringe as a bolus
options.rationale: This changes the prescribed method without an order and still uses a Luer device on an enteral route.

options.text: Label the Luer set clearly as enteral
options.rationale: Labeling is required, but a label does not stop a Luer tip from fitting an IV port. It does not remove the wrong route risk.

questions.takeaway: Enteral feeding equipment uses ENFit connections so that formula cannot be connected to an IV line. Never improvise a connection; get the right equipment.
questions.strategy: Three options make the wrong equipment work. Ask which option removes the risk of wrong route administration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A Luer tip on a feeding set can be connected to the IV.
ENFit connectors fit only enteral devices.
Taping, a Luer syringe bolus and a label all keep the Luer hazard in place.
Get a feeding set with an ENFit connector.

elimination.verdict: A. Get a feeding set with an ENFit connector.

questions.objective: Administer feedings, formula, water flushes and medications safely

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient who will go home with a gastrostomy tube, bolus feedings and medications given through the tube. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will flush with water before and after each medication."
options.rationale: Flushing before, between and after medications keeps the tube open and is correct.

options.text: "I will give each of my medications one at a time."
options.rationale: Medications are given separately with flushes, not mixed together. This is correct.

options.text: "I will stay sitting up during and after each feeding."
options.rationale: Upright positioning during and after intermittent feeding reduces aspiration risk. This is correct.

options.text: "If the tube clogs, I will push a little cola through it."
options.rationale: Carbonated drinks and juice should not be used to unclog a feeding tube. A clog is treated with gentle water flushing, never forced, and the patient should seek help if water does not clear it.

questions.takeaway: Teach that a clogged tube gets gentle warm water flushing, never force, and never cola or juice. Use teach back to confirm the patient can state the plan.
questions.strategy: Three statements match safe practice. Look for the home remedy that sounds helpful but is not recommended.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the incorrect statement.
Flushing around medications, giving them one at a time and sitting upright are all correct.
Cola is a common home remedy, but carbonated drinks and juice are avoided for clogs.
The cola statement.

elimination.verdict: D. "If the tube clogs, I will push a little cola through it."

questions.objective: Provide oral, nasal and site care, teach the patient and document

questions.nursesNote: 0800: Patient with cancer of the larynx had a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube placed 3 weeks ago, takes nothing by mouth, and receives continuous feeding at 60 mL per hour. Oriented to person only, was oriented to person, place and time yesterday. Mucous membranes dry and sticky. Heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 102/64 mm Hg, oral temperature 37.1 °C. Head of bed at 35 degrees. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, bowel sounds active. PEG site clean and dry, external mark at 3 cm at the skin, matches the documented length. Urine dark amber, 140 mL in the past 8 hours. Weight 59.6 kg, was 61.4 kg 3 days ago. Sodium 151 mEq/L. Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 34 mg/dL.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 0800 note of a patient receiving continuous gastrostomy tube feeding. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Oriented to person only, was oriented to person, place and time yesterday
segments.rationale: New confusion is a change in mental status. In a patient who cannot drink, it can reflect a fluid deficit and a high sodium.

segments.text: Mucous membranes dry and sticky
segments.rationale: Dry, sticky mucous membranes are a sign of dehydration. The patient cannot drink to correct it.

segments.text: Heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 102/64 mm Hg
segments.rationale: A fast heart rate with a low blood pressure suggests the body is compensating for low circulating volume.

segments.text: Head of bed at 35 degrees
segments.rationale: This is within the 30 to 45 degrees used during feeding.

segments.text: Lungs clear
segments.rationale: Clear lungs do not suggest aspiration or fluid overload.

segments.text: PEG site clean and dry, external mark at 3 cm at the skin, matches the documented length
segments.rationale: A clean site and a mark at the documented length do not suggest infection or displacement.

segments.text: Urine dark amber, 140 mL in the past 8 hours
segments.rationale: Concentrated, low volume urine shows the kidneys are conserving water. This is a key sign of dehydration.

segments.text: Weight 59.6 kg, was 61.4 kg 3 days ago
segments.rationale: A loss of 1.8 kg in 3 days is mostly fluid, not tissue. Rapid weight change reflects fluid balance.

segments.text: Sodium 151 mEq/L
segments.rationale: The sodium is high (normal about 135 to 145 mEq/L), which fits a water deficit.

segments.text: Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 34 mg/dL
segments.rationale: A raised BUN (normal about 10 to 20 mg/dL) is consistent with dehydration.

questions.takeaway: Fluid imbalance is a metabolic complication of tube feeding. A patient who takes nothing by mouth depends entirely on the formula and the water flushes, so dry mucosa, tachycardia, concentrated urine, rapid weight loss, a high sodium and new confusion point to dehydration.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into two groups: findings about the feeding setup (position, site, mark) and findings about the patient's fluid status. The fluid findings all point the same way.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Head of bed, lungs, abdomen and PEG site are all as expected.
Dry mucosa, heart rate, blood pressure, urine, weight, sodium and BUN all show a deficit.
New confusion is a change from yesterday and needs follow up.
The seven fluid and mental status findings.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.scenario: At 0830 the nurse reviews the patient's records. Chart so far: gastrostomy tube placed 3 weeks ago, nothing by mouth, continuous feeding at 60 mL per hour; weight 59.6 kg, was 61.4 kg 3 days ago; sodium 151 mEq/L; urine dark amber; new confusion. Records: water flushes of 30 mL are prescribed every 4 hours, and 2 of 6 were given in the past 24 hours because the pump was alarming. Four liquid stools in the past 24 hours. Furosemide 20 mg by gastrostomy tube daily. Pump set at the prescribed 60 mL per hour. Head of bed kept at 30 to 45 degrees. PEG site cleaned daily.
questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing the records of a patient with signs of dehydration who receives continuous gastrostomy tube feeding. For each finding, indicate whether it is a likely contributor to the fluid deficit.

rows.text: Only 2 of 6 prescribed water flushes given
rows.rationale: Flushes are part of the patient's total fluid intake. Missing two thirds of them removes water the patient cannot get any other way.

rows.text: Four liquid stools in the past 24 hours
rows.rationale: Diarrhea loses water and electrolytes, and its cause (medications, contamination, infection or formula tolerance) needs assessment.

rows.text: Daily furosemide
rows.rationale: A diuretic increases urine water loss in a patient whose intake is already short.

rows.text: Pump running at the prescribed 60 mL per hour
rows.rationale: The formula is running as prescribed, so it is not the source of the shortfall.

rows.text: Head of bed at 30 to 45 degrees
rows.rationale: Positioning prevents aspiration and has no effect on fluid balance.

rows.text: PEG site cleaned daily
rows.rationale: Site care prevents skin breakdown and infection and does not change fluid balance.

questions.takeaway: When a tube fed patient becomes dehydrated, look at every way water comes in (formula, flushes) and every way it goes out (stool, urine, medications that increase losses). Missed flushes are an easily overlooked cause.
questions.strategy: For each row ask: does this add water, remove water, or neither?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only 2 of 6 flushes given means less water in.
Liquid stools and a diuretic mean more water out.
The pump rate is correct, and positioning and site care do not affect fluid balance.
Three contributors, three not.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 2 and 3: likely contributor. Rows 4, 5 and 6: not a likely contributor.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
At 0900 the patient is restless and keeps reaching for the abdominal dressing. Chart so far: gastrostomy tube placed 3 weeks ago, nothing by mouth, continuous feeding at 60 mL per hour; weight 59.6 kg, was 61.4 kg 3 days ago; sodium 151 mEq/L; urine dark amber; new confusion. Records show missed flushes, four liquid stools in 24 hours and daily furosemide. Lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft.

The nurse's priority concern is [[1]], shown by [[2]].

Because of the new restlessness, the patient is also at risk for [[3]].

options.text: dehydration
options.rationale: The pattern of low intake, high losses, rapid weight loss, high sodium and concentrated urine is a fluid deficit.

options.text: aspiration of formula
options.rationale: Clear lungs, no cough and the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees do not point to aspiration.

options.text: fluid overload
options.rationale: The patient has lost weight and has concentrated urine, the opposite of overload.

options.text: refeeding syndrome
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome follows restarting nutrition in a severely undernourished patient. This patient has been fed for 3 weeks, and the findings are about water, not phosphorus or potassium.

options.text: rising sodium with falling weight and urine output
options.rationale: These three findings together describe a water deficit.

options.text: a soft abdomen with active bowel sounds
options.rationale: These are expected findings and do not support any problem.

options.text: a heart rate of 108/min alone
options.rationale: Tachycardia supports the deficit but has many causes. Alone it does not show the problem.

options.text: the head of the bed at 35 degrees
options.rationale: This is correct positioning and is not a sign of any problem.

options.text: dislodging the gastrostomy tube
options.rationale: A confused, restless patient reaching for the dressing can pull the tube out of place. Securement and close observation become a priority.

options.text: a clogged tube
options.rationale: Clogs come from formula, medications and missed flushes, not from restlessness.

options.text: a pressure injury of the naris
options.rationale: This patient has a gastrostomy tube, not a nasal tube.

options.text: hypoglycemia from the feeding
options.rationale: Nothing in the findings points to low blood glucose, and the feeding is running continuously.

questions.takeaway: Name the problem from the pattern, not one finding: high sodium, weight loss and low concentrated urine together mean dehydration. Then anticipate the next risk: new confusion puts the tube itself in danger.
questions.strategy: Choose the problem that explains all the findings, then ask what the new behavior threatens.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dehydration explains every abnormal finding; aspiration and overload contradict the data.
Sodium, weight and urine together show the deficit; a single sign or a normal finding does not.
Reaching for the dressing threatens the tube.

elimination.verdict: 1: dehydration. 2: rising sodium with falling weight and urine output. 3: dislodging the gastrostomy tube.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: At 0930 the provider prescribes water flushes of 200 mL every 4 hours, holds the furosemide, and orders a daily weight, a basic metabolic panel each morning and a stool test. Chart so far: gastrostomy tube placed 3 weeks ago, nothing by mouth, continuous feeding at 60 mL per hour; weight 59.6 kg, was 61.4 kg 3 days ago; sodium 151 mEq/L; urine dark amber; new confusion. The patient is restless and reaching for the dressing. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give each flush on schedule and record it as intake
options.rationale: Flushes are prescribed treatment here and count toward total fluid intake. Recording each one shows whether the deficit is being corrected.

options.text: Give all four missed flushes now to catch up
options.rationale: Extra water beyond the new prescription is not ordered and can overshoot. The nurse follows the prescribed volume and schedule.

options.text: Weigh the patient daily on the same scale
options.rationale: Daily weight under the same conditions is the best measure of fluid change.

options.text: Record intake and output, including each stool
options.rationale: Liquid stool is a fluid loss, so intake and output must include it to show the true balance.

options.text: Secure the tube and cover it with a binder
options.rationale: Securing the tubing reduces pulling and excessive pressure, and covering it keeps it out of the patient's reach.

options.text: Apply wrist restraints to protect the tube
options.rationale: Restraints are a last resort that need an order. Less restrictive steps, such as securing and covering the tube, come first.

questions.takeaway: Correct a fluid deficit in a tube fed patient by giving the prescribed flushes, counting them and all losses, and weighing daily. Protect the tube with the least restrictive measure.
questions.strategy: Keep actions that carry out the new orders and protect the patient; reject actions that go beyond the orders or are more restrictive than needed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scheduled flushes recorded as intake, daily weight, intake and output with stools, tube securement with a binder.
Extra water is not prescribed.
They need an order and come after less restrictive measures.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, E.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.stem: At 1300 the nurse finds the patient holding the gastrostomy tube, and formula is leaking onto the gown. The external mark is at 8 cm at the skin, documented at 3 cm. The feeding pump is running. Chart so far: gastrostomy tube placed 3 weeks ago, nothing by mouth, continuous feeding at 60 mL per hour; weight 59.6 kg, was 61.4 kg 3 days ago; sodium 151 mEq/L; urine dark amber; new confusion. Flushes have been given on the new schedule since 0930. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Push the tube back in to the 3 cm mark
options.rationale: Pushing a displaced tube back in blindly can place it outside the stomach and lead to formula entering the abdominal cavity. Placement must be verified, not guessed.

options.text: Stop the feeding and hold all tube use
options.rationale: With suspected displacement, the priority is to stop tube use so no more formula or water goes through a tube that may not be in the stomach. Verification follows.

options.text: Flush with 30 mL of water to check patency
options.rationale: A flush through a possibly displaced tube can deliver water outside the stomach. Patency does not confirm placement.

options.text: Notify the provider of the displacement
options.rationale: The provider must be told and placement verified, but formula is still running into a tube that may be out of place. Stopping it comes first.

questions.takeaway: Suspected displacement: stop tube use first, then verify placement. Do not push the tube back, flush it or keep feeding while placement is uncertain.
questions.strategy: Every option is something that may happen next. Ask which one stops harm that is happening right now.

steps.detail: The mark moved from 3 cm to 8 cm and formula is leaking while the pump runs.
Formula may be going outside the stomach right now.
Pushing it in and flushing use a tube of unknown position; notifying the provider leaves the pump running.
Stop the feeding and hold all tube use.

elimination.verdict: B. Stop the feeding and hold all tube use.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

questions.scenario: Two days later at 0800, the provider has replaced the tube, placement has been verified, and feeding with 200 mL water flushes every 4 hours resumed. Chart so far: dehydration 2 days ago with weight 59.6 kg, sodium 151 mEq/L, dark amber urine and new confusion; usual weight 61.4 kg; tube displacement at 1300 that day. Findings now: sodium 140 mEq/L. Urine pale yellow, 480 mL in the past 8 hours. Oriented to person, place and time, not reaching for the tube. Heart rate 84/min. Weight 63.1 kg. Fine crackles in both lung bases, new today. Five liquid stools in the past 24 hours.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating the response to treatment of a patient with dehydration who receives continuous gastrostomy tube feeding. For each finding, indicate whether it shows the treatment is effective or requires follow up.

rows.text: Sodium 140 mEq/L, was 151 mEq/L
rows.rationale: The sodium has returned to the normal range (about 135 to 145 mEq/L), showing the water deficit has been corrected.

rows.text: Urine pale yellow, 480 mL in the past 8 hours
rows.rationale: Dilute urine at a good volume shows the kidneys are no longer conserving water.

rows.text: Oriented to person, place and time, not reaching for the tube
rows.rationale: Mental status has returned to baseline, which also lowers the risk of another displacement.

rows.text: Weight 63.1 kg, was 59.6 kg 2 days ago, usual 61.4 kg
rows.rationale: Some gain was the goal, but a 3.5 kg gain in 2 days that is now 1.7 kg above the usual weight is too fast and points to fluid excess.

rows.text: Fine crackles in both lung bases, new today
rows.rationale: New bilateral crackles with the rapid weight gain suggest the water replacement has now overshot into fluid overload. The nurse reports it so the flushes can be adjusted.

rows.text: Five liquid stools in the past 24 hours
rows.rationale: The diarrhea has continued and is a source of fluid and electrolyte loss. Its cause still needs to be found.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate against the goal, not just the direction of change. A deficit that is corrected can be overcorrected: weight above the usual baseline with new crackles means fluid overload, even though the sodium and urine now look right.
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with the goal (the usual baseline), not only with 2 days ago.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sodium, urine and mental status are back to the goal.
Weight is above the usual weight and new crackles have appeared.
Liquid stools continue.
Three effective, three requiring follow up.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 2 and 3: effective. Rows 4, 5 and 6: requires follow up.

questions.objective: Monitor feeding tolerance and respond to complications

skills.title: Cardiac Assessment
skills.subtitle: Pulse and apical pulse, cardiac monitoring, recording and reading a 12 lead ECG, heart sounds, and a heart failure home visit

questions.stem: Before giving digoxin, the nurse cannot palpate the apical impulse on a patient with large breasts. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Lift the breast and auscultate the apex for 1 minute
options.rationale: The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line. A patient with large breasts is asked to lift the breast. The impulse cannot be felt in every patient, and the count is still made by listening for 1 full minute.

options.text: Count the radial pulse for 1 full minute instead
options.rationale: A full minute is right, but the site is wrong. An impulse that cannot be felt is not a reason to change sites, and the apical pulse is heard, not only felt.

options.text: Auscultate the right 2nd intercostal space for 1 minute
options.rationale: A full minute with the diaphragm is right, but this is the aortic area. The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line.

options.text: Lift the breast and auscultate the apex for 30 seconds, doubled
options.rationale: The site and the breast are handled correctly, but the apical pulse before digoxin is counted for 1 full minute.

questions.takeaway: The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line. Listen with the diaphragm for 1 full minute. Ask a patient with large breasts to lift the breast. Not feeling the impulse is not a reason to switch sites.
questions.strategy: Each option gets something right, and two options match on site and breast. Check the site first, then the length of the count.

steps.detail: 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line.
1 full minute, by listening.
The patient lifts the breast.
An impulse that cannot be felt is common and expected in some patients.

elimination.verdict: Have the patient lift the breast, listen at the 5th intercostal space on the left midclavicular line, and count 1 full minute.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is locating the apical pulse of a patient by landmarks. Place the steps in the order the nurse performs them.

options.text: Move just to the left of the sternum into the 2nd intercostal space
options.rationale: The 2nd intercostal space lies just beside the angle of Louis, so it is the first space the nurse can name with certainty.

options.text: Find the sternal notch between the clavicles
options.rationale: The sternal notch is the starting landmark.

options.text: Place the diaphragm and count for 1 full minute
options.rationale: Listening comes after the site is found, and the count is a full minute.

options.text: Find the angle of Louis, the ridge on the sternum
options.rationale: The angle of Louis is the next landmark below the notch.

options.text: Count down to the 5th intercostal space on the left midclavicular line
options.rationale: From the 2nd space, the nurse counts down the spaces along the midclavicular line to the 5th.

questions.takeaway: To find the apical pulse: sternal notch, angle of Louis, 2nd intercostal space just to the left, then down the midclavicular line to the 5th space, then listen for 1 full minute.
questions.strategy: Start with the landmark that cannot be mistaken, the notch, and let each step name the next one. The space cannot be counted until the 2nd space has been found.

steps.detail: The sternal notch.
The angle of Louis comes next, below the notch.
2nd intercostal space, just left of the angle of Louis.
Midclavicular line to the 5th space, then listen.

elimination.verdict: Notch, angle of Louis, 2nd space, down the midclavicular line to the 5th space, listen for 1 full minute.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give digoxin to a patient. The apical pulse, counted for 1 full minute, is 56/min and regular. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. The patient is alert and says, "My pulse is always in the fifties. My doctor knows about it." Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the digoxin and document the patient's statement
options.rationale: The patient's report and the lack of symptoms matter, but the rate is below the range wanted before digoxin. The nurse does not decide alone that a low rate is acceptable; the statement is reported, not acted on.

options.text: Hold the digoxin and report the rate to the provider now
options.rationale: Before digoxin the heart rate should be within 60 to 100/min. At 56/min the dose is held, and the report gives the provider both the rate and the patient's statement so a decision can be made now.

options.text: Hold the digoxin and recheck the rate before the next dose
options.rationale: Holding is right, but a held dose and the reason are reported at the time. Whether a rate in the fifties is acceptable for this patient is the provider's decision, and without a report the patient simply misses the medication.

options.text: Recount the apical pulse and give the digoxin if it is higher
options.rationale: The first count was already a full apical minute with a regular rhythm. A recount only looks for a number that permits the dose.

questions.takeaway: Count the apical pulse for 1 full minute before digoxin. The adult range wanted is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Below 60, hold the dose and report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Two options hold the dose. The deciding cue is who may accept a rate below 60 beats per minute: the provider, today, not the nurse and not the next shift.

steps.detail: Apical 56 beats per minute for a full minute.
60 to 100 beats per minute before digoxin.
It is reported, not acted on alone.
One reports now. One leaves the decision until the next dose.

elimination.verdict: Hold the digoxin and report the rate with the patient's statement.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: Before cardiac monitoring, the nurse notes an alert patient's chest is damp with sweat and has thick hair. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Dry the skin, then press and tape electrodes over the hair
options.rationale: Drying is right, but hair still prevents good contact, and tape does not fix that.

options.text: Obtain consent, clip, and apply electrodes to the damp skin
options.rationale: Consent and hair removal are right, but the skin must be dry.

options.text: Dry the skin and clip the hair at the sites with consent
options.rationale: Skin should be clean and dry with good contact. With the patient's consent, hair at the electrode sites is removed. Some guides say shave; current US practice is to clip, because a razor can nick the skin and cause irritation under the electrode.

options.text: Dry the skin, clip the sites, then explain the clipping
options.rationale: Both problems are solved, but consent comes before hair removal. This patient is alert.

questions.takeaway: For cardiac monitoring the skin must be clean and dry with good electrode contact. Chest hair at the sites is removed with the patient's consent, by clipping rather than shaving in current US practice.
questions.strategy: Check three things in each option: dry skin, hair removed, and consent given first.

steps.detail: Moisture and hair.

steps.action: Drop options that leave one unsolved
steps.detail: Tape over hair, or damp skin.

steps.action: Compare the two that solve both
steps.detail: Consent before clipping, or explanation after.

elimination.verdict: C. Dry the skin and, with consent, clip the hair at the electrode sites.

questions.objective: Consider when cardiac monitoring may be used for a patient and how the clinician might apply this

questions.nursesNote: 1030, review of a 12 lead ECG recorded as a routine baseline: Calibration box is 2 large squares high and speed is 25 mm per second. One P wave comes before each QRS complex. PR interval is 7 small squares on every beat. QRS width is 2 small squares. R waves are evenly spaced, 4 large squares apart. ST segment is raised above the baseline in leads II, III and aVF.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a 12 lead ECG recorded as a routine baseline. Highlight the findings that are outside the expected range and must be reported.

segments.text: Calibration box is 2 large squares high and speed is 25 mm per second
segments.rationale: This is the standard calibration: 1 millivolt equals 2 large squares, and the speed is 25 mm per second.

segments.text: One P wave comes before each QRS complex
segments.rationale: One P wave per QRS is the expected finding.

segments.text: PR interval is 7 small squares on every beat
segments.rationale: The PR interval should be 3 to 5 small squares. Consistently longer could indicate first degree heart block.

segments.text: QRS width is 2 small squares
segments.rationale: The QRS should be 3 small squares or less, so 2 small squares is within range.

segments.text: R waves are evenly spaced, 4 large squares apart
segments.rationale: The rhythm is regular, so 300 divided by 4 gives 75 beats per minute, within the adult range of 60 to 100 beats per minute.

segments.text: ST segment is raised above the baseline in leads II, III and aVF
segments.rationale: ST elevation could indicate myocardial infarction. Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall of the heart.

questions.takeaway: Read an ECG in order: clean trace, calibration, rhythm, one P per QRS, measurements (PR 3 to 5 small squares, QRS 3 or less, rate by the 300 rule), then scan for ST and T wave changes.
questions.strategy: Take each line of the note as one of the six steps and test it against its normal. Two lines fail: one measurement and one finding from the scan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 large squares and 25 mm per second: correct.
PR 7 is long. QRS 2 is in range. 300 divided by 4 is 75 beats per minute.
ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF needs review now.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: While the nurse records a 12 lead ECG, the patient talks and shifts, and the baseline is thick and wavy. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Send the printout with a note that the patient moved
options.rationale: A note is honest, but interference should be sorted at the point of recording. A poor trace can hide or mimic changes.

options.text: Replace all electrodes and record the ECG again at once
options.rationale: Recording again is right, but the cause is movement and talking. New electrodes do not remove it, and the second trace will look the same.

options.text: Estimate the rate from the visible R waves and report it
options.rationale: Reporting is reasonable, but a rate taken from a poor trace may be wrong, and the trace can be fixed now.

options.text: Have the patient lie still and quiet, and repeat it
options.rationale: The first step in interpreting an ECG is a clean trace. Interference is fixed at the time of recording, so the cause is removed by having the patient lie still with the hands relaxed at the sides and not talk, and the ECG is recorded again.

questions.takeaway: Step 1 of reading a 12 lead ECG is a clean trace. Fix interference at the point of recording and record again if in doubt.
questions.strategy: Two options record again. Only one removes the cause stated in the stem, movement and talking.

steps.detail: Talking and moving during the recording.

steps.action: Ask whether it can be fixed now
steps.detail: Yes: the patient lies still and the ECG is repeated.

steps.action: Drop the options that miss the cause
steps.detail: A note, an estimated rate, or new electrodes.

elimination.verdict: Have the patient lie still and quiet, and record again.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who reports chest pain that began 20 minutes ago, rated 6 of 10. A 12 lead ECG recorded 5 minutes ago shows a clean trace, correct calibration, and no ST elevation in any lead. The pain is still 6 of 10. A colleague says, "There is no ST elevation. Let the patient rest." Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Record a second ECG now to compare with the first
options.rationale: Repeat ECGs are real practice, which makes this tempting, but the first trace is 5 minutes old, clean, and correctly calibrated. A second recording delays the report of pain that has lasted 20 minutes.

options.text: Recheck vital signs and the pain rating in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Monitoring vital signs is right, but the pain has already been reassessed and is unchanged at 6 of 10. Waiting 15 minutes delays the report.

options.text: Report the ongoing pain and get the ECG reviewed
options.rationale: A myocardial infarction can be present without ST elevation. The pain is unchanged, so the nurse reports now and has the ECG reviewed by a competent clinician.

options.text: Check lead placement and repeat the ECG
options.rationale: The trace was clean and correctly calibrated. Nothing suggests a recording error, and repeating it delays the report.

questions.takeaway: ST elevation could indicate myocardial infarction, but an infarction can be present without it. Ongoing chest pain is reported, and a competent clinician reviews the ECG.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Three options do something useful before reporting. The deciding cues are that the pain is unchanged at 6 of 10 after 20 minutes and that the ECG is already clean and 5 minutes old, so nothing needs to come before the report.

steps.action: Separate the ECG from the patient
steps.detail: ECG: no ST elevation. Patient: pain still 6 of 10.
An infarction can be present without ST elevation.
A repeat ECG and vital signs are useful, but not before the report.
Clean trace and correct calibration.

elimination.verdict: Report the ongoing chest pain and the ECG now for review.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.scenario: The home health nurse is visiting a patient with heart failure. The patient's furosemide was increased from 40 mg to 80 mg once a day last week because of weight gain and swollen ankles. The patient's spouse weighs the patient every morning and keeps the record. The patient also takes simvastatin at night.
questions.stem: For each finding at today's visit, indicate whether it is an expected finding or requires follow up.

rows.text: Weight is 2 kg lower than before the dose was increased
rows.rationale: The diuretic was increased to remove extra fluid. A lower weight shows it is working.

rows.text: The patient reports feeling light headed when standing up from the bed
rows.rationale: A doubled diuretic can remove too much fluid. Light headedness on standing is a new symptom that needs assessment and reporting.

rows.text: Respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 97% and no increased shortness of breath
rows.rationale: These findings show no sign that fluid is affecting the breathing.

rows.text: The patient says the simvastatin has been skipped for the last 3 nights
rows.rationale: Medication adherence is part of the assessment. A missed medication is explored and addressed with the patient.

rows.text: Radial pulse is 62 beats per minute and regular, the hand is warm, and capillary refill is 2 seconds
rows.rationale: The rate is within 60 to 100 beats per minute, the rhythm is regular, and the limb is well perfused.

rows.text: The spouse is tearful and says, "I am not sleeping. I lie awake listening to the breathing."
rows.rationale: A holistic assessment includes the wellbeing of the family. A caregiver who is not sleeping needs attention and support.

questions.takeaway: After a diuretic increase, a lower weight with a respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, pulse and capillary refill in range is expected. New light headedness on standing, missed medication, and a caregiver who is not sleeping each need follow up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into what the dose was meant to achieve and what is new or going wrong. Follow up is not only for abnormal vital signs: adherence and the caregiver count too.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the goal of the change
steps.detail: Less fluid: lower weight, less swelling.
All in range.
A new symptom, a missed medication, and a tearful caregiver.

elimination.verdict: The lower weight, the breathing findings, and the radial pulse findings are expected. Light headedness, skipped simvastatin, and the spouse's distress require follow up.

questions.objective: Interpret the findings from a patient assessment to identify the priorities for planning care

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure had a diuretic dose increase last week. Which statement by the home health nurse best explores how the patient is managing?

options.text: "You have been taking the new dose every morning, haven't you?"
options.rationale: This is a leading question. It invites the patient to agree and makes a missed dose harder to admit.

options.text: "Tell me how things have been since the dose changed."
options.rationale: An open question lets the patient describe what matters most, including problems the nurse did not think to ask about.

options.text: "How is your breathing today compared with last week?"
options.rationale: This is open, but it covers one symptom on one day, not how the patient has been managing since the change.

options.text: "What side effects have you noticed since your water pill was increased?"
options.rationale: This is open in form, but it limits the answer to side effects and assumes there are some.

questions.takeaway: Open questions let the patient tell the nurse how things are going. A leading question or a question limited to one topic narrows what the patient will say.
questions.strategy: Three options are questions the patient can answer at length. Match each to the stated goal: how the patient has been managing since the change.

steps.detail: "Haven't you?" invites agreement.
One asks only about breathing today.
One assumes side effects.
"Tell me how things have been since the dose changed."

elimination.verdict: B. "Tell me how things have been since the dose changed."

questions.objective: Interpret the findings from a patient assessment to identify the priorities for planning care

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has an S2 at the pulmonic area that splits on inspiration and is single on expiration. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Report a new abnormal heart sound to the provider
options.rationale: Reporting is right for a new abnormal sound, but a second heart sound that splits only on inspiration is a normal finding.

options.text: Move to the 5th intercostal space, where S2 is loudest
options.rationale: The second heart sound is loudest at the aortic and pulmonary areas, where the nurse already is. The mitral area is where the first heart sound is best heard.

options.text: Document a murmur at the pulmonic area for routine review
options.rationale: A murmur is an extra sound. Here the second heart sound itself divides, and only on breathing in, which is a normal finding and not a murmur.

options.text: Document the split S2 and continue the assessment
options.rationale: On inspiration more blood returns to the right side of the heart, so the pulmonary valve closes slightly after the aortic valve. This physiologic splitting of the second heart sound is expected.

questions.takeaway: S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing, loudest at the 2nd intercostal spaces. A split on inspiration that disappears on expiration is physiologic and expected.
questions.strategy: A patient with heart failure and an unusual sound pulls toward reporting. The deciding detail is the timing: two sounds only on breathing in.

steps.detail: S2, heard at the pulmonary area.
Split on inspiration, single on expiration.
Physiologic splitting is expected.
S2 is loudest at the base, not the apex.

elimination.verdict: Document the split on inspiration and continue the assessment.

questions.objective: Identify how to undertake cardiac auscultation and what these sounds represent in relation to the cardiac cycle

questions.stem: The nurse is starting 5 lead continuous cardiac monitoring for a patient with heart failure. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Select lead II for the monitor display
options.rationale: Lead II is usually selected for monitoring because it is easily interpreted.

options.text: Place the right arm electrode just below the right clavicle
options.rationale: The right arm electrode sits under the right clavicle near the shoulder, on the chest and inside the rib cage frame.

options.text: Place the leg electrode on the upper left thigh
options.rationale: The leg electrode is placed on the chest, at the lower edge of the left rib cage below the pectoral muscles, not on the limb.

options.text: Place the chest electrode at the 4th intercostal space, left sternal margin
options.rationale: The space is right but the side is wrong. On a 5 lead system this electrode sits at the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal margin.

options.text: Set alarm limits to this patient's condition
options.rationale: Alarm limits are set based on the patient's clinical condition, so they warn of change that matters for this patient.

options.text: Leave the low heart rate alarm at the unit default
options.rationale: A default limit ignores the patient's condition. Every alarm limit, high and low, is set based on this patient's clinical condition.

questions.takeaway: For continuous monitoring: lead II on display, electrodes on the chest within the rib cage frame, the 5th electrode at the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal margin, and alarm limits set to the patient's condition.
questions.strategy: Treat each statement on its own. For electrode positions, check two things: is it on the chest inside the rib cage frame, and is it on the correct side.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lead II, easily interpreted: correct.
Right arm under the right clavicle is correct. The leg electrode belongs on the lower left rib cage. The chest electrode belongs at the right sternal margin.
Set to the patient's condition, not left at default.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Consider when cardiac monitoring may be used for a patient and how the clinician might apply this

questions.stem: A new 12 lead ECG has a clean trace, but the calibration box is only 1 large square high. Which action should the nurse take next?

options.text: Measure the PR interval, QRS width, and heart rate
options.rationale: Measurements are step 5. With the wrong calibration the trace cannot be interpreted accurately, so this comes too early.

options.text: Scan every lead for ST and T wave changes
options.rationale: Scanning the leads is the last step. With the wrong calibration the size of ST changes would be misjudged.

options.text: Correct the calibration and record the ECG again
options.rationale: The calibration box should be 2 large squares high, equal to 1 millivolt. A box of 1 large square fails step 2, so the nurse fixes it and records again before interpreting the trace.

options.text: Check the lead II strip for sinus rhythm
options.rationale: This is step 3, the right next step only after calibration is confirmed. Here calibration has failed.

questions.takeaway: Read a 12 lead ECG in order: clean trace, calibration (2 large squares at 25 mm per second), sinus rhythm on lead II, one P wave per QRS, measurements, then scan the leads. A failed step is fixed before you move on.
questions.strategy: Check each step against the patient's trace in order. The first step that fails decides the action, even when a later step sounds more useful.

steps.detail: The trace is clean, so step 1 passes.
The box is 1 large square, not 2. Step 2 fails, so later steps wait. Eliminate A, B and D.
