elimination.verdict: C. Fix the calibration and record again before interpreting the trace.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient on continuous cardiac monitoring who reports palpitations. The lead II rhythm strip, recorded at 25 mm per second, shows spaces between R waves that vary from 2 to 4 large squares with no pattern. The first two R waves are 3 large squares apart. The nurse counts 12 R waves within 30 large squares. Which heart rate should the nurse document?

options.text: 120/min, from 12 R waves in 30 large squares times 10
options.rationale: With an irregular rhythm the rate is found by counting the R waves in 30 large squares, which is 6 seconds, and multiplying by 10. This gives 120 beats per minute, above the expected range.

options.text: 100/min, from 300 divided by the first R to R interval
options.rationale: The 300 rule is a correct method, but only for a regular rhythm. Here the spacing varies from 2 to 4 large squares, so one pair of R waves does not represent the rate, and the result falsely sits inside the expected range.

options.text: 75/min, from 300 divided by the widest R to R interval
options.rationale: The widest space gives the slowest beats only. With an irregular rhythm, no single R to R space gives the rate.

options.text: 110/min, from 11 R to R intervals in 30 large squares times 10
options.rationale: The 6 second method and the multiplier are right, but the method counts R waves, not the spaces between them. 12 R waves have only 11 spaces, so this undercounts by 1 beat in every 6 seconds.

questions.takeaway: Use 300 divided by the large squares between R waves only when the rhythm is regular. When it is irregular, count the R waves in 30 large squares (6 seconds) and multiply by 10.
questions.strategy: Two methods are both correct ways to calculate a rate. The deciding cue is in the stem: the R to R spacing varies with no pattern, so the rhythm is irregular and only the 6 second count applies.

steps.detail: R to R spacing varies from 2 to 4 large squares: irregular.
Any 300 rule answer uses one space that does not represent the rate.
30 large squares is 6 seconds, so multiply by 10.
12 R waves times 10 is 120 beats per minute, above 60 to 100.

elimination.verdict: 120 beats per minute, from 12 R waves in 30 large squares multiplied by 10.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: A patient with ongoing chest pain has ST elevation in leads V1 through V4 only. Which actions and interpretations are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Report changes in the inferior, right coronary artery area
options.rationale: The inferior leads are II, III and aVF. V1 to V4 are the septal and anterior leads.

options.text: Report changes in the left anterior descending artery area
options.rationale: V1 and V2 are septal and V3 and V4 are anterior; both groups are supplied by the left anterior descending artery.

options.text: Conclude that changes in only four leads rule out infarction
options.rationale: ST elevation in any group of leads could indicate a myocardial infarction. The number of leads does not rule it out.

options.text: Report the ongoing pain and ST elevation now
options.rationale: ST elevation could indicate a myocardial infarction, and the pain is still present, so the report cannot wait.

options.text: Stop reassessing pain if a later ECG shows no ST elevation
options.rationale: A myocardial infarction can occur without ST elevation, so ongoing pain still needs assessment and reporting.

options.text: Ask a clinician skilled in ECG interpretation to review it
options.rationale: The nurse asks a competent clinician to help interpret the ECG and confirm the findings.

questions.takeaway: Septal V1 and V2 and anterior V3 and V4 reflect the left anterior descending artery; inferior II, III and aVF the right coronary artery; lateral I, aVL, V5 and V6 the circumflex. ST elevation with ongoing pain is reported now, and an infarction can occur without ST elevation.
questions.strategy: First match the leads to their artery, then decide what the finding means for this patient: ongoing pain plus ST elevation is an urgent report, with expert help to interpret.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: V1 to V4 are septal and anterior: left anterior descending. Keep B; eliminate A.
ST elevation with pain could be an infarction, and its absence does not rule one out. Keep D; eliminate C and E.
A competent clinician reviews the trace. Keep F.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F. Name the artery, report now, and get expert interpretation.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: Before documenting a murmur's timing, the nurse must identify S1 in a patient. Which technique is most reliable?

options.text: The sound louder at the right second intercostal space
options.rationale: The aortic area is where S2, the aortic and pulmonary valves closing, is loudest.

options.text: The sound louder at the left second intercostal space
options.rationale: The pulmonic area is also where S2 is loudest, so this finds S2, not S1.

options.text: The sound louder at the apex
options.rationale: S1 is usually louder at the apex, so this is tempting. A loud murmur or extra sound at the apex can make loudness hard to judge, so loudness alone is less reliable than timing.

options.text: The sound that occurs with the carotid pulse
options.rationale: S1 is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing at the start of systole, and the carotid pulse is felt right after it. Feeling the carotid pulse while listening identifies S1 whatever other sounds are present.

questions.takeaway: S1 is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing at the start of systole. It is usually louder at the apex, but the most reliable way to identify it, especially with a murmur or a fast rate, is to feel the carotid pulse while listening: S1 comes with the pulse.
questions.strategy: Three options rely on where a sound is loudest, which a murmur can distort. Choose the technique that ties the sound to systole itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The right and left second intercostal spaces are where S2 is loudest. Eliminate A and B.
S1 is usually louder there, but a murmur can mask loudness. C is less reliable.
S1 comes with the carotid pulse. D remains.

elimination.verdict: D. The sound that occurs with the carotid pulse is S1.

questions.objective: Identify how to undertake cardiac auscultation and what these sounds represent in relation to the cardiac cycle

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to record a 12 lead ECG for an alert patient. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm the patient's name and date of birth
options.rationale: Identity is confirmed with the name and date of birth before the recording, so the trace belongs to the right patient.

options.text: Ask about chest pain at this moment
options.rationale: Asking about chest pain at the moment of recording is part of preparing the patient, and chest pain is one of the reasons a 12 lead ECG is recorded.

options.text: Have the patient sit upright with hands in the lap
options.rationale: Relaxed hands are right, but the position is wrong. The patient lies back on the bed with the hands relaxed and flat at the sides, which reduces movement interference.

options.text: Place the limb electrodes on the chest, inside the rib cage
options.rationale: Inside the rib cage frame is the placement for continuous monitoring. For a 12 lead ECG the 4 limb electrodes go on the wrists and ankles.

options.text: Palpate the chest to locate electrode landmarks
options.rationale: The chest is palpated to find the landmarks for the chest electrodes, so each one is placed accurately.

options.text: Apply electrodes first, then explain and gain consent
options.rationale: Explanation and consent are right, but they come before the patient is touched. This patient is alert.

questions.takeaway: Before a 12 lead ECG: confirm name and date of birth, explain and gain consent, ask about chest pain, have the patient lie back with the hands relaxed flat at the sides, palpate the chest for landmarks, and place the limb electrodes on the wrists and ankles.
questions.strategy: Check each option for the one detail that is off: the position, the limb electrode site, or the point at which consent is gained.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Name and date of birth first; consent before touching the patient.
Chest pain now is asked about.
Lying back, hands relaxed flat at the sides, not sitting.
Chest landmarks by palpation; limb electrodes on wrists and ankles, not the chest.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: On a lead II monitor, a patient's P waves and QRS complexes suddenly point downward. The patient is unchanged. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the right arm and leg electrode positions
options.rationale: In lead II the right arm electrode is negative and the leg electrode is positive. The wave normally travels toward the leg electrode and points upward, so a sudden downward trace with no change in the patient suggests the electrodes were moved or swapped.

options.text: Report a new conduction problem to the provider now
options.rationale: The patient is unchanged, and the most likely cause is electrode position. Check the equipment before reporting a rhythm change.

options.text: Document the downward complexes as the new baseline
options.rationale: The trace changed suddenly with no change in the patient. Recording it as baseline accepts a probable equipment error.

options.text: Switch the display to a different lead
options.rationale: Lead II is usually selected because it is easily interpreted. Changing leads hides the problem instead of finding its cause.

questions.takeaway: A wave moving toward a positive electrode gives an upward deflection. In lead II the leg electrode is positive and the right arm negative, so the normal trace points up. A sudden downward trace in an unchanged patient points to electrode position first.
questions.strategy: When the monitor changes but the patient does not, suspect the equipment. Check the electrodes before you report or accept the new trace.

steps.detail: The patient is unchanged, so the trace change is likely technical.
Reporting, recording a new baseline or switching leads all skip the check. Eliminate B, C and D.

elimination.verdict: A. Check the right arm and leg electrode positions first.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: A patient with a known systolic murmur has a new whooshing sound after S2 that ends before the next S1. Which conclusions are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: It occurs while the mitral and tricuspid valves are open
options.rationale: After S2 the aortic and pulmonary valves are closed and the mitral and tricuspid valves open so the ventricles can fill.

options.text: It occurs while the ventricles fill
options.rationale: Between S2 and the next S1 is diastole, when the ventricles relax and fill, with atrial contraction at the end.

options.text: It occurs while the aortic and pulmonary valves are open
options.rationale: These valves are open during systole, between S1 and S2. They close to make S2, before this sound begins.

options.text: It is the known systolic murmur
options.rationale: A systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2. This sound falls between S2 and S1, so it is a different, new sound.

options.text: It is a new diastolic murmur to report
options.rationale: A sound between S2 and S1 is diastolic. A new murmur is a change from baseline, so it is reported and documented.

options.text: It can be charted as unchanged
options.rationale: The known murmur is unchanged, but this second sound is new. Charting it as unchanged hides a change the provider needs to know.

questions.takeaway: S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing at the start of diastole. A sound between S2 and the next S1 is diastolic, heard while the mitral and tricuspid valves are open and the ventricles fill. A known systolic murmur does not explain a new diastolic one, which is reported.
questions.strategy: Anchor the new sound to the heart sound it follows. After S2 is diastole, so it cannot be the known systolic murmur, and a new finding is reported.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It follows S2, the start of diastole. Keep A and B; C describes systole. Eliminate C.
The known murmur is systolic; this sound is diastolic, so it is new. Eliminate D and F.
A new diastolic murmur is reported. Keep E.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E. The new sound is diastolic, heard while the ventricles fill, and is reported.

questions.objective: Identify how to undertake cardiac auscultation and what these sounds represent in relation to the cardiac cycle

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient admitted 2 days ago with pneumonia. The radial pulse has been documented at 64 to 70/min, regular, at every check since admission. Today the radial pulse is 98/min and regular, oxygen saturation is 95% on room air, capillary refill is 2 seconds, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document the findings and recheck at the next scheduled time
options.rationale: Each value sits inside its expected range, but the pulse has risen by 28 to 34 beats per minute from this patient's own documented rate. Pulse assessment gives a baseline so that change can be identified, and waiting hides that change.

options.text: Reassess the patient now and report the rise in pulse rate
options.rationale: The pulse has risen from 64 to 70 beats per minute at every check to 98 beats per minute. A change from the patient's own baseline is acted on even when the number is still in range, so the nurse reassesses and reports it.

options.text: Recount the pulse and document it if it remains in range
options.rationale: Rechecking is reasonable, but the plan accepts any rate within the adult range. It still compares the pulse only with that range, not with this patient's usual rate of 64 to 70/min.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L/min and recheck the saturation
options.rationale: The saturation of 95% is within the expected range, and starting oxygen treats one number before the patient has been reassessed. The finding that has changed is the pulse.

questions.takeaway: Pulse is assessed alongside oxygen saturation, blood pressure and capillary refill, and it gives a baseline of what is usual for the patient. A clear change from that baseline needs action even when every value is still within the expected range.
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible because every value is in range. The deciding cue in the stem is the documented rate of 64 to 70 beats per minute at every check since admission.

steps.detail: Every value is within its expected range.
Pulse 98 against a usual 64 to 70 beats per minute: a clear change.
Documenting, or recounting against 100 beats per minute, ignores the baseline.
Oxygen for a saturation inside the range skips reassessment.

elimination.verdict: Reassess now and report the rise from the patient's usual pulse rate.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is completing a cardiovascular assessment of a patient admitted with shortness of breath. Which findings require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apical impulse felt over a 3 cm area
options.rationale: The point of maximal impulse is where the left ventricle touches the chest wall and usually does not exceed 1 cm across. A wider impulse suggests an enlarged ventricle.

options.text: Capillary refill time of 2 seconds
options.rationale: A refill time of 2 seconds shows normal peripheral perfusion.

options.text: Radial pulse regular, grade 2+
options.rationale: A regular pulse graded 2+ is a normal strength pulse.

options.text: S2 that splits on inspiration only
options.rationale: During inspiration more venous blood returns to the right heart and the pulmonary valve closes slightly later. Splitting on inspiration that disappears on expiration is physiologic.

options.text: Radial pulse irregular at 112/min
options.rationale: An irregular pulse that is also fast is a reason to record a 12 lead ECG. It may be an arrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation.

options.text: New whooshing sound between S1 and S2
options.rationale: A whooshing sound between S1 and S2 is a systolic murmur from turbulent flow. A new extra sound is reported and described by location, timing and quality.

questions.takeaway: Know normal first: a point of maximal impulse no wider than 1 cm, a regular 2+ pulse, refill of about 2 seconds, and S2 splitting only on inspiration. A wide impulse, a fast irregular pulse and a new murmur are findings to report.
questions.strategy: Two options describe normal findings that sound abnormal: a split heart sound and a graded pulse. Ask whether each is normal physiology before calling it a problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wider than 1 cm: follow up.
Grade 2+ and regular is normal; irregular at 112/min is not.
Splitting on inspiration is physiologic; a new murmur is not.

elimination.verdict: A, E, F.

questions.objective: Interpret the findings from a patient assessment to identify the priorities for planning care

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a 12 lead ECG recorded for a patient with chest tightness, now 3 of 10. The trace is clean, the calibration is correct, and the rhythm is sinus. ST depression is present in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6, and no lead shows ST elevation. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: Infarction of the inferior wall, from the right coronary artery
options.rationale: The inferior leads are II, III and aVF, supplied by the right coronary artery. The changes here are in other leads, and ST depression suggests ischemia rather than a definite infarction.

options.text: Possible ischemia of the lateral wall, from the circumflex artery
options.rationale: Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 look at the lateral wall, supplied by the left circumflex artery. ST depression or T wave inversion could indicate ischemia. The ECG is reviewed with a clinician skilled in interpretation and reported with the ongoing tightness.

options.text: Possible ischemia of the anterior wall, from the left anterior descending artery
options.rationale: ST depression could indicate ischemia, so half of this is right. But the anterior leads are V3 and V4, with the septal leads V1 and V2, all supplied by the left anterior descending artery.

options.text: No infarction, because no lead shows ST elevation
options.rationale: This sounds reassuring, but a myocardial infarction can occur without ST elevation, and ST depression with chest tightness still needs reporting.

questions.takeaway: Lead groups map to the arteries: inferior II, III, aVF (right coronary); lateral I, aVL, V5, V6 (left circumflex); septal V1, V2 and anterior V3, V4 (left anterior descending). ST elevation could indicate infarction; ST depression or T wave inversion could indicate ischemia; no ST elevation does not rule out infarction.
questions.strategy: You need two cues at once: which leads changed and what the change was. Option C gets the meaning right with the wrong wall, and option D draws a false conclusion from a true observation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: I, aVL, V5, V6: lateral, left circumflex.
ST depression: possible ischemia.
An infarction can occur without ST elevation.

elimination.verdict: B. Possible ischemia of the lateral wall, from the circumflex artery.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing 12 lead ECGs recorded this morning for four patients. Each trace is clean with correct calibration. Which patient's finding should the nurse report first?

options.text: PR interval 6 small squares, unchanged from last year
options.rationale: A PR interval longer than five small squares could indicate first degree heart block. It is unchanged from last year and is reported routinely.

options.text: Tall R waves over the left ventricle with long standing hypertension
options.rationale: Tall R waves over the left ventricle could indicate left ventricular hypertrophy, which fits years of high blood pressure. It is reported, but it is a chronic change.

options.text: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with nausea and sweating
options.rationale: ST elevation could indicate a myocardial infarction, here in the inferior wall supplied by the right coronary artery. Nausea and sweating show it is happening now. Heart muscle is being lost by the minute, so this is reported first.

options.text: Two P waves before some QRS complexes, rate 64/min, no symptoms
options.rationale: More P waves than QRS complexes could indicate second or third degree heart block, which is new and serious and makes this tempting. But the rate of 64/min is maintaining output and the patient has no symptoms, so it is reported right after the acute infarction.

questions.takeaway: Report the finding that shows harm happening now. ST elevation with symptoms suggests an evolving infarction and comes first. A new conduction block with an adequate rate and no symptoms is serious and follows closely. Chronic, unchanged findings are reported routinely.
questions.strategy: Two findings are new and abnormal: the ST elevation and the extra P waves. The deciding cues are the symptoms (nausea and sweating) with the ST elevation, against an adequate rate and no symptoms with the block.

steps.detail: An unchanged PR interval and hypertrophy from long standing hypertension.
An evolving infarction with symptoms against a block with a rate of 64/min and no symptoms.
ST elevation with nausea and sweating.

elimination.verdict: C. ST elevation with symptoms suggests an evolving infarction.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient on continuous cardiac monitoring after admission for palpitations. The central monitor alarms and shows wide, bizarre QRS complexes at 180/min. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the patient's responsiveness and pulse
options.rationale: Wide, bizarre QRS complexes could mean a ventricular origin such as ventricular tachycardia, which can stop effective output. The patient is assessed first: a patient who is unresponsive without a pulse needs resuscitation, and one who is talking points toward artifact.

options.text: Print a rhythm strip to document the event
options.rationale: A strip documents the rhythm, but it does nothing for a patient who may have lost cardiac output.

options.text: Record a 12 lead ECG to confirm the rhythm
options.rationale: A 12 lead ECG may follow once the patient is assessed. Recording one first delays help if the patient has no pulse.

options.text: Check the electrodes for loose skin contact
options.rationale: Loose electrodes can cause a false alarm, which makes this tempting. But the nurse checks the patient, not the equipment, before deciding the rhythm is artifact.

questions.takeaway: Treat the patient, not the monitor. When the monitor shows a dangerous rhythm, the first action is to assess the patient's responsiveness and pulse. Equipment checks, rhythm strips and a 12 lead ECG come after.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Every option is a reasonable step with a monitor alarm. Order them by what could kill the patient in the next minute: only checking the patient answers that.

steps.detail: Wide, bizarre QRS at 180/min could be ventricular tachycardia.
Responsiveness and pulse.
Strip, 12 lead and electrode checks come after.

elimination.verdict: A. Check the patient's responsiveness and pulse.

questions.objective: Consider when cardiac monitoring may be used for a patient and how the clinician might apply this

questions.nursesNote: 0800 Day 2 after bowel surgery. Patient reports a fluttering feeling in the chest that began 30 minutes ago and feels lightheaded when sitting up. Denies chest pain. Radial pulse irregular with no pattern, counted for 30 seconds and doubled to 118/min. Blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg, was 128/78 mm Hg yesterday evening. Respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air. Capillary refill time 2 seconds. Skin warm and dry. Oral temperature 37.1 °C. Wound clean and dry.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 0800 assessment of a patient 2 days after bowel surgery who reports a new symptom. Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: fluttering feeling in the chest that began 30 minutes ago
segments.rationale: A new fluttering sensation is a palpitation, one of the common presenting symptoms of heart disease. It is new since yesterday.

segments.text: feels lightheaded when sitting up
segments.rationale: Lightheadedness suggests the brain is getting less blood, which fits a fall in cardiac output from a fast, irregular rhythm.

segments.text: Denies chest pain
segments.rationale: The absence of chest pain is reassuring and is documented. It does not require follow up on its own.

segments.text: Radial pulse irregular with no pattern
segments.rationale: An irregular pulse with no pattern is a reason to record a 12 lead ECG. It is commonly atrial fibrillation.

segments.text: counted for 30 seconds and doubled to 118/min
segments.rationale: An irregular pulse cannot be counted accurately over 30 seconds; it is counted for 1 full minute. The rate is also above 100/min.

segments.text: Blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg, was 128/78 mm Hg yesterday evening
segments.rationale: A drop from the patient's own baseline, together with lightheadedness, suggests reduced cardiac output. The baseline is what lets the nurse see the change.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air
segments.rationale: Breathing and oxygen saturation are within expected limits.

segments.text: Capillary refill time 2 seconds
segments.rationale: Refill of 2 seconds shows peripheral perfusion is still maintained.

segments.text: Skin warm and dry
segments.rationale: Warm, dry skin shows no sympathetic response with sweating and no fever.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
segments.rationale: There is no fever, which makes infection less likely as the cause of the fast rate.

segments.text: Wound clean and dry
segments.rationale: The wound shows no bleeding or infection, which makes blood loss less likely as the cause of the falling pressure.

questions.takeaway: A new palpitation, an irregular pulse with no pattern, lightheadedness and a fall from the patient's own baseline blood pressure are cues to act. An irregular pulse is counted for a full minute, never for 30 seconds and doubled.
questions.strategy: Read the technique as well as the values. The entry that is easy to skim past is how the pulse was counted, not what it was.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fluttering in the chest and lightheadedness.

steps.action: Check the pulse and how it was counted
steps.detail: Irregular, and counted for only 30 seconds.
Blood pressure lower than yesterday evening.
Breathing, refill, skin, temperature and wound.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing the findings of a patient 2 days after bowel surgery who has a new irregular pulse. Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
0815. Chart so far: day 2 after bowel surgery; fluttering in the chest since 0730; lightheaded when sitting up; no chest pain; radial pulse irregular with no pattern; blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg at 0800, was 128/78 mm Hg yesterday evening; capillary refill time 2 seconds; wound clean and dry. The nurse auscultates the apical pulse for 1 full minute: 132/min and irregular.

The irregular pulse with lightheadedness and a falling blood pressure most likely reflects [[1]].

The test the nurse expects next is [[2]].

On that test, the heart rate is best found by [[3]].

options.text: a new arrhythmia
options.rationale: A fast, irregular pulse with no pattern, lightheadedness and a falling blood pressure point to a rhythm problem that is lowering cardiac output.

options.text: blood loss from the surgical wound
options.rationale: Blood loss can lower blood pressure after surgery, which makes this tempting. But the wound is clean and dry, the refill is 2 seconds, and blood loss does not make the pulse irregular.

options.text: pain after surgery
options.rationale: Pain raises the heart rate, but it does not make the rhythm irregular or lower the blood pressure.

options.text: anxiety about the fluttering
options.rationale: Anxiety can raise the heart rate, but it does not explain an irregular rhythm or a falling blood pressure.

options.text: a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: An irregular pulse, a fast pulse and an unwell patient are each reasons to record a 12 lead ECG.

options.text: a chest x ray
options.rationale: A chest x ray shows the heart and lungs but not the rhythm.

options.text: blood cultures
options.rationale: There is no fever and the wound is clean, so infection is not the leading problem.

options.text: an exercise ECG
options.rationale: Exercise would raise demand on a heart that is already fast and lowering the blood pressure.

options.text: counting R waves in 30 large squares and multiplying by 10
options.rationale: When the rhythm is irregular, the R waves in 30 large squares (6 seconds) are counted and multiplied by 10.

options.text: dividing 300 by the large squares between two R waves
options.rationale: This method works only when the rhythm is regular. With irregular spacing it gives a different answer depending on which two beats are chosen.

options.text: counting the P waves in one large square
options.rationale: One large square is a fifth of a second, far too short, and P waves do not give the ventricular rate.

options.text: using the rate printed on the strip
options.rationale: Machine readings are a guide, but the nurse works systematically through the trace and confirms the rate.

questions.takeaway: A fast, irregular pulse with a falling blood pressure is an arrhythmia until proven otherwise, and it calls for a 12 lead ECG. Count a regular rhythm with 300 divided by the large squares between R waves; count an irregular rhythm with the R waves in 30 large squares times 10.
questions.strategy: Each blank has a tempting alternative: blood loss after surgery, an x ray, and the regular rhythm method. The irregular rhythm rules out each one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Irregular rhythm with low pressure and a dry wound: arrhythmia.
Irregular pulse is a reason for a 12 lead ECG.
Irregular: 30 large squares times 10.

elimination.verdict: 1: a new arrhythmia. 2: a 12 lead ECG. 3: counting R waves in 30 large squares and multiplying by 10.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.scenario: At 0830 the nurse reviews the 12 lead ECG. Chart so far: day 2 after bowel surgery; fluttering in the chest since 0730; lightheaded when sitting up; no chest pain; radial pulse irregular with no pattern; blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg at 0800, was 128/78 mm Hg yesterday evening; capillary refill time 2 seconds; wound clean and dry. Apical pulse 132/min and irregular at 0815. ECG: clean trace; calibration box 2 large squares high; speed 25 mm per second. No clear P waves; the baseline between complexes is wavy. Spacing between R waves varies with no pattern. 13 R waves in 30 large squares. QRS width 2 small squares. No ST elevation or depression. The patient is still lightheaded, blood pressure 100/64 mm Hg, and denies chest pain.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 12 lead ECG of a patient with a new irregular pulse. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Start continuous cardiac monitoring with lead II displayed
options.rationale: Monitoring gives continuous assessment of rate and rhythm and shows the response to treatment. Lead II is usually selected because it is easily interpreted.

options.text: Report the ECG findings and symptoms to the provider now
options.rationale: A new fast arrhythmia with lightheadedness and a falling pressure needs treatment, and a clinician skilled in interpretation should review the ECG.

options.text: Repeat the ECG because the baseline is wavy
options.rationale: The trace is clean, the calibration is correct, and the waviness sits between complexes where P waves should be. Repeating the test delays the report.

options.text: Help the patient walk to ease the fluttering
options.rationale: Walking a lightheaded patient with a falling pressure risks a fall and raises demand on the heart.

options.text: Recount the radial pulse for 30 seconds
options.rationale: An irregular pulse is never counted for 30 seconds, and the ECG has already given the rate.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with a fast rate
options.rationale: No clear P waves, a wavy baseline and R waves with no pattern fit atrial fibrillation, the most common irregular rhythm. 13 R waves in 30 large squares times 10 gives about 130/min.

options.text: Second degree heart block
options.rationale: Heart block shows more P waves than QRS complexes. Here there are no clear P waves at all.

options.text: Ventricular tachycardia
options.rationale: A ventricular rhythm gives wide, bizarre QRS complexes. These are 2 small squares wide, which is normal width.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia
options.rationale: Sinus tachycardia is fast but regular, with one P wave before each QRS. This rhythm is irregular with no clear P waves.

options.text: Heart rate and rhythm on the monitor
options.rationale: The rate shows whether treatment is slowing the heart, and the rhythm shows whether it changes.

options.text: Blood pressure and lightheadedness
options.rationale: These show whether cardiac output is recovering as the rate comes down.

options.text: Wound drainage
options.rationale: The wound is clean and dry and is not the cause of this problem.

options.text: Bowel sounds
options.rationale: Bowel sounds are part of routine care after bowel surgery but do not track this problem.

options.text: Oral temperature
options.rationale: There is no fever, and temperature does not track the rhythm.

questions.takeaway: An irregular rhythm with no clear P waves and a normal width QRS is commonly atrial fibrillation. Find the rate by counting R waves in 30 large squares and multiplying by 10. Put the patient on continuous monitoring in lead II, report now, and follow the rate, rhythm, blood pressure and symptoms.
questions.strategy: Work the six steps in order: clean trace, calibration, rhythm, P waves for each QRS, measurements and rate, then the ST segments. Each wrong condition fails one step: block needs extra P waves, ventricular tachycardia needs a wide QRS, sinus needs P waves and regularity.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clean, 2 large squares, 25 mm per second: the waviness is not interference.
Irregular, no clear P waves: atrial fibrillation.
2 small squares wide; 13 x 10 is about 130/min.
Monitor and report; follow rate, rhythm, pressure and symptoms.

elimination.verdict: Condition: atrial fibrillation with a fast rate. Actions: start monitoring in lead II; report now. Parameters: heart rate and rhythm; blood pressure and lightheadedness.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.scenario: At 0900 the provider prescribes continuous cardiac monitoring and an IV drug to slow the heart rate. Chart so far: day 2 after bowel surgery; fluttering in the chest since 0730; lightheaded when sitting up; no chest pain; radial pulse irregular with no pattern; blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg at 0800, was 128/78 mm Hg yesterday evening; capillary refill time 2 seconds; wound clean and dry. ECG: atrial fibrillation at about 130/min. The patient is still lightheaded when sitting up. The chest is damp with sweat from a warm room and has thick hair at the electrode sites.
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with new atrial fibrillation who is starting continuous cardiac monitoring. For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.

rows.text: Explain the monitor and why it is needed
rows.rationale: Explaining fully and reassuring the patient comes first. A new symptom and new equipment are frightening.

rows.text: Dry the skin and, with consent, clip hair at the electrode sites
rows.rationale: Electrodes need clean, dry skin and good contact for a clear trace. Chest hair is clipped, not shaved, with the patient's consent, because a razor nicks the skin.

rows.text: Set the alarm limits to this patient's condition
rows.rationale: Alarm limits are set based on the patient's clinical condition and the plan to slow the rate, not left at a default.

rows.text: Place the right arm electrode on the upper arm
rows.rationale: The right arm electrode goes under the right clavicle near the shoulder, within the frame of the rib cage, which keeps the trace clear when the arms move.

rows.text: Silence the alarms overnight so the patient can sleep
rows.rationale: Silenced alarms miss a change in rhythm or a rate that becomes too fast or too slow with the new drug.

rows.text: Have the patient walk to the bathroom alone
rows.rationale: The patient is lightheaded with a fast, irregular rhythm and is at risk of falling. The nurse assists.

questions.takeaway: Apply monitoring with the patient in mind: explain and reassure, keep privacy and dignity, prepare clean, dry skin with consent for clipping hair, place electrodes within the rib cage frame, display lead II, and set alarm limits to the patient's condition. Keep the alarms on and keep the lightheaded patient safe.
questions.strategy: Think of three goals: a clear trace, alarms that will catch a change, and a patient who will not fall. Every not indicated row breaks one of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry skin, consented clipping, right arm electrode under the clavicle.
Limits set to the patient; never silenced.
Explain, and do not leave a lightheaded patient to walk alone.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: rows 1, 2, 3. Not indicated: rows 4, 5, 6.

questions.objective: Consider when cardiac monitoring may be used for a patient and how the clinician might apply this

questions.stem: At 1030, during the IV drug infusion, the patient reports a heavy pressure in the chest, 6 of 10, that began 5 minutes ago. Chart so far: day 2 after bowel surgery; fluttering in the chest since 0730; lightheaded when sitting up; no chest pain; radial pulse irregular with no pattern; blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg at 0800, was 128/78 mm Hg yesterday evening; capillary refill time 2 seconds; wound clean and dry. Monitor: atrial fibrillation at 128/min. Blood pressure 98/62 mm Hg. Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stay with the patient and recheck the blood pressure
options.rationale: New chest pain in a patient with a fast arrhythmia and a low pressure needs the nurse at the bedside, watching for further deterioration.

options.text: Record a 12 lead ECG while the pain is present
options.rationale: Chest pain is a reason to record a 12 lead ECG. Recording it during the pain gives the best chance of showing ST changes of ischemia or infarction.

options.text: Report the chest pain and ECG to the provider now
options.rationale: New chest pain in this patient is reported at once, with the ECG for review by a clinician skilled in interpretation.

options.text: Count the radial pulse for 1 full minute first
options.rationale: A full minute count is the right technique for an irregular pulse, which makes this tempting. But the monitor is already showing the rate, and a minute spent counting delays the ECG during the pain.

options.text: Disconnect the monitor to place the 12 lead electrodes
options.rationale: The patient is in a fast arrhythmia with chest pain. Continuous monitoring stays on while the 12 lead electrodes are placed.

options.text: Wait to see whether the pain eases with rest
options.rationale: The patient is already resting. Waiting lets an ECG change go unrecorded and delays treatment.

questions.takeaway: New chest pain is a reason for an immediate 12 lead ECG, recorded during the pain. Stay with the patient, keep continuous monitoring on, and report the pain and the ECG now.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options are good nursing in another moment: a full minute pulse count and placing electrodes. Here each one delays the ECG or removes the monitoring during chest pain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At the bedside, recheck the pressure.
12 lead ECG during the pain, monitor left on.
Pain and ECG to the provider now.
Counting the pulse and waiting both lose time.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.scenario: At 1400 the nurse reassesses the patient. Chart so far: day 2 after bowel surgery; fluttering in the chest since 0730; lightheaded when sitting up; no chest pain; radial pulse irregular with no pattern; blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg at 0800, was 128/78 mm Hg yesterday evening; capillary refill time 2 seconds; wound clean and dry. At 0830 the rate was about 130/min in atrial fibrillation; at 1030 the patient had chest pressure 6 of 10, and a 12 lead ECG showed no ST changes. The IV drug was given as prescribed.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a patient with new atrial fibrillation after treatment to slow the heart rate. For each finding, indicate whether it shows expected progress or requires follow up.

rows.text: Apical pulse 86/min, counted for 1 full minute
rows.rationale: The rate has come down from about 130/min, counted with the correct technique for an irregular rhythm. Slowing the rate was the goal of the drug.

rows.text: No lightheadedness when sitting up
rows.rationale: With a slower rate the ventricles fill better between beats, so output to the brain recovers.

rows.text: Blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg
rows.rationale: The pressure is back near the patient's baseline of 128/78 mm Hg.

rows.text: No chest pressure since 1100
rows.rationale: The chest pressure has resolved as the rate came down.

rows.text: A flat line in lead II while the patient is talking
rows.rationale: A patient who is talking has a heartbeat, so the flat line is an equipment problem such as a lead that has come off. Monitoring is not working until it is fixed.

rows.text: An electrode peeling off damp skin on the lower left rib cage
rows.rationale: Poor contact causes a noisy trace and false alarms. The skin is dried and the electrode replaced.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate against the goals of treatment: a slower rate counted correctly, symptoms gone, blood pressure back near baseline, no chest pain. Also evaluate the monitoring itself: a flat line in a talking patient is a lead problem, and a peeling electrode means the trace cannot be trusted.
questions.strategy: The four clinical findings show the plan working. The two that need follow up are about the equipment, and they matter because a monitor that does not work cannot catch the next change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 86/min over a full minute: progress.
No lightheadedness and pressure near baseline: progress.
A flat line while talking and a peeling electrode: follow up.

elimination.verdict: Expected progress: rows 1 to 4. Requires follow up: rows 5 and 6.

questions.objective: Interpret the findings from a patient assessment to identify the priorities for planning care

skills.title: Infusion Therapy
skills.subtitle: IV solutions, blood products, access devices and site care, the infusion system, drip rates, complications, older adults, alternative routes and documentation

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with severe hyponatremia and new confusion who is receiving 3% sodium chloride. Which assessment is the priority?

options.text: Capillary blood glucose every 4 hours
options.rationale: Glucose checks matter with dextrose solutions such as 10% dextrose in water. A saline solution does not change the glucose.

options.text: Peripheral pulses below the IV site
options.rationale: Distal pulses are not the risk of a hypertonic saline infusion. The risks are systemic: sodium shifts, brain changes and fluid overload.

options.text: Serum sodium and neurologic status
options.rationale: 3% sodium chloride is hypertonic and pulls water out of cells into the vessels. Its key risks are hypernatremia, cell dehydration and circulatory overload, so serum sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance are monitored closely. Confusion is both the presenting problem and the early sign of a sodium shift.

options.text: Urine color at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Urine color once a shift is too infrequent and too indirect for a high risk hypertonic infusion.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic solutions (3% sodium chloride for severe hyponatremia or cerebral edema, 10% dextrose in water for hypoglycemia) pull water out of cells. Watch serum sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance, because the risks are hypernatremia, cell dehydration and circulatory overload.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Match the monitoring to the solution. A saline solution changes sodium, and sodium changes show up first in the brain.

steps.detail: 3% sodium chloride is hypertonic saline, not dextrose, so glucose is off target.
Hypernatremia, cell dehydration and circulatory overload.
Serum sodium and neurologic status, not a once a shift urine color or a local pulse.

elimination.verdict: Serum sodium and neurologic status.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.stem: A nursing student suggests 5% dextrose in water (D5W) to restore volume after blood loss because the bag is isotonic. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Once the dextrose is used, the water moves into cells."
options.rationale: D5W is isotonic in the bag, but the body metabolizes the dextrose quickly and what is left acts as free water, which is hypotonic. Free water shifts into cells instead of staying in the vessels, so D5W does not expand blood volume. Isotonic 0.9% sodium chloride or lactated Ringer's is used for volume expansion.

options.text: "D5W is hypertonic, so it pulls fluid into the vessels."
options.rationale: D5W is not hypertonic. It is isotonic in the bag and becomes hypotonic once the dextrose is metabolized.

options.text: "Isotonic fluids stay in the vessels, so this will work well."
options.rationale: This repeats the student's error. It is true of 0.9% sodium chloride, but D5W stops acting isotonic once the dextrose is used.

options.text: "D5W is a good choice if it runs in quickly."
options.rationale: Speed does not change where the water goes. Run fast, D5W still ends up as free water that moves into cells.

questions.takeaway: D5W is isotonic in the bag but hypotonic in the body, because the dextrose is metabolized and leaves free water that moves into cells. It does not expand volume and is avoided where cells must not swell, such as cerebral edema.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: The student's reasoning stops at the label on the bag. The best response follows the fluid into the body.

steps.action: Spot the gap in the student's logic
steps.detail: Isotonic in the bag is not the same as isotonic in the body.
D5W is never hypertonic.
Agreeing with the student, at any rate, leaves the error in place.

elimination.verdict: Once the dextrose is used, the water moves into cells.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing IV prescriptions for four patients on a neuroscience unit before hanging the fluids. No patient has diabetes or a glucose problem unless stated. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: 3% sodium chloride for severe hyponatremia in a patient who just had a seizure
options.rationale: This looks dangerous because the solution is hypertonic, but it is the indicated treatment. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia is the main use of 3% sodium chloride. The nurse gives it and monitors serum sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance closely.

options.text: 10% dextrose in water for hypoglycemia in a patient who cannot swallow safely
options.rationale: 10% dextrose in water is hypertonic, but hypoglycemia is one of its listed uses, and a patient who cannot swallow cannot take oral glucose. It is appropriate with glucose and fluid monitoring.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride for a patient with a head injury and low blood pressure
options.rationale: Isotonic saline causes no net water shift into brain cells and supports blood pressure, which protects cerebral perfusion. It is appropriate after head injury.

options.text: 5% dextrose in water at a maintenance rate for cerebral edema after a stroke
options.rationale: This is the one to question. 5% dextrose in water is labeled isotonic, but once the dextrose is metabolized it acts as free water, which is hypotonic and moves into cells. Hypotonic fluid is contraindicated with cerebral edema or raised intracranial pressure because it swells brain cells.

questions.takeaway: Judge a fluid by how it behaves in the body, not by the label on the bag. 5% dextrose in water becomes hypotonic and worsens cerebral edema. Hypertonic 3% sodium chloride and 10% dextrose in water carry real risks (hypernatremia, cell dehydration, circulatory overload), but they are indicated for severe hyponatremia and hypoglycemia.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Three options sound risky and one sounds routine. The two hypertonic fluids are high risk but indicated, and the isotonic saline protects perfusion. The routine sounding maintenance fluid is the one that turns hypotonic in a patient whose brain is already swollen. Cue: cerebral edema plus a dextrose fluid with no glucose problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypertonic does not mean wrong. 3% sodium chloride and 10% dextrose in water each match their indication.
0.9% sodium chloride after head injury with low blood pressure supports perfusion without shifting water into cells.

steps.action: Follow 5% dextrose in water into the body
steps.detail: The dextrose is used up, free water remains, and it enters brain cells that are already swollen.

steps.action: Confirm there is no reason for dextrose
steps.detail: The stem rules out a glucose problem, so nothing justifies it.

elimination.verdict: 5% dextrose in water at a maintenance rate for cerebral edema after a stroke.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.stem: A patient with active gastrointestinal bleeding is NPO and vomiting. Which explanation by the nurse about the IV pantoprazole is accurate?

options.text: "It works slower but lasts longer than a pill."
options.rationale: IV delivery gives an immediate systemic effect, not a slower one.

options.text: "It bypasses the digestive tract for an immediate effect."
options.rationale: Infusion therapy delivers drugs directly into the vascular system, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract and first pass metabolism, for a rapid, predictable effect. That is why it is used when oral intake is not possible, as with vomiting and NPO status.

options.text: "It is safer, so it needs no aseptic technique or monitoring."
options.rationale: Direct access to the bloodstream requires strict aseptic technique and ongoing monitoring. IV is not automatically safer.

options.text: "It must pass through the liver first before it can act."
options.rationale: That describes an oral drug. IV delivery bypasses first pass metabolism in the liver.

questions.takeaway: Infusion therapy delivers fluids, medications, blood products and nutrients directly into the vascular system, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract and first pass metabolism for an immediate effect. Its four purposes: fluid replacement and maintenance, medication administration, blood product transfusion and nutritional support with total parenteral nutrition.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Ask what the IV route skips. It skips the gut and the liver's first pass, so the drug acts at once.

steps.detail: "No aseptic technique or monitoring" is never true of IV therapy.
Immediate versus slower: IV acts immediately.
Passing through the liver first is what IV avoids.

elimination.verdict: It bypasses the digestive tract for an immediate effect.

questions.objective: Define Infusion Therapy

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with major bleeding who is receiving several blood products. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the platelets at room temperature until hung
options.rationale: Platelets are stored at room temperature with agitation. Refrigeration damages them.

options.text: Infuse thawed fresh frozen plasma within 24 hours
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors and is infused within 24 hours of thawing.

options.text: Recheck vital signs only at the end of each unit
options.rationale: Vital signs are taken at baseline, 15 minutes after the start, every 30 to 60 minutes and at completion. Most severe reactions show early.

options.text: Complete each red blood cell unit within 4 hours
options.rationale: Each unit is transfused over no more than 4 hours to limit bacterial growth.

options.text: Pick up the next unit before consent is signed
options.rationale: Consent must be on file before the product is retrieved from the blood bank.

options.text: Give O negative red cells in an emergency before crossmatch
options.rationale: O negative is the universal donor for red blood cells in emergencies when there is no time to wait for crossmatch.

questions.takeaway: Platelets at room temperature, fresh frozen plasma within 24 hours of thawing, each red cell unit within 4 hours, O negative as the emergency universal donor, consent on file before pickup, and vital signs at baseline, 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Run each option against the product rule it names: storage, time limit, consent or monitoring.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Platelets stay at room temperature: correct.
Plasma 24 hours after thaw, red cells 4 hours per unit: correct.
Consent comes before pickup, and vital signs start at 15 minutes, not at the end.
O negative red cells when crossmatch cannot wait: correct.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with massive bleeding and a clotting disorder who is receiving several blood products. Before hanging each product, the nurse checks how it was handled. Which product requires the nurse to stop and contact the blood bank before use?

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma thawed 20 hours ago and kept refrigerated
options.rationale: Twenty hours sounds long, but thawed fresh frozen plasma may be infused within 24 hours of thawing, and refrigerated storage is correct for thawed plasma. It can be used.

options.text: Platelets placed in the unit refrigerator for an hour
options.rationale: This is the product to stop. Platelets are stored at room temperature, 20 to 24 °C, with agitation. Cold storage damages their function, so the blood bank decides whether the unit can still be given.

options.text: Cryoprecipitate thawed 2 hours ago for a low fibrinogen level
options.rationale: Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII and von Willebrand factor and is the right product for low fibrinogen. Two hours after thawing is within the time limit for use.

options.text: O negative red cells started before the crossmatch resulted
options.rationale: Giving red cells before crossmatch sounds like an error, but O negative is the universal donor for red cells in emergencies. Massive bleeding is that emergency.

questions.takeaway: Each blood product has its own handling rule. Platelets: room temperature with agitation, never refrigerated. Fresh frozen plasma: within 24 hours of thawing. Cryoprecipitate: for fibrinogen deficiency, used soon after thawing. Red cells: within 4 hours, with O negative as the emergency universal donor.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Every option contains something that sounds wrong: 20 hours, before crossmatch, a thawed product. Test each against the specific product's rule. Only one breaks it. Cue: refrigerator plus platelets, the one product that must stay warm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 20 hours after thaw is under the 24 hour limit, and thawed plasma is kept cold: acceptable.
Right product for low fibrinogen, 2 hours after thaw: acceptable.
Massive bleeding justifies O negative before crossmatch: acceptable.
Platelets must stay at room temperature. Refrigeration breaks the rule: stop.

elimination.verdict: Platelets placed in the unit refrigerator for an hour.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse needs IV access for maintenance fluids in an older adult with fragile, hard to see veins. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Choose a 22 gauge catheter
options.rationale: 22 to 24 gauge is recommended for older adults and fragile veins and is enough for maintenance fluids.

options.text: Choose a 16 gauge catheter for better flow
options.rationale: 14 to 16 gauge is for trauma, major surgery and rapid resuscitation. It would traumatize a fragile vein.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to dilate the veins
options.rationale: Warmth dilates veins and improves visibility in older adults.

options.text: Use vein illumination in place of palpating the vein
options.rationale: Vein illumination helps show surface veins, but it does not replace clinical assessment. The vein is still palpated for a soft, straight, resilient feel.

options.text: Request ultrasound guided insertion after failed attempts
options.rationale: Ultrasound guided insertion is the standard of care for difficult access and reduces failed attempts.

options.text: Choose an 18 gauge catheter as the standard size
options.rationale: 20 gauge is the standard adult size. 18 gauge is preferred for blood and contrast media.

questions.takeaway: Gauge by purpose: 14 to 16 for trauma and rapid fluids, 18 for blood and contrast, 20 for standard adult infusions, 22 to 24 for older adults, children and fragile veins. For difficult access, ultrasound guided insertion is the standard; vein illumination helps but never replaces assessment.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Match each gauge to its purpose, then ask whether each device supports or replaces the nurse's assessment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Maintenance fluids in fragile veins: 22. Not 16, not 18.
A warm compress dilates veins.
Ultrasound is the standard for difficult access. Vein illumination supports, but does not replace, palpation.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient with cancer will receive chemotherapy every 3 weeks for 6 months and wants to keep swimming between treatments. The patient had a nontunneled central line during a recent intensive care stay.

The device that best fits this plan is [[1]].

To access it, the nurse uses [[2]].

Between treatment cycles, when the device is not in use, it is flushed [[3]].

Before any newly placed peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) is used, the nurse confirms [[4]].

options.text: An implanted port
options.rationale: A port is a totally subcutaneous reservoir with the lowest infection risk. It is ideal for intermittent long term therapy and has no external catheter, so the patient can swim and bathe freely.

options.text: A tunneled catheter with a cuff
options.rationale: A tunneled catheter is long term and its cuff anchors the line and reduces infection, but the external catheter needs daily care and cannot be submerged for swimming.

options.text: A nontunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: Nontunneled lines are for short term acute care and carry the highest catheter related bloodstream infection risk of central lines.

options.text: A hemodialysis catheter
options.rationale: A hemodialysis catheter is dedicated to dialysis and is never used for routine infusions.

options.text: A non coring (Huber) needle
options.rationale: A port is accessed only with a non coring Huber needle, which spares the septum.

options.text: A standard hollow needle
options.rationale: A standard needle cores out pieces of the septum and damages the port.

options.text: A short peripheral IV catheter
options.rationale: A peripheral catheter is not used to access a port.

options.text: Monthly
options.rationale: A port that is not in use is flushed monthly.

options.text: Every 8 hours
options.rationale: That frequency fits a line in active use, not a port between cycles.

options.text: Every 6 months
options.rationale: Six months is far too long. The port could occlude.

options.text: Tip placement by x ray
options.rationale: X ray confirmation of the tip is required before a PICC is used. Tip location, not insertion site, makes a line central.

options.text: A brisk blood return
options.rationale: Blood return shows patency, not where the tip lies.

options.text: An upper arm insertion site
options.rationale: The insertion site does not define a central line. The tip location does.

questions.takeaway: Implanted port: lowest infection risk, intermittent long term therapy, Huber needle, monthly flush when not in use, no external catheter. Tunneled: cuff, daily care. Nontunneled: short term, highest catheter related bloodstream infection risk. Hemodialysis catheter: dialysis only. PICC: x ray tip confirmation before use.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Let the patient's plan pick the device: intermittent, long term and wants to swim. Then recall how that device is accessed and maintained.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Intermittent and long term with no external line for swimming: implanted port.
Huber needle, monthly flush when idle.
X ray of the tip, not blood return or insertion site.

elimination.verdict: An implanted port, a non coring Huber needle, monthly, tip placement by x ray.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an NPO patient who needs total parenteral nutrition (TPN). A vascular access specialist placed a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) in an upper arm vein with ultrasound guidance 30 minutes ago. The PICC flushes easily with a brisk blood return. The chest x ray has been taken but not yet read. The patient also has a working forearm peripheral IV, and the TPN is due now. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Start the TPN through the PICC, since blood return is brisk
options.rationale: Blood return confirms the catheter is patent and in a vein, not that the tip sits in the lower superior vena cava. An expert insertion with ultrasound still needs x ray confirmation.

options.text: Start the TPN through the forearm IV until the reading
options.rationale: This avoids the unconfirmed PICC but sends a highly concentrated solution through a peripheral vein. TPN requires central access.

options.text: Keep the PICC unused until tip placement is confirmed
options.rationale: X ray confirmation of tip placement is required before a PICC is used. Tip location, not the arm insertion site or a blood return, is what makes the line central and safe for TPN. A short delay in starting TPN is the safer choice.

options.text: Start the TPN slowly through the PICC and monitor closely
options.rationale: A slow rate does not make an unconfirmed tip safe. A misplaced tip can cause vessel damage or infuse into the wrong vessel at any rate.

questions.takeaway: A PICC is a central line because of where its tip ends, not where it enters. X ray confirmation of tip placement is required before first use, however skilled the inserter and however good the blood return. TPN needs central access, so it waits rather than going peripheral.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option solves the delay. Two use the PICC with something reassuring (blood return, a slow rate), and one moves TPN to a peripheral vein. The deciding cue is the x ray that is not yet read, and the rule that tip confirmation comes before any use.

steps.detail: The x ray is taken but not read, so tip placement is unconfirmed.
Blood return shows patency, not tip location. A slow rate does not fix a misplaced tip.
TPN needs central access, so the forearm IV is not an option.
Hold the PICC until the tip is confirmed.

elimination.verdict: Keep the PICC unused until tip placement is confirmed.

questions.objective: Apply Clinical Judgment

questions.stem: The nurse is hanging a new primary infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Scrub the needleless connector for at least 15 seconds
options.rationale: Scrubbing the hub for at least 15 seconds before access prevents catheter related bloodstream infection.

options.text: Label the tubing to change in 96 hours or per policy
options.rationale: Administration sets are changed every 96 hours or per facility policy and labeled with the date.

options.text: Plan to replace the bag within 24 hours of spiking
options.rationale: Once spiked, a bag hangs no longer than 24 hours.

options.text: Use a bag with a few particles if it is not expired
options.rationale: A bag must be clear and free of particles as well as unexpired.

options.text: Choose a microdrip set for a rapid large volume infusion
options.rationale: Microdrip (60 drops per mL) is for small, precise volumes. Macrodrip (10 to 20 drops per mL) suits larger volumes and faster rates.

questions.takeaway: Bag: clear, no particles, unexpired, no more than 24 hours once spiked. Tubing: every 96 hours or per policy. Hub: scrub at least 15 seconds. Macrodrip 10 to 20 drops per mL for larger volumes, microdrip 60 drops per mL for small precise volumes.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Check each piece of the system against its rule: hub, tubing, bag and drip set.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At least 15 seconds of scrubbing: correct.
96 hours for tubing, 24 hours for a spiked bag: correct.
Any particles mean the bag is not used.
Microdrip is for small volumes, not rapid large ones.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse will infuse 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's over 8 hours by gravity with tubing that delivers 15 drops per mL. Which rate should the nurse set?

options.text: 125 drops per minute
options.rationale: 125 is the rate in mL per hour (1,000 mL divided by 8 hours), not drops per minute. The drop factor and minutes were never applied.

options.text: 21 drops per minute
options.rationale: This uses a drop factor of 10: 125 times 10 divided by 60 is about 21. The tubing delivers 15 drops per mL.

options.text: 42 drops per minute
options.rationale: This uses a drop factor of 20: 125 times 20 divided by 60 is about 42. The tubing delivers 15 drops per mL.

options.text: 31 drops per minute
options.rationale: 1,000 mL over 8 hours is 125 mL per hour. Drops per minute equal volume times drop factor divided by time in minutes: 125 times 15 divided by 60 is 31.25, rounded to 31.

questions.takeaway: Drops per minute equal total volume times drop factor divided by time in minutes. Find mL per hour first (volume divided by hours), then multiply by the drop factor and divide by 60. With microdrip (60 drops per mL), drops per minute equal mL per hour.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the slides.
questions.strategy: Do it in two steps: mL per hour, then drops per minute with the drop factor on the package.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 1,000 divided by 8 is 125 mL per hour.
1,875 divided by 60 is 31.25, so 31 drops per minute.
125 skips the conversion; 21 and 42 use the wrong drop factor.

elimination.verdict: 31 drops per minute.

questions.objective: Apply Clinical Judgment

questions.scenario: The nurse is checking seven infusions on a medical surgical unit at the start of the shift. Drop counts were taken over a full minute. Facility policy is to change primary tubing every 96 hours.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it requires action or no action is needed.

rows.text: Gravity infusion of 1,000 mL over 8 hours, tubing 15 drops per mL, running at 31 drops per minute
rows.rationale: 1,000 mL over 8 hours is 125 mL per hour. 125 times 15 divided by 60 is 31.25, so 31 drops per minute is correct.

rows.text: Pump infusion of 1,000 mL prescribed over 6 hours, pump set at 125 mL per hour
rows.rationale: 1,000 mL over 6 hours is about 167 mL per hour. 125 mL per hour is the 8 hour rate, so the pump is set too slow.

rows.text: Microdrip infusion prescribed at 50 mL per hour, running at 50 drops per minute
rows.rationale: With microdrip tubing (60 drops per mL), drops per minute equal mL per hour. 50 drops per minute is correct.

rows.text: Bag of 0.9% sodium chloride spiked 26 hours ago, with 200 mL left at the prescribed rate
rows.rationale: A spiked bag hangs no longer than 24 hours. It is replaced now even though it would finish soon.

rows.text: Primary tubing labeled with a date 3 days ago
rows.rationale: Three days is 72 hours, within the 96 hour change interval set by policy.

rows.text: Nurse about to give an IV push drug after a 5 second alcohol wipe of the hub
rows.rationale: The hub is scrubbed for at least 15 seconds before access to prevent catheter related bloodstream infection. A quick wipe is not enough.

rows.text: Gravity piggyback of 100 mL over 30 minutes, tubing 10 drops per mL, running at 33 drops per minute
rows.rationale: 100 times 10 divided by 30 is 33.3, so 33 drops per minute is correct.

questions.takeaway: Check every infusion two ways: the math (drops per minute equal volume times drop factor divided by minutes; mL per hour equal volume divided by hours) and the system rules (spiked bag 24 hours, tubing 96 hours or per policy, hub scrub at least 15 seconds).
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the slides.
questions.strategy: Do the math on every rate row instead of trusting a familiar number. 125 mL per hour looks right because it is a common rate, but not for 6 hours. On the system rows, count hours: 3 days is under 96 hours, 26 hours is over 24.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rows 1, 3 and 7 match their prescriptions. Row 2 is the 8 hour rate on a 6 hour order.
Bag at 26 hours is over 24. Tubing at 72 hours is under 96.
5 seconds is short of the 15 second scrub.

elimination.verdict: Requires action: rows 2, 4 and 6. No action needed: rows 1, 3, 5 and 7.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: A patient's IV of 0.9% sodium chloride crosses the wrist and shifts with each bend. The vein is now red and tender. Which type of phlebitis does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Chemical, from the solution
options.rationale: Chemical phlebitis comes from an irritating solution. Isotonic 0.9% sodium chloride is not an irritant, so the solution is not the cause.

options.text: Bacterial, from a break in asepsis
options.rationale: Bacterial phlebitis follows poor aseptic technique and may bring purulent drainage. Nothing in the stem points to a break in asepsis.

options.text: Mechanical, from catheter movement
options.rationale: A catheter that shifts with every bend of the wrist rubs the vein wall. Movement of the catheter is the cause of mechanical phlebitis. The nurse stops the infusion, removes the catheter, applies a warm moist compress, notifies the provider and documents the grade.

options.text: Postinfusion, after catheter removal
options.rationale: Postinfusion phlebitis appears after a catheter comes out. This catheter is still in place.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall: pain, redness, warmth, a streak or a palpable cord. Name the type by its cause: mechanical (catheter movement), chemical (irritating solution) or bacterial (poor asepsis). Stop, remove, apply a warm moist compress, notify the provider and document the grade.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Match the cause the stem gives you to the type. A catheter that moves with a joint is the mechanical cause; an isotonic solution rules out chemical.

steps.action: Find the cause in the stem
steps.detail: The catheter shifts with each bend of the wrist.
0.9% sodium chloride is isotonic, not an irritant.
No break in asepsis is described, and the catheter is still in.

elimination.verdict: C. Mechanical, from catheter movement.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: After a missed IV attempt, the nurse sees bruising and swelling forming at the site. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Apply gentle pressure; choose a new site
options.rationale: Bruising and swelling at the site after an attempt is a hematoma. Gentle pressure limits the bleeding, the same site is not used again, and the nurse watches for the hematoma to expand.

options.text: Retry the same vein after the swelling stops
options.rationale: The injured site is not cannulated again. A new attempt goes to a different site.

options.text: Press firmly and massage the area
options.rationale: Pressure is gentle, not firm, and massage disturbs the tissue and can spread the bleeding.

options.text: Restart the IV just below the bruise
options.rationale: A site below the injury drains through the damaged vein. The same site, and sites distal to it, are avoided.

questions.takeaway: Hematoma: blood leaking into the tissue at the insertion site, with bruising, swelling and tenderness. Apply gentle pressure, do not cannulate the same site again, and monitor for expansion.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Name the complication first. Bruising with swelling right after an attempt is a hematoma, and the only plan that both treats it gently and moves away from the injured vein is right.

steps.detail: Bruising and swelling after a missed attempt: hematoma.
Same vein and just below the bruise both use the damaged site.
Firm pressure and massage spread the bleeding.

elimination.verdict: A. Apply gentle pressure; choose a new site.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.scenario: The nurse on a medical surgical unit reviews new findings in six patients receiving IV therapy.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the complication it most likely represents.

rows.text: Burning and tingling shoot into the fingers as the catheter is advanced
rows.rationale: Burning, shooting pain, numbness or tingling during insertion is nerve injury. The nurse stops at once, removes the catheter, assesses neurologic function, and documents and reports it.

rows.text: The whole arm with a peripherally inserted central catheter is swollen and painful, and the pump shows slowed flow
rows.rationale: A swollen, painful limb with a slowing flow rate points to a clot in or around the catheter. Treatment is anticoagulants and catheter removal as prescribed.

rows.text: Flushing, headache and chest tightness begin after a piggyback planned for 30 minutes empties in 5
rows.rationale: A drug given far too fast causes flushing, headache, chest tightness and can progress to shock. An infusion pump, a verified rate and never giving concentrated drugs as a bolus prevent it.

rows.text: An older adult has new crackles and confusion after a day of IV fluids at 150 mL per hour
rows.rationale: Older adults have less total body water and less renal reserve, so fluid builds up quickly. Crackles, dyspnea and new confusion signal overload. Lower flow rates prevent it.

rows.text: Burning and a red streak along the vein begin during a potassium chloride infusion
rows.rationale: Redness and a streak along the vein are phlebitis. An irritating solution like potassium chloride makes it the chemical type.

rows.text: A firm cord and purulent drainage appear at a site placed during an emergency without a full skin prep
rows.rationale: A palpable cord with purulent drainage is phlebitis at the top of the scale, and poor asepsis makes it the bacterial type. The nurse documents the grade.

questions.takeaway: Read the timing and the location. During insertion with tingling: nerve injury. At the vein with redness, a streak or a cord: phlebitis. The whole limb with slowed flow: thrombosis. Minutes after a too fast infusion: speed shock. Lungs and mental status after hours of fluid in an older adult: fluid overload.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Ask where the finding is and when it started. A local vein problem, a whole limb problem and a whole body problem each point to a different complication.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: During insertion: nerve injury. Minutes after a fast infusion: speed shock.
