Along the vein: phlebitis. The whole limb with slowed flow: thrombosis.

steps.action: Then the whole body over hours
steps.detail: Crackles and confusion in an older adult on fluids: fluid overload.

elimination.verdict: Nerve injury: row 1. Thrombosis: row 2. Speed shock: row 3. Fluid overload: row 4. Phlebitis: rows 5 and 6.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is starting a peripheral IV for an older adult with thin, fragile skin. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Select a 22 gauge catheter
options.rationale: The smallest effective gauge, 22 to 24, is used for older adults with fragile veins. It limits vein trauma and still delivers most therapies.

options.text: Apply gentle traction to the skin during insertion
options.rationale: Gentle traction anchors fragile, rolling veins without tearing thin skin.

options.text: Choose a forearm vein over a dorsal hand vein
options.rationale: Dorsal hand veins are avoided in older adults when possible. Thin skin there tears and bruises easily.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to dilate the vein
options.rationale: A warm compress dilates the vein and makes it easier to see and enter.

options.text: Tighten the tourniquet firmly to raise the vein
options.rationale: An overtightened tourniquet can burst a fragile vein and cause a hematoma. It is applied snugly, not tightly.

options.text: Use an 18 gauge catheter for better flow
options.rationale: A large catheter damages fragile veins and is not needed for most therapies in an older adult.

questions.takeaway: For older adults: smallest effective gauge (22 to 24), gentle skin traction, a warm compress to dilate, no overtightened tourniquet, avoid dorsal hand veins, and document skin condition before and after every attempt.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Picture thin skin and a fragile vein. Every correct action protects them; every wrong one puts force or size on them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Small gauge, warm compress, gentle traction.
Forearm over dorsal hand.
A tight tourniquet and an 18 gauge catheter injure fragile veins.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: An older adult receiving IV fluids develops crackles, shortness of breath and new confusion. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Notify the provider of the new findings
options.rationale: The provider is notified, but slowing the fluid that is causing the overload comes first.

options.text: Draw blood cultures for a possible infection
options.rationale: New confusion can come from infection, but crackles and dyspnea during IV fluids point to fluid overload. Cultures are not the first step.

options.text: Increase the rate for possible dehydration
options.rationale: More fluid worsens the overload. Confusion here comes with crackles, not with signs of dehydration.

options.text: Slow the infusion and sit the patient up
options.rationale: Crackles, dyspnea and new confusion during IV fluids signal fluid overload. Slowing the infusion to the lowest rate policy allows stops more fluid, and sitting upright eases breathing. Then the nurse notifies the provider.

questions.takeaway: Older adults have less total body water and less renal reserve, so they tolerate rapid infusion poorly. Infuse at lower rates, and assess often for crackles, dyspnea and confusion. If overload appears, slow the infusion, sit the patient up, then notify the provider.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the slides.
questions.strategy: Every option is something a nurse might do. The first action removes the cause and protects breathing before the call is made.

steps.detail: Crackles and dyspnea during IV fluids: fluid overload.
Increasing the rate worsens it.
Blood cultures chase infection, not the fluid.
Slow the fluid and sit the patient up, then notify.

elimination.verdict: D. Slow the infusion and sit the patient up.

questions.objective: Apply Clinical Judgment

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient who had a midline catheter placed 9 days ago for a non vesicant IV antibiotic. The pharmacy lists the osmolarity of each solution. The nurse reviews four new prescriptions before giving them through the midline. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider?

options.text: Continue the antibiotic at 450 mOsm/L for 2 more weeks
options.rationale: Two more weeks brings the total dwell to 23 days, which is within the 4 week limit. A non vesicant antibiotic under 600 mOsm/L is a listed midline use.

options.text: Start peripheral parenteral nutrition at 850 mOsm/L
options.rationale: Under 900 mOsm/L fits a short peripheral IV, but a midline is limited to under 600 mOsm/L and is not used for parenteral nutrition. Current Infusion Nurses Society standards also advise against parenteral nutrition through a midline. This needs clarifying.

options.text: Start dextrose 10% in water at 505 mOsm/L for low glucose
options.rationale: Dextrose 10% is hypertonic, which makes it look risky, but at 505 mOsm/L it is under the 600 mOsm/L midline limit and is not a vesicant.

options.text: Give an IV analgesic at 580 mOsm/L every 4 hours
options.rationale: Close to the limit, but 580 mOsm/L is still under 600, and analgesics are a listed midline use.

questions.takeaway: A midline tip ends below the axilla, so it is not a central line. It dwells up to 4 weeks and takes non vesicant drugs under 600 mOsm/L, such as antibiotics, analgesics and hydration. It is not for vesicants, parenteral nutrition or continuous vasopressors. The 900 mOsm/L figure is the limit for short peripheral access, not for a midline.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Three options carry a tempting cue: a long course, a hypertonic dextrose, a number near the limit. Check each against the two midline limits, 4 weeks and 600 mOsm/L. The deciding cue is that 850 passes the peripheral limit of 900 but fails the midline limit of 600.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 9 days plus 2 weeks is 23 days, under 4 weeks.
450, 505 and 580 pass; 850 fails.
Parenteral nutrition is excluded from midlines regardless of number.

steps.action: Ignore the labels that only sound risky
steps.detail: Hypertonic dextrose under 600 is still within the limit.

elimination.verdict: B. Start peripheral parenteral nutrition at 850 mOsm/L.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a peripheral IV. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the site every 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: The site is inspected every 1 to 2 hours for redness, swelling or pain.

options.text: Change a transparent dressing every 2 days
options.rationale: A transparent dressing is changed every 7 days, or sooner if it is damp, loose or soiled. Every 2 days is the interval for gauze.

options.text: Label the tubing and site with the date
options.rationale: Tubing and site are labeled with the date so the next nurse knows when each is due.

options.text: Change a gauze dressing every 2 days
options.rationale: Gauze does not let the nurse see the site and is changed every 2 days.

options.text: Plan site rotation per policy, about every 72 to 96 hours
options.rationale: Sites are rotated per facility policy. Many policies use 72 to 96 hours, which matches Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance. Infusion Nurses Society standards favor replacing a catheter when it is clinically indicated, so follow your facility's policy.

options.text: On removal, hold pressure until bleeding stops and inspect the tip
options.rationale: After removal, pressure is held until hemostasis, and the tip is inspected to confirm the whole catheter came out.

questions.takeaway: Monitor the site every 1 to 2 hours. Transparent dressing every 7 days, gauze every 2 days. Label tubing and site with the date. Rotate sites per policy (72 to 96 hours). On removal, hold pressure until hemostasis and inspect the catheter tip.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options name the same interval for two dressings. Only one dressing gets changed every 2 days: the one you cannot see through.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every 1 to 2 hours is right.
Gauze every 2 days; transparent every 7 days.

steps.action: Check the rest of the care
steps.detail: Labeling, rotation per policy and removal with pressure and tip inspection are all correct.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, E, F.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse is assisting with insertion of a nontunneled central line. Which actions reduce the risk of a catheter related bloodstream infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before the procedure
options.rationale: Hand hygiene before any catheter insertion or access is the single most effective prevention measure.

options.text: Use a full body drape and full sterile attire
options.rationale: Maximal barrier precautions, with sterile gloves, gown, mask, cap and a full body drape, lower infection rates during central line insertion.

options.text: Prep the skin with chlorhexidine in alcohol and let it dry
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine in alcohol, scrubbed back and forth and allowed to dry fully, beats povidone iodine at reducing skin flora.

options.text: Prefer the femoral site to the subclavian site
options.rationale: The femoral site carries the highest infection risk. The subclavian site is preferred when possible.

options.text: Ask each day whether the line is still needed
options.rationale: Dwell time is a main risk factor. A daily review of need leads to prompt removal.

options.text: Leave the line in until discharge in case it is needed
options.rationale: Every extra day raises the risk. The line comes out as soon as it is no longer needed.

questions.takeaway: The prevention bundle: hand hygiene, maximal barrier precautions, chlorhexidine in alcohol allowed to dry, the subclavian site over the internal jugular or femoral (femoral is highest risk), and a daily review of whether the line is still needed.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Walk through the bundle in order: hands, barriers, skin, site, daily need. Anything that lengthens dwell time or picks a dirtier site is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hand hygiene, full barriers, chlorhexidine allowed to dry.
Subclavian over femoral.
Review need daily; do not keep a line just in case.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient in the intensive care unit who had a nontunneled central line placed in the femoral vein during a resuscitation 4 days ago. The patient is now alert, eating, and receiving only oral medications, and a working peripheral IV is in place. The central line dressing is clean, dry and intact. Which action by the nurse best reduces the patient's risk of a catheter related bloodstream infection?

options.text: Scrub the hub for 15 seconds before each access
options.rationale: Scrubbing the hub is correct practice for a line in use, but this line no longer has a use. It lowers the risk of each access, not the risk of the line staying in.

options.text: Change the dressing using a chlorhexidine skin prep
options.rationale: The dressing is clean, dry and intact, so it is not due. Changing it adds handling without removing the main risk.

options.text: Request the line be replaced at the subclavian site
options.rationale: The subclavian site is preferred over the femoral site, but only when a central line is needed. Replacing it adds a new insertion with its own risks for a patient who needs no central access.

options.text: Ask the provider whether the line can be removed
options.rationale: Dwell time is a primary risk factor, and every extra day raises it. The patient takes only oral medications and has a working peripheral IV, so the line is no longer needed. Prompt removal is the bundle's last step.

questions.takeaway: The daily question for every central line is: is it still needed? Dwell time is a primary risk factor for a catheter related bloodstream infection, and the femoral site carries the highest risk. When the need is gone, the line comes out.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Every option is part of central line care. The deciding cues are that the patient needs no central access (oral medications only, a working peripheral IV) and the line sits in the highest risk site. Removing a line beats caring for it well or moving it.

steps.action: Ask whether the line is needed
steps.detail: Oral medications only and a working peripheral IV: no.

steps.action: Reject care for a line with no use
steps.detail: Hub scrubbing and a dressing change keep a line that should come out.
Subclavian is better only for a patient who still needs a central line.
Ask whether it can come out.

elimination.verdict: D. Ask the provider whether the line can be removed.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for patients receiving infusions by alternative routes. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Plan to replace intraosseous access within 24 hours
options.rationale: Intraosseous access is an emergency route and is limited to 24 hours, so other access is arranged before then.

options.text: Monitor respirations closely during an epidural opioid infusion
options.rationale: Intraspinal opioids can cause respiratory depression. Respiratory and neurologic status are monitored closely.

options.text: Warm dialysate to body temperature before instilling it
options.rationale: Dialysate warmed to body temperature reduces discomfort during peritoneal dialysis.

options.text: Report cloudy effluent during peritoneal dialysis
options.rationale: Cloudy effluent is a sign of peritonitis and is reported along with abdominal pain or fever.

options.text: Avoid giving blood through an intraosseous line
options.rationale: An intraosseous line can deliver all IV fluids, medications and blood products.

options.text: Use clean technique for epidural catheter care
options.rationale: Intraspinal catheters need strict aseptic technique because infection there can reach the central nervous system.

questions.takeaway: Intraosseous: emergency access for fluids, drugs and blood, limited to 24 hours. Intraspinal (epidural or intrathecal): strict asepsis, watch for respiratory depression and catheter migration. Intraperitoneal: warm the dialysate, track inflow and outflow, and report cloudy effluent, pain or fever.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Tie each route to its signature risk: time limit for intraosseous, breathing for intraspinal, infection of the peritoneum for intraperitoneal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 24 hour limit; it can carry blood.
Watch respirations; strict asepsis, not clean technique.
Warm the dialysate; cloudy effluent means peritonitis.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Define Infusion Therapy

questions.nursesNote: 0900: Peripheral IV inserted in the left forearm, cephalic vein, 1 attempt. 20 gauge catheter. Vein soft and straight before insertion. Transparent dressing applied and labeled with the date. Patient tolerated the procedure without pain. Site to be inspected every 4 hours. 1300: Site red and tender with a palpable cord along the vein. Phlebitis noted. Infusion stopped, catheter removed with pressure held until bleeding stopped, tip intact. Warm moist compress applied and provider notified. 1330: New 20 gauge IV inserted in the left hand, below the inflamed site. Gauze dressing applied, next change due in 7 days. Antibiotic restarted; allergy history to be reviewed at end of shift.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the infusion documentation for a patient receiving an IV antibiotic. Highlight the entries that require follow up.

segments.text: Peripheral IV inserted in the left forearm, cephalic vein, 1 attempt
segments.rationale: Site location, vein and number of attempts are required insertion documentation, and a forearm cephalic vein is a preferred site.

segments.text: Vein soft and straight before insertion
segments.rationale: Vein condition is a required element of insertion documentation.

segments.text: Transparent dressing applied and labeled with the date
segments.rationale: The dressing applied is documented, and labeling with the date is correct maintenance care.

segments.text: Site to be inspected every 4 hours
segments.rationale: The site is inspected every 1 to 2 hours. Every 4 hours lets infiltration or phlebitis progress unseen.

segments.text: Phlebitis noted
segments.rationale: Complications are documented by grade. Redness, tenderness and a palpable cord should be graded on the phlebitis scale, not just named.

segments.text: Infusion stopped, catheter removed with pressure held until bleeding stopped, tip intact
segments.rationale: Stopping, removing, holding pressure until hemostasis and inspecting the tip are the correct discontinuation steps.

segments.text: Warm moist compress applied and provider notified
segments.rationale: A warm moist compress and notifying the provider are the correct phlebitis interventions.

segments.text: New 20 gauge IV inserted in the left hand, below the inflamed site
segments.rationale: Sites distal to a prior phlebitis are avoided, because fluid would drain through the inflamed vein. A new site goes on the other arm or above the injury.

segments.text: Gauze dressing applied, next change due in 7 days
segments.rationale: Gauze is changed every 2 days. Every 7 days is the interval for a transparent dressing.

segments.text: Antibiotic restarted; allergy history to be reviewed at end of shift
segments.rationale: Allergies are checked before any infusion begins. The infusion checklist starts with the patient: allergies and access history.

questions.takeaway: Document insertion by site, gauge, number of attempts, vein condition, dressing applied and patient tolerance. Document complications by grade. Inspect every 1 to 2 hours, change gauze every 2 days and transparent dressings every 7 days, avoid sites distal to prior phlebitis, and check allergies before any infusion starts.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Read each entry twice: once for whether the action was right, and once for whether the note is complete. The subtle misses are a correct word without its grade, a correct dressing with the wrong interval, and a monitoring plan that is too far apart.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Site, vein, attempts, gauge, vein condition, dressing and tolerance are all present.
Every 4 hours is too infrequent.
The phlebitis is named but not graded; the interventions are correct.

steps.action: Check the new site and dressing
steps.detail: Distal to phlebitis, and gauze on a 7 day schedule, both need follow up.
Allergies come before the infusion, not after.

questions.objective: Document Infusion Care

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient receiving a second dose of an IV antibiotic piggyback that was hung by gravity to run over 30 minutes. Five minutes later the bag is empty, and the patient reports a pounding headache, a flushed face and tightness in the chest. There are no hives, no wheezing and no swelling of the lips or tongue. The first dose caused no reaction. After the patient is assessed and the provider is notified, which action best prevents this problem with the next dose?

options.text: Request an antihistamine before the next dose
options.rationale: Premedication targets an allergic reaction. Flushing and chest tightness can look allergic, but there are no hives, wheezing or swelling, and the first dose was tolerated.

options.text: Report a new allergy to the antibiotic
options.rationale: Labeling an allergy would remove a drug the patient tolerated. The reaction came from the rate, not the drug.

options.text: Give the next dose by infusion pump
options.rationale: A 30 minute dose that ran in 5 minutes, followed by headache, flushing and chest tightness, is speed shock. An infusion pump at a verified rate prevents it.

options.text: Dilute the next dose in a larger bag
options.rationale: A larger volume still runs by gravity with nothing to control the rate. Speed shock is prevented by controlling the rate, not the volume.

questions.takeaway: Speed shock follows a drug or fluid given too fast: flushing, headache, chest tightness and possible shock. Prevent it with an infusion pump, by verifying the rate before starting, and by never giving concentrated drugs as a bolus.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two hypotheses fit flushing and chest tightness: an allergic reaction and speed shock. The deciding cues are the timing (a 30 minute bag empty in 5) and what is missing (no hives, wheezing or swelling, and a first dose with no reaction). Once the cause is the rate, the fix is the pump.

steps.detail: Allergy or speed shock.
The bag ran in 5 minutes instead of 30.
No hives, wheezing or swelling, and the first dose was tolerated: not allergy.
Control the rate with a pump; dilution by gravity does not control it.

elimination.verdict: C. Give the next dose by infusion pump.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury and low blood pressure has a new prescription for 0.45% sodium chloride. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Start the infusion with hourly neurologic checks
options.rationale: Hourly neurologic checks are good care, but 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic. It moves water into cells, including brain cells, and it is contraindicated with head trauma and low blood pressure.

options.text: Start the infusion at a slower rate
options.rationale: A slower rate still moves water into brain cells. The problem is the type of fluid, not the speed.

options.text: Hold the infusion and question the prescription
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid is contraindicated with head trauma, raised pressure in the skull and low blood pressure. This patient has both a head injury and low blood pressure, so the order is questioned before it starts.

options.text: Hang 0.9% sodium chloride instead
options.rationale: An isotonic fluid may well be what this patient needs, but the nurse cannot change the type of fluid without an order.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid (0.45% or 0.225% sodium chloride) moves water into cells. Do not give it with head trauma, raised pressure in the skull, low blood pressure or third spacing. Question the order before starting.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options give the ordered fluid and one changes it without an order. Ask what the fluid does once it is in the vein, then match that against the head injury.

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic.
Into cells, including brain cells.
Head injury and low blood pressure: both are contraindications.
Question the order. Do not swap fluids without one.

elimination.verdict: C. Hold the hypotonic fluid and question the prescription.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the IV fluid orders for six patients on a medical surgical unit.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the IV fluid prescriptions for six patients on a medical surgical unit. For each patient, indicate whether the ordered fluid is appropriate or the order should be questioned.

rows.text: A patient bleeding after a car crash, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, ordered 0.9% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and is used for volume expansion and hemorrhage resuscitation.

rows.text: A patient with new confusion and serum sodium 118 mEq/L, ordered 3% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: 3% sodium chloride is the hypertonic fluid for severe hyponatremia. Sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance are watched closely.

rows.text: A patient with ascites from fluid shifting into the abdomen, ordered 0.45% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Third spacing is a contraindication to hypotonic fluid. More water would leave the vessels.

rows.text: A patient with blood glucose 48 mg/dL, ordered D10W
rows.rationale: D10W is a hypertonic dextrose solution used for hypoglycemia.

rows.text: A patient with intracranial pressure 24 mm Hg, ordered D5W as the continuous maintenance fluid
rows.rationale: Once the body uses the dextrose, D5W leaves free water. It acts as a hypotonic fluid and moves water into brain cells.

rows.text: A patient about to receive packed red blood cells, ordered Lactated Ringer's to prime the blood tubing
rows.rationale: Blood products run with 0.9% sodium chloride only.

questions.takeaway: Match the fluid to where the water goes. Isotonic stays in the vessels, hypertonic pulls water out of cells, hypotonic pushes water into cells. D5W behaves as hypotonic once the dextrose is used.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Judge each row on its own. For each fluid ask where the water goes, then ask whether that helps or harms this patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.9% isotonic. 3% and D10W hypertonic. 0.45% hypotonic. D5W acts as hypotonic once the dextrose is used.
Third spacing and raised intracranial pressure rule out hypotonic fluid.
0.9% sodium chloride only with blood.

elimination.verdict: Appropriate: rows 1, 2 and 4. Question: rows 3, 5 and 6.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.stem: The nurse is receiving a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis from the emergency department, where the blood pressure was 82/50 mm Hg and the patient received 2 L of 0.9% sodium chloride. Blood pressure is now 118/72 mm Hg, heart rate 92/min, and the patient is alert and oriented. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L. The provider prescribes 0.45% sodium chloride at 150 mL/hour. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Question the prescription before starting the infusion
options.rationale: This is the near miss: hypotonic fluid is contraindicated with low blood pressure, and the blood pressure was 82/50 mm Hg in the emergency department. It is now 118/72 mm Hg after 2 L of isotonic fluid, so the contraindication is no longer present.

options.text: Start the infusion and monitor sodium and neurologic status
options.rationale: In diabetic ketoacidosis, hypotonic fluid follows the initial isotonic resuscitation. The blood pressure is in range, the patient is alert and the sodium is high, so the order fits. Sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance are the checks.

options.text: Request a change to Lactated Ringer's solution
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid was the first step and the blood pressure has recovered. Lactated Ringer's does not give the cells the free water a sodium of 147 mEq/L calls for.

options.text: Hold the infusion until a repeat sodium level results
options.rationale: The sodium is already known to be above range. Waiting delays the ordered next step of the fluid plan.

questions.takeaway: Diabetic ketoacidosis fluid plan: isotonic fluid first to restore volume, then hypotonic fluid once the blood pressure has recovered. Hypotonic fluid is unsafe while blood pressure is low.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options seem defensible: start the hypotonic fluid, or question it because of the emergency department blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg. The deciding cue is the current blood pressure, 118/72 mm Hg.

steps.action: Find where the patient is in the plan
steps.detail: 2 L of isotonic fluid already given.
Blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg: no longer low.
147 mEq/L: water is needed in the cells.
Lactated Ringer's adds no free water. Waiting for a repeat sodium delays care.

elimination.verdict: B. Start the infusion and monitor sodium and neurologic status.

questions.objective: IV Solution Types

questions.stem: The bedside check for a unit of packed red blood cells is complete. The patient has a 22 gauge IV with Lactated Ringer's infusing. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Start an 18 or 20 gauge IV with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Blood runs with 0.9% sodium chloride only, through an 18 or 20 gauge catheter. This solves both problems with the current line. Current standards allow 20 to 24 gauge for adults; for your exam use 18 to 20 gauge.

options.text: Use the 22 gauge IV with 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: Dextrose solutions cause red cells to clump and hemolyze, so 5% dextrose in water never runs with blood, whatever the catheter size.

options.text: Infuse the unit through the existing line
options.rationale: Verification is complete, but the line is the wrong size and Lactated Ringer's cannot run with blood.

options.text: Keep the unit at the bedside until a new IV is placed later
options.rationale: Packed red cells must be infused within 4 hours of issue. A new line is needed now, not later in the shift.

questions.takeaway: Every blood product needs two nurse verification, an 18 to 20 gauge catheter and 0.9% sodium chloride only. Packed red cells are infused within 4 hours of issue.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: The verification is done, which makes using the current line tempting. Check the solution first, since only 0.9% sodium chloride runs with blood, then the catheter size.

steps.detail: Only 0.9% sodium chloride runs with blood. Lactated Ringer's and 5% dextrose in water are out.
Blood needs 18 to 20 gauge, so the 22 gauge line is replaced.
4 hours from issue: do not wait until later in the shift.

elimination.verdict: A. Start an 18 or 20 gauge IV with 0.9% sodium chloride.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse receives a prescription to transfuse packed red blood cells. Baseline vital signs are recorded. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Pick up the unit from the blood bank
options.rationale: The unit is collected only after consent is confirmed, so this comes second.

options.text: Confirm signed consent is on file
options.rationale: Consent must be on file before the unit is picked up from the blood bank. It is the first step.

options.text: Verify the unit with a second nurse at the bedside
options.rationale: Two licensed nurses verify the unit at the bedside, which is after the unit has been collected.

options.text: Reassess vital signs at the bedside
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs are already recorded. The next reassessment is 15 minutes after the transfusion starts.

questions.takeaway: Blood order: consent on file, then pick up the unit, then two nurse bedside check, then start, then vital signs at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes and at completion.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Anchor the first step. Consent comes before the unit leaves the blood bank, and every other option needs the unit in hand or the transfusion running.

steps.detail: Baseline vital signs are recorded; the unit has not been picked up.
Consent must be on file before the unit is retrieved.
Pick up, two nurse bedside check, start, then recheck at 15 minutes.

elimination.verdict: B. Confirm signed consent is on file.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing the IV site of a patient receiving 0.9% sodium chloride. Which findings indicate infiltration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cool, pale skin around the site
options.rationale: Fluid in the tissue cools the skin and makes it pale: a sign of infiltration.

options.text: Edema around the site
options.rationale: Fluid leaking into the tissue causes swelling around the site.

options.text: A slowed drip rate
options.rationale: Fluid going into the tissue meets resistance, so the drip slows.

options.text: Patient reports tightness at the site
options.rationale: Fluid collecting in the tissue stretches it, so the patient feels tightness or discomfort at the site: a sign of infiltration.

options.text: No redness or streak along the vein
options.rationale: Redness and a streak are signs of phlebitis. Their absence does not point to infiltration.

options.text: Capillary refill of 2 seconds beyond the site
options.rationale: Normal capillary refill shows circulation beyond the site is intact. It is not a sign of infiltration.

questions.takeaway: Infiltration: cool, pale skin, edema, tightness at the site and a slowed drip; there may be no blood return, but that finding alone is not reliable. Phlebitis: pain, redness, warmth, a streak and a cord along the vein.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into infiltration, phlebitis or normal. Only the infiltration findings are selected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool, pale, swollen, and tight.
A slowed drip.
No phlebitis signs and a normal capillary refill.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing the forearm IV site of a patient receiving an IV antibiotic through a 20 gauge catheter. There is mild swelling at the site, redness and warmth along the vein, a red streak 3 cm above the site, and a firm cord when the vein is palpated. Pain at the site is 5 of 10. The infusion runs at the prescribed rate, and there is a blood return. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Flush the catheter and continue the infusion
options.rationale: Warm, red skin with a streak and a cord points to phlebitis rather than infiltration, and the catheter does not stay. Flushing and continuing keeps irritating an inflamed vein.

options.text: Remove the catheter, elevate the arm, and apply a compress
options.rationale: This is the infiltration plan, with the compress chosen for the solution. Swelling is present, but the skin is warm and red with a streak and a cord, not cool and pale, and blood still returns. That points to phlebitis.

options.text: Remove the catheter, apply warm moist heat, and notify the provider
options.rationale: Redness, warmth, a streak and a palpable cord are phlebitis. The plan is stop the infusion, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress, notify the provider and document the grade.

options.text: Stop the infusion, leave the catheter, and apply a warm moist compress
options.rationale: The compress is right, but a catheter in an inflamed vein is removed, not saved.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis: pain, redness, warmth, a streak and a palpable cord. Stop, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress, notify the provider and document the grade.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options stop and remove the catheter. The swelling suggests infiltration. The deciding cue is warm, red skin with a streak and a cord, which means phlebitis, not the cool, pale skin of infiltration.

steps.detail: Red, warm, streak, cord: phlebitis.
A catheter in an inflamed vein comes out, whatever the flow or blood return shows.
Warm moist compress and notify for phlebitis. Elevate and compress by solution for infiltration.

elimination.verdict: C. Remove the catheter, apply warm moist heat, and notify the provider.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.scenario: The tubing of a patient's central line separates at the hub while the patient is sitting up in a chair. Within a minute the patient reports sudden shortness of breath and chest pain. Blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg, heart rate is 124 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation is 86%. A churning sound is heard over the heart.
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient whose central line tubing has separated at the hub. Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Return the patient to bed on the left side with the head down
options.rationale: Left lateral Trendelenburg traps the air in the right side of the heart, away from the lungs.

options.text: Lay the patient flat on the back with the legs raised
options.rationale: A shock position does not trap the air in the right side of the heart. The left side with the head down does.

options.text: Clamp the catheter
options.rationale: Clamping stops more air from entering the vein.

options.text: Remove the central line
options.rationale: The line is clamped, not removed, in this emergency.

options.text: Flush the line with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Flushing pushes more of what is in the line into the vein.

options.text: Fluid overload
options.rationale: Fluid overload builds over hours of infusion. This began within a minute of the line opening.

options.text: Catheter related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: Infection brings fever and chills over time, not a sudden onset after a disconnection.

options.text: Speed shock
options.rationale: Speed shock follows a fast infusion, with flushing, headache and chest tightness. Nothing was infusing fast.

options.text: Air embolism
options.rationale: An open line, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, low blood pressure and a churning sound over the heart.

options.text: Urine specific gravity
options.rationale: This does not guide care in the next minutes.

options.text: Blood pressure
options.rationale: 82/48 mm Hg shows the heart is struggling to pump.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Temperature does not track an air embolism.

options.text: Appearance of the insertion site
options.rationale: The problem is in the heart and lungs, not at the skin.

options.text: Oxygen saturation
options.rationale: 86% shows the air is blocking blood flow to the lungs.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, low blood pressure and a churning murmur after air enters a line. Clamp the tubing, turn onto the left side head down, call rapid response and give 100% oxygen.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Link the timing to the event: an open central line, then sudden breathing and chest symptoms. Then choose actions that stop more air and keep the air away from the lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Central line open at the hub.
Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a churning sound.
Clamp.
Left side, head down.
Oxygen saturation and blood pressure.

elimination.verdict: Clamp the catheter and turn onto the left side head down. Air embolism. Watch oxygen saturation and blood pressure.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a patient going home with a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Which statements indicate understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will cover the site when I shower."
options.rationale: Showering is allowed with a waterproof cover over the site.

options.text: "I can swim laps once the site heals."
options.rationale: The arm is not submerged: no swimming and no baths while the PICC is in.

options.text: "No blood pressure cuffs on my PICC arm."
options.rationale: No blood pressure cuffs and no needle sticks on the PICC arm.

options.text: "If the flush is hard to push, I will push harder."
options.rationale: Resistance during a flush means stop and do not use the line. Force can break the catheter.

options.text: "I will call if my temperature reaches 38.2 °C."
options.rationale: A fever above 38 °C is a warning sign to report at once.

options.text: "I can carry my 20 lb laundry basket with that arm."
options.rationale: Heavy lifting over 10 lb with the PICC arm is avoided.

questions.takeaway: PICC teaching: keep the dressing dry, shower with a cover, no swimming, no blood pressure cuff or needle sticks on that arm, nothing over 10 lb, never force a flush, and report a fever above 38 °C.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Treat each statement as true or false against the PICC rules: water, that arm, lifting, flushing and fever.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shower with a cover. No swimming.
No blood pressure cuff, no lifting over 10 lb.
Resistance means stop.
Above 38 °C: call.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: The registered nurse is making assignments for a licensed practical nurse (LPN) and assistive personnel (AP). Which assignment is appropriate?

options.text: Ask the LPN to hang checked platelets
options.rationale: Starting any blood product stays with the registered nurse, even after the check.

options.text: Ask the AP to decide whether an IV comes out
options.rationale: The AP can report how a site looks. Deciding what the finding means is the registered nurse's judgment.

options.text: Ask the LPN to start a heparin infusion
options.rationale: Heparin is a high alert IV medication, which the registered nurse gives.

options.text: Ask the LPN to flush an established IV line
options.rationale: Flushing an established line is within the LPN's role, per the state practice act. The registered nurse stays accountable.

questions.takeaway: The registered nurse keeps insertion, site selection, starting blood, high alert IV drugs, interpreting findings and teaching. The LPN can monitor sites, flush established lines and hang non high alert fluids. AP take vital signs and report what a site looks like.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Each option hands off a real task. Ask whether the task needs judgment, starts blood or involves a high alert drug; any of these stays with the registered nurse.

steps.detail: Platelets: registered nurse.
Deciding a catheter comes out: registered nurse.
Heparin: registered nurse.
Flushing an established line: LPN.

elimination.verdict: Assign the flush of an established line to the LPN.

questions.objective: RN Responsibility & Delegation

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing vascular access plans for four patients receiving non vesicant therapy. For which patient is a midline catheter the best fit?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride for 2 days after minor surgery
options.rationale: Short term isotonic fluid can run through a short peripheral IV, which is less invasive than a midline.

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Total parenteral nutrition requires central access. A midline is not used for it, however long the therapy lasts.

options.text: A continuous vasopressor for several days
options.rationale: A midline is not used for continuous vasopressors. Over several days a continuous vasopressor needs central access.

options.text: An IV antibiotic at home for 3 weeks
options.rationale: Therapy longer than 6 days warrants a midline or PICC. A midline can dwell up to 4 weeks and suits non vesicant antibiotics, so it is the less invasive choice.

questions.takeaway: Choose access by duration and solution. Short term isotonic fluid: short peripheral IV. Non vesicant therapy longer than 6 days, up to 4 weeks: midline. Total parenteral nutrition or continuous vasopressors: central line.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each patient: how long, and what is going in. Total parenteral nutrition and a continuous vasopressor go straight to a central line, and 2 days of fluid does not need a midline.

steps.detail: Total parenteral nutrition and a continuous vasopressor need a central line.
2 days of isotonic fluid fits a short peripheral IV.
3 weeks of a non vesicant antibiotic is longer than 6 days and under 4 weeks: midline.

elimination.verdict: D. An IV antibiotic at home for 3 weeks.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: The nurse observes a student insert a peripheral IV for an older adult with lymphedema of one arm after mastectomy. Which student actions require follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Selected a 22 gauge catheter
options.rationale: A 22 to 24 gauge catheter is recommended for older adults with fragile veins and is enough for maintenance fluid.

options.text: Scrubbed with chlorhexidine back and forth for 30 seconds
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine applied with a back and forth scrub for at least 30 seconds is the correct prep.

options.text: Fanned the site to speed drying
options.rationale: The antiseptic must air dry completely. Fanning, blotting or wiping is not done.

options.text: Palpated the vein again after the prep
options.rationale: Touching the cleansed site again with unsterile fingers contaminates it and cancels the prep.

options.text: Kept advancing after the patient reported shooting pain
options.rationale: Shooting pain, burning, numbness or tingling during insertion signals nerve injury. Insertion stops immediately, the catheter is removed and neurologic function is assessed.

options.text: Chose a hand vein on the lymphedema arm as backup
options.rationale: The lymphedema arm after mastectomy is avoided. Dorsal hand veins are also avoided in older adults when possible.

questions.takeaway: Air dry the chlorhexidine without fanning, never touch the site again after prep, stop at once for shooting pain or tingling during insertion, and avoid the arm on the mastectomy side and the dorsal hand in older adults.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Read each action against three checklists: the skin prep steps, the sites to avoid and the nerve injury signs. Select only what breaks a rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scrub for 30 seconds is right. Fanning and touching the site again are wrong.
The lymphedema arm and the dorsal hand are wrong for this patient.
Shooting pain during advancement means stop, not finish.
A 22 gauge catheter needs no follow up.

elimination.verdict: C, D, E, F.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: A patient with a central line has new fever, chills, hypotension, and confusion. The lungs, urine, and insertion site show no other source. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Two sets of blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Fever, chills, hypotension and new confusion with no other source in a patient with a central line point to a catheter related bloodstream infection. Treatment is blood cultures twice, IV antibiotics, and catheter removal if needed.

options.text: One set of blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotics are right, but blood cultures are drawn twice, not once.

options.text: A warm moist compress over the insertion site
options.rationale: This is a phlebitis intervention. The site has no redness, and the findings point to the bloodstream.

options.text: An oral antipyretic and a temperature recheck in 1 hour
options.rationale: An antipyretic treats the fever but not its source. Fever, chills, hypotension and new confusion with a central line call for cultures and antibiotics, not watchful waiting.

questions.takeaway: Catheter related bloodstream infection: fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status with no other source. Draw blood cultures twice, start IV antibiotics and remove the catheter if needed.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: First rule out every other source the stem hands you: lungs, urine and site. What is left with a central line is the bloodstream infection. Then match each treatment to the complication it belongs to.

steps.detail: Clear lungs, clear urine, clean site: the line is the source.
No redness for phlebitis; an antipyretic treats the fever, not the source.
A and B share antibiotics; cultures are drawn twice, not once.

elimination.verdict: A. Two sets of blood cultures and IV antibiotics.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient, 87 years old, receiving hospice care in a long term care facility who has had poor oral intake for 3 days. The patient is alert and oriented, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 96/min, and the oral mucous membranes are dry. The provider prescribes fluid replacement. Three peripheral IV attempts with a vein illumination device have failed. Ultrasound guided insertion would require transfer to the hospital, and the hospice plan of care documents the patient's wish to avoid transfer. Which route should the nurse recommend to the provider?

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion in the abdomen at about 1 mL per minute
options.rationale: Subcutaneous infusion is used for mild to moderate dehydration in older and palliative patients and is avoided only in severe dehydration or shock. The abdomen is a common site and about 1 mL per minute is the maximum rate. It needs no transfer.

options.text: Hospital transfer for ultrasound guided IV insertion
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the standard for difficult access, but it requires a transfer the patient has declined, and mild to moderate dehydration in a palliative patient can be treated subcutaneously.

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion in the thigh at about 5 mL per minute
options.rationale: The route and site are right, but about 1 mL per minute is the maximum rate for subcutaneous infusion.

options.text: Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia
options.rationale: Intraosseous access does deliver all IV fluids when IV access fails, but it is for emergencies such as cardiac arrest or trauma and is limited to 24 hours. This patient is alert with a blood pressure in range.

questions.takeaway: When IV access fails, match the alternative to the patient's goals and urgency. Ultrasound guided insertion is the standard for difficult access. Subcutaneous infusion (hypodermoclysis) suits mild to moderate dehydration in older or palliative patients at about 1 mL per minute and is avoided in severe dehydration or shock. Intraosseous access is for emergencies and is limited to 24 hours.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible: ultrasound guided IV insertion, the standard for difficult access, and subcutaneous infusion. The deciding cue is the documented wish to avoid hospital transfer, with findings that show neither severe dehydration nor shock.

steps.detail: Alert, blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per minute: not shock, not an emergency.
Ultrasound requires a hospital transfer the patient has declined.
Intraosseous access is for cardiac arrest, trauma or pediatric emergencies and lasts 24 hours at most.
Same route, but the rate limit is about 1 mL per minute, not 5.

elimination.verdict: A. Subcutaneous infusion in the abdomen at about 1 mL per minute.

questions.objective: Apply Clinical Judgment

questions.stem: The nurse is making rounds on four patients receiving infusion therapy. Which finding requires immediate follow up?

options.text: A bag of 0.9% sodium chloride spiked 20 hours ago
options.rationale: A spiked bag may hang up to 24 hours. At 20 hours it is still within the limit; the nurse plans the change.

options.text: A PICC transparent dressing applied 5 days ago, intact
options.rationale: A transparent dressing is changed every 7 days, or sooner if damp, loose or soiled. An intact 5 day dressing is within the limit.

options.text: A peripheral IV inserted 70 hours ago, site without redness
options.rationale: Many policies rotate peripheral sites at 72 to 96 hours. At 70 hours with a normal site, the nurse plans rotation per policy.

options.text: An aching PICC arm, 3 cm larger around than on admission
options.rationale: A swollen, painful limb with a central catheter points to thrombosis, a clot in or around the catheter. It needs prompt assessment and reporting, and treatment with anticoagulants or removal as prescribed.

questions.takeaway: Know the time limits so they do not distract you: spiked bag 24 hours, transparent dressing 7 days, gauze 2 days, tubing 96 hours or per policy, peripheral site rotation per policy (often 72 to 96 hours). A swollen, painful PICC arm is thrombosis until proven otherwise.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Three options test a time limit, and each is close to but inside its limit. The finding that requires immediate follow up is the one that describes a change in the patient, not a date on a label.

steps.detail: Bag 20 of 24 hours, dressing 5 of 7 days, site 70 hours with rotation at 72 to 96.
An aching arm that has grown 3 cm.
Swelling and pain in the PICC arm: thrombosis.

elimination.verdict: D. An aching PICC arm, 3 cm larger around than on admission.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with kidney failure who has a tunneled hemodialysis catheter. The only peripheral IV infiltrated, and an IV antibiotic is due now. Two attempts at a new peripheral IV have failed. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose through the dialysis catheter after a flush
options.rationale: A hemodialysis catheter is dedicated to dialysis and is never used for routine IV infusions. Using it risks infection and clotting of the patient's dialysis access.

options.text: Request the vascular access specialist for new access
options.rationale: After failed attempts, the vascular access specialist, with ultrasound guidance, improves first attempt success in difficult access. The dose is given through the new access, and the nurse documents the delay.

options.text: Ask the dialysis nurse to give the dose through the catheter
options.rationale: The dialysis nurse manages the catheter for dialysis, but the catheter is still not used for routine infusions. Who gives the dose does not change the rule.

options.text: Give the dose through the infiltrated IV at a slower rate
options.rationale: The fluid is going into the tissue, not the vein. A slower rate still infiltrates, and the drug does not reach the bloodstream.

questions.takeaway: Hemodialysis catheters are large bore, dedicated to dialysis, managed by dialysis trained staff and never used for routine IV infusion or blood draws. For difficult access, call the vascular access specialist, who can use ultrasound guidance.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options use the dialysis catheter, one with a flush and one with a specialist. If the rule is about the device, changing the person does not fix it.

steps.detail: Fluid into tissue is not a route.
A dialysis catheter is for dialysis only, whoever uses it.
The vascular access specialist handles difficult access.

elimination.verdict: B. Request the vascular access specialist for new access.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: The registered nurse is planning infusion care with a licensed practical nurse (LPN) and assistive personnel (AP) on a medical unit. Which tasks may the nurse delegate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the LPN to hang the next bag of maintenance 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hanging fluids that are not high alert may go to the LPN, per the state nurse practice act and facility policy.

options.text: Ask the AP to report when a patient says the IV site hurts
options.rationale: AP may measure vital signs, report site appearance and patient comfort. Reporting pain lets the nurse assess the site.

options.text: Ask the LPN to assess a new admission's veins and choose an IV site
options.rationale: Initial vascular access assessment and site selection stay with the registered nurse.

options.text: Ask the LPN to start the prescribed insulin infusion
options.rationale: Insulin is a high alert medication. Administering high alert IV medications stays with the registered nurse.

options.text: Ask the LPN to teach a patient going home how to care for a PICC
options.rationale: Patient and family education on infusion therapy stays with the registered nurse.

options.text: Ask the LPN to check established peripheral IV sites each hour
options.rationale: Routine monitoring of established IV sites may go to the LPN. The registered nurse interprets any change and keeps accountability.

questions.takeaway: The registered nurse keeps initial assessment and site selection, insertion, starting blood, high alert IV medications, interpretation, education and care plan updates. The LPN may monitor sites, flush established lines and hang fluids that are not high alert, per the state act. AP may measure vital signs and report site appearance and comfort. Delegation never transfers accountability.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: For each task ask: does it need assessment, judgment, teaching or a high alert drug? If yes, it stays with the registered nurse. Routine, predictable tasks on established lines can be delegated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vein assessment and site choice, teaching: registered nurse.
Insulin infusion: registered nurse.
Maintenance fluid and site checks to the LPN; reporting pain to the AP.

elimination.verdict: A, B, F.

questions.objective: RN Responsibility & Delegation

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a patient with a bleeding gastric ulcer who received 2 units of packed red blood cells this morning. Before the first unit: hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mm Hg, oral temperature 37.0 °C. One hour after the second unit, the nurse evaluates the response. Which finding requires follow up?

options.text: Oral temperature 37.4 °C
options.rationale: The rise is less than 1 °C. A febrile reaction is a rise of 1 °C or more, with chills; this small change is watched but does not suggest a reaction.

options.text: Heart rate 98/min
options.rationale: The heart rate fell from 118/min. It is not yet at a normal resting level, but the trend shows a response to the restored volume.

options.text: Hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL
options.rationale: Each unit of packed red blood cells raises hemoglobin about 1 g/dL, so about 8.8 g/dL was expected. A rise of only 0.3 g/dL suggests the bleeding is continuing, and the nurse reports it.

options.text: Blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg
options.rationale: The pressure rose from 96/58 mm Hg, which shows the transfusion is supporting circulating volume.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate a transfusion against its expected result: hemoglobin rises about 1 g/dL per unit of packed red blood cells. A much smaller rise in a bleeding patient points to ongoing blood loss. A temperature rise of 1 °C or more, with chills, suggests a febrile reaction.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options are vital signs that are not yet perfect, and one is a temperature change that sounds like a reaction. The deciding cue is arithmetic: two units should raise the hemoglobin about 2 g/dL, not 0.3.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 6.8 plus about 2 g/dL is about 8.8; 7.1 is far short.
A 0.4 °C rise is below the 1 °C reaction threshold.
Heart rate down and blood pressure up: responding.
The small hemoglobin rise suggests continued bleeding.

elimination.verdict: C. Hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL.

questions.objective: Apply Clinical Judgment

questions.nursesNote: Day 10 after bowel surgery with a prolonged ileus. NPO. Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) placed 9 days ago. 20 gauge forearm peripheral IV, saline locked. 0800: Alert and oriented, oral temperature 37.1 °C, heart rate 84/min, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg. 1400: Shaking chills, oral temperature 38.9 °C. Heart rate 116/min. Blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg. Asks the nurse the date three times in 10 minutes. PICC site clean and dry, no redness or drainage. Transparent dressing dated 3 days ago, intact. Lungs clear. Urine clear yellow. Incision edges together, no drainage.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the 1400 note of a patient receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Highlight the findings that require immediate follow up.

segments.text: Shaking chills, oral temperature 38.9 °C
segments.rationale: A new fever with shaking chills in a patient with a central line is a cue for a bloodstream infection.

segments.text: Heart rate 116/min
segments.rationale: The heart rate rose from 84/min, consistent with a body wide response to infection.

segments.text: Blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg
segments.rationale: The pressure fell from 122/74 mm Hg. Hypotension is a listed sign of a catheter related bloodstream infection and of sepsis.

segments.text: Asks the nurse the date three times in 10 minutes
segments.rationale: The patient was alert and oriented at 0800. New confusion is altered mental status, a key cue.

segments.text: PICC site clean and dry, no redness or drainage
segments.rationale: The site looks normal. This is useful information, but a clean site does not rule out an infection of the bloodstream from the catheter.

segments.text: Transparent dressing dated 3 days ago, intact
segments.rationale: A transparent dressing is changed every 7 days or sooner if damp, loose or soiled. An intact 3 day dressing is within the limit.

segments.text: Lungs clear
segments.rationale: No lung source is found, which matters for the next step but is not abnormal.

segments.text: Urine clear yellow
segments.rationale: No urinary source is found.

segments.text: Incision edges together, no drainage
segments.rationale: No wound source is found.

questions.takeaway: Fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status in a patient with a central line, with no other identifiable source, are the signs of a catheter related bloodstream infection. A normal looking insertion site does not rule it out.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Highlight what changed for the worse since 0800. The normal site, lungs, urine and incision are reassuring about other sources, but they are not findings that need follow up themselves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Temperature, heart rate, blood pressure and mental status all worsened.
Dressing within its limit, site clean.
Lungs, urine and incision are normal.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing the 1400 findings of a patient receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
Chart so far: day 10 after bowel surgery, NPO, TPN through a PICC placed 9 days ago, 20 gauge forearm peripheral IV. At 0800 alert, oral temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg. At 1400 shaking chills, oral temperature 38.9 °C, heart rate 116/min, blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg, repeating questions about the date; PICC site clean with no redness; lungs clear, urine clear, incision closed with no drainage.

The findings are most consistent with [[1]].

The clean, dry PICC site [[2]].

The clear lungs, clear urine, and closed incision [[3]].

options.text: phlebitis at the PICC insertion site
options.rationale: Phlebitis shows at the vein: pain, redness, warmth, a streak or a cord. This site has no redness, and phlebitis does not cause hypotension and confusion.

options.text: a catheter related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: Fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status with no other identifiable source in a patient with a central line are the listed signs. TPN through the line adds risk.

options.text: thrombosis of the PICC arm
options.rationale: Thrombosis causes a swollen, painful limb and a slowing flow rate, not fever and hypotension.

options.text: speed shock from the TPN
options.rationale: Speed shock follows a rapid infusion and causes flushing, headache and chest tightness. Nothing suggests the TPN ran too fast.

options.text: rules out an infection of the catheter
options.rationale: Organisms can travel along or inside the catheter into the blood without any redness at the skin.

options.text: does not rule out this complication
options.rationale: A catheter related bloodstream infection often shows no local signs. The systemic findings decide.

options.text: means the PICC can stay in use
options.rationale: A clean site does not clear the catheter. Removal is considered when it is the likely source.

options.text: make another source less likely
options.rationale: With no lung, urinary or wound source, the central line becomes the most likely source. That matches the definition: no other identifiable source.

options.text: point to a hidden wound infection
options.rationale: A closed incision with no drainage does not point to a wound infection.

options.text: show the patient is not septic
options.rationale: The patient has an infection with hypotension and confusion. Normal findings in other systems do not cancel that.

questions.takeaway: Catheter related bloodstream infection: fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status in a patient with a central line, with no other identifiable source. The insertion site often looks normal. Ruling out other sources points the nurse to the catheter.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Match the pattern to the complication. Local complications show at the vein or limb; this patient's findings are systemic, and the normal site and other systems are the clue that points to the line.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fever, hypotension and confusion are systemic.
Lungs, urine and incision are normal: the catheter is left.
A clean insertion site does not rule out infection of the line.

elimination.verdict: 1: a catheter related bloodstream infection. 2: does not rule out this complication. 3: make another source less likely.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: At 1415 the nurse rechecks the patient. Capillary glucose is 236 mg/dL, was 150 mg/dL at 0800. Blood pressure 92/54 mm Hg, heart rate 120/min, and the patient still asks for the date. The TPN is running at the prescribed rate. Chart so far: day 10 after bowel surgery, NPO, TPN through a PICC placed 9 days ago, 20 gauge forearm peripheral IV. At 0800 alert, oral temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg. At 1400 shaking chills, oral temperature 38.9 °C, heart rate 116/min, blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg, repeating questions about the date; PICC site clean with no redness; lungs clear, urine clear, incision closed with no drainage. Which problem is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Falling perfusion from a bloodstream infection
options.rationale: The blood pressure keeps dropping, the heart rate keeps rising and the brain is already affected. A bloodstream infection from the line can move quickly to septic shock, so this is the threat to address first.

options.text: High glucose from the dextrose in the TPN
options.rationale: The glucose rise is real and is treated, but infection and stress raise glucose too. A glucose of 236 mg/dL is not the immediate threat to life here.

options.text: New confusion caused by the high glucose
options.rationale: The glucose is tempting as an explanation, but this level rarely causes confusion. With fever and hypotension, the confusion points to poor brain perfusion.

options.text: Poor nutrition from the prolonged ileus
options.rationale: Nutrition is a real long term problem and the reason for the TPN, but it is not urgent compared with falling perfusion.

questions.takeaway: When an infection and a metabolic change appear together, look for the cause that links them. Sepsis raises glucose and causes confusion; the falling blood pressure is the life threatening part. Treat the glucose, but address perfusion first.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options blame the TPN glucose, which is the new number in the stem. Ask which problem explains the falling blood pressure. Only one does.

steps.detail: Blood pressure 94/56 to 92/54 mm Hg with a rising heart rate.
Infection and stress raise glucose; the rise is a clue, not the cause.
Hypotension and fever point to poor perfusion, not glucose at this level.
Nutrition matters but is not urgent.

elimination.verdict: A. Falling perfusion from a bloodstream infection.

questions.objective: Apply Clinical Judgment

questions.scenario: At 1430 the nurse has escalated care for a probable catheter related bloodstream infection. Blood pressure 92/54 mm Hg, heart rate 120/min, capillary glucose 236 mg/dL. Chart so far: day 10 after bowel surgery, NPO, TPN through a PICC placed 9 days ago, 20 gauge forearm peripheral IV. At 0800 alert, oral temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg. At 1400 shaking chills, oral temperature 38.9 °C, heart rate 116/min, blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg, repeating questions about the date; PICC site clean with no redness; lungs clear, urine clear, incision closed with no drainage.
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing potential prescriptions for a patient with a PICC and a probable catheter related bloodstream infection. For each potential prescription, indicate whether it is anticipated or not anticipated for this patient.

rows.text: Two sets of blood cultures, one through the PICC and one by venipuncture
rows.rationale: Blood cultures times 2 are part of the treatment. Paired samples from the line and a vein help show whether the line is the source.

rows.text: IV antibiotics after the cultures are drawn
rows.rationale: IV antibiotics treat the bloodstream infection. Cultures first so the organism can be identified, then the antibiotic without delay.

rows.text: Removal of the PICC
rows.rationale: The catheter is removed if needed, and with hypotension and no other source it is the likely source.

rows.text: Warm moist compress over the PICC vein
rows.rationale: A warm moist compress treats phlebitis. The site shows no phlebitis, and a compress does not treat a bloodstream infection.

rows.text: Left lateral Trendelenburg position
rows.rationale: This position traps air in the heart during an air embolism. Nothing suggests air entered the line.

rows.text: Anticoagulant to dissolve a clot in the PICC
rows.rationale: Anticoagulants treat thrombosis, which shows as a swollen, painful limb and slowing flow. Neither is present.

rows.text: Move the TPN to the forearm peripheral IV
rows.rationale: TPN is hypertonic, above 900 mOsm/L, and needs central access. A peripheral vein would be injured.

questions.takeaway: For a catheter related bloodstream infection: blood cultures times 2, IV antibiotics, and removal of the catheter if needed. Each local or mechanical complication has its own treatment; do not borrow it. TPN never moves to a peripheral vein.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the slides.
questions.strategy: Several rows are the correct treatment for a different complication. Ask of each: does this treat the problem this patient has?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cultures times 2, IV antibiotics, remove the source.
Compress for phlebitis, position for air embolism, anticoagulant for thrombosis.
TPN needs central access.

elimination.verdict: Anticipated: rows 1, 2 and 3. Not anticipated: rows 4 to 7.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: At 1530 the blood cultures have been drawn and the first IV antibiotic dose has finished through the forearm IV. The provider prescribes: stop the TPN, remove the PICC, and start 10% dextrose in water (D10W) through the forearm IV at the TPN rate. Blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg after a fluid bolus. Chart so far: day 10 after bowel surgery, NPO, TPN through a PICC placed 9 days ago, 20 gauge forearm peripheral IV. At 0800 alert, oral temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg. At 1400 shaking chills, oral temperature 38.9 °C, heart rate 116/min, blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg, repeating questions about the date; PICC site clean with no redness; lungs clear, urine clear, incision closed with no drainage. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Start the D10W when the TPN is stopped
options.rationale: TPN carries a high dextrose load. Stopping it suddenly can drop the glucose, so D10W replaces it right away to prevent rebound hypoglycemia.

options.text: Place the patient supine for the PICC removal
options.rationale: Lying flat raises venous pressure at the site and lowers the chance of air entering the vein as the catheter comes out.

options.text: Inspect the tip to confirm the catheter is intact
options.rationale: After removal the nurse inspects the tip to confirm the whole catheter came out and documents it.

options.text: Hold pressure until bleeding stops, then apply an occlusive dressing
options.rationale: Pressure until hemostasis is part of removal. An occlusive dressing seals the tract so air cannot enter.

options.text: Sit the patient upright to ease breathing during removal
options.rationale: Sitting up lowers venous pressure at the site and raises the risk of air embolism. Breathing is not a problem in this patient.

options.text: Restart the TPN through the forearm IV after removal
options.rationale: TPN is above 900 mOsm/L and needs central access. A peripheral vein would be injured.

questions.takeaway: When TPN stops suddenly, start dextrose right away to prevent hypoglycemia. For central catheter removal: position flat, withdraw, hold pressure until hemostasis, apply an occlusive dressing, inspect the tip, and document. TPN never goes into a peripheral vein.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the slides.
questions.strategy: Two risks drive this item: low glucose when the dextrose stops, and air when the catheter comes out. Every correct action prevents one of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: D10W at once, no gap.
Supine position, pressure and an occlusive dressing.
Inspect the tip.
Upright removal and peripheral TPN.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.scenario: Two days later, the patient is on IV antibiotics through the forearm IV, and D10W is prescribed at a continuous rate through the same IV. Chart so far: day 10 after bowel surgery, NPO; TPN through a PICC stopped 2 days ago at 1530 and the PICC removed for a probable catheter related bloodstream infection; at that time oral temperature 38.9 °C, blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg, confused about the date.
questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating a patient 2 days after removal of an infected PICC. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or requires follow up.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.2 °C
rows.rationale: The fever has resolved from 38.9 °C.

rows.text: Blood pressure 120/72 mm Hg
rows.rationale: The pressure is back near the 0800 baseline of 122/74 mm Hg.

rows.text: Oriented and knows the date
rows.rationale: Mental status has returned to baseline.

rows.text: Heart rate 88/min
rows.rationale: The heart rate is back near the baseline of 84/min.

rows.text: Capillary glucose 62 mg/dL with the D10W bag empty for 1 hour
rows.rationale: The dextrose stopped when the bag ran out, and the glucose is low. The nurse treats the low glucose per protocol and replaces the bag.

rows.text: Red streak and tenderness along the forearm IV vein
rows.rationale: These are signs of phlebitis. D10W is hypertonic and can irritate a peripheral vein, the chemical type. The nurse stops the infusion, removes the catheter, applies a warm moist compress, notifies the provider and documents the grade.

rows.text: Former PICC site dry with no bleeding
rows.rationale: The removal site has sealed without bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate the infection and the new risks the treatment created. The fever, blood pressure, mental status and heart rate show the infection responding. Low glucose when dextrose stops and chemical phlebitis from a hypertonic solution in a peripheral vein both require follow up.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Check two lists: did the original problem respond, and did the treatment cause anything new? The vital signs answer the first; the glucose and the forearm vein answer the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Temperature, blood pressure, mentation and heart rate are back to baseline.
Empty bag and a glucose of 62 mg/dL: needs action.
A red streak and tenderness with D10W: chemical phlebitis.

elimination.verdict: Shows improvement: rows 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7. Requires follow up: rows 5 and 6.
